hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS BUDGET - BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (DOH)

topics.topic: HFEP shortfall, utilization, reversions, and FY2027 catch-up funding
topics.summary: Members raised a reported HFEP shortfall of about 15 billion, low or delayed utilization, unused equipment, uneven construction standards, and hospital-specific infrastructure gaps. DOH said the shortfall reflected the difference between requested and granted funding, acknowledged the need to synchronize construction and equipment, and cited stronger project-management systems, site-readiness rules, local investment plans, and catch-up planning. Members also sought additional funding for hospitals in Negros Occidental, Northern Mindanao, Region 12, and other localities, while the agency discussed referral networks, phased construction, alternative equipment financing, and hospital prioritization. The committee highlighted 26 percent combined infrastructure and equipment disbursement, a proposed FY2027 catch-up amount of roughly 14 billion, and lower proposed capital outlay of 14.5 compared with 22.3 in the prior GAA. The chair required DOH to submit utilization and catch-up data by Friday, September 11th and prioritized funding information by Wednesday at 12 noon. The hearing was terminated and the proceedings on House Bill No. 10858 were suspended, leaving the FY2027 HFEP amount dependent on the requested submissions.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much HFEP funding had been allocated, released, utilized, delayed, or reverted; why infrastructure and equipment remained incomplete; and how much FY2027 funding was justified by a catch-up plan. Members also asked how HFEP and related hospital investments should be prioritized, standardized, and monitored before the committee acted on the proposed budget.
topics.agency_position: DOH said HFEP implementation should be governed by omnibus guidelines, site readiness, local health investment plans, and stronger project management linking construction, equipment, personnel, and operations. The agency acknowledged implementation and utilization problems, committed to submit historical utilization, reversion, release, and catch-up data, and said the FY2027 request should be based on historical performance and current project needs.
topics.outcome: The committee did not settle the appropriate FY2027 HFEP amount. It required DOH to submit historical utilization, reversions, implementation, equipment, and catch-up information, plus prioritized and hospital-specific funding lists, before the committee and plenary deliberated further.

positions.position: Supported additional, phased HFEP funding for hospital expansion in Negros Occidental and asked DOH to consider district and local-government requests.
Argued that the HFEP shortfall could not be considered separately from utilization, equipment-delivery delays, unused assets, and project management.
Raised concern that proposed HFEP and other DOH budget reductions could impair operations.
Called for uniform construction and equipment standards and completion of existing facilities before beginning new construction.
Sought prioritization of specialty and large tertiary hospitals, including capital-outlay support for facilities with reduced or inadequate capacity.
Supported additional infrastructure and referral-network investment to address Northern Mindanao Medical Center overcrowding and requested annual monitoring against hospital-development targets.
Appealed for additional regional-hospital and outpatient-department funding and support for the conversion and staffing of SokSargen General Hospital.
Supported proactive HFEP investment and planning for flood-resilient or relocated hospital facilities.
Supported exploring lease-to-own, pay-per-use, PPP, and other financing arrangements to reduce pressure on capital-outlay appropriations.
Said FY2027 HFEP funding decisions should be based on historical utilization, reversions, implementation status, and a credible catch-up plan within limited fiscal space.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jeffrey Ferrer
thread.said: He asked how much HFEP allocation was proposed for the 4th District of Negros Occidental and raised the need for hospital expansion in the district.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official stated that the FY2027 HFEP amount for the district was “52200000 bop,” followed by “2.52” and “200000 bop”; the exact figure and wording were unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jeffrey Ferrer
thread.said: He said the district and local government sought a larger amount, possibly 200000000, and proposed funding the hospital expansion in phases, with part in the next year and part in 20 28.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said the request would be noted and aligned with the program.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Serge Memon
thread.said: He asked whether DOH had previously admitted an HFEP shortfall of 15000000000 and whether the amount represented a deficiency against the agency's desired budget.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official clarified that 15000000000 was the difference between what DOH requested and what was granted in the net budget.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Serge Memon
thread.said: He pressed that the issue was not only the size of the appropriation but also utilization, particularly project-by-project utilization.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official agreed that utilization mattered and referred to construction phases and the need to match infrastructure completion with equipment delivery.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Serge Memon
thread.said: He cited a health center begun in 20 23 where equipment took 3 years to arrive and asked what reforms would prevent infrastructure from being completed before the corresponding equipment was delivered.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official pointed to HFEP omnibus guidelines requiring site conditions and alignment with the province's local investment plan for health.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Serge Memon
thread.said: He said unused DOH equipment had amounted to almost 300000000 and asked whether DOH had completed an inventory and determined how much equipment had been wasted, apart from expired medicines.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said an inventory of facilities and equipment issues was being pursued and described plans to strengthen the HFEP project-management team, monitor construction progress, and prepare a catch-up plan.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official reported combined infrastructure and equipment disbursement at 26 percent as of the end of the 3rd quarter and going into the 4th quarter.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Serge Memon
thread.said: He asked whether DOH could still utilize the 20 26 budget with only 3 more remaining months and requested a report identifying where funds would be downloaded.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said, “we will comply with the request,” including the requested report.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He cited a reported 34 percent reduction in HFEP and asked how the proposed reductions across DOH programs would affect operations.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: In discussing the comparison, the official cited MOOE of 11000000000 and compared HFEP figures from 14 to 29000000000; the surrounding explanation was unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Caroline Agyao
thread.said: She said HFEP facilities lacked uniform designs, procurement amounts, infrastructure, and equipment standards, and questioned the repeated construction of incomplete facilities.

thread.speaker: Rep. Caroline Agyao
thread.said: She referred to a construction amount of 2.7 applied across the Philippines; the unit and context were unclear.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said DOH used concept and system standards covering health stations, RHUs, MHUs, district and provincial hospitals, and apex hospitals, aligned with local health investment plans and health-care provider networks.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He asked how HFEP allocations for the 75 DOH retained hospitals were prioritized among national and regional medical centers, specialty hospitals, large tertiary hospitals, and training hospitals.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said HFEP for specialty centers was based on identified specialties, existing regional hospitals, referral needs, and the needs of the relevant catchment area.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He raised the absence of an FY2027 HFEP capital-outlay allocation for a specialty hospital whose capacity had been reduced by rebuilding and asked about the planned west-wing reconstruction.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said specialty centers would be expanded outside Metro Manila, while GOCC specialty hospitals would generally pursue projects through DPWH, multiyear agreements, retained earnings, and PhilHealth coverage; national-government support would still require inclusion in the DOH proposal.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official referred to a 200000000 proposal for medical equipment for East Avenue but said there was no corresponding HFEP capital-outlay proposal; the exchange was partly unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Karen Lagbas
thread.said: She said Northern Mindanao Medical Center was handling 7 60 to 7 80 patients against 6 92 implemented beds, with an emergency room designed for 29 beds handling 117 patients and operating at 403 percent utilization. She asked why the hospital had not reached the 1200-bed mandate under RA 1 1 7 1 6.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official cited pending releases from previous years, absorptive capacity, and the lag between infrastructure construction and operations. As an interim measure, DOH was considering private hospitals' 10 percent no-balance-billing beds, PhilHealth negotiations, and referral-network measures to relieve apex hospitals.

thread.speaker: Rep. Karen Lagbas
thread.said: She asked for a monitoring mechanism based on the hospital development plan, with annual budget requirements, accomplishments, target dates, and a monitoring team for Northern Mindanao Medical Center.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official committed to stronger project oversight, forecasting, year-to-year project management, and a catch-up plan so infrastructure would be ready to receive equipment and personnel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Karen Lagbas
thread.said: She asked whether DOH had conducted a referral-flow analysis to determine which patients could have been treated elsewhere if other government hospitals had adequate specialists, equipment, ICU beds, operating rooms, and diagnostics.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official referred to an interreferral network, specifically for Northern Mindanao, but the answer was incomplete in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Rep. Karen Lagbas
thread.said: She asked whether Misamis Oriental General Hospital had a yearly allocation for completing infrastructure, how much was needed, and how much had been funded.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official stated that the 20 27 allocation was 270000000 and said future requirements had to be determined strategically and based on the plan.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official requested submission of the list of expired and expiring medicines since 20 22 and the inventory of HFEP equipment that had been condemned or wasted.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He appealed for additional HFEP capital-outlay funding for a continuing regional-hospital construction project and for its outpatient department.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He cited 20 25 construction funding of 250000020 25 and 20 26 funding of 269000000; the first figure was garbled.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He said the FY2027 proposal included 50000000 in capital outlay and 10000000 in MOOE, and recommended increasing capital outlay by 10000000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He sought an additional 400000000 in 20 27 for the outpatient department, with completion targeted for 20 28.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said Rep. Hernandez's appeal and manifestation were noted and would be considered by the committee.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Anna York Bondoc
thread.said: She asked what DOH planned to do about equipment and hospitals damaged by flooding, including a district hospital whose CT scan, ward, and operating room had been flooded.

thread.speaker: Committee/DOH official
thread.said: The official said DOH would work with the member on a second floor or possible relocation, temporarily transfer services to an existing facility, arrange a roving van for outpatient care, and deploy architects to plan the response.

thread.speaker: Rep. Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked whether DOH had explored lease-to-own or similar arrangements for essential equipment because capital-outlay funding was tight.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official stated that last year's GAA capital outlay was 22.3 and the FY2027 net proposal was 14.5.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said hospitals already used pay-per-use dialysis and reagent tie-up arrangements, while larger projects could use PPP, joint-venture, or private-sector contracts, subject to reliable PhilHealth payment.

thread.speaker: Rep. Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked DOH to provide a list of equipment arrangements tied to the proposed budget so the committee could assess alternatives to capital-outlay funding.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official agreed to provide the list and financial modeling, including return-on-investment and breakeven information.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He asked what funding was allocated to finish SokSargen General Hospital after its proposed conversion from a 2nd-level facility into a Region 12 regional medical center.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said FY2027 included another 50000000 for a cancer center apart from the 130 mentioned earlier.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He asked the secretary to support the hospital's conversion, plantilla positions, and additional employees and doctors, including coordination with DBM.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official recognized the need for a Region 12 regional hospital and said DOH would enable the transition of the facility into a DOH hospital.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: The chair said many member concerns centered on years of HFEP implementation delays, inadequate funding for important hospitals, and undelivered infrastructure and equipment.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: She requested HFEP utilization rates from as far back as 2023, including utilized, reverted, and continuing appropriations, and cited a dialysis center funded in 2021 or 2022 whose building was completed in 2024 but whose machines remained undelivered.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: She said roughly 14000000000 was budgeted in FY2027 for a DOH catch-up plan and asked the committee to assess how much of the proposed HFEP amount was actually still needed.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official agreed to provide historical and current HFEP data, including project stages, releases, implementation, and the basis for the FY2027 request, and said DOH would strengthen project management for both infrastructure and equipment.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: She specifically asked DOH to include 2023 and 2024 HFEP line items, reversions, and the 20 26 HFEP status, and to examine implementation through DOH, CHD, DPWH, PPP, and LGU modalities.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: She asked when DOH could submit the utilization and catch-up information because it was needed to determine the FY2027 HFEP allocation.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official committed to submit the requested HFEP data on Friday, September 11th.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: The chair said any HFEP decision would account for limited fiscal space and would be based on historical utilization and the catch-up plan.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said an additional 11, 12000000000 for DOH hospitals would be used to cover zero-balance billing; the spoken figure was unclear.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair Micaela Suansing
thread.said: The chair said the 12000000000 request could not be committed given fiscal constraints and asked for a hospital-by-hospital breakdown and prioritization.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official committed to provide the prioritized hospital funding breakdown by Wednesday at 12 noon.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Majority Leader Albert Garcia
thread.said: He summarized that the committee expected the wish list by Wednesday at 12 noon and the HFEP catch-up plan by Friday.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He moved to terminate the committee hearing on the FY2027 DOH budget, including attached agencies and corporations under House Bill No. 10858.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Majority Leader Albert Garcia
thread.said: With no objection, the committee approved the motion to terminate the DOH budget hearing.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He moved to suspend the committee hearing on House Bill No. 10858.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Majority Leader Albert Garcia
thread.said: With no objection, the committee hearing was suspended.

topics.topic: DOH proposed budget reductions and priority funding requests
topics.summary: Members questioned how substantial reductions in medical assistance, HFEP, commodities, hospitals, emergency preparedness, and other programs would affect service delivery. DOH said it would rely on primary-care expansion, payment reform, procurement improvements, and efficiency measures, while requesting additional support for PhilHealth benefits, zero-balance billing, hospitals, and selected commodities. The committee raised specific concerns about a reported medical-assistance reduction from about 51 billion to about 24 billion, lower capital outlay from 22.3 to 14.5, and a possible additional hospital zero-balance-billing requirement of about 11 to 12 billion, although some transcript figures were unclear. Members also sought support for specialty hospitals, a regional hospital and outpatient department, senior-citizen flu vaccination, maternal care, primary-care facilities, and national hospital data systems. DOH committed to submit corporate-budget figures, prioritized funding lists, hospital-by-hospital zero-balance-billing needs, and equipment-financing information. The issue remained subject to further committee deliberation within limited fiscal space.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 reductions would affect medical assistance, hospital operations, medicines, immunization, HFEP, commodities, and zero-balance billing. It also sought to identify priority additions to the DOH and PhilHealth budgets, including capital outlay, primary care, and hospital-specific needs.
topics.agency_position: DOH said it would manage the reductions through primary-care expansion, payment and procurement reform, efficiency measures, and better hospital and financial-data systems. It maintained that additional support was needed for PhilHealth benefit expansion, zero-balance billing, hospitals, and selected commodities, but acknowledged that fiscal space was limited and several requested amounts required further breakdown or documentation.
topics.outcome: The committee did not settle the adequacy of the reduced FY 2027 DOH budget or the final funding level for zero-balance billing, hospitals, HFEP, and capital outlay. DOH committed to submit the requested budget, hospital-prioritization, and equipment-financing information for further committee deliberation.

positions.position: Supported stronger funding and controls for zero-balance billing, immunization, essential medicines, and professional-fee accountability, and pressed DOH to prevent procurement delays.
Raised concern that extensive proposed reductions could impair medical assistance, HFEP, commodities, emergency preparedness, hospitals, laboratories, and disease-control programs.
Argued that specialty and large tertiary hospitals required more explicit capital-outlay and HFEP support, particularly for capacity expansion and major hospital rebuilding.
Pressed DOH to correct flu-vaccine procurement delays and protect senior-citizen vaccination.
Supported expanding maternal-care assistance and increasing DOH funding for provincial hospitals whose shortages were shifting patients and resources to private hospitals.
Sought assurance that expanded zero-balance billing would cover DOH and non-DOH government hospitals, including isolated provinces, and questioned whether the reduced MAIFIP budget was sufficient.
Supported centralized health data, expanded primary care, lower out-of-pocket spending, and alternative equipment-financing arrangements to offset lower capital outlay.
Supported possible expansion of YACAP and requested a prioritized, data-based list of additional DOH and PhilHealth funding needs, including hospital-level zero-balance-billing requirements.

The agency proposed moving away from fee-for-service toward global or value-based payments to control incentives and professional-fee margins.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The agency said schedules would depend on seasonality, including for flu and pneumonia vaccines, as well as HPV procurement and vaccine shelf life.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Yamsuan

topics.topic: Zero-balance billing and MAIFIP coverage for DOH and LGU hospitals
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Yamsuan and Rep. Edgar Erice questioned how zero-balance billing could continue after the proposed MAIFIP reduction and other DOH budget cuts. The DOH described a prospective, rules-based payment model and said PhilHealth packages would form the first tier, with MAIFIP providing complementary assistance. The agency cited R51 billion dollars falling to about R24 billion in MAIFIP, while another committee member noted that the 20 26 General Appropriations Act had a dedicated zero-balance-billing amount that was not clearly identified in the 20 27 National Expenditure Program. Vice Chair JC Rahman Nava then asked whether coverage would apply to all DOH hospitals and expand to LGU hospitals; the agency referred to 300 plus LGU hospitals and said a special provision was needed. The agency also said about 85 percent of LGU-hospital bills were already covered by PhilHealth, with the remaining 10, 15 percent to be addressed through expanded packages and MAIFIP. The committee accepted the agency's stated direction but left the sufficiency and final legal and budgetary basis of the expansion as matters requiring follow-through.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how zero-balance billing would be financed in FY 2027 after reductions in MAIFIP and related DOH programs. It also asked whether the coverage would apply to all DOH hospitals and be expanded to LGU and other non-DOH government hospitals, and how PhilHealth packages would complement MAIFIP.
topics.agency_position: The DOH said zero-balance billing would operate through complementation: PhilHealth packages would cover the first tier, with MAIFIP addressing the remaining eligible costs. The agency indicated that coverage was intended to include DOH hospitals and 300 plus LGU hospitals, but acknowledged that a special provision was needed for 20 27 and that expanded PhilHealth packages and rules for outliers were still being negotiated.
topics.outcome: The agency stated that MAIFIP would complement PhilHealth and that the intended coverage would include DOH hospitals and 300 plus LGU hospitals, subject to a 20 27 special provision. The adequacy and dedicated identification of funding remained a concern, with PhilHealth package expansion and the final budget authority not fully settled.

He treated the reduction in MAIFIP and the absence of a clearly dedicated 20 27 zero-balance-billing allocation as a policy and operational concern.

He recognized the adequacy of MAIFIP as a concern and expressed support for extending zero-balance billing to local government hospitals.

topics.topic: Vaccine procurement delays, coverage, and the FY2027 immunization budget
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Yamsuan asked about the FY2027 immunization budget, which an agency official stated as 6855000000, and about vaccine scheduling and essential-medicine procurement. Vice Chair Julienne Baronda challenged the DOH to justify additional funding while suppliers had an ongoing portfolio of about 15 billion and asked for delivery percentages and statuses for major vaccine and medicine procurements. The DOH reported awards or notices of award for several vaccines but acknowledged procurement delays, bid changes, and incomplete visibility over delivery percentages; Baronda requested a supplier-by-supplier performance matrix and the chair required a full report. Rep. Girlie Veloso cited coverage of almost 4 out of 10 children not being fully vaccinated and received a DOH plan focused on community outreach, trust-building, last-mile services, forecasting, cold-chain management, and digital records. Members then pressed the DOH over flu-vaccine delays, including the failure to procure for 20 25, emergency vaccination of only 2500 individuals, and planned coverage of 25 percent to 50 percent of senior citizens versus a cited 75 percent standard. The DOH committed to early procurement and the chair indicated that another small purchase could be made, but members said the explanation was insufficient.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the DOH had sufficient FY2027 funding and a reliable procurement system to deliver vaccines on time, particularly childhood, influenza, pneumococcal, HPV, rabies, and other priority vaccines. Members also asked how the DOH would address low childhood coverage, vaccine hesitancy, supply-chain weaknesses, and delayed flu vaccination for senior citizens.
topics.agency_position: The DOH said procurement delays were driven largely by bidding failures, procurement procedures, inadequate forecasting, and timing challenges for a vaccine with a one-year shelf life, rather than by a lack of vaccine availability. It said it was moving to early procurement, clearer terms of reference, stronger supply and cold-chain management, improved forecasting and digital information systems, community-level outreach, and a strategy targeting 25 percent of senior citizens annually, while acknowledging that coverage remained inadequate.
topics.outcome: The DOH explained the procurement delays and outlined corrective strategies, but members remained dissatisfied with the flu-vaccine record and low coverage. The DOH was expected to submit procurement-performance information, pursue early procurement, and consider another small purchase; the underlying delivery and coverage problem remained open.

positions.position: Supported clarifying the FY2027 immunization allocation and procurement arrangements so essential medicines and vaccines could reach constituents and close supply gaps.
Opposed adding substantial funds without assurance that suppliers would deliver on time and urged uniform enforcement of procurement law, contract standards, and remedies for supplier nonperformance.

Pressed the DOH to respond aggressively to low childhood vaccination coverage through trust-building, wider barangay-level access, transportation and cold-chain support, and active follow-up of children who missed doses.
Pressed the DOH over flu-vaccine procurement delays and supported an increase in the DOH budget and stronger vaccination delivery for senior citizens.
Criticized the failure to procure flu vaccines for 20 25, questioned the delayed arrival and limited emergency vaccination, and demanded better planning and an immediate procurement option.

topics.topic: Essential-medicine and TB-drug procurement, stockouts, and expirations
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Yamsuan asked how DOH would schedule immunization procurement and match essential medicines to local needs; the agency cited the approved FY 2027 immunization amount of about 6.86 billion and described bidding, centralized procurement, and inventory-management measures. Deputy Minority Leader Percy Sandania raised HIV test-kit and TB-drug stockout risks, and DOH said HIV procurement was nearing post-qualification and that the TB award was expected within the month or by the following month; the committee required a regional TB balance and risk report covering the suspended 3225000000 procurement. Rep. Caroline Agyao questioned medicine overstocking and expirations, and DOH said it was improving electronic inventory visibility and forecasting. Vice Chair Julienne Baronda questioned major vaccine and TB procurements, citing an ongoing portfolio of about 15.4 billion and a procurement pipeline of about 21.68 billion, and demanded a supplier-by-supplier performance matrix. Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron sought an updated Yakap medicine list, while Vice Chair Anna York Bondoc criticized delayed flu vaccine procurement and obtained a commitment for another small purchase. The issue therefore landed with agency follow-up commitments and requested documents, rather than a fully resolved finding.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DOH could procure essential medicines, TB drugs, vaccines, and HIV test kits on time while maintaining accurate inventories and preventing stockouts, overstocking, and expirations. Members also asked for supplier-by-supplier performance data, regional balances, and corrective measures for delayed or failed procurement.
topics.agency_position: DOH said procurement was governed by terms of reference, bidding, post-qualification, and other statutory procedures, while harder-to-procure vaccines, anti-HIV medicines, and TB medicines were centralized. The agency said it was improving inventory visibility and forecasting, reviewing the Yakap medicine list, pursuing delayed awards, and applying supplier-performance remedies, but several deliveries and requested data remained pending.
topics.outcome: The agency gave partial explanations and several procurement-status updates, but the committee required additional reports on TB stocks, expired medicines, inventory, and supplier performance. Flu vaccine procurement remained a point of dissatisfaction, while the promised data submissions and corrective actions were left for follow-up and plenary consideration.

positions.position: Essential-medicine procurement should be matched to local needs and should close gaps in medicine access for constituents.
Delayed HIV test-kit and TB-drug procurement created serious risks of stockouts and treatment interruption; DOH needed to provide regional and local stock-balance data.
DOH needed to address overstocking, expired medicines and vaccines, and incomplete or insufficient inventory reporting.
The committee should not approve additional medicine and vaccine funding without assurance of timely supplier performance and uniform enforcement of contract remedies.
The Yakap medicine list needed to be updated to reflect commercially available medicines and practical pharmacy pricing and availability.
DOH's delayed flu vaccine procurement was inadequate, particularly for senior citizens and areas needing immediate vaccination, and required better planning and an immediate procurement response.

topics.topic: YAKAP medicines, Gamut pharmacy access, and benefit expansion
topics.summary: Rep. Miro Quimbo and Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron supported Yakap while raising implementation, medicine-list, and pharmacy-access concerns. PhilHealth said it was reviewing the list, including medicines that were unavailable or obsolete, but was not prioritizing differential reimbursement between hospital and retail pharmacies. Rep. Rachel Singson pressed for a solution in provinces without Gamut pharmacies; PhilHealth discussed FDA-regulated mobile pharmacies, alternative licensing, and possible action within 30 days. Chair Mika Suansing cited the reported 20000 allocation per patient and encouraged future expansion subject to actuarial and fiscal review. PhilHealth and DOH committed to submit a prioritized list of possible benefit and funding changes and a hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the additional request, including about 12 billion as spoken in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Yakap medicine list remained relevant and whether beneficiaries could access Yakap medicines in areas without Gamut-accredited pharmacies. It also examined possible changes to pharmacy reimbursement, the reported 20000 allocation per patient, and priorities for expanding PhilHealth benefits.
topics.agency_position: PhilHealth said it was reviewing and rationalizing the Yakap medicine list using provider feedback and was not currently prioritizing differential reimbursement between hospital and retail pharmacies. For areas without Gamut pharmacies, it was pursuing FDA rules for mobile pharmacy outreach, considering alternative pharmacy licensing, and supporting further Yakap expansion subject to actuarial review, available fiscal space, and program calibration.
topics.outcome: The medicine-list review and access problems were acknowledged, but differential pharmacy reimbursement and alternative accreditation remained under study. PhilHealth and DOH committed to follow-up coordination and to submit prioritized funding and hospital-level information; Yakap expansion was encouraged but not decided.

positions.position: Supported Yakap as an important preventive program and favored broad private-sector participation, strong monitoring, and additional government funding.
Supported Yakap but pressed PhilHealth to update obsolete medicine listings and address price and reimbursement differences that could limit pharmacy participation.
Supported Yakap but said access and accreditation were too slow in provinces without Gamut pharmacies and urged mobile pharmacies and alternative accreditation arrangements.
Supported possible Yakap expansion but required actuarial and fiscal review, a prioritized benefits list, and clearer distinctions between lateral reallocations and additional funding requests.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: He said Yakap was a strong program but would succeed only if implemented well and fully. He supported broad access, strong monitoring, and post-release audits, while warning that isolated abuses should not undermine the program.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: He said LGUs could not handle Yakap registrations alone because they lacked the necessary capacity and manpower. He urged deep private-sector participation, with the DOH and PhilHealth exercising monitoring and enforcement functions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: He said Yakap would require more government funding and described bringing preventive services directly to citizens as an outstanding intervention. He expressed hope that DOH and PhilHealth would monitor the program effectively.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron
thread.said: He asked whether PhilHealth had reviewed the medicines covered by Yakap. He relayed reports that some listed medicines were no longer commercially available, had become obsolete, or were offered in different dosage forms.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth president Beverly Ho
thread.said: She said PhilHealth had nearly a year of data and provider feedback and was reviewing and updating the list. The review would add medicines while rationalizing the list so pharmacies could carry more of the covered medicines.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron
thread.said: He asked whether PhilHealth was aware that retail prices differed substantially between stand-alone or chain pharmacies and hospital pharmacies.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth president Beverly Ho
thread.said: She said PhilHealth was aware of the price differences, explaining that retail pharmacies were more competitive while hospitals could mark up prices because patients sought medicines there out of necessity.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron
thread.said: He said hospital pharmacies faced higher operating costs and might be unable to meet Yakap requirements because their prices were higher than those of stand-alone retail pharmacies.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth president Beverly Ho
thread.said: She said some hospitals had separated their inpatient and outpatient pharmacy operations, which helped address the pricing issue. She added that hospitals could view the planned Yakap expansion, including Gamut and outpatient laboratories, as one portfolio rather than separate revenue streams.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth president Beverly Ho
thread.said: She said PhilHealth was not yet considering differential reimbursement for hospital and retail pharmacies because the objective was greater access and pressure on prices. She said the issue could be studied but was not among the agency's immediate priorities.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron
thread.said: He followed up by asking whether PhilHealth would consider a different type of reimbursement for hospital pharmacies.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth president Beverly Ho
thread.said: She replied that PhilHealth could study differential reimbursement, but it was not at the forefront of its priorities.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rachel Singson
thread.said: She asked what PhilHealth's direction was for constituents who wanted to use Yakap but lived in areas with no Gamut pharmacies.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said the current direction remained to use FDA-licensed pharmacies. PhilHealth was discussing mobile pharmacies with the FDA so existing pharmacies could conduct regular outreach in areas without Gamut pharmacies, and it was increasing the number of accounts that could operate simultaneously per pharmacy from 2.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rachel Singson
thread.said: She asked whether pharmacies could already apply to operate as mobile pharmacies.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said the FDA first had to issue licensing guidelines because mobile pharmacies would be extensions of existing licensed pharmacies. PhilHealth would provide immediate or automatic accreditation once the guidelines were issued, and said the policy might be issued within 30 days.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rachel Singson
thread.said: She said that in her province Yakap services existed but constituents could not obtain Gamut medicines because there were no Gamut pharmacies, and asked how the situation could be addressed.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said PhilHealth would work with the member's team to assess available infrastructure. The agency was also studying whether existing pharmacies could be accredited under a possible category B license for pharmacies dispensing specific medicines.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rachel Singson
thread.said: She said private clinics wanted Yakap accreditation but could not meet a requirement for a memorandum of agreement with a Gamut pharmacy where no Gamut pharmacy existed. She asked how clinics could be accredited under those circumstances.

thread.speaker: PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said PhilHealth was working on the issue and would coordinate with its regional vice president on specific initiatives in the member's area.

topics.topic: PhilHealth and private-hospital payment, billing, and reimbursement rules
topics.summary: Members questioned DOH and PhilHealth on private-hospital payment terms, balance billing, professional fees, claims processing, and the treatment of hospital and physician charges. The agency said it was moving toward direct negotiations, rules-based global payments, and selective advance payments, with hospitals expected to provide no-balance-billing beds and include physicians in the payment arrangements. Reported figures included payment processing in about 15 to 20 days, a 10 percent no-balance-billing bed requirement, a 15000000000 HFEP shortfall, and estimated unallocated PhilHealth-related collections of about 199 billion in total. The agency also committed to guidelines by October 2026, provider-network targets by end-2027, an HMO complementation agreement, and studies or reports on billing and HFEP concerns. The issue was not fully resolved because specific payment terms, professional-fee safeguards, and remittance and billing reforms remained under development.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DOH and PhilHealth would pay private hospitals and physicians, including payment timing, advance or global payments, professional fees, claims processing, and safeguards against balance billing. Members also asked how private-provider networks, PhilHealth benefits, and hospital contracting would ensure timely, transparent, and affordable care.
topics.agency_position: DOH and PhilHealth said they were moving toward negotiated, rules-based and potentially global-budget payments rather than relying exclusively on fee-for-service reimbursement. Advance payments would be piloted selectively in exchange for no-balance-billing beds, predictable professional-fee arrangements, and lower patient out-of-pocket costs; provider networks would be built with LGUs and private providers, but several implementation guidelines and billing issues remained under study.
topics.outcome: The agency answered the committee's principal questions by outlining negotiated and global-payment models, selective advance payments, no-balance-billing conditions, and provider-network targets. However, the payment terms, professional-fee controls, private-hospital invoice rules, remittance delays, and several implementing guidelines remained subject to study, negotiation, or future reports.

positions.position: Private-hospital agreements should specify payment timing and prevent patients from being charged unexplained balances after PhilHealth or DOH payment.
DOH must protect zero balance billing and create transparent controls against duplicate, abusive, or inconsistent professional-fee billing.
Hospital expansion requests in Negros Occidental should be considered, while charges and doctors' fees in private-provider arrangements must be controlled.
HFEP utilization and equipment delivery must be synchronized, and private-hospital invoice requirements should not impose avoidable burdens on hospitals and physicians.
The UHC Act's no-balance-billing bed rule, portable public-private networks, timely PhilHealth remittances, and HMO complementation required concrete implementation and accountability.
Advance payments could address private hospitals' liquidity and reimbursement delays, but PhilHealth should also ensure that private physicians receive professional fees on time.

topics.topic: Professional-fee regulation and transparency in health-care billing
topics.summary: Rep. Miro Quimbo requested a written DOH update on professional-fee regulation, citing the growing share of professional fees in medical expenses and asking what legislative authority the department needed. Rep. Brian Yamsuan later asked how the DOH would address professional-fee controls amid a reported budget decrease stated as "50 per 53 percent" and zero balance billing. The agency discussed primary care, provider negotiations, fee-for-service, rent-seeking behavior, and a shift toward rules-based global payments, but did not give a detailed billing-control system. Yamsuan specifically sought safeguards against abusive or duplicate billing and a way to reconcile charges. The agency later said that professional fees should be transparent and accountable and that a mechanism should be established, while also mentioning "15, 20 days," whose context was unclear. The matter remained open pending the requested written update and more specific mechanisms.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOH could regulate, monitor, and require transparency for professional fees charged in government and private hospitals. It also sought mechanisms to prevent abusive or duplicate billing and to clarify what legislative tools or institutional arrangements the DOH needed.
topics.agency_position: The agency indicated that it was considering provider negotiations, a shift away from fee-for-service, and rules-based global payments to reduce rent-seeking and control payment incentives. It also agreed in principle that professional fees should be transparent and accountable and that a mechanism should be established, but it did not specify the mechanism, enforcement authority, or implementation timetable.
topics.outcome: The agency acknowledged the need for transparent and accountable professional-fee practices and referred generally to provider negotiations, global payment arrangements, and a future mechanism. The requested written update and the specific regulatory, billing-verification, and enforcement arrangements were not provided in the transcript.

positions.position: Professional fees had become a substantial component of medical expenses, especially in private hospitals, and the DOH needed to identify legislative tools to strengthen its regulatory authority.
The committee needed safeguards against abusive, duplicate, or nontransparent professional-fee billing and a way to verify and reconcile charges.
Professional-fee practices should be transparent and accountable, with a mechanism covering both government personnel and doctors.

topics.topic: Hospital capacity, specialty facilities, and regional hospital development
topics.summary: Members raised concerns that hospital capacity and infrastructure had not kept pace with statutory bed expansions and patient referrals. Ferrer sought phased additional funding for Negros Occidental, while Suntay questioned the absence of capital outlay for specialty and large tertiary hospitals such as East Avenue Medical Center. Lagbaf reported severe overcrowding at Northern Mindanao Medical Center, including 760 to 780 patients against 692 beds and emergency-room utilization of 403 percent; DOH cited delayed releases, infrastructure lag, and the need for a stronger referral network. Baronda pressed for action on Western Visayas Medical Center and its cancer center, and the chair required a full report. Hernandez sought additional funding for a regional hospital and outpatient department, while DOH indicated that a 100-bed regional hospital could cost more than 1 billion and recognized the need to support conversion of SokSargen General Hospital. DOH also committed to flood-response planning, standardized hospital data systems, equipment-financing analysis, and a hospital-by-hospital breakdown of additional funding requests before plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 budget would adequately expand and staff DOH hospitals, specialty facilities, and regional referral networks. Members also asked how DOH prioritized capital outlay, addressed overcrowding and delayed construction, and would support hospital conversions and flood-resilient infrastructure.
topics.agency_position: DOH said hospital and specialty-facility funding should be based on catchment-area needs, referral networks, hospital development plans, project readiness, and equipment and staffing requirements. The agency acknowledged infrastructure and data-system gaps, supported interim referral and private-hospital arrangements, and undertook to submit catch-up plans, reports, financial models, and hospital-level funding priorities.
topics.outcome: The committee did not finally resolve the requested hospital-expansion and capital-outlay increases during the hearing. DOH was directed or undertook to submit hospital-level funding priorities, development and catch-up plans, and reports before plenary, leaving the amounts subject to further committee deliberation.

Pressed for urgent action on Western Visayas Medical Center's overcrowding, staffing, equipment, and cancer-center construction and requested a full DOH report.
Sought additional construction and outpatient-department funding and advocated DOH support for converting SokSargen General Hospital into a Region 12 regional medical center.
Said a new regional hospital could cost more than 1000000000 and advocated considering conversion of an existing provincial hospital as a potentially more cost-effective option.
Called for immediate and long-term DOH support for flood-damaged hospitals, including temporary outpatient services and climate-resilient infrastructure.
Supported standardized hospital data systems and asked DOH to explore lease-to-own and pay-per-use equipment arrangements to supplement limited capital outlay.
Sought a prioritized, hospital-level breakdown of additional funding requests before the committee considered amendments, given limited fiscal space.

topics.topic: Pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing localization
topics.summary: Deputy Speaker Serge Memon raised the risk of renewed foreign medicine-supply disruptions and asked how the government would support local pharmaceutical manufacturers. The DOH cited negotiated rates, procurement-volume shifts, DTI manufacturing provisions, and the Clark pharma hub as possible incentives, and said an ITRM vaccine study was underway. Memon argued that a 6 year tax holiday was insufficient and pointed to Malaysia's 70 percent government-purchase market share, suggesting at least 50 percent sustainable support for manufacturers. TS Miron separately urged the government to establish vaccine fill-and-finish capacity using imported bulk vaccine. He said the arrangement could save billions, but the agency made no specific commitment to establish the facility or adopt the proposed procurement targets.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what the DOH planned to do to support local pharmaceutical manufacturing and reduce dependence on foreign medicine suppliers. It also considered whether the government should develop domestic vaccine fill-and-finish capacity and adopt stronger procurement or market incentives.
topics.agency_position: The DOH stated that it was considering incentives for local pharmaceutical suppliers, including negotiated rates, procurement-volume shifts, DTI manufacturing-plant provisions, and the Clark pharma hub. It also said an ITRM study on vaccines was underway, but it did not provide a specific commitment to establish a government fill-and-finish facility or adopt the proposed procurement shares.
topics.outcome: The DOH presented general incentive and procurement approaches and noted an ongoing vaccine-related study, but no specific fill-and-finish project, procurement-share policy, or implementation timetable was adopted during the exchange. The proposals remained for further consideration.

positions.position: Supported stronger, longer-term government support for local pharmaceutical manufacturing, including preferential government procurement and a possible government manufacturing arm.

topics.topic: FDA medicine-registration backlog and regulatory-fee policy
topics.summary: Rep. Caroline Aguil raised the recurring FDA registration backlog and requested data covering at least 50 widely used generic medicines, with separate counts for principal CPRs, related CPRs, and CLIDPs or “baby CPRs.” The FDA director general said the agency would provide information for the past 4 years and reported a total backlog of 19000 applications, including almost 15000 in CDRR. A member identified by the chair as DS Baron proposed 2 years of provisional registration for certain products, automatic renewal of medical devices, and use of the FDA's retained income of about 2 billion through a DBM business plan. The member also objected to a regulatory-fee increase described as 1000 percent and sought its deferral. The FDA said it would revisit the policies, and the chair required an update, but the proposed reforms and fee deferral remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the scale and composition of the FDA's medicine-registration backlog, including the distinction between principal CPRs and related or “baby” CPRs and CLIDPs. Members also asked whether policy reforms, additional manpower, use of retained FDA income, provisional registration, and fee-policy changes could reduce the backlog and improve access to generic medicines.
topics.agency_position: The FDA acknowledged a current backlog of 19000 applications, including almost 15000 in CDRR, and committed to provide data for the past 4 years. The director general said the FDA would revisit its policies, including the reforms raised by the members, to align them with the mandate to make medicines available to the public.
topics.outcome: The FDA answered the headline backlog question and committed to submit historical and disaggregated data. It also undertook a policy review, but no decision was recorded on provisional registration, automatic device renewal, use of retained income, or deferral of the fee increase.

positions.position: The FDA should submit detailed registration-backlog data for widely used generic medicines, distinguish principal CPRs from related CPRs and CLIDPs, analyze the CDRR workload, and consider manpower and CPR-review reforms.

positions.who: a member identified by the chair as DS Baron
positions.position: The FDA should consider provisional registration for medicines with a wide margin of safety, automatic renewal of medical devices, use its retained income through a DBM business plan, and defer the implementation of substantially higher regulatory fees.

topics.topic: Universal health-care provider networks and PhilHealth financing flows
topics.summary: Assistant Minority Leader Robert Nazal Jr. questioned DOH on the 10 percent private-bed requirement and whether public-private provider networks were functioning seven years after the UHC law's approval. DOH cited Bataan as a model, said LGUs should manage province-wide or citywide systems, and committed to targets of 10 primary care networks and 5 HCP networks by the end of 2027. The committee also asked about estimated delayed PhilHealth allocations, which DOH placed at about 133 billion in unallocated sin taxes and an unclear figure of around 66 for PCSO and Pagcor, while the member characterized the combined amount as 199 billion. DOH said reserves had fallen from about 2 years of coverage to 8 to 9 months and that discussions with DBM and DOF were ongoing. It also reported that an HMO complementation MOA had been prepared and that some HMOs were ready to sign. The hearing therefore produced agency commitments, but the delayed fund transfers and some implementation details remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish DOH's progress in implementing Universal Health Care provider networks, including the 10 percent private-bed requirement, public-private referrals, and province-wide or citywide networks. It also asked about delayed PhilHealth fund allocations, HMO complementation, and the timeline for integrating medicines into the field health system.
topics.agency_position: DOH said provider networks should be organized around province-wide or citywide systems led by LGUs, with private providers complementing public capacity and patients routed to appropriate accredited facilities. It reported ongoing work on private-bed guidelines, initial HMO complementation agreements, and discussions with DBM and DOF on delayed PhilHealth-related allocations, while maintaining that benefit expansion should continue.
topics.outcome: DOH provided implementation targets and undertook further work on private-bed guidelines, LGU networks, HMO complementation, and medicines integration. The delayed PhilHealth allocations and the precise status and cause of the outstanding funds were not fully resolved during the exchange.

topics.topic: Health data systems and national capacity planning
topics.summary: Vice Chair Javi Benitez asked how a national data repository could track patients, diseases, beds, hospital capacity, and budget needs, and how primary-care expansion could reduce out-of-pocket spending. The DOH said it was developing a repository integrating Yakap and eventually inpatient records, while targeting 60 percent Yakap enrollment by 20 28 and at least 50 percent by that year in its more cautious projection. Officials said the country lacked around 3000 primary-care facilities, that 52 percent had a Gamut provider, and that around hundred 20000000000 in reimbursements could ideally go to primary care; the amount was unclear as spoken. The secretary said 800000000000 was an aggressive health-care requirement, cited a projected PhilHealth payout of 420000000000, and said additional subsidies and reforms were necessary. Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez then raised fragmented DOH hospital data systems and lower capital outlay, with the DOH reporting 22.3 previously approved versus 14.5 proposed for 20 27. The DOH committed to standard reporting and to provide equipment-financing and financial-modeling information.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOH would build an integrated national health data system, use it to plan capacity and reduce out-of-pocket spending, and expand primary-care access. It also asked whether DOH hospitals could standardize their data systems and how the agency would address lower capital-outlay funding for equipment.
topics.agency_position: The DOH said it was pursuing a national health data repository integrating Yakap outpatient records and eventually inpatient records, while standardizing hospital financial and operational reporting. It said primary-care expansion and lower out-of-pocket spending required additional subsidies, efficiency reforms, value-based payment, expanded Yakap and Gamut coverage, and a mix of public and private providers; it also supported examining pay-per-use, PPP, and other equipment-financing arrangements.
topics.outcome: The DOH answered the data, primary-care, and capital-outlay questions and undertook to standardize hospital reporting and provide equipment-financing information. The broader funding requirement and the timeline for achieving national coverage remained dependent on additional subsidies, efficiency reforms, and future implementation.

positions.position: He supported centralized, patient- and disease-level data to improve capacity planning and budget allocation, pressed for primary-care expansion to reduce out-of-pocket costs, and endorsed exploring private-sector equipment-financing arrangements.

He said DOH hospital data systems were fragmented and urged the agency to use middleware or comparable integration and to examine lease-to-own or other arrangements to address lower capital-outlay funding.

He said the proposed 800000000000 requirement was aggressive, that additional subsidy and efficiency reforms were necessary, and that the DOH would standardize hospital reporting and explore financing models for equipment.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked about real-time tracking of patients, diagnoses, hospital beds, occupancy, available beds, and excess capacity throughout the country.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The DOH said it was creating a national health data repository, initially integrating the outpatient EMR known as Yakap and gradually including inpatient records. It intended to track disease entities and interconnect hospitals to identify excess capacity.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He said logging each patient and disease would improve tracking and help determine budget requirements at different levels of the health-care sector, including coordination between the national government and local government units.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked how much budget would be needed to address health-care needs in the Philippines, including emergency care, triage, and different levels of disease and sickness.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said no country could cover 100 percent of its full health-care needs. The DOH was using out-of-pocket spending as a measure, citing a WHO standard of 15 percent, a medium-term development goal of 28 percent, and an estimate reaching 38 percent.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary gave a back-of-the-envelope estimate of 800000000000 in out-of-pocket spending, with the surrounding transcript indicating the figure was associated with a 20 to 28 percent range; the wording is unclear.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He repeated the figure, saying “800000000000.”

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said reducing out-of-pocket spending by 9 percent, or bringing it toward roughly 25 to 30 percent, would substantially reduce catastrophic spending. Catastrophic spending was defined as spending more than 10 percent of total household income on health.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked where the 800000000000 should be focused, including whether priority should be given to early or later years of life and to public or private providers.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The DOH said the focus should be primary care “from womb to tomb,” rather than a particular age group. Its aspiration was to shift 25 percent of health-care spending to primary care, which it said could reduce admissions by 33 percent to 35 percent and produce net savings of 10 percent.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said primary care should use a mix of public and private providers and require private-sector engagement as a whole-of-society approach. The DOH targeted 60 percent of the population being enrolled in Yakap by 20 28.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked how many primary-care facilities were needed and whether reaching 60 percent enrollment in 20 28 was achievable at the current rate.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said every municipality had a Yakap provider, while only 52 percent had a Gamut provider. The goal was to have enough providers to reach one for every 20000 people, rather than merely one Yakap and one Gamut provider per municipality.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said the country still lacked around 3000 primary-care facilities. The DOH hoped that more generous Yakap and Gamut programs would provide predictable financing and attract providers, while the government would need to do more in areas where private provision was not viable.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He recapped that about 3000 primary-care facilities were needed and that Yakap and Gamut partners would be required to reach the target, asking whether that understanding was correct.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official added that the target involved 60000000 people.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked how much the primary-care expansion would cost.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official estimated that around hundred 20000000000 of reimbursements would ideally go to primary care in the best-case scenario. The spoken amount is unclear as written.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He summarized the proposed approach as requiring a central database, 800000000000 for health care, primary-care facilities and Yakap and Gamut partners for 60000000 people, and lower out-of-pocket spending, then asked whether that was correct.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official answered yes.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Javi Benitez
thread.said: He asked how many years the objective would take and how confident the DOH was that it could be achieved.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said 800000000000 was very aggressive and would require more than the usual funding. He said current sin-tax funding was insufficient and that additional subsidies, efficiency measures, and a shift from fee-for-service to value-based payment would be needed.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said PhilHealth's current payout was projected to be 420000000000 by this year, while the usual budget from sin taxes was not enough.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said the objective was for at least 50 percent of Filipinos to be enrolled in Yakap by 20 28, with broader implementation expected to take time and continuing into the next 5 years.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez
thread.said: He said DOH hospital data had been difficult to extract because hospitals appeared to use different systems, and asked whether that was correct.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said initial feedback and an analysis of some hospitals showed a need to work with hospital finance personnel on standard reporting templates, including consistent accounting standards.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said the DOH had already formed a hospital operations cluster whose work streams included finance. It would implement common reporting lines using COA and public-hospital accounting manuals, with an ADB consultant helping standardize the chart of accounts.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez
thread.said: He said a middleware system could extract data across the different DOH hospital systems for planning and execution, noting that the DOH head office otherwise lacked visibility into conditions on the ground.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez
thread.said: He asked whether proposed capital outlay for the coming year was the same as, higher than, or lower than the prior year's approved amount.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said the net capital-outlay amount was lower than the prior year's Gaha-approved amount: the prior year was 22.3, while the 20 27 net amount was 14.5.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez
thread.said: He asked whether the DOH had explored lease-to-own or similar arrangements for essential equipment, using supplier agreements linked to hospital and PhilHealth payments.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary said hospitals already used pay-per-use arrangements, including for dialysis, and reagent tie-ups for laboratory equipment. Larger arrangements could involve a joint venture or PPP, but the hospital would need assurance that PhilHealth would pay on time.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez
thread.said: He asked the DOH to prepare a list based on its equipment budget request and the existing equipment-arrangement options, so the Appropriations Committee could assess alternatives to capital outlay.

thread.speaker: DOH secretary
thread.said: The secretary agreed to provide the list and possibly a financial template showing return on investment, expected break-even points, and related financial modeling.

topics.topic: Maternal care, rare-disease treatment, and PhilHealth package coverage
topics.summary: Rep. Howard Guintu asked whether dystonia qualified under Republic Act number 1 7 4 7 and whether PhilHealth had a treatment package for it. The agency said dystonia was not yet included but was being considered through qualification criteria, newborn screening, medicine indications, and a planned rare-diseases package. Guintu then asked about prenatal checkups and coverage for difficult pregnancies and deliveries. The agency said the expanded maternal care package covered prenatal visits, tests, supplements, and deliveries, with coverage described as having increased by almost 150 percent, although the exact wording was unclear. Guintu urged the committee to consider increasing the DOH budget because provincial hospitals lacked funds and patients were being directed to private hospitals. The rare-disease package represented an agency commitment, while dystonia eligibility and provincial-hospital funding remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether dystonia qualified for coverage under the Rare Diseases Act and whether PhilHealth packages covered prenatal checkups, complicated pregnancies, deliveries, and related maternal care. It also raised whether DOH funding for provincial hospitals should be increased because patients were being directed to private hospitals.
topics.agency_position: The agency stated that dystonia was not yet included as a rare disease but was under review for qualification, newborn screening, and possible medicine indications. It said PhilHealth was developing a rare-diseases package and that the expanded maternal care package covered prenatal visits, required tests, and deliveries, subject to stated accommodation and copay provisions.
topics.outcome: The agency provided information on ongoing rare-disease package development and existing expanded maternal-care coverage. Dystonia's eligibility and the requested increase in provincial-hospital funding were not resolved during the exchange.

positions.position: He supported faster access to dystonia treatment, sought broader and clearer maternal-care coverage for pregnant women, and urged increased DOH funding for provincial hospitals to reduce reliance on private hospitals.

topics.topic: Drug-treatment and rehabilitation program funding
topics.summary: Assistant Minority Leader Renee Co asked the DOH to explain its drug-treatment and rehabilitation programs, their consent and referral safeguards, and its shift toward a health-based response. The DOH said it operated 27 of 87 nationwide treatment and rehabilitation centers and supplied them with personnel, medicines, rehabilitation programs, and psychiatric support. For 2027, the official cited a total budget of about 2.4 billion, including about 1.466 billion for center operations, 747 million in MOOE, and 168000020 for drug-related illness programs; the spoken figure 2.213 was unclear. Ko also requested a budget history, the latest implementation review, cost per beneficiary, and comparisons with alternative harm-reduction models. The DOH committed to submit those materials, leaving the requested effectiveness comparison for follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOH funded and administered drug-treatment and rehabilitation programs, including which programs were voluntary, compulsory, or court-referred and what safeguards protected informed free consent. Members also sought a facility- and program-level budget breakdown, beneficiary costs, and comparisons with alternative harm-reduction models.
topics.agency_position: The DOH characterized drug use and related illness as a medical and potential epidemic issue, supported treatment and rehabilitation centers, and said it was expanding primary-care, health-promotion, and community-based responses. It agreed to provide historical budget data, implementation reviews, and cost-per-beneficiary and alternative-model comparisons.
topics.outcome: The DOH answered the facility-count and budget questions but did not provide the requested beneficiary-cost analysis or alternative-model comparison during the hearing. It committed to submit the requested budget breakdown, implementation review, and comparative cost information.

positions.position: Drug responses should be community-centered, rehabilitation-focused, and based on informed free consent rather than primarily criminalizing drug use; the DOH should provide detailed budget and effectiveness information.

topics.topic: DICT FY2027 proposed budget reduction and priority funding wish list
topics.summary: DICT presented a proposed FY 2027 budget of about 19.49 billion for the department and its attached agencies, including about 7.6 billion for the DICT Office of the Secretary. Representatives Salvador Pleyto and Joeboye Aquito supported the budget, with Aquito also seeking 5000000 for a digital transformation center project. Representative Rufus Rodriguez questioned a reported reduction of hundred 33000000 and cited a reduction of 1100000000 related to a capacity-building proposal of 1800000000. Secretary Aguda did not explain the reduction on the record but asked to submit DICT's wish list in writing. The stated additional requests included around 450 million for CICC, less than 200 million for NTC, around 303 hundred million from an agency whose attribution was unclear, and 50000000 for an unclear Pinoy-related implementation request. Rodriguez proposed augmentation of at least 1 billion, subject to consideration at the proper time, and the committee then terminated the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DICT's FY 2027 proposed budget had been reduced despite the department's reported digitalization and connectivity accomplishments. It also sought DICT's and its attached agencies' priority funding requests or wish list for possible augmentation.
topics.agency_position: DICT presented its FY 2027 proposed budget as supporting connectivity, digital government, cybersecurity, digital skills, and related services. When asked for additional priorities, Secretary Aguda requested permission to submit a written wish list; the stated agency requests included around 450000000 for CICC, less than 200000000 for NTC, and an additional request of around 303 hundred million whose agency attribution is unclear.
topics.outcome: The reduction was identified and questioned, but the transcript did not record a substantive explanation for why the budget was reduced. DICT and the attached agencies were directed to submit a written priority wish list, while Representative Rodriguez proposed at least 1000000000 in augmentation; the motion was reserved for later consideration and the hearing was terminated.

topics.topic: DICT budget utilization, unobligated funds, payables, and project bottlenecks
topics.summary: Rep. Romeo Momo and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned DICT's low utilization, unobligated balance, payables, project delays, and manpower capacity. Members cited about 61.7 percent obligation and 22 percent disbursement for 20 25, a 9 percent 20 26 obligation figure, and an unobligated balance of about 20.5 billion, while DICT reported a 24 percent BUR and said it had released 89 percent of downloaded funds. DICT attributed delays to the 85 percent BUR threshold, late fund downloads, extended implementation periods, procurement cycles, World Bank rules, and insufficient personnel; DBM had approved 115 of about 500 requested positions. Members also pressed DICT to clarify its claim of 100 percent DepEd school connectivity and to identify unpaid e-government service providers, while DICT agreed to submit lists and reports. Rep. Iris Marie Montes raised the Philippine Digital Infrastructure Project, and DICT acknowledged two failed biddings and a 6-month delay but projected BUR shares of 3.03 by September, 45 percent by October, and 80 percent by December. DICT also confirmed that a COA-directed UIS GDA payment for services rendered without a renewed contract had already been paid and said current contracts would be handled more strictly.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT could efficiently utilize its existing and proposed appropriations, identify the causes of unobligated funds and unpaid obligations, and explain project implementation delays. Members also asked whether DICT had sufficient manpower and procurement capacity to deliver connectivity and digital infrastructure projects.
topics.agency_position: DICT said its reported BUR was 24 percent as of June, rather than the 9 percent figure attributed to COA, and said it would reconcile the difference with COA. The agency attributed weak utilization and project delays to late fund downloads, an 85 percent BUR threshold, project implementation periods extending into the following year, manpower shortages, unusual procurement cycles, and World Bank procurement rules. DICT said it had paid the COA-directed UIS GDA claim, would submit lists and reports on payables and unpaid providers, and was taking steps to accelerate procurement and project execution.
topics.outcome: DICT provided competing utilization figures and explanations for delayed implementation, but the discrepancy between the 9 percent COA figure and the 24 percent DICT/DBM figure remained subject to reconciliation. The agency undertook to submit multiple lists and reports and to accelerate procurement, while the project delays, payables, and detailed coverage claims were not fully resolved during the hearing.

positions.position: DICT should demonstrate faster obligation and disbursement of its increased appropriations, resolve its manpower and implementation bottlenecks, and use its available talent to consume appropriations.

DICT needed to account for the unobligated balance, identify and explain delayed projects and payables, clarify what school connectivity coverage meant, and ensure that digital services did not fail because providers were unpaid.
DICT's additional funding should be justified by improved utilization, particularly given competing fiscal needs and delays in the Philippine Digital Infrastructure Project.
The committee should require reliable implementation, timely payment of obligations, avoidance of unused ICT capacity, and safeguards against outages caused by nonpayment.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Rep. Momo questioned DICT's obligation and absorptive capacity, noting that its budget had increased by 7 percent compared with 20 26. He asked how DICT could assure Congress that it could spend the proposed 20 27 budget quickly and effectively.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: He said DICT's 20 25 obligation rate was only 61.7 percent against appropriations and its disbursement was 22 percent versus obligations, describing DICT as the lowest among national government agencies in absorptive capacity.

thread.said: Secretary Uy said the issue was not the size of the budget but DICT's ability to comply with its BUR. He said DICT was on track to reach 90 percent for the 25, sorry, 26 budget and would front-load deployment of 20 27 funds beginning in October.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Rep. Momo warned that funding for 20 25 would be lost by December if it was not used, and said the 7 percent increase in the 20 27 budget could pile up if implementation did not accelerate.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: He raised a separate utilization figure, saying DICT's reported obligation for the 20 26 budget was only 9 percent as of June and was the lowest among national offices.

thread.speaker: DICT head of support and finance

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
