thread.said: He said Congress had appropriated 3700000000 in the 20 26 budget for 7 projects, including ICT systems, government systems support, e-government, the digital national ID, free Wi-Fi, and digital health solutions. He said 3040000000 of these projects remained unimplemented.

thread.speaker: DICT head of support and finance
thread.said: The finance official confirmed that 3400000000 remained unimplemented, principally involving Congress-initiated amendments. DICT had been unable to obtain the funds because DBM required an 85 percent BUR before allocation or downloading, and DICT had not reached that threshold the previous year.

thread.speaker: DICT head of support and finance
thread.said: The official said that after explaining the situation to DBM, DICT obtained an additional allocation of about 500000000 dollars and an additional 700000000 dollars from that fund. The transcript identifies these figures with a dollar symbol.

thread.speaker: Ivan Uy, DICT Secretary

thread.speaker: DICT head of support and finance
thread.said: The finance official said DICT had requested about 500 additional positions because its existing organizational staffing pattern dated from 20 19 and no longer matched current operations. DICT had about 1700 JOs or SOs, and DBM approved 115 additional positions, or one-fourth of the request.

topics.topic: Free public Wi-Fi funding, coverage, site counts, and actual usage
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co questioned whether the Free Wi-Fi program's beneficiary targets matched actual usage and asked how DICT would reach about 15 million users. DICT reported about 10.37 million unique users across 11,836 locations and 29,091 access points, with 99.39 percent of 45,328 DepEd schools connected and 220 SUCs in the first phase. It said a Free Wi-Fi request of about 5 billion would sustain existing locations, while additional deployment would require projects and coordination with other programs. Rep. Romeo Momo cited COA deficiencies and asked for inactive-site data; DICT described network monitoring and a 72-hour provider-resolution process but said it would check the inactive percentage. Rep. Elmer Catulpos elicited that 1,726 of 42,208 barangay halls and 766 of 4,000 LGUs had operational Free Wi-Fi, and the chair required a 2027 site list. The chair also requested an ASEAN spending comparison after citing 22.4 pesos per unique beneficiary per month. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez praised local connectivity, questioned the budget reduction, requested a priority wish list, and moved for a later augmentation of at least 1 billion; the chair said the motion would be taken up at the proper time.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Free Public Internet Access Act program was meeting its beneficiary, school, barangay hall, site, and usage targets, and whether its funding was producing reliable service. Members also sought performance data, comparative ASEAN spending, and the agency's priorities amid a proposed DICT budget reduction.
topics.agency_position: DICT said the program had about 10370000 unique users across 11836 locations and 29091 operational access points, with 99.39 percent of DepEd schools connected as of August 31. It maintained that the requested Free Wi-Fi funding would sustain existing sites, while additional sites and reliable connectivity would require further projects, efficiency gains, and coordination with other programs; it also said monitoring and beneficiary-use data were part of performance assessment.
topics.outcome: DICT provided current user, location, access-point, school, barangay hall, and LGU figures, but did not provide the inactive-site percentage during the exchange. The committee required additional submissions, including site lists, inactive-site data, ASEAN comparisons, and wish lists; the proposed budget augmentation was left for later consideration.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Renee Co asked whether the reported target of 10200000 individual beneficiaries for 20 26 and 4500000 users for 20 27 was correct, noting that the prior target had been 15800000 individual beneficiaries set in 20 25.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The agency reported about 10370000 unique users as of August 31, covering 11836 locations and 29091 operational access points. The locations included schools, markets, tourist spots, public places, barangay halls, and public plazas.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked whether the program's characterization of unique users as beneficiaries was correct.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The assistant secretary confirmed that the users were being treated as beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked how the program would operationalize the target of 15000000 or 15800000 beneficiaries and whether it would simply add access points and users.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The agency said it aimed to reach 15000000 unique users by the end of the year through projects in the pipeline that were nearing post-qualification and award. Additional access points would be deployed in public markets, tourist spots, schools, and regional rural health units.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked whether the 15800000 target beneficiaries would be maintained for the year.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The assistant secretary answered yes.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co requested progress on the statutory connectivity requirement for public basic education institutions and state universities and colleges.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: As of August 31, 99.39 percent of DepEd schools were connected, based on 45328 schools. The agency was implementing a first phase to connect 220 state universities and colleges nationwide and said the balance would be connected the following year.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co requested a list of schools, SUCs, priority markets, public areas, and the target of 15000000 beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The assistant secretary said the agency would comply.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked whether the Free Wi-Fi request was still 5000000000 and whether it represented 3 percent of the BSF.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The agency said the request for free Wi-Fi was about 5 5000000000 pesos from the SUF.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked whether the request differed from the prior year's 7500000000 request for the Free Public Internet Access Act.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The agency said 5000000000 would sustain existing locations, but adding locations and reliable school connectivity would require synergy with other programs. It said every added Free Public Wi-Fi budget would contribute to last-mile connectivity.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Rep. Momo noted that the program received 5000000000 in 20 26 while reporting 29091 active access points in 11836 locations. Citing COA findings on signage, connection instructions, awareness, inoperative sites, limited hours, speed, reliability, and delayed complaint resolution, he asked how many deficient or inauthentic sites had already been connected.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The agency reiterated that it covered 11836 locations with about 29091 access points and said it used a network monitoring system. Offline sites were referred to providers for resolution or reconnection within 72 hours; the agency acknowledged room for improvement and said missing signages had been addressed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Rep. Momo asked what percentage of the 11836 locations was inactive as of the hearing.

thread.speaker: DICT assistant secretary Chris
thread.said: The agency said it would check the figure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Rep. Momo asked whether the program's performance indicator was the number of sites established or actual usage, speed, reliability, and citizen satisfaction.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Ivan Uy
thread.said: Secretary Ivan Uy said all of those indicators mattered, emphasizing citizen benefit. He said the agency had statistics on usage and bandwidth and that the service had to redound to beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Rep. Momo asked that the number of inactive sites be submitted to the committee.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair directed the agency to submit the requested information to plenary.

thread.speaker: Rep. Elmer Catulpos
thread.said: Rep. Catulpos asked about Free Wi-Fi coverage in public schools and public places, specifically barangay halls, and asked for the 20 27 site count.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The agency said it prioritized DepEd schools, followed by SUCs, and was connecting tourist areas, public markets, and health services.

thread.speaker: Rep. Elmer Catulpos
thread.said: Rep. Catulpos specifically asked whether barangay halls were included.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The agency clarified that community centers, including barangay halls, were included.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The agency reported that the universe of barangay halls was 42208, of which 1726 were currently enjoying Free Wi-Fi. It also reported 4000 LGUs, with 766 having operational Free Wi-Fi.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The agency said the 20 26 Free Wi-Fi budget was 5000000000 pesos and that retaining the same amount for 20 27 would be enough to sustain sites, while additional sites could result from efficiency gains upon renewal. It undertook to submit the site list.

thread.speaker: Rep. Elmer Catulpos
thread.said: Rep. Catulpos requested the site-count list for 20 27.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair directed the agency to submit the requested list to the committee.

thread.speaker: Chair

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair cited the reported spending of 22.4 pesos per unique beneficiary per month, describing the comparison as relevant to defending the Free Wi-Fi budget and assessing investment in citizens.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez praised the program's reported accomplishments, said all public schools in his area had been connected and 80 percent of barangay halls had been connected, and asked why DICT's budget had been reduced despite those achievements.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez cited a decrease of hundred 33000000 and a reduction of 1100000000 from a proposal of 1800000000 for capacity building and related items. He asked for DICT's priority wish list.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda

topics.topic: School and regional connectivity targets, including SUCs and disadvantaged areas
topics.summary: The chair required DICT to show that reported connectivity translated into reliable, usable, and affordable service, particularly in schools and disadvantaged communities. DICT reported about 10370000 free Wi-Fi beneficiaries, 11836 locations, 2 29091 access points, and 99.39 percent connectivity across 45328 DepEd schools, while saying it initially targeted 220 SUCs and would connect the balance later. Representative Renee Co questioned inconsistent free Wi-Fi targets and the about 5 5000000000 pesos SUF request, and DICT said additional deployments would support a 15000000-user goal. Representative Roberto Nazal challenged the meaning of school coverage, and DICT did not establish that all schools had full-school usable connectivity. Representative Pagianos requested regional targets because household access ranged from 68.7 percent in NCR to 21.2 percent in the Zamboanga Peninsula, while the agency promised a detailed submission. Secretary Aguda reported a 92.5 percent reduction in cost per gigabyte, from 149 to 11.19, and the committee said it would assess the broader price-reduction commitment through 2028. The hearing landed on agency commitments and document requests, with key school, SUC, regional, and disaster-resilience measures still requiring verification.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT's 2027 connectivity targets represented reliable, usable, affordable service on the ground, particularly in DepEd schools, SUCs, regions, rural and geographically disadvantaged areas. Members also asked for verifiable regional targets, broadband-price reductions, disaster-resilient links, and the funding and implementation needed to meet those targets.
topics.agency_position: DICT maintained that connectivity was expanding and becoming more affordable through free public Wi-Fi, infrastructure sharing, competition, the National Fiber Backbone, and satellite and fiber deployments. It reported 99.39 percent DepEd school connectivity, planned to reach 100 percent, was connecting 220 SUCs initially, and committed to submit school, SUC, regional, and project lists; however, it did not provide all requested regional targets or a definitive current SUC percentage.
topics.outcome: DICT provided national connectivity and free Wi-Fi figures and undertook to submit school, SUC, regional, and project-level documentation. The committee did not receive during the hearing a definitive SUC coverage percentage, full-school usability breakdown, or complete regional 2027 targets, leaving verification and affordability outcomes open.

positions.position: Connectivity should be judged by reliable, usable, sufficient, and affordable service on the ground rather than by reported sites or nominal coverage.
Free public Wi-Fi targets, school and SUC coverage, access-point deployment, and funding needed to be reconciled and documented.
DICT's 100-percent DepEd coverage claim required a precise definition and a school-by-school breakdown distinguishing full usable connectivity from limited hotspots or SIM-based service.
National connectivity averages concealed major regional disparities, and DICT needed measurable regional household, speed, reliability, latency, and price outcomes.
DICT's broadband price-reduction commitments through 2028 should be monitored against actual delivery.
DICT needed to demonstrate that provincial and regional connectivity reports were independently and consistently validated.
Connectivity programs had to distinguish installed access points from sustainable, operational, disaster-resilient Internet service in remote communities and schools.
South Cotabato and other Region 12 areas needed to be specifically identified in the National Broadband Program and related project lists.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the committee would examine not only reported connected sites, access points, fiber kilometers, and institutions, but whether people actually received reliable, usable, and affordable Internet. He emphasized that school connectivity had to work throughout the school day and support teachers, students, digital learning, and government systems.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Secretary Aguda said DICT's 2027 framework called for inclusive technology, reliable and affordable connectivity, and digital infrastructure closer to communities, especially in geographically disadvantaged areas.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Herzon Asidao
thread.said: Undersecretary Asidao reported that telecommunications towers had increased from close to 18000 in 2020 to about 35000 in 2023, while connected Filipinos increased from 77000000 in July 2022 to about 99000000 by June 2026.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Herzon Asidao
thread.said: He reported that mobile download speeds had more than doubled since 2022 and that Internet use had increased to about 67 percent in 2024. Households with Internet access had increased from 17.7 percent to about 48.8 percent.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Herzon Asidao
thread.said: DICT reported up to 70 percent cost efficiencies in its free public Internet program, about 10370000 unique beneficiaries, 1 27490000 user sessions, and an estimated cost of about 22.4 pesos per unique beneficiary per month, with expansion focused particularly on geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas.

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Co
thread.said: Representative Co asked DICT to reconcile the free public Internet targets: 10200000 individual beneficiaries for 2026, 4500000 users for 2027, and the previously cited 15800000 target set in 2025. She asked for progress and the basis for the target.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT reported about 10370000 unique users as of August 31, covering 11836 locations and 2 29091 operational access points. The locations included schools, markets, tourist spots, public places, barangay halls, and plazas.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: The official said DICT aimed to reach 15000000 unique users by year-end through projects nearing post-qualification and award, with additional access points in public markets, tourist spots, schools, and regional rural health units.

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Co
thread.said: Representative Co asked whether the 15800000 target would be maintained and requested the progress of coverage for public educational institutions and SUCs, as required under the law.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT said the 15800000 target would be maintained. For DepEd schools, it reported 99.39 percent connectivity as of August 31 out of 45328 schools, while a free Wi-Fi project was connecting 220 SUCs in phase one and would connect the balance the following year.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: In response to Representative Co's request for a list of schools, SUCs, priority markets, and public areas, DICT said, "we will comply."

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Co
thread.said: Representative Co asked whether the free Wi-Fi budget request remained 5000000000 and whether it represented 3 percent of the BSF.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT answered that the free Wi-Fi request was about 5 5000000000 pesos from the SUF. The official said 5000000000 would sustain existing locations, while additional locations and schools would require synergies with the National Broadband Program and other programs.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Representative Nazal challenged DICT's statement that it had covered 100 percent of target DepEd schools and asked what "covered" meant: full usable connectivity throughout a school, one Wi-Fi hotspot or access point, or SIM-based connectivity.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT clarified that the DepEd universe was 45328 schools and reported 99.39 percent at the end of August, with deployment continuing toward 100 percent. The answer did not establish that every school had full-school usable connectivity.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Representative Nazal pressed DICT to identify the breakdown of schools covered through DepEd maintenance and other operating expenses, DICT free Wi-Fi, private ISPs, and limited hotspot or SIM-based service, and asked whether the reported coverage meant three access points and a low-earth-orbit modem at every school.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT said it would submit the deployment breakdown. It described a standard template involving three access points and a low-earth-orbit dish modem for its free Wi-Fi deployments, but the transcript did not establish that this template applied to all 45328 DepEd schools.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT said initial deployment covered 4770 schools, another deployment involved 5400, and a further 4700 were then being deployed. It separately said the SUC project initially aimed to connect 220 schools, including 120 by fiber and 116 remote SUCs through available fiber or low-earth-orbit satellite; the spoken figures are internally unclear.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT said it was considering savings from renewals and synergies with other connectivity programs, particularly the National Broadband Program, to address remaining school gaps. The chair clarified that DICT was saying DepEd schools would reach 100 percent while SUCs were not yet at 100 percent.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: When asked for the current SUC percentage and a list of uncovered SUCs, DICT did not provide the percentage during the hearing and committed to submit the list. The chair said an answer was expected.

thread.speaker: Representative Elmer Catulpos
thread.said: Representative Catulpos asked about data-transmission participation and broadband implementation in Region 12 and South Cotabato, including the National Broadband Program's 2027 proposal.

thread.speaker: DICT official Pinky
thread.said: DICT said South Cotabato was part of phase 5 of the National Fiber Backbone. It said the World Bank PDIP project would cover phases 4 and 5, including the area, with implementation in 2027.

thread.speaker: Representative Elmer Catulpos
thread.said: Representative Catulpos asked whether the PDIP loan and a proposed second loan would include the requested South Cotabato program and requested a list covering Koronadal City, South Cotabato, General Santos, Tacurong, and other cities.

thread.speaker: DICT official Pinky
thread.said: DICT said the Class 3 loan would be 400000000 and would be implemented in August 2027. It agreed to provide the requested nationwide list.

thread.speaker: Representative JP Pagianos
thread.said: Representative Pagianos cited 48.8 percent household Internet access in 2024, compared with 68.7 percent in NCR, 21.2 percent in the Zamboanga Peninsula, and 27.7 percent in BARM, with 58.3 percent of households without home Internet citing high subscription cost. He asked what 2027 outcome would be produced for these families and requested regional targets covering household access, minimum speed, latency, reliability, and average retail price.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: The DICT official attributed expected improvements to the Connectadong Pinoy law, competition, additional connectivity investment, and telcos launching fiber services in the regions. The official said DICT would submit a detailed and more comprehensive regional list, but did not provide the requested 2027 regional targets during the hearing.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: A minority member cited DICT statements that Internet costs could fall by 50 percent by 2028 in underserved areas and that broadband prices could drop by 40 to 80 percent. The member asked Secretary Aguda to address the targets and their implementation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Secretary Aguda reported a 92.5 percent reduction in cost per gigabyte, from 149 to 11.19, across blended fiber, mobile, and satellite services.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The member described the price-reduction statement as an important progressive realization commitment through 2028 and said the committee would wait until 2028 to assess delivery.

thread.speaker: Representative Sergio Dagooc
thread.said: Representative Dagooc asked how DICT monitored and validated connectivity at the provincial and regional level, expressing concern that reported connectivity might not reflect actual service.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said it had validation through regional offices and regular monitoring, but the official said the specific region would have to be checked. No regional validation results were provided in the exchange.

thread.speaker: Representative Caroline Agyao
thread.said: Representative Agyao asked about emergency communications and rapid restoration in calamity-prone and geographically disadvantaged areas, including deployable satellite phones, portable cell sites, mobile command centers, radio systems, and emergency Wi-Fi. She also asked how quickly assets could be activated, how many sites were operational and reliably connected, maintenance cost per site, and how many communities without commercial signal could realistically be connected in 2027.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT said disaster-resiliency measures included satellite services, cell sites, generators, and other providers. It reported 24 disaster emergency communication facilities for the current year and 12 for the following year, while several other spoken figures about availability and coverage were unclear.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT said it was lengthening contract durations to improve restoration and reduce rates, with procurement expected to be expedited. For managed services, the official cited a 72-hour requirement to repair or restore connectivity in an affected area.

thread.speaker: DICT official Chris
thread.said: DICT said remote areas were a priority and described a nationwide project covering 5400 plus schools to gain economies of scale. It also said low-earth-orbit satellite service, including Starlink, and solar power would support resilient connectivity in disaster-affected schools, including island and floating schools.

topics.topic: National Broadband Program and Philippine Digital Infrastructure Project delays
topics.summary: Rep. Elmer Catulpos asked about the National Broadband Program proposal of about 113 billion and its coverage of South Cotabato and nearby cities. DICT said the National Fiber Backbone was still being built and that the World Bank-funded PDIP would cover phases 4 and 5, with a stated loan figure of 400000000 and implementation in August 20 27. Catulpos requested a complete list of covered locations, and the chair directed DICT to submit it. Rep. Iris Marie Montes questioned DICT's utilization, citing 87 percent for 20 24 and 9 percent for the first semester of 20 26, while DICT attributed the figures partly to procurement timing and denominator issues. DICT acknowledged two failed biddings caused by difficulties matching World Bank rules with local bidders, but said it was working with the World Bank to recognize local bidders and expected sharing to rise from 0.54 percent to 80 percent by December. The agency said the project was originally scheduled through 20 28 but was delayed by 6 months, leaving document and procurement follow-up commitments outstanding.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status, funding, coverage, procurement problems, and implementation timetable of the National Broadband Program and the World Bank-funded Philippine Digital Infrastructure Project (PDIP), including its intended coverage of South Cotabato and other areas. Members also questioned DICT's budget utilization and whether procurement delays would affect delivery of the infrastructure.
topics.agency_position: DICT said the National Broadband Program and PDIP were advancing the National Fiber Backbone, with PDIP intended to cover phases 4 and 5 in the Visayas and Mindanao, including the area identified by the member as South Cotabato. The agency attributed the delay to unfamiliar World Bank procurement rules and mismatches with local bidders, but said it had reached an arrangement to recognize local bidders, projected increased budget sharing through December, and expected implementation to proceed six months behind the original schedule.

topics.topic: Government data centers, cloud subscriptions, and data sovereignty
topics.summary: Members questioned DICT about the location and security of government data, the use of foreign cloud services, and the adequacy of domestic data-center capacity. DICT said about 80 percent of government data was outside the Philippines and that some eGov storage was in Singapore and the United States, while its first Subic facility held only about 60 racks. DICT estimated that complete sovereign data-center infrastructure would cost around 20 billion, with a return on investment in about 4 to 5 years, and said unified data management could yield roughly 50 to 60 percent savings. Officials said cloud subscriptions were procured through competitive bidding, eGov used AWS for about 80 percent of its public-cloud service, and migration would occur gradually. The department also said eGov was government-owned, its source code was maintained by DICT, and underlying data remained decentralized with the responsible agencies. DICT committed to issue EO 119 guidelines, develop government-wide data standards, convene an oversight committee, and submit procurement and infrastructure information, but no firm localization timetable was established.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish where government data was stored, how data sovereignty and localization would be implemented, and whether DICT had sufficient domestic data-center capacity. Members also asked about the cost of foreign cloud subscriptions, the proposed cost and savings from sovereign data centers, procurement safeguards, cybersecurity, and the timetable for moving critical government workloads locally.
topics.agency_position: DICT said EO 119 would establish a risk-based classification and residency framework under which top-secret and other sensitive national-security data would remain in the Philippines, while lower-classified data could be contracted out within Philippine jurisdiction. DICT acknowledged substantial reliance on foreign cloud services but said it was building domestic capacity, reducing duplicated data, using encryption and decentralized agency control, and gradually migrating workloads to locally owned and managed sovereign data centers.
topics.outcome: DICT acknowledged that much government and eGov data remained on foreign public-cloud infrastructure, while presenting domestic sovereign data centers as the long-term solution. The department committed to issue EO 119 guidelines, develop standards, provide procurement information, and progressively migrate data, but the hearing did not settle the precise 2027 infrastructure requirement or a firm timetable for full localization.

topics.topic: Cybersecurity program funding and protection of government systems
topics.summary: The Chair framed cybersecurity as a national-security responsibility and asked whether the proposed program would measurably protect government systems, critical infrastructure, and Filipino data. DICT reported NSOC monitoring of 99 agencies and about 6.7 billion security alerts, while proposing expanded VAPT, private-sector certification, professional registration, and cybersecurity laboratories. Rep. Presley de Jesus questioned overseas cloud storage, data-center capacity, encryption, and control of eGov data; DICT said data was decentralized, used double-layered encryption, and could be localized through a projected investment of about 20 billion with estimated savings of 50 to 60 percent. Rep. JP Pagianos asked what protection would result from the 1094000000 cybersecurity program after reported website compromises and an eGov disruption; DICT answered that the budget covered currently protected agencies but not the whole country or all critical infrastructure. DICT and CICC said they were investigating a reported Department of Labor portal incident, while the NPC described expanded breach monitoring and faster registration validation. The committee received commitments for reports, targets, procurement records, case figures, and regional validation, so the issue was not fully resolved during the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT's cybersecurity program would provide measurable protection for government systems, critical infrastructure, and Filipino data, especially after reported government-portal compromises. It also examined whether data localization, cloud arrangements, privacy enforcement, and agency responsibilities were sufficient to reduce cyber risks.
topics.agency_position: DICT said its cybersecurity approach combined NSOC monitoring, encryption, decentralized data custody, agency assistance and training, VAPT, private-sector certification, professional registration, and proactive breach monitoring. It acknowledged that the proposed cybersecurity budget was sufficient for agencies currently covered but insufficient to protect the entire country and all critical infrastructure, and it said data localization and consolidation could reduce costs and duplication.
topics.outcome: DICT presented existing cyber-monitoring, encryption, training, VAPT, and privacy-monitoring measures, but acknowledged that the proposed cybersecurity funding would not protect the whole country or all critical infrastructure. Several measurable targets and documents, including cybersecurity outcomes, procurement records, eGov usage data, case figures, and regional validation, were left for submission or follow-up.

positions.position: Cybersecurity was a national-security responsibility, and the budget had to demonstrate real protection of government systems, critical infrastructure, and Filipino data.

thread.said: The official said about 80 percent of government data was not stored in the Philippines and that the policy sought to localize data and eliminate duplication across agencies, which was making data maintenance expensive.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Rep. Dino cited the historical and proposed data-center infrastructure budgets and asked DICT to explain why the proposed amount consisted largely of maintenance and other operating expenses.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said the budget was connected to building the first data center in Subic and that about 700000000 had been spent there.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Rep. Dino asked how cloud services were selected and whether procurement used competitive or negotiated bidding.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official answered that the services were procured through competitive bidding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Rep. Dino requested information on the data-center infrastructure budget from 20 16 to 26, including procurement details and applicable standards.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official agreed to provide the requested information to the committee.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said some data centers were on premises, while some eGov app and cloud storage was located in Singapore and the United States.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said the first DICT data center in Subic could hold around 60 racks and would initially be sufficient for archiving.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said DICT had a study indicating that around 20000000000 would be needed to build government data-sovereignty data centers, with an estimated return on investment of around 4 to 5 years.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: Rep. de Jesus asked how much the government currently paid for foreign cloud services.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said the total cloud-subscription request was 30 to 40000000000.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official estimated that unified data management could produce around 50 to 60 percent savings by reducing duplicated data.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: Rep. de Jesus pressed DICT on the safety of its storage facilities and documents against hackers, noting that DICT held highly sensitive information.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said eGov used a double-layered encryption model and expressed confidence that it would prevent hacking. The official added that data remained decentralized among government agencies rather than being held entirely by DICT.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said a single-source-of-truth model would reduce duplication, citing 92000000 digital national IDs and 48000000 e-signatures as data that should not be repeatedly captured by different agencies.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: Rep. de Jesus asked how DICT could assure the committee that a centralized eGov platform and source code would be protected against sabotage and hacking.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official distinguished the source code, which DICT maintained, from the data, which stayed with individual agencies. DICT's cybersecurity bureau provided training and assistance to those agencies.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: Rep. de Jesus said the committee should examine the arrangement seriously, but stated that he supported the DICT budget.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Rep. Pagianos cited 19 government websites reportedly compromised in September 20 25 and a 2 day eGov PH disruption in April 20 26, then asked what measurable protection Congress would receive from the 1094000000 cybersecurity program.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT said cybersecurity was urgent and described recent agency attacks, including defacement and the Marina ransomware incident. It said the proposed program would expand private-sector cybersecurity capacity, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, professional certification, and proactive monitoring.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: The official said DICT had certified 43 private-sector cybersecurity providers and that combining them with DICT capacity could raise vulnerability-assessment and penetration-testing output to 3000 to 4000.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT said the budget was enough to protect the agencies currently covered, but not enough to protect the whole country or all critical infrastructure, including power and banking, much of which was privately operated.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT identified targets of registering 100000 cybersecurity professionals next year, expanding the current 5 to 10000 professional program, certifying 100 VAPT providers, and establishing 3 private cybersecurity laboratories.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Rep. Pagianos asked whether DICT had resolved the reported hacking of a Department of Labor client portal used for permits, certifications, and regulatory submissions.

thread.speaker: Director Rodil
thread.said: Director Rodil said the incident had been reported the previous night and involved a subdomain not under DICT's control. DICT coordinated a takedown, while its team and CICC were investigating and working to determine whether data had been exfiltrated.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Rep. Pagianos questioned the NPC's increased proposed spending despite lower listed performance targets, including fewer compliance checks and a lower complaint-resolution target.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC said it was not promising less because the 20 26 and 20 27 net targets were actually the same. The additional budget would expand eSprint monitoring from 20 websites to 50, improve personal-information-controller registration, and reduce validation time from around 7 days to 3 days or, where possible, 1 day.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: On online-lending complaints, the NPC said it had issued a joint advisory with the SEC and DICT on borrowers' data rights and lenders' obligations. It could provide the committee with the specific number of cases filed from 20 24 to 20 26.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Rep. Pagianos expressed full support for the DICT budget and additional requests, while stressing that support had to be matched by measurable cybersecurity results, completed transactions, affordable connectivity, and accountability.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: In response to a question on NGCP, Secretary Aguda said that, because NGCP was critical infrastructure, DICT's cyber bureau could participate in efforts to secure it.

thread.speaker: DICT undersecretary for support services
thread.said: The official said the Data Privacy Act covered NGCP employee or customer personal information, but nonpersonal operational data such as power-outage statistics was outside the NPC's privacy mandate. The official added that the national government should have visibility over data held by its concessionaires.

thread.speaker: DICT regional official
thread.said: The regional official said DICT had validation through regional offices but would have to check the specific region and provide further confirmation.

topics.topic: eGov PH sustainability, operating costs, personnel, and service continuity
topics.summary: DICT presented eGov as a widely used, government-owned platform with about 61 million downloads, 56 million verified users, more than 1.2 billion eGovDX transactions, and 1,332 integrated services. The chair and Representative Richard Gomez asked whether the in-house system could survive changes in administration; DICT said continuity was assured but that low government salaries threatened staffing and that a Magna Carta for IT professionals was needed. Members also challenged DICT over unobligated funds, payables, an outage attributed to an unexpected surge in usage, and the lack of precise information on unpaid providers. DICT said local data sovereignty would require about 20 billion, while unified data management could produce roughly 50 to 60 percent savings against cloud costs of 30 to 40 billion. The agency reported that eGov data were decentralized, encrypted, and integrated through eGovDX, although much cloud storage remained in Singapore and AWS accounted for about 80 percent of eGov cloud services. Members requested written reports on usage, connectivity, payables, school and SUC coverage, regional targets, and data infrastructure, while DICT committed to additional legislative, standards, cybersecurity, and digital nomad visa work.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT's in-house eGov platform could remain operational across administrations, whether it had sufficient personnel and funding, and whether its usage, cloud arrangements, cybersecurity, and data infrastructure were sustainable. Members also asked what measurable connectivity and digital-service outcomes would result from the FY 2027 budget.
topics.agency_position: DICT maintained that eGov was a government-owned, in-house platform with guaranteed institutional continuity, but said sustained operations depended on adequate funding and competitive compensation for IT personnel. It supported moving toward sovereign local data infrastructure, standardized and decentralized data exchange, stronger cybersecurity capacity, and continued congressional support, while acknowledging that several requested lists, targets, cost reconciliations, and timelines remained to be submitted.
topics.outcome: The committee received DICT's assurance that eGov was government-owned, in-house, and capable of administrative continuity, but accepted that staffing, compensation, cloud costs, and service-continuity funding required further action. Multiple written submissions and legislative follow-up were requested; the precise unpaid obligations, SUC coverage, end-to-end usage, regional targets, local-data migration cost and timeline, and full budget reconciliation remained open.

positions.position: Supported continuity of eGov but pressed DICT to clarify whether staffing and funding would permit the platform to survive changes in administration.
Supported institutionalizing IT personnel compensation and said he would file legislation addressing DICT's request, including a Magna Carta for IT professionals.
Demanded explanations and written documentation on unobligated funds, payables, project delays, and the actual meaning of DepEd school connectivity coverage.

Supported DICT's budget but insisted that digitalization funds produce reliable services, timely payments, lower recurring costs, local data infrastructure, and stronger protection against outages and hacking.
Pressed DICT for region-specific connectivity outcomes, meaningful eGov usage statistics beyond downloads, reconciliation of eGov funding requests, and measurable cybersecurity results.
Supported DICT's work while seeking government-wide data standards, a costed assessment of Cadena, transparent eGov ownership and usage data, and sovereign local data centers.

thread.speaker: Herzon Asidao, DICT undersecretary for support services
thread.said: He reported that the eGov Super App had 61000000 plus downloads, more than 56000000 verified accounts, over 1200000000 eGovDX transactions, and 1332 integrated government e-services. He also cited more than 92000000 digital national IDs and over 300000000 digital ID transactions.

thread.speaker: Herzon Asidao, DICT undersecretary for support services
thread.said: He presented DICT and its attached agencies' proposed FY 2027 budget of 19491000000, including 1692000000 for personal services, 13900000000 for maintenance and other operating expenses, and 3892000000 for capital outlay.

thread.speaker: Appropriations chair
thread.said: The chair noted the eGov figures and asked what would happen when current officials were no longer in office, specifically whether the in-house platform created a continuity problem because it had no contractors.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: The official confirmed that eGov was developed in-house without contractors. He said sustainability required congressional help, particularly because government salaries were too low to attract and retain programmers compared with the private sector.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: He said the eGovernment Act created an office under DICT to sustain the platform and included a Magna Carta provision intended to improve IT salaries, although government pay remained below private-sector compensation.

thread.speaker: Appropriations chair
thread.said: The chair sought clarification on whether there was a guarantee that eGov could transition from administration to administration, apart from questions about the number of personnel and funding.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: The official answered yes, indicating that continuity was guaranteed, while personnel levels and funding remained the practical concerns.

thread.speaker: Richard Gomez, member
thread.said: Gomez asked whether eGov's sustainability required another law or an amendment so that the successful platform would continue beyond the next administration.

thread.speaker: DICT secretary or senior DICT official
thread.said: The official said the eGovernment Act already institutionalized digitalization, but sustainability was primarily a funding and personnel concern not yet fully addressed by the law. An amendment could be explored.

thread.speaker: DICT secretary or senior DICT official
thread.said: The official said developers were at salary grades 12, 15, and 17. Another DICT official said IT positions at salary grade 22 paid about 59000 to 89000 a month at the maximum, while most programmers at salary grades 19 and 20 received around 50 to 60000 only.

thread.speaker: Richard Gomez, member
thread.said: Gomez asked for the key purpose of the eGovernment Act, identified in the transcript as RA 1 2 2 5 4.

thread.speaker: DICT secretary or senior DICT official
thread.said: The official said the law institutionalized government digitalization, enabled DICT to pursue proprietary functions and raise revenue, and harmonized IT investments across government.

thread.speaker: Richard Gomez, member
thread.said: Gomez said the committee should institutionalize the salary grade of IT workers in DICT.

thread.speaker: DICT secretary or senior DICT official
thread.said: The official appealed to Congress to prioritize a Magna Carta for IT professionals, saying it would help DICT retain IT talent in the country.

thread.speaker: Richard Gomez, member
thread.said: Gomez said he would file a bill addressing DICT's request, and the chair said the committee would support and potentially coauthor it.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., member
thread.said: Nazal said DICT and its attached agencies had 22519000000 in allotments as of June 30 but only 2000000000 obligated, or around 9 percent. He asked for the three largest projects behind the 20500000000 unobligated balance, the amount unpaid or overdue, and the amount DICT would obligate and pay by year-end.

thread.speaker: Herzon Asidao, DICT head of support and finance
thread.said: Asidao said DICT's reported budget utilization rate was 24 percent as of June, compared with the 9 percent figure reported to Congress, and that DICT would reconcile the figures with COA. He said 89 percent of downloaded funds had been spent or released, while significant payables related to prior years remained.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., member
thread.said: Nazal asked DICT to submit a list of payables and problematic or delayed projects, showing amounts appropriated, obligated, and disbursed, as well as the bottlenecks causing delays.

thread.speaker: Herzon Asidao, DICT head of support and finance
thread.said: Asidao agreed to submit the requested report and list, including an explanation of the implementation and funding-timing issues.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., member
thread.said: Nazal asked what DICT meant when it reported 100 percent coverage of DepEd schools: full usable connectivity, one hotspot or access point, or SIM-based connectivity.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for school connectivity
thread.said: The official said the DepEd universe consisted of 45328 schools and that coverage was 99.39 percent at the end of August, with deployment continuing toward 100 percent through different connectivity arrangements.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., member
thread.said: Nazal questioned whether the reported coverage meant that all 45000-plus schools had the same three-access-point, low-Earth-orbit dish and modem configuration. DICT indicated that coverage involved a mix of DepEd, private ISP, and DICT Free Wi-Fi arrangements.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for school connectivity
thread.said: The official cited an initial deployment to 4770 schools, another deployment of 5400, and a current deployment of 4700, using the stated connectivity template.

thread.speaker: Appropriations chair
thread.said: The chair asked what percentage of state universities and colleges was currently connected, after distinguishing the DepEd target from the not-yet-fully-covered SUC program.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT did not provide the SUC percentage during the exchange and agreed to submit the list and answer. The chair said an answer was expected.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The member asked about the reported eGov outage lasting several hours because of nonpayment: what was unpaid, how much was owed, to whom, and why payment was delayed.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall attributed the incident primarily to an unexpected surge in use, described in the transcript as a 700 times percent increase over 1.1 and a half years. He said DICT had expected 30000000 downloads in 2028, but reached 61000000 in 2026, while the digital national ID and integration of about 1300 government systems also increased demand.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: As a short-term measure, DICT disabled eGov's backup and used it as the primary server operation. He also cited a 2025 e-government budget and later funding releases for digital national ID and eGov sustainability.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The member asked whether the relevant funding came from the special purpose fund and pressed DICT on the source of the money used to sustain eGov.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall said DBM had released a budget for eGov sustainability, that DICT would begin the bidding process, and that the incident was considered isolated but required a sustainability budget in the following year.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The member asked DICT to identify unpaid or overdue cloud, hosting, internet, software, and managed-service providers, including an aging of the obligations.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall agreed to submit the requested list of unpaid providers and overdue obligations.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The member asked what DICT needed to bring more government data infrastructure into the Philippines, how much it would cost, whether it was included in the FY 2027 proposal, and the timeline for moving critical data and workloads locally.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: The official said DICT would convene a joint oversight committee and an interagency process on data classification and data residency under EO 1 1 9. The resulting data and numbers would inform the transition of national government agencies to local capacity.

thread.speaker: Presley de Jesus, member
thread.said: De Jesus asked whether government data, including eGov data, was stored outside the country and recalled DICT's earlier commitment to build local storage facilities.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said it had on-premises data centers, but some eGov and other cloud storage was in Singapore and the United States. It said the first DICT data center in Subic could hold around 60 racks and was sufficient for archiving.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall said a study estimated approximately 20000000000 to build a government data-sovereignty data center, with an estimated ROI of around 4 to 5 years. He said localizing data would reduce reliance on foreign cloud services.

thread.speaker: Presley de Jesus, member
thread.said: De Jesus asked how much government currently paid for foreign cloud services.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall said the total cloud-subscription request was 30 to 40000000000. He estimated that unified data management could generate around 50 to 60 percent savings.

thread.speaker: Presley de Jesus, member
thread.said: De Jesus asked how secure the storage facilities and government documents were against hackers.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall said eGov used a double-layered encryption model. He explained that the data remained decentralized with the responsible agencies rather than being held by DICT, while eGovDX provided an integration and data-exchange platform.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: The official said the system had 92000000 digital national IDs and 48000000 eSignatures, and that using existing national-ID data could reduce duplicate data collection across agencies.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: He said eGovDX connected about 1300 government systems while the underlying data stayed with agencies such as PSA and PhilHealth. The cybersecurity bureau was responsible for training and assisting agencies in protecting their own data.

thread.speaker: JP Pagianos, member
thread.said: Pagianos cited household Internet access of 48.8 percent nationally, 68.7 percent in NCR, 21.2 percent in the Zamboanga Peninsula, and 27.7 percent in BARM, with 58.3 percent of unconnected households citing subscription cost. He asked for specific FY 2027 regional targets covering household access, speed, latency, reliability, and retail price.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: The official attributed improved connectivity pressure partly to the Connectadong Pinoy framework and said DICT would submit a detailed and more comprehensive regional list and report for FY 2027.

thread.speaker: JP Pagianos, member
thread.said: Pagianos asked DICT to distinguish downloads and API calls from completed transactions, and requested unique active users, end-to-end completions, monthly active users, logins, document views, and completed transactions.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: The official said eGov had 56000000 unique verified Filipinos out of 61000000 downloads and agreed to provide monthly end-to-end service data.

thread.speaker: JP Pagianos, member
thread.said: Pagianos asked DICT to reconcile the publicly announced 2700000000 e-government request, including 800000000 for the Super App, with the precise net programs and objects of expenditure.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for the eGov program
thread.said: The official said the 2700000000 request was associated with the new eGovernment law, but DBM provided only 1.8.

thread.speaker: JP Pagianos, member
thread.said: Pagianos asked what measurable protection Congress would receive from the 1094000000 cybersecurity program after reported compromises of government websites and a two-day eGov disruption in April 2026.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: The official said DICT was expanding cybersecurity monitoring, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, private-sector certification, and professional registration. He said the budget was sufficient for agencies currently protected but not for the whole country or all critical infrastructure.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: The official cited 43 certified private-sector cybersecurity providers, compared with only a few hundred assessments previously, and said the combined capacity could reach 3000 to 4000 VAPT engagements.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT said it was targeting 100000 cybersecurity professionals next year, compared with 5 to 10000 in the current program, 100 VAPT-certified providers, and 3 private cybersecurity laboratories.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez, member
thread.said: Benitez asked whether the government had comprehensive data standards under EO 1 1 9, beyond DBM's existing identifiers and codes.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said an interagency technical working group would begin meeting that week and would craft government-wide data standards, with a formal convening planned by the following week.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez, member
thread.said: Benitez asked whether the proposed Cadena blockchain system was feasible for government and how much it would cost.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said Cadena was feasible, but the cost depended on whether the legislature chose a public or private chain and how broadly it was implemented. The official said it would be worth the cost if it achieved greater transparency.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez, member
thread.said: Benitez asked whether Cadena would solve corruption and whether a minimal-budget version could be pursued.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said Cadena would be a tool to curb corruption and increase transparency, not a complete solution. Uploading an already published budget to a public chain could be done for free, but an end-to-end system from the NEP to expenditure would require substantial work.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez, member
thread.said: Benitez asked who owned eGov and its source code, how many monthly active users it had, how much it cost per user or transaction, how it was funded, and whether private contractors were involved.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said ownership was with the government and that DICT was the custodian and owner of the source code. The platform was developed internally without contractors.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall said eGov had 61000000 downloads and 56000000 unique users, with average daily downloads of about 70000 to 100000 and approximately 3000000 monthly downloads.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: He estimated the current budget impact at around 9 pesos per user. He said DICT had more than 30 programmers working on the platform and paid for staff, storage, cloud, cybersecurity, and other non-development expenses.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez, member
thread.said: Benitez asked where eGov's cloud was stored and whether DICT supported sovereign data centers in the Philippines.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall, DICT official
thread.said: Almirall said eGov was stored in Singapore through public cloud services, using AWS for about 80 percent, with other services in Google Cloud and existing colocation facilities. He agreed that locally owned and managed sovereign data centers were the ideal arrangement.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez, member
thread.said: Benitez asked for the status of the digital nomad visa.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official
thread.said: DICT said the digital nomad visa remained in the planning and consultation stage, with work involving the Department of Foreign Affairs and the cybersecurity bureau. DICT would provide an update once it had a timeline.

topics.topic: National ID integration, social-media registration, and online age verification
topics.summary: Minority members Renee Co and Antonio Tinio questioned whether national-ID-based social-media registration would be effective, privacy-protective, and compatible with rights, particularly after DICT and NTC acknowledged limits in SIM registration. DICT said the national ID could provide a stronger identity and age-verification record, with Roblox targeted for compliance by October and Meta engagement continuing before the end of the year. Members also pressed DICT and NTC on fake IDs, scam complaints, the number of acceptable IDs, and the proposed reduction from 17 IDs to 3. The NPC and DICT acknowledged unresolved risks involving data minimization, surveillance, data sovereignty, and access to government databases. DICT linked the issue to data localization, citing about 92 million digital national IDs, an estimated 20 billion data-center requirement, potential savings of 50 to 60 percent, and continuing reliance on foreign cloud services during migration. The committee obtained commitments for a position paper, procurement and budget information, implementing guidelines, technical standards, an online-gaming age-verification standard, and continued consultation, but the broader policy remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT could technically and legally integrate the national ID into social-media, SIM, and online-gaming age and identity verification, and whether such integration would be effective, privacy-protective, and enforceable. Members also examined the related use of national ID and government data systems, data sovereignty, cloud storage, and cybersecurity.
topics.agency_position: DICT supported using the national ID as a higher-confidence source for identity and age verification, potentially linked through PSA systems and APIs while limiting the information disclosed to platforms. DICT said implementation remained technically and legally complex, required public consultation, stronger platform compliance, data-minimization safeguards, data localization, interoperable standards, and cybersecurity controls. It undertook to develop standards, submit position papers and procurement information, recommend online-gaming age-verification standards, and pursue migration toward Philippine data centers.
topics.outcome: DICT answered the technical and policy questions but did not establish that social-media registration or national-ID integration had been fully implemented, tested, or accepted by all stakeholders. The matter remained subject to public consultation, platform compliance, proposed SIM-registration amendments, technical standards, implementing guidelines, and multiple promised submissions.

positions.position: Questioned whether social-media registration would be effective after SIM registration had failed to prevent scams and raised concerns about rights, privacy, and implementation.
Supported stronger enforcement against Meta and Roblox, a Philippine jurisdictional presence, national-ID age verification, and child-safety measures.
Argued that DICT should take a firmer position toward Meta because of its large Philippine user base and influence over children and political discourse.
Pressed for concrete action against SIM-registration scams and for stronger controls on the IDs and SIMs that could be used.
Raised unresolved concerns about national-ID access, privacy, surveillance, and the sovereignty implications of integrating the ID with social-media platforms.
Sought assurance that government data would remain sovereign and requested scrutiny of data-center spending, procurement, and security standards.
Sought a national standard for online-gaming age verification and clarification of Smart City funding.
Supported DICT funding but demanded stronger assurance that decentralized government data and eGov systems would be protected from hacking.
Supported DICT's digital infrastructure work while pressing for common government data standards, transparent digital systems, and sovereign data storage.
