thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: Renee Co asked for DICT's specific plan or implementation phasing for social-media registration, citing school violence, online communications, and rights groups' concerns.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda described a Singapore meeting involving Meta, Roblox, the National Privacy Commission, NTC, CICC, NBI, and DepEd. He said the discussion covered identity verification using the national ID and the technical and policy issues involved.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Roblox's principal problem was age verification. Facial-recognition software could identify age only within roughly plus or minus 1 or 2 years, while Roblox needed to distinguish users aged 9 and below, 9 to 16, and 16 and above.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: He described a possible national-ID solution using the physical or digital card, biometrics, and Philippine Statistics Authority API calls, so that Roblox could verify personal information and provide age-appropriate content without receiving unnecessary information.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said the Philippines would be the first country to integrate a sovereign national ID into a social-media platform and characterized the effort as technically complex.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: He said a technical working team would study the proposal within the next 2 weeks and that Roblox's technical and policy templates could serve as models for other social-media platforms.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: Co questioned the proposed social-media registration after the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group reportedly said SIM registration had not fulfilled its promise of ending cybercrime and SMS scams. She asked why another registration system should be expected to address trolls, fake accounts, and scams when other registration policies had not done so.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda acknowledged that SIM registration had not lived up to its full promise and that false identities and mule accounts remained problems. He said identity and age verification on social-media platforms should rely on the national ID because it offered a stronger basis for verification.

thread.speaker: a committee member
thread.said: The member said the privacy issue required further discussion and noted the current understanding that verification data would not be stored anywhere other than for government verification of the details. The member said policies still had to be worked out so that the system would not intrude on the right to privacy.

thread.speaker: Ann Matibag
thread.said: Matibag asked DICT to provide a clear timeline, mechanism, and framework for monitoring Meta's and Roblox's compliance with child-protection and age-verification requirements. She emphasized the need to establish offices or a jurisdictional presence so the platforms would follow Philippine law.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Roblox should comply no later than October. He identified five demands, including child-focused platform controls, restrictions on chats and keywords related to sexual acts, default parental controls, compliance with Philippine requirements, and age verification through the national ID.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Roblox's Philippine compliance involved about 300 people working through a Roblox partner rather than directly through Roblox.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Meta representatives were expected to meet with the technical working group, FBI, police, and other authorities. He said legislation and subpoenas could be used and that a realistic deadline would be before the end of the year.

thread.speaker: Ann Matibag
thread.said: Matibag urged DICT to secure a Philippine office or equivalent jurisdictional arrangement from Meta. She also asked how DICT coordinated with PNP, NBI, CICC, DepEd, and other agencies to respond quickly to grooming, cyberbullying, sexual exploitation, and violent online content.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said DICT had sought additional authority and referred the detailed coordination and enforcement-process question to the CICC executive director.

thread.speaker: Edi Aboy
thread.said: Aboy said the CICC executive committee, chaired by the DICT secretary and involving the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group, NBI, and DOJ, provided the coordination structure. He said the Threat Monitoring Center was operational and brought law-enforcement, partner agencies, private-sector partners, and advocacy groups together for rapid response.

thread.speaker: the chair
thread.said: The chair said DICT had been too accommodating toward Meta, noting that the Philippines was Meta's 5th-largest audience and represented 3 percent of its online population, or 1 out of every 32 users. The chair urged DICT to assert Philippine sovereignty and demand stronger protections for children and the country's political discourse.

thread.speaker: Sarah Elago
thread.said: Elago asked about NTC's response to SIM-registration-related tech scams and spoofed government messages, including fake LTO traffic-violation notices. She questioned what concrete action agencies had taken against the reported complaints.

thread.speaker: NTC Commissioner Ella
thread.said: Commissioner Ella said the reported complaint figure came from the NTC consumer hotline and did not include reports filed with CICC or other government agencies. She explained that scammers could send messages to a captured range of cellphone numbers using fake government websites and said recent operations had involved NBI, CICC, DICT, and PNP, with cases being prepared for prosecution.

thread.speaker: the chair
thread.said: The chair pressed DICT to provide the agency's position on limiting the number of acceptable IDs for SIM registration, rather than leaving the issue only to other agencies.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said linking a bank account and a SIM registration to the national ID could create a single 'golden record.' He said the SIM Registration Act currently allowed multiple IDs and SIMs, but that a proposed amendment could limit both the acceptable IDs and the number of SIMs a person could buy.

thread.speaker: the chair
thread.said: The chair requested an official DICT position paper on limiting acceptable IDs and SIM ownership.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda agreed that DICT would submit the requested position paper.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: A member asked whether DICT intended to recognize only a few government-issued IDs for SIM registration, given that many agencies issue valid IDs.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy said that, for SIM registration, DICT considered 17 IDs too many and that reducing the list to 3 could limit the use of fake IDs.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked how DICT would decide which government-issued IDs should be recognized, including a driver's license, passport, national ID, and firearms license.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy said the national ID should serve as the single record of truth for identity and that other IDs could be verified against it. He clarified that a firearms license could stand on its own, while the person's name, age, and other identity information could be checked through the national ID and PSA.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether digital verification could be completed within seconds or at least a minute, and whether that would remove the need to choose only 3 IDs.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy said digital verification could be completed in seconds. He nevertheless maintained that the problem with the 17-ID system was that many IDs had links to the national ID and could be double-checked through the PSA.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio raised concerns about access to the national ID, privacy, surveillance, and the use of social-media registration as a potential surveillance instrument.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy said the Philippine Statistics Authority was continuing to onboard people and expected national-ID registration to be completed within the next 2 years. He referred the privacy and surveillance questions to the National Privacy Commission.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC official said linking Meta verification to the national ID raised risks involving data minimization, the information disclosed to Meta, security of the government database, and government access to account-holder information. The official said these issues required extensive public consultation with public authorities, Meta, and Filipino stakeholders.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio emphasized that the proposed integration would be the first of its kind globally and raised concerns about data sovereignty.

thread.speaker: DICT Secretary Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy confirmed that, based on DICT's understanding, the Philippines would be the first country to integrate a sovereign ID into a social-media platform.

thread.speaker: DICT Undersecretary Sarah
thread.said: Undersecretary Sarah said DICT had helped develop EO 119 and was conducting roadshows to explain data sovereignty. She clarified that the policy concerned government data, not commercial private data, and said top-secret and other national-security-classified data would remain in the Philippines; lower-level data could be contracted out only within Philippine jurisdiction.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty
thread.said: The official said implementing guidelines for data sovereignty were about to be issued and would set encryption, certification, and contractor-qualification requirements.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said data sovereignty meant more than storing data in the Philippines: it also required reducing duplication and repeated copying of data among agencies. DICT said that about 80 percent of government data was not then in the Philippines and that localizing data could save resources.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Rep. Dino requested information on the national-government data-center infrastructure budget and procurement from 2016 to 2026, including whether competitive bidding was used and what standards were applied.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official agreed to provide the requested procurement and budget information. The chair emphasized that the standards applied to international companies should be no lower than those required of local providers.

thread.speaker: Jay Vergara
thread.said: Vergara asked about the Smart City program and later asked whether DICT had a national standard for age verification in online gaming, including parental controls and coordination with gaming platforms, telcos, and internet-service providers.

thread.speaker: DICT secretary or senior DICT official
thread.said: The DICT official said there was no specific Smart City execution item in the current budget and undertook to check and report the details to the committee.

thread.speaker: Jay Vergara
thread.said: After being asked to rephrase, Vergara directly asked whether DICT had a national standard for age verification in online gaming.

thread.speaker: DICT secretary or senior DICT official
thread.said: The official answered yes and said DICT would recommend a standard, with further details to be provided later.

thread.speaker: Presley de Jesus
thread.said: De Jesus asked whether government data and eGov cloud storage were located outside the country and recalled DICT's earlier commitment to build Philippine data facilities.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said DICT had on-premises facilities but that some eGov and cloud storage was in Singapore and the United States. DICT's first data center in Subic could hold about 60 racks and was initially intended mainly for archiving.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall said DICT's study estimated that building the government's data-sovereignty data-center capacity would cost around 20000000000, with an estimated return on investment in 4 to 5 years.

thread.speaker: Presley de Jesus
thread.said: De Jesus asked how much DICT currently paid for foreign cloud services.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall said the total cloud-subscription request was 30 to 40000000000, while noting that the amount was affected by duplicated and bloated data.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall said a unified data-management model could produce estimated savings of 50 to 60 percent. He said DICT would continue using foreign cloud services during migration and move most data locally over time.

thread.speaker: Presley de Jesus
thread.said: De Jesus pressed DICT on the security of its storage facilities and government documents against hackers.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall said eGov used a double-layered encryption model and expressed confidence in its security. A DICT official added that data remained distributed among government agencies rather than being held entirely by DICT.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said there were 92000000 digital national IDs containing names, pictures, and biometrics, while eGov had 48000000 electronic signatures. DICT argued that using these existing records could reduce repeated data capture.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said the eGovDX data-exchange platform connected around 1300 government systems, while the underlying records remained with agencies such as PSA and PhilHealth. DICT's role was to enable integration without duplicating the data.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official clarified that DICT held the source code but not the underlying agency data. The data remained decentralized, and the Cybersecurity Bureau trained and assisted agencies in protecting their own systems.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez
thread.said: Benitez asked whether government had a common data standard and whether EO 119 would produce unified identifiers across budgeting and disbursement systems.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said an interagency technical working group would convene by the following week, or during that week, to craft data standards under EO 119.

thread.speaker: Albee Benitez
thread.said: Benitez asked who owned eGov and its source code, how many active users it had, what it cost to operate, and where its cloud data was stored.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: DICT said ownership of eGov and custody of its source code rested with the government and DICT.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall reported 61000000 downloads and 56000000 unique users, with average daily downloads of about 70000 to 100000 and approximately 3000000 monthly downloads.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall estimated eGov's current budget impact at around 9 pesos per user.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: He said eGov was developed in-house, with more than 30 programmers, and that DICT paid for storage, cloud, cybersecurity, and other non-development expenses rather than an outside software contractor.

thread.speaker: Isaac Almirall
thread.said: Almirall said eGov data was stored in Singapore through public cloud services, with AWS accounting for about 80 percent, alongside Google Cloud and existing colocation facilities. He agreed that locally owned and managed sovereign data centers were the ideal arrangement.

topics.topic: Online scams, child safety, and technology-facilitated abuse response
topics.summary: The chair raised complaints about harmful online content, including 197 Facebook links, and directed DICT and CICC to review and report on them while asking Meta to explain its dispositions. Representative Ann Matibag pressed for timelines and mechanisms requiring Meta and Roblox to comply with Philippine law and protect children; DICT committed to Roblox compliance by October and described interagency threat-monitoring operations. Members questioned whether SIM registration had reduced scams, and DICT and NTC acknowledged gaps, supported stronger national-ID verification, and committed to submit a position paper on limiting IDs and SIM ownership. The committee also examined a hacked portal, NPC spending and privacy-monitoring targets, and 47446 online-lending complaints. NPC explained that additional funding would expand breach monitoring and registration capacity and agreed to provide specific online-lending case numbers. The issue landed with several agency commitments, but major enforcement and legislative questions remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT and its attached agencies had effective, enforceable, and privacy-compliant mechanisms to address unlawful online content, scams, child exploitation, technology-facilitated abuse, and data breaches. Members also examined whether platform compliance, SIM-registration controls, interagency response, and privacy-enforcement targets were adequate and funded.
topics.agency_position: DICT said existing mechanisms could coordinate platform compliance, law-enforcement response, scam investigations, and child-safety interventions, but acknowledged that SIM registration had not fully achieved its objectives and that stronger ID controls might require legislation. DICT and attached agencies undertook platform engagements, operationalized the CICC threat-monitoring center, supported national-ID verification, expanded privacy monitoring, and agreed to submit or provide requested materials.
topics.outcome: The agencies answered the operational questions and made commitments on complaint review, Roblox compliance, an ID position paper, breach investigation, and NPC case data. However, stronger Meta enforcement, legislative limits on acceptable IDs and SIMs, and concrete enforcement results for online-lending complaints remained open.

positions.position: Government must respond to unlawful online conduct without becoming an arbiter of lawful opinion, and DICT must take a firmer, more accountable stance toward Meta and protect children and public data.

Meta and Roblox should comply with Philippine law, establish meaningful local accountability, and support faster interagency action against child exploitation, grooming, cyberbullying, and digital violence.
Social-media registration should be considered because SIM registration had not stopped scams and other registration policies had failed to address fake accounts and trolls.
DICT and NTC needed stronger action against text scams and should explain and limit the IDs and SIMs that could be used for registration.
He supported the DICT budget but demanded measurable results, accountability, effective cybersecurity, and specific information on privacy enforcement and online-lending complaints.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said members had sought government assistance over fake, false, manipulated, defamatory, threatening, and otherwise harmful online content. He cited a case involving 197 Facebook links referred by Congressman Miro Kimbo's office, some of which remained online after Meta found no community-standards violation.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked how the agency could help and whether there was a solution, while emphasizing that government should not arbitrate opinions but must respond to impersonation, fraud, threats, coordinated deception, and other unlawful conduct.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair formally turned over consolidated complaints and supporting materials to DICT and CICC, furnished Meta a copy, and asked DICT and CICC to review the cases individually and report actions taken, pending matters, available legal or technical steps, and policy gaps.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair requested that Meta review the reported content, explain referral dispositions, and clarify review or escalation mechanisms when content was found not to violate community standards.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The member cited a Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group statement that SIM registration had failed to end SMS scams and asked whether DICT would pursue social-media registration after other registration avenues and policies had failed.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said SIM registration had not fulfilled its full promise because bank mules and false identities could still be used. He supported identity and age verification on social-media platforms through the national ID, subject to privacy safeguards.

thread.speaker: Committee secretary
thread.said: The committee secretary said the privacy issue required further discussion and sought assurance that verification data would not be stored elsewhere beyond government verification of the details.

thread.speaker: Representative Ann Matibag
thread.said: Matibag asked for a clear timeline, monitoring mechanism, and framework for Meta and Roblox compliance, including age and identity verification, and urged the establishment of a Philippine office or other arrangement giving the platforms jurisdictional accountability under Philippine law.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Roblox should comply no later than October. He listed five demands made since May: a child-focused Roblox platform or setting, attention to sexual-content-related keywords in chat, another chat-related measure, default parental controls, Philippine compliance involving 300 people through a Roblox partner, and age verification through the national ID.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Facebook authorities were expected to meet with the technical working group, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the police the following week. He said legislation and subpoenas could be considered and that a deadline was realistically expected before the end of the year.

thread.speaker: Representative Ann Matibag
thread.said: Matibag pressed for Meta to establish an office in the Philippines, saying the existing Meta representative could do only so much and that an office or stronger compliance arrangement was needed.

thread.speaker: Representative Ann Matibag
thread.said: Matibag asked how DICT coordinated with the PNP, cybercrime units, NBI, CICC, DepEd, and other agencies to respond faster to online sexual exploitation, grooming, cyberbullying, violent content, harassment, and technology-facilitated abuse.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said additional authority and the details of coordination would be better explained by the CICC executive director, whom he asked to respond.

thread.speaker: CICC Executive Director Edi Aboy
thread.said: Aboy said the CICC executive committee, chaired by the DICT secretary, included the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group, NBI, and DOJ. He said the threat monitoring center was operational and brought law-enforcement, partner agencies, private-sector partners, and advocacy groups together for rapid response to scams and online crimes.

thread.speaker: Representative Ann Matibag
thread.said: Matibag requested Wi-Fi for an elementary school in her district and proposed coordination among DICT, DepEd, and NBI to protect children. She supported adequate DICT funding to improve infrastructure and build a safer digital environment.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the Philippines was Meta's fifth-largest audience, representing 3 percent of Meta's online population, or 1 out of every 32 users. He contrasted this with X, where the Philippines ranked 12th and represented 1.7 percent, and urged DICT to take a firmer position with Meta.

thread.speaker: Representative Sarah Elago
thread.said: Elago asked about NTC's response to 15507 tech-scam or spam complaints and cited spoofed messages pretending to come from LTO. She sought concrete agency action against these scams.

thread.speaker: NTC Commissioner Ella Blanca Lopez
thread.said: Lopez said the reported figure came from the NTC consumer hotline and did not include reports filed with CICC or other agencies. She explained that scammers obtain a range of cellphone numbers and send messages impersonating government agencies, hoping recipients will click links to fake websites.

thread.speaker: NTC Commissioner Ella Blanca Lopez
thread.said: Lopez said recent operations had resulted in a capture the previous week and that the case was being built with NBI, CICC, DICT, and the PNP for prosecution.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the issue of limiting fake identities and the number of IDs used for registration should come from DICT and be effective.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said the national ID could provide a single identity record when used for both bank-account opening and SIM verification. He noted that limiting acceptable IDs and the number of SIMs per person would require an amendment to the SIM-registration law.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair requested an official DICT position paper on limiting acceptable IDs and SIM ownership.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda agreed that DICT would submit the requested position paper.

thread.speaker: A member
thread.said: A member asked whether the secretary intended to recognize only a limited number of government-issued IDs for SIM registration, noting that many agencies issue valid IDs.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy said 17 IDs were too many for SIM registration and that reducing the number to 3 might limit the use of fake IDs. He said other IDs could be verified against the national ID as the single record of truth.

thread.speaker: A member
thread.said: The member asked whether IDs such as a PNP firearms license could be recognized and whether government could verify an ID within seconds or a minute.

thread.speaker: DICT senior official Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy said digital verification could take seconds. He explained that the problem with accepting 17 IDs was that licenses and passports had links to the national ID, making identity provenance and cross-checking central to the solution.

thread.speaker: Representative JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos asked whether DICT had resolved a hacked portal that had affected permit, certification, regulatory, and labor-related requests for 18 hours.

thread.speaker: DICT Director Rodil
thread.said: Rodil said the incident had been reported the previous night and involved a subdomain not under DICT control. DICT coordinated a takedown, while DOLE, the Department of Migrant Workers, and CICC were helping investigate and determine whether data had been exfiltrated.

thread.speaker: Representative JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos questioned the National Privacy Commission's increased spending despite lower FY 2027 targets for compliance checks, satisfaction, technical assistance, and complaint resolution.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC official said the agency was not promising less because the relevant targets for 2026 and 2027 were actually the same. The additional budget would expand breach monitoring from 20 websites to 50, improve registration-platform capacity, reduce manual validation from around 7 days to 3 days or, if possible, 1 day, and increase registered personal information controllers beyond the current 17000.

thread.speaker: Representative JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos asked why the NPC had left 83000000 unused in 2025.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The official said much of the 83000000 was fit-out capital outlay released late in 2025. About 37000000 remained unutilized after the contractor backed out, following delays associated with securing a long-term lease and procurement.

thread.speaker: Representative JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos asked how many of the 47446 online-lending complaints reported by PAOCC reached the NPC and what concrete enforcement followed.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC official said the agency, SEC, and DICT had issued a joint advisory on borrowers' data-subject rights and online platforms' obligations, including restrictions concerning access to contacts. The official said online-lending cases had declined from their pandemic peak and committed to provide specific case numbers for 2024 to 2026.

thread.speaker: Representative JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos manifested full support for DICT's proposed budget and additional requests, but said support had to be matched by measurable connectivity, cybersecurity, service, and accountability results.

topics.topic: Digital Workforce Hub renewal and beneficiary expansion
topics.summary: Representative Sarah Elago questioned the renewal of the Digital Workforce Hub, its public cost, whether it was locally developed, and the sharp increase in beneficiaries targeted for 2027. Undersecretary Aguirre said the platform had cost 60000000 in the current year and that renewal was estimated at 40000000, with an unlimited-user license. He described a free platform that matched CVs to jobs, identified skills gaps, and directed users to training and micro-credentials. Aguirre said the platform was localized for the Philippines but originally developed by a Singaporean entity. He attributed the increase from 94778 beneficiaries in 2026 to 631251 in 2027 to the shift from face-to-face to online delivery and broader implementation through LGUs and other partners. The rationale was stated, but the transcript did not show detailed supporting metrics or a final resolution of the target's validity.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the public cost and development status of the Digital Workforce Hub renewal, and why the target number of digital-economy beneficiaries would rise sharply from 2026 to 2027. It also sought the expected reach and benefits of the platform.
topics.agency_position: DICT said the Digital Workforce Hub would be renewed for an estimated 40000000 and could serve an unlimited number of users under the procured license. The agency said the platform was localized for the Philippines but originally developed by a Singaporean entity, and that the higher beneficiary target reflected online delivery, toolkits, and expanded implementation through partner institutions.
topics.outcome: DICT provided the renewal cost, described the platform's functions and partnerships, clarified that it was localized rather than wholly locally developed, and attributed the higher 2027 target to online and partner-based implementation. The transcript did not show a further challenge, document submission, or separate validation of the beneficiary projection.

positions.position: She sought justification for the renewal cost, questioned whether the platform was locally developed, and challenged the basis for the sharp increase in targeted beneficiaries.

He supported renewal and broader platform utilization through government and educational partnerships, while explaining the beneficiary increase through the shift to online and partner-based implementation.

thread.speaker: Henry Roel Aguda, DICT official
thread.said: Aguda asked that Undersecretary Aguirre respond because he was in charge of the program.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: Aguirre said the Digital Workforce Hub would be launched that Wednesday. He described it as an ecosystem connecting job seekers and employers, with employers uploading job descriptions and applicants uploading their CVs.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: He said accounts would be free, and artificial-intelligence analysis of a user's CV would identify suitable jobs and skills gaps. The platform would direct users to training available through DICT courseware or external learning-management-system partners and would provide micro-credentials.

thread.speaker: Representative Sarah Elago
thread.said: Elago asked about the project's renewal for the following year and how much public money would be spent on it.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: Aguirre said the platform had been procured for 60000000 for the current year and that renewal was estimated at 40000000. He added that the license covered an unlimited number of users.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: He said DICT was partnering with BSP, TESDA, the National Privacy Commission, other government agencies, and state universities and colleges to maximize platform utilization.

thread.speaker: Representative Sarah Elago
thread.said: Elago asked whether the platform had been developed locally.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: Aguirre said the platform had been localized for the Philippine situation, but indicated that it was originally developed by a Singaporean entity. The transcript's reference to local partners was incomplete.

thread.speaker: Representative Sarah Elago
thread.said: Elago asked why the digital-economy participation target would increase from 94778 in 2026 to 631251 in 2027, describing it as a huge increase in target beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: Aguirre attributed the increase to changes in implementation of the Digital Workforce Program. DICT had shifted from face-to-face delivery to online modalities and planned to distribute toolkits through local-government-unit and partner institutions.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Aguirre
thread.said: He said the toolkits would provide alternative livelihood support for freelancers and had been developed with freelancers and MSMEs, including material on tax compliance and BIR registration. He said implementation would increasingly occur online and through DICT's various partners.

topics.topic: National Privacy Commission funding, enforcement, and performance
topics.summary: Members questioned DICT and the NPC on whether national-ID-based social-media verification could protect privacy after SIM registration had fallen short of its promises. DICT said the Philippines could be the first country to integrate a sovereign ID into a social-media platform, while the NPC said data minimization, database security, lawful processing, and public consultation were necessary. DICT described data-sovereignty safeguards, including encryption, contractor qualification, and keeping sensitive government data in the Philippines, and committed to issue implementing guidelines and procurement information. Rep. Dino also questioned data-center spending, including a cited historical budget of about 8.7 billion and a disputed 20 27 figure, while DICT said about 700 million had been spent on the first Subic data center. Rep. Pagianos challenged the NPC's increase from about 440 million to 505 million despite lower stated targets; the NPC said the funds would expand breach monitoring from 20 to 50 websites and accelerate controller registration from 7 days to 3 days or 1 day if possible. The NPC attributed 83000000 in unused funds mainly to a delayed fit-out and committed to provide online-lending case numbers, while regional connectivity validation and the final privacy framework remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the National Privacy Commission and DICT had sufficient funding, enforcement capacity, and safeguards to protect personal and government data. Members also asked whether proposed national-ID-based social-media verification, data-sovereignty rules, privacy enforcement, and breach monitoring would produce measurable results and respect privacy rights.
topics.agency_position: DICT and the NPC maintained that national-ID-based verification and data-sovereignty measures could be implemented with data minimization, security, consultation, encryption, contractor qualification, and lawful processing safeguards. The NPC defended its increased 20 27 request as funding for expanded breach monitoring, faster registration validation, and more registered controllers, while explaining that unused funds were mainly linked to a delayed and ultimately abandoned fit-out contract.
topics.outcome: The agency answered the committee's principal policy and funding questions but left several implementation matters for consultation, guidelines, and documentary submissions. The NPC defended the additional budget, explained the unused funds, and committed to provide online-lending case data; privacy safeguards and the final design of national-ID-based social-media verification remained unresolved.

positions.position: Questioned whether social-media registration was justified after SIM registration's reported shortcomings and sought a phased, technically feasible plan that would protect privacy.

Raised concerns that national-ID-linked social-media registration could impair privacy and become a surveillance instrument, and questioned whether the Philippines should be the first country to adopt it.
Pressed DICT on data sovereignty, national government data-center spending, procurement safeguards, and the privacy implications of officials' personal online posts.
Supported the DICT budget but demanded measurable results, questioned the NPC's increased funding and unused funds, and sought concrete enforcement data on online-lending complaints.
Sought clarification on DICT's access to NGCP data, the scope of NPC privacy jurisdiction, and whether regional connectivity claims were independently validated.

actions.action: Convene a technical working team to study national-ID integration for age and identity verification.
Conduct extensive public consultation on linking Meta verification to the national ID.
Issue implementing guidelines on data sovereignty, classification, localization, encryption, and contractor qualification.
Provide the committee with historical data-center infrastructure budgets, procurement information, terms, bidding procedures, and standards.
Submit specific NPC online-lending case numbers for 20 24 to 20 26.
Check and provide specific information on regional connectivity validation.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: Renee Co asked about DICT's plan or phasing for social-media registration, noting school violence and rights groups' concerns about using the national ID for verification.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda described discussions among Meta, Roblox, the NPC, NTC, CICC, NBI, and DepEd on identity and age verification. He said Roblox had proposed using the national ID, with facial recognition considered insufficiently precise for age verification.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said Roblox wanted to distinguish users aged 9 and below, 9 to 16, and 16 and above. A national-ID API could verify age without disclosing unnecessary personal information to Roblox.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: Co asked for an update on the technical complexity of integrating the Philippine national ID into a social-media verification system.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said the Philippines would be the first country to integrate a sovereign national ID into a platform of this kind. He undertook to convene a technical working team within the next 2 weeks.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said the Roblox technical and policy template could become a model for other social-media platforms.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: Co questioned whether social-media registration was justified after the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group reportedly said SIM registration had not delivered its original promise of ending cybercrime and SMS scams.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda acknowledged that SIM registration “didn't live up to its full promise,” citing the use of mules and false identities. He nevertheless argued for using the national ID for social-media identity and age verification because it had a higher chance of containing reliable information.

thread.speaker: Committee secretary
thread.said: The committee secretary said the privacy issue remained under discussion and understood that data would not be stored elsewhere beyond government verification of the details. The secretary said further policy discussions were needed to avoid intruding on the right to privacy.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Antonio Tinio raised concerns about access to the national ID, privacy, the right to privacy, social-media activity, and the possibility that registration could become a surveillance instrument.

thread.speaker: Ivan Uy
thread.said: Ivan Uy said the Philippine Statistics Authority was continuing to onboard people to the national ID system, including areas that still needed coverage, and was poised to complete registration in the next 2 years. He referred the privacy and surveillance questions to the NPC.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC official said linking Meta verification to the national ID involved risks concerning data minimization, the information disclosed to Meta, security features protecting the government database, and access to account-holder information. The official said these issues required extensive public consultation with government authorities, Meta, and Filipino stakeholders.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether the proposed system would be the first of its kind globally and connected that concern to data sovereignty.

thread.speaker: Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy confirmed that, based on DICT's understanding, the Philippines would be the first to integrate a sovereign ID into a social-media platform.

thread.speaker: Ivan Uy
thread.said: Uy referred the data-sovereignty question to DICT's legal officials, who had worked on the executive order harmonizing data classification, sovereignty, and localization.

thread.speaker: DICT undersecretary for legal affairs
thread.said: The undersecretary said DICT had helped craft EO 119 and was conducting roadshows to explain data sovereignty. She clarified that the policy concerned government data, not commercial private data.

thread.speaker: DICT undersecretary for legal affairs
thread.said: The undersecretary said top-secret and other national-security data would remain in the Philippines, while only lower-ranking classified data could be contracted out, still within Philippine jurisdiction. She said DICT had assured national-security agencies that their classifications would be respected.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said DICT was about to issue implementing guidelines on data sovereignty and that the guidelines would be released shortly.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Rep. Dino asked how the government would maintain sovereignty over Filipinos' data and what safeguards would apply.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official cited government encryption standards and said contractors would undergo rigorous certification and qualification, to be detailed in the implementing guidelines.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said data sovereignty was intended to bring government data into the Philippines and reduce duplication across agencies. He said about 80 percent of the data was not currently in the Philippines and that agencies were therefore more likely to subscribe to foreign cloud services.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Rep. Dino cited a 20 16 to 20 26 budget of 8700000000 for national government data-center infrastructure and a 20 27 proposal of 949000000000 million, then corrected the latter to 806000000 in maintenance and other operating expenses and 143 in capital outlay. He asked for the breakdown.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official said the maintenance and other operating expenses largely reflected the buildup of the first data center in Subic, where about 700000000 had been spent.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Dino asked how cloud services, including Google Cloud Platform, were selected and whether procurement used competitive or negotiated bidding.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official answered that the services were selected through competitive bidding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Dino requested information on the national government data-center infrastructure budgets from 20 16 to 20 26 and on procurement terms and standards.

thread.speaker: DICT official responsible for data sovereignty and data-center infrastructure
thread.said: The official agreed to provide the requested information to the committee. The chair emphasized that the committee also wanted the bidding standards, including whether international providers were held to standards no less stringent than those applied locally.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dino
thread.said: Dino asked the NPC about the privacy implications of a government official personally vlogging a video involving a teacher who had committed a traffic violation.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC said no formal complaint had yet been filed and therefore avoided ruling on the specific incident. It explained that capturing and uploading the video were separate processing activities, each requiring a lawful basis, and that the distinction between an official public channel and a personal vlog could affect the analysis.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC added that proportionality and data minimization had to be assessed even if the subject's image was blurred. It said any processing of personal information required a lawful basis under the Data Privacy Act and that the personal information controller had the burden of showing that basis.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos noted that the NPC's total spending program increased from 440000000 in 20 26 to 505000000 in 20 27, while reported performance targets declined. He asked whether the NPC was seeking more funds while promising less.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC official said the agency was not promising less and that the 20 26 and 20 27 net targets were actually the same. The added funding would expand eSprint breach monitoring from 20 websites to 50 websites, enhance the registration platform, and increase the number of registered personal information controllers.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The official said manual validation of registrations currently took around 7 days and that the upgraded system aimed to reduce this to 3 days, or 1 day if possible, through automated validation and verification. The NPC currently had 17000 registered personal information controllers, compared with around 700000 registered companies in the SEC.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos asked why the NPC had left 83000000 unused in 20 25.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC said a large part of the 83000000 was fit-out capital outlay released late by the DBM. About 37000000 remained unutilized after the contractor backed out, following the NPC's move to its current Quezon City premises in March 20 25.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos cited 47446 complaints involving online-lending firms from August 20 24 to January 20 26 and asked how many reached the NPC and what concrete enforcement followed.

thread.speaker: National Privacy Commission official
thread.said: The NPC said it had issued a joint public advisory with the SEC and DICT on borrowers' data-subject rights and online platforms' obligations, including access to contact lists. It said online-lending cases had tapered from pandemic levels and committed to provide the specific case numbers for 20 24 to 20 26.

thread.speaker: Rep. JP Pagianos
thread.said: Pagianos manifested full support for the DICT's proposed budget and additional requests, while stressing that support should be matched by measurable connectivity, cybersecurity, public-service, and accountability results.

thread.speaker: Secretary Henry Roel Aguda
thread.said: Aguda said NGCP, as critical infrastructure, could be accessed for appropriate cybersecurity and oversight purposes and that DICT's cyber bureau actively participated in securing critical infrastructure.

thread.speaker: DICT official for legal and privacy matters
thread.said: The official explained that the Data Privacy Act covered personal and sensitive personal information, such as employee or customer data, but not all forms of NGCP data. Nonpersonal operational data would generally fall outside the NPC's purview.

thread.speaker: Sergio Dagooc
thread.said: Dagooc asked whether the NPC was familiar with electricity-market operations and whether wholesale electricity spot-market data was personal information that could be shared.

thread.speaker: DICT official for legal and privacy matters
thread.said: The official said the NPC was not familiar with electricity-market operations because they were outside its mandate. He said wholesale spot-market data generally did not contain personal data, although distribution utilities could hold customer information covered by the privacy law.

thread.speaker: Sergio Dagooc
thread.said: Dagooc asked whether DICT monitored and validated connectivity in the provinces through regional offices, rather than relying solely on reported figures.

thread.speaker: DICT official
thread.said: The official said DICT had regional-office validation and regular monitoring but would need to check the specifics for the region concerned. The exchange ended with Dagooc seeking a commitment on validation.

topics.topic: Disaster communications and connectivity restoration
topics.summary: Caroline Agyao asked DICT how it would provide emergency communications and rapidly restore connectivity in calamity-prone and commercially underserved areas. She sought details on deployable assets, activation time, operational sites, maintenance costs, 2027 coverage, and funding for school and community power supplies. DICT cited improved availability of about 60 percent in affected areas, telecommunications-provider availability of 99.8 percent, and a contractual restoration period of 72 hours. The agency also described longer contracts, a nationwide project covering about 5,400 schools, and a DepEd partnership to install solar-powered Starlink. The committee did not receive clear answers to all requested budget and operational figures, so the issue remained unresolved despite the agency's described projects and commitments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what DICT programs, assets, funding, and response times would support emergency communications and rapid connectivity restoration in calamity-prone areas. It also asked how many sites and schools had reliable connectivity, how DICT would serve communities without commercial signal, and whether schools could maintain links during disasters.
topics.agency_position: DICT said it was strengthening disaster communications through deployable assets, telecommunications and satellite arrangements, longer service contracts, and a nationwide school-connectivity project. It presented Starlink, including solar-powered installations with DepEd, as a resilient option for schools and remote communities, while stating that managed-services contracts required restoration within 72 hours.
topics.outcome: DICT provided a general operational response, citing a 72-hour restoration requirement, longer contracts, coverage of 5400 plus schools, and solar-powered Starlink for resilient school connectivity. The transcript did not show a precise response to the requested budget amounts, site counts, per-site maintenance costs, or funding for power-supply units.

positions.position: She sought stronger assurance that DICT could provide emergency communications, restore connectivity quickly, maintain reliable service beyond merely installing Wi-Fi access points, and support schools and communities during disasters.
He characterized the concern as a fair point and linked the proposed approach to DICT's mandate to connect disadvantaged and geographically disadvantaged communities.

thread.speaker: Caroline Agyao
thread.said: Caroline Agyao asked the Secretary to identify programs ensuring emergency communications and rapid restoration of connectivity in calamity-prone areas.

thread.speaker: Caroline Agyao
thread.said: She asked what deployable assets DICT had, including satellite phones, portable cell sites, mobile command centers, radio systems, and emergency Wi-Fi, and how quickly they could be activated after a disaster.

thread.speaker: Caroline Agyao
thread.said: She asked the agency to provide information on the approved amount, including the transcript's references to '20 20' and '1000000000,' and another '1000000000' for communications signal.

thread.speaker: Caroline Agyao

thread.speaker: Caroline Agyao

topics.topic: DICT IT staffing and compensation capacity
topics.summary: Rep. Romeo Momo questioned DICT’s low absorptive capacity, citing a 61.7 percent obligation rate, 22 percent disbursement against obligations, and a disputed June obligation figure of 9 percent versus DICT’s reported 24 percent. DICT attributed implementation difficulties partly to funding-release requirements and manpower constraints, saying it had about 1700 JOs or SOs, had requested about 500 positions, and received about 115 additional positions. The committee then asked whether the in-house eGov super app could continue across administrations; DICT said continuity was assured but required adequate staffing and funding, particularly more competitive IT salaries. DICT cited developer salary grades of 12, 15, and 17, IT salary grades of 20 and 22, and programmer pay of around 50 to 60000, with a maximum range of around 59000 to 89000 a month. Rep. Richard Gomez and the chair committed to pursuing legislation on IT salary grades and a Magna Carta for IT professionals. The utilization discrepancies and project-implementation figures remained unreconciled, but legislative and administrative follow-up was undertaken.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DICT had sufficient budget-utilization and manpower capacity to implement its growing appropriations and sustain systems developed in-house, particularly the eGov super app. It also examined IT salary levels and whether legislative action, including a Magna Carta for IT professionals, was needed to retain technical personnel.
topics.agency_position: DICT said implementation capacity had been constrained by staffing, outdated organizational and staffing structures, and the inability to offer compensation competitive with the private sector. It maintained that the eGov app could continue across administrations because it was developed in-house, but said sustained funding, adequate personnel, and legislative action on IT compensation and a Magna Carta for IT professionals were needed.
topics.outcome: DICT’s continuity assurance for eGov was accepted as conditional on resolving personnel and funding needs. The COA-versus-DICT utilization figures and the unimplemented-project amounts were not reconciled during the hearing, while legislative action on IT compensation and a Magna Carta was committed for follow-up.

positions.position: DICT needed to improve its budget utilization and resolve manpower and execution bottlenecks before receiving and consuming a larger 2027 budget.
eGov continuity was possible, but depended on adequate personnel and funding; the chair also viewed IT staffing as a legislative concern.
The committee should institutionalize IT salary grades and pursue legislation, including a bill and a Magna Carta for IT professionals, to sustain eGov and retain technical personnel.

topics.topic: FY2027 Judiciary budget proposal of about 86.27 billion
topics.summary: Justice Estuesta presented a proposed FY2027 Judiciary budget of about 86.27 billion, compared with about 70.611 billion under the FY2026 General Appropriations Act. He detailed proposed allocations for the Supreme Court and lower courts, PET, Court of Appeals, Sandigan Bayan, and Court of Tax Appeals, and sought about 5.344 billion in further augmentations, including court-complex requirements and sheriff hazard pay. Representative Roman Romulo asked whether DBM had commented on the proposal and whether the amount would support the Judiciary's programs; the Judiciary said it had not received DBM's comments and that funding all programs was its goal. Patal also questioned electronic discovery procedures, and the Judiciary said electronic evidence rules were still under review, with privacy, relevance, materiality, and forensic issues requiring consideration. Representatives Jan Rurik Padiernos and Biloso expressed support, with Padianos conditioning support on measurable performance and accountability. The committee invited augmentation letters by Wednesday before lunch, promised consideration subject to fiscal space, and then terminated the hearing.
topics.question: What was the Judiciary's proposed FY2027 budget, how was it divided among the courts, and what additional augmentations or program-related funding did the Judiciary seek? The committee also sought to establish whether DBM had reviewed the proposal, whether the budget would support the Judiciary's programs, and how electronic discovery reforms were progressing.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary supported its proposed FY2027 budget of PHP 86271000000 and said the amount was intended to fund all planned programs. It additionally sought 5344000000 in augmentations, including court-complex requirements and sheriff hazard pay, while electronic-discovery procedures remained under review through revisions to the rules on evidence.
topics.outcome: The committee terminated the hearing after the Judiciary presented its original proposal and requested further augmentation. Additional funding remained subject to the courts' Wednesday submissions, subcommittee review, and available fiscal space; DBM comments and finalized electronic-discovery protocols were not yet available.

positions.position: Supported examining the proposed increase and sought clarification on the unavailable DBM comments, the budget's sufficiency for planned programs, and concrete protocols for electronic discovery.
Fully supported the proposed Judiciary budget, subject to measurable performance, reduced case delays, stronger digital systems, and greater transparency.
Manifested full support for approval of the proposed 2027 Judiciary budget.
Supported the Judiciary and invited the courts to submit augmentation requests for committee consideration.
Was willing to consider additional Judiciary funding requests, subject to review through the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee and limited fiscal space.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta introduced the Judiciary's original budget proposal under the Fiscal Autonomy Act and said the presentation would cover its programs, priorities, and resource requirements.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He said the FY2026 General Appropriations Act Judiciary budget was PHP70.611 billion and that, given the fiscal envelope, the Judiciary had limited the increase to 22 percent. He identified the Supreme Court and lower courts' allocation as 60489000000, with the remaining allocations to be presented by court.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He presented the proposed FY2027 Judiciary budget of PHP 86271000000: 73837000000 for the Supreme Court and lower courts, PHP193.43 million for the PET, PHP7.605 billion for the Court of Appeals, PHP3.282 billion for the Sandigan Bayan, and PHP1.354 billion for the Court of Tax Appeals.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He compared the FY2026 and FY2027 proposals, citing increases of PHP13.347 billion for the Supreme Court and lower courts, PHP 13560000 for the PET, PHP 1513000000 for the Court of Appeals, PHP559 million for the Sandigan Bayan, and 2 27000000 for the Court of Tax Appeals.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He said the total proposed budget represented an increase of 15660000000, or 22 percent, over the previous budget.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He explained that the Supreme Court's capital outlay increased by 3758000000, while the Court of Tax Appeals' capital outlay decreased by 4528000, resulting in a total capital-outlay decrease of 3218000000. The Supreme Court and lower courts' breakdown included personal services of 8 5 900000000 and MOOE of 3246000000.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He attributed the capital-outlay change principally to the FY2026 allocation for the Manila Hall of Justice, which was not carried in the FY2027 proposal; the proposal instead included 200000000 for the Cebu NCDO judiciary complex.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He said the consulting services had submitted the construction design and engineering documents for the Hall of Justice in the judiciary complex and that an additional allocation was needed for Cagayan de Oro, although the amount was unclear in the transcript. For Cebu City, he cited 4541000000, for a total of 5041000000.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He requested that the Cebu and Cagayan de Oro requirements be carried in the FY2027 budget and asked that hazard pay for sheriffs be included. He stated the sheriff hazard-pay request as 3 0 3000000 and said the Judiciary was augmenting its original proposal by 5344000000 in total.

thread.speaker: Representative Roman Romulo
thread.said: Representative Patal noted that the proposal increased by about just over PHP15 billion and asked the Judiciary to share DBM's comments and recommendations, which the chart indicated had been appended to the submission.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: The Judiciary answered that, as of the previous day and up to the hearing, it had not received DBM's comments. Patal then asked whether 86270000000 was the amount being proposed, and the Judiciary confirmed that it was.

thread.speaker: Representative Roman Romulo
thread.said: Patal asked whether the proposed increase would allow the Judiciary to pursue all of its planned programs.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: The Judiciary answered that pursuing all of the planned programs was the goal.

thread.speaker: Representative Roman Romulo
thread.said: Patal asked about the status of the electronic discovery project, focusing on how individual litigants could obtain electronically stored information such as email from companies with greater resources and information.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Estuesta said the rules on civil procedure had recently been amended and were again undergoing amendment, while electronic evidence was being addressed in the ongoing revision of the rules on evidence. He said electronic evidence had become a substantial part of evidence presentation.

thread.speaker: Representative Roman Romulo
thread.said: Patal asked how aggressive the Judiciary's approach would be while the rules remained under review, including whether parties would be required to establish protocols covering access, metadata, production format, custodians, and deadlines for potentially millions of pages of email.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Estuesta said electronic mail, Facebook posts, and instant messages raised issues involving forensic evidence, anonymous senders, data privacy, and the relevance and materiality of evidence. He did not identify a finalized discovery protocol, stating that the matters were part of the ongoing rules review.

thread.speaker: Representative Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: Padianos manifested full support for the proposed Judiciary budget, saying the Judiciary should equalize access to justice. He cautioned that support was not a blank check and that a larger budget should produce measurable results, including fewer delayed cases, shorter waiting times, stronger digital systems, and greater transparency.

thread.speaker: Representative Biloso
thread.said: Representative Biloso said he had no further question and manifested full support for approval of the proposed 2027 Judiciary budget.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked the Supreme Court, Sandigan Bayan, Court of Tax Appeals, and Court of Appeals to submit the items they believed should be augmented. He said the chair was ready to receive four letters of augmentation.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said institutional amendment requests would be routed through the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee for open, line-by-line deliberation, and asked the courts to submit additional funding items before the committee convened ahead of plenary.

thread.speaker: Court Administrator Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Estuesta accepted the opportunity to seek augmentation and committed to submit requests from all courts by Wednesday before lunch.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the House would do its best to accommodate the Judiciary's submitted items, subject to limited fiscal space.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez moved to terminate the committee hearing on the Judiciary's proposed FY2027 budget.

topics.topic: About 4.3 billion MOOE increase for case backlogs
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co asked how much of the roughly 4.3 billion MOOE increase would directly clear backlogs, particularly in lower courts reporting first-half disposal rates of about 65 to 69 percent. Justice Estuesta answered that the funds would support case-flow management, ICT systems, monitoring through the CMO data hub, and lower-court personnel upgrading, but he did not give a specific backlog-allocation amount. He reported 4 6300 judge vacancies, or 16.7 percent of authorized positions, and undertook to pursue funding measures while the Judiciary was asked to submit staffing lists. Rep. John Tracy Cagas raised delays in election cases and obtained an assurance that a time-bound election protest would hopefully be resolved before the next election. The agency also committed to look for funding for a Davao Sur House of Justice at 150000000, while Rep. Charah Jain Ilago’s request for detailed spousal- and child-support outcomes was only partially answered. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos supported the budget subject to measurable reductions in delays and stronger accountability.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the roughly 4.3 billion MOOE increase would directly address case backlogs and speed case processing, particularly in first-level courts. It also examined whether staffing and judicial vacancies were limiting disposition rates and whether the Judiciary had measurable steps to reduce delays.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary said the MOOE increase would support case-flow management, monitoring through the CMO data hub, ICT and digital systems, and the upgrading and reclassification of lower-court personnel. It also said judge vacancies were constrained by the lack of NOSCAs and promised efforts to secure funding and accelerate time-bound election cases, but it did not provide a specific amount of the MOOE increase dedicated solely to backlog reduction.
topics.outcome: The Judiciary explained the systems and personnel measures that would support case disposition but did not identify a specific portion of the 4300000000 MOOE increase dedicated to clearing backlogs. Staffing data and commitments on election cases and the Davao Sur facility were noted, while the support-case outcome data requested by Rep. Ilago remained incomplete.

positions.position: Pressed for a direct accounting of the MOOE increase’s allocation to backlog reduction, improved calendaring, additional personnel, and the filling of judicial and court-personnel vacancies.
Commended the Judiciary’s reported disposition rates but urged faster resolution of election cases and sought funding for a Davao Sur House of Justice.
Sought outcome data on spousal- and child-support cases, including grants of support and execution of support orders.
Supported the Judiciary budget subject to measurable performance, fewer delays, shorter waiting times, stronger digital systems, and greater transparency.
Requested a fast-track approach for election cases and supported revising and recommending the Davao Sur House of Justice request.
