thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Justice Estuesta identified case disposition as the Judiciary’s major final output and linked improvements in justice delivery to the SPJI institutional transformation program.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: For the first half of 2026, regional trial courts had an 81 percent accomplishment rate. The Supreme Court had disposed of 2662 cases against a half-year target of 3000, for an 89 percent accomplishment rate.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Family Courts posted a 91 percent first-half accomplishment rate; metropolitan trial courts posted 95 percent, with actual disposal of 46033 against a target of 48313.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Municipal trial courts in cities had a 79 percent first-half accomplishment rate, while municipal trial courts had 69 percent.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Municipal circuit trial courts had a 65 percent first-half accomplishment rate, and Sharia Circuit Courts had 67 percent.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: For the first half of 2026, the Court of Appeals had a 130 percent accomplishment rate, the Sandigan Bayan 178 percent, and the Court of Tax Appeals 127 percent.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co noted the proposed budget’s 22 percent increase and the 65 to 69 percent disposal rates in some first-level courts. She asked how much of the 4300000000 MOOE increase was specifically allocated to clear backlogs and enable swift processing, especially in lower courts.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He said disposal targets function as performance benchmarks and that the relevant budget support would include proper case-flow management. The CMO data hub and the statistics and records division would monitor caseloads, resolutions, and disposals to support a case-flow management system covering calendaring and hearings.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co followed up on whether ICT upgrades would improve backlog reduction, particularly calendaring. She described how overloading a calendar with 30 cases could force the remaining cases to be rescheduled and cause delay, and asked about additional personnel and other measures.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He replied that, beyond ICT upgrades, the increase for lower courts—spoken as “0.959 increase or million increase,” which is unclear—would support personnel upgrading and reclassification. He said more competitive pay would improve personnel engagement and, in turn, justice delivery.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He said a salary grade 1 utility worker still received 15000 pesos, describing the longstanding lack of salary-grade upgrades for lower-court personnel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co raised the contribution of vacant judicial and court-personnel positions to backlogs and asked how many judge and court-personnel positions remained unfilled after the creation of new regional trial and family courts.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Justice Estuesta explained that newly created courts could not be filled until a NOSCA was issued; these were considered unorganized courts. He then reported that judge vacancies stood at 4 6300, representing 16.7 percent of authorized judicial positions.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He said the vacancies could be remedied through the Fiscal Autonomy Act and that, if DBM did not act within 120 days, the Supreme Court would resort to appropriate measures to secure funding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked that the Judiciary submit lists of judges and court personnel, including the relevant Judiciary items.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He said the submission would reflect the total number of judges and court personnel and identify unorganized courts, including their branch numbers and territorial locations.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Tracy Cagas
thread.said: Rep. Cagas commended the reported disposition performance of the appellate courts, citing the Court of Appeals’ 130 percent rate and the Sandigan Bayan’s 178 percent rate. He also acknowledged the Supreme Court’s 89 percent and the regional trial courts’ 81 percent first-half rates but raised concerns about unresolved cases.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Tracy Cagas
thread.said: Rep. Cagas asked about delays in election cases, including cases involving status quo orders issued by the Supreme Court, and urged the Judiciary to address the delays without requiring him to discuss the merits of particular cases.

thread.speaker: Raul Villanueva, agency official
thread.said: Villanueva explained that election cases filed under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 undergo a procedure requiring comments from the parties, collation of pleadings, assignment, and deliberation by a Supreme Court division.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair summarized the request that the Supreme Court develop a fast-track procedure for election cases because elected congressional and local officials serve three-year terms.

thread.speaker: Raul Villanueva, agency official
thread.said: Villanueva said three Supreme Court members had been made aware that election protests were time-bound and assured the committee that the case would hopefully be resolved before the next election.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Tracy Cagas
thread.said: Rep. Cagas thanked the Judiciary for the assurance and continued to press for the timely movement of election cases.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Tracy Cagas
thread.said: Rep. Cagas requested support for a Davao Sur House of Justice, stating that the district already had a lot and that the construction cost requested was about 50000000 pesos.

thread.speaker: Raul Villanueva, agency official
thread.said: Villanueva said the indicative construction cost for a House of Justice on a 5000 square meter property was 500000000 pesos.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair asked the Judiciary to revise the request for a one-story building costing 1 50, understood in context as 150000000, rather than a two- or three-story building, and said the committee would strongly recommend it.

thread.speaker: Raul Villanueva, agency official
thread.said: Villanueva committed to look for funding and realign Judiciary funds if the requested amount was 150000000.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Tracy Cagas
thread.said: Rep. Cagas said he no longer wished to pursue a proposed court creation after the discussion, having been informed that courts could remain unfilled and unorganized for 2 years.

thread.speaker: Rep. Charah Jain Ilago
thread.said: Rep. Ilago asked how many filed spousal- and child-support cases had been granted, how many granted orders had been successfully executed, and how courts ensured that support orders were regularly enforced.

thread.speaker: Agency official
thread.said: The agency official said the cases were classified in a cluster as violence against women and children under Republic Act 9262. The official provided aggregate case figures but did not separately answer how many support orders had been granted or successfully executed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: Rep. Padianos supported the proposed Judiciary budget but said support was not a blank check. He called for measurable results, including fewer delayed cases, shorter waiting times, stronger digital systems, and greater transparency.

topics.topic: Funding and NOSCAs for newly created courts and plantilla positions
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co asked how the proposed budget increase would reduce case backlogs and how many judge and court personnel positions remained unfilled in newly created courts. Justice Estuesta said staffing depended on NOSCAs, reported 4 6300 judge vacancies, and said the Fiscal Autonomy Act could provide a solution after the 120-day DBM period. The chair pressed the Judiciary to complete the IRR and use its fiscal autonomy, while Justice Marquez said approval would be pursued in September October and that the Judiciary could program positions for funding. DBM described a proposal including 46 family courts worth 541103000 and stated that it had no opposition to the Judiciary's legal authority. Justice Villanueva reported 135 courts requiring about 1.4 billion in additional funding and committed to submit the relevant requests and amounts. The chair directed that the FY 2027 budget consideration focus on NOSCA requests for which the 120-day period had elapsed, leaving broader implementation pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how funding and staffing would address vacancies in newly created courts, including the number of unfilled judicial and court personnel positions and the status of required NOSCAs. It also pressed the Judiciary and DBM on whether the Fiscal Autonomy Act allowed the Judiciary to proceed with staffing and funding without waiting for DBM action.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary said staffing newly created courts depended on NOSCAs under the prior process, but it recognized that RA 1 2 2 3 3 and the Fiscal Autonomy Act could allow programming and funding positions after DBM failed to act within 120 days. The Judiciary committed to pursue the IRR, identify eligible courts and positions, and submit additional funding requirements, while DBM stated that it had no opposition to the Judiciary's authority under the law.
topics.outcome: The matter was left with a commitment by the Judiciary to submit the NOSCA and funding information for the 135 courts and to pursue implementation of the Fiscal Autonomy Act. The chair limited immediate budget consideration to requests meeting the 120-day condition, while the broader timing of the IRR and staffing of all newly created courts remained open.

positions.position: The Judiciary should identify unfilled judge and court personnel positions and explain how the proposed MOOE and staffing increases would address backlogs and vacancies.

The Judiciary should exercise its Fiscal Autonomy Act authority where legally available, but the FY 2027 budget should include only NOSCA requests for which the 120-day period had elapsed, giving DBM an opportunity to act on the rest.
DBM had no opposition to the Judiciary assuming authority over classification and salary levels under the new law.
The Judiciary could program and seek funding for the positions under RA 1 2 2 3 3, with some provisions considered self-implementing.
The Judiciary should add funding for newly created courts, including courts for which NOSCAs had been requested and DBM had not acted within the statutory period.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co cited the proposed FY 2027 Judiciary budget totaling 86271000000, a 22 percent increase from the FY 2026 GAA, and low first-level-court disposal rates of 65 to 69 percent. She asked how much of the 4300000000 increase in MOOE was specifically intended to clear backlogs and speed case processing in lower courts.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said disposal targets were performance benchmarks and that case-flow management was the principal administrative response. The CMO data hub and statistics and records division monitored caseloads, resolutions, and disposals to support a case-flow management system.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co followed up on whether ICT upgrades would reduce backlogs, particularly calendaring problems that caused cases to be moved when too many were scheduled on one day. She also asked about additional personnel and other measures to enable faster case processing.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said that, apart from ICT upgrades, the 0.959 increase or million increase in the lower-court budget would support upgrading and reclassifying personnel. He said lower-court salary grades had not been upgraded for a very long time and cited a salary grade 1 utility worker receiving 15000 pesos.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co raised the creation of new courts and the continuing lack of judges and plantilla personnel. She asked how many judge and court personnel positions remained unfilled following the creation of new RTCs and family courts, and how the Supreme Court would ensure that personal-services funding matched the staffing needs of those courts.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta explained that staffing depended on whether a NOSCA had been issued. Courts without NOSCAs were considered unorganized courts and could not be filled despite the Judiciary's intention to staff them; he then reported 4 6300 judge vacancies, representing 16.7 percent of authorized judicial positions.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said the vacancies would hopefully be remedied by the Fiscal Autonomy Act, under which DBM had 120 days to act. Otherwise, he said, the Supreme Court would resort to appropriate measures to have the positions funded.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked that the Judiciary submit a list of judges and court personnel positions, including Judiciary items.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said the submission would reflect the total number of judges and court personnel in the Judiciary. He added that it would also identify unorganized courts about to be created, their branch numbers, and their territorial jurisdictions.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the Judiciary had already exercised the 120-day authority under the Fiscal Autonomy Act to proceed when DBM did not issue NOSCAs, emphasizing that the country needed judges for courts already approved for creation.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said the Judiciary had not yet exercised that authority because the implementing rules and regulations were still under review by the Supreme Court and Bank. He said the IRR had already been submitted and would be issued soon.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair urged the Supreme Court to finish and promulgate the IRR, noting that some courts had been created 5 to 7 years earlier and that districts, cities, and provinces had a felt need for them. He asked for a definite timeline for approval.

thread.speaker: Associate Justice Jose Maidas Marquez
thread.said: Justice Marquez said the IRR had been submitted to the court and was being reviewed. He stated that the Judiciary would push for approval in September October, and said some provisions were self-implementing.

thread.speaker: Associate Justice Jose Maidas Marquez
thread.said: Justice Marquez said the Judiciary could proceed as a fiscally autonomous institution with the filling of the courts, including opening applications for judges through the JBC and subsequently filling court personnel positions.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the Judiciary could proceed without waiting for the IRR and whether the resulting positions were included in the FY 2027 budget or would have to wait until FY 2028.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said the appropriation would come from DBM because the NOSCA should carry the appropriation for the positions.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair challenged that position, stating that the Fiscal Autonomy Act authorized the Judiciary, after 120 days, to proceed without waiting for DBM and include the positions in its automatically funded budget. He requested a definite answer because members had pending courts and judge requests.

thread.speaker: Associate Justice Jose Maidas Marquez
thread.said: Justice Marquez said this was the first implementation of RA 1 2 2 3 3 and that prior practice had required waiting for DBM NOSCAs. He said the Judiciary believed it could program the positions and ask Congress to fund them.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair called on DBM to state its position on the Fiscal Autonomy Act and the proposed plantilla positions, emphasizing that the provision was already law and that members were waiting for implementation.

thread.speaker: Carlo of DBM
thread.said: The DBM official said the Judiciary budget proposal included new positions, including 46 family courts worth 541103000, as well as additional Sharia district and circuit court judges at large, Judicial Integrity Office positions, and Office of the Regional Court Managers positions. He said there were 3 3 pending requests involving the creation of positions, subject to coordination with the Organization, Position Classification and Compensation Bureau, and referred to the Judiciary's miscellaneous personal benefits fund upon request.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked DBM whether it opposed the Judiciary assuming jurisdiction over the classification and salary levels of court judges and personnel under the new law.

thread.speaker: Carlo of DBM
thread.said: The DBM official answered that DBM had no opposition, responding affirmatively when the chair characterized the authority as granted by law.

thread.speaker: Justice Raul Villanueva
thread.said: Justice Villanueva clarified that newly created courts established by law had not been included in the FY 2027 proposal because the Judiciary usually waited for NOSCAs. He said the IRR was expected to be approved perhaps by October and that, under RA 1 2 2 3 3, a DBM request with no action within the prescribed period would be deemed approved.

thread.speaker: Justice Raul Villanueva
thread.said: Justice Villanueva committed that, through the court administrator, the Judiciary would add the amounts needed for newly created courts under laws already passed by Congress so they could be implemented in 2027 even if DBM did not act within the period required by law.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair clarified that the law's 120-day rule applied only to courts for which the Judiciary had already submitted requests to DBM and on which DBM had failed to act. The chair said the Judiciary should give DBM an opportunity to act before including other courts.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked Justice Villanueva to submit the requests already sent to DBM for which 120 days had elapsed.

thread.speaker: Justice Raul Villanueva
thread.said: Justice Villanueva agreed to submit the information. He proposed separating courts for which NOSCAs had already been requested from courts for which requests had not yet been made, and submitting the funding amounts needed for consideration in the FY 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair said it would be premature to include courts for which NOSCAs had not been requested because DBM might still approve them. The chair directed the Judiciary to include only requests for which the 120-day period had already lapsed, to limit the fiscal impact.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked how many positions had been submitted to DBM as of the hearing date for which 120 days had already elapsed, so those amounts could be considered in the budget.

thread.speaker: Justice Raul Villanueva
thread.said: Justice Villanueva reported that 135 courts needed funding and that NOSCAs had already been requested for them. He said the additional funding requirement was 1400000000 pesos.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked which of the requests had not been acted on by DBM within 120 days and therefore could proceed under the law.

thread.speaker: Justice Raul Villanueva
thread.said: Justice Villanueva answered that all 135 requests had been submitted to DBM before the deliberation.

thread.speaker: The chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the 135 courts were already included or whether the Judiciary would submit an additional request, then directed the Judiciary to submit the additional request for courts approved by DBM.

topics.topic: Judiciary digitalization, cybersecurity, and court technology
topics.summary: The Judiciary presented digital infrastructure and reform projects including the eCourt pilot, CMO data hub, Philippine Judicial Platform, electronic payments, e-notarization, video conferencing, and data-center upgrades. Rep. Renee Co asked how the roughly 4.3 billion MOOE increase would clear lower-court backlogs, but the agency described case-flow management and personnel reclassification without identifying a specific backlog allocation. Rep. Sarah Elago asked whether the 20 22–20 27 strategic plan remained on schedule, and the agency said digital infrastructure supported the transition to the next Chief Justice while gender-related digital and court initiatives were being implemented. Roman Romulo questioned electronic discovery, metadata, privacy, and access to corporate emails; the agency said electronic-evidence rules were still under review. The agency also reported that electronic-notary applications had opened on August 10, 20 26 and that electronic documents and payments were being processed online. Rep. Jay Vergara received a stated Supreme Court digital-infrastructure figure of about 5.21 billion and requested specific figures for digitalization, training, and cybersecurity, leaving those details committed for later submission.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Judiciary's proposed budget adequately supported digital court infrastructure, cybersecurity, electronic evidence and discovery, electronic notarization, video conferencing, and related online services. Members also asked whether these systems were improving case management, access to justice, and accountability, and what remained to be funded or submitted.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary presented digitalization as a central component of its judicial-transformation plan, citing operational systems, court connectivity, cloud and data-center infrastructure, eCourt pilots, electronic payments, e-notarization, video conferencing, and electronic-evidence rule revisions. It said electronic discovery and evidence remained under rules review and acknowledged that specific digitalization, training, and cybersecurity figures would be provided separately.
topics.outcome: The Judiciary explained its existing digital systems and said electronic evidence and discovery rules were still under review. Specific allocations for digitalization, training, and cybersecurity were not fully provided during the hearing and were to be submitted to Rep. Vergara's office.

positions.position: Supported improving digital calendaring and court staffing but questioned whether the proposed MOOE increase had a specific, adequate allocation for backlog reduction.
Pressed for evidence that the strategic digital-reform plan was on schedule and that digital and court reforms incorporated gender responsiveness and access concerns.
Advocated stronger and clearer electronic-discovery mechanisms, electronic notarization, and fair service-of-process procedures that would improve access for individual litigants.
Supported the Judiciary budget subject to measurable performance, stronger digital systems, reduced delays, transparency, and fiscal accountability.
Supported the proposed Judiciary budget and requested specific digitalization, training, cybersecurity, and infrastructure figures.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Justice Estuesta identified the Scriptix artificial-intelligence voice-to-text transcription system and the Judiciary's ICT governance framework. He said the Judiciary was assessing human-centered augmented artificial intelligence for the Supreme Court and had a five-year ICT strategic plan and operations manual.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He described the digital infrastructure program, including a software-defined wide-area network, cloud infrastructure, Wi-Fi and WAN GPS backup connectivity, and a procurement project for data-center servers and backup-storage infrastructure for the Supreme Court.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He listed online and electronic systems including the Judiciary electronic payment solution, eCourt pilot, e-procurement, the CMO data hub, the Philippine Judicial Platform, e-notarization, the Olas legal-aid portal, and an interim promulgation application. He also cited online registration and application systems, e-voting, human-resource and financial-management systems, and courthouse-management systems.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co noted the proposed budget of 86271000000 and lower-court disposal rates of 65 to 69 percent in the first half of 20 26. She asked how much of the 4300000000 increase in MOOE was specifically allocated to clearing backlogs and speeding case processing.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: Justice Estuesta said case-disposal targets were performance benchmarks and that case-flow management, supported by the CMO data hub and the Court Management Office's statistics and records division, would monitor caseloads, calendaring, hearings, resolutions, and dispositions. He did not identify a specific MOOE amount dedicated to backlog reduction.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co pressed for details on how ICT upgrades would improve calendaring, noting that scheduling many cases on one date could force cases to be re-calendared and cause delay. She also asked whether additional personnel or court rules were needed to address backlogs.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta, Court Administrator
thread.said: He answered that, beyond ICT upgrades, the 0.959 increase or million increase in the lower courts' budget would support personnel upgrading and reclassification. He said improved compensation was intended to produce a sufficient, attractive, and competitive salary structure and improve justice delivery, but he did not provide a separate digitalization or cybersecurity allocation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sarah Elago
thread.said: Rep. Elago asked whether the Supreme Court's 20 22 to 20 27 Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations remained on schedule in the middle of 20 26. She also asked how specific SPJI activities integrated gender-and-development mandates.

thread.speaker: Raul Villanueva, Judiciary official
thread.said: Raul Villanueva said the plan was highlighted by the courts' digital infrastructure and remained oriented toward 20 27, which he described as a critical transition year between the current SPJI and the next Chief Justice's projects. He said the 20 27 budget proposals were intended to open a gateway for the next phase.

thread.speaker: Charah Jain Ilago, Judiciary official
thread.said: The Judiciary official said amended video-conferencing guidelines allowed video conferencing in all cases in the first- and second-level courts, the Court of Appeals, and the Court of Tax Appeals. For international video conferencing requested by overseas Filipinos, the requesting party paid the related costs and expenses.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Rep. Patal asked for the DBM's comments and recommendations on the proposed 20 27 budget, which reflected an increase of about just over PHP15 billion. He also asked about the status of the electronic-discovery project and how individual litigants could obtain relevant electronic information, including emails, from corporate parties.

thread.speaker: Judiciary official
thread.said: The Judiciary official said DBM comments had not yet been received. The official confirmed that 86270000000 was the Judiciary's proposal and said the goal was to pursue the planned programs with the increase.

thread.speaker: Judiciary official
thread.said: The official said electronic discovery was being addressed through pending revisions to the rules on civil procedure and evidence. Electronic emails, messages, and other electronic evidence were undergoing review, with relevance, materiality, data privacy, sender identification, and forensic issues requiring consideration.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Rep. Patal asked what electronic-discovery protocols were in place or being developed for disclosure, metadata, production format, custodians, deadlines, and the potentially very large volume of email records. He emphasized the value of electronic information to individual litigants deciding whether to proceed or settle.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Rep. Patal asked why electronic notarization could not address the distance and inconvenience of personal appearance before a notary. He also raised concerns about service of process in criminal cases where a respondent might receive only one side of the story.

thread.speaker: Judiciary official
thread.said: The official said applications for lawyers to become electronic notaries public had opened on August 10, 20 26. The Supreme Court had established a legal framework for electronic documents, and notary submissions and electronic payments were being handled online through JEPS, reducing paper-based processing.

thread.speaker: Judiciary official
thread.said: On service of process, the official said personal service was generally required for personal actions, with substituted service available only under specified circumstances. Sheriffs or process servers had to verify service and submit strict returns before the court could proceed, including declaring a defendant in default.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: Rep. Padianos expressed full support for the proposed Judiciary budget but said the support was not a blank check. He conditioned support on measurable results, fewer delayed cases, shorter waiting times, stronger digital systems, greater transparency, and fiscal accountability.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jay Vergara
thread.said: Rep. Vergara asked how much was allotted for digitalization and sought the Judiciary's specific figures, including cybersecurity and infrastructure requirements.

thread.speaker: Judiciary official
thread.said: The Judiciary official stated that total digital infrastructure for the Supreme Court was 5208182274.71. The official indicated that more specific figures, including for training personnel and cybersecurity, could be provided to the member's office.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jay Vergara
thread.said: Rep. Vergara instructed the Judiciary to provide the specific digitalization, training, and cybersecurity figures to her office.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jay Vergara
thread.said: Rep. Vergara manifested full support for approval of the Judiciary's proposed budget.

topics.topic: Hall of Justice and court-facility construction funding
topics.summary: Justice Estuesta presented the Judiciary’s capital-outlay position, explaining that the 2027 proposal included 200000000 for the Cebu NCDO judiciary complex and that Cebu City required 4541000000, with a total facility requirement cited as 5041000000; the Cagayan de Oro amount was unclear in the transcript. Rep. John Tracy Cagas requested funding for a Davao Sur House of Justice, noting that the lot was already available. The Judiciary initially cited an indicative cost of 500000000 pesos for a 5000 square meter property, but the chair directed that the request be revised to a one-story 150000000 project. The Judiciary agreed to include the revised request and look for or realign funds. Rep. Jay Vergara supported the Judiciary’s proposed budget, while Vice Chair Jam Baranda requested priority funding for a new Iloilo City Hall of Justice and cited safety and site concerns. The chair promised assistance for Iloilo, but the facility additions were not shown as finally incorporated into the enacted budget.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish what the Judiciary had proposed or needed for Hall of Justice and court-facility construction, including projects in Cebu, Cagayan de Oro, Davao Sur, and Iloilo City. It also sought to determine whether additional, augmented, or realigned funding could support these facilities and related digital infrastructure.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary said the 2027 proposal included 200000000 for the Cebu NCDO judiciary complex but that additional facility requirements had emerged for Cagayan de Oro and Cebu City. For Davao Sur, the agency initially cited an indicative construction cost of 500000000 pesos for a 5000 square meter property, then agreed to include and seek or realign funds for the committee’s revised 150000000 one-story request.
topics.outcome: The Davao Sur request was revised to a one-story 150000000 project, with the Judiciary undertaking to look for or realign funds and the chair saying it would be strongly recommended. Iloilo City was identified as a priority facility project and received the chair’s promise of assistance, while the additional Cagayan de Oro and Cebu City requirements and the detailed digitalization figures remained subject to budget processing or submission.

topics.topic: Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations and gender responsiveness
topics.summary: The Chair framed the budget discussion around the 138 unorganized courts and the Judiciary’s continuing reforms under SPJI. Justice Estuesta presented a proposed Judiciary budget of about 86.3 billion and described digital, infrastructure, case-disposition, and justice-sector convergence milestones supporting the 2022–2027 plan. Rep. Sarah Elago asked whether SPJI was on schedule and how it integrated gender and development; the Judiciary answered that the plan was on track and cited gender-sensitivity training, gender-fair language, gender-neutral comfort rooms, legal-feminism research, and a digital GAD corner. The Judiciary also discussed justice zones and a Justice Sector Convergence Program, but the proposed amount was garbled and inconsistent in the transcript. Rep. Jay Vergara requested detailed digitalization figures after being told that Supreme Court digital infrastructure totaled about 5.21 billion, and the agency undertook to provide them. Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. supported an adequate budget increase, citing nearly 99 percent obligation of available allotments and improved GAD-budget utilization.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Judiciary’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations was on schedule, how its reforms were being funded, and whether gender and development commitments were integrated into the plan and budget. Members also examined digitalization and justice-sector convergence funding, including whether the Judiciary could absorb additional resources.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary stated that SPJI was on track and that its 2027 budget was designed both to sustain current reforms and to support transition to the next Chief Justice. It said gender responsiveness had been institutionalized through training, gender-fair language, gender-neutral facilities, legal-feminism research, a digital GAD corner, and related justice-sector initiatives, while additional digitalization details would be submitted separately.
topics.outcome: The Judiciary’s SPJI was presented as on track, with gender responsiveness described as institutionalized through multiple programs and facilities. Members expressed support for additional resources, but detailed digitalization figures were left for submission and the Justice Sector Convergence Program amount remained unclear in the transcript.

positions.position: Supported examining the Judiciary’s budget alongside its operational reforms and emphasized the need to address unorganized courts and strengthen access to justice.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair highlighted 138 newly created first- and second-level courts that remained unorganized and nonoperational pending notices of organization, staffing, and compensation. The delay was said to affect judicial capacity and the timely administration of justice.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair said the Judiciary was seeking support not only for additional resources but also for reforms under the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations, or SPJI, to make the justice system more responsive and accessible.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta presented the Judiciary’s proposed budget and the budgets of its component courts, including the Supreme Court and lower courts, the Presidential Electoral Tribunal, the Court of Appeals, the Sandigan Bayan, and the Court of Tax Appeals.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He stated that the proposed Judiciary budget attached to the National Expenditure Program was PHP 86271000000, including PHP 73837000000 for the Supreme Court and lower courts.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He said the proposed budget represented an overall 22 percent increase from the 2026 General Appropriations Act, with increases for the Supreme Court, PET, Court of Appeals, Sandigan Bayan, and Court of Tax Appeals.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He stated that the proposed budget represented an increase of PHP 15660000000, or 22 percent overall.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He explained that the reduction in capital outlay for the Supreme Court and lower courts was mainly because the 2026 budget had included the Manila Hall of Justice, while the 2027 proposal included only the Cebu NCDO judiciary complex.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He said consulting services had submitted the detailed architectural and engineering design for the Hall of Justice in the judiciary complex and that additional funding would be needed for Cagayan de Oro and Cebu City.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: Justice Estuesta requested inclusion of hazard pay for sheriffs, which had not been included in the original proposal, and said the Judiciary was augmenting its proposal by PHP 5344000000.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He linked the Judiciary’s case-disposition performance to institutional transformation under SPJI and described the plan as the blueprint for judicial transformation from 2022 to 2027.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He identified SPJI milestones including the Scriptix artificial-intelligence voice-to-text transcription system, an ICT governance framework, a five-year ICT strategic plan, digital infrastructure, and cloud, network, data-center, and backup systems.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He described software-defined wide-area networking, cloud infrastructure, Wi-Fi and WAN backup connectivity, and procurement of a Judiciary data-center server and backup-storage infrastructure refresh.

thread.speaker: Justice Estuesta
thread.said: He listed additional SPJI-related systems, including online learning, JBC online applications, electronic voting, electronic payment of docket fees, continuing legal education, human-resource and financial-management systems, eCourt, e-procurement, and court-data hubs.

topics.topic: Judicial security and protection of judges and legal professionals
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Ko raised concerns about attacks, threats, and killings involving judges and legal professionals, citing 35 security operations and the Judiciary's proposed increase of 15000000000. The Judiciary said its Office of the Judiciary Marshals was still being staffed, lacked sufficient manpower for independent investigations, and relied heavily on the PNP and NBI. Rep. Ko requested information on extrajudicial killings, attacks, and threats covering 2025 through 2026 before plenary deliberations. The Judiciary said Supreme Court committees were revising the rules on Amparo, Habeas Data, and other remedies, and hoped to pass them before November 6, within the next 2 months. The chair directed submission of the requested materials but ruled that internal drafts could only be provided after approval.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of threats, attacks, and killings involving judges and legal professionals; the Judiciary's capacity to investigate and protect them; and whether updated protective-writ rules, including the writ of Kalayaan, were being developed and could be submitted before plenary deliberations.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary said the Office of the Judiciary Marshals was responding to security risks involving judges but was still being staffed and lacked sufficient manpower for independent investigative work. It said the Judiciary therefore relied heavily on the PNP and NBI, while Supreme Court committees were revising the rules on Amparo, Habeas Data, and other remedies as part of the strategic plan for judicial innovation.
topics.outcome: The Judiciary committed to provide the requested information and materials, while the chair ruled that still-internal draft rules could not be demanded. The status of the proposed budget increase and the Judiciary's independent investigative capacity remained dependent on further submissions and staffing support.

positions.position: Sought stronger and more independent protection and investigation of threats, attacks, and killings involving judges and legal professionals, and requested updates and implementation of the protective-writ rules.
Required submission of the requested materials but ruled that internal draft rules could not be demanded before approval.

topics.topic: Election-case disposition and delayed Supreme Court resolutions
topics.summary: Rep. John Tracy Cagas raised concerns about Supreme Court election cases that remained pending, including matters that had been unresolved for almost a year. He cited reported judicial disposition rates and 16509 cases resolved, while asking why cases involving status quo orders had not yet reached resolution. The court administrator explained that petitions under Rules 64 and 65 required party comments, collation of pleadings, assignment, and division deliberation. The Chair emphasized that election cases required expedited handling because elected officials were limited to three terms and a three-year term. The court administrator said three Supreme Court members were aware of the time-sensitive petitions and assured the committee that the election protest would hopefully be resolved before the next election. The specific supporting case details were to be provided after the hearing, leaving the formal fast-track request not fully settled.

topics.outcome: The Judiciary explained the ordinary procedural steps for election petitions and assured the committee that Supreme Court members were aware of the time-sensitive nature of the cases. topics.topic: Electronic service of process and preliminary-investigation access
topics.summary: Roman Romulo asked whether electronic notarization could reduce the distance and inconvenience of personal appearance. A Judiciary official said applications for electronic notaries public had opened on August 10, 20 26, and that the Supreme Court had established a legal framework for electronic documents and online submissions through JEPS. Rep. Patal then raised the risk that a respondent in a criminal case could have proceedings move forward after only one side had been heard, effectively denying preliminary investigation. The Judiciary answered that personal service was generally required, with substituted service allowed only under specified conditions and documented by the sheriff or process server's return. The official said strict verification was required before a defendant could be declared in default. Rep. Patal suggested the issue might be one of implementation, and the official agreed.

topics.topic: Judicial accountability, performance measurement, and absorptive capacity
topics.summary: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos supported the Judiciary’s proposed budget but said increased funding should produce measurable improvements in case disposition, waiting times, digital systems, and transparency. Rep. Jay Vergara raised digitalization and infrastructure questions; the Judiciary cited 5208182274.71 for Supreme Court digital infrastructure and agreed to provide additional specific figures, including for cybersecurity. Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. cited the Judiciary’s almost 99 percent obligation rate in 2025 and improved GAD utilization as grounds for supporting an adequate increase. The committee chair and Rep. topics.topic: Preliminary-injunction bonds and judicial jurisdiction
topics.summary: Rep. Eli San Fernando raised questions under Rule 58, Section 4(b), about whether approval of an injunction bond was required before a preliminary-injunction writ could issue. A Judiciary official explained that the injunction was an ancillary provisional remedy and that the bond protected the adverse party against damages from implementation. The member tested the rule using a hypothetical bond of x amount, and the official confirmed that the bond was a prerequisite. The exchange was summarized as no bond, no injunction. The official further discussed jurisdiction and stated that a decision could be appealed, while an interlocutory order could be challenged under Rule 65 certiorari; parts of that discussion were unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to clarify whether approval and posting of an injunction bond was a prerequisite to the issuance of a writ of preliminary injunction, and what remedy was available for a court order issued in an interlocutory matter involving jurisdiction.
topics.agency_position: The Judiciary official stated that approval of the requisite injunction bond is a prerequisite to issuance of a writ of preliminary injunction, because the bond secures potential damages to the adverse party. The official also indicated that final decisions may be appealed, while interlocutory orders may be challenged through Rule 65 certiorari, although the jurisdiction discussion was partly unclear.
topics.outcome: The agency confirmed the bond requirement in the formulation that no bond means no injunction. The discussion also identified appeal and Rule 65 certiorari as possible remedies depending on whether the order was a decision or an interlocutory order, but the jurisdiction portion was not fully developed.

positions.position: He sought confirmation that an injunction could not issue without the requisite bond and clarification of the remedy for interlocutory orders involving jurisdiction.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET : (DepEd)

topics.topic: Classroom backlog, construction, repairs, and capital-outlay cuts
topics.summary: Members repeatedly challenged DepEd’s proposed facilities funding against a classroom backlog variously cited at about 142000 to 165000 and against substantial repair and disaster-damage needs. Secretary Angara said the FY 2027 plan would complete 700 classrooms but supported a broader target of roughly 4000 to 5000, while PPP arrangements targeted 16000 classrooms and repairs were funded at about 5 billion. He attributed delivery problems to absorptive capacity, procurement timing, rising construction costs, DPWH and LGU implementation, and the two-year construction cycle, while citing early procurement and decentralization as corrective measures. Members raised district shortages, delayed buildings, missing furniture, earthquake damage, remote-area costs, and possible GAA-PPP duplications. The Secretary committed to prioritize affected districts, coordinate with DPWH and LGUs, submit or provide project lists, and consider additional funding, while Rep. Rodriguez moved for a possible 20000000000 augmentation. The central funding and backlog issues were not finally resolved during the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DepEd’s proposed FY 2027 facilities funding would materially reduce the classroom backlog, address repairs and disaster damage, and be implemented efficiently through DepEd, DPWH, LGUs, and PPP arrangements. Members also pressed for the actual classroom targets, construction costs, procurement timelines, furniture provision, and transparency of project locations.
topics.agency_position: DepEd said the FY 2027 facilities allocation was insufficient to eliminate the nationwide backlog, but represented an effort to expand construction, repairs, LGU participation, PPP delivery, early procurement, and regional implementation. The agency acknowledged persistent delays, rising construction costs, disaster-related damage, and absorptive-capacity constraints, and sought higher infrastructure funding through the budget process.
topics.outcome: The committee received DepEd’s explanation that the 700 figure covered classroom completions, while the broader FY 2027 construction target was roughly 4000 to 5000 classrooms, with repairs funded at about 5 billion and PPP targeting 16000 classrooms. Members sought higher appropriations, priority lists, transparency, and district-specific action; several commitments were made, but the backlog, funding reduction, project duplication, and delivery delays remained unresolved.

positions.position: The committee would support education but would judge the budget by actual classrooms built, repairs completed, project transparency, and delivery of learning infrastructure.
The proposed reduction in basic education facilities and related infrastructure programs was unacceptable in light of classroom congestion and other education needs.
Poor and remote districts required priority treatment because they faced severe classroom shortages, extensive repair needs, and weak access to national infrastructure support.
DepEd needed to resolve furniture backlogs, provide school-level facilities together with buildings, and prevent duplication between GAA and PPP-funded school sites.
Congress should fully support DepEd so classroom construction and repair investments produced safer and more conducive learning environments.
Declining infrastructure funding was counterproductive while the classroom deficit continued, and sustained education investment and effective LGU participation were necessary.
DepEd deserved budget augmentation, including a priority-project package of about 20000000000, because classroom shortages in Cagayan de Oro were acute.
School-building costing should account for difficult terrain, transport, and last-mile conditions rather than applying a uniform amount nationwide.
Earthquake-damaged classrooms in General Santos and nearby areas required urgent repair funding.
Delayed school-building projects should be completed promptly, with furniture and other necessary school investments included.
The gap between classroom appropriations, construction targets, and actual accomplishments required a clear explanation and stronger implementation.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair said the committee would examine DepEd’s plans for schools through the basic education facilities program and the computerization program, and would measure whether prior appropriations produced classrooms and stronger schools.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara presented the proposed FY 2027 DepEd budget, including attached agencies, as 975960000000 dollars. He later said the FY 2027 level was 39350000000 dollars lower than FY 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: He said capital outlay had a large decrease of 67000000000 compared with the FY 2026 GAA. For the learning environment, he identified 17310000000 dollars for more than 4000 classrooms.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar
thread.said: Rep. Edgar highlighted a negative 64.2 percent reduction in basic education facilities, along with reductions in computerization and other education programs, and asked the department to explain the proposed cuts.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said classroom construction normally averaged around 5000 per year. He said the current year had around 60000000000 for infrastructure and new classrooms, representing around 18000 classrooms, while PPP could add another 16000.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: He said the combined effort could produce about 34000 classrooms but remained far short of the 140-plus-thousand classroom deficit accumulated over the years.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar
thread.said: Rep. Edgar sought support for 150 classrooms for his district and asked about the number of teacher laptops under the FY 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said the FY 2027 budget funded only 50000 laptops and that DepEd was requesting an additional 10 b. The figure was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Rep. Adrian Amato
thread.said: Rep. Amato described his district as having a classroom shortage of more than 700 and more than 1000 classrooms needing minor or major repairs, and asked for an update.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd had signed memoranda of agreement with more than 350 local government units, representing over 20000000000 pesos worth of classrooms. He said the next PPP batch would focus significantly on Mindanao and that he would try to include Rep. Amato’s district.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: He said the repair backlog was probably larger than the classroom construction backlog because many buildings were already more than 50 years old. He identified 5000000000 for FY 2027 repairs, compared with only a few billion in earlier years, and warned that some buildings were being kept in use despite needing condemnation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: In response to concerns about learning materials in remote areas, Secretary Angara said DepEd was undertaking early procurement and had closed the gap in procuring textbooks, while acknowledging that timely delivery remained unacceptable and needed improvement.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez asked about the FY 2027 budget for repairing and rehabilitating existing schools, including guidance facilities, comfort rooms, and water and sanitation facilities. He cited initial damage in his province of around 561000000, including 300 damaged wash facilities.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said the FY 2027 repair and rehabilitation budget was 5170000000 dollars and would allow DepEd to repair around 7900 classrooms. He said Rep. Rodriguez’s province would be prioritized.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said there was 1900000000 for FY 2027 and that DepEd could build around 131 classrooms. The surrounding exchange concerned last-mile electrification and the transcript does not clearly identify the precise program attached to the figure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bernadette Escudero
thread.said: Rep. Escudero raised the continuing problem of completed and inaugurated school buildings lacking furniture and asked whether furniture procurement and delivery were centrally managed.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said furniture was supposed to be bundled with the schools. He later clarified that DPWH was involved in classroom completion, while DepEd would coordinate with Rep. Escudero regarding furniture shortages.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: He attributed some furniture delays to the requirement that 20 percent of school furniture be engineered bamboo, which made nationwide sourcing difficult.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd had 3690000000 for furniture, that a new batch was being procured, and that DepEd would ensure an allotment for Rep. Escudero’s district.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bernadette Escudero
thread.said: Rep. Escudero asked how PPP school sites were selected and whether DepEd was aware that some school buildings appeared to be funded both through the GAA and PPP.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said PPP selection was largely based on congestion. He said the first batch involved more than 1000 sites, around 600 of which required demolition, and that the PSIP 3 package targeted 16000 classrooms, with all 16000 hoped to be awarded by December 2026.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bernadette Escudero
thread.said: Rep. Escudero pressed DepEd to address possible duplications between GAA-funded and PPP-funded school sites.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said PPP implementation was slower because it required multiple regulatory and multilateral approvals. He did not provide a specific list resolving the alleged duplications.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair asked how much of the FY 2027 budget was allocated to constructing and repairing last-mile schools, including typhoon-resilient buildings.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said the FY 2027 last-mile schools budget was 1910000000 dollars.

thread.speaker: Rep. Babayan
thread.said: Rep. Babayan referred to funding for 4945 new classrooms and repairs to 11140 classrooms and asked whether Congress could be assured that these investments would produce safer and more conducive learning environments.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said improving learning outcomes and creating a holistic, safe school community were the department’s aims. He linked the physical learning environment with mental health, school counselors, parent-teacher associations, and barangay engagement.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: Relaying civil-society questions, the Chair noted that basic education facilities funding was reportedly down 64.2 percent despite a classroom backlog and schools operating in two or three shifts. The Chair asked why DepEd continued to target relatively few classrooms and how it addressed unfinished projects and disaster-related rehabilitation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd had requested 98000000000 from DBM to match or exceed the current year’s infrastructure allocation, but the request was not granted. He said the backlog was approximately 142000 rather than more than 160000, although calamities continually increased it.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: He said DepEd had expanded implementation beyond one or two infrastructure agencies by engaging more than 350 government instrumentalities, LGUs, private corporations, PPP proponents, and multilateral agencies. He identified this as a response to absorptive-capacity constraints.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair asked when DepEd would publish a complete allocation list showing the locations of classrooms to be built, as requested by civil-society groups for transparency and monitoring.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara referred to placing classroom locations on the website, but the response was incomplete in the transcript. The commitment was not further specified in that exchange.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair asked how many FY 2027 classrooms would depend on LGU counterpart funding or PPP arrangements and what would happen where LGUs could not provide a counterpart.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd currently had no counterpart-funding arrangement, although LGUs played an important role in building classrooms. He said the PC3 PPP package targeted 16000 classrooms.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair asked what would change in FY 2027 to improve delivery despite COA findings of chronic under-obligation in computerization and facilities, and questioned why construction funding should be cut while the backlog grew.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara cited early procurement as the principal response to absorptive-capacity concerns. He later added decentralization, recurring procurement procedures, and downloading funds to regional offices so suppliers could prepare earlier.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair asked how DepEd planned to construct semi-permanent learning continuity spaces during disasters given corruption and efficiency concerns and the existing classroom backlog.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd had built 169 learning continuity spaces in the preceding three months. He said the structures used sandwich panels, carried a 20-year warranty, and cost under 2000000.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: In discussing the budget history, Secretary Angara said infrastructure funding had been around 65000000000 for new classrooms and was now around 14000000000, or possibly 13000000000. He said the reduction would affect the pace of addressing the approximately 142000-classroom deficit.

thread.speaker: A representative
thread.said: A representative said capital outlay was 32330000000 for FY 2027 compared with approximately 99447000000 for FY 2026, a roughly 67.5 percent reduction, and asked why funding was falling despite the classroom shortage.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara attributed the FY 2026 capital-outlay level largely to congressional-stage increases and said collections may not have been as strong as anticipated. He acknowledged that the lower level would affect classroom construction.

thread.speaker: A representative
thread.said: The representative cited a FY 2025 target of 6099 new classrooms with a reported accomplishment rate of 1.65 percent, a FY 2026 target of 4869, and asked about the FY 2027 target and performance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara cited absorptive capacity, infrastructure-agency workload, and project priorities as reasons for the shortfall. He said DepEd had signed memoranda with about 350-plus LGUs and expected results to improve as LGUs bid out projects.

thread.speaker: A representative
thread.said: The representative asked whether DepEd had a master list for prioritizing school buildings and whether the list was published.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd used a congestion index, prioritizing crowded schools operating in two or three shifts, particularly in urban regions. He agreed to provide the master list so it could be followed publicly.

thread.speaker: Rep. Elmer Catulpos
thread.said: Rep. Catulpos said the FY 2027 classroom target was 700 compared with 4869 in FY 2026 and against a backlog stated as 145024, and asked how carryover and delayed construction affected delivery.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said classroom completion depended on LGU project timelines and that construction generally required a two-year horizon. He said more than 30000 classrooms should be completed by the first months of 2027, although the transcript does not clearly identify whether this referred to cumulative or ongoing projects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez said Cagayan de Oro had a classroom shortage of more than 3000, with students attending morning and afternoon shifts or classes outside classrooms. He asked when DepEd would download funds to DPWH or LGUs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said DepEd had already transmitted the funds to DPWH and that DPWH had commenced procurement, although the funds appeared still to be with DPWH’s central office.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez requested a list of priority projects totaling about 20000000000 and moved for an augmentation of 20000000000 for DepEd, in addition to the proposed budget.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara agreed to submit the requested priority-project list.

thread.speaker: Rep. Caroline Agyao
thread.said: Rep. Agyao questioned the uniform costing of school buildings, citing approximately 2500000 per school building even in mountainous or hard-to-access areas where transport and repeated handling increased costs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said the current range was 3 to 3500000 and that the figure had been agreed with DPWH. He said last-mile schools were treated as a priority and agreed to consider the higher costs of remote areas.

thread.speaker: Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles
thread.said: Rep. Bañas-Nograles said a 7.8 earthquake had damaged approximately 1400-plus classrooms in General Santos City and asked whether repairs were included in the FY 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said the FY 2027 budget contained a 5000000000 repair item and promised to prioritize General Santos, Sarangani, and Davao Occidental, which had suffered major earthquake damage.

thread.speaker: Rep. Koko Yap
thread.said: Rep. Yap renewed a concern about 15 delayed school buildings involving around 40 classrooms that had remained unfinished for approximately two years, and asked DepEd to complete them.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said there was a FY 2026 fund for completion of school buildings, would inquire with DPWH about what could be accommodated, and assured Rep. Yap that the district’s needs would receive top priority.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Chan
thread.said: Rep. Chan contrasted a reported FY 2025 target of 6000 classrooms and an actual figure of 99, with 5887 marked ongoing, against a nationwide shortage of around 165000. He asked what bottleneck explained the gap between appropriations and actual construction, including procurement, land, contractors, releases, and implementing arrangements.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara clarified that the 700 figure represented classrooms to be completed, while the broader FY 2027 target was at least 4000 to 5000 classrooms. Using 2500000 per classroom would imply more than 6000 classrooms, but with current costs of 3 to 3.5, the likely output was about 5000-plus, or approximately 4000 to 4900 on the optimistic side.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Chan
thread.said: Rep. Chan asked how long DepEd expected completion of the broader classroom program to take.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
thread.said: Secretary Angara said the reasonable expectation was one and a half to two years, with a longer period where demolition was required.

topics.topic: FY2027 DepEd budget reductions and MOE falling to 174 billion
topics.summary: Members, led by Rep. Edgar, Rep. Nelson Legacion, Rep. Antonino Roman III, Rep. Elmer Catulpos, and the Chair, questioned reductions in DepEd's FY 2027 proposal, especially MOE falling from 207 billion to 174 billion and capital outlay declining sharply. Secretary Angara acknowledged that the reductions would shorten school feeding from 180 days to 120 days, reduce classroom construction, limit laptops to 50000 teachers, and affect per-learner funding and other services. He attributed much of the decline to the unusually high FY 2026 congressional-stage allocation and said DepEd had requested about 1.1 trillion from DBM. The Chair said a net budget increase of about 41.3 billion was largely absorbed by a roughly 57.8-billion increase in personal services, leaving about a 16-billion reduction in MOE and capital outlay. The committee also examined utilization, carryover funds, classroom implementation, voucher safeguards, and the effects on feeding and inclusive education. DepEd agreed to submit a reprioritized list, and the committee committed to consider restoration or augmentation, but no final adjustment was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DepEd's proposed FY 2027 budget reduced maintenance and other operating expenses (MOE), capital outlay, and several core programs despite persistent classroom, learning, feeding, and teacher-support needs. Members also asked what the reductions would mean for service coverage and whether Congress should restore or augment the affected programs.
topics.agency_position: DepEd acknowledged that the FY 2027 proposal reduced MOE, capital outlay, feeding days, classroom construction capacity, and some program coverage, largely because FY 2026 funding had been increased during the congressional stage and because the agency's larger request was not adopted. The agency maintained that the cuts would have concrete effects on feeding, classrooms, learning materials, and other services, and asked Congress to restore or augment priority items while offering to submit a reprioritized list.
topics.outcome: The committee did not accept the reductions as a settled policy choice. DepEd was asked to submit a reprioritized list, while the committee indicated that it would consider restoring or augmenting feeding, inclusive education, ARAL, mental-health, classroom, and other priority programs; the final funding outcome remained open.

positions.position: The Chair supported examining the reductions and indicated that the committee should consider restoring funding for priority education programs, particularly those reduced outside personal services.
Rep. Edgar opposed the reductions in basic education facilities, feeding, textbooks, personnel, computerization, vouchers, and other programs and urged consideration of additional funding.
Rep. Nelson Legacion expressed full support for DepEd's request for additional budget and questioned the effect of the MOE reduction on per-learner funding and local education services.
Rep. Presley de Jesus argued that education should receive a larger national budget share and expressed support for stronger computerization, connectivity, and education investment.

Rep. Antonino Roman III questioned the decline in appropriations and capital outlay despite education and classroom shortages, supported decentralization and stronger LGU participation, and said he supported DepEd.
Rep. Elmer Catulpos pressed DepEd on the sharp capital-outlay decline, carryover and unspent funds, reduced classroom targets, textbook funding, ARAL tutoring, and school safety requirements.
Rep. Audrey Zubiri supported increasing the ARAL program and National Museum funding, arguing that relatively small per-learner investments could produce substantial educational and cultural returns.

positions.who: Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara
positions.position: Secretary Angara supported restoring or augmenting the affected programs, particularly feeding, classrooms, laptops, ARAL, inclusive education, and teacher training, while recognizing implementation and absorptive-capacity constraints.
Jeremy Barnes said the National Museum needed additional MOE and exhibition funding so new facilities could be staffed, maintained, and opened without becoming underused facilities.
