hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET:  (CHR)

topics.topic: FY2027 CHR budget reduction and restoration request
topics.summary: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato presented an original FY 2027 proposal of about 2.75 billion against a 2027 NEP allocation of about 1.27 billion, describing an almost 53% reduction and the elimination of capital outlay. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez sought restoration of the 74,000,000 Tier 1 reduction and asked the CHR to identify its highest-priority Tier 2 items; Palpalato identified preventive monitoring, mandatory expenses, productivity, capacity building, information systems, and international participation, with the exchange pointing to a package of roughly 200 million to 250 million. Another vice chairperson confirmed with Palpalato that capital outlay had been completely wiped out, while Vice Chair Sia Agyong supported reinstatement or a substantial increase. De Lima and Aris Montes separately supported restoration and received answers on the CHR’s monitoring and gender-ombud functions, while Salazar said the 592,000,000 trust fund remained with the Bureau of the Treasury and had not been released. In response to the NGO caucus, Palpalato reiterated the 2,749,000,000 proposal, the roughly 1.27 billion NEP amount, the 53% reduction, and a 34,000,000 MOOE cut, although some figures in that exchange were unclear. The committee required a consolidated, prioritized wishlist with the Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission by September 9, and the hearing was terminated without a final restoration decision.
topics.question: What was the extent and effect of the reduction in the CHR’s FY 2027 proposed budget, and which Tier 1 and Tier 2 items did the committee seek to restore or augment? The committee also sought to establish how the reduced funding would affect the CHR’s statutory and constitutional functions and requested a prioritized written wishlist.
topics.agency_position: The CHR said its original FY 2027 proposal of 2,749,000,000 was reduced by almost 53% in the NEP, with capital outlay eliminated and MOOE reduced. It asked Congress to restore the reduced funding and support prioritized Tier 2 requirements for preventive monitoring, mandatory operating expenses, productivity, capacity building, information systems, infrastructure, and related mandates.
topics.outcome: The committee did not finally resolve the restoration amount during the hearing. Members expressed support for restoring the CHR’s reduced funding and increasing it for prioritized Tier 2 requirements, while the CHR committed to submit a written, consolidated and prioritized wishlist.

positions.position: Supported restoration and augmentation of the CHR budget, including the 74,000,000 Tier 1 reduction and a prioritized Tier 2 package, and indicated support for an increase of 250,000,000.

Supported reinstating the original CHR request or securing at least a substantial increase, arguing that the CHR could not adequately perform its mandate without capital outlay and operating resources.
Supported restoration of the CHR budget and said she would join Rodriguez in insisting on restoration of the needed amount.
Supported restoring the original proposal, particularly because additional resources were needed for the CHR’s gender-ombud and special-law functions.

positions.position: Sought a complete explanation of the budget reduction, its operational effects, and the CHR’s requested congressional augmentation.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato said the CHR’s original FY 2027 proposed budget was 2,749,000,000, consisting of 1,173,000,000 under Tier 1 and 1,576,000,000 under Tier 2.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He said the CHR’s allocation under the 2027 National Expenditure Program had been reduced by almost 53%, equivalent to 1,272,592,000, leaving a deficit of 1,477,000,000 compared with the CHR’s Tier 1 and Tier 2 proposal.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He presented the NEP breakdown as 718,000,805 for personal services, plus 61,330,000 for automatic appropriations for a total of 780,138,000, and 492,000,454 for maintenance and other operating expenses.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Compared with the 2026 GAA budget of 1,347,000,000, the 2027 NEP amount of 1,272,592,000 represented an overall decrease of 74,882,000. He attributed the decrease primarily to the lack of capital outlay.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He said MOOE had a negative variance of 34,888,000, while personal services increased by 103,549,000 because of filled positions, the fourth tranche of the salary standardization law, and automatic appropriations for retirement.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato appealed for reconsideration of the budget and identified Tier 2 priorities, beginning with 108,223,700 for the expanded places of deprivation of liberty visitation and torture-prevention program, including mandatory expenses for central and regional offices.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He identified 18,416,000 for capacity-building activities for Human Rights Action Center officers and local government units, and 10,114,000 for CHR information systems.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He identified 1,934,000 for regional human-rights-mechanism activities and 195,523,000 for additional human-rights resources and wages, including ICT personnel. He also described infrastructure requests, including a permanent central-office building and land acquisition.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said he supported strengthening and increasing the CHR budget, noting that it had fallen from last year’s level. He said the reduction meant the budget would not strengthen the commission.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked whether the 74,000,000 reduction included the combined Tier 2 request and whether the CHR wanted the 74,000,000 restored.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato answered that the Tier 2 request was “1,500,000,000. 76,000,000,000,” which was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked the CHR to submit the 74,000,000 Tier 1 restoration request and its highest-priority Tier 2 items, rather than assuming that the entire request could be funded.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked about the 34,000,000 MOOE reduction and the absence of capital outlay, including whether the capital outlay was for buildings or transportation.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato said the capital-outlay items were mostly for retrofitting, an ICT building, and ICT vehicles.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said those items were required and indicated that he would seek increases for the Tier 1 restoration and a substantial portion of the Tier 2 priorities.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato identified the top priority as strengthening the preventive mandate, including the remaining funding after the DBM increase.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He said the remaining preventive-mandate request was around 4,000,000 after an additional 16,000,000 from DBM, although the exchange also referred to “21 additional 16” and was partly unclear.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He identified 59,000,505 for mandatory expenses for the central and regional offices and said the preventive and mandatory-expense items together enhanced productivity, stated in the exchange as 108,000,237.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He identified 18,416,000 for capacity building and 10,000,000 for rollout training for the central and regional offices on newly developed CHR information systems.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato referred to 227,000,000 for databases and ISSP activities and later described the total priority request as 227,000,000.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He said the request for participation in global and regional national human-rights-institution organizations was 1,900,000.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez concluded that the prioritized package would be about 200 plus, rather than 400, and said the priorities were clear.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez directed the CHR to put the priorities in writing and submit them by the following day, ahead of the committee’s Wednesday deadline.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato committed that the CHR would submit the written priority letter by the next day.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said that, at the proper time, he would move for approval of the budget plus an increase based on the CHR’s computation of 250,000,000.

thread.speaker: An unidentified vice chairperson
thread.said: The vice chairperson said the CHR’s capital outlay had apparently been “completely wiped out” and asked Palpalato to confirm.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato confirmed that the capital outlay had been completely wiped out.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Sia Agyong
thread.said: Agyong said the reduction was inconsistent with expectations that the CHR coordinate with local government units and maintain regional offices. He argued that the CHR needed sufficient funding to perform its mandate.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Sia Agyong
thread.said: Agyong asked how the reduction would affect the CHR’s obligations under international human-rights conventions and its participation in global and regional human-rights institutions.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The agency official identified the original budget as 2.7 billion, with the exact amount spoken as “2.7, yeah, billion.”

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Sia Agyong
thread.said: Agyong manifested that he would support reinstating the original request or securing at least a substantial increase through the budget amendment review process.

thread.speaker: Rep. Leila de Lima
thread.said: De Lima asked whether the CHR intended to include oversight of NTF-ELCAC in its work despite the agency’s monitoring role.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The official said the CHR had no oversight function over NTF-ELCAC because it was under the Office of the President and the CHR was an independent institution. The CHR could monitor activities and investigate violations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Leila de Lima
thread.said: De Lima asked whether 597,742,802.78 in martial-law reparation-trust interest required under the 2026 GAA had been released during FY 2026, noting that the provision was absent from the 2027 NEP.

thread.speaker: Executive Director Lorette Salazar
thread.said: Salazar said the trust fund remained intact with the Bureau of the Treasury and that no release had been made because no amount had been requested. A release could be made only after a request to DBM.

thread.speaker: Rep. Leila de Lima
thread.said: De Lima asked whether the trust fund came from the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund and asked for the status of that fund.

thread.speaker: Executive Director Lorette Salazar
thread.said: Salazar said distribution of reparations had been completed. She described the remaining trust fund as 592,000,000 intended for memorialization, after the agency that completed the reparations mandate had been dissolved.

thread.speaker: Rep. Leila de Lima
thread.said: De Lima expressed full support for the CHR budget and said she would join Rodriguez in insisting on restoration of the needed amount.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Aris Montes
thread.said: Montes asked the CHR to clarify its role in protecting and promoting the human rights of women and girls as the gender ombud.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato said the CHR was designated gender ombud under the Magna Carta of Women and monitored the Philippine government’s compliance with treaty obligations under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Aris Montes
thread.said: Montes asked whether the gender-ombud function included receiving and investigating complaints involving discrimination, violence, harassment, and other violations of women’s human rights.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato answered yes and said the function included investigating gender-based violations through walk-in, telephone, email, and digital or online complaint channels.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Aris Montes
thread.said: Montes asked whether the reduction from the original proposal to the NEP level would significantly affect the CHR’s gender-ombud functions.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato said the commission adapted to meager resources, but additional funding—particularly a dedicated budget for gender-ombud compliance—would help the CHR perform the function and its other special-law mandates.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Aris Montes
thread.said: Montes joined colleagues in calling for restoration of the CHR’s original proposed budget.

thread.speaker: Committee representative presenting the NGO caucus question
thread.said: The NGO caucus asked the CHR to state its total FY 2027 proposal, the amount recommended in the NEP, the shortfall in peso and percentage terms, DBM’s reason for the reduction, the excluded personal-services, MOOE, and capital-outlay items, the operational effects, and the items for which the CHR sought congressional augmentation.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato gave a partly garbled response identifying a Tier 1 amount as “one billion one hundred seventy three million two hundred thirty seven” and another sequence as “1,000,000,000 1,272,000,020.26 1,374,000,000.” The exact intended figures were unclear in this exchange.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He restated that the total proposal was 2,749,000,000 and the NEP amount was 1,272,000,000, representing a reduction of 53%.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato said the capital-outlay reduction affected infrastructure, ICT equipment, software, and transport vehicles, referring to “ND152 million” in the transcript, which was unclear.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: He identified a 34,000,000 MOOE reduction attributed to a decrease in the ISSP.

thread.speaker: Committee chairing official
thread.said: The committee requested that the CHR submit a consolidated wishlist with the Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission by Wednesday, September 9, with the items prioritized.

thread.speaker: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato
thread.said: Palpalato said the CHR would gladly comply with the request.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sarah Elago
thread.said: Elago moved to terminate the hearing on the proposed FY 2027 CHR budget, including the Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission under House Bill number 10,858.

thread.speaker: Committee chairing official
thread.said: With no objection, the chair approved the motion to terminate the hearing.

topics.topic: Tier 2 priority requests and written funding list
topics.summary: CHR Richard Palpalato presented an original FY 2027 proposal of about 2.75 billion, including about 1.58 billion in Tier 2 requests, and identified productivity enhancement, preventive visitation and torture prevention, mandatory expenses, capacity building, information systems, infrastructure, and institutional roles as priorities. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez supported restoring the CHR’s reduction and asked for the first three Tier 2 priorities in writing. Palpalato identified a remaining preventive-mandate request of around 4,000,000, mandatory expenses of 59,000,505, productivity enhancement of 108,000,237, capacity building of 18,416,000, information-systems training of 10,000,000, and regional and global institutional activities of 1,900,000, while also stating a total priority figure of 227,000,000 whose breakdown was unclear. Rodriguez said he would seek an increase based on the CHR’s computation of 250,000,000, subject to fiscal space. In response to the NGO caucus, Palpalato said the CHR had no administrative or programmatic oversight over NTF-ELCAC or the Support to the Barangay Development Program, but needed resources for field monitoring, investigations, assistance, and human-rights education in vulnerable communities. The committee required a consolidated, prioritized CHR and Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission wishlist by September 9, and the CHR agreed to comply.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the CHR’s Tier 2 priorities, the amounts required for each, and which requests should be considered for possible restoration or augmentation. topics.topic: Capital outlay reduced to zero
topics.summary: The CHR chairperson said the FY 2027 NEP was reduced mainly because it contained no capital outlay, affecting the commission’s proposed infrastructure, ICT, facilities, and vehicle requirements. The deputy minority leader asked how zero capital outlay would affect mandate delivery, and the chairperson answered that it would constrain ICT infrastructure, facilities, and regional-office workplaces. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez and Vice Chair Sia Agyong supported restoring or substantially increasing the CHR budget, with Rodriguez specifically identifying retrofitting, ICT, buildings, and vehicles. Rodriguez requested a written list of the CHR’s highest priorities, and the chairperson committed to submit it by the next day. Representative Reneko linked funding needs to jail visitation, torture prevention, rapid response to red-tagging, and digital evidence capabilities; the CHR provided a total protection-program figure of 323,278,000 but did not provide the exact jail-visitation allocation. In the later NGO-caucus exchange, the chairperson restated the proposal as 2,749,000,000 and the NEP as 1,272,000,000, and cited a capital-outlay amount transcribed unclearly as “ND152 million.” The issue was left for subsequent budget amendments rather than finally resolved during the hearing.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed zero allocation for capital outlay would affect the Commission on Human Rights’ infrastructure, ICT capabilities, regional offices, transportation, and delivery of its constitutional mandate. Members also sought the restoration of the capital outlay and clarification of the related Tier 1 and Tier 2 funding requests.
topics.agency_position: The CHR stated that the absence of capital outlay would constrain ICT infrastructure, facilities, retrofitting, regional-office workplaces, software, and transport vehicles, thereby limiting mandate delivery. It sought restoration of the capital-outlay component and broader support for its Tier 2 infrastructure and digital-capability requests.
topics.outcome: Members broadly supported restoring or substantially increasing CHR funding, including the eliminated capital-outlay component, but no restoration was formally approved in the transcript. The CHR committed to submit a written priority list, while the capital-outlay issue remained subject to subsequent budget amendment deliberations.

topics.topic: Case backlog and capacity to resolve investigations
topics.summary: Leila de Lima asked which CHR mandate faced the greatest resource constraints and whether the commission had case backlogs. CHR identified prevention as the most resource-constrained mandate and reported that it had resolved 95.8 percent of a historical backlog of about 28,000 cases, leaving roughly 1,200 pending. De Lima and Antonio Tinio separately pressed CHR on drug-war investigations; CHR cited 493 cases for reinvestigation, 289 cases investigated or concluded by the task force, and 140 cases for resolution, with delays attributed to lack of evidence, noncooperation, missing documents, and reprisal risks. CHR committed to prioritize the 140 cases within the year and submit a written update before plenary. An NGO caucus raised regional staffing and workload concerns, and CHR acknowledged that Regions 4-B, 7, and the Negros Island Region remained affected by manpower and geographic constraints. CHR agreed to submit regional personnel figures, but the additional staffing and FY 2027 appropriation required remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of CHR case backlogs, the status and resolution rate of investigations—particularly drug-war cases—and whether CHR had sufficient personnel and resources to discharge its mandates. topics.topic: Jail visitation and monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty
topics.summary: CHR Richard Palpalato reported that the commission visited 960 facilities in 2024, 985 in 2025, and 617 during the first semester of 2026, but could reach only about one third of 2,920 detention facilities with existing resources. He said DBM had provided 16,000,000 and 19,000 for the expanded visitation program, although the context of the 19,000 figure was unclear, and requested 108,223,700 under Tier 2 for visitation and torture prevention. Representative Reneko supported restoring the budget and pressed for more frequent jail visits, rapid-response legal teams for red-tagging, and digital-forensics capabilities. The CHR gave 323,278,000 as the total protection-program allotment but did not provide a separate jail-visitation or red-tagging amount. Leila de Lima asked which mandate faced the greatest resource gap, and the CHR identified prevention because it shared funding with protection and lacked a dedicated allocation. The CHR agreed to submit rapid-response guidelines, while funding restoration and digital evidence resources remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had sufficient funding and personnel to conduct regular visitation and preventive monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty. Members also asked how the CHR's prevention mandate was funded, including jail visitation, torture prevention, rapid response to red-tagging, and related investigative capabilities.
topics.agency_position: The CHR stated that prevention services, including visitation and monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty, were its most resource-constrained mandate because they lacked a dedicated budget and shared resources with protection services. It maintained that additional funding would permit more frequent and wider facility coverage, earlier risk identification, corrective recommendations, and torture prevention.
topics.outcome: The need for additional funding for jail visitation and prevention services was presented and supported, but the exact dedicated jail-visitation allocation was not supplied during the exchange. The CHR committed to submit rapid-response guidelines, leaving the requested funding restoration and the digital-forensics funding question unresolved.

positions.position: Supported restoration of the CHR budget and particularly supported the Tier 2 request for places-of-deprivation-of-liberty visitation, torture prevention, rapid-response legal deployment, and stronger digital evidence capabilities.
Supported restoration of the CHR's requested budget and regarded funding for its constitutional human-rights mandates, including prevention, as an important investment.

topics.topic: Digital privacy, cyber threats, and digital evidence capacity
topics.summary: A committee member asked whether the CHR had a dedicated program for digital privacy, online harassment, cyberbullying, misinformation, and artificial-intelligence risks. CHR chairperson Richard Palpalato said the Commission had focal officials, research, policy monitoring, and protection activities concerning emerging technology and human rights. Representative Reneko later connected red-tagging to online campaigns, doxing, and deepfakes and asked about rapid-response protocols and funding for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, and secure databases. The CHR cited a broader protection-program allotment of 323,278,000 but did not identify a separate digital-evidence allocation. The CHR agreed to submit guidelines or related materials, while the specific digital-capacity funding question was left unanswered.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had programs, funding, protocols, and operational capacity to address digital privacy violations, online harassment, cyberbullying, misinformation, artificial intelligence risks, and digitally enabled red-tagging. It also asked whether the CHR had digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, secure databases, and systems to preserve digital evidence.
topics.agency_position: The CHR stated that it had institutional activities on emerging technology and human rights, including focal officials, research on artificial intelligence, monitoring of gender-based violence and disinformation, and protection-related work involving technology. However, it did not state a specific budget for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring systems, or secure digital-evidence databases; it only identified the broader protection-program allotment of 323,278,000 and agreed to submit requested guidelines or related material.
topics.outcome: The CHR described existing emerging-technology and human-rights activities and provided the broader protection-program figure, but it did not answer with a dedicated amount for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, or secure database infrastructure. The request for guidelines was accepted for submission, while the digital-evidence funding question remained open.

topics.topic: NTF-ELCAC and barangay development-program monitoring
topics.summary: Rep. Reneko supported restoring the CHR budget and sought funding for jail visitation, rapid-response legal teams, and digital evidence capabilities in response to red-tagging. The CHR said its total protection-program allotment was 323,278,000 but did not identify a separate red-tagging allocation, and it agreed to submit relevant recommendations and guidelines. Rep. Leila de Lima asked about resource gaps, case backlogs, drug-war investigations, ICC membership, and NTF-ELCAC oversight; the CHR reported that 95.8 percent of about 28,000 backlog cases had been resolved, with around 1,200 pending, and identified 493 drug-war cases for reinvestigation. The CHR supported rejoining the ICC but said it had no formal oversight over NTF-ELCAC, limiting its role to monitoring compliance and investigating violations. An NGO caucus then asked about the roughly 740 million Support to the Barangay Development Program and the safeguards and resources needed in vulnerable communities. CHR Richard Palpalato said additional demands would involve more field monitoring, investigations, protection, documentation, and human-rights education, and reiterated the agency's tier-two resource proposal.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHR had sufficient resources and authority to monitor, investigate, and respond to human-rights risks associated with NTF-ELCAC and the Support to the Barangay Development Program. topics.outcome: The committee received the CHR's clarification that it could monitor and investigate human-rights violations connected with NTF-ELCAC and the Barangay Development Program but could not exercise formal oversight over them. topics.topic: ICC reengagement and human-rights implications
topics.summary: The deputy minority leader asked whether the CHR would lead advocacy for the Philippines’ reengagement with the ICC. The CHR said it supported rejoining the ICC and the Rome Statute and had issued statements, policy recommendations, public-information materials, and an EJK report concerning ICC-related developments. The member urged the CHR to speak more visibly for victims and against false narratives surrounding the ICC proceedings involving former president Rodrigo Duterte. Leila de Lima later asked about the status of drug-war investigations and the CHR’s ICC position. The CHR reported 493 cases for reinvestigation and described the task force as having concluded “208 289” cases, an unclear figure, while citing lack of evidence, hostile conditions, noncooperation, and unavailable police documents as obstacles. The CHR unequivocally maintained that rejoining the ICC and Rome Statute would provide an additional assurance of accountability for human-rights violations.

topics.outcome: The CHR gave a clear and consistent answer that it supported the Philippines rejoining the ICC and the Rome Statute and described its related advocacy and investigative work. topics.topic: Community monitoring, dialogues, and human-rights education
topics.summary: A committee member asked CHR to explain its grassroots monitoring, local-government coordination, community-based dialogues, and mechanisms for referring cases to the DOJ. CHR cited barangay human rights action centers, regional coordination, complaints channels, legal clinic caravans, sectoral validation, DOJ engagement under Administrative Order Number 35, and a DOJ referral agreement. When asked for case outputs and status, CHR said it would provide the data, and the member said the committee would await it. The discussion also covered CHR activities on emerging technology, artificial intelligence, digital harms, and disinformation. Sarah Elago asked about community dialogues and human-rights education; CHR reported 34 dialogues in 2025, 122,950 participants in promotion activities, and 51,716 participants as of June 2026, although one intervening figure was transcribed as "20 in five." The agency cited partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher-education institutions, and the Philippine Association of Law Schools. A committee member also indicated support for increasing the CHR budget, whose stated total was about 1.27 billion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHR had sufficient mechanisms and resources for grassroots human-rights monitoring, community-based dialogues, local partnerships, and human-rights education. It also asked how CHR coordinated with the DOJ on referrals and prosecutions, tracked case outcomes, and addressed emerging digital and artificial-intelligence-related human-rights issues.
topics.agency_position: CHR said it already had extensive grassroots mechanisms, including barangay human rights action centers, local-government and interagency coordination, community-based dialogues, complaints channels, legal clinic caravans, and sectoral validation exercises. It also stated that it had DOJ referral arrangements, emerging-technology activities, and partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher-education institutions, and law schools to advance human-rights education.
topics.outcome: CHR's existing programs and partnerships were presented without substantive challenge, but the committee did not receive the requested case-status data during the discussion. The data submission was committed, while the proposed budget increase was only indicated and not shown as formally acted upon in the transcript.

topics.topic: Martial-law reparation trust-fund interest and release status
topics.summary: Rep. Leila de Lima asked whether about 597.7 million in martial-law reparation trust-fund interest had been released in fiscal year 2026 and sought the status of the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund. CHR Executive Director Lorette Salazar answered that the trust fund remained intact with the Bureau of the Treasury and that no amount had been released because the commission had not made a request. She said a request to the DBM would be necessary before any release. Salazar identified the fund as sourced from the 10,000,000,000 reparations fund, said distribution of reparations was complete, and described 592,000,000 as intended for memorialization. The exchange did not resolve the discrepancy between the reported interest amount and the agency's stated trust-fund amount.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether 597,742,802.78 in martial-law reparation trust-fund interest had been released during fiscal year 2026, why the corresponding provision was absent from the proposed 2027 budget, and the current status of the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund.

It said the reparations distribution was complete and that the remaining trust-fund balance was for memorialization purposes.
topics.outcome: The CHR answered that no release had occurred and that the trust fund remained with the Bureau of the Treasury, while stating that reparations distribution was complete and the remaining balance was for memorialization. The difference between the reported 597,742,802.78 interest amount and the 592,000,000 amount cited by the agency was not explained, and no release or follow-up submission was committed during the exchange.

topics.topic: CHR program allocations for personal services, MOOE, and Arleap
topics.summary: Sarah Elago and the committee reviewed the CHR's proposed allocations for personal services, MOOE, Arleap, and its protection, promotion, policy, and jail-visitation programs. The agency reported a stated total of about 1.27 billion, along with program allocations and participation figures for community dialogues and promotion activities. Elago asked whether activities represented expansions and how human-rights education could be institutionalized; the agency cited regional dialogues and partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher educational institutions, and law schools. An NGO and civil-society representative then asked for the CHR's total proposal, the NEP recommendation, the shortfall, the reasons for reductions, affected expenditures, operational consequences, and requested augmentation. Richard Palpalato cited a proposal of about 2.75 billion, an NEP amount of about 1.27 billion, a stated 53% reduction, a capital-outlay figure of "ND152 million," and an MOOE reduction of 34,000,000. The excerpt ended without a complete answer on the DBM rationale, all operational effects, or the requested augmentation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the CHR's proposed FY 2027 budget was distributed among personal services, MOOE, Arleap, and core programs, and how those allocations supported community dialogues and human-rights education. It also asked what budget the CHR proposed to the DBM, what the NEP recommended, the resulting shortfall, and the operational effects of reductions or exclusions.
topics.agency_position: The CHR presented its proposed allocations for personnel services, MOOE, Arleap, and its protection, promotion, policy, and jail-visitation programs. It said regional offices conducted community dialogues and described partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher educational institutions, and law schools to advance human-rights education. On the FY 2027 reduction, the CHR attributed the MOOE decrease to a reduction in the ISSP and identified effects on capital outlay, but did not clearly answer every question concerning DBM's reasons, operational consequences, or requested augmentation.
topics.outcome: The committee received the CHR's program allocations, participation figures, partnership information, and partial explanation of the FY 2027 reduction. The questions on the precise shortfall, DBM's reasons, operational effects, and congressional augmentation were not fully resolved in the excerpt.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (DOTr) - PART 2

topics.topic: Public Transport Modernization Program funding and continuity
topics.summary: Members led by Rep. Carl Legaspi, Rep. Renee Co, Rep. Lim, Rep. Chan, Rep. Rodge Gutierrez, and Rep. Bonispares questioned the sharp reduction in PTMP funding and its effect on operators, commuters, vehicle supply, and program continuity. DOTr said the reduced 2027 amount would support only limited operations, ground preparation, route rationalization, industry consolidation, stakeholder support, and monitoring, while seeking congressional help for subsidies and service contracting. The agency reported a 1,500,000,000 unobligated amount in one update, and explained that the 2026 1,500,000,000 budget had only recently received its cash allotment. Members also challenged inconsistent consolidation figures, including the agency's correction from 86.23% to 83.64%, and requested updated franchise and unit data. The Secretary committed to written explanations within the following week, while other questions on utilization, passenger demand, GPS transmission, reporting baselines, and passenger infrastructure were not fully answered. The issue therefore landed with agency submissions and congressional efforts to restore funding still pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the sharply reduced FY 2027 funding would allow the Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP) to continue, including subsidies, route rationalization, consolidation, service contracting, and support for operators and commuters. Members also sought explanations for prior unobligated funds, current utilization, vehicle and consolidation data, and the department's plans to address financing distress and passenger needs.
topics.agency_position: DOTr said PTMP remained necessary but acknowledged that implementation and utilization had been problems. It said the reduced 2027 allocation would sustain limited operations and ground preparation, while the department intended to pursue equity subsidies, support for distressed transport groups, and congressional restoration or augmentation of PTMP, fuel subsidy, and service-contracting funds.
topics.outcome: The committee did not accept the reduced PTMP funding as sufficient and members repeatedly indicated that they would seek restoration or augmentation of PTMP, fuel subsidy, service contracting, and related active-transport funds. DOTr committed to written explanations and updated consolidation data, but questions about utilization, passenger-capacity effects, route viability, GPS compliance, baselines, and the full continuity plan remained unanswered.

positions.position: Supported increasing PTMP and other commuter-oriented transportation funding and questioned the sharp reduction from the requested amount.
Questioned the passenger-capacity effects of modernization, the large unobligated balances, the viability of the program, and the need for sustained PTMP and active-transport funding.
Supported restoring or increasing funding for PTMP, fuel subsidy, and EDSA Busway operations to protect drivers, operators, and commuters.
Supported restoring fuel subsidy and service-contracting funds and pressed the department to address modernization-loan distress.
Supported refunding active transport, PTMP, fuel subsidy, and service-contracting programs, citing their importance during the oil crisis.
Supported continuing PTMP and requested a clear agency commitment, updated consolidation and utilization data, and additional funding for cooperatives and operators.

positions.who: Move As One coalition and participating civil-society organizations
positions.position: Called for evidence-based utilization reporting, route and demand assessment, GPS accountability, passenger-side infrastructure, active transport, service contracting, and fuel subsidy.

thread.speaker: Rep. Carl Legaspi
thread.said: Legaspi said the department had requested 2,170,000,000 for PTMP but received around 177,000,000, a roughly 91% decrease. He asked how PTMP implementation would proceed under the reduced allocation and questioned why commuter-oriented projects were cut while large projects continued.

thread.speaker: an agency official
thread.said: The official said the department needed the PTMP modernization budget "now more than ever," but did not provide a detailed response to the funding question.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co cited the Philippines' ranking of 63 out of 70 countries in a 2024 urban mobility readiness report and said mass-transport availability remained a concern for commuters.

thread.speaker: LTFRB official
thread.said: The official gave updated June 2026 figures, including 137,218 traditional PUJs, around 7,600 units identified as "fill cup," 23 to 24,000 provincial and city buses, and 13,516 modern PUJs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co compared the current vehicle figures with earlier publicly available data showing about 300,000 operating PUJs. She said the reduction to about 128,000 operating PUJs implied roughly 171,000 units had been lost through modernization and asked the department to account for the resulting passenger-capacity gap.

thread.speaker: LTFRB official
thread.said: The official attributed the decrease in authorized units primarily to route rationalization and said the number of units was not simply a measure of modernization. The answer did not directly quantify the lost daily passenger capacity.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co said DOTR website data showed nearly 9,000,000,000 in PTMP funds from 2018 and asked why amounts remained unobligated, including 200,000,000 or 1,000,000,000 in some years. She specifically requested an explanation for the 2022 unobligated balance.

thread.speaker: LTFRB official
thread.said: The official said data downloaded around May or June showed 1,500,000,000 unobligated, including the continuing 2025 budget of 400 plus million, and said the funds related to modernization amortization and beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co cited 1,600,000,000 unobligated in 2022, described as 93% of the PTMP allocation, and again asked for an explanation.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation
thread.said: The Secretary said the current administration had assumed office only the previous year and had to move forward with PTMP implementation so funds could be obligated and disbursed. He undertook to submit a written explanation, including the role of officials who had handled PTMP in earlier years.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co requested a written report covering PTMP budgets and unobligated funds from 2018 through 2025, including the 2022 to 2025 balances.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked the Secretary to provide a submission timetable.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation
thread.said: The Secretary committed to submit the requested documents "within next week."

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co said the issue affected the livelihoods of jeepney drivers and operators as well as commuters, and questioned the viability and continuing implementation of PTMP.

thread.speaker: Rep. Lim
thread.said: Lim asked what PTMP activities would be affected by the proposed budget of 1,350,000,000, later identified by the agency as a net amount of 176,830,000.

thread.speaker: DOTr PTMP official
thread.said: The official said the 176,830,000 budget would sustain only limited program operations and ground preparations. The planned uses included 60,000,000 for financing and validation of defaulted or distressed units, 20,000,000 for route rationalization, 10,000,000 for LPTRP, 20,000,000 for industry consolidation and development, 10,000,000 for stakeholder support, and 56,300,000 for communications, monitoring, evaluation, and technical and administrative personnel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Chan
thread.said: Chan cited published comparisons showing PTMP falling from 2,500,000,000 to 176,800,000, service contracting from 1,000,000,000 to zero, and fuel subsidies from 2,500,000,000 to zero. He asked whether the proposed budget reflected the department's request for a moratorium on modernization loans and whether the department intended to restore fuel subsidy and service-contracting funds.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said the department planned a 1,500,000,000 subsidy-amortization program for distressed modernization borrowers and referred to a 1,000,000,000 LTFRB budget. He said the department would seek congressional help for service contracting, PTMP, active pathways, and fuel subsidy.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: Gutierrez said active transport and safe pathways had been cut by 97%, from the proposed 1,100,000,000 to 34,000,000, while PTMP had fallen from a proposed 2,000,000,000 to 177,000,000. He asked how the department could implement these programs at those levels.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official attributed the reductions to limited fiscal space and said the department would ask the committee for the same budgets as previously requested.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: Gutierrez said fuel subsidy was a priority because the 2025 budget had been used while the absence of 2026 funding required reliance on DSWD. He said he would support restoring fuel subsidy and service-contracting funds.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares asked about PTMP implementation since 2017 and the funding proposed for 2026 and 2027.

thread.speaker: DOTr PTMP official
thread.said: The official said the agency had requested 11,760,000,000 but was left with 176,300,000 for 2027, described as funding to sustain program operations and ground preparations for recalibration. The official said the department hoped for a more substantial PTMP budget in 2028 and identified a 1,500,000,000 equity subsidy for distressed transport groups facing foreclosure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares asked for updated consolidation data after citing 165,334 franchises out of 191,730, or 86.23%, as consolidated by the November 2024 deadline.

thread.speaker: DOTr/LTFRB official
thread.said: The official corrected the figure, saying the LTFRB's cleansed listing showed 83.64% of groups consolidated rather than 86.23%.

thread.speaker: DOTr/LTFRB official
thread.said: The official reported 2,946 cooperatives or corporations in 2024, 2,956 in 2025, and 3,019 in 2026.

thread.speaker: DOTr/LTFRB official
thread.said: The official undertook to submit the actual number of individual franchises consolidated by the following Monday.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares asked for data on consolidated provisional authorities and modernized CPCs, including the number of units represented by the consolidation figures.

thread.speaker: DOTr/LTFRB official
thread.said: The official said the requested unit-level data would be included in the submission the following week.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares asked how much of the 1,500,000,000 2026 PTMP budget had been utilized.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official explained that the 2026 cash allotment had only been downloaded during the hearing week, so the 1,500,000,000 could not yet show substantial utilization. The official said the budget covered administrative costs, equity subsidy, route rationalization, and other PTMP activities.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation
thread.said: The Secretary said the 2026 PTMP funding included a 400,000,000 equity subsidy, a continuing 2025 fuel subsidy, and service-contracting funding, with the 1,500,000,000 program to be implemented in the following months.

thread.speaker: DOTr PTMP official
thread.said: The official said the 176,000,000 would fund ground preparations and the program grant for 2027, but did not provide a full continuity plan.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares asked how the department could continue PTMP with 176,000,000 in 2027 compared with 1,500,000,000 in 2026, 2,500,000,000 for fuel subsidy, and 1,000,000,000 for service contracting. He also asked what would happen to cooperatives that had invested in modernization and faced foreclosure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares pressed the department to state its position on whether it was serious about continuing PTMP, including equity subsidy, fuel subsidy, service contracting, consolidation, and support for transport groups.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation
thread.said: The Secretary said the PTMP concept was sound but acknowledged that implementation was the problem.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: Bonispares said the House and committee were supportive of the transport sector and would seek to provide more funding so the program could continue, but requested the agency's commitment and supporting data.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked how the department evaluated low budget utilization when reducing FY 2027 public-transport funding.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official said low utilization was one reason for the reduced PTMP proposal and explained that the department had pivoted its policy. The official said an NCA of 1,000,000,000 would be obligated and downloaded to LTFRB for subsidy to modern transport operators and drivers; the transcript's reference to an additional 11,000,000,000 is unclear.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked whether DOTR first assessed passenger demand and route viability before cooperatives incurred debt for modern vehicles.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked what percentage of modern PUVs transmitted valid GPS data to government monitoring systems each day.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official referred generally to fleet-management personnel and the public-utility-vehicle regulatory office but did not provide a percentage.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked what measurable improvement commuters should experience from PTMP and requested clarification of the denominator and baseline for reported modernization and ridership accomplishments.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official said consolidation was only one aspect of modernization and referred to consolidation rates and modernized PUJs, but did not provide the requested baseline or denominator.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked what PTMP did to modernize the passenger side of trips, including stops, terminals, sidewalks, crossings, lighting, passenger information, and interchange facilities, and which level of government was accountable.

thread.speaker: Committee official
thread.said: The committee asked how many personnel handled PTMP route planning, data analysis, monitoring, and evaluation, and how many were plantilla personnel, COS, job-order, or consultants.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official said the exact number was not available and referred generally to road-infrastructure contracting of service and LTFRB manpower.

thread.speaker: People's Budget Coalition representative
thread.said: The coalition's questions emphasized commuter vulnerability to fuel prices, high-capacity public transport, active transport, and continued fuel subsidy and service-contracting programs.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official said the department could not agree more with the Move As One position.

topics.topic: Active transport, bike lanes, and Safe Pathways funding
topics.summary: Members Renee Co, Rep. Lim, Rep. Chan, Rep. Rodge Gutierrez, the Ways and Means Committee chairman, and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the sharp reduction in active-transport, bike-lane, and Safe Pathways funding. The proposed amount was cited variously as 33,900,000 or 33,000,000, compared with about 105 million in the prior year, while another presentation described a reduction from 1,100,000,000 to 33,000,000 or 34,000,000. DOTr said the proposed amount would support only about six kilometers in one exchange and 33 kilometers of Class One bike lanes in another, while DBM cited 2.66% utilization of the 60,000,000 2025 allocation and limited absorptive capacity. DOTr attributed delays to LGU partnerships and tranche-based downloading, and said it would complete procurement for a sidewalk project funded at more than 60 million and use the remaining 34,000,000 with an LGU. Members sought restoration, convergence with DPWH, clearer congressional oversight, and a report on 3,800,000,000 appropriated from 2022 to 2026. The issue remained unresolved as to the final 2027 appropriation, but the agency made implementation and reporting commitments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why active-transport, bike-lane, and Safe Pathways funding had been sharply reduced, whether the proposed amount could deliver meaningful infrastructure, and whether low utilization justified the reduction. Members also asked how projects were being implemented with LGUs, what oversight and monitoring would apply, and whether funding should be restored or amended.
topics.agency_position: DOTr and DBM attributed the reduced active-transport and Safe Pathways proposal primarily to limited fiscal space and low utilization or absorptive capacity, while DOTr said LGU partnerships and tranche-based downloading had delayed liquidation and disbursement. DOTr maintained that active-transport implementation was coordinated with, rather than formally devolved by policy to, LGUs, and undertook to accelerate procurement, use remaining funds, improve monitoring, and submit a progress report.
topics.outcome: The reduction was not restored during the hearing. DOTr and DBM defended the proposed amount on fiscal-space and utilization grounds, while members continued to press for restoration and better oversight; DOTr committed to implementation steps and a progress report, leaving the adequacy of the 2027 funding unresolved.

positions.position: The active-transport allocation should be sustained or restored because bike lanes and connected facilities were necessary for commuters, pedestrians, persons with disabilities, and elderly people.
The committee should help restore active-transport funding and support the department's requested programs.
The committee should support restoring active pathways and other transport-support lines alongside modernization, service contracting, and fuel subsidy.

The 97% reduction in active transport and Safe Pathways funding required committee restudy and restoration; he considered active transport a priority and supported a broader convergence program for maintenance and safety.
The committee needed clarity on whether active-transport construction was being practically devolved to LGUs and stronger congressional oversight of implementation and fund use.

The proposed active-transport and Safe Pathways budget was inadequate despite the program's importance, and the committee needed a comprehensive utilization, achievement, and implementation report before accepting the reduction.

thread.said: She flagged that the proposed 2027 active-transport budget was only 33,900,000, compared with 105,300,000 last year, describing the reduction as roughly two-thirds. thread.speaker: Rep. Chan

thread.said: He said the department planned to restore, with congressional help, a 1,500,000,000 program for modernization-loan amortization or subsidy support. He also referred to 1,000,000,000 in the LTFRB budget for 2027 and requested support for service contracting, PTMP, active pathways, and fuel subsidy.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: He said the active transport bike-share system and Safe Pathways had been slashed by 97% from the proposed 1,100,000,000 to 34,000,000. He also cited PTMP at 177,000,000 against a proposed 2,000,000,000 and asked how these projects could operate with such small net allocations.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: The secretary's response, as transcribed, attributed the reductions to the fiscal-space problem and indicated that the department would ask the committee for the same budgets, hoping the committee would provide them.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: He urged the committee to restudy zero allocations, particularly the fuel subsidy and service-contracting program, and said he would support restoring those programs. He also said active transport was more important than the stalled EDSA Greenways project.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: He asked whether DOTr had a convergence program with DPWH for the construction and maintenance of roads and facilities affecting bicycle riders, noting that cracks and poor riding surfaces could be dangerous, particularly at night.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: He referred to a convergence program with DPWH and said that access roads and rehabilitation formed part of an overall DPWH, MMDA, and DOTr convergence effort concerning connectivity and mobility. The transcript does not show a detailed commitment specific to bike-lane maintenance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: He reiterated support for restoring the affected programs and urged the committee and DOTr to explore expanding convergence beyond busways, including measures that could address broader road-safety and maintenance needs.

thread.speaker: Ways and Means Committee chairman
thread.said: He asked whether it was now DOTr policy to download or delegate construction of bikeways and active-transport infrastructure in the metropolis to LGUs, given the Local Government Code and the concern about double handling.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: He said it was not DOTr policy to devolve the function, but that the department requested local governments to implement active-transport projects. He referred to special provisions, coordination with cities, and the need to address implementation and disbursement.

thread.speaker: Ways and Means Committee chairman
thread.said: He responded that, under the Local Government Code, the function was practically devolved and questioned whether DOTr directly allotted funds to LGUs. He also raised an oversight concern, saying members were not always invited to project groundbreakings or inaugurations.

thread.speaker: Secretary Vince Dizon
thread.said: He said his general instruction was to invite relevant leaders and agreed that participation was important so Congress could verify the proper use of funds. He indicated that special provisions could allow funds to be downloaded to the proper barangay and that reporting to the concerned congressman could be provided.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He questioned the declining active-transport bike-share and Safe Pathways allocations, citing the historical figures from 2022 through the proposed 2027 budget. He asked why a program prominently discussed in the department's presentation had a proposed budget of only 33,000,000.

thread.speaker: Agency implementing official
thread.said: The official confirmed that the budget proposal had fallen from 1,100,000,000 to 33,000,000. He said the 33,000,000 corresponded to 33 kilometers of bike lane and confirmed that the facilities referred to actual separate Class One bike lanes.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked for an explanation of the reduction from more than 1,000,000,000 to 33,000,000. The agency official again cited limited fiscal space.

thread.speaker: Director Abogado, DBM
thread.said: He explained that the reduction was based on absorptive capacity and utilization. For 2025, current-year obligations were described as only three percent, with active transport specifically at 2.66% for the 60,000,000 allocation, while limited fiscal space required prioritizing projects with adequate absorptive capacity.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He clarified whether the 2026 total appropriation was 105,300,000,000 and asked how much had actually been released. The DBM official answered that the total appropriation was 105.376 and that 69.376 had been comprehensively released through the GAA as an allotment order.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Castor
thread.said: She confirmed that the utilization figures were accurate, but explained that most projects were implemented with LGUs and that downloading in tranches from 2023 to 2024 delayed liquidation and disbursement. She said more than 60 million had been launched for sidewalk expansion and committed that procurement would be completed within the next two months, with civil works starting thereafter; she also undertook to use the remaining 34,000,000 in partnership with Barangayaki City.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked whether the department considered the availability of continuing appropriations when judging the 2025 utilization rate, since a 60,000,000 budget might be used in 2026 rather than entirely in 2025.

thread.speaker: Director Abogado, DBM
thread.said: He said DBM generally intended projects and funds to be implemented and utilized within the same fiscal year, but the GAA allowed MOE and capital-outlay extensions until the end of the next fiscal year. He added that DOTr could catch up under its implementation plan.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He requested a DOTr report covering 2022 to 2026, including the total 3,800,000,000 appropriated for bike lanes, active transport, Safe Pathways, and related items; utilization, savings or reverted amounts, concrete achievements, and the department's institutional plan or amendments.

thread.speaker: DOTr implementing official
thread.said: The official agreed to comply with a status and progress report on active transport from 2022 onward. The response also indicated that future budgeting would consider utilization and LGU implementation, although the exact submission deadline was not stated.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked the chair to note the requested deadline for submission and emphasized that pedestrians and bike commuters needed bike lanes and sidewalks. The transcript ends with a reference to 3,033,000,000 for next year, but its precise meaning is unclear.

topics.topic: EDSA Busway zero FY2027 allocation and operating support
topics.summary: Rep. Carl Legaspi first raised concern that the EDSA Busway had a proposed budget of about 1.79 billion but received zero allocation, alongside a sharp reduction in public-transport modernization funding. Rep. Claudine Botisdalim and Rep. Lim then asked what the zero line item would mean for busway operations, maintenance, safety, accessibility, and station rehabilitation. DOTr officials said maintenance, security, accessibility equipment, and station improvements remained necessary, and Senior Undersecretary Pastor identified a FY2027 request of about 1.7 billion to rehabilitate 12 more stations and facilities. Pastor also cited ridership rising from 90,000 to 190,000 passengers per month at one renovated station. Rep. Lim appealed for the full request, while Rep. Rodge Gutierrez later supported restoring transport programs and examining convergence arrangements. The hearing did not record a committee decision restoring the allocation, leaving the issue unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the EDSA Busway had no FY2027 line-item allocation and whether the absence of funding would disrupt its operations, maintenance, safety, accessibility, and rehabilitation. Members also sought clarification on the amount needed to sustain and improve the busway.
topics.agency_position: DOTr officials did not indicate that the EDSA Busway would cease operating. They described continuing maintenance, safety, accessibility, security, and station-rehabilitation requirements and identified 1,700,000,000 as the FY2027 request to rehabilitate 12 additional stations and facilities. The agency also said EDSA Greenways had been pivoted to other projects because it was not progressing as expected.
topics.outcome: DOTr identified 1,700,000,000 as the FY2027 requirement for rehabilitation of 12 additional EDSA Busway stations and facilities, and members supported restoring or funding the request. No committee ruling or confirmed restoration of the zero FY2027 allocation was recorded.

positions.position: Opposed the zero allocation for the EDSA Busway and questioned reductions affecting daily commuters, while expressing support for increasing DOTr funding.
Raised concern that the EDSA Busway had been defunded for the first time and sought an explanation of the operational implications.
Supported providing the requested 1,700,000,000 for EDSA Busway maintenance and operations.
Supported restoring transport programs with zero or sharply reduced allocations and favored exploring a DOTr-DPWH convergence approach for mobility-related infrastructure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Lim
thread.said: Rep. Lim asked what impact the defunding of the EDSA Busway would have and whether DOTr services, projects, or programs would be disrupted. The question covered the maintenance, safety, accessibility, cleanliness, and renovation of the stations.

thread.speaker: Giovanni Lopez, Secretary of Transportation
thread.said: Secretary Lopez deferred the response to Senior Undersecretary Pastor.

thread.speaker: Senior Undersecretary Pastor
thread.said: Undersecretary Pastor described FY2027 requirements for busway maintenance, service providers, maintenance of lifts and elevators for persons with disabilities, security services, and the project management office. thread.said: Undersecretary Pastor highlighted busway-station improvements and rehabilitation, explaining that one station's ridership increased from 90,000 to 190,000 passengers per month after renovation of its manlift and elevator. He said this represented an increase of more than 100%.

He explained that it had been pivoted to other projects because it was not progressing as expected, while emphasizing the continuing need for an active-transport budget.

He supported restoring the programs discussed and suggested that convergence funding could help address mobility and infrastructure concerns.

topics.topic: PTMP consolidation, franchise data, and route capacity
topics.summary: Congresswoman Renee Co raised conflicting fleet data and argued that modernization may have removed about 171,000 PUJ units and roughly 34,000,000 in daily passenger capacity, while the agency attributed the decline mainly to route rationalization and authorized-unit limits. She also questioned nearly 9 billion in PTMP funding and cited 1.6 billion in unobligated 2022 funds; the Secretary committed to submit written explanations and a budget report within the next week. Congressman Bonispares challenged the reported 86.23% franchise-consolidation rate, and the agency corrected it to 83.64% while promising more detailed franchise and provisional-authority data. He also questioned how a 176 million FY 2027 request could sustain a program previously associated with amounts including 1,500,000,000, 2,500,000,000, and 1,000,000,000; the Secretary maintained that the program would continue but acknowledged implementation problems. Civil-society questions sought route-demand testing, GPS compliance, modernization baselines, staffing data, and passenger infrastructure, but several received no precise answer. The issue therefore landed with documentary commitments but material data and accountability questions unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the actual number of public transport units and franchises before and after modernization, whether consolidation reduced passenger-carrying capacity, and how route rationalization affected authorized units. It also examined PTMP funding utilization, the basis for the proposed FY 2027 allocation, and whether the program would continue with adequate data, monitoring, and passenger infrastructure.
topics.agency_position: DOTr and LTFRB officials said the reduced unit counts were substantially attributable to route rationalization and authorized-unit limits, not solely to modernization. They maintained that PTMP would continue, but acknowledged implementation and utilization problems, proposed to use newly downloaded cash authority for subsidies, and undertook to submit updated consolidation, franchise, and budget-utilization data.
topics.outcome: The agency explained that route rationalization and authorized-unit limits contributed to lower vehicle counts and acknowledged that PTMP implementation had been problematic. Updated fleet, franchise, consolidation, and unobligated-fund documents were committed, but the passenger-capacity calculations, GPS reporting rate, route-demand assessment, modernization baseline, and passenger-infrastructure responsibilities remained unanswered or insufficiently supported.

positions.position: She questioned whether modernization had reduced overall passenger capacity, challenged conflicting fleet and consolidation data, and argued that unobligated PTMP funds and insufficient active-transport funding required explanation.

He supported continuing PTMP in principle but demanded reliable consolidation and franchise data, a clear implementation plan, and an explanation of how a much smaller FY 2027 request could sustain the program.
They sought evidence that routes could support modern-vehicle debt, valid GPS monitoring, transparent modernization and ridership baselines, and coordinated passenger infrastructure.
He said the PTMP concept remained valid, acknowledged implementation difficulties, and committed to written explanations and supporting documents.

topics.topic: Unobligated and underutilized transport-modernization funds
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co questioned the loss of transport capacity and cited unobligated PTMP amounts, including nearly 9 billion and 1.6 billion in 2022; DOTr attributed lower vehicle counts to route rationalization and acknowledged that earlier funding required further explanation. The secretary committed to submit a written PTMP report from 2018 through 2025 within the following week. Other members challenged reductions in PTMP, fuel subsidy, service contracting, EDSA Busway, and active-transport funding; DOTr said limited fiscal space, delayed releases, and weak absorptive capacity contributed to the reductions and sought congressional help to restore funds. The agency described the proposed PTMP budget as about 177 million, including financing, route rationalization, consolidation, stakeholder support, and monitoring activities, and said a 1 billion NCA would fund subsidy support. DBM cited 2.66% active-transport utilization for 2025, while DOTr attributed low utilization partly to tranche-based LGU releases and committed to accelerate procurement and submit progress data. Civil-society questions on passenger-demand testing, GPS validity, modernization baselines, passenger infrastructure, and staffing were read into the record, but several answers, especially the GPS percentage and staffing figures, remained incomplete.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why transport-modernization and related public-transport appropriations were unobligated or underutilized, and whether reduced FY2027 funding would impair PTMP continuity, fuel subsidy, service contracting, active transport, and passenger infrastructure. Members also sought updated consolidation, utilization, and monitoring data and asked whether the agency would provide documents or seek restoration of funds.
topics.agency_position: DOTr attributed low utilization and reduced proposed funding primarily to limited fiscal space, delayed or tranche-based releases, and implementation or absorptive-capacity problems. It nevertheless stated that PTMP would continue through a policy pivot, subsidy support, and requests to restore service contracting, fuel subsidy, active transport, and other reduced lines.
topics.outcome: The committee did not resolve the causes and extent of historical PTMP unobligated funds or the adequacy of the reduced FY2027 allocations. DOTr and LTFRB undertook to submit updated data and reports, while members manifested support for restoring or increasing several programs.

positions.position: Questioned whether modernization had reduced available passenger capacity and demanded explanations and historical reports on unobligated PTMP funds. She opposed the sharp reduction in active-transport funding.
