thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: She presented commuter and public-transit data and asked for updated counts of traditional and modern PUJs, buses, UV Express units, and other mass-transport vehicles.

thread.speaker: LTFRB official
thread.said: The official gave June 2026 figures, including 137,218 traditional PUJs, around 7,600 units described unclearly as 'fill cup,' 23 to 24,000 provincial and city buses, and 13,516 modern PUJs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: She requested updated vehicle numbers for the committee.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Using publicly available data, she argued that the number of operating PUJs had fallen from about 300,000 to 128,000 plus or minus, implying roughly 170,000 units lost through modernization. She asked how the system could replace the associated passenger capacity.

thread.speaker: LTFRB official
thread.said: The official attributed the lower number of units principally to route rationalization and the number of authorized units, rather than solely to modernization.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: She cited DOTr website data showing nearly 9,000,000,000 in PTMP funds from 2018 and unobligated amounts of 200,000,000 or even 1,000,000,000 in some years, and asked for an explanation.

thread.speaker: LTFRB official
thread.said: The official said the 2025 unobligated figure was 1,500,000,000, including the 2025 continuing budget of 400 plus million, and said the funds related to modernization amortization and beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: She specifically cited 1,600,000,000 unobligated in 2022, described as 93% of the PTMP allocation, and requested an explanation.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation Vince Dizon
thread.said: He said the current leadership had assumed office only the previous year and could not fully explain earlier obligations, but undertook to submit a written explanation covering the relevant years.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: She requested a written PTMP budget report from 2018 through 2025, including unobligated amounts and the funds available on the website.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The secretary was asked for a submission timetable and committed to provide the documents within next week.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: She warned that PTMP remained insufficiently explained and noted that the proposed active-transport budget was only 33,900,000 versus 105,300,000 the previous year.

thread.speaker: Senior Undersecretary Pastor
thread.said: For FY2027, the agency requested 1,700,000,000 to rehabilitate 12 additional EDSA Busway stations and facilities.

thread.speaker: Rep. Lim
thread.said: She appealed for approval of the requested 1,700,000,000 to maintain and operate the EDSA Busway.

thread.speaker: Rep. Lim
thread.said: She asked how the 2025 fuel-subsidy allocation of 2,500,000,000 had been used and raised concern that FY2027 had zero funding.

thread.speaker: Giovanni Lopez
thread.said: He said the 2,500,000,000 fuel subsidy was downloaded to LTFRB and fully disbursed, less an estimated 5% administrative and engineering component.

thread.speaker: Rep. Lim
thread.said: She asked whether DOTr would request fuel subsidies for FY2027 in case of another oil crisis.

thread.speaker: Giovanni Lopez
thread.said: He said the requested amount was, if he was not mistaken, 5,000,000,005 billion.

thread.speaker: Senior Undersecretary Pastor
thread.said: He said the active-transport budget had fallen from 105,000,033,400,000 to 33,000,000 and that the latter would fund approximately six kilometers of bike lane coverage nationwide.

thread.speaker: Rep. Lim
thread.said: She asked which PTMP activities would be affected by the reduced proposed budget of 1,350,000,000.

thread.speaker: PTMP official
thread.said: The official described a net budget of 176,830,000, with 60,000,000 for financing distressed or defaulted units, 20,000,000 for route rationalization, 10,000,000 for LPTRP, 20,000,000 for industry consolidation and development, 10,000,000 for stakeholder support, and 56,300,000 for communications, monitoring, evaluation, and personnel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Chan
thread.said: She cited reductions in PTMP from 2,500,000,000 to 176,800,000, service contracting from 1,000,000,000 to zero, fuel subsidy from 2,500,000,000 to zero, and the EDSA Busway line from 88,700,000 to zero. She asked whether the budget reflected DOTr's request for a loan moratorium and whether the zeroed-out lines would be restored.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation Vince Dizon
thread.said: He said the department planned to restore the programs with congressional help, citing 1,500,000,000 for amortization subsidy and 1,000,000,000 in the LTFRB budget, while also seeking support for service contracting, active pathways, and fuel subsidy.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rodge Gutierrez
thread.said: He said active transport, bike share, and safe pathways had been cut by 97% from the proposed 1,100,000,000 to 34,000,000, while PTMP had fallen from the proposed 2,000,000,000 to 177,000,000. He supported restoring these funds, including fuel subsidy and service contracting.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation Vince Dizon
thread.said: The agency attributed the reductions to limited fiscal space and said it would ask the committee for the same budgets.

thread.speaker: PTMP/LTFRB official
thread.said: The official undertook to submit the actual number of individual franchise consolidations and related current data by the following Monday.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: He asked how the 1,500,000,000 FY2026 PTMP budget had been utilized and whether the department had current consolidation data, including individual franchises and modernized units.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official explained that the 1,500,000,000 FY2026 budget had only recently been downloaded through a notice of cash allotment, so utilization from January to July could not yet reflect full implementation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: He asked how PTMP could continue with 176,000,000 in FY2027 compared with 1,500,000,000 for equity subsidy, 2,500,000,000 for fuel subsidy, and 1,000,000,000 for service contracting in earlier periods, especially amid possible cooperative foreclosures.

thread.speaker: Secretary of Transportation Vince Dizon
thread.said: He acknowledged that the concept of PTMP was sound but that implementation was the problem.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bonispares
thread.said: He sought and expressed support for a DOTr commitment to continue PTMP and requested supporting data and the agency's position for the committee.

thread.speaker: DBM Director Abogado
thread.said: DBM said the active-transport reduction reflected very low utilization, citing 2.66% utilization for 2025, together with limited fiscal space and the need to fund projects with adequate absorptive capacity.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Castor
thread.said: He said the low utilization figures were accurate but partly reflected tranche-based downloading to LGUs. He committed to complete procurement within the next two months, begin civil works, and utilize the remaining 34,000,000 in partnership with LGUs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He requested a DOTr report for 2022 through 2026 covering the 3,800,000,000 appropriated for bike lanes, active transport, and safe pathways, including utilization, savings or reversions, concrete achievements, and the department's implementation plan.

thread.speaker: DOTr official
thread.said: The official agreed to submit the active-transport status and progress information.

thread.speaker: Safe Travel PH question read by the committee
thread.said: The civil-society question asked precisely how underutilization had been evaluated as a basis for reducing FY2027 public-transport funding.

thread.speaker: DOTr/PTMP official
thread.said: The official confirmed that low utilization was one reason for the reduction, but said the department had pivoted its PTMP policy and would use an NCA of 1,000,000,000 to provide subsidy to modern transport operators and drivers.

thread.speaker: Committee reading civil-society questions
thread.said: The committee asked whether DOTr tested passenger demand before cooperatives assumed vehicle debt, what percentage of modern PUVs transmitted valid GPS data daily, what measurable commuter improvements modernization should produce, and what baselines supported reported accomplishment and ridership figures.

thread.speaker: DOTr/PTMP official
thread.said: The GPS response was incomplete and referred generally to fleet-management personnel and the regulatory office; the official did not provide the requested percentage.

thread.speaker: Committee reading civil-society questions
thread.said: The committee asked what program would modernize passenger-side infrastructure such as stops, terminals, sidewalks, crossings, lighting, passenger information, and interchange facilities, and which government level was accountable.

thread.speaker: Committee reading civil-society questions
thread.said: The committee also asked how many personnel handled PTMP route planning, data analysis, monitoring, and evaluation, and how many were plantilla, COS, JO, or consultants.

thread.speaker: DOTr/PTMP official
thread.said: The official said he did not have the exact personnel number and referred generally to sector, road-infrastructure, service-contracting, and LTFRB manpower.

topics.topic: Fuel subsidy and public-transport service contracting
topics.summary: Rep. Lim questioned the effects of reduced or zero funding for the EDSA Busway, fuel subsidy, active transport, and public-transport modernization. DOTr said the 2025 fuel-subsidy allocation of about 2.5 billion had been downloaded to the LTFRB and fully disbursed, while the agency's stated 2027 fuel figure was garbled and unclear. The agency said about 176.83 million for modernization would support only limited operations, including financing, route rationalization, LPTRP, industry consolidation, stakeholder support, and personnel. Rep. Chan and Rep. Rodge Gutierrez separately pressed for restoration of fuel subsidy and service contracting and highlighted steep reductions in active transport and modernization. DOTr attributed the reductions to limited fiscal space and said it would seek congressional help. The committee members manifested support, but no restoration or appropriation was finally adopted in the transcript.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 budget would affect the EDSA Busway, fuel subsidy, active transport, public-transport modernization, and service contracting. Members also asked whether DOTr intended to restore zeroed-out support for transport operators and drivers, particularly amid an oil crisis and financial pressure on modernized jeepney cooperatives.
topics.agency_position: DOTr said the 2025 fuel-subsidy allocation had been downloaded to the LTFRB and fully disbursed, subject to an unclear administrative deduction. Agency officials said the proposed allocations could sustain only limited modernization and active-transport activities, attributed the reductions to limited fiscal space, and sought congressional help to restore fuel subsidy, service contracting, modernization, and active-transport funding.
topics.outcome: The agency answered how the 2025 fuel subsidy was used and identified limited proposed funding for modernization and active transport. However, restoration of the zeroed-out fuel-subsidy and service-contracting lines, and significant increases for active transport, modernization, and the EDSA Busway, remained subject to congressional action.

positions.position: Supported restoring 1,700,000,000 for EDSA Busway maintenance and operations, 5,000,000,000 for fuel subsidy, and additional support for active transport and public-transport modernization.
Supported restoring fuel subsidy and service contracting and addressing the financial problems of modernized jeepney operators and cooperatives.
Supported restoring active transport, public-transport modernization, fuel subsidy, and service contracting, and favored expanding convergence work with DPWH.
Supported seeking congressional assistance to restore the affected programs and cited limited fiscal space as the apparent reason for the reductions.

topics.topic: North-South Commuter Railway funding, utilization, and completion
topics.summary: Committee members first sought the status of relocation for 637 affected families and were told that none had yet been relocated, although site construction and inspection were ongoing. The DOTr right-of-way official gave April 2027 as the target for completion and was asked to submit detailed relocation and turnover data. Chairman Franz Pumaren questioned whether inadequate funding could affect NSCR utilization. Representative Bong Son Dai then examined the NSCR allocation of about 123.8 billion, foreign-assisted project utilization, right-of-way acquisition, and the financing gap; the DOTr reported an NSCR funding total of about 67 billion, an obligation rate of 89.89%, and a disbursement rate of 47.94% as of June 2026. The Department said the first phase was targeted for December 2027, the Clark demonstration run for June 2028, and revenue operations toward Clark for the last quarter of 2028. The financing gap and a firm full-project completion date remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) had adequate and usable funding, including foreign-loan and GOP counterpart financing, and whether obligations and disbursements were keeping pace. Members also asked about right-of-way constraints, relocation, utilization, and the realistic dates for partial and full operations.
topics.agency_position: The DOTr said NSCR implementation was progressing but depended on continuing foreign-loan proceeds and GOP counterpart funding, with right-of-way acquisition being prioritized. It reported high obligations but substantially lower disbursement for NSCR and gave operating targets of December 2027 for the initial segment and the last quarter of 2028 for revenue operations toward Clark.
topics.outcome: The Department provided utilization, financing, right-of-way, and operating targets, but the hearing did not resolve the funding gap or establish a firm full-project completion date. Relocation information was to be submitted to the committee, with April 2027 given as the resettlement target.

positions.position: He questioned whether insufficient program funds could affect NSCR utilization and pressed the Department to explain how funding increases would translate into effective railway operations.

He supported prioritizing mass-transport railways but criticized undertaking projects without full funding and warned that incomplete financing could waste limited fiscal resources through additional interest costs.
The member sought a firm relocation timetable and detailed documentation on families affected by the South Commuter Railway.

topics.topic: Metro Manila Subway and other railway completion targets
topics.summary: Rep. Bong Son Dai questioned the scale and utilization of railway appropriations, emphasizing that the North-South Railway and Metro Manila Subway together represented about 191.3 billion and roughly 76% of the DOTr-OSEC expenditure program. DOTr officials reported an 82 obligation rate as of July 2026, 33 billion in June and July disbursements for foreign-assisted NSCR and subway projects, and 89.89% obligations against 47.94% disbursements for NSCR as of June. They said about 90% of NSCR and subway right of way had been acquired, while funding remained incomplete, including only 26 billion of a 47 billion GOP counterpart requirement. The agency targeted December 2027 for initial NSCR partial operations, June 2028 for a demonstration run, late 2028 for revenue operations, and around 2031 for Metro Manila Subway operations. Rep. France separately questioned whether the PNR South Long Haul investment was justified, and a PNR official cited current ridership of about 1,600 daily and projected ridership of 20 to 25,000 under the original alignment. PNR committed to submit written data and justification before plenary consideration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 railway allocations were being utilized effectively, whether right-of-way and counterpart-funding constraints could be managed, and when the North-South Commuter Railway and Metro Manila Subway would reach operations. It also asked whether the proposed PNR South Long Haul investment was financially justified and requested supporting ridership and investment data.
topics.agency_position: The DOTr said railway implementation was progressing, with high NSCR obligations, substantial recent disbursements for foreign-assisted projects, and most NSCR and subway right of way acquired. It maintained targets of December 2027 for initial NSCR partial operations, roughly the last quarter of 2028 for NSCR revenue operations after a June 2028 demonstration run, and around 2031 for Metro Manila Subway operations; PNR officials continued to support rehabilitation and requested additional capital funding for South Long Haul.
topics.outcome: The DOTr provided indicative completion and operations targets, utilization figures, and right-of-way status, but funding gaps and counterpart-fund requirements remained concerns. The PNR South Long Haul question was committed for further review through a written submission before plenary consideration.

positions.position: Supported continued railway investment but warned that projects should not be undertaken without full funding, timely counterpart funds, and credible implementation plans because unfinished projects could waste scarce fiscal resources.
Questioned whether the PNR South Long Haul investment was worth its cost and required written ridership and investment-justification data before plenary consideration.
Maintained that South Long Haul remained viable if rehabilitation and additional capital outlay were provided, citing projected increases in daily ridership.

topics.topic: LRT-2 capacity and improvement funding
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co raised LRT-2's record ridership of 250,578 passengers and cited 197,000,000,000 in proposed rail transport funding for improvement. The LRTA or rail administrator said LRT-2 had begun with 18 train sets, that the trains were more than twenty-two years old, and that aging equipment constrained peak-hour capacity. The agency said the Gen Four train sets were financed through an ODA loan and described LRMC revenues, including about 31 billion in total revenues, about 14 billion for rehabilitation, and about 6 billion in 2015 operating expenses. Rep. Renee Co also questioned LRMC's responsibility for leaks, flooding, cleanliness, and other service failures; the administrator cited 121,000,000 in outstanding penalties. The agency undertook to submit NNIC revenue and passenger-service-charge data, while Rep. Renee Co said she would submit a formal written request. The capacity and debt issues were not fully resolved in the hearing segment.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed rail transport investment would address LRT-2's rising ridership and limited train capacity. It also examined the financing and use of rail revenues, responsibility for LRT-1 service deficiencies, and whether additional revenue and passenger-service data would be submitted.
topics.agency_position: The agency said LRT-2's principal challenge was its aging train fleet, with trains more than twenty-two years old and insufficient capacity during peak periods. It stated that Gen Four train sets were ODA-loan financed, that LRMC revenues were being used for system rehabilitation and operations, and that LRMC could be penalized for concession-agreement violations.
topics.outcome: The agency explained that aging LRT-2 trains were the main capacity constraint and confirmed that additional train procurement was part of the budget proposals, but it did not provide a clear capacity projection or directly resolve the public-debt question. Revenue, accountability, and NNIC data matters were left for written submissions and follow-up.

positions.position: The proposed rail investment and train-set procurement should be assessed against LRT-2's record ridership and passenger-capacity needs. She also pressed for accountability from LRMC for service-quality failures and requested detailed revenue and remittance data from NNIC.
LRT-2's aging trains and limited train availability were the principal capacity constraints, while LRMC was responsible for concession performance and subject to penalties for violations.

topics.topic: PNR South Long Haul Express investment

topics.topic: General Santos Airport repairs and passenger boarding bridges
topics.summary: Dennis Hernandez raised the status of repairs at General Santos Airport and sought a firm completion timetable. The DOTr said ongoing repair and rehabilitation works were targeted for November, with the latest date extending to the first week of December. Hernandez recalled that the agency had accepted a 200,000,000 repair budget and argued that it should also cover redesign and passenger boarding bridges. He warned that boarding-gate congestion would worsen once the airport became fully operational and handled more flights. The agency referred to aircraft separation requirements for Airbus three thirty operations, but did not fully explain the technical plan for resolving congestion. The matter landed with a timetable commitment, while the detailed boarding-bridge and expansion plan remained incompletely answered.

topics.topic: Naga Airport runway and right-of-way funding
topics.summary: Rep. Nelson Legacion raised the Naga Airport's prolonged delay, attributing it to property acquisition and right-of-way problems dating back to the project's decision in 2014. He asked whether the 2027 allocation of about 900 million would complete the 2.1-kilometer runway earthworks and also start the concrete runway. The Secretary of Transportation and agency project officials said the allocation would complete the 2,100 embankment activities and commence initial pavement or concreting simultaneously. The agency said Phase One was expected by January and Phase Two by the first quarter of 2027, while acknowledging a six-month delay and contractor price-escalation concerns. The Secretary also committed to closer implementation and a catch-up plan if needed. The issue landed with agency commitments, although some dates and the cited accomplishment figure remained unclear in the transcript.

topics.agency_position: The agency said the 2027 allocation of 900,000,000, also referred to as N900 million, would complete the 2,100 runway embankment or earthworks and allow initial pavement or concrete runway activities to begin concurrently. topics.topic: Calbayog Airport upgrading and runway completion
topics.summary: Representative Stephen James Tan raised the need to complete the Calbayog Airport upgrade and restore a direct Manila flight. He cited 2026 funding of about 62 million for strip grade correction and 100 million for perimeter fencing and asphalt overlay, and identified requirements of about 117 million for road transfer, 100 million for right of way, and 350,000,000 for runway completion. Secretary Giovanni Lopez cited general right-of-way funding of about 2.7 billion and said DOTr would coordinate with CAAP. A CAAP official said procurement was ongoing and that the works were being targeted for completion by 2027, subject to the contract of award and coordination with DOTr. CAAP also said the matter would be elevated to top management, but did not expressly confirm the requested 350,000,000 2027 allocation.

CAAP said procurement for the ongoing airport works was proceeding, expected completion by 2027, and that the matter would be elevated to top management, but it did not expressly confirm a 350,000,000 2027 allocation.
topics.outcome: CAAP indicated that the ongoing works were being procured and targeted for completion by 2027, with the matter to be elevated to top management. topics.topic: Tuguegarao Airport infrastructure and multiyear funding
topics.summary: Joseph Lara raised the importance of Tuguegarao Airport as the Region 2 gateway and questioned whether earlier and multiyear appropriations would be implemented. He cited a previous amount spoken as 150,000,020.24 and sought 100% assurance on the multiyear funding. Secretary Banoy identified 150,000,000 and a corporate operating budget multiyear allocation of 477,000,000, while saying the corporate operating budget would be used. On runway and safety issues, Banoy referred to an unclear amount and the DOTr general right-of-way fund. Lara also requested tower and equipment improvements, all-weather capability, and a night rating. Banoy gave a qualified assurance that the night-rating program would proceed if it met organizational priorities, leaving the implementation details open.

topics.outcome: The agency identified multiyear corporate operating budget support and pointed to the general right-of-way fund for possible runway and safety-related needs. topics.topic: Ozamis City Airport modernization funding
topics.summary: Representative Inviu Aminal raised Ozamis City Airport modernization as a regional and presidential priority targeted for completion by 2028. DOTr officials confirmed that the project had received no DOTr funding from 2023 onward and cited limited fiscal space and low obligation or utilization rates as possible reasons. The secretary mentioned about 300 million in connection with the proposal, while the implementing authority confirmed a ballpark modernization requirement of about 2.1 billion. The agency also cited 169 million for site acquisition, a transcribed phase-one amount of 303,300,000,000, and 891,000,000 for the FY2027 phase-two asphalt overlay. The secretary declined to commit to a specific final FY2027 amount without board consultation and undertook to get back to the committee, leaving completion funding unresolved.

topics.topic: Palawan port and airport development
topics.summary: Rep. Carl Legaspi requested updates on Palawan’s ports and airports, including Port San Fernando, Buliluyan Port, Taytay-Sandoval Airport, and Busuanga Airport. PPA said San Fernando and Borac ports were being prepared for turnover to the provincial government, after which the province would handle further development, including a passenger terminal at San Fernando. It reported ongoing Buliluyan expansion and commitments for further RoRo and Cagayancillo facilities. DOTr officials said Busuanga had an allocation of about 573 million, an ongoing 2,100-meter runway, and a 2027 allocation of about 950 million for landside development. They also said procurement for the Taytay-Sandoval feasibility study would proceed within the month, with a hoped-for award by November. The matter landed with agency implementation commitments rather than a new committee funding action.

It said Buliluyan expansion was ongoing and committed to further port facilities, while DOTr officials reported ongoing Busuanga works, planned feasibility-study procurement for Taytay-Sandoval, and 2027 funding for Busuanga landside development.
topics.outcome: The agency provided status updates and timelines, including commitments on port turnover, Buliluyan expansion, Taytay-Sandoval feasibility-study procurement, and Busuanga runway completion. The record did not show a final committee ruling or additional funding action beyond the stated 2027 Busuanga allocation.

topics.topic: MARINA cybersecurity, seafarer systems, and processing charges
topics.summary: Chairman Franz Pumaren asked MARINA to confirm the cyber incident, identify system accountability, and explain the effect on seafarer-document processing. MARINA clarified that the incident occurred on August 13 and said the affected system was about seven years old, with a technology refresh and disaster-recovery system included in its Tier 2 proposal. The agency said it had used a temporary system, preserved data, and resumed operations in a controlled environment. The chairman then raised reports that the usual 1,000 charge had become 10,000 to 20,000 for fast-track processing. MARINA agreed to investigate the alleged charges and possible middlemen, while the chairman requested a report. The issue therefore landed as committed rather than resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether MARINA's IT system had suffered a cyberattack, who was accountable for the system and its recovery, and whether the agency had adequate funding for a technology refresh and disaster-recovery system. It also sought an explanation for reports that seafarers were being charged substantially higher amounts for fast-track processing.
topics.agency_position: MARINA said the cyber incident had not resulted in data loss and that operations had resumed through a temporary and controlled system. It said the system required a technology refresh and disaster-recovery capability, while the alleged fast-track charges would be investigated.
topics.outcome: MARINA answered that DICT was investigating the cyber incident and that the agency needed funding for system modernization and recovery capability. The alleged fast-track charges remained under investigation, with MARINA committed to provide a report.

positions.position: He pressed MARINA on system accountability and funding needs, and expressed concern that seafarers were allegedly being charged between 10,000 to 20,000 for fast-track processing instead of the usual 1,000.

topics.topic: Philippine Coast Guard vessels and disaster-response support
topics.summary: Chairman Franz Pumaren pressed the DOTr and Coast Guard on the need for additional vessels and outboard motors, citing a request for "seven or eight" vessels and obsolete motors. Secretary Banoy referred to a commitment to provide Coast Guard support by year four, but the transcript did not clarify the exact scope. Rep. Anna York Bondoc described flooding that caused ten to twelve hours of delay and required Army six-by-six trucks and Navy assistance in affected areas. Secretary Vince Dizon said the DOTr could pursue a feasibility study and longer-term elevated public transport through coordination with DPWH. Bondoc commended the Coast Guard's rescue work and requested full budgetary and operational support during disasters. No specific additional Coast Guard appropriation was announced.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget adequately supported Philippine Coast Guard vessels, outboard motors, and disaster-response operations. Members also asked how the DOTr would maintain transportation and provide coordinated support in areas affected by flooding.
topics.agency_position: The DOTr acknowledged the Coast Guard's vessel request and referred to a commitment to provide support by year four, while the exact scope was unclear. On broader disaster-response transportation, the agency pointed to feasibility studies, elevated public transport, and coordination with DPWH, but did not state that additional vessels, outboard motors, or full Coast Guard funding had been secured.
topics.outcome: The agency acknowledged the Coast Guard vessel request and cited a support commitment by year four, while the chairman separately requested additional vessels and outboard motors for appropriations consideration. Rep. Bondoc's request for full Coast Guard support was recorded, but no specific additional funding or final allocation was stated.

positions.position: The Coast Guard required additional vessels and outboard motors, with obsolete motors replaced and the agency's operational priorities presented for appropriations consideration.

The Coast Guard deserved full budgetary and operational support because it was conducting rescue operations during flooding and other disasters; affected communities also required reliable public transportation.
Long-term disaster-response mobility required elevated public transport and a whole-of-government approach coordinated with DPWH.

topics.topic: NLEX flooding mitigation and alternative transport routes
topics.summary: Rep. Anna York Bondoc raised the severe NLEX flooding and traffic disruption, reporting delays of about ten to twelve hours over roughly 10 kilometers. Vince Dizon cited short-term measures including raising the pavement by about point six meters northbound and point five meters southbound, flood walls, dredging, floodgates, sheet piles, and heavy-duty pumps. He also said TRB had issued NLEX a notice to explain, was studying possible reimbursement, and had sought toll-free passage and proactive advisories. Bondoc pressed for alternative expressways or viaducts, unfinished bridges and bypass roads, and public transport options because McArthur Highway and railway access were flooded. Dizon said the agency would coordinate with other officials and ask its planning office to study additional rail infrastructure, while identifying elevated public transport as a long-term solution. Bondoc also requested full Coast Guard support and cited the clearing of 15,000 items or material, although the transcript's description of that figure was unclear. The issue landed with agency commitments and further coordination, but without a complete resolution of the alternative-route and public transport gaps.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DOTr and other agencies would address recurring NLEX flooding and severe traffic disruptions, including immediate flood-control measures, alternative roads and bridges, public transport options, and longer-term elevated or rail infrastructure. It also sought clarification on the status of related PPP infrastructure and support for emergency responders.
topics.agency_position: DOTr, through Vince Dizon, said NLEX flooding required coordinated short-, medium-, and long-term action involving TRB, NLEX, DPWH, and other agencies. The agency supported immediate road, drainage, floodgate, pumping, and information measures, while identifying elevated public transport and whole-of-government coordination as longer-term requirements; several route and rail proposals still required further coordination or study.
topics.outcome: DOTr described immediate NLEX flood-control, drainage, pumping, toll-management, and information measures, while longer-term viaduct, bridge, floodway, and elevated public transport proposals remained subject to coordination, feasibility work, or DPWH action. The public transport and alternative-route concerns were therefore not fully resolved during the exchange.

positions.position: Highway and flood-related infrastructure should be pursued through a group effort, including locally funded roads and possible PPP or BOT projects.

topics.topic: Maritime passenger safety, insurance, and vessel regulation
topics.summary: Rep. France questioned MARINA about Orient classification society's continued preventive suspension and whether it was being favored or treated differently from other societies. MARINA said Orient had not been blacklisted because an appeal was pending before the Office of the President, and described a system involving three local classification societies and seven international IACS members. Rep. France remained concerned about how the system could properly classify roughly 6,000 to 7,000 boats and urged that only inspected, seaworthy, and properly insured vessels receive operating authority. He also asked about prior committee recommendations on passenger insurance. MARINA said it had drafted an increase in passenger coverage for submission to its Board, while Undersecretary Castor said the existing personal passenger accident insurance program covered 400,000 for hospital or injury expenses. The insurance increase was committed for Board submission, but the Orient justification and broader adequacy concerns were not fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why Orient classification society remained under preventive suspension without being blacklisted, how MARINA regulated and accredited classification societies for domestic vessels, and whether passengers were adequately insured before vessels were authorized to operate. It also asked what had happened to prior committee recommendations on passenger insurance.
topics.agency_position: MARINA said Orient remained under preventive suspension, had not yet been blacklisted, and had an appeal pending before the Office of the President. It said the classification framework included three local societies and seven international IACS members, denied favoritism, and reported that an increase in passenger insurance coverage had been drafted for submission to the MARINA Board.
topics.outcome: The agency answered that Orient was still suspended but not blacklisted and that its appeal remained pending, but the committee did not receive a fully developed justification for the classification society's treatment. MARINA reported a pending insurance-coverage increase, while the existing program was stated to cover 400,000; the adequacy of the classification system and insurance arrangements remained subject to further action.

positions.position: Rep. France questioned the basis for Orient's continued suspension and possible blacklisting, expressed concern about whether classification societies could properly handle the domestic vessel fleet, and insisted that vessels be inspected, seaworthy, and properly insured before receiving operating authority.
Tony Boy Roman stressed that changing weather and the rainy season could create serious passenger-safety risks and said the committee needed to protect the riding and traveling public.

topics.topic: Land acquisition and distribution balances and the 2027 target
topics.summary: Secretary Estrella reported accelerating land-title distribution, including 410,179 titles covering 556,088 hectares under the Marcos administration as of 08/12/2026. Members questioned whether the 2027 target of about 20,000 to 22,000 hectares was adequate, and DAR acknowledged that the target was constrained by the DBM budget ceiling and was not enough. The civil society representative highlighted conflicting LAAD balances of 147,493 hectares, about 700,000 hectares, and 563,076 hectares; Secretary Estrella said 750,000 hectares was the more accurate figure and suggested DAR might reduce it to 500 or a little less during the year. DAR said much of the larger balance related to partializing collective CLOAs rather than entirely new acquisitions. The agency also described its balance-cleansing process under MC 4 series of 2014 and said it was reviewing the policy to impose stricter, Secretary-level controls. DAR committed to provide official LAAD figures and Agrarian Reform Fund utilization data, but the committee did not resolve which balance should govern the 2027 budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish DAR's actual land-acquisition and distribution balance, the figure underlying the President's 2027 title-distribution directive, and whether the proposed funding and targets were sufficient. It also examined how DAR cleanses the LAAD balance, reports accomplishments, and addresses land titles affected by legal or documentation problems.
topics.agency_position: DAR maintained that the practical balance was 750,000 hectares, while distinguishing land still requiring acquisition from parcels being processed through SPLIT and partialization of previously distributed collective CLOAs. It attributed the limited 2027 LAAD target and funding proposal to the DBM budget ceiling, acknowledged that existing landowners' compensation balances remained, and said it was reviewing the rules for deleting or cleansing land from the LAAD balance.
topics.outcome: DAR identified 750,000 hectares as the more accurate practical balance, but the record also retained the conflicting figures of 147,493 hectares, about 700,000 hectares, and 563,076 hectares. The agency attributed its 20,000-hectare target and limited funding request to the DBM ceiling and agreed to provide official balance, accomplishment, and fund-utilization data; the underlying balance and adequacy of funding remained contested.

positions.position: Supported the DAR budget and SPLIT project but questioned whether the project and its funding were sufficient to complete individual titling before the 2027 expiration.
Pressed DAR to explain its 2027 land-distribution targets, documentation backlog, funding constraints, and the continuing protection of farmers affected by the Saraya case.
Sought updated reports on land distribution, revalidation, land conversion, SPLIT implementation, and electronic titles.
Contested the conflicting LAAD balances, questioned the legality and transparency of land-balance deletions, and sought full funding and accomplishment reporting.

topics.topic: LAAD funding, land deletions, and the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance
topics.summary: A civil society representative questioned DAR's conflicting LAAD balances, which ranged from 147,493 hectares and 563,076 hectares to about 700,000 hectares and a response referring to 750,000 hectares. The representative challenged DAR's 20,000-hectare target, the deletion of land from the balance, and the agency's ability to preserve the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance. DAR said it was following MC 4 series of 2014 but was reviewing and seeking to amend the deletion process, including possible centralization under the Secretary. On funding, DAR attributed its proposal to the DBM ceiling and cited about 7 billion in landowners' compensation, including 2.2 billion in cash, while the representative presented substantially larger amounts for completing the balance. DAR agreed to publish official LAAD figures and requested one or two days to submit missing ARF utilization data. It also reported 135,884 validated collective CLOA-equivalents, 1,481,491 hectares, 1,075,672 beneficiaries, and 330,497 e-Titles, but the central balance and funding questions remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which LAAD balance DAR was using for budgeting, the legal and procedural basis for deleting land from that balance, and how DAR could meet the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance. It also sought official accomplishment, funding, and utilization data supporting DAR's reported figures.
topics.agency_position: DAR said it was using existing procedures under MC 4 series of 2014 to validate and remove low-priority or legally problematic landholdings from the LAAD balance, but was revisiting and seeking to amend those procedures. The agency attributed its proposed funding to the DBM budgetary ceiling, cited 2,200,000,000 as the cash portion of a reported 7,000,000,000 landowners' compensation balance, and agreed to publish official LAAD figures and submit missing ARF data.
topics.outcome: DAR provided partial explanations and some accomplishment figures but did not resolve the conflicting LAAD balances, establish a definitive legal basis for deletions, or provide the requested ARF utilization data during the hearing. It undertook to publish official LAAD figures and submit the missing ARF tally within one or two days.

positions.position: The representative questioned the reliability of DAR's competing LAAD balances, challenged the legality and due-process implications of deleting land from the balance, and pressed DAR to request funding sufficient to meet the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance.
The undersecretary maintained that DAR was following MC 4 while reviewing it, and supported stricter, more centralized deletion procedures to protect farmers.
Palmares presented DAR's reported project accomplishments, including validated collective CLOAs, hectares covered, beneficiaries, and e-Titles.

topics.topic: SPLIT project, World Bank loan, collective CLOAs, and e-titles
topics.summary: Rep. Leila de Lima asked whether SPLIT remained a DAR priority, whether its World Bank loan was exhausted, and whether the project could be completed before its 12/31/2027 expiration. Secretary Conrad Estrella III said SPLIT was proceeding at full speed, remained a priority, and had an unexhausted loan, while explaining that it was needed to parcelize collective CLOAs. DAR officials said the DBM ceiling supported about 20,000 hectares annually, or roughly 20,000 to 22,000 hectares in 2027, at an estimated 10,000 per hectare, which they acknowledged was insufficient. De Lima requested regional 2025–2026 output data and the loan's disbursement status, but those figures were not supplied in the transcript. DAR also reported about 703,000 debt-condonation certificates distributed, cumulative distribution of 4,800,000 hectares from the start of CARP, ongoing regional shapefile work, and digitalization estimated at 80 to 90%. The matter landed with DAR commitments to validate excluded beneficiaries and complete shapefile work, while requested SPLIT performance and disbursement details remained outstanding.

topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DAR about the landowners’ compensation budget, the 2026 allocation of about 500 million, and the proposed 2027 amount of about 100 million. The agency explained that 70% could be paid through government bonds and 30% in cash, with Land Bank issuing the bonds and handling valuation. DAR said the 2026 allocation had zero utilization because OP approval for its release was still pending, and that payments followed a first-in, first-out process. The agency committed to provide a supporting list of pending landowners’ compensation payments.

It said the 2026 allocation of 500,000,000 had not yet been utilized because OP approval for its release was pending, and committed to provide a supporting list of pending payments.
topics.outcome: The committee received answers on the backlog, the 30% cash and 70% bond structure, Land Bank’s role, and the zero utilization of the 2026 allocation pending OP approval. DAR undertook to provide a supporting list of pending compensation payments.

positions.position: He pressed DAR to account for the 2026 cash allocation, explain the compensation balance and cash-versus-bond structure, identify the bond issuer, and support the proposed funding with a list of pending payments.

topics.topic: PBBM Bridges foreign-assisted project and FY2027 loan treatment
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio asked whether the PBBM Bridges project was financed by a Republic of Korea loan and how its proposed funding of about 1.4 billion would be reflected in the FY 2027 budget ceiling. The foreign-assisted-projects undersecretary answered that the total loan package was 22 billion and said the loan contract was scheduled for final signing on Monday. Rep. Salvador Plato separately asked whether the project was grant-funded or ODA, and a DAR official answered that it was ODA. Rep. Marlo Bancoro asked whether at least six bridges in his district could be implemented, while DAR said it was trying to implement projects that year and conservatively expected one third of the list to proceed. Rep. Tim Cayton asked about selection criteria and a Nueva Vizcaya crossing; DAR cited validation, farmer beneficiaries, food security, and economic internal rate of return, after reviewing 1,200 locations and approving "three fifty" sites as transcribed. The financing reconciliation and definitive 2027 schedule were not resolved, but DAR made implementation and follow-up commitments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the PBBM Bridges project was financed by a Republic of Korea loan or ODA, how loan proceeds and the GOP counterpart would be reflected in the FY 2027 budget ceiling, and whether proposed bridges could be implemented in 2027. Members also asked how bridge sites were selected and whether a specific Nueva Vizcaya crossing could be considered.
topics.agency_position: DAR said the PBBM Bridges project was associated with a 22,000,000,000 loan package requiring final loan-contract signing, while another agency answer characterized the project as ODA. DAR said implementation was being pursued as early as the current year, with one third of the list conservatively expected to proceed, and said bridge selection was based on validation, farmer beneficiaries, food-security potential, and economic internal rate of return.
topics.outcome: The agency provided different characterizations of the financing—as a loan package requiring final signing and as ODA—but the transcript does not show a definitive reconciliation of the loan, ODA, GOP counterpart, and budget-ceiling treatment. DAR undertook to pursue implementation, assigned an undersecretary to examine the district concern, and received a request for a Nueva Vizcaya feasibility study; the specific 2027 implementation schedule and funding treatment remained open.

topics.topic: Agrarian debt condonation and land-tenure security
topics.summary: Secretary Conrad Estrella III presented debt condonation as a central DAR and presidential priority under Republic Act No. 11,953 and said the statutory 06/30/2026 completion deadline had been met. DAR reported about 703,000 certificates distributed, covering about 901,246 hectares, while the identified statutory scope involved approximately 57,760,000,000 in agrarian debt; some debt figures in the transcript were inconsistent or unclear. Representative Leila De Lima asked whether SPLIT and its World Bank loan remained priorities, and Estrella answered that SPLIT was proceeding at full speed, the loan was not exhausted, and the project would expire on 12/31/2027. DAR officials said the DBM ceiling supported only about 20,000 to 22,000 hectares annually and that 10,000 per hectare was insufficient. The chair questioned why some beneficiaries had not received certificates, and DAR cited the BARM distribution as the remaining verified gap while undertaking to validate other alleged exclusions and submit a detailed explanation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status and completion of DAR’s agrarian debt-condonation program, including the number of beneficiaries and obligations covered, any exclusions, and the remaining distribution of certificates. It also examined whether the SPLIT project and World Bank financing remained priorities for FY 2027 and whether the proposed land-tenure-security funding was sufficient.
topics.agency_position: DAR stated that debt condonation under Republic Act No. 11,953 had been completed within the statutory deadline, with only final certificate distribution in the BARM area remaining. It also stated that SPLIT remained a priority for FY 2027 and that the World Bank loan was not exhausted, but acknowledged that the DBM-imposed land-tenure-security funding ceiling was insufficient for DAR’s preferred coverage.
topics.outcome: The agency answered that debt condonation was substantially completed, with only final distribution in the BARM area remaining, but the committee requested validation and further explanation regarding allegedly excluded beneficiaries. SPLIT remained a stated FY 2027 priority, while the adequacy of its land-tenure-security funding and the requested regional and loan-disbursement data remained open for submission.

topics.topic: Protection of CLOA holders and ARBs in land disputes
topics.summary: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella raised the Wanderlust title overlap and asked DAR to identify the affected land, titles, ARBs, and barangays. DAR reported around 745 hectares affected, 63 collective titles covering about 677 hectares, 276 affected ARBs, and around four ARBs directly affected by fencing, while confirming the initial 438.5-hectare projection. DAR's legal undersecretary said conflicting titles required cancellation of one title and that eligible and disposable portions covered by CLOAs should remain free from Wanderlust claims. DAR said it was coordinating with the OSG and DNR, investigating the missing survey plan, and collating areas for possible reversion action, but gave no timetable. Fuentebella requested certified lists and technical survey materials within the week, and the chair committed to pursuing the concern. Rep. Elijah San Fernando separately questioned 2027 land-distribution backlogs, which DAR attributed primarily to insufficient funding and DBM budget ceilings, and raised the unresolved Saraya case and protection of CLOA holders.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of the Wanderlust title overlap, the number of affected hectares, titles, and ARBs, and DAR's legal position and timetable for protecting CLOA holders. It also sought explanations for DAR's 2027 land-distribution targets, funding constraints, and the status of the Saraya case and related protection of farmers.
topics.agency_position: DAR stated that it was mandated to protect ARBs and that CLOAs issued on eligible and disposable land should remain free from Wanderlust claims. It was coordinating with the OSG and DNR, investigating the questionable title and survey records, and collating the land areas needed for possible legal action, but gave no filing timetable.
topics.outcome: DAR confirmed the reported overlap, the affected collective CLOAs and ARBs, and its general duty to protect the beneficiaries, but it had not determined a filing timetable or resolved the title conflict. The committee requested technical records and pressed DAR to expedite coordination and legal action; the Saraya-related timetable and protections remained open.

positions.position: He supported DAR's budget and pressed for expedited legal, survey, and administrative action to protect Saroma farmers, ARBs, and CLOA holders from the Wanderlust overlap and fencing.

thread.said: He asked whether the Wanderlust title overlapped at least two barangay sites in Saroma, identified in the transcript as Salvacion and San Ramon, and asked about the affected population and CLOA coverage.

thread.speaker: DAR official
thread.said: The official confirmed the overlap with Salvacion and San Ramon and gave an approximate population of 2,000. The official said 63 collective CLOAs covering 677 hectares overlapped with the Wanderlust title and confirmed that DAR's initial projection of 438.5 hectares was based on a survey by DNR.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked how many individual ARBs were affected by the overlap and how many were affected by Wanderlust fencing activities. He also requested a list of the affected ARBs.

thread.speaker: DAR official
thread.said: The official said around 276 individual ARBs were affected by the overlap and that around four were directly affected by the fencing activities.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella
thread.said: He cited the reported issuance of the Wanderlust title on 02/14/2024 and DAR's distribution in December 2025 of 3,497 land titles to 2,697 ARBs covering 5,929.336 secondtors of agricultural land, including land in Sonoma. He asked whether the distribution had occurred as described.

thread.speaker: DAR official
thread.said: The official answered, "As far as I know, yes, sir," regarding the reported title distribution and attendance of the DAR secretary and the Camarines Sur governor. The official said no concern had been raised to DAR by the provincial governor regarding the Wanderlust title, CLOAs, or overlaps.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella
thread.said: He requested within the week a certified list and technical plotting or survey plan showing the CLOAs and collective CLOAs overlapping the Wanderlust title, as well as all portions of the NARA settlement overlapping it. He also asked whether OCTs, TCTs, and CLOAs issued to ARBs received equal treatment as titles issued under other government grants.

thread.speaker: DAR official
thread.said: The official answered that ARB titles received equal treatment and identified OCTs in response to the question about free patents and sales patents. On the legal position regarding the overlap, the official said DAR was exploring its options and that some ARBs had filed a case involving disturbance of possession arising from the fencing.

thread.speaker: DAR undersecretary for legal concerns
thread.said: The undersecretary characterized the matter as two conflicting titles over the same parcels. He said that under Republic Act 496, as amended by Presidential Decree 1529, one title must be canceled, and that a reversion action under Commonwealth Act 141, as amended by Presidential Decree 705, should be filed by the Office of the Solicitor General. He stated that CLOAs issued on portions found to be alienable and disposable should remain free from claims by Wanderlust.

thread.speaker: DAR undersecretary for legal concerns
thread.said: He said DAR was coordinating with the OSG and the DNR regarding the interrelated matter and the reversion case being considered by DNR. He stated that DAR was mandated to protect the interests of its ARB partners and was pursuing the matter, but was still collating and segregating the portions that were alienable and disposable from forest and timberland portions allegedly included in the Wanderlust title.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked whether DAR had located the purported Wanderlust survey plan SI 2676 and how its absence affected the alleged title.

thread.speaker: DAR undersecretary for legal concerns
thread.said: The undersecretary said DAR was trying to locate the approved survey plan and noted that DNR normally did not approve original survey plans on forest and timberland. He added that the title appeared to have been reconstituted under Republic Act 26 using an owner's duplicate copy that DAR could not locate, and said the absence of the survey plan had a very great effect on the title's validity, although the title could not simply be collaterally attacked.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnulf Bryan Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked the secretary to expedite action and protect the people of Saroma, stating that he intended to investigate the matter further and pursue legislation. The chair responded that the committee would get to the bottom of the matter as soon as possible and recognized it as a valid concern.

thread.speaker: Rep. Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: He asked the secretary to explain the 2027 targets for landholdings entering initial documentation, approved surveys, registration, and actual land distribution, including the budget implications and the backlog between front-end and downstream targets.

thread.speaker: DAR undersecretary for field operations
thread.said: The undersecretary said DAR was still completing documentation for landholdings, including holdings already distributed but lacking documentation and holdings distributed while landowner compensation remained unpaid.

thread.speaker: DAR undersecretary for field operations
thread.said: He attributed the backlog primarily to lack of funding and said DAR's funding proposal was based mainly on the budget ceiling issued by DBM.

thread.speaker: Rep. Elijah San Fernando

thread.speaker: DAR official

The transcript does not contain a clear answer on the timetable for the task force terminal report or the requested protections.

topics.topic: Agricultural land-use conversion, inactivity penalties, and renewable-energy projects
topics.summary: A committee member first asked how DAR monitored and enforced reported illegal agricultural land conversions. Secretary Conrad Estrella said local government units were responsible for many conversions, while DAR called them out, directed parties to the proper procedure, and reported that many had complied. Rep. Sarah Elago then raised a study showing a decline in agricultural land from 50.19% to the transcript's unclear 47.64333.3%, alongside solar-farm expansion, and questioned a proposed PacSilica project involving 4,000 acres or an unclear hectare figure. Estrella said DAR would contest PacSilica's or BCDA's eminent-domain exercise, and a DAR undersecretary reported distribution of about 13,775 hectares while offering updated data. Elago requested reports covering conversion applications, approvals, converted lands, and related implementation for specified years. Rep. Salvador Plato separately asked whether the penalty for agricultural inactivity and premature conversion under the cited statutory provision was strictly enforced, and DAR answered yes. The enforcement position was stated, but detailed conversion data remained subject to submission.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DAR was adequately monitoring and enforcing agricultural land-use rules, including illegal conversion, renewable-energy projects, agricultural inactivity, and premature conversion. Members also asked for data on land conversion, ARB land status, and DAR's implementation of related programs and mandates.
topics.agency_position: DAR said it monitored and called out illegal agricultural conversions, communicated with local governments, and reported that some parties returned to the proper procedure and complied. On renewable-energy-related conversion, DAR said it would defend its mandate and contest the validity of eminent-domain exercises affecting agricultural land and farmers. DAR also stated that the penalty for agricultural inactivity and premature conversion was strictly implemented.
topics.outcome: DAR answered that it monitored illegal conversion, enforced the inactivity and premature-conversion penalty, and would defend farmers against disputed renewable-energy-related land takings. topics.topic: ARB revalidation and inclusion in the RSBSA database

topics.topic: FY2027 DAR budget, utilization, and support-services allocation
topics.summary: The committee reviewed DAR’s FY2027 proposed allocation and its utilization of prior appropriations. The chair cited a proposed net budget of about 14.691 billion and identified allocations for land tenure security, agrarian justice, and beneficiary development and support. Secretary Conrad Estrella III reported support-services accomplishments and utilization rates, including a 47% obligation rate and 70% disbursement rate for FY2026 as of June. DAR committed to complete remaining debt-condonation work, improve implementation and utilization, and continue land, justice, and support-service programs. topics.question: The committee was establishing DAR’s FY2027 proposed budget, how it had used prior appropriations, and whether the requested resources were aligned with land tenure, agrarian justice, debt condonation, and support-services priorities. It also sought to determine what DAR committed to deliver with the proposed allocation.
topics.agency_position: DAR maintained that its prior appropriations had supported substantial land-distribution, debt-condonation, justice, and support-services accomplishments. It defended the FY2027 request as necessary to complete remaining condonation work, sustain land distribution, strengthen agrarian justice, and provide productive support to beneficiaries, while acknowledging the need to improve implementation and utilization pace.
topics.outcome: The agency presentation established DAR’s stated budget, utilization record, support-services accomplishments, and FY2027 priorities. The committee then terminated the briefing without a recorded challenge to the agency’s budget figures; remaining implementation commitments were left for agency follow-through.

topics.topic: DOH FY2027 budget reduction and priority-item restoration
topics.summary: The committee chair highlighted a proposed DOH budget of about 354 billion and described a reduction of roughly 95 billion, or 21.2%, against the FY2026 enacted level. Secretary Mercado said the DOH had requested 837,000,000,000 but received approval for 353,000,000,000, and identified the indirect-member PhilHealth gap, HFEP, and hospital operations as priority restoration items. PhilHealth officials described an indirect-member benefit requirement of about 2.44 or R244 billion dollars against an allocation of 74, with an additional 170 identified as necessary to reach breakeven. Mercado cited PHP19 billion requested for HFEP against PHP14.5 billion provided and about 12,000,000,000 for hospital operations. Rodriguez supported the DOH and PhilHealth budgets and said he would seek the requested increases. The committee also requested rare-disease lists and earmarked-revenue information, but the exact 2027 sin-tax and rare-disease funding figures were not established.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 DOH budget was sufficient to sustain the Department's five pillars, universal health-care commitments, hospitals, facilities, and PhilHealth-related benefits. It also sought to identify the priority items and amounts that should be restored, and to clarify the funding gap for indirect-member premium subsidies and earmarked revenues.
topics.agency_position: DOH officials maintained that the FY2027 net budget of 353,800,000,000 supported the Department's five pillars, hospital operations, HFEP, primary care, and universal health care. They nevertheless identified major restoration priorities: about 170 for indirect-member benefit payments, PHP15.1 billion as stated for the HFEP shortfall, and about 12,000,000,000 for hospital operations. PhilHealth officials said the 74 allocation was insufficient against an expected indirect-member benefit payout of about 2.44 or R244 billion dollars, and said they would coordinate with DBM on unavailable earmarked-revenue estimates.
topics.outcome: The agency identified the indirect-member PhilHealth benefit gap, HFEP, and hospital operations as the principal restoration priorities, and Rodriguez expressed support and said he would seek increases. The rare-disease funding request and 2027 earmarked-revenue estimates remained incomplete, with documents and coordination left for follow-up.

Sought a clear accounting of earmarked PCSO, PAGCOR, and sin-tax revenues and suggested that collection of these revenues could substantially address the PhilHealth funding gap.

topics.topic: Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) cuts, utilization, and reverted funds
topics.summary: Members questioned the reduction of HFEP funding from the DOH request of about 19 billion to an allocation of about 14.5 billion, although the Secretary also gave an inconsistent stated shortfall of PHP15.1 billion. Representative Suntay cited an audit showing only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities operational, or roughly 33 percent, and challenged facility planning and political allocation. The Secretary said site conditions, catchment planning, facility standards, and a rules-based referral network would guide future projects, and undertook to improve compliance and oversight. Representative Garin raised low HFEP obligation and disbursement figures and called for projects to have complete designs, programs of work, budgets, and procurement arrangements before inclusion. Representative Nava said completed super health centers remained unequipped and asked for primary-care standards and the amount of funds reverted to the National Treasury. The Secretary said active construction would be completed before new projects were started, and the Chair directed the DOH to submit reverted-funds data before plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the HFEP allocation was reduced, how effectively HFEP-funded facilities and projects were being used, and whether projects were being prioritized according to health-network needs rather than political requests. Members also asked what funds had been reverted to the National Treasury and whether those funds could be restored or repurposed for health facilities.
topics.agency_position: The DOH said HFEP allocations should be governed by site conditions, facility standards, catchment-area planning, and a rules-based Universal Health Care referral network rather than by political requests. It acknowledged implementation and utilization problems, said active projects should be completed before new projects were started, and undertook to provide data on reverted funds and develop standards for primary-care and super health facilities.
topics.outcome: The HFEP reduction, low utilization, facility planning problems, and politicization concerns were not resolved during the hearing. The DOH committed to standards, closer oversight, and coordination, while the Chair required submission of reverted-funds data before plenary; the specific reverted amount and any restoration of HFEP funding remained outstanding.

positions.position: Supported restoring HFEP funding because rural health facilities needed renovation, expansion, and equipment, and identified HFEP as one of the House's principal restoration priorities.
Sought additional HFEP support for Bukidnon and a health center in Moolog, arguing that the approved amounts were inadequate for facilities and equipment in a province without a DOH hospital.
Argued that low facility utilization and unequal district treatment showed failures in planning and possible politicization of HFEP, and demanded concrete corrective measures.

Asked how hospitals, ongoing projects, super health centers, and health centers were prioritized.
