thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado presented an HFEP allocation of 14,500,000,000, covering facilities, infrastructure, and equipment.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Vice Chair Rodriguez said a 60,000,000 allocation for his area would support renovation, expansion, and equipment for rural health centers, and then asked how much the DOH had proposed and how much had been cut.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said the DOH's total request was 837,000,000,000 and the approved amount was 353,000,000,000, describing the difference as R485 dollars; the wording and currency of the difference were unclear.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: In response to Vice Chair Rodriguez's request for restoration priorities, Secretary Mercado identified HFEP as a priority because local governments needed to become sustainable and properly equipped.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said the DOH requested PHP19 billion for HFEP but received PHP14.5 billion, and stated a shortfall of PHP15.1 billion. The figures do not reconcile in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Vice Chair Rodriguez summarized HFEP as one of the three main restoration priorities, alongside the PhilHealth gap and DOH hospital operations, and said the House should try to restore those amounts.

thread.speaker: Representative Audrey Zubiri
thread.said: Representative Zubiri said Bukidnon partners had requested 2,000,000,000 for district health facilities but only approximately a little less than 5,000,000 had been approved. She asked how provincial allocations were determined and whether they were based on population or another standard.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The official said HFEP required certain site conditions before a locality could be included in the budget and undertook to coordinate with Representative Zubiri's office about the apparent deficiencies.

thread.speaker: Representative Audrey Zubiri
thread.said: She raised a Bagong Filipinas health center in Moolog and said the local request was 19,000,000 for X-ray sets, generators, and a water-impounding facility, while only 2,700,000 had been allocated. She requested that the DOH review the amount.

thread.speaker: Representative Bong Suntay
thread.said: Representative Suntay cited an audit indicating that only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities were operational, or roughly 33 percent. He questioned whether facilities had been built in locations where local governments could not support the required personnel.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said HFEP's omnibus guidelines required site conditions before a locality was considered. He added that the DOH was moving toward assessing the complete catchment of a region or province and applying standards for health centers, district hospitals, and provincial hospitals when allocating infrastructure or equipment resources.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said HFEP would now be viewed as part of a holistic regional network under the Universal Health Care law, with referral routes providing continuity of care to an apex hospital.

thread.speaker: Representative Bong Suntay
thread.said: Representative Suntay pressed the Secretary for concrete steps and asked why the original HFEP guidelines had apparently not been followed, warning that the same problem would recur unless the flaws were acknowledged.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado attributed the difficulty partly to the devolved nature of health care, under which local chief executives and local health personnel were under local-government purview. He said that during his term he would be more engaged in ensuring that HFEP requirements were followed and communicated to local chief executives.

thread.speaker: Representative Bong Suntay
thread.said: Representative Suntay alleged that health care was being politicized and that facilities were constructed in response to political requests, producing unequal treatment among districts. He asked what would be done for constituents who had been unable to obtain assistance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado agreed that health-service delivery should not be a political favor and said the DOH was developing a rules-based procedure to promote equity and access. He said he could not speak for past decisions.

thread.speaker: Representative Janette Garin
thread.said: Representative Garin asked for HFEP obligation and disbursement figures.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado reported that the 2025 HFEP allotment was 13,700,000,000, with 12.4 obligated, described as almost 90.8 percent, and disbursement at 47.03.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: For 2026, he cited an HFEP amount of 11.9, with 1,964,000,000 obligated, or 16 0.4; the transcript is garbled and the meaning of the final figure is unclear.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He also cited 20,483,000,000, with 5,000,000,000 obligated and disbursed 7.58, followed by an obligation rate of 24.64 and disbursement of 15.04. The relationship among these figures is unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Representative Janette Garin
thread.said: Representative Garin characterized the 2026 HFEP figures as approximately less than 1 percent disbursement and around 47 percent obligation, and asked the DOH to confirm whether lengthy documentary, design, and approval requirements caused projects to move back and forth between regional and central offices for more than a year.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said the current omnibus HFEP guidelines required applications, site conditions, and other requirements to be complete before the budget was included.

thread.speaker: Representative Janette Garin
thread.said: Representative Garin said implementation requirements should include an actual design, program of works, approved budget, and procurement arrangements before a project entered the GAA. She attributed reversions partly to frequent changes in undersecretaries and directors and called for adjustments to prevent a repeat.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: In response to Representative Jay Vergara's question about hospital prioritization, the official said existing hospitals, ongoing projects, HFEP super health centers, and health centers were being prioritized.

thread.speaker: Representative JC Rahman Nava
thread.said: Representative Nava asked whether the DOH was standardizing primary-care facilities and what minimum services each facility should provide, because those standards would determine the equipment required.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said licensing requirements for primary-care facilities had been deferred because they were too stringent, but would be revisited. He said the intent was to provide access to consultation rather than require every facility to have a birthing center, minor operating room, and dental clinic.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He identified consultation, basic laboratory services, basic X-ray, and a pharmacy as the services currently being provided through Yakap, and said a super health center would be a higher-level primary-care facility that could potentially include outpatient surgery.

thread.speaker: Representative JC Rahman Nava
thread.said: Representative Nava said two super health centers in his district had been completed structurally but remained nonfunctional because they were not fully equipped, reportedly for about two years. He said there was no 2027 budget for equipping them and asked for the DOH's plan.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said the DOH would set standards using a spoke-and-hub arrangement: basic services at primary facilities, a higher-level super health center potentially in each district, a tertiary facility in each province, and an apex hospital in each region. He said the roadmap would align facilities with the Universal Health Care referral network.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: After Representative Nava raised the construction and implementation arrangements, Secretary Mercado said he had received word that the questioned facility was a DPWH-funded project.

thread.speaker: Representative JC Rahman Nava
thread.said: Representative Nava said HFEP projects had been channeled through DPWH regional offices in 2023–2024 and that substantial amounts had consequently been reverted to the National Treasury. He asked for the amount reverted and whether the committee could work to return the funds to health purposes.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said the reverted DPWH funds were being used for priority projects and that his guidance was to complete projects already under active construction, with no new projects to be started.

thread.speaker: Representative JC Rahman Nava
thread.said: Representative Nava again requested the specific reverted amount, saying the funds might be brought back because they had originally been intended for health.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said the DOH would coordinate on the data and that the funds could be repurposed, although the remainder of his answer was garbled.

thread.speaker: Committee Chair
thread.said: The Chair directed the DOH to submit the reverted-funds data to the committee before plenary so Representative Nava could use it in his review.

topics.topic: PhilHealth subsidy gap for indirect contributors and earmarked revenues
topics.summary: Perci Cendaña and other members questioned the distinction between direct and indirect contributors and the implementation of PhilHealth's differential-benefits policy. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula asked PhilHealth to reconcile its headcount-based requirement of 76,000,000,000 with the much higher breakeven-based payout estimates, while the agency cited a proposed allocation of PHP79 and a maximum expected payout of 500,000,000,000. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez pressed DOH and PhilHealth on the shortfall, and Beverly Ho said an additional 170 was needed to reach breakeven. Eli San Fernando and Rep. JC Rahman Nava then sought a complete accounting of earmarked sin-tax, PCSO, and PAGCOR revenues. PhilHealth cited 54,000,000,000 in FY 2027 sin-tax earmarking, 127,000,000,000 in PCSO/PAGCOR revenues through the second quarter of 2026, and 224,000,000,000 expected from direct contributors for 2026. The hearing ended with requests for supporting data and a commitment to coordinate with DBM, while the total available 2027 earmarked revenue and its application to the subsidy gap remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the difference between PhilHealth's mandated or projected subsidy requirement for indirect contributors and the amount proposed for FY 2027. It also asked whether earmarked sin-tax, PCSO, and PAGCOR revenues were fully available and allocated to cover that gap.
topics.agency_position: DOH and PhilHealth said the proposed funding was below the amount needed for indirect-contributor benefit payments. PhilHealth presented both a headcount-based premium requirement and a higher breakeven-based payout estimate, while saying it would continue studying differential benefits and coordinate with DBM on the 2027 sin-tax estimate.
topics.outcome: The committee established that the proposed PhilHealth allocation was substantially below the agency's projected indirect-contributor payout requirement, with the gap described as about 170. The precise FY 2027 earmarked-revenue total and its full allocation remained open, subject to data submission and DBM coordination.

positions.position: Pressed PhilHealth to reconcile the mandated or estimated FY 2027 indirect-contributor subsidy requirement with the lower NEP allocation and sought supporting data.
Supported restoring funding for the PhilHealth indirect-contributor gap and identified the requested additional amount as 170.

Argued that the committee needed a complete accounting of earmarked revenues because collecting them could substantially address PhilHealth's funding requirements.
Questioned the treatment of direct and indirect contributors and the implementation implications of PhilHealth's differential-benefits policy.

topics.topic: PhilHealth differential benefits for direct and indirect contributors
topics.summary: Perci Cendaña first raised the distinction between PhilHealth’s direct and indirect contributors under universal health care. PhilHealth answered that an approved Board resolution on differential benefits had not yet been implemented because the agency was studying its medical-inflation, database, collection, and operational implications. Eli San Fernando later asked whether the measure had been tested and whether it would disadvantage marginalized indirect contributors. The agency reiterated that it was still studying the policy and committed to examining its implications thoroughly before implementation. PhilHealth cited about 54 billion as earmarked from sin taxes for 2027 and 69.78 billion pesos as the approved 2026 budget, but did not clearly establish that all earmarked revenues would finance indirect-contributor subsidies. The issue therefore remained under agency study, with the allocation question not fully answered.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PhilHealth’s proposed differential benefits for direct and indirect contributors were legally and operationally ready, consistent with universal health care, and supported by sufficient and properly allocated revenues. Members also asked how much excise-tax and other earmarked revenue PhilHealth would receive in FY 2027 and whether those funds would finance indirect-contributor subsidies.
topics.agency_position: PhilHealth stated that an approved Board resolution on differential benefits existed, but the policy had not yet been implemented because the agency was still studying its operational, fiscal, database, collection, and policy implications. It indicated that 54,000,000,000 was earmarked for PhilHealth from sin taxes in 2027, based on BIR and BOC certification, but did not establish that all legally earmarked revenues were fully allocated specifically to indirect-contributor subsidies.
topics.outcome: The agency confirmed that the Board resolution existed but had not been implemented and remained under study. The committee did not receive a clear confirmation that all legally earmarked FY 2027 excise-tax revenues would be fully allocated to indirect-contributor subsidies.

positions.position: Questioned the distinction between direct and indirect contributors and its consistency with universal health care, implicitly seeking assurance that indirect contributors would not receive inferior treatment as so-called freeloaders.

Questioned whether differential benefits had been tested and whether the measure would improperly disadvantage marginalized indirect contributors. He also sought confirmation that earmarked excise-tax revenues would fully support indirect-contributor subsidies.

topics.topic: DOH-retained hospital operations, MOE, and personnel-service cuts
topics.summary: Representative Antonio Tinio raised concerns that DOH-retained hospitals and some GOCC hospitals faced personnel-services and MOE cuts, including an 8% personnel-services reduction and 112,000,000 pesos in one hospital example and an 11,000,000 MOE cut at the National Center for Mental Health. The DOH said the personnel-services differences reflected unfilled positions, while total plantilla positions remained unchanged; vacancies resulted from noncompetitive salaries and the temporary nature of residency and fellowship posts. On MOE, the DOH cited normative financing, income retention and the need to assess GAA funds alongside PhilHealth and other revenue streams. A majority member moved, and Representative Tinio seconded, a request for hospital-level PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP allocations and MOE utilization. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez later asked about the overall DOH reduction, and the Secretary said the request was 837,000,000,000 against an approval of 353,000,000,000, with the difference stated unclearly as R485 dollars. The Secretary identified the PhilHealth indirect-member gap, HFEP and hospital operations as restoration priorities, including about 12 billion for hospital operations, while the committee left the funding restorations open pending further deliberation and documents.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 budget would affect DOH-retained and government-owned hospitals, particularly hospital operations, personnel services, and maintenance and other operating expenses (MOE). Members also asked whether the apparent cuts were justified by unfilled positions, normative financing, PhilHealth reimbursements, Medical Assistance for Indigent Patients and Families (MAIFIP), or the implementation of Zero Balance Billing (ZBB), and what funding the DOH wanted restored.
topics.agency_position: The DOH said the apparent personnel-services reductions largely reflected unfilled positions rather than a reduction in the total plantilla, and that vacancies resulted from noncompetitive compensation and the temporary nature of residency and fellowship posts. It said hospital MOE was based on normative financing and should be assessed together with income retention, GAA funding, PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP and ZBB-related financing; it also identified hospital operations, HFEP and the PhilHealth indirect-member gap as priority funding needs.
topics.outcome: The DOH provided explanations for the personnel-services and MOE differences, but the committee requested hospital-level reimbursement, MAIFIP and MOE-utilization data and a comprehensive written explanation of unfilled positions. The committee also identified major restoration priorities, but no restoration was approved during the excerpt.

topics.topic: Hospital staffing shortages and unfilled plantilla positions
topics.summary: Members raised the inability of hospitals to operate at their intended levels because plantilla positions remained vacant despite available facilities and equipment. DOH said vacancies stemmed from noncompetitive salaries, specialty requirements, limited applicants, and temporary residency or fellowship posts; it reported 6,774 unfilled positions as of July 2026, mostly in DOH hospitals. The committee also questioned whether the country was producing and retaining enough physicians, and DOH cited 82 medical schools, about 5,600 annual physician passers, and a garbled figure of 'seventeen ninety seven' temporary migrant doctors annually. Representative Renee Ko challenged mental-health budget reductions and shortages of psychiatrists and other professionals, while DOH cited MH-GAP training, hotline expansion, salary-grade adjustments, and PhilHealth-based income streams. Chair Romeo Momo separately questioned regional allocations and a hospital staffing gap of about 989 personnel, including a request for 185 positions amounting to 212,471,000. The hearing landed on commitments for written explanations, mental-health documentation, hospital visits, and further review, while the broader staffing shortage remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DOH hospitals had substantial unfilled plantilla positions despite available facilities and hospital upgrades, how personnel-service allocations were determined, and what DOH was doing to address shortages of doctors and mental-health professionals. Members also asked whether medical-education production, migration, compensation, and accreditation rules were contributing to the workforce gap.
topics.agency_position: DOH attributed unfilled hospital positions to noncompetitive salary grades, stringent specialty requirements, few applicants for some professional posts, and positions structured for temporary residency or fellowship service. It maintained that the overall plantilla and personnel-services budget remained available, while proposing recruitment, revised accreditation and training arrangements, compensation adjustments, PhilHealth income streams, and direct review of affected hospitals.
topics.outcome: DOH explained the vacancies and outlined recruitment, compensation, training, accreditation, and workforce-retention measures, but several hospital-specific staffing and budget questions remained subject to written data, direct review, or future allocation decisions. The committee obtained commitments for written submissions and hospital follow-up, but did not resolve the underlying nationwide staffing gap.

positions.position: Facilities and equipment could not deliver their intended services when hospitals lacked personnel; DOH needed to address almost 5,000 reported unfilled positions and help her district hospital.
Personnel-services reductions and the treatment of unfilled positions required a comprehensive explanation, including the nature and causes of the vacancies.
The country needed more medical schools and allied-health training, better alignment between health-worker production and national needs, and stronger measures to retain doctors in the Philippines.

Mental-health budget reductions were inconsistent with the scale of the mental-health crisis and should be reversed or accompanied by stronger workforce, community-service, and child-focused interventions.

Regional allocations and hospital staffing needed to reflect actual service gaps, functional bed capacity, hospital upgrades, and underserved regions rather than concentration of facilities in the NCR.

thread.said: Secretary Mercado reported 77,000 cumulative calls since 2019: 3,000 in 2019, 11,000 in 2020, 21,000 in 2021, 18,000 in 2022, 16,000 in 2023, and 23,000 in 2024.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said the hotline had 38 open lines and eight dedicated lines and operated 247 hours, although the final operating figure was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Ko
thread.said: Representative Ko raised the shortage of mental-health professionals, noting that there were fewer than 2,000 licensed psychiatrists for around 110,000,000 Filipinos. She also cited a student-to-guidance-counselor ratio of one to 401, compared with a stated standard of one to 50.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said MH-GAP training covered 100% of nurses in the mental-health programs. DOH was working to authorize academic institutions as additional certification bodies so training could occur more frequently and produce a multiplier effect.

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Ko
thread.said: Representative Ko asked whether the persistent supply gap among psychiatrists and other mental-health professionals was caused only by certification issues, noting competition from overseas opportunities and concerns about compensation and quality of life.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH had adjusted psychiatrist and psychologist positions from salary grade 18 to salary grade 20. He also cited practice- and facility-based income streams funded through PhilHealth for psychiatrists, psychologists, and developmental pediatricians.

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Ko
thread.said: Representative Ko requested a copy of DOH's current mental-health initiatives, particularly those involving PhilHealth, and emphasized the need for adequate funding during a mental-health crisis.

thread.speaker: Representative Renee Ko
thread.said: Representative Ko asked for an update on implementation of the Mental Health Strategic Framework 2024–2028, especially interventions affecting children.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado cited peer-to-peer facilitator engagement in schools and a facilitator handbook as part of the response. He said DOH would provide more concrete achievements from the past four years.

thread.speaker: Chair Romeo Momo
thread.said: Chair Momo said the unused appropriation was almost 50,000,000,020.25, but the transcript's wording and intended magnitude were unclear. He linked the concern to DOH absorptive capacity and service delivery.

thread.speaker: Chair Romeo Momo
thread.said: Chair Momo questioned why the National Capital Region continued to receive the largest regional allocation despite its concentration of hospitals and beds. He asked whether allocations considered population, poverty, disease burden, geographic isolation, bed shortages, and health-workforce gaps.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The DOH official said normative budgeting used a mix of factors, including occupancy rate, average length of stay, and other facility indicators. The complete explanation was garbled in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Chair Romeo Momo
thread.said: Chair Momo said a hospital recently upgraded from level two to level three had a reported personnel gap of about 989 personnel. He said the hospital had requested 185 positions amounting to 212,471,000.

thread.speaker: Chair Romeo Momo
thread.said: Chair Momo said the DOH allocation was only 4,000,000, enough to hire two medical officers and one administrative position, and asked how the hospital could obtain the additional personnel needed after the upgrade.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The DOH official said staffing depended on the hospital's operational capacity and functional or operating beds rather than simply its full bed capacity. The official said DBM adjustments were based on functional capacity.

thread.speaker: Chair Romeo Momo
thread.said: Chair Momo invited the DOH undersecretary for operations to visit hospitals in the Caraga region so the staffing and operational-capacity issues could be assessed directly.

thread.speaker: Chair Romeo Momo
thread.said: Chair Momo cited an orthopedic and rehabilitation building with phase one funded at 80,000,000, phase two at 50,000,000 in the 2026 budget, and phase three at 50,000,000 for completion in 2027.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The DOH official indicated that allocations for equipment and facilities could be modified in a meeting to support project completion.

topics.topic: Zero Balance Billing, no-balance-billing beds, and professional fees
topics.summary: Members pressed DOH and PhilHealth on how the President’s ZBB commitment would cover hospital costs and professional fees without leaving patients to seek political assistance. DOH said fixed costs should be covered by hospital MOE and personnel-services funding, while PhilHealth would pay for variable costs and MAIFIP would address outliers. The agency cited a target to reduce out-of-pocket spending from 41% in 2025 to about 37.8% by 2028, while members sought stronger targets and a single-digit outcome. Members also demanded enforcement of the 90% government and 10% private no-balance-billing bed requirements and cited a case involving a 1,000 hospital bill and a 60,000 professional fee. DOH committed to issue private-hospital guidelines within the year, negotiate standardized professional-fee arrangements, improve reimbursement timing, and use PhilHealth or licensing leverage to improve compliance. The committee requested hospital reimbursement, MAIFIP, MOE, and capacity data, but compulsory physician participation and full ZBB enforcement remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the President’s Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) commitment would be financed and enforced, including coverage of professional fees. Members also asked how PhilHealth, DOH hospital budgets, MAIFIP, and private hospitals would be coordinated to prevent patient balance billing and reduce out-of-pocket spending.
topics.agency_position: DOH said ZBB should be financed through hospital MOE and personnel-services funding for fixed costs, PhilHealth payments for variable costs and ordinary cases, and MAIFIP or other assistance for outliers. The agency supported stronger monitoring, clearer rules for private-hospital no-balance-billing beds, faster PhilHealth reimbursement, and negotiated or standardized professional-fee arrangements, but acknowledged implementation gaps and that private-doctor participation remained partly optional.
topics.outcome: The agency outlined a financing model and committed to guidelines, reporting, negotiations with professional societies, stronger monitoring, and faster reimbursement. However, enforcement of private-hospital bed requirements and compulsory acceptance of MAIFIP by private doctors remained under development rather than fully resolved.

positions.position: Medical assistance should be consolidated and made easier for constituents to access so patients would not have to seek political assistance.

The committee needed to determine whether DOH hospital MOE reductions were justified by PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP allocations, or other financing, and needed a plan and report on hospital capacity relevant to ZBB.
Doctors should be compelled, or at least placed under a prenegotiated structure, to accept MAIFIP for professional fees.
Professional-fee compliance should be linked to PhilHealth accreditation or another enforceable licensing mechanism.
ZBB was a presidential promise that required identifiable funding and enforcement; existing basic-accommodation rules were not adequately reflected on the ground.
The government needed a concrete target and timeline to reduce out-of-pocket health spending and a streamlined system that would prevent patients from seeking assistance from legislators.
DOH needed to enforce the statutory 10% private-hospital no-balance-billing-bed requirement, issue clear guidelines, and provide detailed MAIFIP allocation and utilization data.
ZBB implementation had to include timely reimbursement of facilities and professional fees, including for doctors practicing in private hospitals.
The 90% government and 10% private no-balance-billing requirements needed active monitoring, limits on professional fees, and accountability for implementation.

actions.action: DOH was to submit each hospital’s PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP allocation, and actual MOE utilization.
DOH was requested to submit a report on the administration’s hospital-capacity expansion achievements and plans.
DOH was to pursue inclusion of a special-provision requirement concerning doctors’ acceptance of MAIFIP.
DOH was to negotiate an opt-in hospital and physician arrangement tied to agreed professional-fee rates and patient volume.
DOH and PhilHealth were to work with professional societies and use accreditation or licensing leverage to improve professional-fee compliance.
DOH committed to issue clear private-hospital ZBB guidelines within the year.

DOH was requested to provide MAIFIP allocations for 2024, 2025, and 2026 by region, hospital, and health facility, including downloads, augmentations, utilization, patients served, balances, and referring office where applicable.
The committee parked Rep. Emano’s remaining time while awaiting the regional director’s answer on the Northeastern Misamis hospital site.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ian Amatong
thread.said: He asked whether the government could consolidate medical assistance and related health programs to make assistance easier for constituents and reduce the need for patients to seek help from politicians.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said public hospitals should have 90% of their beds under no-balance-billing arrangements and would need mechanisms to obtain additional support from LGUs and other funding sources. The official described this as an implementation challenge alongside PhilHealth rate adjustments.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ian Amatong
thread.said: He said it was difficult to explain to constituents why they still had to beg politicians for medical assistance despite higher PhilHealth premiums.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said hospital bills consist of hospital fees and professional fees and that DOH had begun discussions with professional societies. The aim was to make professional-fee payments more predictable and to make provider enrollment and frontline PhilHealth processes easier.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official committed to making it easier for providers to participate in PhilHealth benefit packages and to improve frontline services for providers.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said enhanced BarangayAKAP policies would include liveness checks, patient biometrics, provider controls, and other safeguards to verify patients and claims.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said Yakap would serve as the foundational primary-care program and an entry point into the health system, with controls intended to integrate previously separate programs.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair noted that a special provision in the 2026 GAA covered 100% of professional fees separately from the hospital bill.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said professional fees, particularly in the private sector, could contribute to runaway hospital bills and should be addressed through guidelines.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said PhilHealth already provided generous coverage, including coverage exceeding 1,000,000 for some conditions, but that catastrophic cases should be more effectively converted into Z benefits and coordinated with other funds.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He questioned cuts to the maintenance and other operating expenses of DOH hospitals and asked whether the reductions reflected higher MAIFIP and PhilHealth reimbursements or a DBM decision.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH hospital operations in Metro Manila were proposed to decline from PHP 30,000,000,000 in 2026 to PHP 26,900,000,000, a reduction described as 10.2%. He also said the allocation covered 26.9% against projected MOE requirements of 31.7%.

thread.speaker: A majority member
thread.said: The member moved for DOH to submit each hospital’s PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP allocation, and actual MOE utilization so the committee could determine whether higher external funding justified the MOE cuts.

thread.speaker: DOH hospital finance official
thread.said: The official said hospital MOE requirements followed DOH normative financing. The official added that part of the financing approach related to implementing ZBB.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH hospitals were allowed income retention and that the committee should examine GAA funding, retained revenues, and other sources together to avoid double financing. He characterized the arrangement as a sector-wide, 'left pocket, right pocket' transaction.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked about DOH hospital bed capacity, surge requirements during outbreaks such as leptospirosis and dengue, and the number of beds added by the administration, particularly in relation to ZBB.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said the department was pursuing shorter hospital stays and greater efficiency, while recognizing that additional physical expansion of DOH hospitals would still be needed. He also referred to private hospitals providing 10% of their beds for no-balance-billing arrangements.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He requested a report on the administration’s achievements in expanding DOH hospital capacity and its plans through the end of the administration, noting that ZBB would inevitably involve private hospitals.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado cited an estimated authorized bed capacity of 30,045, although the transcript’s reference to the year is unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bambi Emano
thread.said: While waiting for an answer about the Northeastern Misamis hospital site, he asked whether doctors could be compelled to accept MAIFIP as payment for professional fees.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH was proposing a special-provision requirement making doctors accept MAIFIP, although he clarified that this was not an amendment but an inclusion in the special provision.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said acceptance was currently optional and that DOH was negotiating with specialty societies on a standardized professional-fee structure based either on a multiple of PhilHealth coverage or an HMO RVU code.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH was considering packaging professional fees with hospital services through an opt-in mechanism. Hospitals and doctors that accepted the agreed rate could receive a volume of referred patients.

thread.speaker: A majority member
thread.said: The member said DOH had repeatedly promised since 2023 to resolve doctors’ professional fees within one month and said the guidelines already contemplated 50% coverage of doctors’ fees by MAIFIP. The member urged linking compliance to PhilHealth accreditation, with reprimand, suspension, or revocation for noncompliance.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado agreed that DOH should work with PhilHealth and possibly the PRC because accreditation or licensing leverage could compel compliance. He also agreed that the professional-fee structure needed to be addressed jointly with PhilHealth.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He asked how DOH planned to achieve the President’s ZBB promise under the proposed budget and what funding sources besides DOH appropriations would be used.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH hospital MOE and personnel-services allocations should cover fixed costs, while PhilHealth should cover variable costs related to the actual delivery of care. He described PhilHealth as the first payer and MAIFIP as a second payer for outliers.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He warned that patients interpreted ZBB as a promise of no hospital bill and said the commitment was difficult to achieve unless DOH ensured the necessary funding.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said charity or basic accommodation should be subject to strict no-balance-billing rules, while acknowledging that outliers could fall between the cracks. He referred to MAIFIP as a second-line mechanism and to Z benefits with 70% coverage, although the surrounding wording was unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Maximo Rodriguez Jr.
thread.said: He cited the continuing level of Filipino out-of-pocket health spending and asked for a concrete plan, target, and timeline to reduce it substantially, including whether it could reach single digits.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said out-of-pocket spending had declined from 44% to 41% in 2025, while PhilHealth’s share of total health expenditure rose from 13.4% to 19.5%.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said the Philippine Development Plan target was to reduce out-of-pocket spending from 41% in 2025 to around 37.8% by 2028. Reaching single digits was described as an aspiration requiring additional fiscal commitment.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said PhilHealth should be paid first, followed by other support, and that DOH was working toward a common statement of account and one-stop-shop processing in DOH hospitals to coordinate MAIFIP and other assistance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: He asked whether the one-stop shop could be strengthened so patients would no longer have to seek assistance from congressmen and senators and could have all available assistance facilitated in one place.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH was pursuing joint contracting with PhilHealth, including global payments and a separate layer for outliers, with ordinary PhilHealth-covered cases handled automatically and other cases supported by PhilHealth and MAIFIP.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: He asked why DOH was not enforcing the Universal Health Care Act requirement that at least 10% of private hospital beds be basic or ward accommodation subject to no balance billing, and requested clear implementation guidelines.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado said DOH was strengthening monitoring and intended to implement the private-hospital ZBB requirement. He cited an across-the-board 30 and 50 expansion of the ZBB arrangement, although the transcript’s reference to '95' is unclear.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: Secretary Mercado committed to issuing clear guidelines within the year and said licensing and ongoing monitoring would be used to support compliance.

thread.speaker: DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: On professional fees, he said DOH was coordinating with major specialty societies on a structure based on an HMO RVU multiplier or a percentage of PhilHealth coverage. He also said faster PhilHealth payment, including payment in 15 days, could help secure physician participation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked about the 2026 implementation of ZBB, including reimbursement of health facilities and payment of doctors’ professional fees, particularly when doctors affiliated with private hospitals treated patients under the program.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said special provisions covered professional fees, but private-practice doctors in private hospitals had to accept MAIFIP as payment. The official acknowledged that payment delays were a concern and that faster reimbursement was necessary for private doctors to participate.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edwin Cruzado
thread.said: He reiterated that 90% of government-hospital beds and 10% of private-hospital beds should be allocated for no-balance billing. He urged limits and monitoring because private medical centers had limited capacity and doctors could charge high professional fees.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edwin Cruzado
thread.said: He cited a case in which an outpatient hemorrhoidectomy had a hospital bill of 1,000 but a doctor’s fee of 60,000, illustrating the need to regulate and monitor professional fees.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edwin Cruzado
thread.said: He also raised hospital-waste costs, saying facilities were paying 30.50 to 85,000 per kilo for collection, treatment, storage, and disposal.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official proposed a network approach linking government hospitals, private hospitals, and charity beds. The official gave PGH and Cardinal as an example of a private-government arrangement in which the private hospital could pay or cover part of the operating cost and add outlier support.

topics.topic: Consolidation and coordination of medical assistance programs
topics.summary: Members pressed DOH and PhilHealth to integrate medical assistance, hospital subsidies, and PhilHealth payments so patients would not have to seek help from politicians or remain liable for unpaid balances. The agency said PhilHealth should be the first payer, with DOH, MAIFIP, PCSO, and other programs addressing outliers, and proposed shared statements of account, one-stop shops, joint contracting, and global payments. Members also challenged politically influenced HFEP and medical-assistance allocations, citing only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities as operational and demanding rules-based distribution. Secretary Edwin Mercado committed to DOH-PhilHealth financial alignment, simpler medical assistance, stronger monitoring, allocation reports, and private-hospital no-balance-billing guidelines within the year. The agency reported a fall in out-of-pocket spending from 44% to 41% and a 2028 target of 37.8%, but said single-digit spending would require additional fiscal resources. The hearing therefore produced several reporting and implementation commitments, while full consolidation and reliable zero-balance billing remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PhilHealth, DOH medical assistance, PCSO, and related hospital-support programs could be coordinated or consolidated to reduce out-of-pocket costs, simplify access, and prevent patients from being left unpaid. Members also asked whether assistance and hospital allocations were being distributed through objective, rules-based systems rather than political channels.
topics.agency_position: DOH and PhilHealth officials supported greater alignment and a clearer order of payment, with PhilHealth covering ordinary or first-payer obligations and MAIFIP, DOH, PCSO, and other programs addressing outliers. The agency said it was developing one-stop shops, shared statements of account, joint contracting, rules-based allocation, stronger monitoring, and private-hospital no-balance-billing guidelines, but several operational details and data requests remained pending.
topics.outcome: The committee obtained commitments for financial alignment, hospital and MAIFIP allocation data, liquidation and program-breakdown reports, stronger monitoring, and private-hospital no-balance-billing guidelines. The broader question of fully consolidating assistance programs and eliminating political intermediation remained open, with implementation dependent on future guidelines, data submissions, fiscal resources, and coordination among DOH, PhilHealth, LGUs, and providers.

positions.position: Medical assistance programs should be consolidated or integrated so patients do not have to seek political help and constituents can access benefits more easily.
DOH should explain hospital MOE reductions and show whether PhilHealth reimbursements and MAIFIP allocations offset or justified those cuts.
The committee needed hospital-level data on PhilHealth reimbursements, medical-assistance allocations, and MOE utilization.

Patient detention and hospital debt practices required stronger monitoring and enforcement, while assistance programs for reproductive health, protection units, and cancer care needed transparent breakdowns and adequate support.
HFEP and medical assistance had been affected by poor planning and politicization; DOH needed objective rules and a credible mechanism to deliver zero balance billing.
DOH and PhilHealth should restore financial alignment, eliminate double financing, simplify medical assistance, and prevent medicines and commodities from expiring unused.

The government needed measurable targets to reduce out-of-pocket spending, stronger one-stop hospital assistance, transparent and objective allocation data, and enforcement of the 10% private-hospital no-balance-billing-bed requirement.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: He asked whether the government could consolidate medical assistance and related programs so constituents could access support more easily, and said the committee was seeking a legislative solution.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said public hospitals should have 90% of their beds under no-balance-billing arrangements and that DOH, LGU, and MAIFIP support would need to be coordinated. The official described implementation and payment-rate adjustments as continuing challenges.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: He said the system was difficult to explain to patients who ended up begging politicians for help, and urged PhilHealth to fund as much of the patients' needs as possible.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said hospital bills consisted partly of hospital fees and professional fees and that the DOH would continue discussions with professional societies to make professional charges more predictable.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official committed to making it easier for providers to participate in PhilHealth benefit packages and to simplify frontline provider services.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said BarangayAKAP 2.0 would include stronger controls, including liveness checks, patient biometric verification, and other provider-related mechanisms.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said the department would work with LGUs to convene public, private, and nonprofit providers, including through Yakap centers and possible HFEP and health-human-resource support. PhilHealth payments, the official said, should result in patients receiving the appropriate services.

thread.speaker: DOH/PhilHealth official
thread.said: The official said Yakap would serve as the foundational primary-care entry point for programs that currently appeared disparate, and that the department would put controls in place while integrating those programs.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: He asked for a clearer explanation of how the programs would be integrated and what legislation could help achieve consolidation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He responded that program assessment involved determining patients' capability or social status, but the machine-generated transcript did not preserve the complete answer.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair identified hotline 1555 as the central response and complaint center for hospital complaints, including complaints involving public and private hospitals.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair noted that the 2026 special provision provided 100% professional fee coverage apart from the hospital bill and said the committee should work on hospital and professional-fee charges.

thread.speaker: Rep. Quino
thread.said: He raised reductions in maintenance and other operating expenses for DOH hospitals, citing Hirivo Memorial Medical Center and the National Center for Mental Health, and asked whether the reductions reflected a DBM decision or another justification.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: The secretary said the operating budgets for DOH hospitals in Metro Manila would decline from PHP 30,000,000,000 in 2026 to PHP 26,900,000,000, a 10.2% reduction. He also referred to a projected maintenance-and-operating requirement of 31.7% but a grant of 26.9%.

thread.speaker: Rep. Talosa
thread.said: He moved that DOH submit each hospital's PhilHealth reimbursements, medical assistance-program allocation, and actual MOE utilization, including whether higher MAIFIP and PhilHealth reimbursements explained the MOE cuts.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He seconded the document request and again asked for the justification for reducing the MOE of DOH hospitals, including the effect of zero-balance billing.

thread.speaker: DOH finance official
thread.said: The official said hospital MOE requirements followed DOH normative financing. The official added that a portion was being used to implement CBB, but the rest of the answer was unclear.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: The secretary said DOH hospitals were allowed income retention and that the figures should be viewed in totality to account for GAA financing and other revenue streams. He described the arrangement as avoiding double financing and as a sector approach.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago
thread.said: She asked whether DOH had data on unsettled promissory notes and patient collectibles and whether it actively monitored the scale of collateral being foreclosed or seized because of those debts.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: The secretary said the department would need to provide detailed data. He referred to hotline 1555, PhilHealth involvement, and DOH field-office investigations with due process for complaints.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago
thread.said: She asked whether the 1555 action center was outsourced or internally managed, including who handled its administration, staffing, and funding.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said the action center was internally managed, although his prior PhilHealth experience involved an outsourced service. He said the system generated statistics on calls, drop calls, resolutions, common complaints, and escalation to regional directors and the central office.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago
thread.said: She called for a review of implementation of the Anti-Hospital Detention Act, saying that allowing arrangements under RA 9439 did not justify leaving patient detention conditions unchanged.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He stated that the 2027 family-planning and reproductive-health allocation was 664,000,000.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH could provide a breakdown of the reproductive-health allocation, including commodities, women and children's protection, safe motherhood, adolescent health, and family-planning support.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said 51,000,000 was allocated for women and children's protection support in 51 hospitals, inclusive of expansion.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH would provide the actual breakdown of the 51,000,000, including sexual-assault investigation kits, and would review whether the funding was sufficient.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He confirmed that the kits had been developed by DOST and said DOH could incorporate them into its terms of reference.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said amendments to the cancer fund expanded coverage to blood products and nutritional support, which had initially been limited to medicines. He said the cancer fund had increased by 25.6% to account for the additional support.

thread.speaker: Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago
thread.said: She requested DOH reports on compliance with its gender-and-development mandate and documents concerning the National HIV Policy Act, reproductive health, and the Integrated Cancer Control Program.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He asked that the requested anti-detention data also be included.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He said an audit showed only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities were operational, or roughly 33%, and asked whether facilities had been built in locations where LGUs could not support personnel requirements.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said HFEP omnibus guidelines required site conditions before a locality was considered. Going forward, DOH would assess regional and provincial catchments, use facility standards, and allocate infrastructure or equipment according to network needs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said HFEP would be viewed as a holistic regional network under the Universal Health Care law, with referral routes providing continuity of care up to apex hospitals.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He pressed DOH to identify the concrete steps taken after the apparent failure to follow the original guidelines and to acknowledge the flaws that could otherwise recur.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He attributed implementation problems partly to devolved health care and said that, during his term, he would be more engaged in ensuring that guidelines were followed and communicated to local chief executives.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He argued that health care and medical assistance were being politicized, with facilities constructed in response to political requests and districts receiving unequal access to aid.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said health-service delivery should not be a political favor but should be based on equity and access, and that DOH was developing a rules-based procedure. He said he could not speak for past decisions.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH had begun strengthening direct links, starting with DOH hospitals and LGUs, with the goal of eventually including SUCs, GOCCs, and private hospitals.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He asked how DOH would achieve the President's zero-balance-billing promise under the proposed budget and what other funding sources would be used.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH hospital MOE and personnel-services allocations should cover fixed costs, while PhilHealth should cover variable consumable costs and serve as the first payer, with assistance programs covering outliers.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Suntay
thread.said: He warned that patients interpreted zero balance billing as a promise of no hospital bill, which he said was difficult to achieve without additional DOH support.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He referred to rules for charity or basic accommodation and said basic-accommodation patients should have no balance billing, while acknowledging that outliers could fall between the cracks and referring to MAIFIP as a second layer.

thread.speaker: Rep. Janette Garin
thread.said: She asked Secretary Mercado to commit to reviving alignment between DOH and PhilHealth to prevent double financing, noting that an earlier alignment initiative had later collapsed.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He agreed to alignment through the single-agenda work streams and said a separate finance work stream for hospitals was being developed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Janette Garin
thread.said: She asked about the unearmarked donation to WHO, including who handled its use and whether DOH could provide liquidation of the amount already spent.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Meilyne Beltran
thread.said: She said the pledge of around 10,000,000 US dollars had been made during the October 2024 investment round and acknowledged the need to account for its use.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Meilyne Beltran
thread.said: She committed to provide the committee a report on the liquidation of the 5,000,000 already spent.

thread.speaker: Undersecretary Meilyne Beltran
thread.said: She confirmed that 167,000,277 pesos for the donation had been included in the 2027 net budget under her office.

thread.speaker: Rep. Janette Garin
thread.said: She raised recurring expiration of nutrition commodities and mental-health medicines and asked whether unused medicines could instead be redirected to medical assistance or the Philippine Cancer Fund.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH would examine the proposal and that the long-term direction was for PhilHealth to pay for medicines and commodities, reducing double financing through financial alignment.

thread.speaker: Rep. Janette Garin
thread.said: She cited documented instances in which DOH-procured chemotherapeutic drugs were supplied to hospitals and then reimbursed by PhilHealth, calling this double financing and urging the department to correct the system.

thread.speaker: Rep. Janette Garin
thread.said: She proposed simplifying medical assistance for renal, cardiac, and cancer patients by bringing it back to the Medical Assistance Program, so patients could use it more effectively after PhilHealth and private insurance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He agreed that the directive was to make the process simpler and said DOH would examine the Medical Assistance Program.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He cited out-of-pocket health spending of around 44% in the Philippines versus around 9% in Thailand and asked for a concrete plan, target, and timeline to substantially reduce it.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said the out-of-pocket share had fallen from 44% to 41% in 2025, while PhilHealth's share of total health expenditure had risen from 13.4% to 19.5%.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said the Philippine Development Plan target was to reduce out-of-pocket spending from 41% in 2025 to around 37%, specifically a 37.8% target, by 2028.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether the government had a plan to reduce out-of-pocket spending to single digits.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official said single-digit out-of-pocket spending remained an aspiration but would require additional fiscal resources; the department's present planning horizon was 2028.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether PhilHealth, MAIFIP, hospital subsidies, PCSO, and other assistance could be coordinated so that qualified patients would not be left with a balance.

thread.speaker: DOH official
thread.said: The official described a clear order of payment, with PhilHealth first and other support following. DOH was considering a shared statement of account and one-stop shops in DOH hospitals so MAIFIP evaluators and other assistance providers could work from the same information.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He said patients still had to seek assistance from congressmen and senators and asked whether one-stop shops could be strengthened so the entire process would be facilitated for them.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH was pursuing joint contracting with hospitals and PhilHealth, global payments, and an outlier or second-layer approach in which ordinary cases would be covered automatically and other assistance would address remaining cases.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether DOH allocations by region and hospital were based on a scientific formula incorporating poverty, population, disease burden, patient volume, utilization, and actual need.

thread.speaker: DOH official Sheila Pabila
thread.said: She said funds downloaded to DOH hospitals were determined by hospital level and absorptive capacity.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He cited 41,000,000,000 and a 61.3% disbursement figure and questioned whether the allocation basis and remaining balances were consistent with the goal of eliminating balance billing.

thread.speaker: DOH official Sheila Pabila
thread.said: She clarified that the updated 2025 obligation rate was 86%, while the 2026 obligation rate was 50% because DOH was still waiting for the notice of cash allocation.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He questioned the continued allocation of funds despite hospitals' requests for additional support for referred patients and asked whether allocations were being made objectively.

thread.speaker: DOH official Sheila Pabila
thread.said: She said all referred patients under the MAIFIP program were assessed by medical social workers against eligibility requirements.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He requested that DOH submit before plenary the complete MAIFIP allocations for 2024, 2025, and 2026 by region, hospital, and health facility, including additional downloads, augmentations, utilization, patients served, remaining balances, and the requesting or referring office.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair directed DOH to provide the requested data.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked why DOH was not enforcing the Universal Health Care Act requirement that at least 10% of private-hospital beds be basic or ward accommodation with no balance billing.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH was strengthening monitoring and intended to implement the requirement through licensing and expanded zero-balance-billing arrangements.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked when clear guidelines for enforcing the private-hospital no-balance-billing requirement would be available and urged implementation before the budget hearing ended.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He committed that the guidelines would be issued within the year.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said DOH was coordinating with major specialty societies to develop payment arrangements for private providers, potentially based on an HMO-style RVU multiplier or a percentage of PhilHealth coverage.

thread.speaker: Secretary Edwin Mercado
thread.said: He said the future system could combine case rates and global payments, with front-loaded or virtual reimbursement and negotiated referral volume to encourage private-hospital participation.

topics.topic: YAKAP prevention, medical missions, and provider accreditation
topics.summary: Rep. Ian Amatong sought easier, consolidated medical assistance and asked how YAKAP could serve as an integrated primary-care entry point. Rep. Patrin Gorazeta pressed PhilHealth on prevention beyond screening, the low number of GAMOT-accredited centers, expanded medicines, and flexible mental-health and autism-provider accreditation; the agency said it was reviewing standards, considering mobile and outreach pharmacies, and planning unbundling and provider expansion. Rep. Bong Suntay cited roughly 33% operational HFEP facilities, challenged politicized allocation, and alleged abuse of YAKAP through barangay medical missions; Secretary Edwin Mercado and Undersecretary Beverly Ho committed to rules-based allocation and YAKAP 2.0 safeguards. Rep. Jay Vergara asked about YAKAP capacity, with PhilHealth citing 4,423 centers and 17,200,000 assigned beneficiaries, although the transcript also captured 4,426 and an unclear 15.2? figure. Rep. Christopher received confirmation that ambulance transport was covered and asked for strict enforcement of the one-year transfer rule and the three-month GAMOT receipt rule. The hearing ended with commitments and a requested provider list, while alleged abuse and implementation capacity remained subject to follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether YAKAP was delivering genuine prevention and primary-care services, whether its centers and providers had adequate capacity, and whether accreditation and payment controls prevented abuse. Members also asked how medical missions, GAMOT accreditation, facility planning, and zero-balance-billing arrangements would be corrected or expanded.
topics.agency_position: The agency maintained that YAKAP was the foundation of primary care and that YAKAP 2.0 would strengthen prevention, patient verification, consent, provider controls, performance-based incentives, and information systems. It also supported more flexible accreditation through mobile pharmacies, outreach arrangements, unbundled packages, professional-society accreditation, and expanded provider training, while developing rules-based infrastructure and assistance procedures.
topics.outcome: The agency provided explanations and undertook multiple policy, accreditation, and control improvements, but the committee's concerns about provider abuse, medical missions, center capacity, HFEP placement, and politicized access were not fully closed. The requested accredited-provider list and several promised guideline and system changes remained for submission or implementation.

positions.position: Supported consolidating medical assistance and sought legislation or policy that would make access easier for constituents and integrate YAKAP with other programs.

Supported YAKAP and expanded benefit packages but argued that prevention must go beyond screening and that GAMOT, autism, and other provider-accreditation requirements were too restrictive for rural and lower-income municipalities.

Argued that HFEP planning and medical assistance had been politicized, demanded rules-based access, and warned that YAKAP medical missions could be abused without stronger provider and patient controls.
Sought clarification on hospital and YAKAP-center prioritization and whether center capacity was adequate for assigned beneficiaries.
Supported YAKAP and GAMOT but called for strict enforcement of accreditation-transfer and medicine-dispensing rules and for effective ambulance-coverage implementation.

topics.topic: GAMOT pharmacy accreditation and medicines coverage
topics.summary: Rep. Patrin Gorazeta raised the limited reach of GAMOT, reporting only 15 of 47 accredited facilities in her district and identifying pharmacist, space, and licensing requirements as barriers in poorer municipalities. PhilHealth said it was reviewing the standards, considering four accounts per pharmacy, and planning mobile pharmacies and outreach arrangements. She also sought broader medicine coverage, and PhilHealth said thyroid medicines were already in its pipeline. Members later raised alleged YAKAP abuse through barangay medical missions; Dr. Beverly Ho described YAKAP 2.0 safeguards, revised incentives, and planned IT changes, and was asked to provide the accredited-provider list. Rep. Christopher then asked about patient transfers and GAMOT dispensing, and PhilHealth confirmed a one-year transfer rule, three-month receipt validity, and dispensing of only one month's medicines. The hearing produced commitments and requests, but the final accreditation revisions and provider list were not presented in the excerpt.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether GAMOT accreditation requirements were preventing pharmacies and rural health facilities from participating, and whether medicine coverage and dispensing rules were adequate. Members also asked how PhilHealth would address access, provider accreditation, and alleged abuse of YAKAP and related packages.
topics.agency_position: PhilHealth said it was reviewing GAMOT accreditation standards and considering flexible arrangements such as multiple accounts per pharmacy, outreach services, and mobile pharmacies. It also said medicine coverage was being expanded, provider participation was being widened through package unbundling and other accreditation changes, and YAKAP controls and incentives were being revised to address abuse.
topics.outcome: PhilHealth answered the members' questions and undertook several accreditation, package-expansion, and YAKAP-control reforms. The specific list of accredited YAKAP providers and the final revised GAMOT accreditation standards were not supplied during the excerpt, so implementation remained partly unresolved.

positions.position: GAMOT accreditation requirements were a major barrier, particularly for fourth-class municipalities, and the medicines list should be expanded to include thyroid, liver-support, vitamin B complex, and calcium medicines.
Accreditation requirements for autism and other expanded packages should be simplified so more centers and providers could participate.
YAKAP was vulnerable to provider abuse through poorly controlled barangay medical missions and required clearer guidelines, verification, and accountability.
PhilHealth should strictly enforce the GAMOT dispensing and receipt-validity rules, including the three-month rule, to prevent patients from receiving less medicine than the receipt implied.
