thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: The DOE reported that renewable energy accounted for 25.04% of the 2025 generation mix, equivalent to 31.65 terawatt hours. It also reported household electrification of 94.93%, with around 28,750,000 households energized out of 30,280,000 potential households.

thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: Through the Green Energy Auction program, the DOE said it had awarded 20.7 gigawatts of renewable-energy capacity and planned another 25 gigawatts for auction from 2027 to 2035. It also cited 187 endorsed renewable-energy projects amounting to 5,460,000 pesos since 2023.

thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: The DOE said it was pursuing additional green-energy auctions for waste-to-energy, offshore wind, agrosolar, solar on stilts, solar on irrigation canals, and off-grid areas.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: He asked whether generation costs should be regulated, after noting that system-loss and inflation formulas had previously been discussed. He pressed for protection against high generation costs.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary
thread.said: The secretary said direct regulation was not necessary, but safeguards were. The DOE was developing policies requiring greater accountability from generation companies, including compliance with their energy mix, replacement-power obligations, and requirements imposed by APRA, ERC, and their contracts.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary
thread.said: The secretary cautioned that regulating generation companies could dislodge investment appetite, while arguing that stronger accountability and safeguards were needed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: Using the solar situation in Occidental Mindoro, he questioned whether renewable-energy projects had delivered the supply promised in their service contracts and referred to 24,000,000.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary
thread.said: The secretary said there were about 33 contracts, most under the Green Energy Auction, totaling about 1.3 gigawatts. Had that capacity been delivered, DOE simulations indicated a reduction in the generation rate of about 2 pesos, or at least 1 peso; the secretary emphasized that the issue was the cost to consumers, not merely penalties.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: He pressed the DOE on whether it foresaw cancellation of renewable-energy service contracts when developers failed to deliver contracted supply.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary
thread.said: The secretary said all contracts were being reviewed and cleaned up, and that the DOE had canceled about 100 plus two hundred two hundred renewable-energy service contracts. The DOE was also implementing a generation-company accountability policy with escalating sanctions, including possible cancellation of the COE or blacklisting after repeated noncompliance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Anko
thread.said: He asked the DOE about solar projects, including projects on hillsides, and raised the planned target of 50% solar and wind generating capacity by an unclear year. The question also referred to checking records, but the transcript is garbled.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The DOE official said the issue was beyond the department's mandate but that the Renewable Energy Management Bureau would check it. If a violation were found, the DOE could reprimand or take action against the generation company under its permit.

thread.speaker: Yusick, agency official
thread.said: The official raised the need for hydrological studies for solar plants and other plants, apparently to assess whether solar power plants could divert water or impose excessive costs. Several portions of the statement were unclear.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: In response to the chair's request, the agency official committed to include the matter in the next report and report back. The transcript does not clearly identify the exact scope of the report.

thread.speaker: Rep. Salvador Pleyto
thread.said: He asked how the DOE would meet the 2027 renewable-energy capacity targets if ground-mounted solar projects were restricted by the Department of Agriculture's fencing criteria. He proposed protecting about 3,000,000 hectares of flat agricultural land, particularly rice-producing areas, as the country prepared for the next Green Energy Auction.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The DOE said solar power plants would require proof of possessory rights and that projects involving large irrigation systems or rice fields had to address the Department of Agriculture's requirements. The response indicated that agricultural land should remain available for productive agricultural activities.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary
thread.said: The secretary added that the DOE was consulting local government units, which could issue ordinances to protect food production and could impose their own LGU permitting requirements.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: On the Green Energy Option Program, the DOE explained that retail competition and open access had an ERC threshold of 100 kilowatts as of June 26, while the DOE's Green Energy Option threshold was 50 kilowatts. The response also referred to the Department of Agriculture's retail aggregation program and renewable-energy suppliers.

thread.speaker: Rep. Salvador Pleyto
thread.said: He said the presentation fully supported approval of the DOE's 2027 proposed project budget. He had also raised a farm-to-energy framework and renewable-energy supply for cold-storage and post-harvest facilities, although portions of that question were unclear.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary
thread.said: The secretary said the DOE was discussing with the Department of Agriculture how Green Energy Auction solar farms could coexist with farms producing vegetables or other products and with fishponds. The secretary said the agencies were designing an approach that could benefit local beneficiaries and provinces.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: The member asked how DOE certificates of endorsement for renewable-energy tax incentives under RA 9513 accounted for indigenous communities that could be displaced by renewable-energy projects. The question referred to an income tax holiday for the first seven years, duty-free importation for 10 years, and net operating loss carryover for seven taxable years.

thread.speaker: Atty. Leila, DOE official
thread.said: The DOE official said service-contract requirements included prior informed consent and a memorandum of agreement involving the NCIP and the developer before the department issued the service contract. The official indicated that these requirements applied during project predevelopment before benefits and incentives under the Renewable Energy Act could be obtained.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: Rep. Reneko asked the DOE to amend or strengthen its framework and guidelines so renewable-energy incentives would take account of indigenous communities and displacement. The member referred to the 19 guidelines, but the precise reference was unclear.

thread.speaker: Atty. Leila, DOE official
thread.said: The DOE official said the department would consider the suggestion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: The member asked how waste-to-energy projects were treated under the DOE renewable-energy framework and whether the DOE had existing partnerships with private institutions or approved waste-to-energy facilities.

thread.speaker: Atty. Leila, DOE official
thread.said: The DOE said a special auction for waste-to-energy projects was ongoing. It also referred to memoranda of agreement with local government units, feedstock agreements between developers and LGUs, technology standards, and environmental safeguards under the Clean Air Act and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: The member clarified that waste-to-energy developers would need LGU and feedstock agreements and asked whether the DOE was involved in or had records of such agreements and projects.

thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: The undersecretary said finding feedstock was primarily the developer's responsibility, although the issue had long affected waste-to-energy projects. He said developers joining the auction were presumed to be looking for feedstock and that the law could help make the arrangements more sustainable.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: Rep. Reneko requested a list of current waste-to-energy agreements and asked whether the DOE had information on projects being developed at an industrial level.

thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: The undersecretary said the DOE did not have the information at hand but would check through the LGUs or the DENR and determine whether it could provide the requested information.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: The member cited a 2023 study reporting 1,707 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour from U.S. waste-to-energy incinerators and argued that waste-to-energy could be among the dirtiest power sources. Rep. Reneko asked why it was classified as renewable energy and what plans existed to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions.

thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: The undersecretary said waste-to-energy was classified as such because the law placed it under the renewable-energy law. The DOE would not accept technology that failed Philippine requirements, would consider technologies used in Japan, Switzerland, Singapore, and China, and said Philippine emissions requirements were stricter than Switzerland's.

thread.speaker: Rep. Reneko
thread.said: Rep. Reneko asked the department to reconsider classifying waste-to-energy under renewable energy, citing documented health and environmental concerns near proposed sites and offering to provide additional studies for consideration.

thread.speaker: Youssef Bacordo, DOE undersecretary
thread.said: The undersecretary said the DOE could not reclassify waste-to-energy because it lacked the mandate to do so. If the member proposed a change, the DOE could participate in the discussion and study.

topics.topic: Rooftop solar, net metering, and distribution-system cost allocation
topics.summary: Rep. Jay Vergara asked the ERC how rooftop-solar exports, net metering, back-feed, and system losses would affect distribution utilities and whether non-solar consumers could be protected from shifted costs. The ERC said batteries, two-way metering, distribution impact studies, interconnection standards, and future review of the Philippine Grid and Distribution Codes would address the risks; it expected system-loss impacts to be minimal because exported power would be consumed locally. An unclear portion of the exchange referred to a 20-kilowatt capacity and a system-loss document dated 08/26/2026. Rep. Felimon Espares then raised the inability of some electric cooperatives to provide net metering for solar-powered rice mills, cold storage, and residential facilities. DOE Secretary Sharon said most utilities could accommodate net metering and committed to reinforce information and capacity building. The chair directed submission of a report listing capable utilities, leaving the detailed cost-allocation issue not fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the ERC evaluates the technical and cost impacts of rooftop solar exports, net metering, back-feed, and system losses, and what safeguards prevent those costs from being shifted to non-solar consumers. It also sought to determine which distribution utilities and electric cooperatives could accommodate net metering, particularly for solar-powered post-harvest facilities.
topics.agency_position: The ERC said rooftop-solar exports could affect distribution-utility markets, rates, technical operations, and supply quality, but expected local consumption of exported energy to limit impacts on existing system losses. It relied on two-way metering, distribution impact studies, interconnection standards, further code studies, and possible customer investments or refusal of connections above the net-metering threshold. The DOE said most distribution utilities and electric cooperatives could accommodate net metering and committed to check the specific cases and reinforce information and capacity-building efforts.
topics.outcome: The ERC provided a preliminary explanation centered on two-way metering, distribution impact studies, interconnection standards, and future code review, but the transcript leaves the detailed cost-allocation discussion unclear. The DOE and agency officials were directed to check and submit a list or report on utilities capable of net metering.

positions.position: Sought safeguards against shifting the costs of rooftop-solar interconnection, back-feed, and system losses to non-solar consumers.

Supported expanded solar use for rice mills, cold storage, and residential facilities, but sought a list of utilities capable of net metering because some electric cooperatives were reportedly unable to provide it.

thread.said: The official said the ERC was aware of the possibility of cost and operational impacts as rooftop installations increased across distribution-utility networks. The ERC was considering distributed energy resources, including batteries, to ease the impact of solar exports.

thread.speaker: an ERC official
thread.said: The official said increasing solar exports could cannibalize the distribution utility's market and would require attention to rate-setting and technical operations. Intermittent exports could also affect the quality of electricity supplied to other customers.

thread.speaker: an ERC official
thread.said: The ERC said it was conducting further studies on how distribution utilities should prepare and what amendments might be needed after the 2026 Philippine Grid Code. It also intended to revisit the Philippine Distribution Code and provide appropriate interconnection standards, especially for larger rooftop systems that would fall under distributed energy resources.

thread.speaker: an ERC official

thread.speaker: an ERC official

The study would assess the connection and prescribe requirements such as new metering facilities, or allow refusal of connection above the net-metering threshold unless the intending customer made specified investments.

topics.topic: Catanduanes and island high-cost generation assistance
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought an emergency subsidy and long-term transmission solution for Catanduanes, where diesel dependence was driving high electricity costs. DOE declined to commit to a subsidy but promised a task force, fuel and electric-cooperative assessment, coordination with NAPOCOR, and work toward a grid connection or other long-term solution. Rep. Stephen James Tan then raised funding for an off-grid solar project, fuel allocation for an island system, pole relocation, a submarine-cable option, solar-plant fee relief, and the Luzon-Visayas transmission upgrade. The agencies cited about 300 million requested for pole-relocation advances, 50 million in a 2026 DPWH allocation, roughly 60 million in donated solar support, and roughly 100,000 a month in fees, while NAPOCOR said one island was operating at eight hours with peak demand stated unclearly as “a 100 kilo 108 kilowatts.” The issues were not finally resolved, but DOE, NEA, Transco, and NAPOCOR undertook follow-up studies, coordination, and presentations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what emergency assistance, fuel allocation, and regulatory or budgetary mechanisms could reduce high electricity costs and improve reliability in Catanduanes and other island or off-grid systems. It also sought the status and funding of solar, pole-relocation, submarine-cable, and Visayas transmission projects.
topics.agency_position: DOE and its attached agencies did not commit to a temporary subsidy, saying DOE was not authorized to support one. They instead supported task-force assessment, fuel and system reviews, reduced diesel dependence, grid or submarine-cable alternatives, pole-relocation coordination, and a longer-term Visayas plan based on more self-sufficient island systems.
topics.outcome: The temporary subsidy request was not accepted because DOE said it lacked authority to support it. The matters were left with agency commitments to conduct assessments, coordinate on funding and infrastructure, process or prioritize transmission options, and submit or present further information.

positions.position: Sought emergency generation-cost assistance for Catanduanes while pressing DOE to facilitate funding, regulatory approvals, and a long-term grid or submarine-cable connection.

Sought funding and operational support for off-grid solar, fuel allocation, pole relocation, submarine-cable resilience, fee relief for a donated solar project, and accelerated transmission planning. He supported greater use of local energy sources.

topics.topic: Ancillary services, stranded costs, and excess renewable capacity
topics.summary: A majority member asked the ERC to address stranded costs that could arise when distribution utilities retained excess contracted capacity while consumers shifted toward solar power. The ERC pointed to carve-out provisions in post-2023 power-supply agreements and said it would examine assistance for utilities and captive customers. A member also questioned ancillary charges, stating that about 60 percent of transmission charges were ancillary charges and citing a reserve-market price of 25 pesos per kilowatt hour; the ERC said a lower-price proposal was under consultation. Javi Benitez connected transmission delays in Negros and Panay to possible renewable curtailment involving roughly 1,300 megawatts of projects, with risks described as about 10% and possibly 20% to 30%, while DOE cited 50 megawatts of proposed battery storage in Negros. A minority member pressed for CSP amendments, greater NGCP accountability for ancillary services, and solar-plus-storage in place of uneconomic line extensions, citing 200,000,000 for the proposed funding step. The matters were not finally resolved, but the ERC and DOE undertook further review and reporting.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how stranded costs from excess or curtailed renewable capacity would be allocated, whether distribution utilities and consumers could be protected from those costs, and whether ancillary-service and reserve-market charges could be reduced and made more accountable. It also examined whether transmission constraints were contributing to renewable curtailment and whether solar-plus-storage could substitute for uneconomic line extensions.
topics.agency_position: The ERC said existing and post-2023 power-supply agreements could use carve-outs or other mechanisms to unload excess contracted capacity, and it was considering a reserve-market proposal intended to lower pricing. DOE said transmission was lagging generation, supported battery storage as an alternative or supplement, and would monitor and report on NGCP transmission commitments.
topics.outcome: The ERC described existing contractual and reserve-market mechanisms for excess capacity and undertook to consider a proposal intended to reduce reserve-market prices. Transmission-related curtailment, ancillary-service accountability, and the proposed CSP and solar-plus-storage changes remained open for further action.

positions.position: Solar power should reduce consumer costs, but the ERC should address stranded capacity and prevent consumers from bearing stranded-cost charges.
Transmission delays could cause substantial renewable curtailment in Negros and Panay; NGCP project timelines and performance required clarification.
The CSP should be amended, NGCP should provide stronger ancillary-service accountability, and solar panels with battery storage should be considered instead of uneconomic rural line extensions.
Battery storage, including a proposed 50 megawatts in Negros, could help manage excess renewable power and transmission constraints.

topics.topic: ER 194 host-community remittances and unresolved claims
topics.summary: Rep. Presley De Jesus asked the DOE for the total ER 194 host-community remittances and questioned the apparent gap in benefits. The DOE reported audited post-remittance figures as of 06/20/2026, including about 1.8 billion for Nordell Luzon and 8 million for the National Capital Region, with specified allocations for electrification, development, watershed rural health, DLF, and water management. The chair required the DOE to submit the audit-based records, and the DOE agreed. The DOE also reported roughly 160,000 pending right-of-way claims and committed to an outsourced settlement program targeting 50,000 claims in two years and all claims by 2034. It estimated the total cost at about 220 billion based on a 2016 zonal valuation, excluding unregistered and public land, but Rep. De Jesus questioned whether that amount was realistic.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much ER 194 host-community benefits had been remitted, including the allocation of post-remittance benefits, and whether the DOE could provide audited records. It also sought to determine the scale, cost, and timetable for resolving pending right-of-way claims associated with transmission lines.
topics.agency_position: The DOE said audited records showed direct remittances and post-remittance benefits for host communities and agreed to submit those records to the committee. It said the right-of-way backlog would be addressed through nationwide outsourcing, with a target of reducing the claims by 50,000 in two years and clearing them by 2034, but acknowledged that the projected 220,000,000,000 cost was only an estimate based on a 2016 zonal valuation.
topics.outcome: The DOE committed to submit audited remittance records and outlined a settlement program for the roughly 160,000 right-of-way claims. The 220,000,000,000 estimate was challenged by the member and remained subject to validation; the committee did not resolve the underlying claims or funding obligation.

positions.position: He sought a complete accounting of ER 194 host-community remittances and questioned the scale of the estimated cost for resolving the right-of-way claims.

topics.topic: Nuclear-energy roadmap, SMR feasibility, and regulatory framework
topics.summary: Rep. Marco Anko pressed the DOE over the PNPP Unit 1 feasibility study, saying it was needed for House bill eight five six seven and other nuclear-policy decisions. The DOE said the study was controlled under its agreement with KHNP and could not be photocopied or transmitted, but committed to submit the arriving hard copy by Monday and compare and certify it against the DOE-held version. Rep. Tino then asked about the status, technology, cost, and providers for Philippine nuclear development. Secretary Sharon said the country had a roadmap and a target for nuclear energy in the next decade, but was reconsidering SMRs in favor of conventional technology because SMR options appeared limited. She said regulatory organization and implementing rules remained to be completed, and gave indicative costs of 10,000,000,000 for conventional technology and 4,000,000,000 for an SMR. The DOE said development would rely mostly on private funding and that it was exploring providers from Korea, China, Japan, Canada, the United States, and France.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status and availability of the DOE's PNPP Unit 1 feasibility study, including whether the committee would receive the same document held by the DOE. It also asked about the country's nuclear roadmap, the choice between small modular reactors (SMRs) and conventional reactors, regulatory readiness, technology providers, and indicative costs.
topics.agency_position: The DOE said the Philippines had a nuclear roadmap and still targeted nuclear energy in the next decade, but was reconsidering an SMR-centered approach because options appeared limited and conventional technology might be pursued instead. The agency said regulatory and safety requirements were still being completed, nuclear development would rely mostly on private funding, and technology and provider options remained under study.
topics.outcome: The feasibility-study issue landed on a commitment for the DOE to submit the copy arriving from Korea by Monday and to compare and certify it against the DOE-held copy. The broader nuclear roadmap remained exploratory: the DOE had not settled the SMR-versus-conventional choice, regulatory framework, provider, or financing arrangement.

topics.topic: Strategic energy projects and West Philippine Sea service contracts
topics.summary: Antonio Tinio questioned the DOE about the Energy Secure Philippines program, which he described as having 24 million in funding, and asked whether it included energy storage. The DOE said the activities were mostly technical studies, with a containerized solar-battery system described as providing 10 kilowatts and higher. Tino also raised the ownership and use of fuel-storage facilities, including a 1,000,000-barrel facility announced through the US Embassy; the secretary said the DOE had not been officially informed but that any energy or fuel project required DOE permits. The DOE said PNOC was pursuing a Philippine strategic reserve, beginning with 1,000,000 barrels, requiring about 8 billion, and potentially taking a year and a half to construct. Tino requested public clarification of US Embassy energy announcements, and the secretary undertook to assess and clarify them as needed. On the West Philippine Sea, the DOE said oil and gas joint activity had to use the service-contract system, while work in the relevant area was under a moratorium because of geopolitical issues.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the DOE's involvement in US-linked energy programs and announcements, the ownership and use of fuel-storage facilities, and the implications for Philippine energy security. It also sought clarification on the status of offshore oil and gas service contracts and any proposed joint development in the West Philippine Sea.
topics.agency_position: The DOE said most US-linked Energy Secure Philippines activities were technical studies rather than infrastructure or capital-outlay projects, and that all energy and fuel projects would require DOE permits. It supported developing a Philippine strategic reserve through PNOC, while stating that offshore joint activity had to proceed through service contracts and that work in the relevant West Philippine Sea area was subject to a moratorium.
topics.outcome: The DOE undertook to review and clarify the US-linked announcements and said Philippine permits would be required for any energy or fuel project. It presented PNOC's proposed strategic reserve but did not resolve the status of the announced foreign facility or the West Philippine Sea activity, which remained subject to a moratorium and broader geopolitical concerns.

positions.position: The DOE should clarify public US Embassy energy announcements, provide information on fuel-storage arrangements, protect Philippine energy security through domestic reserve capacity, and explain the status and legal basis of West Philippine Sea resource development.

topics.topic: Offshore-wind development and supporting port and grid infrastructure
topics.summary: Rep. Jan Franz Chan asked whether the cited target of 21 gigawatts by 2040, or about 21% of national electricity, remained the administration's working offshore-wind target. The DOE secretary said offshore wind continued to be promoted but did not confirm the 21% figure, pending a new energy-mix simulation expected at the end of the year. A DOE undersecretary said an offshore-wind auction covering 3,300 megawatts was ongoing. Chan then asked about budget support for port works and grid preparation. The Philippine Ports Authority said offshore-wind ports would require about 30 tons per square meter, compared with six to eight tons for existing ports, and identified projects in Pambuhan and Santa Clara, with stated construction timelines. Curimao Port was described as intended for floating offshore wind and not to be contracted under the current administration because the auction mainly covered fixed-bottom projects. No specific budget amount for grid preparation was committed, but the port project timelines and DOE's year-end energy-mix update were stated.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the administration still supported the Philippine Energy Plan target of 21 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2040, supplying about 21% of national electricity. It also asked what budget and interagency support were needed for port works and grid preparation, including for off-grid islands.
topics.agency_position: The DOE said it continued to support offshore-wind development but could not yet confirm that the 21% share target remained unchanged. It was conducting a new energy-mix simulation, expected by the end of the year, while offshore wind remained included; the Philippine Ports Authority described port projects and their implementation timelines as the principal enabling infrastructure discussed.
topics.outcome: The committee received confirmation that offshore wind remained part of DOE planning and that a 3,300-megawatt auction was ongoing, but the secretary did not confirm the specific 21% target. Port infrastructure plans and timelines were provided, while specific 2027 budget amounts or grid-preparation funding commitments were not established.

positions.position: Supported continued offshore-wind planning and asked that the budget provide coordinated port and grid-preparation support, with off-grid islands included.

topics.topic: ERC consumer complaints and regional access to hearings
topics.summary: A committee member questioned the ERC about complaint volumes, informal and formal complaint handling, and case disposition. The discussion cited about 5,380 complaints as of mid-August, 5,329 complaints in 2025, 3,289 in 2024, and 4,000, or 77%, of 2026 complaints concerning service-bureau status. The ERC also cited 3,657 ongoing informal or letter complaints, 620 2026 letter complaints, and a combined figure of 27, although some categories were unclear. The member requested submission of the complaint data, and the ERC agreed. Marlo Bancoro then raised the difficulty of access for complainants facing around 10 hours of land travel and sought regional hearings. The ERC said online hearings were the default but consumers could request in-person proceedings, and committed to prioritizing Cagayan de Oro for Mindanao hearings subject to transportation funding while studying the cost of hearing staff and related expenses.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the volume and disposition of ERC consumer complaints, including the number of informal and formal complaints and who was handling them. It also asked whether consumers could access ERC hearings regionally or online instead of traveling long distances.
topics.agency_position: The ERC said online video-conference hearings were the default, while consumers could request in-person hearings. It said it had previously held locality-based or satellite-office hearings and committed to prioritizing Cagayan de Oro for in-person Mindanao hearings, subject to transportation funding, while studying how to fund the required hearing staff and related costs.
topics.outcome: The ERC agreed to submit complaint data and committed to prioritizing Cagayan de Oro for qualifying in-person Mindanao hearings, while studying the funding of hearing staff and related costs. The full complaint disposition data and the feasibility and funding of regular regional hearings remained subject to submission or further study.

topics.topic: DOE special-fund authority and retained agency income
topics.summary: Rep. Robert Nassal asked whether the proposed 20% authority would ensure DOE access to PD number 910 earmarked funds and what programs would be financed. Secretary Sharon Garin said DOE did not receive the full statutory share because GOCCs were also covered, but identified automation, grid management, regional facilities, green buildings, and energy research as potential uses. She projected that 20% of 2027 Malampaya collections could be about 5.4 billion. DOE officials said more than 2 million households remained without electricity and that about 10 billion a year would be needed for electrification, compared with current annual funding of about 2 billion to 3 billion. Later, DOE requested authority to retain 3% for administrative and engineering costs, but the chair said DBM had previously found no legal basis for similar requests. The committee requested prioritized lists and supporting details by the following day and deferred the legal issue for discussion with DBM before plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed 20% special-fund authority would allow DOE to access legally earmarked PD Number 910 funds, what programs would be financed, and whether the additional fiscal space could accelerate total electrification. It also examined whether DOE-related agencies could retain income for administrative and engineering costs and whether the proposed special provisions had a legal basis.
topics.agency_position: DOE supported inclusion of the 20% authority so it could obtain greater access to legally earmarked funds, although Secretary Garin said DOE had historically received less than the full amount because other GOCCs were also covered. DOE identified electrification, automation, grid management, regional facilities, green buildings, and energy research as potential uses, while the retained-income request remained subject to DBM's legal position.
topics.outcome: The committee generally supported DOE's access to legally earmarked funds and the need for higher electrification resources, but required program details and prioritized special-provision language. The retained-income request was not resolved during the hearing and was deferred for consultation with DBM before plenary.

positions.position: Supported the proposed 20% special provision if it ensured access to legally earmarked DOE funds, subject to DOE clearly identifying lawful and implementable uses. He also supported increasing electrification funding.
Expressed support for DOE and ERC funding needs but required detailed prioritized lists and further consultation with DBM before deciding on special provisions involving retained income.

Supported access to the earmarked special fund and identified substantial unfunded DOE programs, while stating that DOE would not request a general budget increase and would instead seek support for ERC and appropriate special provisions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal cited Section 21 of Republic Act number seven six three eight, which provides that 20% of the outstanding balance of the PD number nine one zero special fund may be disbursed for expenses necessary for DOE's powers and functions. He asked whether expressly including the 20% authority in the proposed 2027 special provision was intended to ensure DOE could access funds already earmarked to it by law.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: He noted that the 2025 GAA reflected 896,000,000 from the same fund and that the 2026 GAA reflected 1,300,000,000, but neither contained the express 20% language proposed for 2027.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin said the 20% could amount to about 2,000,000,000 if based on roughly 10,000,000,000 from Malampaya. She explained that DOE was not the only recipient because the calculation also included amounts given to GOCCs, but said DOE would appreciate full access and would make do with what it received.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal asked what amount DOE expected from the 20% authority and what specific programs, projects, and expenses DOE would fund from it.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin said DOE's tier-one items were the projects normally granted, while tier-two items included projects DOE wished to pursue, such as regional offices, green buildings, improved automation, support for the grid management committee and ERC, and energy-related research and development.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: She said that if the relevant fund reached 20,000,000, the 20% share would normally be 4,000,000,000, while DOE would probably receive about 1,000,000. The transcript's reference to 20,000,000 is unclear in context.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal summarized that DOE was receiving more or less 10%, and said that if the 20% authority were reached, the amount could be 4,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin projected that Malampaya collections alone in 2027 could reach 27,000,000,000, with 20% amounting to 5,400,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal said he supported the provision if it was intended to ensure DOE could access funds legally earmarked to it. He added that DOE should clearly identify the funded programs so Congress could verify that the money remained within legally authorized purposes.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal asked whether improved access to earmarked funds, assuming 4,000,000,000, could be used to accelerate total electrification. He asked how many CTOs and households remained without electricity as of 08/31/2026 and how much it would cost to electrify all of them.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin pointed to DOE's Total Electrification Program and the NAES budget, and asked that the impact of increasing the program to 2,000,000,000 or so be considered.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: A DOE official said the current total electrification program budget was 500,000,000 per year and that more than 2,000,000 households remained without electricity.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official cited 100,000,000,000 pesos every year, 10,000,000,000 a year, and a range of two to 3,000,000,020.22, followed by references to 2028, 2038, and 2043 electrification computations. The statement is garbled and its intended figures are unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal asked how much would be needed annually beginning in 2028.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The DOE official answered that 2028 would require 10,000,000,000 a year from government, while DOE was receiving only about 2,000,000,000 to 3,000,000,000 per year.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal supported increasing the electrification budget and reiterated that DOE should have access to its earmarked funds.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing asked DOE and ERC to identify programs and projects not funded in the NEP that they wanted the budget amendments review subcommittee to consider, including requested special provisions.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin said most of DOE's requested items would not involve additional funding. She identified proposed provisions concerning electric vehicles and a separate request involving administrative costs, but the transcript is unclear on the exact wording of the latter.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin referred to a special provision on the use of 55% for administrative purposes, after which another speaker corrected the figure to 3%. The transcript is unclear on the precise provision.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: She referred to a request allowing CPNOC to reserve 8,000,000,000 in corporate funds for construction of a facility, and said the request would not involve additional funding.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin said DOE had collected 6,000,000,000 pesos from Malampaya that year and expected next year's collections to increase to about 27,000,000,000. She said the increase was about 21,000,000,000 and that the funds would go to the national coffers; the statement also contains an unclear reference to 200,000,000.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: A DOE-related official asked whether a 3% executive and administrative cost could be kept as general income of Naya to cover additional engineers needed to inspect and certify solar home system projects.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official said the agency was struggling to implement the project on time and needed additional manpower. The request was to use EIO for salaries and wages of additional personnel; the transcript does not clearly identify the acronym or entity.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing said the committee would confer with DBM because a similar ERC request to use retained income had been rejected in the previous year. She said DBM's position was that there was no legal basis to allow such use.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing said the committee would obtain DBM's position on the retained-income request and address the legal complexity separately rather than wait for a DBM representative during the hearing.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing said the committee would settle the special-provision issue after conferring with DBM, Secretary Garin, and the vice chair, preferably before the matter reached plenary.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing requested a prioritized list of DOE's proposed special provisions and other items by the end of the week, ultimately specifying submission by tomorrow, so the subcommittee could deliberate on them.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing extended the request for detailed information to ERC, including the details supporting its additional requirements and proposed special provisions.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin agreed to coordinate on the requested submissions and special-provision language.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (DOTr)

topics.topic: DOTr FY2027 budget proposal and infrastructure priorities
topics.summary: The chair opened scrutiny of the proposed 300,960,000,000 DOTr FY 2027 budget, emphasizing that only 30 of 179 proposed infrastructure projects were in the NEP. DOTr presented 2025 and July 2026 obligation and disbursement rates, including an overall 2025 obligation rate of about 89.35% and a July 2026 obligation rate of about 74.1%. It said capital outlay accounted for about 81.05% of the proposal and described major railway, road, aviation, maritime, and right-of-way requirements, with only a portion of the proposed projects funded. Representative Romeo Momo questioned the increase from 158,000,000,000 to 300,960,000,000 pesos and raised concerns about absorptive capacity. DOTr answered that foreign-assisted projects, including NSCR and the subway, used cash availment authority that affected the comparison of disbursement rates. The committee's questions on implementation capacity and allocation among regions and sectors remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed DOTr FY 2027 allocation was justified by transport priorities, project coverage in the NEP, and the department's capacity to obligate and disburse funds. It also examined how the large capital-outlay allocation would be distributed among sectors and projects.
topics.agency_position: DOTr maintained that the FY 2027 proposal was needed for a large capital-outlay program, particularly foreign-assisted rail and other transport infrastructure, while locally funded projects remained equally important. The agency asserted that its obligation and disbursement performance was stronger than the figures cited by Representative Momo and explained that foreign-assisted projects used cash availment authority in addition to regular NCA accounting.
topics.outcome: The agency presented the proposed allocation, infrastructure mix, NEP coverage, and reported obligation and disbursement rates. Representative Momo challenged the department's absorptive capacity and began a further inquiry into regional and sectoral allocations; that inquiry was not completed in the provided transcript.

positions.position: Supported careful scrutiny of the proposed allocation, especially the gap between 179 proposed infrastructure projects and the 30 projects accommodated in the NEP, and sought assurance that investments would deliver mobility, safety, accessibility, and commuter benefits.
Asked Congress for guidance on the FY 2027 proposal and stated that locally funded projects were as important as foreign-assisted projects.

Questioned whether DOTr could absorb and disburse a budget that nearly doubled from 2026, stressing that allocation size mattered less than implementation speed and raising concerns about regional and sectoral distribution.

actions.action: The chair invited DOTr to present its FY 2027 budget proposal in detail.
Giovanni Lopez requested legislative guidance and support on the FY 2027 budget proposal.
The secretary requested permission to show a short approximately seventeen-minute audiovisual presentation.
The chair granted permission for the presentation to proceed.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair stated that the proposed FY 2027 DOTr and attached-agency budget was 300,960,000,000.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The bulk of the allocation was for capital outlay, including foreign-assisted and locally funded projects in railways, roads, aviation, and maritime transport.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair noted that only 30 of 179 proposed infrastructure projects had been accommodated in the NEP and called for scrutiny of whether priority projects would be implemented efficiently and equitably.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair asked whether the investments were aligned with long-term mobility goals and whether they addressed congestion, safety, accessibility, and tangible relief for ordinary commuters.

thread.speaker: Secretary Giovanni Lopez
thread.said: Giovanni Lopez sought Congress's legislative wisdom, authority, and guidance on the FY 2027 budget proposal, saying the department would present its 2026 NEP and accomplishments.

thread.speaker: Secretary Giovanni Lopez
thread.said: Giovanni Lopez assured the committee that the department would work with whatever budget Congress provided and said locally funded projects were equally important as foreign-assisted projects.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter introduced the FY 2027 budget proposal and began with the Office of the Secretary and Central Office's obligation and disbursement accomplishments.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: For January to December 2025, the Office of the Secretary and Central Office had a 90.45% obligation rate and a 57.45% disbursement rate.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: As of July 2026, the Office of the Secretary and Central Office had an 82.4% obligation rate and a 51.73% disbursement rate. The presenter said the rates were expected to improve before year-end.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: For the entire DOTr agency and attached agencies in 2025, the obligation utilization rate was 89.35% and the disbursement rate was 56.94%.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: As of July 2026, the entire DOTr group had a 74.1% obligation rate and a 56.18% disbursement rate.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter said the FY 2027 NEP amount reflected an increase of billion dollars or 52.52%, compared with a 2026 NEP figure of 197.3. The wording and currency of the increase were unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter compared the proposal with a 2026 GAA amounting to R137.846 billion and described the increase as unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter stated that the increase was 163,114,000,000 or 118%.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The Office of the Secretary, including LTO, LTFRB, MRT3, CAL, and CADCA, received 83.71% or R251 billion dollars out of the R300 million dollars stated in the presentation.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The Philippine Coast Guard received R45.51 billion dollars or 15.12%; the remaining allocation went to other attached agencies.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Capital outlay represented 81.05% or R243 billion dollars out of the total R300 billion dollars. Personnel services amounted to R35.35 billion dollars or 11.75%.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter said 97% of the capital-outlay allocation, described as billion dollars, was for locally funded and foreign-assisted projects. Of 97,300,000,000, 95% was for foreign-assisted projects and locally funded projects represented 2.1%.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Of 179 proposed projects, 30 had NEP allocations. The presenter said the total 2027 proposal was billion dollars, but only R237 billion dollars was provided; the amount is unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The railway sector proposed 22 projects worth R194 billion.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Road transport proposed 19 projects worth R37 billion, with IPT projects worth PHP15 billion.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Aviation proposed 42 projects worth PHP23 billion; the amount for projects accommodated was spoken as PHP and then became unclear.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Maritime proposed 94 projects worth R18.1 billion. The presenter also cited foreign-assisted projects including the LRT Line One Cavite extension, Metro Manila Subway, MRT Line 3 rehabilitation, and the North-South Commuter Railway.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter said locally funded railway projects were being developed and that the DBM amount totaled R97.9 billion.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The presenter cited a proposal of R19 billion and an allocation of R15 billion dollars, leaving a calculated difference of R4.7 billion.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Locally funded road transport projects involved five projects, described as totaling 12 items.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The amount for the road transport items was stated as 12,000,000,979.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: For aviation foreign-assisted projects, the proposal was R3.8 billion and the other amount was 1,900,000,000.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The aviation locally funded proposal involved 40 projects totaling an unclear amount, within a total proposal of R19.30 billion.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: For maritime foreign-assisted projects, the presenter said the total proposal was an unclear amount but only R18.13 billion was provided.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: The right-of-way proposal was R98 500,000,000, while the amount provided was NIS 2,790,000,000. The presenter said the latter was insufficient even for the NSCR requirement.

thread.speaker: DOTr budget presenter
thread.said: Budgetary support to government corporations, including LRTA and PNR Corporation, totaled 1,200,000,000.

thread.speaker: Representative Romeo Momo
thread.said: Representative Momo questioned the near doubling of the DOTr budget from 158,000,000,000 in 2026 to 300,960,000,000 pesos in 2027 and raised concern about absorptive capacity, particularly with capital outlay at 81.9% of the budget.

thread.speaker: Representative Romeo Momo

topics.topic: MRT-3 subsidy, operations, and possible privatization
topics.summary: A minority member raised unresolved MRT-3 safety and labor complaints, including alleged train-protection and operating concerns, and pressed DOTr for the status of its investigation. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said three foreign experts had reviewed the safety issue, noted MRT-3's average ridership of about 500,000 passengers daily, and undertook to implement a Civil Service Commission resolution on labor violations and provide the committee a copy. Congressman Antonio then asked about MRT-3's subsidy, direct government operation, and maintenance arrangement with Sumitomo, including a transcript figure of 35,000,000,000 whose context was unclear. The agency described the fare support as a 50% discount, illustrating it with a 12-peso fare reduced to 6 pesos, and characterized the underlying subsidy as a noncash loss of revenue. The agency said the subsidy was included in the 2027 proposal but did not state its exact amount. It also said market sounding for a possible PPP covering MRT-3 operations and maintenance was underway, with affordability still to guide any eventual concession.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status and cost of MRT-3 operations, including the government subsidy and any maintenance-related obligations. It also asked whether the MRT-3 operation might be privatized through a public-private partnership and what safeguards would preserve affordability and safety.
topics.agency_position: DOTr said MRT-3 remained government-operated and subsidized, with the subsidy described principally as a noncash revenue loss associated with discounted fares. It was conducting market sounding for a possible PPP covering MRT-3 operations and maintenance, but said the concession terms, exact amount, and bidding process were not yet final.
topics.outcome: The committee received the agency's explanation that MRT-3 was government-operated, subsidized, and subject to a possible PPP after market sounding. The exact subsidy amount and final PPP terms were not established during the exchange, while safety and labor matters remained subject to further agency and commission action.

topics.topic: MRT-7 right-of-way acquisition, alignment, and costs
topics.summary: Members questioned DOTr about MRT-7’s station timetable, common-station delays, and the project’s unresolved right-of-way and alignment. DOTr cited a target of the second quarter of 2027 for the 12-station segment and said the common station was expected to be partially operational in the first quarter of 2028. The minority member pressed the agency on whether property associated with Greggy Araneta was involved; DOTr distinguished the old alignment from a new alignment but did not definitively settle the property question. DOTr later said SMC was responsible for the right-of-way property and gave an unclear estimate recorded as “15,000,000,009,500,000,000,” with the Chair also referring to “9,500,000,000.” The agency committed to submit the alignment, agreement details, amounts, and related information, subject to coordination with SMC. The issue therefore remained open but with agency follow-up committed.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish MRT-7’s implementation timetable, including the opening of its stations and common-station arrangements, and to determine the status, alignment, and cost of right-of-way and site acquisition. topics.agency_position: DOTr stated that MRT-7’s station targets were being pursued under a catch-up plan, but that right-of-way and alignment details required coordination with SMC, the PPP partner. It said SMC was responsible for the right-of-way property and that the estimated cost covered the entire 14-station right-of-way, including resettlement and related activities, while the exact alignment and property implications remained subject to documentation and confirmation.
topics.outcome: DOTr provided an unclear right-of-way cost figure and stated that SMC was responsible for the right-of-way property, but it did not conclusively resolve the current alignment or the alleged property involvement. topics.topic: MRT-7 station completion and commuter mitigation
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Cendaña asked when the MRT-7 stations and the Trinoma common station would be completed and how commuter disruption would be mitigated. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said the 12-station portion and the 13th and 14th stations were targeted for the second quarter of 2027, while the common station was delayed but expected to be partially operational, including signaling, in the first quarter of 2028. The department cited coordination with Trinoma, a dedicated lane, station rehabilitation, headway maintenance, and joint MRT-3/MRT-7 transport management. Rep. Adore Plato later sought clarification on MRT-7's road component, North-South Commuter Railway progress, right-of-way funding, and a 5,000,000 feasibility-study grant. Agency officials reported 62% overall progress on the North-South Commuter Railway, including a 35-kilometer, nine-station segment with 99% right-of-way acquisition and December 2027 passenger operations targeted, but the MRT-7 station timing and road-component budget treatment remained unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish when MRT-7 stations, including the 13th and 14th stations and the common station, would be completed and operational. topics.agency_position: The department said the 12-station MRT-7 portion and the 13th and 14th stations were targeted for the second quarter of 2027, although another agency statement placed the latter stations by 2028. It said the common station was delayed but targeted for partial operation, including signaling, in the first quarter of 2028, with coordination, dedicated access, rehabilitation, headway management, and transport-management measures intended to mitigate commuter impacts.
topics.outcome: The department provided target dates and described interim coordination and operational measures, but the transcript contained inconsistent timing for the 13th and 14th MRT-7 stations—second quarter of 2027 in one answer and 2028 in another. The road-component budget treatment and the questioned right-of-way amount were not fully resolved in the exchange.

topics.topic: North-South Commuter Railway right-of-way and operations
topics.summary: Rep. Adore Plato asked the DOTr to clarify the North-South Commuter Railway's overall requirement, right-of-way funding, project progress, and feasibility-study support. The agency reported 62% overall progress, 99% right-of-way acquisition for a 35-kilometer, nine-station segment, and 85% acquisition for a 53-kilometer segment. It targeted passenger operations for December 2027 on the first segment and construction completion in 2028 for the other segment, while reporting 64% acquisition for the south segment. The agency also confirmed a 5,000,000 feasibility-study grant. The committee's question about whether 150,000,000,000 was a separate right-of-way amount, and the related road-component budget discussion, remained unclear in the transcript.

topics.topic: Mindanao Railway Phase Three and bridge-and-rail feasibility studies
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez asked what DOTr had done to advance Mindanao Railway Phase Three from Villanueva and Tagoloan through Cagayan de Oro to Laguindingan. The agency referred to a prior prefeasibility study and an unclear commitment concerning the following week. Rodriguez also asked how DOTr and DPWH would study a bridge carrying or accompanying railway infrastructure and cited earlier feasibility-study funding of about 450 million and 50 million. The agency said bridges, roads, and railways should be covered by an integrated transport plan and stated a cost of 75 million per study. The chair acknowledged the proposal as equivalent to an additional 10% of the DOTr budget, but the increase was not approved in the excerpt.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted projects, loan proceeds, and commitment fees
topics.summary: A committee member and Congresswoman Mula asked DOTr to identify its foreign-assisted projects, account for delays and commitment fees, and clarify the status and financing of loan-funded projects. DOTr identified major rail, Cebu BRT, and other projects, estimating about seven, and confirmed that commitment fees form part of loan contracts. DOTr said DOF makes the payments and undertook to coordinate with DOF and submit the DOTr-related figures, while Congresswoman Mula cited about 308 million pesos for 2024, 3.4 billion pesos in DOF-reported fees from 2022 to the present, and about 1.6 billion in the DPWH hearing. In the later exchange, the committee cited a foreign-assisted-project budget of about 232 billion and discussed GAA figures including 122 b in 2025 and 20,000,000,000. The member questioned whether congressional insertions had a financing source once loan proceeds were allocated elsewhere. The Chair directed the Secretariat to note the comments, while the precise commitment-fee and insertion-financing data remained pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which DOTr foreign-assisted projects were covered by perfected loan agreements, whether delays had generated commitment fees, and how loan proceeds and congressional insertions were being handled. It also sought project lists, timelines, and financial data, including amounts paid by DOF for or on behalf of DOTr projects.
topics.agency_position: DOTr stated that its foreign-assisted projects included major rail, bus rapid transit, and other projects, estimated at about seven projects, although the official cautioned that the count might be wrong. It confirmed that commitment fees form part of loan contracts, but said DOF makes the payments and undertook to coordinate with DOF and submit the relevant figures and project information.
topics.outcome: DOTr confirmed the contractual nature of commitment fees and said DOF was responsible for paying them, but the precise DOTr-related amount remained to be coordinated and submitted. The committee also recorded concerns about the financing source for foreign-assisted-project insertions; the issue was not fully resolved during the hearing.

topics.topic: Delayed or canceled transport projects and congressional insertions
topics.summary: A committee member asked DOTr to account for foreign-assisted projects, delays, penalties, and commitment fees, and DOTr estimated that there were about seven such projects. DOTr confirmed that commitment fees were part of loan contracts, while Congresswoman Mula cited about three hundred eight million pesos for 2024, 3,400,000,000 pesos in DOF-cited fees for DPWH and DOTr from 2022 to the present, and about one point six billion at the DPWH hearing. DOTr said DOF actually paid the fees and undertook to coordinate with it and report back, while the member requested complete project, timeline, and financial data. Congresswoman Mula also asked about the terminated Zamboanga Port passenger-terminal contract, and PPA reported about 52% accomplishment, with rebidding or reimplementation discussed but no clear roadmap supplied. The chair later cited a foreign-assisted-project budget of 232,000,000,000 and questioned the funding basis for congressional insertions. The agency confirmed that loan agreements were perfected, but the detailed appropriation and insertion issues remained subject to clarification and document submission.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which DOTr foreign-assisted projects had been delayed, canceled, or placed under unprogrammed appropriations; the commitment fees paid or incurred for them; and whether congressional insertions had funding and valid loan support. It also sought an update on the terminated Zamboanga Port passenger-terminal contract.
topics.agency_position: DOTr said foreign-assisted projects included the NSCR, subway, Cebu BRT, and other projects, estimated at about seven, and confirmed that commitment fees were part of the loan contracts. It said DOF actually paid the commitment fees and undertook to coordinate with DOF and submit the relevant information; it also confirmed that the cited loan agreements were perfected, while several detailed funding and insertion questions remained unclear.
topics.outcome: DOTr answered the general questions about the existence of foreign-assisted projects, contractual commitment fees, and perfected loan agreements, but detailed project, fee, and insertion data were deferred for submission or coordination with DOF. The Zamboanga project was reported at about 52% accomplishment and subject to reimplementation or rebidding, but no complete timeline or roadmap was provided.

topics.topic: MARINA vessel-safety inspection personnel and capacity
topics.summary: Congresswoman Mula asked MARINA about its 2027 plan to address nationwide vessel-safety inspection staffing and capacity gaps. MARINA said its MOOE was so far sufficient but that it needed additional personnel and continuing technical capacity building for highly technical maritime-safety work. The agency said it had submitted a comprehensive manpower proposal under the Government Optimization Plan, which would be evaluated by DBM and used to strengthen regional offices. It also appealed for consideration of another tier-two proposal for 2027. Congresswoman Mula called for continued monitoring of reforms, budget utilization, inspection compliance with international conventions, and maritime-industry oversight. The request remained subject to evaluation and committee consideration, with no final funding decision recorded.

It had submitted a comprehensive manpower proposal under the Government Optimization Plan and appealed for consideration of an additional tier-two proposal for 2027.
topics.outcome: MARINA explained that its MOOE was generally sufficient but that additional personnel and technical capacity building were needed. A manpower proposal had been submitted for DBM evaluation, while the requested tier-two support remained subject to consideration; no final funding action was recorded.

topics.topic: DOTr absorptive capacity and regional allocation
topics.summary: DOTr presented 2025 and July 2026 obligation and disbursement rates and said it was confident its performance would improve. Rep. Romeo Momo questioned the proposed increase from about 158 billion to about 301 billion and the agency's ability to absorb a capital-outlay-heavy budget. DOTr answered that its whole-agency 2025 rates were about 89.35% for obligations and 56.94% for disbursements, while July 2026 rates were 74.1% and 56.18%, respectively, and attributed differences to foreign-assisted projects using cash availment authority. Momo also questioned the regional distribution, citing about 0.1% for his region versus Davao's roughly 15.3 billion or 5.1%. The committee pressed for completion of Tandag Airport and improved facilities in Surigao del Sur. DOTr targeted Tandag completion by year-end, said it would reevaluate the project, and committed to prepare a 2027 program for Surigao del Sur.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DOTr could absorb and disburse its substantially increased FY 2027 budget, particularly its capital-outlay allocation. It also questioned whether the proposed allocation adequately covered regions such as Surigao del Sur and whether specific airport and transport projects would be completed.
topics.agency_position: DOTr maintained that its absorptive capacity was stronger than the member's cited figures suggested, reporting a 2025 whole-agency obligation rate of 89.35% and disbursement rate of 56.94%, and July 2026 rates of 74.1% and 56.18%. It attributed apparent disbursement differences to foreign-assisted projects being funded through cash availment authority rather than regular NCA and committed to evaluate Tandag Airport and prepare a 2027 program for Surigao del Sur.
topics.outcome: DOTr defended its reported absorptive-capacity rates, but the member's concern about the scale and regional equity of the proposed capital-outlay budget remained open. The agency made commitments on Tandag Airport completion and a 2027 Surigao del Sur program.

positions.position: The proposed increase, especially the large capital-outlay component, required proof that DOTr could absorb and disburse the funds quickly. He also argued that the regional distribution was inequitable because his region received about 0.1% compared with Davao's 5.1%, despite having port and airport needs.
The member pressed for completion and turnover of Tandag Airport and sought additional transport infrastructure and funding for Surigao del Sur.

topics.topic: Tandag Airport completion and Surigao del Sur transport facilities
topics.summary: A committee member criticized the area's reported allocation of only about 1% of the DOTr budget and pressed the agency on Tandag Airport's completion. The member said the airport appeared to be roughly 97% to 98% complete and sought turnover so airlines could be engaged. The DOTr said the project was almost substantially complete, identified the seven-story control tower, apron, grade corrections, and perimeter fence, and targeted completion of the vertical structures by year-end. The member pushed for completion within the month and cited 7% disbursement absorptive capacity, while the agency undertook to revisit the accomplishment. The member also sought improvements to Surigao del Sur's port and Kagwa Airport facilities, and the agency committed to immediately prepare a program for 2027.

topics.topic: NLEX disruption response, toll reimbursement, and traffic management
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Cendaña raised the NLEX disruption, asking about traffic management, toll treatment, and short-, medium-, and long-term mitigation. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said the TRB would examine possible reimbursement within three days, while emphasizing proactive warnings through SMS, RFID-holder notices, variable message signs, and other public-information channels. Cendaña noted that toll-fee collection had continued for more than twenty four hours, and Lopez said toll suspension was governed by the toll-operations agreement and that more reimbursement was needed. Lopez also said the TRB had issued NLEX a notice to explain regarding the toll holiday and liability. Rep. Adore Plato separately questioned the response to severe-weather stranding and the implementation of early-warning protocols. NLEX representative Robin Ignacio said advisories had begun on August 28, but no final reimbursement or protocol determination was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DOTr and the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) responded to the NLEX disruption, including traffic management, toll collection or reimbursement, and communication with motorists. It also examined whether NLEX and the TRB had adequate early-warning protocols for severe-weather events.
topics.agency_position: The DOTr said traffic management, infrastructure mitigation, proactive motorist communication, and possible toll reimbursement were the appropriate responses. Giovanni Lopez said the TRB was examining reimbursement within three days and had required NLEX management to explain the toll-holiday and liability issues, while NLEX said it had issued severe-weather advisories through multiple channels.
topics.outcome: The DOTr described ongoing TRB review of possible reimbursement and confirmed that NLEX had been directed to explain the toll-holiday and liability issues. The record did not show a final reimbursement decision, a completed liability determination, or a specific new severe-weather protocol.

positions.position: Pressed for concrete short-, medium-, and long-term measures, faster action on toll collection or reimbursement, and an explanation for the delay affecting motorists during the NLEX disruption.

topics.topic: LTFRB Region 3 hearing-officer requirements and discipline
topics.summary: Eli San Fernando raised an allegation that LTFRB Region 3 hearing officer Attorney Jennifer Rodriguez arbitrarily required additional documents and 40,000 on the same day they were submitted. He also questioned why the hearing officer was operating from a private law office in the LTFRB office and asked who had disciplinary authority, citing possible collusion or conflict of interest and a memorandum dated 02/19/2026. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said it was his first time hearing of the matter and stated that disciplinary authority over appointed officials belonged to the appointing authority. An LTFRB board member identified as Greg said a notice to explain had been issued, a complaint was pending before the LTFRB disciplinary board, and Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office. The board member also said the regional director had begun hearing the complaint and that the LTFRB had filed its comment with the CSC. The immediate allegations and the broader oversight concerns remained open, although the agency reported ongoing disciplinary action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether an LTFRB Region 3 hearing officer had improperly imposed additional requirements and a 40,000 payment on the same day, and whether the regional director or another authority had disciplinary jurisdiction. It also sought the status of the disciplinary case and corrective action, including whether similar conflicts could occur in other regions.
topics.agency_position: The DOTr Secretary said he had only learned of the matter during the hearing and stated that disciplinary authority over appointed officials rested with the appointing authority. The LTFRB board member said a disciplinary complaint was pending, Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office, the regional director had begun hearing the complaint, and the LTFRB had already filed its comment with the Civil Service Commission.
topics.outcome: The agency reported that disciplinary proceedings were pending, Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office, and the LTFRB had submitted its comment to the CSC. The committee's concerns about the alleged 40,000 requirement, the regional director's disciplinary authority, and possible broader conflicts were not fully resolved during the exchange.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (DA and NIA)

topics.topic: DA FY2027 budget restoration and agency funding priorities
topics.summary: Christopherson Yap supported the DA budget and possible increases, highlighting soil laboratories, irrigation reforms, and local food security planning. The chair later asked DA officials for their top three priorities for possible restoration or additional funding and said the remaining requests could be submitted in writing. DA administrator Paul presented a written-request wishlist that included about 8.7 billion for fertilizer assistance, as much as 10 billion for Rice for All, roughly 9.2 billion for farm-to-market bridges, and about 20 billion for NMIS operating-budget restoration and DA realignment funds. He also cited requests for solar irrigation, laboratories, coconut planting, sugarcane, Ube, dairy, and agricultural food hubs. The committee did not approve a specific restoration during the recorded exchange, but the agency's requests were placed on the record for continuing budget-amendment deliberations.
topics.question: The committee sought to determine which DA programs and projects should be considered for budget restoration or additional funding during institutional amendments. The chair specifically asked the DA leadership to identify its top three priorities and provide the remaining requests in writing.
topics.agency_position: The DA sought restoration or additional funding across fertilizer assistance, agricultural infrastructure, laboratories, irrigation, food production, and commodity-specific programs. Its administrator presented a broad funding wishlist, including items in a written request dated 07/07/2026, but the transcript did not identify which three items were the formal top priorities.

topics.topic: NIA FY2027 budget restoration and irrigation project flexibility
topics.summary: Sheen Gonzales sought DA intervention and rehabilitation planning for irrigation facilities in Dolores, Eastern Samar, and Secretary Kiko Laurel committed to inspect the area in October for possible 2027 action. Carl Cari asked what rapid funding mechanisms NIA had for typhoon-damaged irrigation facilities; an NIA official cited a request of about 2.8 billion and a proposal of 66,000,000, with repairs requested through OCD. NIA Administrator Ed Gillian said NIA had requested about 233 billion for FY2027, but only 46 billion was included, compared with nearly 64 billion in FY2026. He warned that the reduction could delay ongoing irrigation projects and asked that the budget be restored to a program-based presentation. The chair distinguished that request from the special provision on project modifications and required safeguards, validation, and accountability. NIA agreed to submit proposed special-provision language and a prioritized list of items for the budget amendment subcommittee.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what support was available for irrigation rehabilitation and emergency repairs, and whether NIA’s FY2027 funding was sufficient to complete ongoing projects. It also examined whether NIA should receive greater flexibility to modify project line items while retaining congressional safeguards and accountability.
topics.agency_position: NIA said its FY2027 allocation was substantially below both its request and the FY2026 budget, creating a risk of delays to ongoing and critical irrigation projects. It sought restoration to a program-based budget presentation and a special provision allowing appropriate project-line modifications for technical, right-of-way, and site-readiness problems, while maintaining strict compliance, safeguards, and congressional oversight.
topics.outcome: The committee expressed support for considering NIA budget restoration and greater implementation flexibility, subject to safeguards and continued oversight. NIA was expected to submit a prioritized list and proposed special-provision language; no final restoration amount or approved modification authority was established during the hearing.
