topics.topic: El Niño, drought, and climate-resilient farmer assistance
topics.summary: Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA how the 2027 budget would help farmers and Palawan fisherfolk withstand climate-related losses and access inputs, insurance, equipment, and markets. The DA cited solar irrigation, solar pumps, solar-powered aerators, drought- and heat-resistant seeds, fertilizer support, crop insurance, recovery loans, and soil laboratories, as well as Palawan port and ice facilities. Carl Cari later asked about direct assistance during a prolonged El Niño and drought, and the DA answered that it would coordinate with DSWD and provide alternative seeds, fertilizer, and land-preparation support. NIA cited a request of about 2.8 billion and a proposal of 66,000,000 for repair-related needs, but did not clearly explain a rapid-release mechanism. The Chair then asked for El Niño contingency funding, and the DA cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and an increase in the fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar aerators and solar pumps. The DA committed to submit detailed, separately prioritized information, while the final adequacy of contingency and emergency-repair funding remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what the 2027 budget would provide for farmers and fisherfolk facing climate-related crop and fisheries losses, especially prolonged El Niño, drought, and water shortages. It also examined whether contingency funds, irrigation repairs, insurance, inputs, equipment, and recovery assistance would be available and quickly released.
topics.agency_position: The DA said it was responding to climate risks through solar irrigation and pumping, solar-powered aerators, water impounding, drought- and heat-resistant seeds, fertilizer and replanting support, insurance, loans, and soil testing. For El Niño specifically, it cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and an increase in the fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar aerators and solar pumps; NIA identified repair requests but did not clearly establish a rapid-release mechanism.
topics.outcome: The DA presented existing and proposed climate-resilience measures and identified 8,700,000,000 for El Niño fertilizers and a higher BFAR allocation for solar equipment. The Chair requested a separately identified priority list and the DA committed to provide details; the adequacy of the funding and NIA's rapid-release repair mechanism remained unresolved.

positions.position: Supported stronger climate-resilient assistance and expressed support for expanded farmer and fisherfolk livelihood and production programs, particularly in Palawan.
Sought direct, timely financial, input, equipment, and irrigation-repair assistance for farmers affected by El Niño, drought, and typhoon damage, and supported the DA and NIA budgets.
Favored dedicated or separately identified contingency and recovery resources for El Niño and fisherfolk assistance, while recognizing the limits of available fiscal space.

thread.said: The Secretary said Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation coverage normally applied every cropping season and that indemnity checks were normally issued within 21 days after affected farms were verified, although verification could cause delays. The Secretary said processing capacity remained limited compared with 20 plus units, but maintained that soil testing helped farmers use inputs more accurately and reduce costs.

topics.topic: African swine fever response, farmer payouts, and vaccine validation
topics.summary: An Iloilo member questioned the DA's claim that its ASF vaccine was safe and effective, citing the contrary positions of two FDA veterinary experts and the US Department of Agriculture. The DA reported that it had distributed about half a million doses and observed efficacy of about 85% to 90%, then committed to send the supporting clinical-trial documents. Representative Carl Cari asked about 2027 funding for community pig-raising facilities, faster indemnification, and low-cost biosecurity training, citing 4,900,000 in prior indemnification aid in Southern Leyte. topics.topic: Rice procurement, floor-price implementation, and Rice for All
topics.summary: Rep. Sarah Elago asked how EO 100's rice floor price applied and sought clarification on NFA procurement, Rice for All funding, storage, and EO 101 implementation. The agency said NFA was buying at 21 and cited dry-rice prices of 25 to 27 pesos per kilo, while reporting 9,000,000,000 for NFA and 10,000,000,000 for Rice for All. An agency official said NFA warehouse capacity had risen from 500,000 tons to 800,000 tons, with procurement discussed at 20,000 to eventually 40,000 tons a month. The chair then questioned reports that LGU suppliers were selling imported rice instead of local rice and called for validation and investigation. The agency committed to providing details, and reported that the Sagibsaka desk had about 2,000,000, stated as exactly 1,950,000 for ICT equipment, with an additional 95,000,000 figure that was unclear in context.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how Executive Order 100's rice floor-price policy was being implemented, including whether it applied to private-sector buyers, and how NFA procurement, Rice for All funding, and storage capacity supported the policy. It also sought clarification on supplier validation, the implementation of Executive Orders 100 and 101, and funding for the Sagibsaka desk.
topics.agency_position: The agency said EO 100's floor-price mechanism was principally a government measure with limited application to the private sector. It maintained that NFA's warehouse capacity and available funding were sufficient for the planned procurement volumes, while stating that supplier arrangements were being validated and the Sagibsaka desk had funding, including 1,950,000 for ICT equipment as described in the transcript.
topics.outcome: The agency said procurement capacity, funding, and storage were substantially improved, but the committee requested further details and validation of supplier practices. The record does not show that the supplier-validation concerns or the unclear Sagibsaka figures were fully resolved.

topics.topic: Rice storage capacity and delayed Iloilo processing facility
topics.summary: The Iloilo member pressed the DA over a rice processing facility that had remained unimplemented despite a commitment made about three years earlier. PhilMech described a warehouse of about 1,200 square meters, a 12-ton dryer, and a processing system with a stated capacity of three tons per hour, while DBM clearance for hauling trucks remained pending. The DA committed the rice processing system for June 2027 and scheduled tractors and combined harvesters for distribution from October through December. Sarah Elago then asked about EO 100, temporary storage, and NFA use of private warehouses. The agency cited Rice-for-All funding of about 10 billion, NFA funding of about 9 billion, and a stated total of 19,000,000,020.26, while reporting NFA internal storage capacity of 800,000 tons and procurement of 20,000 to eventually 40,000 tons a month. topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the Iloilo rice processing facility had not been implemented despite earlier commitments, what equipment and delivery dates were covered, and whether storage capacity was sufficient for rice procurement and the Rice-for-All program. topics.outcome: The Iloilo facility was given a revised implementation commitment, but DBM clearance for hauling trucks was still pending. The storage and funding discussion produced agency figures and assurances, but no definitive committee ruling or resolution on temporary and private-warehouse arrangements was recorded.

topics.topic: Fish ports, deepwater ports, and fisheries infrastructure
topics.summary: Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA about fisheries livelihood and production support in Palawan, and the agency cited a 15 hectare Puerto Princesa-area port with ice, cold-storage, and blast-freezer facilities, along with solar-powered ice plants with five to 10 tons per day capacity. Rep. Howard Guintu questioned PFDA’s fish-port funding, which was stated as 3,800,000,003.08 and then 3,800,000,000, while another response cited 8,000,000,000 for old and new ports after an unclear initial figure of 88,000,000,000. He also raised the effect of US restrictions on blue swimming crab, noting that 90% of the market was in the United States; the fisheries undersecretary answered that the issue involved fishing gear and Irrawaddy dolphin interactions and cited a reduction of the gill-net limit to 500 meters. The chair asked about deepwater-port implementation and fisherfolk contingency assistance, and the DA said Mindoro construction would be bid out, cited 8,700,000,000 for El Niño fertilizers, and reported an increase in the BFAR fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000. The chair requested that fisherfolk needs be separately prioritized, and the DA committed to submit the requested details.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much funding was proposed for fish ports and deepwater ports in 2027, how existing and new projects would be financed and implemented, and what support would improve fisheries communities’ access to ice, cold storage, markets, and fishing gear. Members also asked how the agency would protect fisheries market access, particularly for blue swimming crab, and whether contingency support would be available for fisherfolk affected by climate and fuel-related disruptions.
topics.agency_position: The DA and its fisheries officials presented port, ice-plant, cold-storage, seaweed, and climate-response interventions as support for fisheries communities. The agency said Mindoro deepwater-port construction would be bid out, committed to regulatory and local-government measures addressing the blue swimming crab market-access issue, and agreed to submit details and a prioritized fisheries wish list.
topics.outcome: The agency answered the infrastructure and market-access questions and undertook to bid out the Mindoro deepwater port and submit further fisheries details. The precise allocation between ongoing and new fish-port projects remained unclear, while additional funding for PFDA, fish ports, and the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk program was left for further budget consideration.

topics.summary: Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA what assistance would be available to Palawan fisherfolk, including fuel, ice, gear, insurance, and market support. The DA cited a port facility near Puerto Princesa, solar-powered ice plants, seaweed and livestock programs, and proposed ice-plant capacities of about five to 10 tons per day. Rep. Howard Guintu questioned PFDA fish-port funding and raised the US restrictions affecting blue swimming crab exports; BFAR explained the Marine Mammal Protection Act issue, the Irrawaddy dolphin risk, the 500-meter gill-net limit, and its assistance and reporting commitments. The committee also sought support for fisherfolk affected by fishing bans and military exercises, but the duration and precise assistance remained unclear. The Chair later pressed the DA on deepwater-port implementation, the depleted Presidential Assistance program, and El Niño contingency funding; the DA cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and a BFAR budget increase from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar equipment. The DA agreed to submit detailed, separately identified fisherfolk priorities.

topics.outcome: The agency provided program descriptions, infrastructure plans, regulatory measures, and selected funding figures, but several fish-port figures were inconsistent or unclear. The matter landed with commitments to submit detailed priorities, pursue the Mindoro port bidding, report on dolphin-protection compliance, and coordinate on assistance for fisherfolk affected by fishing bans.

topics.topic: RSSI sugarcane infestation control and the 35,000,000 LGU allocation
topics.summary: Sarah Elago raised concerns about the cost and environmental effects of chemical pesticides and asked whether lower-cost biological controls could reach all RSSI-affected sugarcane farms. The DA reported 134,000 hectares affected and 67,443 hectares verified, while the administrator said chemicals had covered about 35,000 hectares. The DA said it had provided 209,000,000, including 23,000,000 for chemical pesticides, had an additional 10,000,000 for chemicals, and estimated about 120,000,000 more for the initial response. It identified slow fungal production and limited laboratory capacity as the principal constraints, while citing an earmarked 300,000,000 for laboratories. The DA committed 35,000,000 directly to LGUs, based on verified affected areas, for Negros Island, with further quick response funding as needed. Expansion of biocontrol production was committed, but the complete transition away from chemical control was not fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of RSSI infestation in sugarcane farms, the cost and coverage of chemical pesticide assistance, and whether lower-cost biological or nature-based controls could replace or complement chemical measures. It also asked what immediate assistance could be provided before the FY 2027 budget, including how the 35,000,000 LGU allocation would be distributed.
topics.agency_position: The DA said chemical pesticides were being used as the initial response because RSSI infestation was intense and biocontrol production was too slow. It supported expanding fungal biocontrol production through DA, government, university, and proposed LGU laboratories, while releasing immediate chemical assistance to LGUs and additional quick response funds as needed.
topics.outcome: The DA answered the committee's questions with infestation figures, existing pesticide assistance, and estimated funding needs. It committed immediate 35,000,000 LGU assistance for Negros Island and longer-term laboratory expansion, but the broader shift to integrated pest management and the final funding required for all affected areas remained dependent on additional budgets and production capacity.

positions.position: She pressed the DA to provide assistance to all affected farms, disclose the full resource requirement, and shift from chemical-intensive control toward cheaper, less harmful nature-based solutions and integrated pest management.
He supported expanding domestic production of biocontrol agents and said the DA would fund the development of mass production capacity.
He defended chemical pesticides as the necessary first response but supported fungal biocontrol and laboratory expansion as the longer-term approach.

topics.topic: Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund delivery
topics.summary: Carl Cari asked how the PCA and DA would use the 2027 Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund resources to reduce paperwork and ensure timely delivery of free fertilizer and planting materials. An agency official said the PCA budget was mostly for replanting, with a target of 100,000,000 trees and an expected 40,000,000 trees planted by the end of the year. The official also said coco levy funds needed to be unlocked through the new bill and referred to value-adding facilities, scholarships, and education for coconut farmers. No specific process for reducing paperwork or accelerating input delivery was provided. Cari later supported the DA and NIA budgets, but the Trust Fund delivery question remained unresolved.

topics.outcome: The agency described replanting and the proposed unlocking of coco levy funds but did not directly answer how paperwork and delivery bottlenecks would be reduced or how inputs would reach farmers on time. topics.topic: Farm-to-market road prioritization and eligibility
topics.summary: A committee member raised the requirements for qualifying and identifying farm-to-market roads. An agency official said the Philippines had 55,000 kilometers of farm-to-market road networks and that 16,000,000,000 would cover only about 1,000 kilometers per year. The official listed poverty incidence, the road influence area, the number of farmer, fish, and fruit beneficiaries, connectivity, road condition, climate-change adaptation, and average daily traffic as prioritization factors. The official added that the roads benefited local communities and the broader local economy, not only agriculture. The exchange ended with the criteria stated and no additional action recorded.
topics.question: What criteria does the Department of Agriculture use to qualify and prioritize farm-to-market road proposals, given the size of the road network and limited annual funding?
topics.agency_position: The agency official said farm-to-market roads are prioritized under the master plan using factors such as beneficiary coverage, poverty incidence, network connectivity, road condition, climate-change adaptation, and traffic. The official also emphasized that these roads support local economies beyond agriculture, while available funding covers only a limited portion of the 55,000-kilometer network each year.
topics.outcome: The agency provided the stated qualification and prioritization criteria and explained the funding limitation. No further document, funding adjustment, or other action was recorded.

topics.topic: Eastern Samar rehabilitation, irrigation, and fisheries research facilities
topics.summary: Sheen Gonzales asked the Department of Agriculture and fisheries officials about rehabilitation of Eastern Samar's research and training center and the Dolores Valley irrigation facilities. The National Fisheries Research and Development Institute reported about 10,600,000 for research-facility rehabilitation and a BFAR counterpart of around 2,500,000, with improvements to be completed by October this year as Phase One. The institute committed to submit the full rehabilitation plan. On Dolores Valley, the agency indicated that a proposal was hoped to be implemented next year, but no detailed scope or amount was provided. Secretary Kiko Laurel committed to visit Eastern Samar in October and address the situation in 2027.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether fisheries research and training facilities in Eastern Samar would be fully rehabilitated, including the total rehabilitation plan and funding. It also asked whether the Department of Agriculture would intervene to rehabilitate the Dolores Valley irrigation facilities and support Eastern Samar's food sufficiency.
topics.agency_position: The fisheries research institute stated that rehabilitation was already under way, with identified funding and a commitment to submit the full rehabilitation plan. The Department of Agriculture indicated that a Dolores Valley rehabilitation proposal was hoped to be implemented next year, while the Secretary committed to an October site visit and action for 2027.
topics.outcome: The fisheries facility issue resulted in a commitment to submit a rehabilitation plan, while the broader rehabilitation scope remained open. The Dolores Valley irrigation issue was not resolved during the exchange; the Secretary committed to an October inspection and action in 2027.

positions.position: He pressed for full rehabilitation of the Eastern Samar fisheries research and training center and for government intervention to restore the Dolores Valley irrigation facilities and strengthen food sufficiency.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET: (OVP)

topics.topic: FY2027 OVP budget overview, program delivery, and utilization
topics.summary: The chair limited the briefing to the OVP budget and then recognized the agency to present its FY 2027 proposal. The OVP presented a proposed budget of about 785 million, with over 70% for operating expenses and about 193.1 million for goods and grants under socioeconomic program delivery. It described delivery through 10 satellite offices and one extension office, with a target of about 1.4 million beneficiaries. The agency reported that it served about 1.396 million individuals and groups in 2025, obligated about 851.8 million, and disbursed about 687.8 million. For the first half of 2026, it reported about 773,858 beneficiaries served, 43% obligation of the available allotment, and a 62% disbursement rate, although the spoken disbursement amount was unclear. The presentation ended without a recorded challenge, request, or commitment.
topics.question: What was the OVP's proposed FY 2027 budget, how would it be distributed across personnel, operating expenses, capital outlay, and direct program delivery, and what did the OVP report about program reach and budget utilization? The committee also sought to establish the implementation structure supporting nationwide delivery.
topics.agency_position: The OVP presented the proposed FY 2027 budget as a lean, focused allocation centered on direct socioeconomic assistance, satellite-office operations, and nationwide service delivery. It maintained that its historical utilization, beneficiary reach, project completion, partnerships, and satisfaction ratings demonstrated effective implementation.
topics.outcome: The OVP completed its budget and performance presentation, covering the proposed allocation, delivery structure, beneficiary reach, and utilization record. No member question, document request, commitment, or contested issue was recorded in this stretch.

topics.topic: Beneficiary selection and duplication controls
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Ko asked how the OVP selected beneficiaries for bags, wheelchairs, and Aljanaza kits and how it avoided duplication with LGUs and other agencies. OVP Director for Operations Norman Baloro said the Department of Education and people's organizations identified recipients, with priority for GIDA and last-mile schools, while wheelchairs could be provided upon requests from organizations, LGUs, or walk-in clients. He cited dashboard monitoring and a Department of Education-verified master list as safeguards against duplication. The discussion also covered the proposed OVP charter, House Bill Number 4 2 1 5, which the OVP said would establish a dedicated policy-research function; current policy work was handled by the Strategic Management Office. Rep. Ko asked for the OVP or Vice President's position on “Paxilica,” but the agency official declined to comment, said the question would be noted, and the Chair requested any response in writing.

topics.agency_position: The OVP said beneficiary selection relied on Department of Education identification, people's-organization requests, priority targeting of GIDA and last-mile schools, and requests from organizations, LGUs, and walk-in clients. It said dashboard monitoring, a Department of Education-verified master list, and supporting documents were used to control duplication. The OVP said policy research was currently handled by the Strategic Management Office, while a proposed OVP charter would establish a dedicated policy-research office.
topics.outcome: The committee received the OVP's explanation of beneficiary identification and duplication controls, but the extent of coordination with agencies beyond the Department of Education was not fully detailed. The question on the Vice President's position on “Paxilica” remained unanswered and was to be addressed, if at all, in a written response.

topics.topic: OVP maintenance and other operating expenses and program manuals
topics.summary: A committee member questioned whether OVP programs had publicly accessible manuals and requirements because the OVP directly implemented its programs. The OVP said all nine core programs had regularly updated manuals, although the You Can Be VP procedure was not in the citizens charter. OVP officials explained that the You Can Be VP allocation included program activities and reported five recipients against a target of two learners. The member also questioned Libreng Sakay's cited beneficiary totals and 22,000,000 budget; the OVP described nine buses, private and government partnerships, two buses being purchased, and POL costs charged to the OVP. The OVP cited 46 passengers per bus and a daily figure recorded inconsistently as 442 and 422, with operations during morning and afternoon peak hours. The exchange ended with a request for a list of providers and related You Can Be VP information, while the beneficiary calculations remained unclear.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARINGS OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (CSC)

topics.topic: JO/COS absorption, plantilla vacancies, and professionalization funding
topics.summary: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. led the inquiry into 919,868 JO and COS workers, vacant plantilla positions, and the absence of measurable absorption and vacancy-reduction targets. CSC described preferential rating, qualification requirements, Prime ESG, agency optimization, and a target covering 40 agencies, but said it could not establish a direct correlation between the programs and JO/COS absorption. The agency distinguished regular and necessary functions that should be staffed permanently from temporary or episodic work, and proposed reviews of LGU personnel-service caps and DBM's scrap-and-build policy. Representative Elijah San Fernando and Representative Kaloy Bulilla raised worker precarity, political accommodation, public-sector unionism, and a DSWD worker's case, while CSC discussed joint work with DBM and COA and possible benefits coverage. Representative Democrito Mendoza questioned 224999 vacancies, examination pass rates, and proposed equivalency legislation; CSC said the principal problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete vacancies, staffing constraints, and merit-and-fitness concerns. The issue remained unresolved, with several administrative and legislative follow-ups contemplated.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how CSC would reduce plantilla vacancies and government-wide reliance on job-order (JO) and contract-of-service (COS) workers, including whether qualified long-serving workers could be absorbed into permanent positions. Members also asked what measurable results would come from the proposed professionalization and modernization allocations and whether CSC would support legislative and monitoring mechanisms.
topics.agency_position: CSC said it could facilitate eligibility, improve HR systems, monitor or analyze JO/COS deployment, and recommend legislative and administrative changes, but could not guarantee absorption into permanent civil service positions. It distinguished workers performing regular and necessary functions, who should be reduced or regularized through proper staffing, from workers performing temporary or episodic functions, for whom JO/COS arrangements remained necessary.
topics.outcome: The committee obtained CSC's explanation of the existing preferential-rating, modernization, optimization, and public-sector unionism measures, but no government-wide numerical targets for vacancy reduction or JO/COS absorption were committed. Legislative equivalency, monitoring, LGU staffing limits, and the precise scope of CSC jurisdiction remained open for further policy or legislative action.

positions.position: Pressed CSC to provide government-wide, measurable targets for filling vacancies, reducing JO/COS reliance, monitoring workers, and demonstrating results from the professionalization and modernization allocations.

Supported regularization or reduction of JO/COS use for workers performing regular and necessary functions, while recognizing that some temporary work required such arrangements. He identified perpetual hiring and political accommodation as major concerns.
Supported the CSC budget and sought a remedy for the precarious situation of a DSWD JO worker transferred to Pasay LGU.
Sought a legislative equivalency pathway for qualified long-serving workers, questioned persistent vacancies and examination pass rates, and urged CSC support for House Bills 93 and 92.
Recognized the operational importance of JOs and COS workers but said legal and governance constraints had to be addressed while CSC continued reviewing policies.

actions.action: CSC said it would continue reviewing policies and working to make civil-service entry and absorption more efficient and accessible.
CSC was asked to provide or develop Prime ESG guidance and measurable modernization results for Congress.
CSC said it hoped to recommend within the year a way forward on mandatory and optional LGU positions and their effect on long-serving JO/COS workers.
CSC, DBM, and COA were to work together on the joint memorandum circular and mechanisms concerning JO/COS benefits and grievances.
Representative Kaloy Bulilla manifested support for passage of the CSC budget.
Representative Democrito Mendoza requested CSC support for House Bill 93 and later House Bill 92.
The CSC official said there was no problem with the proposed public-sector labor representation, subject to the mechanisms already being discussed.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked what CSC was doing about unfilled plantilla positions and continued reliance on JO and COS workers. He cited CSC's inventory of 919,868 JO and COS workers and asked for a government-wide plan to match qualified workers with vacant positions, help workers obtain eligibility, and provide measurable targets and a timeline.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC was reluctant to give absorption targets because appointing authorities must apply qualification requirements to positions. CSC's current measure was preferential rating for JO and COS workers in the civil service examination, while workers still had to meet education, experience, training, and eligibility requirements.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official described the preferential-rating measure as a 70% grade score and a 10% avenue to enter government service, subject to passing the civil service eligibility examination and meeting other qualification requirements.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said workers with ten years of experience could apply the preferential rating, with five years satisfying the government-service experience requirement. Training and education remained potential barriers, although workers meeting first-level or second-level educational qualifications could enter government service if the other requirements were met.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked when the change was implemented. The CSC official answered that it was implemented early this year, after the budget deliberations.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official reported an increase in applicants and passers under the preferential-rating measure but said CSC could not establish a direct correlation between those measures and JO/COS absorption. CSC would continue working to make absorption more efficient and accessible.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal pressed CSC for a concrete response, noting that departments issue plantilla positions while qualified JO and COS workers remain outside the regular service.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC needed a data-management system to establish the relationship between the preferential-rating program and absorption. CSC could not guarantee employment because qualification standards still applied, and the Commission was not generally empowered to employ JOs and COS workers; the official suggested reviewing the laws, with legislation potentially addressing the issue.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal cited the proposed CSC civil service professionalization and workplace cooperation allocation of 725,700,000 and asked what measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and reliance on JOs and COS workers Congress should expect.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal cited budget notes showing 202 unfilled CSC proper positions and 28 unfilled positions in the other CSC unit identified in the transcript as 'CSV.'

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC did not have indicators establishing a correlation between the spending and reductions in JO/COS reliance. The official emphasized that JOs and COS workers were not government employees under civil service jurisdiction and were subject to regulations issued by DBM.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal argued that civil service should monitor JOs and COS workers, particularly because many had worked in government for more than ten years, and asked whether the CSC official agreed.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official agreed that, ideally, CSC could design a system to monitor JOs and COS workers, but did not present an existing system or numerical target.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal cited the proposed Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project funding of 1,450,000,000 and asked what measurable improvements would be delivered by the end of 2027 in hiring time, appointment processing, vacancy filling, HR records, and payroll. He requested numerical targets, metrics, or key result areas to be reported to Congress.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said Prime ESG, replacing Prime HRM, was intended to improve recruitment and selection, performance management, learning and development, and rewards and incentives through the HRM information system. The stated PCSMP target was to reach 40 agencies across all sectors, but no vacancy or JO/COS-absorption target was provided.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official agreed that some long-serving workers performing regular and necessary functions should already have been made permanent. However, COS and JO arrangements remained important for temporary or episodic work, including welfare distribution, and it would be financially irresponsible to make those workers permanent.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official proposed reviewing LGU personnel-service caps with DILG and DBM, considering regulation of JO/COS numbers in LGUs, and improving CSC assistance to LGUs in recruitment and appointments. The official said 70% of the total number of JOs and COS workers in government were in LGUs.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC was discussing the issue and hoped within this year to recommend a way forward on whether mandatory LGU positions should be mandatory or optional, including the effect on LGUs' ability to create plantilla positions for long-serving JO and COS workers.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official recommended that DBM move away from scrap-and-build as the default policy so agencies could create legitimately needed positions without first identifying positions to scrap. The official also supported analyzing obsolete vacant positions and removing them from the plantilla inventory when justified.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official proposed agency-by-agency staffing analysis and possible trigger points for automatic review when an agency repeatedly hired JOs or COS workers for the same position over a number of years. The stated objective was to minimize the first category of workers performing regular, desirable, and necessary functions while retaining JO/COS arrangements for temporary and episodic work.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the DBM-CSC joint memorandum circular required agencies to maintain updated inventories showing where JOs and COS workers were deployed and what functions they performed. Better implementation and analytics could provide the evidence needed for policies facilitating entry into government service, although CSC could not guarantee absorption at that time.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official described political and electoral realities, particularly in local governments, as part of the reason JO and COS arrangements persisted, while maintaining that these workers were essential to service delivery. The official said legal barriers to integration had to be addressed and that CSC would continue reviewing and rationalizing policies.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando agreed that some JOs and COS workers were essential but said perpetual use of such arrangements created the problem. He identified political accommodation, especially in LGUs, as a concern, and the chair indicated agreement.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked about the public-sector unionism subprogram, citing an allocation of around 30,000 pesos to 88,000 pesos per regional office and asking about its outputs and targets.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the program covered organizing and registering public-sector employee organizations, encouraging their creation, recognizing exclusive bargaining units, and registering collective negotiation agreements. The official cited a target to recognize organizations within seven days.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando raised the precarious situation of JO and COS workers and said the issue required political reform. He deferred additional questioning to a second round.

thread.speaker: Representative Kaloy Bulilla
thread.said: Bulilla manifested support for passage of the CSC budget but raised the case of a DSWD job-order worker transferred from the national central office to the local government of Pasay. He sought CSC assistance on the worker's situation.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said CSC had not clearly had jurisdiction over JOs and COS workers under the earlier framework, but the President asked CSC to participate in formulating the joint memorandum circular with DBM and COA. CSC interpreted the circular as covering JO/COS workers' entitlement to the seven-day solo-parent leave benefit, subject to refining the mechanism and coordination with DBM.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta explained that CSC's participation in the joint memorandum circular gave it jurisdiction to issue rules concerning JOs and COS workers to that extent, including the application of the solo-parent law to such workers in DSWD.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the civil service examination passing rate was 80% in the context of the preferential-rating discussion, but clarified that five years of JO service did not automatically create a permanent appointment. Workers remained subject to the necessary qualifications and availability of a permanent position item.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza asked about 224999 vacant plantilla positions as of July and whether the figure came from CSC or DBM. Acosta answered that it came from the inventory of government human resources.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza said the number of vacant positions remained at roughly the same level and asked for the plan to reduce it, including whether some positions were obsolete.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said there was anecdotal evidence that agencies kept obsolete positions vacant for scrap-and-build purposes. He recommended moving away from scrap-and-build as the default, evaluating genuine agency needs, and having the optimization program monitor long-vacant positions.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said CSC had met workers halfway through a preferential-rating policy: ten years of COS or JO service could provide 10 points, provided the worker had served five years in the position.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza asked whether CSC would support House Bill 93, an equivalency bill under which at least three years of satisfactory service and demonstrated competence could establish eligibility. He offered to work with CSC on a legislative solution.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said CSC did not have a shortage of eligible applicants, reporting that it produced 160 plus thousand eligibles every year compared with 14,000 positions. He identified the main problems as agencies keeping obsolete vacancies, difficulties creating positions, and LGU personnel-service caps, rather than a lack of eligibles.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza questioned the civil service examination pass rate, citing figures in the transcript as 158080%, 75, 80%, and 15% nationwide, with a separate barangay figure of 25% and 48%. He argued that the results were discouraging.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said he personally took the examination whenever it was administered and vouched for the fairness of the items. He attributed the low passing rate to the quality of education and the examinees, not to poor examination questions.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza again asked whether CSC would support an equivalency bill allowing workers with fifteen years or ten years of service, or at least three years of good service, to qualify for permanent positions.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official opposed an automatic three-year equivalency because it could encourage LGUs to hire unqualified people and wait three years to qualify them. The official said CSC's bottom line was to preserve merit and fitness, while noting that the view expressed was personal and not necessarily the Commission's formal position.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza asked whether CSC was open to House Bill 92, which would create an independent public-sector labor dispute mechanism and alter labor representation in the PSLMC, including in light of ILO Convention 151.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said labor representatives already participated in the PSLMC and regional congresses, from which labor-sector representatives would be nominated. When the chair asked about supporting the bills, the official said there was no problem with the proposed representation and noted that the committee had previously discussed the matter.

topics.topic: Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and digital transformation
topics.summary: CSC presented the PCSMP as a central part of its digital transformation, covering Prime ESG, HRMIS plus payroll, a national learning platform, electronic administrative justice, and a civil-service data management system. The agency cited a proposed PCSMP allocation of about 1.34 billion in the budget breakdown, while the opening presentation separately cited 453 million for implementation. Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. pressed for measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and JO/COS dependence, but CSC acknowledged that it had no indicators establishing those correlations and could not guarantee absorption into the civil service. A committee member confirmed that the contact center used written referrals and that CSC's electronic case system could track cases nationwide. Representative Ryan questioned cybersecurity, online oath-taking authentication, SALN rules, and the failed data-center bidding; CSC undertook to submit a cybersecurity cost breakdown and defended the failed bidding as a privacy safeguard. Representative Elijah San Fernando raised delayed administrative cases, and CSC said CLASS would be implemented in 2027 to enable online filing and digital transmission of case records.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and related digital-transformation spending would produce measurable improvements in recruitment, appointment processing, HR records, payroll, case resolution, cybersecurity, and service delivery. Members also asked whether CSC had concrete targets for reducing vacancies and dependence on job-order and contract-of-service workers, and whether safeguards would protect sensitive personnel and SALN data.
topics.agency_position: CSC said modernization and digitalization were necessary to improve HR governance, appointment processing, learning, payroll, records, administrative justice, and public assistance. It described planned systems and implementation targets, but acknowledged that it did not yet have measurable indicators linking PCSMP spending to vacancy reduction or JO/COS absorption and did not provide a specific cybersecurity or CLASS budget breakdown during the hearing.
topics.outcome: The committee received CSC's explanation of the planned modernization systems and implementation timetable, but the agency did not provide the requested measurable targets linking PCSMP spending to vacancy reduction, hiring time, or JO/COS absorption. Cybersecurity cost disaggregation was requested for later submission, while CLASS and the data-management systems remained implementation commitments rather than completed outcomes.

positions.position: Modernization spending should be tied to measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and reliance on JOs and COs, with numerical targets and reports to Congress.
Digital expansion required a specific cybersecurity budget and strong authentication and privacy safeguards, particularly for online oath-taking, electronic filing, SALN data, and the data center.
Long delays in administrative cases were unacceptable, and CLASS should be funded and implemented to accelerate case transmission and disposition.

positions.who: Committee member who asked about the Contact Center Nangbayan
positions.position: The committee needed to establish whether the contact center and case systems gave complainants meaningful tracking and written feedback.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: CSC proposed a total FY 2027 budget of 3,890,000,000, an increase of 1,140,000,000 or 41.4% from the FY 2026 approved budget of 2,890,000,000. The presenter said 453,000,000 of the increase was intended for the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: The PCSMP would support modernization of the human-resource system through the rollout of Prime Embedded Systems Governance, the HRMIS Payroll system, and a national learning management system.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: CSC had begun allowing digital signatures on CSC records, online oath-taking, and online submission of appointments as part of its digital transformation.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: CSC said appointments were being fully digitized and that this would improve the action rate and speed the issuance of appointments.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: CSC was hoping to digitalize legal processes and services and was intensifying efforts to address aging cases.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: The World Bank-funded PCSMP aimed to strengthen HR capabilities, modernize HR systems, and digitize personnel management.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: The HRMIS plus payroll component initially identified 40 pilot government agencies. CSC said it was trying to add 20 more agencies.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: After a stress test, CSC hoped to operationalize the civil-service data management system by November 2026, including a fully digital personal data sheet across the central and regional offices.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: CSC targeted nationwide rollout of the civil-service data management system across the civil service by the end of 2026, with analytics to support evidence-based policy and program planning.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: The DBM-approved ceiling was described as 4,040,000,000, with 1,340,000,000 attributed to PCSMP and 2,580,000,000 to the regular budget subsidy.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: MOOE was said to increase from 789,000,000 to 1,200,000,000 because of inflationary adjustments, ICT requirements, and PCSMP.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: CSC said the HRMIS plus payroll system could go live as early as the last quarter of 2026, with full go-live, testing, and customization targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: CSC targeted migration of at least 20 existing CSC e-learning courses into an operational national learning platform in 2027.

thread.speaker: CSC opening presenter
thread.said: The planned digital administrative-justice platform would provide electronic filing and service of pleadings, electronic clearances, online payment, paperless transactions, and real-time case-status monitoring.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked what CSC was doing about unfilled plantilla positions and dependence on JO and COS workers. He requested a government-wide plan, measurable targets, and a timeline to match qualified workers with vacant positions and reduce contractual dependence.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: The chairperson said she was reluctant to set targets for absorbing JOs and COs because appointing authorities must apply qualification requirements. She cited preferential ratings and the civil-service eligibility examination as avenues into government service.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: She said the experience requirement for preferential rating had been reduced from 10 years to five years, implemented early in the year after budget deliberations.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the data management system might eventually establish a correlation or support an absorption program, but CSC could not guarantee employment because qualification standards applied. The official suggested reviewing laws affecting JOs and COs, noting that CSC was not empowered to employ them and that legislation might be needed.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked what measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and reliance on JOs and COs Congress should expect from the proposed spending.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC did not yet have indicators establishing a correlation between the program and JO/COS absorption, emphasizing that JOs and COs were not government employees under CSC jurisdiction and were subject to DBM regulations.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: In response to whether CSC should monitor JOs and COs, the official said that, ideally, CSC could design a monitoring system.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked what specific measurable improvements the PCSMP spending would produce by the end of 2027, including improvements in hiring time, appointment processing, filling vacancies, HR records, and payroll. He requested numerical targets, metrics, or key result areas to be reported to Congress.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: CSC answered that Prime ESG and the HRMIS plus payroll system were intended to improve recruitment and selection, performance management, learning and development, and rewards and incentives. The PCSMP target was described as covering 40 agencies across all sectors, but specific performance metrics were not supplied.

thread.speaker: CSC assistant commissioner
thread.said: The Contact Center Nangbayan allowed citizens to report violations or anomalies in agencies. CSC referred reports to the proper agency and monitored the action taken.

thread.speaker: CSC assistant commissioner
thread.said: The contact center used a written mechanism to record reports and provided a written report to the complainant, allowing the complainant to know the status of the matter.

thread.speaker: Committee member
thread.said: A committee member asked whether a digitized case-management system would track administrative and other cases and make their status available.

thread.speaker: CSC assistant commissioner
thread.said: CSC said its electronic case and document management system could track and monitor cases filed nationwide. It was being improved through the Civil Service Legal and Administrative Service System, or CLASS.

thread.speaker: Representative Ryan
thread.said: Ryan asked where CSC stood on cybersecurity and noted that he could not identify a specific cybersecurity budget item. He also asked about security and authentication measures for online filing and online oath-taking.

thread.speaker: CSC assistant commissioner
thread.said: CSC said cybersecurity was integral to Prime ESG and HRMIS plus payroll. It was drafting a data-privacy and cybersecurity manual and said its digital programs for the next three years would contain robust cybersecurity provisions.

thread.speaker: CSC assistant commissioner
thread.said: CSC said it could not identify a specific cybersecurity amount within the integrated programs but undertook to submit a disaggregated breakdown of Prime ESG, HRMIS plus payroll, and other digital-program costs.

thread.speaker: CSC official responsible for oath-taking and digital signatures
thread.said: For online oath-taking, the official said the oath administrator must verify the identity of the person taking the oath and allow the oath only after being personally convinced that the person was genuine.

thread.speaker: Representative Ryan
thread.said: Ryan pressed whether authentication consisted merely of a Zoom confirmation and warned that AI could impersonate a person in a live feed.

thread.speaker: CSC official responsible for oath-taking and digital signatures
thread.said: The official said all precautions should be taken to verify identities and that oath administrators had been notified that they could incur liability if online oath-taking was fictitious or otherwise improper.

thread.speaker: Representative Ryan
thread.said: Ryan asked whether CSC was coordinating with DICT, PNP, NBI, or other law-enforcement bodies to guarantee the authenticity of online oath-taking.

thread.speaker: CSC official responsible for oath-taking and digital signatures
thread.said: CSC said it had a continuing partnership with DICT on ICT matters and would include the concern in matters raised with DICT.

thread.speaker: Representative Ryan
thread.said: Ryan asked for guidelines on the SALN category 'others,' particularly for online and electronic filing.

thread.speaker: CSC official responsible for oath-taking and digital signatures
thread.said: CSC explained that personal properties could generally be grouped under 'others,' while cash, registered personal properties such as motor vehicles and guns, and other registered assets had to be separately or individually declared under the new rules.

thread.speaker: Representative Ryan
thread.said: Ryan noted that 212,000,000 pesos had been set aside to upgrade the central-office data center and said the project was being rebid.

thread.speaker: CSC official responsible for oath-taking and digital signatures
thread.said: CSC said the procurement had only one bidder, which failed to comply with the required confidentiality guarantee. The technical working group recommended declaring a failure of bidding, and the responsible officials agreed.

thread.speaker: Representative Ryan
thread.said: Ryan commended CSC for prioritizing data privacy over expediting the data-center procurement and said the project should be rebid with terms of reference that protected privacy.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando raised a 2019 Land Bank employees' association case involving a claimed constructive demotion and a loss of allowances and benefits amounting to 100,000 pesos annually. He questioned why the case took six years to resolve and asked what CSC was doing about its backlog.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: The chairperson said she had addressed administrative-case delays by adopting a six-month target depending on case complexity, using regular decision templates, dedicating commission sessions to adjudication, and requiring fact sheets and pre-commission reviews.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: The chairperson said CSC's target was to reduce the relevant cases by at least 10% or 5% by year-end, depending on the numbers, and said the agency would try to make case disposition faster.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked about the recommended 2027 budget allocation for CLASS and how it would affect case disposition.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: CSC did not provide a figure but explained that CLASS would permit online filing of pleadings, digital transmission of documents among receiving, records, legal, regional, and executive offices, and work from scanned copies rather than physical files.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson Mary Marilyn Yap
thread.said: CSC said the target implementation of CLASS was 2027. The existing electronic case and document management system was already being used by the Office of Legal Affairs.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: CSC reported an inventory of 7,781 cases, including 5,228 nondisciplinary cases and 553 disciplinary cases; the transcript's categorization is internally unclear.

thread.speaker: CSC official

topics.topic: CSC administrative justice, case backlog, and electronic adjudication
topics.summary: CSC reported that it had disposed of about 10,052 cases in 2024, 9,148 in 2025, and 4,897 in 2026, while aging-case resolution remained an active priority. A committee member asked whether Contact Center 888 provided complainants with status information, and CSC said reports were referred, monitored, and answered in writing. Rep. Solomon Chungalao submitted a pending regional-office complaint involving state-university students, which CSC agreed to check. Rep. Eli San Fernando questioned why a Land Bank employees’ complaint filed in 2019 took six years to resolve and cited 100,000 pesos in removed benefits and incentives. CSC described procedural reforms and said CLASS would permit online filing and digital transmission of case records, with implementation targeted for 2027. CSC did not state the requested CLASS budget figure, leaving the funding impact and specific complaints open while committing to follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CSC’s administrative-justice reforms and proposed digital systems would reduce the backlog, shorten the time for resolving complaints, and give complainants reliable case-status information. Members also asked how the 2027 budget would support electronic adjudication and followed up on specific pending complaints.
topics.agency_position: CSC said it had introduced procedural measures, dedicated adjudication sessions, pre-commission reviews, templates, and targets to reduce its administrative-case backlog. It maintained that CLASS and related electronic systems would improve tracking, speed document transmission and case processing, and support faster disposition, but it did not provide the requested 2027 CLASS budget figure during the exchange.
topics.outcome: CSC explained its existing case-tracking tools, procedural backlog measures, and planned 2027 CLASS implementation, and undertook to check specific pending cases. The requested CLASS budget figure and a concrete resolution of the cited complaints were not established during the hearing.

thread.said: CSC described its planned administrative justice system as a digital platform for legal and administrative services, including electronic filing and service of pleadings, electronic processing of CSC clearances, online payment, paperless transactions, and real-time case-status monitoring.

thread.speaker: a committee member
thread.said: The member asked about the role of Contact Center 888, including whether it merely referred complaints to the agency concerned or also provided redress and follow-up.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: CSC explained that citizens could report violations or anomalies observed in government agencies. The Contact Center would call the concerned agency’s attention to the report, refer it to the proper agency, and monitor what action was taken.

thread.speaker: a committee member

thread.speaker: a committee member

thread.speaker: CSC Assistant Commissioner

thread.speaker: Rep. Solomon Chungalao

thread.speaker: Rep. Eli San Fernando

He said CSC dismissed it after six years, finding that the removal of allowances, benefits, and incentives amounting to 100,000 pesos was pursuant to law and did not constitute demotion, and questioned the delay and CSC’s policy for addressing its backlog.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson
thread.said: The Chairperson said administrative cases were intended to be resolved within six months, depending on their complexity. CSC had adopted regular decision templates, dedicated commission-meeting sessions for adjudication, and pre-commission review requiring fact sheets and case-file checks.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson
thread.said: The Chairperson said cases were reviewed through the Office of Legal Affairs, executive offices, and pre-commission meetings before action by the commission. She said the agency aimed to reduce the case inventory by at least ten percent or five percent by year-end, depending on the numbers.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson
thread.said: The Chairperson said CSC had adopted remedial measures and would try very hard to make case disposition faster. She identified CLASS, the Civil Service Legal and Administrative Services electronic system, as a project that could help address pending cases.

thread.speaker: CSC Chairperson

thread.speaker: CSC agency official

topics.topic: Cybersecurity, online oath-taking, and the 212,000,000 data center
topics.summary: Rep. Ryan asked the CSC to identify its cybersecurity allocation, noting a modernization figure of about 1.4 billion, and requested a breakdown because cybersecurity was integrated across digital programs. The CSC said it was drafting a data privacy and cybersecurity manual and committed to submit a disaggregated budget breakdown. Ryan questioned whether online oath-taking relied only on Zoom and warned about AI-enabled impersonation; the CSC said oath administrators had to verify identity, ask questions, and accept liability for inadequate precautions. The CSC said it had a continuing ICT partnership with DICT and would raise the authentication concerns there. On SALN filing, the CSC explained that personal properties could be grouped under "others," while cash and registered properties had separate treatment under rules issued in 2025. Ryan also raised the roughly 212 million pesos data-center project, and the CSC said the sole bidder failed confidentiality requirements, leading to a declared failure of bidding and rebidding. Ryan endorsed that decision, but the cybersecurity breakdown and rebidding outcome were not yet resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the CSC's modernization budget was specifically devoted to cybersecurity, how online oath-taking and SALN filing would be authenticated and protected, and why the central-office data-center procurement failed. It also sought assurances that the rebidding would preserve data confidentiality and that the failed bidding would not prejudice the CSC's budget.
topics.agency_position: The CSC said cybersecurity was integrated across its digital programs and that it was preparing a data privacy and cybersecurity manual, but it could not provide a specific disaggregated cybersecurity amount during the exchange. It maintained that online oath-taking required identity verification and administrator accountability, that SALN rules clarified the treatment of personal and registered properties, and that the data-center bidding was properly declared failed because the sole bidder did not satisfy confidentiality safeguards.
topics.outcome: The CSC's explanations on oath-taking authentication, SALN treatment, and the failed data-center bidding were provided, and Rep. Ryan endorsed the privacy-based failure of bidding. The requested disaggregated cybersecurity budget and the result of the data-center rebidding remained open.

positions.position: Supported stronger, separately identifiable cybersecurity funding and more robust authentication for online oath-taking and filing. He supported the CSC's decision to reject the data-center bid to protect data privacy and asked that the rebidding and failed procurement not prejudice the CSC's budget.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan

thread.speaker: Agency official

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: Rep. Ryan requested the CSC's cybersecurity budget, including whether it was a separate allocation or lumped into another budget item, because the commission was expanding digital services.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: He asked what safety and authentication measures would apply to online filing and online oath-taking, including protection against impersonation and AI-enabled deception.

thread.speaker: Agency official
thread.said: The agency official explained that the new omnibus rules required verification of the identity of the person taking the oath by the oath administrator. The administrator could proceed only after being personally convinced that the person taking the oath was the actual individual.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: Rep. Ryan asked whether the authentication process consisted merely of confirming identity through Zoom.

thread.speaker: Agency official
thread.said: The agency official said the oath administrator would ask identity-related questions during the Zoom session and would have to be personally convinced that the person taking the oath was the owner of the SALN.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: Rep. Ryan warned that AI technology could make a person appear to be someone else in a live video feed and could enable scams or impersonation of a public or government official.

thread.speaker: Agency official
thread.said: The agency official said all precautions should be taken to verify the real identities of the persons involved. Oath administrators had been notified that they could incur liability and had to ensure that online oath-taking was genuine and did not involve a fictitious oath-taker.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: Rep. Ryan asked whether the CSC was partnering with DICT, the PNP, the NBI, or another law-enforcement body to guarantee the authenticity of online oath-taking.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan

thread.speaker: Agency official

Cash in bank or cash on hand was to be declared separately, while registered personal properties such as motor vehicles and guns had to be individually identified.

thread.speaker: Agency official

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan

thread.speaker: Agency official

thread.speaker: Agency official
thread.said: The official said the terms of reference contained specific safeguards for information confidentiality. The technical working group recommended declaring a failure of bidding, and the reviewing members agreed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: Rep. Ryan applauded the CSC for declaring the failed bidding because it prioritized data privacy over expediting the procurement.

thread.speaker: Rep. Ryan
thread.said: He urged the CSC to apply again with proper terms of reference protecting privacy and asked that the failed bidding not be held against the commission in considering its budget.

topics.topic: Civil-service examinations, eligibility, and equivalency pathways
topics.summary: Representative Nassal pressed the CSC for a government-wide plan, measurable targets, and concrete results from proposed programs addressing vacancies and dependence on about 919,868 JO and COS workers. The CSC described preferential rating, including the 70% grade score, 10% avenue, and experience-based treatment, but said it could not guarantee appointments or establish a direct correlation with absorption. Representative Ismula raised possible preferential eligibility for IPMRs, and the CSC said it could work toward extending coverage after consultations and subject to legal requirements. Representative Mendoza later urged support for House Bill 93, which would create an equivalency pathway after at least three years of satisfactory service, but the CSC warned that this could encourage agencies to retain unqualified hires and undermine merit and fitness. The CSC said it was producing more than 160 thousand eligibles annually and that the central problems were vacancies, obsolete positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates rather than a shortage of eligibles. The hearing ended without a clear CSC commitment to support House Bill 93 or deliver numerical vacancy and absorption targets, although the agency undertook related work on IPMR preferential rating, modernization guidance, and JO/COS regulation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the CSC would help qualified JO and COS workers obtain eligibility, fill vacant plantilla positions, and reduce reliance on contractual arrangements. Members also examined preferential-rating and equivalency pathways, civil-service examination standards and pass rates, and the CSC's position on related legislation.
topics.agency_position: The CSC said preferential rating could help qualified JO, COS, and potentially IPMR workers obtain eligibility, but it did not guarantee appointment because education, training, experience, eligibility, and position-specific qualification standards still applied. The agency maintained that the main problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete or unavailable positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates; it cautioned that automatic equivalency after three years could undermine merit and fitness.
topics.outcome: The CSC explained its existing preferential-rating pathway and indicated that IPMR coverage could be expanded subject to legal and qualification requirements. The broader issues of measurable vacancy-reduction targets, automatic equivalency under House Bill 93, and the causes of low examination pass rates remained open.

positions.position: The CSC should produce measurable government-wide targets and timelines to fill vacancies, monitor JOs and COS workers, reduce contractual dependence, and demonstrate concrete results from modernization spending.
The CSC should consider preferential eligibility treatment for IPMRs and support improved compensation and benefits for government personnel.
The CSC budget should be supported, while the continuing JO and COS problem and the treatment of experienced contractual workers should be addressed.

The CSC should support House Bill 93 to create an equivalency pathway for experienced, competent government workers and should address low examination pass rates and the lack of a pathway to permanent employment.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked what the CSC was doing about the large number of unfilled plantilla positions and the government's continued reliance on JO and COS workers. He cited the CSC inventory of 919,868 JO and COS workers and asked for a government-wide plan, measurable targets, and a timeline.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official was reluctant to give absorption targets because appointing authorities must apply the qualification requirements for each position. The CSC's existing pathway included preferential rating for JOs and COS workers.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said preferential rating could provide a 70% grade score and a 10% avenue to enter government service, but applicants still had to pass the civil-service eligibility examination and meet experience, training, and educational requirements.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official explained that workers with ten years of experience could apply for civil-service preferential rating, with the five-year government-service experience requirement treated as fulfilled. Training or competency hours and educational qualifications remained possible barriers.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked when the preferential-rating change had been implemented.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said it had been implemented early this year, after the budget deliberations.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official reported an increase in applicants and passers under the civil-service preferential-rating system, but said the CSC could not establish a direct correlation between those measures and the absorption of JOs and COS workers. The CSC would continue working to make absorption more efficient and accessible.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He pressed the CSC to state concretely what it would do while departments continued creating plantilla positions despite having qualified JOs and COS workers.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the CSC needed a data-management system to establish a correlation and prepare an absorption program. The CSC could not guarantee civil-service employment because qualification standards applied, and the official suggested reviewing the laws affecting JOs and COS workers because the CSC was generally not empowered to absorb them; legislation could address the issue.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He cited the proposed 725,700,000 for the CSC civil-service professionalization and workplace cooperation program and asked what measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and reliance on JOs and COS workers Congress should expect. He also cited 202 unfilled CSC Proper positions and 28 unfilled positions in the transcript's reference to the CSC.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the CSC did not have indicators establishing a correlation between the spending and reductions in JO and COS reliance. JOs and COS workers were not government employees under the law and were subject to regulations issued by DBM.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He argued that the civil service should monitor JOs and COS workers, particularly because many had worked in government for more than ten years.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official agreed that, ideally, the CSC could design a system to monitor JOs and COS workers, but did not present a concrete monitoring target.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He cited the proposed 1,450,000,000 for the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and asked what measurable improvements would be delivered by the end of 2027 in hiring time, appointment processing, vacancies, human-resource records, and payroll. He asked whether CSC would commit to numerical targets or key result areas and report them to Congress.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the primary target of Prime ESG, replacing Prime HRM, was improved human-resource management through the HRM system and embedded programs covering recruitment and selection, performance management, learning and development, and rewards and incentives. The PCSMP target mentioned was 40 agencies across all sectors.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair asked the CSC chair to provide the Prime ESG guide and said the committee looked forward to the digitalization program being realized and replicated in national government offices.

thread.speaker: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked about civil-service eligibility for Indigenous Peoples mandatory representatives, including representatives at the barangay, municipal, and provincial levels under the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act or RA 8371.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said a prior budget hearing had prompted a study of preferential treatment for Indigenous peoples as a class, with consultations requested from field offices in the Visayas and Mindanao. The CSC recognized that preferential rating could affect qualifying standards but said it could work toward a preferential-rating system for IPMRs.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official indicated that the CSC could extend civil-service preferential-rating eligibility to IPMRs, provided the legal basis and applicable requirements were satisfied.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official proposed recognizing IPMR service by crediting the required years of government experience, such as treating one, two, or three years as representatives as applicable toward the five-year experience requirement for civil-service preferential rating.

thread.speaker: Representative Kaloy Bulilla
thread.said: In discussing the DSWD JO case and the status of JO and COS workers, he asked about the civil-service examination passing rate and the preferential-rating system, including whether five years of JO service meant the worker automatically passed the examination.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official clarified that preferential rating did not automatically make a worker eligible without further conditions. The worker remained subject to the necessary qualifications and requirements for appointment to a permanent position.

thread.speaker: CSC Assistant Commissioner Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: He said the CSC had met JO and COS workers halfway through its preferential-rating policy: ten years of COS or JO service, plus 10 points, could apply so long as the worker had served the government in the position for five years.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: He asked whether the CSC would support House Bill 93, an equivalency law under which at least three years of satisfactory service and demonstrated competence would establish eligibility. He linked the proposal to the large number of JOs and COS workers and unfilled positions.

thread.speaker: CSC Assistant Commissioner Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: He said the CSC did not view the problem as a shortage of eligibles, because it was producing more than 160 thousand eligibles every year while only 14,000 were needed, as spoken in the transcript. He identified obsolete positions, agencies' difficulty creating positions, and LGU personnel-service caps as the more fundamental problems.

thread.speaker: CSC Assistant Commissioner Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: He recommended optimizing government positions, monitoring vacant positions, and using an oversight mechanism. He said the CSC's optimization program could help address the vacancy problem.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: He continued to urge CSC support for House Bill 93, citing his own long experience as a permanent casual worker who had to sign annually and arguing that the bill could provide a pathway to permanence for experienced government workers.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
