topics.topic: Public-sector unionism and labor-management representation
topics.summary: Rep. Eli San Fernando asked about the public-sector unionism subprogram's allocation, outputs, and targets and raised the precarious status of job order and contract of service workers. The stated allocation was 30,000 pesos to 88,000 pesos per regional office, and a CSC official said organizations were to be credited and recognized within seven days. The committee did not receive a complete account of the 2026 and 2027 output indicators, and Rep. San Fernando said he would return to the JO/COS issue in the second round. Rep. Democrito Mendoza then questioned the quality of civil-service examinees and sought CSC support for an equivalency or pathway-to-permanency bill based on three years of service. A CSC commissioner said that position was personal and warned that the proposal could undermine merit and fitness. Mendoza also sought support for a labor-representation bill, and a CSC official expressed openness while describing the existing PSLMC selection mechanism. The issues therefore remained partly open, with further consideration implied rather than fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the allocation, output indicators, and targets for CSC's public-sector unionism subprogram, including the registration and recognition of public-sector employee organizations. On equivalency, the responding commissioner personally opposed a three-year route that could weaken merit and fitness, while the agency official was open to labor representation proposals and described the existing PSLMC nomination process.
topics.outcome: CSC provided the stated allocation range and a seven-day recognition target, but the transcript did not establish complete 2026 and 2027 output indicators or targets. topics.topic: Anti-sexual-harassment compliance and workplace wellness leave
topics.summary: Congresswoman Ilago asked whether agencies were complying with the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act and maintaining functional committees on decorum and investigation. The CSC said the mechanisms were legally required, regional offices conducted regular inspections, and the agency could handle certain cases involving officials and employees of other agencies. It said sexual-harassment and Safe Spaces Act provisions had been integrated into the RACs and related CSC rules, but it did not provide a clear timeline for new Convention 190 guidelines. The CSC cited a special emergency leave policy issued in 2013 that provided five days annually to calamity victims who could show proof. The chair directed the CSC to submit data and a status report, including on wellness leave, leaving those requested materials and the separate wellness-leave issue pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether agencies had functional mechanisms for preventing and investigating sexual harassment, how the Civil Service Commission (CSC) enforced compliance, and whether the CSC had issued or planned guidelines implementing ILO Convention 190. It also sought the status of workplace wellness leave and related employee protections.

It cited an existing special emergency leave policy for calamity victims but did not state a substantive position or timeline on a separate workplace wellness leave policy or fully answer the requested Convention 190 implementation timeline.
topics.outcome: The CSC described existing compliance rules and inspection practices and undertook to submit inspection data and a status report. The requested timeline for CSC guidelines implementing ILO Convention 190 and the substantive status of a separate wellness leave policy remained open.

positions.position: She pressed for evidence of functional agency compliance, clarification of CSC enforcement responsibilities, implementation of ILO Convention 190, and a status report on wellness leave.

topics.topic: Solo-parent leave and benefits for JO/COS workers
topics.summary: Minority member Roberto Nazal Jr. raised whether qualified JO and COS solo parents were entitled to the seven-day solo-parent leave under Republic 11/1961 and the 2025 joint circular. CSC answered that it interpreted section 11.2 as covering benefits granted under existing laws and said it had recognized seven-day solo-parent leave since 2004. Nassal warned that departments remained hesitant because of audit concerns. CSC undertook to reiterate the provision to departments and said it was coordinating with DSWD, the primary implementing agency, while DBM's position was still needed. Representative Kaloy Bulilla later supported the CSC budget and raised the plight of a DSWD JO worker. CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta reaffirmed coverage of JO and COS workers and committed to work with DBM and COA on a mechanism for implementation and grievances.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether qualified solo-parent job order (JO) and contract of service (COS) workers were entitled to the seven-day solo-parent leave under Republic Act 11/1961 and the applicable joint memorandum circular. It also sought to determine whether CSC had communicated and would enforce that interpretation across departments despite audit and implementation concerns.

CSC said DSWD remained the primary implementing agency for the Act, that DBM's position was still needed, and that CSC would reiterate the relevant provision and work with DBM and COA on implementation and grievance mechanisms.
topics.outcome: CSC affirmed that its interpretation covered qualified JO and COS workers and their entitlement to seven-day solo-parent leave, but said DBM's position and coordination with DSWD remained relevant. CSC committed to reiterating the provision and developing an implementation or grievance mechanism with DBM and COA.

thread.said: The official said CSC interpreted the Solo Parents Welfare Act as allowing a seven-day leave for qualified solo parents, whether male or female. The official also cited a CSC issuance from 2004 allowing seven days of solo-parent leave.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: Nassal asked whether CSC had already communicated this interpretation to government departments.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The CSC official said the matter would be circularized to departments, while cautioning that DSWD was the principal implementing authority for the Solo Parents Welfare Act.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC was engaged in ongoing dialogues with DSWD because DSWD was the primary implementing agency for the Act.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official reiterated that CSC had recognized seven-day solo-parent leave as early as 2004 and recognized the joint circular issued by CSC, DBM, and COA.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC could issue a reiterative issuance on the application of the seven-day solo-parent leave if still necessary, although the official believed the relevant issuance had already been made.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: Nassal pushed back that many departments remained afraid to implement the law because of audit concerns.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official acknowledged the audit concern and suggested that the pertinent section of the joint memorandum circular could be reiterated to departments.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official concluded, "We will do that," undertaking to reiterate the relevant provision.

thread.speaker: Kaloy Bulilla, representative
thread.said: Kaloy Bulilla said the treatment of contract-of-service workers was a continuing issue and personally important to him. He manifested support for passage of the CSC budget, while raising the situation of a DSWD national central office job-order employee assigned to the local government of Pasay.

thread.speaker: Ryan Alvin Acosta, CSC official
thread.said: Acosta said he understood Bulilla's desire to improve the situation of COS and JO workers. He explained that CSC's role in the 2025 joint memorandum circular had developed after the President asked CSC to participate in its creation.

thread.speaker: Ryan Alvin Acosta, CSC official
thread.said: Acosta said the concrete result of CSC's work with DBM and COA was the formulation of the joint memorandum circular. He stated that CSC interpreted section 11.2 as granting JO and COS workers the benefit under the Solo Parents Welfare Act, including the seven-day leave.

thread.speaker: Ryan Alvin Acosta, CSC official
thread.said: Acosta said that, under CSC's interpretation, JO and COS workers were covered by the legal provision granting solo-parent leave. He added that CSC still needed DBM's position on the matter.

thread.speaker: Ryan Alvin Acosta, CSC official
thread.said: Acosta said CSC, DBM, and COA could develop a mechanism for JO and COS workers to air grievances and determine whether a contractor or agency arrangement violated the joint circular or the relevant contract.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair pressed for a yes-or-no clarification from CSC on its jurisdiction and involvement in governing JO and COS workers under the joint memorandum circular.

thread.speaker: Ryan Alvin Acosta, CSC official
thread.said: Acosta gave an affirmative answer, explaining that CSC's involvement in the JO/COS joint memorandum circular necessarily gave it jurisdiction to issue rules governing that class of workers.

thread.speaker: Ryan Alvin Acosta, CSC official
thread.said: Acosta clarified that CSC's jurisdiction extended to its role in the joint circular, while DSWD retained subject-matter authority as the implementing agency for the Solo Parents Welfare Act. He said the Act, as applied to JOs and COS workers, was therefore an area involving both CSC's circular-related role and DSWD's implementing authority.

topics.topic: Hospital and agriculturist qualification standards for appointments
topics.summary: Rep. Romeo Momo requested that Adela Siorati Memorial Hospital be allowed to use the higher qualification standards in DOH Administrative Order 2016-003 after its upgrade from a second-level to a third-level hospital. CSC said the hospital had to submit supporting documents, including the DOH circular, and undertook to review the request and act immediately. The Chair then raised a civil-society question citing Republic Act 12215, section 31, and the law's stated effect on agriculturist appointments in national and local government. CSC said draft qualification standards for agriculturists were under Commission consideration and could possibly be finalized after a scheduled September meeting, although the scheduling reference was unclear. The committee requested copies of the relevant materials, but the transcript did not resolve the status of the final circular, nonregistered appointments, or salary adjustments.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CSC would approve higher qualification standards for appointments at Adela Siorati Memorial Hospital and how it was addressing the statutory qualification requirements for agriculturist positions. It also sought clarification on pending CSC guidelines, appointments of nonregistered agriculturists, and related salary adjustments.
topics.agency_position: CSC said it could review and potentially approve the hospital's request for higher qualification standards, subject to submission and verification of the supporting DOH documents. On agriculturist positions, CSC said draft qualification standards were under Commission consideration and could possibly be finalized after the scheduled Commission meeting, but the transcript did not establish a final decision on the circular, nonregistered appointments, or salary adjustments.
topics.outcome: CSC undertook to review the hospital's supporting documents and act immediately, but no approval of the higher qualification standards was recorded. For agriculturist positions, draft standards were under Commission consideration and documents were to be submitted, while the issues of the final circular, existing nonregistered appointments, and salary adjustments remained open.

positions.position: Supported adopting the higher qualification standards under DOH Administrative Order 2016-003 for Adela Siorati Memorial Hospital to enable the urgent filling of vacant positions.

topics.topic: CSC compliance and enforcement of personnel rules
topics.summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula questioned how the CSC enforced its expanded gambling ban and whether it covered online gambling. The CSC said complaints could be filed anonymously through contact centers and complaints desks in regional and field offices, and Assistant Commissioner Ariel Ronquillo said the prohibition covered both on-site and online gambling. Ismula also asked about preferential civil-service eligibility for IPMRs; the CSC said it would consult Indigenous Peoples communities and could develop a preferential-rating system, potentially crediting one to three years of representative service toward a five-year experience requirement, subject to law. The member raised a 2,000 pesos compensation reform and House Bill Number 3874, and the CSC expressed support for increased benefits and continued discussions with DBM. Rep. Isabel Segabaria then challenged the CSC's authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule. The CSC acknowledged the need for legal basis but defended the rule under the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly, leaving the scope of the agency's authority unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the CSC monitored and enforced its expanded gambling prohibition, whether it could provide preferential civil-service eligibility treatment for indigenous peoples mandatory representatives (IPMRs), and what reforms it supported for government compensation. It also sought to clarify whether the CSC had statutory authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule.
topics.agency_position: The CSC said gambling was prohibited both on-site and online and that compliance could be monitored through complaints received by its contact center and complaints desks in regional and field offices. It indicated that preferential eligibility treatment for IPMRs could be developed subject to law, while defending the common-law nepotism rule as an anti-circumvention measure grounded in Supreme Court reasoning, although it acknowledged that an administrative rule must have legal basis.
topics.outcome: The gambling-ban questions were answered with the CSC's position that online gambling was already covered and that complaints systems provided the monitoring mechanism. The IPMR eligibility and compensation matters were left at the level of proposed study, consultation, and continuing dialogue, while the statutory authority for including common-law relationships in the nepotism rule remained contested.

positions.position: Supported strict enforcement and possible legislative expansion of the gambling ban to online gambling, sought preferential civil-service treatment for IPMRs, and urged sustainable and equitable compensation reforms.

Questioned whether the CSC could expand the statutory nepotism prohibition to common-law relationships without clear congressional authorization and suggested that any new substantive restriction should be enacted through legislation.
Expressed support for the compensation legislation or benefit increase under discussion.

thread.said: She asked whether the CSC had a current budget for monitoring compliance.

thread.said: She asked whether the CSC would support a law banning all government employees from engaging in online gambling.

thread.speaker: Assistant Commissioner Ariel Ronquillo
thread.said: He answered that gambling was prohibited both on-site and online, indicating that the existing resolution already covered online gambling even without enactment of a separate bill.

thread.speaker: A CSC agency official
thread.said: The official said the CSC could extend preferential-rating eligibility to IPMRs based on their representative role in key government bodies. thread.said: The official said any preferential treatment would have to be provided by law and recognize the unique situation of IPMRs. The official also compared the proposal with treatment of JOs, COs, and military and uniformed personnel.

thread.speaker: A CSC agency official
thread.said: The official said the CSC supported legislation increasing PERA and other financial or nonfinancial benefits for government personnel. On broader compensation reform, the official said the CSC could continue discussions with DBM on matters such as position classification and qualification standards, while resource allocation remained the government's prerogative.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She urged the CSC to recommend reforms to make the compensation system sustainable and ensure equitable incentives for government personnel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Isabel Segabaria
thread.said: She questioned the CSC's statutory basis for treating a common-law relationship as equivalent to marriage under the 2025 omnibus rules on appointments and other human-resource actions. She asked whether this expanded or modified statutory nepotism prohibitions and whether the issue should instead be addressed through legislation.

thread.speaker: A CSC agency official
thread.said: The official recognized the validity of the concern and agreed that the CSC could not create a rule without legal basis that would prejudice affected persons. The official nevertheless defended the rule as preventing favoritism and relied on Supreme Court pronouncements that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.

thread.speaker: A CSC agency official
thread.said: The official said the same principle had been applied to designations of relatives, even though designation was not expressly covered by the statutory definition of nepotism. The commission's position was that a common-law partner stood in the same place as a spouse for purposes of preventing the same evil.

thread.speaker: Rep. Isabel Segabaria
thread.said: She pressed the official on whether the rule specifically covered common-law partners and noted that the issuance was relatively recent.

thread.speaker: A CSC agency official
thread.said: The official maintained that common-law partners were in the same place as married partners because the same relationship existed among the parties involved. The exchange ended after the official clarified that the rule had been issued before the current chair's assumption.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET: COMELEC

topics.topic: 2028 election-preparation funding and proposed COMELEC budget cuts
topics.summary: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia presented a proposed FY2027 budget of about 29.5 billion, including roughly 23.92 billion for 2028 election preparations, and warned that a reduction of about 9 billion could compromise the election. Rep. Mercy Sindania characterized the NEP level as a recipe for disaster and asked what would happen if the reduction remained; Garcia said COMELEC could sacrifice features such as voter verification but could not compromise core preparation for a presidential and vice-presidential election. Rep. Edgar Erice questioned the 23 billion machine request and suggested that a lower requirement could save about 6 billion, while Garcia defended the need for about 124,000 machines because of voter growth and inflation. Other members supported restoring COMELEC's broader request to about 44 billion. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez moved to approve the budget and sought a special provision allowing about 11 billion in unused Barangay and SK election funds to continue for critical 2028 preparations. Garcia agreed to submit the proposed language, and also committed to provide updates on overseas voting and address vacant positions, but the final funding level and machine allocation remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 funding would give COMELEC sufficient resources to prepare for credible 2028 national and local elections. Members also examined the effect of reduced machine, infrastructure, staffing, overseas-voting, and election-preparation funds, and whether unused Barangay and SK election appropriations could be made available for 2028 preparations.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC stated that the proposed reductions, particularly the roughly 9,000,000,000 reduction in 2028 preparatory funding, could compromise election preparations and the credibility of the 2028 national and local elections. Garcia maintained that COMELEC needed funding for approximately 124,000 machines, ballot printing, certification, logistics, staffing, and infrastructure, while offering to defer lower-priority features or construction and to submit language for a continuing-appropriation special provision.
topics.outcome: The committee broadly supported restoring COMELEC's election-preparation resources and moved to approve the budget together with a special provision for continuing use of unused Barangay and SK election funds. The precise final budget level, machine funding, and implementation of the proposed restoration were not fully resolved in the transcript, while COMELEC's submission of special-provision language and other updates remained pending.

positions.position: The NEP funding level was a “recipe for disaster” and risked failure of the 2028 democratic exercise; government had to find a way to support COMELEC.
COMELEC's machine requirement and 23,000,000,000 machine request appeared excessive; a lower machine cost could produce savings of about 6,000,000,000.
COMELEC's budget should be restored to about 44,000,000,000 to protect electoral credibility, integrity, and a peaceful process.
The committee should approve COMELEC's budget and a special provision allowing continued use of unused Barangay and SK election funds, identified as 11,000,000,000, for 2028 preparations.

The House should prevent a recurrence of the budget-process problem, restore 9,000,000,000 for election-related preparations, pursue party-list and anti-political-dynasty reforms, improve overseas voting, and address COMELEC vacancies.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia presented a FY2027 COMELEC budget of 29,500,000,000 pesos, including 339,880,000 pesos in automatic appropriations for retirement and life insurance premiums. He said new appropriations subject to congressional approval totaled 29,160,000,000 pesos, including 23,920,000,000 pesos for preparation for the 2028 elections.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia appealed for restoration of funds, saying the commission's budget had been reduced by almost 23,000,000,000 pesos. He said preparatory national and local election funding was reduced by about 9,000,000,000 pesos, while the regular budget was about 6,000,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia projected about 74,000,000 registered voters for 2028, compared with 68,000,000 in the 2025 election and a projected 71,000,000 voters before 2028.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He warned that the available number of voting machines could require 800 to 1,000 voters per precinct because COMELEC was limited to about 107,000 precincts nationwide. The machine requirement and allocation were not clearly captured in this portion of the transcript.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said market scoping placed the cost at 155,000 pesos per machine, while procurement offers were 149,000 pesos, producing savings of 800,000,000 pesos through leasing.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He cited 1,500,000,000 as an amount equivalent to roughly 9,000 machines, although the surrounding machine figure was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC's projection was for 1,515,100,000 for machines for the 2028 election and 124,000 machines, but the cut reduced the available preparation budget to 21,660,000,000 from 23,000,000,000. He said the agency would have 8,000 or fewer machines under the reduced amount and would have to increase voters per precinct.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He said COMELEC would target 600 voters per precinct if funds were not restored, but might have to accommodate 800 to 1,000 voters per precinct under the reduced budget.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia cited 124,310 machines and 10,000 contingency machines as the requirement, with contingency machines needed for provincial election officers.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He said the request for ballot and election-material printing was 3,200,000,000, including 1,700,000,000 for official ballots, 800,000,000 for voters information sheets, and 888,000,000 for preprinting the list of voters. Some component descriptions and amounts were unclear or internally inconsistent in the transcript.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia estimated printing costs at about 2,930,000,000 and said printing should begin in December 2027 to prepare for the May 2028 election.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He said the reductions in preparatory national and local election funds could not be compromised because they could compromise the election. He cited a reduction in supplies from 973 to 167, with the associated units and currency unclear.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He estimated international certification at more or less 160,000,000 and local overtime at almost 200,000,000 for six months, or 1,200,867,330 for the period described.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia summarized the requirement as 9,000,000,000 for preparatory national and local elections plus 6,000,000,000 for the agency budget, or about 15,000,000,000 in total.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He told the committee that the 9,000,000,000 reduction would definitely affect the conduct of the 2028 election and could imperil preparations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mercy Sindania
thread.said: Sindania called the NEP budget a “recipe for disaster” and asked Garcia to describe what would happen in 2028 if the basic 9,000,000,000 for national preparatory activities remained unrevised.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC wanted to prevent the 2028 election from being compromised by insufficient funding. He cautioned that the election might be compromised, although the precise year references in the machine-generated transcript were unclear.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He said COMELEC could make sacrifices for a special election, including measures involving indelible ink and ballot security, but not for a presidential and vice-presidential election involving 12 senators and 65 or 66 party-list members.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mercy Sindania
thread.said: Sindania pressed that the issue involved not merely an election failure but a failure of an important democratic exercise, particularly because the budget was being reduced in the year before the election.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said that, if necessary, COMELEC could sacrifice the voter-verification feature of the machines, which would cost 2,000,000,000, and blockchain technology. He reiterated that the 9,000,000,000 for preparation could not be compromised.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mercy Sindania
thread.said: Sindania asked about the absence of major budget items, including school buildings and capital outlay, in the 2028 NEP and the FY2027 NEP.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia answered that COMELEC would have to defer construction and purchases because the budget for them was zero. He also said initiative and referendum funding had been reduced to 11,000,000 based on historical spending, while another contingency figure was captured as 98,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: He said COMELEC was legally required to conduct elections even without a call or budget and would have to find the money. The amount needed was transcribed unclearly as “109 91,000,000.”

thread.speaker: Rep. Mercy Sindania
thread.said: Sindania asked whether a nationwide referendum on anti-political-dynasty legislation would have a stand-alone budget.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC supported the initiative and had lifted a suspension of rules to allow signature gathering for local legislation, but not a constitutional initiative. He did not identify a separate referendum appropriation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice asked about the roughly 46,000,000,000 requirement for the 2028 national and local elections and the difference between COMELEC's 23,000,000,000 request for leased machines and the DBM amount of 21,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia explained that about 26,000,000,000 was for preparatory national and local election activities and about 20,000,000,000 was for the conduct of the election, including teachers' honoraria. He confirmed the DBM proposal was short by 1,500,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia justified the machine requirement by citing 3% inflation and an increase in voters from about 67 or 68,000,000 in 2025 to about 74,000,000 in 2028. He said COMELEC would therefore need 124,000 machines.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice questioned whether machine depreciation meant COMELEC would not need 23,000,000,000 and suggested a machine requirement of 17,800,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said the 2025 machines were leased for one-time use and that COMELEC had already prepared terms of reference for the 2028 lease and transmission provider. He said the 2028 procurement would not necessarily use the same provider.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice argued that the machine requirement could be lower and estimated possible savings of about 6,000,000,000 if spending were below 17,800,000,000 rather than 23,000,000,000. Several other budget figures in his comparison were transcribed as 7,200,000,000,000, 2,000,000,000,000, 3,000,000,000,000, 5,000,000,000,000, 1,100,000,000,000, and 6,100,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said the COMELEC Advisory Council had recommended leasing machines, not necessarily from the same provider, and that additional technical features and the higher number of voters drove the request.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia compared 101,000 machines plus 7,000 contingency machines, or roughly 108,000, with the projected requirement of 124,000 machines. He cited 155,000 per machine and another machine-price figure transcribed as 160,005.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice said that 20,000 additional machines would cost only 3,000,000,000 and maintained that the total machine requirement could be about 6,000,000,000 lower.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC would consider Erice's proposal and work toward a reasonable plan of action at the congressional level, including consideration of restoring the budget.

thread.speaker: A member
thread.said: A member said major cuts could damage COMELEC's credibility, integrity, and the peaceful electoral process. The member supported COMELEC's revised request of about 44,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia raised pending House Bill 7546 and said legislation needed to be approved before the end of the year because COMELEC needed to proceed with September 2027 filing of candidacies and December 2027 ballot preparation for the 2028 election.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez cited a reduction of 15,200,000,000 from the revised proposal and asked whether postponement of the Barangay and SK elections would save PHP9.5 billion. He asked how much COMELEC would need for 2028 preparations and what priorities would be covered by about PHP6,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said a special provision could treat the appropriated 2026 Barangay and SK election funds as continuing appropriations and authorize COMELEC to use them for other critical purposes, subject to audit. He said 11,000,000,000 would address the requirement.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said the committee had language ready for the special provision and would approve it, while asking COMELEC to submit its proposed language. He clarified that the requested continuing amount was 11,000,000,000, not 9,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia undertook to submit the proposed special-provision language to the committee chairperson.

thread.speaker: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia
thread.said: Garcia said the funds already appropriated to COMELEC could not simply be used elsewhere and should remain with COMELEC as a continuing appropriation. He also referred to 16% available fiscal space.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez moved to approve the COMELEC budget and the special provision proposed by COMELEC.

topics.topic: Automated election-machine procurement, leasing, and readiness
topics.summary: COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia warned that the proposed reduction in election-preparation funding could compromise 2028 readiness and said about 74 million voters would require roughly 124,000 machines, including contingency units. He explained that the 2025 lease cost 17,990,000,000 or about 18 billion in the discussion, and covered warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement, while the proposed 2028 lease was discussed at 23,000,000,000. Rep. Edgar Erice challenged that figure and argued that purchase, reuse, or upgrading could reduce the cost to about 17.8 billion and save about 6 billion. A member separately asked about cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting, and COMELEC cited 337,000,000 for ICT equipment, continuous monitoring, enrollment controls, and a projected 55 to 60% overseas turnout. Erice also requested the COMELEC Advisory Council's terms of reference, meeting minutes, and resolution, and Chairman Garcia committed to submit them before plenary debates. The lease-versus-purchase issue remained open, subject to the documents and further congressional budget action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC should lease, purchase, or upgrade automated counting machines for the 2028 elections, and whether the proposed funding would provide enough machines and related readiness measures. Members also asked about machine standards, cybersecurity, overseas Internet voting, and the documents supporting COMELEC's procurement position.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC maintained that leasing new machines for the 2028 election was necessary because of projected voter growth, the need for additional and contingency machines, and the importance of avoiding questions about reused equipment in a presidential election. It said leasing covered warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement, while cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting would be supported through ICT investment, monitoring, enrollment controls, and related safeguards.
topics.outcome: The committee received COMELEC's justification for leasing new machines, but Rep. Edgar Erice continued to contest the amount and the preference for new leased equipment. COMELEC undertook to provide the procurement and Advisory Council documents, leaving the cost and lease-versus-purchase question open for further budget deliberation.

positions.position: He questioned the need to spend 23,000,000,000 on leased machines and argued that purchasing, reusing, or upgrading equipment could reduce the requirement to about 17,800,000,000 and yield savings of 6,000,000,000. He also urged COMELEC to use objective standards for accuracy, reliability, security, auditability, and upgrade capacity.
The member questioned whether leasing was more economical than purchasing or upgrading machines and sought assurances on cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting.

He sought an update on election technology and readiness for the upcoming BARMM barangay parliamentary election, including whether election-related security incidents could affect an orderly and peaceful election.

topics.topic: Barangay and SK election postponement, term fixing, and unused funds
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co questioned whether the BSKE elections would proceed and asked about COMELEC’s pending procurement and overtime obligations. COMELEC said it had obligated about 8 billion for election materials and reported PHP 1,200,000,000 in six months of overtime, while supporting periodic, regular, and definite elections but deferring the policy decision on postponement or term fixing to Congress and the courts. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported fixing the barangay officials’ terms and sought authority to retain unused BSKE funds, with figures discussed ranging from about 9 billion to 11 billion and an estimated unutilized balance of about 10.9 billion. COMELEC proposed that unused BSKE appropriations become continuing appropriations for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes. DBM raised no objection to the concept or proposed wording, but the committee deferred final action and requested a formal submission for consideration by the budget amendments review subcommittee. The Senior Deputy Speaker also confirmed that COMELEC would implement Congress’s term-fixing decision and remain bound by procurement contracts already covered by notices to proceed.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the barangay and SK elections would proceed as scheduled or be postponed or reset through term fixing, and what that would mean for COMELEC’s procurement, overtime, and election appropriations. Members also sought to determine whether unutilized BSKE funds could remain available for the 2028 national and local elections through a special provision.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC said it would comply with the law and implement Congress’s decision on whether to hold, reset, postpone, or alter the term of barangay and SK officials. It supported treating unused BSKE appropriations as continuing appropriations for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes, subject to audit and the committee’s final special-provision language.
topics.outcome: The committee did not finally approve the special provision during the hearing; the motion was deferred to the budget amendments review subcommittee and the proper time. COMELEC committed to submit formal language, while DBM stated that it had no objection, leaving final inclusion and wording for later committee action.

positions.position: She expressed concern that another postponement could harm periodic elections, voter turnout, and the right to genuine representation, while seeking clarity on obligations and preparation costs.
He sought clarification on the legal basis and implications of fixing the terms of barangay officials and the resulting election reset.

He supported term fixing rather than describing the measure as a long postponement and supported a special provision allowing unused BSKE funds to remain available for COMELEC programs and 2028 election preparations.
He supported the special provision and said it should be considered by the budget amendments review subcommittee and reflected in the committee report.
She supported examining a special provision for unutilized BSKE funds, sought DBM’s technical position, and emphasized transparency and fiscal management.
DBM had no objection to the proposed special provision and said COMELEC funds remained valid until fully spent under its constitutional fiscal autonomy, subject to applicable rules.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked whether the barangay and SK elections remained scheduled and sought clarification on COMELEC’s preparations, including pending obligations and the possibility of postponement.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Chairperson Garcia said COMELEC had to comply with the law while the elections remained scheduled. He warned that a Supreme Court restraining order could affect the conduct of the election and said procurement actions were already underway.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC had obligated 8,003,000,000 pesos for procurement. He explained that notices to proceed triggered supplier delivery periods and could constitute a perfected sale or contract of sale.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said delivery schedules were uncertain if the election date changed, although items such as indelible ink and pens could be delivered relatively quickly. He referred to deliveries expected in the second week of September and to approximately 70,000 boxes being delivered to COMELEC warehouses.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co clarified whether about 8,000,000,000 represented the overall amount for pending deliveries.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia identified 8,000,000,000 pesos, with 3,000,000 apparently referring to another component, for printing and other election materials. He listed election forms, ballots, ballot boxes, indelible ink, and pens, and also referred to the total as 8,003,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked about operating and preparation expenses beyond procurement, including office improvements and overtime.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC’s monthly overtime cost was almost MXN 200,000,000, and that overtime for the six months of preparation for the BSKE scheduled for November 2 had reached PHP 1,200,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co restated the figures and asked whether 8,000,000,000 was already obligated or otherwise held for the election.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia confirmed that 8,000,000,000 was obligated and earmarked.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co said another postponement would be the second postponement of the BSKE elections and raised concerns about long-term effects on the right to suffrage, voter turnout, and genuine representation.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC supported the principle that elections should be periodic, regular, and definite. He said proponents of any postponement or term extension would have to defend it against the Supreme Court’s standards.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Rep. Co asked whether the issue was a policy question and whether national and local elections could be spread out for reasons other than budget.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia distinguished the barangay and SK elections from national and local elections and said the budget for barangay and SK elections would be needed in the same year as their conduct.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said the barangay and SK election budget was 19,000,000,000 or 20, while the budget for a national and local election was 2040; the latter figure was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia characterized postponement as a policy and political-question issue. He said postponement extending into 2027 would be critical because COMELEC would begin preparations for the 2028 elections from June onward.

thread.speaker: Rep. Caloy Bolilia
thread.said: Rep. Bolilia asked about the constitutional and legal implications of proposals in the House concerning the fixing of barangay officials’ terms and a possible postponement of the barangay election.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia cited the constitutional rule that local officials serve three years, except that the terms of barangay officials may be fixed by law. He said Congress was the sole authority to fix the term and referred to legislation changing a term from three to four years and then from four to five years.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia distinguished a pure postponement, which he associated with the Supreme Court’s treatment of the 2023 case, from term fixing. He said postponement could be incidental to term fixing if a transition period were needed.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said proponents of postponement or term fixing should be prepared to defend the measure under the Supreme Court’s guidelines. He also stated that certificates of candidacy were scheduled to be filed from September 28 to October 5.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez noted a reduction of 15,200,000,000 from the revised reduced proposal and asked whether resetting the barangay and SK elections by two years would save PHP9.5 billion. He asked how much COMELEC would need for the following year and what priorities would be covered by the approximately PHP 6,000,000,000 requirement he identified.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said COMELEC did not want to compromise the 2020 election, although the year reference was unclear. He said the 2026 BSKE appropriation could, through a special provision, become a continuing appropriation that COMELEC could use for other critical purposes, subject to audit, and referred to 11,000,000,000 as sufficient.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez said the committee had language ready for a special provision and would approve it, subject to the committee process.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia undertook to submit the proposed special-provision language to the committee chairperson.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez said the amount needed for preparation for the 2028 elections was 11,000,000,000, correcting an earlier reference to 9,000,000,000, and asked COMELEC to identify other needs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez asked whether keeping 11,000,000,000 available through a special provision would give COMELEC fiscal space to use the funds for other projects and programs.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said the special provision would provide fiscal space and referred to 16% as available fiscal space. He said appropriations already given to COMELEC could not be used by another agency and should remain with COMELEC as a continuing appropriation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez asked whether Garcia continued to recommend term extension and term fixing rather than calling the measure a long postponement.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said Congress had the sole authority to fix the term of barangay officials. He cited the constitutional wording that barangay officials’ terms may be fixed by law.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez asked whether a Supreme Court action striking down term fixing would amount to judicial legislation and whether Congress should not follow it.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia referred to the 2025 Supreme Court treatment, saying the majority viewed the measure as term-fixing legislation rather than postponement legislation and found it consistent with the Constitution.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez moved to approve the COMELEC budget and the special provision proposed by COMELEC.

thread.speaker: Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong
thread.said: Rep. Adiong said the special provision would be taken up by the budget amendments review subcommittee and reflected in the committee’s report and HGAP. He seconded Rep. Rodriguez’s motion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez acknowledged that the motion was not being filed at the proper time and said he would renew it when the budget amendments review subcommittee considered the matter.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia agreed to provide a copy of the proposed language to the subcommittee chairperson and members. He said COMELEC would submit it by the following day.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker reopened the issue of unutilized BSKE funds and asked DBM to clarify whether a 2027 special provision could govern funds appropriated in the 2026 General Appropriations Act.

thread.speaker: Elena Brilliantes, DBM director
thread.said: Director Brilliantes said COMELEC’s constitutional fiscal autonomy meant that funds it received remained valid until fully spent, subject to applicable rules. DBM had no objection to including a 2027 special provision allowing unused BSKE balances to be used, with the provision serving transparency purposes.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said that if the SK and barangay elections did not proceed, the unutilized balance could be more or less 10,900,000,000. He also referred to more or less 15,000,000,000 and about 10,000,000,000 for preparatory national and local election activities; portions of the statement were unclear.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia proposed language providing that unexpended BSKE appropriations would be deemed continuing appropriations, remain available for 2028 national and local election preparations and other lawful purposes, and remain subject to the committee’s final refinement and recommendation.

thread.speaker: Elena Brilliantes, DBM director
thread.said: Director Brilliantes said DBM had no objection to the proposed wording and left to Congress the decision whether to include it in the COMELEC budget.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker said allowing the continuation of 10,900,000,000 in unutilized funds would help address the committee’s fiscal-management concerns and promote transparency and accountability.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker requested a formal letter from COMELEC setting out the special provision, preferably by the following day, for consideration by the budget amendments review subcommittee.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker asked COMELEC’s position on the proposed fixing of the barangay and SK officials’ terms being considered in plenary.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia reiterated that Congress had the absolute and sole authority to fix the terms of barangay and SK officials. He said COMELEC would implement Congress’s decision, whether the term was five years or involved two consecutive terms.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker asked whether Garcia had taken the same position during Senate deliberations.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia confirmed that he had taken the same position in the Senate: Congress alone had authority to fix the term.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker asked how COMELEC would prepare if Congress approved term fixing, noting that the Senate proposal involved three consecutive terms and that an amendment for two terms might be offered. He also asked about the September 28 filing timeline and whether COMELEC was preparing for the possibility that no election would be held.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia confirmed September 28 as the filing date. He then explained that COMELEC was proceeding with procurement for ball pens, indelible ink, and print takers because notices of award and notices to proceed created supplier obligations and contracts.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker asked whether COMELEC would remain bound by its contracts even if the election were held in November 2020, an unclear year reference in the transcript.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia agreed that COMELEC would remain bound by the procurement contract and said the procurement action was the proper interpretation of its obligation.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker asked whether, if an election were postponed before a notice of award was issued, COMELEC could treat the amount as savings and later budget for the contract.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker asked how fiscal autonomy and the proposed special provision would operate if the election were canceled because of term fixing.

thread.speaker: George Irwin M. Garcia, COMELEC chairperson
thread.said: Garcia said the funds would remain with COMELEC even if not yet officially released by DBM, subject to audit and other requirements under the applicable rules. He referred to the possibility of using the funds for other government purposes through the committee and DBM framework.

thread.speaker: Senior Deputy Speaker
thread.said: The Senior Deputy Speaker moved to terminate the hearing on COMELEC’s proposed FY 2027 budget.

topics.topic: Proposed special provision for unused barangay and SK election funds
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez raised the possibility that resetting the barangay and SK elections would leave substantial funds unused and sought a special provision to preserve those funds for COMELEC's future needs. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said the continuing appropriation could make about 11 billion available, later estimating an unutilized BSKE balance of about 10,900,000,000 and proposing its use for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes. Rodriguez moved to approve the COMELEC budget and provision, but the motion was deferred because the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee had to address the wording. The Senior Deputy Speaker later asked DBM whether a 2027 provision could govern funds appropriated in the 2026 GAA, and DBM said it had no objection because COMELEC's constitutionally autonomous funds remain valid until fully spent. The committee requested a formal letter and left final language and approval to the subcommittee process.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the appropriations for the barangay and SK elections could remain available if those elections were reset or not held, and what special-provision wording would authorize COMELEC to use the funds for other lawful purposes. It also sought DBM's technical position on including in the FY 2027 budget a provision concerning funds appropriated in the FY 2026 GAA.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC maintained that its constitutional fiscal autonomy and a continuing-appropriation special provision could keep unused BSKE appropriations available for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes. It supported submitting formal wording and said it would implement Congress's decision on term fixing, while procurement obligations would remain subject to the applicable contracts, audit, and release requirements.
topics.outcome: The special provision was not finally approved during this portion of the hearing. The motion was parked for the proper time and referred for formal submission and consideration by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee, with DBM stating that it had no objection.

positions.position: Supported approving a special provision allowing unused BSKE funds to remain available for COMELEC's future election preparations and other programs.
Supported the provision but said it should be handled by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee and reflected in the committee's report.
Supported pursuing the provision as a transparency and fiscal-management measure, subject to DBM's view and final refinement by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee.
Raised no objection to including the provision in the FY 2027 COMELEC budget, while leaving the final decision to Congress.

topics.topic: Machine funding requirement of 23,000,000,000 versus DBM funding
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice raised the gap between COMELEC's 23,000,000,000 machine requirement and DBM's 21,000,000,000 funding, while COMELEC described the shortfall as 1,500,000,000. Chairman Garcia justified the requirement by citing inflation, projected voter growth to about 74 million, and a need for 124,000 machines. Erice argued that the machines could cost about 17.8 billion, potentially producing savings of 6 billion, and another member questioned whether purchasing or upgrading would be cheaper than leasing. COMELEC maintained that a one-time lease was appropriate for the critical 2028 presidential election and cited warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement costs. The agency also described cybersecurity measures and its planned overseas Internet-voting enrollment and authentication process. The chairman undertook to consider the lower-cost proposal, but the final funding and procurement approach remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why COMELEC projected a machine requirement of 23,000,000,000 for the 2028 elections when DBM funding was stated at 21,000,000,000, and whether leasing, purchasing, or upgrading machines would provide the most economical and reliable option. Members also examined machine readiness, cybersecurity, and the implementation of overseas Internet voting.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC maintained that leasing machines for the 2028 election was justified by the projected increase in voters, technical requirements, and the importance of the presidential and vice-presidential election. The agency also stated that it was addressing cybersecurity and would implement overseas Internet voting through registration, enrollment, identity verification, and a one-time PIN.
topics.outcome: COMELEC defended the 23,000,000,000 machine requirement but agreed to consider the committee member's lower-cost proposal and seek a reasonable plan. The lease-versus-purchase issue, final machine quantity, and funding gap were not conclusively resolved.

positions.position: Rep. Erice questioned the need for 23,000,000,000 and argued that COMELEC could obtain the needed machines at a lower cost, potentially saving 6,000,000,000.
The member questioned whether purchasing or upgrading machines would be cheaper than leasing them for multiple elections and sought assurance on cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting.

topics.topic: Ballot and voter-information printing cut from 3,280,000,000 to 348,000,000
topics.summary: Rep. John Tracy Cagas raised the reduction in the printing allocation from 3,280,000,000 to 348,000,000, a stated cut of 2,930,000,000. COMELEC Chair George Irwin M. Garcia said the reduction was critical and would affect ballot printing, mandatory voter-information sheets, pre-printing activities, and possible reprinting. He identified 2,940,000,000 pesos for the 2028 budget and said procurement and printing should begin in January 2028. Garcia also said that 74 million ballots might have to be printed and that reprinting related to national candidates could cost 20 million. A member connected the issue to deployment and logistics, while Garcia discussed compromised deployment activities, increased machines from 107,000 to 124,000, and other supplies and specifications. No restoration of funds or other concrete action was recorded, so the adequacy of the reduced allocation remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the effect of reducing the proposed allocation for ballot forms and voter-information sheets, and whether the remaining amount could cover printing, reprinting, deployment, and related election supplies. It also examined the timing and budget needed for the 2028 election.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC's stated position was that the reduction was critical and could affect ballot printing, mandatory voter-information sheets, reprinting, pre-printing activities, and deployment. Garcia said the issue would have to be addressed through the 2028 budget, including 2,940,000,000 pesos, with procurement and printing beginning in January 2028.
topics.outcome: COMELEC explained that the reduction could create significant risks and said the shortfall would need to be addressed in the 2028 budget. The exchange did not record a committee ruling, funding restoration, or document submission, and the sufficiency of the reduced allocation remained unresolved.

positions.position: He questioned whether the sharply reduced allocation could cover ballots, voter-information sheets, production capacity, and the related election requirements.

The member linked the printing reduction to deployment and logistics, asking whether machines and supplies could reach polling places on time, and also raised equipment leasing and enhanced automated-election machines.

topics.topic: BSK election budget, obligations, and remaining balances
topics.summary: Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores questioned why the BSK budget had increased despite reported high absorptive capacity and pressed COMELEC on the large ICT reduction and case-disposition backlog. COMELEC attributed the higher requirement to increased precincts, voters, teachers, honoraria, training, cybersecurity, and procurement, and said case disposition would continue regardless of a budget reduction. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos then examined spending and obligations, citing about 8 billion spent from an approximately 19 billion BSK budget and a possible additional requirement of roughly 2.5 to 3.5 billion; Garcia cited 4 billion earmarked and about 3.9 to 4 billion obligated, although the reconciliation remained unclear. The discussion also covered a Cavite special-election budget of about 200 million, including 128 million in COMELEC funding and a 50 million LGU advance subject to reimbursement. Rep. Renee Co asked about pending deliveries, overtime, and postponement; Garcia cited 8,003,000,000 pesos obligated, six months of overtime totaling PHP 1,200,000,000, and pending delivery of election materials. COMELEC committed to submit case information and updates, but the precise remaining balance and the effect of any postponement were not fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the actual cost, obligations, expenditures, deliveries, and remaining balances for the BSK election, including whether funds could be reused if the election were postponed. It also examined special-election advances, pending procurement, overtime, and the implications of any further postponement.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC maintained that the higher BSK requirement reflected increased precincts, voters, teachers, honoraria, training, procurement, cybersecurity, and overtime. It said substantial funds were already obligated or earmarked, procurement and deliveries were proceeding because the election remained legally scheduled, and any postponement was ultimately a policy and political-question issue subject to legal scrutiny.
topics.outcome: COMELEC defended the BSK budget as necessary for training, procurement, cybersecurity, overtime, and other election operations, but the committee did not receive a fully reconciled accounting of spent, obligated, earmarked, delivered, and remaining funds. Case-list submissions were committed, while the question of postponement remained a policy and political issue rather than a resolved budget determination.

positions.position: Supported restoration of COMELEC's budget because of election-security risks, but urged the Commission to resolve election cases more quickly.
Sought a precise accounting of BSK expenditures, obligations, deliveries, possible reuse of funds, LGU advances, and reported savings.
Raised concerns about the fiscal and democratic consequences of postponing the BSKE elections, including effects on suffrage, representation, turnout, and preparation for the 2028 elections.

topics.topic: ICT, cybersecurity, and election-system security after proposed reductions
topics.summary: Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores questioned COMELEC's ability to protect election data after almost 87.4% of its proposed ICT funding was removed. Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia cited 24-hour monitoring, 32,000,000 Internet attempts before an election, 3,000,000 attempts per month, and 337,000,000 for ICT-related requirements, while saying additional cybersecurity personnel and system improvements were needed. A committee member also questioned the approximately 17,990,000,000 lease for 110,000 ACMs and the readiness and integrity of machines for 2028. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned overseas Internet voting, registration funding, and regulation of social media and artificial intelligence; COMELEC said it supported regulation but acknowledged constitutional and legislative limits. Vice Chair Zia Alonto Adiong asked about security and election-related violence before the BARMM barangay election, and COMELEC reported preparations involving 3,393,000 voters, 5,212 voting centers, and 5,212 machines. COMELEC committed to submit case lists and updates, but the budget restoration and several security and regulatory issues were not finally settled.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC could maintain secure election systems, protect voter and election data, and prepare for the 2028 and BARMM elections despite proposed ICT and other budget reductions. Members also asked how cybersecurity, Internet voting, overseas registration, social-media regulation, and election-related security would be handled.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC said it could continue operating and disposing of cases despite reductions, but maintained that additional ICT resources were necessary for cybersecurity, system improvement, maintenance, and protection against hacking, data compromise, and foreign interference. It supported secure Internet voting and social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation, while recognizing constitutional and legislative limits on COMELEC's regulatory authority.
topics.outcome: COMELEC defended the need to restore or protect ICT and cybersecurity resources and gave operational assurances on monitoring, Internet voting, and election preparation. It committed to submit case information and updates, but the proposed budget restoration, the precise funding level, the social-media task-force question, and the security determination concerning the BARMM incident remained unresolved.

positions.position: He supported restoring COMELEC's budget because of the security risks associated with reduced ICT funding, while urging the agency to resolve election cases more quickly.

She pressed COMELEC for clearer safeguards and accountability concerning overseas Internet voting, continuing registration, social-media political advertising, artificial intelligence, and fair campaigning.
He sought assurance that the BARMM barangay election would proceed peacefully and orderly and that election-related violence and security threats would be addressed.

topics.topic: Election-teacher and poll-worker honoraria
topics.summary: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised the BSK election budget and asked how much had been spent or obligated, particularly for poll-worker training. COMELEC said it would train about 1 million teachers, electoral-board members, and support staff, and cited 4 billion as earmarked and roughly 3.9 4,000,000,000 as obligated, although the reported total was garbled. A member also commended 2 million in savings. Rep. Antonio Tinio then raised election-teacher honoraria, and the COMELEC chairperson cited rates ranging from 10,000 to 15,000, including 15,000 per teacher and 15,000 for the chairman. Tinio sought to increase the appropriation from 2,000,000,000 to 2,500,000,000. COMELEC undertook to support the proposal before the relevant committees and DBM, while Tinio requested formal data and a position paper.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the BSK election budget had been spent or obligated, particularly for poll-worker training and related preparations, and whether additional funding would be needed. It also examined the honoraria rates for election teachers and whether the appropriation should be increased.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC said it needed to train more or less 1,000,000 election teachers, electoral-board members, and support staff, and supported increasing teacher honoraria in light of the circumstances described by the chairperson. The agency indicated that the proposed increase should be formalized and defended for inclusion in the budget.
topics.outcome: The committee and COMELEC aligned on pursuing a higher honoraria appropriation, described as an increase from 2,000,000,000 to 2,500,000,000. COMELEC was expected to provide formal supporting data and a position paper for the proposal's budget defense; the final appropriation was not decided in the exchange.

topics.topic: Overseas voting, Internet voting, and continuing registration
topics.summary: Committee members, led by Rep. Sarah Elago and a minority member, questioned whether overseas registration and Internet voting would close persistent participation gaps. COMELEC said the DFA supervised overseas voting under the law while COMELEC coordinated, and described registration, identity verification, one-time PINs, and enrollment lasting three to five minutes. Garcia cited 1,200,000 overseas voters, a hoped-for increase to 2,000,000, and turnout targets ranging from at least 50% to 55 to 60%; Elago cited a 67,000,000 proposal for overseas voting and continuing registration. Members also pressed for accessible registration, voter education, and social-media accountability, while Garcia cited 3,000,000 deactivated voters and promised to activate them for 2028. The agency committed to update the committee on reforms and turnout, and a member manifested support for restoring COMELEC's proposed 2027 budget cut, but the funding question remained unsettled.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC's overseas registration and Internet-voting arrangements would improve participation, accessibility, and security, particularly for overseas voters. Members also asked how continuing registration, funding, social-media regulation, and staffing would support the 2028 elections.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC supported Internet voting as a means of increasing overseas participation, while emphasizing registration, identity verification, one-time PINs, and security. It said overseas voting was supervised under the law by the DFA in coordination with COMELEC, supported stronger social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation subject to legislative and constitutional limits, and committed to broaden registration and report back on electoral reforms and turnout.
topics.outcome: COMELEC defended Internet voting and described registration, enrollment, and security safeguards, but the committee did not settle the separate overseas-registration funding question or the proposed budget restoration. COMELEC committed to continued registration, activation of deactivated voters, stronger online protections, and a later update to the committee.

topics.topic: Voter registration, education, and inclusion of vulnerable voters
topics.summary: Rep. John Tracy Cagas questioned the reduction in printing funds from about 3.28 billion to about 348 million, warning that it could affect ballot and voter-information-sheet production. COMELEC Chair George Irwin M. Garcia said the reduction would affect 2028 procurement and could force the printing of about 74 million ballots without adequate preparation, while also citing 124,000 registration machines compared with 107,000 in 2025. Rep. Sarah Elago asked about overseas voting, Internet voting, continuing registration, and a revised proposal of about 67 million, and pressed COMELEC on social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation. Garcia said COMELEC coordinated with the DFA, was preparing for secure Internet voting, had limited authority to punish conduct without a law, and could request takedowns of discriminatory material. The discussion also covered roughly 3 million deactivated voters, Indigenous peoples, elderly voters, and registration in geographically isolated areas. COMELEC committed to inclusive registration and manifested support for restoring its 2027 budget cut, but the transcript did not record a committee decision on restoration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether proposed reductions in printing, registration, overseas voting, and voter-education resources would impair the 2028 elections, particularly for overseas voters, deactivated voters, and people in geographically isolated or vulnerable communities. It also examined COMELEC's plans for Internet voting, social-media regulation, and inclusive registration.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC said the printing and registration resources were critical to timely ballot production, machine deployment, voter registration, and the 2028 elections. It maintained that it was coordinating with the DFA on overseas voting, exploring secure Internet voting and technology-enabled registration, and would pursue inclusive registration while respecting legal limits on social-media regulation.
topics.outcome: COMELEC explained the operational risks of the printing and registration reductions and stated that it would pursue expanded registration, reactivation, overseas-voting coordination, and inclusive outreach. The committee received the explanations, but no ruling or restoration of the proposed cut was recorded in the provided transcript.

positions.position: He questioned the large reduction in printing funds because it could affect ballots, voter-information sheets, procurement timing, and election readiness.

topics.topic: Election-cycle costs, QRF, and possible longer election intervals
topics.summary: Representative Jobo Yagino asked about the QRF and whether holding elections every five years could produce savings compared with the existing three-year cycle. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said an automated national and local election required about 26 billion for preparation and 20 billion for the election year, or almost 46 billion, while the BSKE figure was stated as 19.57 and 20 billion, with the combined three-year figure rendered unclearly as 6,066,000,000,000. Garcia said changing the election term might be a solution but would require a constitutional amendment or revision because the Constitution provides three-year terms for specified positions. Yagino asked that the issue be placed on the record and potentially referred to House lawyers. He expressed full support for COMELEC's budget, preferred an increase, and moved for approval, but the excerpt contained no ruling on the motion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much COMELEC's election-related costs could be reduced by lengthening the election interval and whether such a change would affect the proposed budget. It also considered whether the issue required legal or constitutional action and whether COMELEC's budget should be approved.
topics.agency_position: COMELEC's chairperson presented the recurring costs of national, local, and BSKE elections and indicated that lengthening the election term could offer a solution. He also stated that changing the constitutionally specified three-year terms would require a constitutional amendment or revision; he did not state a final position on a five-year election cycle or receive a recorded ruling on the budget motion.
topics.outcome: COMELEC supplied cost figures and stated that a longer election interval would require constitutional amendment or revision. Yagino moved to approve the COMELEC budget, but no ruling or disposition of the motion was recorded in the provided excerpt.

positions.position: Supported examining longer election intervals as a possible way to reduce recurring election costs, supported referring the constitutional issue to House lawyers, and expressed full support for approval of COMELEC's budget, preferably with an increase.

topics.topic: Election-case disposition and political-finance enforcement
topics.summary: Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores asked whether budget reductions would delay disposition of about 14,000 election cases and clarified which COMELEC offices handled them. Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia said cases dated as far back as 2000, involved the Law Department and the Contest and Adjudication Department, and required due process because some were criminal in nature. Garcia assured the committee that disposition would proceed despite budget reductions and said the Political Finance and Affairs Department initiated cases involving overspending. He cited 7,000 SK-related cases involving candidates over 24 years of age and said the prescriptive period was five years. Flores supported restoring COMELEC's budget but urged faster action, while Garcia committed to submit the relevant case list and updates to the committees.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC's budget reductions would affect the disposition of roughly 14,000 election cases, including cases involving political-finance violations and overspending. It also asked whether COMELEC was initiating cases on its own and whether older cases could become time-barred.
