thread.said: The secretary said the Clark food hub had 2,000,000,000 pesos and would be complementary to a 500,000,000 mega cold storage facility. The facilities were described as part of a network intended to absorb production shocks and stabilize markets.

thread.said: The minority member questioned why Benguet had a 1.5 b allocation for farm-to-market roads, including 1,000,000,000 in a single province and a 500,000,000 single project. The concern was relevant to the road network needed to support the Benguet food hub and post-harvest system.

thread.said: The secretary explained that Benguet State University was being developed with a mega cold storage and processing facility costing about 7 minimum of 700,000,000 pesos, with private food hubs and a supporting road network. The secretary said the system would begin in Benguet and later extend to Ifugao and other production areas.

The member specifically raised a 500,000,000 project and questioned whether a road was already present.

thread.speaker: minority member
thread.said: The minority member requested all relevant details for the farm-to-market-road projects, particularly the larger projects, so the committee could verify that the proposed allocations were in order.

thread.speaker: DA secretary
thread.said: The secretary said the DA had the reports on hand and would ask someone to present them to the member's office.

thread.speaker: DA undersecretary for infrastructure
thread.said: The undersecretary said post-harvest losses across commodities amounted to 250,000,000,000 every year and that facilities should include not only dryers but also cold storage. The undersecretary argued that increased post-harvest facilities could improve quality, supply stability, and price stability.

thread.speaker: DA official

topics.topic: Mindanao and regional equity in DA and NIA allocations
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed the DA to raise Mindanao's share to 20%, citing Mindanao's contribution to food production, while DA officials sought additional FMR, post-harvest, fertilizer, and high-value-crops funding. The FMR infrastructure request included about 30 billion for an additional 2,000 kilometers, while post-harvest funding was cited at about 6.5 billion, fertilizer at about 8.73 billion, and the requested high-value-crops increase at about 8 billion over a current 1.7 billion budget. Rep. Reynolds Michael Tan questioned unreleased FMR funds, road standards, and declining Region 8 NIA allocations, and requested province- and project-level breakdowns. Rep. Nelson Legacion challenged FMR reductions and sought proportionate irrigation funding and hatchery support; the DA said its regional director would act on the hatchery concerns. A minority member requested a regional seed-system breakdown, and Secretary Laurel said the DA would review it and commit to funding it. Minority member Soberi linked Bukidnon's output of about 36.09 billion to the need for NIA support, but the apparent district allocation discrepancy remained unresolved while NIA undertook to update the figures.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DA and NIA allocations for Mindanao, regions, provinces, and congressional districts were proportionate to agricultural output, irrigable land, validated projects, and implementation needs. Members also asked whether FMR, irrigation, post-harvest, fertilizer, high-value-crops, seed-system, and hatchery funding should be increased or reallocated.
topics.agency_position: The DA and NIA said allocations were constrained by available funds, cash flow, priority Tier 1 and ongoing projects, and restrictive special provisions. DA officials nevertheless supported increased or integrated funding for FMRs, post-harvest facilities, fertilizer, high-value crops, and seed-system interventions, while NIA indicated that greater budget flexibility and project-level review were needed.
topics.outcome: The hearing produced support for higher and more flexible regional and program funding, but did not settle the conflicting FMR, Region 8, district irrigation, or Bukidnon figures. The agency undertook to provide or update certain project-level information and to pursue hatchery and seed-system follow-up.

positions.position: Mindanao should receive a 20% share of DA funding because of its major contribution to national food production, and FMR, post-harvest, fertilizer, and high-value-crops funding should be increased.
Region 8's declining NIA allocation required explanation, province-level itemization, and possible adjustment; DA and DPWH FMR standards should also be harmonized.
FMR reductions and insufficient irrigation allocations were inconsistent with validated district projects and farmer needs; he sought proportionate funding and support for legislated hatcheries.
The seed system program required a detailed regional intervention breakdown and possible additional funding.
Bukidnon's leading agricultural output warranted continued DA and NIA support and clarification of the apparent zero or reduced district allocation.

topics.topic: Land-use conversion, geofencing, and agricultural-land protection
topics.summary: Members raised concerns about the PacSilica development, industrial projects, marshland conversion, and solar installations on irrigable or rice land. The DA cited about 1,600 directly affected farmers in the Clark area but said the full agricultural impact had not yet been established. The DA supported geofencing of key crop lands, with 3 million hectares of rice land identified as needed and an 8% slope threshold discussed for land-use decisions. The secretary committed to complete geofencing by the end of this year and to undertake studies on industrial impacts and marshlands, with possible marshland implementation in mid-2027 subject to World Bank support. The DA also said solar-powered pumps could involve 100 megawatts, potential income of 600,000,000, and a proposed rate of 4 pesos per kilowatt hour, but said the agricultural effects of solar use on flat rice land still required research. A minority member additionally requested a breakdown of the 34,000,000 seed system program budget, which the secretary agreed to review.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DA would protect agricultural and irrigable land from conversion, industrial development, and solar projects, including through geofencing and impact studies. Members also asked what studies, implementation timelines, and program-level interventions would be provided for 2027.
topics.agency_position: The DA supported geofencing to reserve prime agricultural and irrigable areas for food production, using crop, slope, soil, water, and moisture-retention characteristics. It acknowledged that studies on industrial developments, marshlands, and solar use on rice land were incomplete, while undertaking to complete or advance several studies and to finish geofencing by the end of this year.
topics.outcome: The DA undertook to submit geofencing materials, complete geofencing by the end of this year, and produce or advance studies on industrial impacts, marshlands, and solar use on agricultural land. The compatibility of solar projects with flat rice land and the full PacSilica agricultural impact remained unresolved, while implementation of the marshland study was contingent on funding and possible World Bank support.

positions.position: Geofencing was a step in the right direction but needed to be accompanied by stricter land-use-conversion rules and stronger protection for prime agricultural land.
Industrial development should be subject to DA studies covering land reclassification, irrigation and hydrologic effects, contamination risks, and impacts on smallholder farmers and cooperatives.
Irrigable land should be protected from conversion to solar subdivisions, and marshland studies and a clear 2027 implementation timetable were needed.
The DA should provide a detailed regional and project-level breakdown of the seed system program's interventions.

topics.topic: National irrigation systems, maintenance, and infrastructure rehabilitation
topics.summary: DA Undersecretary Asis Perez reported that about 2.2 million hectares of an estimated 3.13 million irrigable hectares had been served, while the DA had added about 21,400 hectares and restored about 3,600 hectares through small-scale irrigation and canal works. Representative Juju Cesar Bergara sought action on an irrigation siphon, for which an agency official cited a request for 45,000,000 and a 194.5-meter length. Representative Marlo Bancoro pressed for multi-year irrigation and solar-irrigation implementation; the agency cited a 2027 proposal of about 1.12 billion but only 29,000,000 for the relevant item because of fiscal limits. Members also urged marshland studies, preservation of the Ifugao rice terraces through irrigation, and investigation of stalled solar projects. NIA reported a dam capacity of 54,000,000 cubic meters and discussed rubber-gate lifespans ranging from 15 to 45 years, but the replacement schedule was unclear. Representative Romeo Momo argued that the 5,000,000 NIA maintenance allocation for his district was inadequate, and NIA committed to provide a list of budget modifications or savings.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether irrigation systems, canals, dams, siphons, gates, and solar-irrigation facilities were adequately funded and maintained for 2027. Members also sought to determine which rehabilitation and expansion projects would be prioritized, and whether the agencies would provide studies, revised allocations, or implementation timelines.
topics.agency_position: The agencies said irrigation expansion, canal rehabilitation, dam and gate maintenance, and solar-irrigation projects were necessary but constrained by limited fiscal space. NIA stated that ongoing projects were prioritized and indicated that it would provide additional allocation information, while DA officials committed to coordination, studies, and follow-up discussions on delayed or proposed projects.
topics.outcome: The hearing established that irrigation maintenance and expansion needs exceeded available allocations, particularly for siphon repair, solar irrigation, dam and gate maintenance, and NIA upkeep. topics.topic: Local dairy production and school milk-feeding funding
topics.summary: Krisel Lagman asked the National Dairy Authority and the Philippine Carabao Center about local milk production, import dependence, and the capacity of the school milk-feeding program to create demand for local dairy. The agency reported production of about 29 million liters in 2024 and 43,000,043 liters in 2025, while national milk sufficiency rose from 1% to 2.2% and imported dairy remained at 98 percent. The discussion cited a 2026 target of 44,500,000 and an NDA allocation of about 3 billion for DepEd's program, excluding DSWD's program, while another agency figure was stated as 2,163,000,000,000. Lagman also warned that fermented and flavored milk supplied nine to 21 grams of sugar, or two point two to five teaspoons, per serving. The agency's explanation of its production strategy and future targets was incomplete, and an agency official committed to provide requested sugar and industry data to her office.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the level of local milk production, the extent of reliance on imported dairy, and whether the proposed milk-feeding funding and agricultural support would expand domestic dairy capacity. It also examined the health and sugar implications of serving fermented and flavored milk beverages in schools.
topics.agency_position: The agency said local milk production had increased but remained insufficient to supply the entire milk-feeding program, leaving the country dependent on imported dairy. It presented the milk-feeding program as a source of demand that could help increase production and referred to feed centers and related support, although its detailed production strategy and targets were not fully stated in the transcript.
topics.outcome: The committee received production, sufficiency, import-dependence, target, and budget figures, but the agency did not provide a clear multi-year production plan or quantified future targets. The sugar-related data request was left for later submission.

positions.position: She supported accelerating local dairy production so schoolchildren could receive domestically produced milk, questioned the continuing reliance on imports, and raised concerns about the sugar content of fermented and flavored milk beverages.

He stated that local production and milk sufficiency had improved but remained inadequate, with imported dairy still averaging 98 percent, and indicated that the milk-feeding program could drive further production increases.

topics.topic: Organic agriculture, agricultural credit, and high-value crops
topics.summary: Rep. Marlo Bancoro raised organic agriculture as a national concern and obtained a commitment from DA officials to meet and discuss the program's structure and regional direction. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed the DA on Mindanao's share, citing its contribution to corn, pineapple, banana, and overall food requirements; the Secretary ultimately confirmed a 20% share after an initial unclear response. The high-value-crops official requested an additional 8,000,000,000 over the existing 1,700,000,000 budget, citing targets for annual industry growth, higher farmer income, diversification, value addition, and post-harvest-loss reduction. ACPC requested no additional funding, but asked that credit be integrated into DA programs; it reported annual funding of 2,750,000,000 and lending of 3,250,000,000. The organic-agriculture budget issue was not resolved because the agency said its main concern was program structure and should be handled under another agenda.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the DA would support organic agriculture, integrate agricultural credit into commodity programs, and expand assistance for high-value crops. It also examined Mindanao's funding share and the additional resources requested for diversification, value addition, and post-harvest needs.
topics.agency_position: The DA described high-value crops as a priority requiring a substantial budget increase to address post-harvest losses, diversification, value addition, and climate-related challenges. ACPC did not seek additional funding but wanted credit integrated into commodity programs, while the National Organic Agriculture Program said its main issue was program structure rather than budget.
topics.outcome: The committee received the DA's request for a major high-value-crops budget increase and ACPC's request for credit integration, while the organic-agriculture issue was deferred to a separate discussion on program structure. Mindanao's 20% share was stated as confirmed, but no final budget authorization for the requested increase was recorded.

topics.topic: Palm oil, banana, abaca, and coffee industry development
topics.summary: Rep. Raymond Mendoza sought DA support for urgent certification of the palm-oil and banana bills, stronger palm-oil funding, and a breakdown of pest-control spending. The DA supported the bills, cited a palm-oil roadmap targeting 300,000 hectares, and described funding of 500,000,000 in the first year and 1,000,000,000 in succeeding years, while committing to make an official recommendation and provide the pest-control breakdown. A minority representative requested marshland studies and a timetable for implementation, and the DA said the study would be completed by year-end with implementation potentially beginning in mid 2027. The same member raised coffee development, and the DA cited nurseries, high-yielding varieties, and processing equipment as planned measures. Rep. Romeo Momo Sr. presented the Marihatag Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor, citing 4,140 metric tons of 2025 production, a total project cost of 739,000,000, and a proposed 47,000,000 2027 allocation. The corridor funding was identified as Tier 2 and was not finally resolved during the exchange.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Department of Agriculture would support legislation and provide funding for palm oil, banana, pest-control, coffee, and abaca development. It also examined implementation timelines and funding arrangements for marshland studies and the proposed Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor in Marihatag.
topics.agency_position: The DA supported certification of the palm-oil and banana bills as urgent and planned expanded palm-oil, coffee, pest-control, and abaca-related interventions. It committed to submit or provide information on the palm-oil recommendation, pest-control expenditure breakdown, marshland studies, and coordination on coffee areas, while treating the Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor funding as a Tier 2 matter requiring further budget or financing action.
topics.outcome: The DA expressed support for the palm-oil and banana bills and undertook follow-up recommendations and expenditure disclosures. Palm-oil and coffee plans, marshland implementation, and the Abaca Agro-Industrial Corridor remained dependent on subsequent recommendations, studies, Tier 2 approval, or future funding.

topics.topic: Animal vaccination and the national anti-rabies program
topics.summary: Minority member Reniko asked how the national anti-rabies program would meet its stated elimination targets and what annual vaccination capacity and budget would be required. The DA Undersecretary for Livestock said that twenty twenty five one hundred fifty million had been distributed, although the transcript did not clarify what the figure measured. He said the agency planned to produce its own rabies vaccine and cited around 30 million dogs and cats, with roughly twenty to thirty percent requiring vaccination and a stated need for 27 million vaccinations. Reniko requested population-growth, vaccination-rate, budget, TNR, and impounding data, including information on free-roaming cats and dogs after impounding. The excerpt ended without the requested data being submitted or a firm agency commitment to provide it.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the national anti-rabies program would meet the country's targets for eliminating rabies, including the annual vaccination requirement, available vaccine supply, and the budget needed to vaccinate dogs and cats. The minority member also sought data on population growth, vaccination rates, and the implementation of the TNR and impounding policies for free-roaming animals.
topics.agency_position: The DA, through the Undersecretary for Livestock, said that rabies-related resources had been distributed and that the agency was planning to produce its own rabies vaccine rather than buy it locally. The agency cited a dog-and-cat population of 30,000,000, an estimated vaccination requirement affecting twenty to thirty percent, and a stated need for 27,000,000 vaccinations.
topics.outcome: The agency provided broad population and vaccination figures and stated that it was planning domestic rabies-vaccine production. The requested supporting data on vaccination rates, population growth, budgeting, TNR, and impounding was not provided in the excerpt, and no explicit submission deadline or formal agency undertaking to furnish it was recorded.

positions.position: The minority member pressed for a concrete assessment of the annual vaccination requirement, the program budget and vaccination rate, vaccine supply, and the implementation of TNR and impounding policies for free-roaming animals.
The agency supported developing domestic rabies-vaccine production and undertaking a large-scale vaccination effort based on the estimated dog-and-cat population.

topics.topic: NIA appropriation structure and congressional oversight
topics.summary: Allan Ty questioned the NIA administrator on whether irrigation appropriations should be program-based or rigidly itemized, and whether program-based budgeting still subjected projects to DBM validation, procurement laws, auditing, engineering standards, and congressional oversight. NIA answered that it preferred program-based appropriations supported by a separately submitted and validated project list, because itemization in 2026 had limited its ability to respond to cost changes, rights-of-way problems, calamities, and implementation delays. Robert Nazal Jr. separately questioned the DA's farm-to-market road funding, noting a 55,050-kilometer deficit, a reduction from about 33 billion in 2026 to about 16 billion in 2027, and a stated 51.5% cut. Secretary Laurel said roughly 60 billion annually could build about 4,000 kilometers, with the minimum effort taking ten to twelve years, and said DA had allocated 30% of its 33 billion budget based on absorptive capacity and manpower. Nassal also asked whether special provision number eight had constrained NIA utilization and requested a written proposal before plenary. The issue landed with NIA's requested program-based structure still subject to committee consideration, supported by document submissions, while the answer on whether cuts would leave projects functionally incomplete remained unclear.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether NIA's irrigation appropriations should remain program-based or be itemized by project, and whether either structure preserved DBM validation, procurement and audit compliance, implementation flexibility, and congressional oversight. It also examined whether budget restrictions affected NIA's utilization and whether DA had the capacity to implement the proposed farm-to-market road funding.
topics.agency_position: NIA preferred restoring program-based appropriations under program expenditure classification, with a detailed, validated, and transparent project list submitted separately to DBM and Congress. It maintained that this structure preserved accountability and oversight while allowing adjustments for field conditions, delays, calamities, savings, and implementation readiness.
topics.outcome: NIA's preferred program-based structure was placed on the record, with separate project-list documentation for validation and oversight. The committee requested the Speaker-submitted request and a written implementation proposal; the effect of project cuts on functional completion was not answered clearly.

positions.position: Supported determining whether program-based appropriations could preserve validation, accountability, transparency, and congressional oversight while avoiding the implementation constraints of rigid project line items.

Pressed for budget provisions and appropriations adjustments that preserved transparency but also reflected NIA's implementation capacity and the functional completeness of irrigation projects after cuts.
Questioned whether the proposed farm-to-market road funding was sufficient to reduce the road deficit and whether DA had the absorptive capacity and manpower to implement a larger program.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked the NIA administrator to confirm that NIA was a government-owned and controlled corporation receiving national government subsidies for development, construction, and rehabilitation of the national irrigation system.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator confirmed that NIA was a government-owned and controlled corporation and received national government subsidies for the national irrigation system.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked how NIA expanded, appropriated, and utilized its annual national government subsidy.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NIA evaluated priorities, explained its prioritization, and identified the budget in a program-expenditure form. The phrase describing the form was garbled in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether, in fiscal year 2025 and prior years, NIA's budget was presented under program expenditure classification rather than as an extensive list of individual irrigation projects in the NEP or GAA.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator confirmed that the budget was presented under the program-based structure.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator clarified that NIA submitted a detailed project list as a supporting document, but individual projects were generally not separate line items in the NEP or GAA annex.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether NIA was still required under the program-based framework to submit its proposed project list and supporting documents to DBM for technical evaluation, validation, and budget review.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NIA submitted the project list and supporting documents to DBM. Projects underwent technical validation, prioritization, costing, and assessment of implementation readiness; their absence as individual GAA line items did not mean they were unvalidated or that NIA had unlimited discretion.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the program-based appropriations remained subject to DBM evaluation, procurement laws, auditing rules, engineering standards, and congressional oversight.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator agreed, stating that a program-based budget did not remove accountability. Projects remained subject to DBM evaluation, procurement and auditing requirements, approved engineering plans and specifications, environmental and other regulatory requirements, and monitoring and reporting to Congress.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NIA had written to the Speaker requesting more flexibility, while emphasizing that the flexibility was operational rather than discretion without accountability.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked what operational challenges resulted from itemizing individual NIA projects in fiscal year 2026, particularly in relation to project costs, rights-of-way, emergencies, and calamities.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said that making projects separate budget line items created significant operational difficulties. Changes in detailed engineering, project scope and cost, right-of-way problems, permits, calamities, or other irrigation requirements could require reprioritization, but funds could not readily be redirected to other validated and implementation-ready projects without a lengthy modification or realignment process.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the list submitted to DBM was for planning and validation, subject to final costing and implementation-readiness assessment, rather than a rigid statutory enumeration of projects.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator agreed, explaining that under the previous program-based structure NIA could proceed with another validated, high-priority, implementation-ready project within the same program when a project encountered an unavoidable delay.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether NIA had recommended the dated list of individual projects to DBM or whether DBM had imposed it.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NIA submitted the list during budget preparation, but it should be treated as a planning, prioritization, and validation document. NIA supported submitting a complete and validated project list while recommending that the appropriations remain program-based.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked which structure would better serve farmers: a rigid itemized project list in the GAA annex or program-based appropriations supported by a separately submitted, validated, and transparent project list.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator preferred restoring the program-based structure. He said it would provide operational flexibility to address delays, use legitimate savings, respond to calamities and emerging irrigation needs, and prioritize validated projects ready for implementation without compromising congressional oversight or project-level transparency.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether NIA had submitted, or was submitting, a request to amend its budget from an itemized list to a program- or subprogram-based structure.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator confirmed the request and reiterated that the detailed project list should be submitted as a supporting document for transparency, validation, monitoring, and oversight rather than as rigid line items.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked NIA to submit to the committee the request it had sent to the Office of the Speaker.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Robert Nazal Jr. noted that DA identified a 55,050 kilometer farm-to-market road deficit and that proposed 2027 funding would fall from 33,000,000,000 in 2026 to 16,000,000,000, a 51.5% cut.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked Secretary Laurel whether building around 1,000 kilometers annually was too little to materially reduce the deficit and improve agricultural productivity, production costs, post-harvest losses, market access, and farmer incomes.

thread.speaker: Laurel
thread.said: Secretary Laurel agreed that the level was insufficient and described the criteria used to prioritize roads, including influence area, poverty incidence, farmer or fisherfolk beneficiaries, network connectivity, road condition, climate adaptation, average daily traffic, and new production areas.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked how much would ideally be needed annually for farm-to-market roads and how many kilometers that funding could build.

thread.speaker: Laurel
thread.said: Laurel estimated that 60,000,000,000 annually might be needed and said this could build about 4,000 kilometers, described as a bare minimum over ten to twelve years.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked whether DA could demonstrate lower-cost construction than DPWH in terms of absorptive capacity and whether it had enough manpower.

thread.speaker: Laurel
thread.said: Laurel said DA had a 33,000,000,000 budget that year and had allocated 30% in consideration of its absorptive capacity and manpower. He said DA would be more ready the following year.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked the NIA administrator whether the more specific itemization of projects in fiscal year 2026 and the addition of special provision number eight improved implementation or contributed to the decline in budget utilization.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NIA preferred program-based operations under program expenditure classification, supported by a detailed, validated, and transparent project list submitted separately to Congress and DBM. He said this provided a balance between transparency, accountability, oversight, flexibility, and timely utilization, while not granting unlimited authority to replace projects.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal followed up on whether special provision number eight had limited NIA's room to implement projects and affected utilization.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator cited the difficulty of rigid line items, using a 100-meter irrigation canal with a transcript figure stated as 10,000,005 million as an example. He also said delays in early procurement affected implementation and contrasted NIA's constraints with DPWH's ability to implement projects at any time of year.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked NIA to submit a proposal to the committee, before plenary, identifying provisions that would improve implementation.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked whether a substantially reduced appropriation for a designed and costed irrigation project could still deliver its intended functional output or would result in an incomplete project.

thread.speaker: NIA administrator
thread.said: The administrator began responding, but the answer was interrupted and is not intelligible in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Robert Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal manifested that House or Senate adjustments should consider project implementability, not merely the amount to be cut.

topics.topic: OP FY2027 budget and proposed budget reduction
topics.summary: The chair presented the Office of the President's proposed FY2027 allocation as 10,156,000,000, while Executive Secretary Ralph Recto stated a proposal of MXN 10,150,000,000. Recto said the proposal was about 0.14% of the proposed national budget and was 64% lower than the previous year's level because of reduced operational requirements and the completion of ASEAN Summit activities. He said the amount would support the Office of the President's 49 delivery units and core presidential operations. The minority and majority moved to extend institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminate the committee deliberations. A minority member objected and raised transparency, flood-control, and confidential and intelligence fund questions, including 550,000,000 in such funds. The motion passed with 37 votes in favor and five against, while the chair recorded that outstanding questions would be answered on or before plenary.
topics.question: What was the Office of the President's proposed FY2027 allocation, and why was it reportedly lower than the previous year's level? The committee also sought to determine whether questions on flood control and confidential and intelligence funds would receive answers despite terminating the committee-level deliberations.
topics.agency_position: The Office of the President said its proposed FY2027 budget was sufficient to perform its constitutional and administrative functions. Executive Secretary Ralph Recto attributed the reduction to lower operational requirements and the completion of ASEAN Summit-related activities, and said the agency was ready to answer questions.
topics.outcome: The committee granted institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminated the Office of the President's committee-level budget deliberations by a vote of 37-5. Questions on flood control and confidential and intelligence funds remained for answers on or before plenary.

topics.topic: Confidential and intelligence funds and spending transparency
topics.summary: Members objected to ending the Office of the President budget discussion without scrutiny of confidential and intelligence funds and related accountability issues. One member cited 550,000,000 in confidential and intelligence funds, while other members raised transparency, flood-control, and possible political-patronage concerns. The Office of the President did not give a substantive answer in these stretches, although Executive Secretary Ralph Recto stated that the office respected Congress's authority and was ready to answer questions. Rep. Edgar Erice supported the budget and said confidential funds were necessary, while Rep. Iris Marie Montes said her negative vote defended Congress's duty to scrutinize every peso of public funds. The chair carried the motion to terminate deliberations by a vote of 37 to five and committed the outstanding answers to the plenary stage.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether the Office of the President's confidential and intelligence funds, and related budgetary issues, would receive meaningful congressional scrutiny and transparent accountability before approval. It also sought to determine when the Office of the President would answer the questions deferred by the committee's grant of institutional and interbranch courtesy.
topics.agency_position: The Office of the President stated that it respected Congress's constitutional authority and was ready to answer questions. It did not provide a substantive answer in the cited stretches on the transparency, accountability, or use of confidential and intelligence funds; the chair recorded that responses would be provided on or before plenary.
topics.outcome: The committee granted institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminated the Office of the President budget deliberations, but members' transparency and confidential-fund questions remained unanswered. The chair recorded the Office of the President's responses as due on or before plenary.

topics.topic: Flood-control projects and reported anomalies
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice raised flood-control anomalies while discussing the President's budget, fiscal space, and developmental spending. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported the Office of the President budget and said the flood-control projects in the 2nd District of Cagayan de Oro were completed, compliant, and cleared by COA, NBI, DPWH, and NEDA. He also said persons responsible for irregularities should face justice through the Ombudsman. A separate member said plenary answers remained due and raised questions about flood control, possible kickbacks, and the transparency of confidential and intelligence funds. The member cited 550 million in confidential and intelligence funds, while other budget figures raised during the related discussion included about 58 billion in presidential pork and about 1.1 trillion for developmental projects. topics.topic: PCO and attached-agency budget reductions and restoration request
topics.summary: Secretary Dave M. Gomez presented a PCO and attached-agency FY 2027 proposal of about 2.62 billion, 6.6% below the 2026 level, while the net department allocation was about 2.48 billion. Robert Nazal Jr. questioned the reductions and the PIA increase, and Gomez attributed the PCO reduction primarily to the end of ASEAN-hosting requirements while saying the PIA increase would fund retrofitting of its 44-year-old building. Gomez said IBC 13 received no subsidy because it was being prepared for privatization, while IBC officials described arbitration and operating pressures. Representative Zia Alonto Adiong pressed whether PCO could meet rising digital and anti-disinformation demands with a reduced budget; Gomez said it could remain effective but would perform much better with additional resources, including the 128,000,000 pesos requested for Bagong Filipinas Studios. Adiong formally sought restoration of the original PCO and attached-agency requests, and Representative Brian Yamsuan supported increasing and restoring the budget. The committee left restoration for a later review and required PCO to submit its original request, identify the cuts, and justify restoration.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the PCO and most attached agencies received reduced FY 2027 allocations, whether the reductions would impair government communications and digital-information services, and whether the original budget requests should be restored. Members also asked what justified the Philippine Information Agency increase, how IBC 13's privatization affected its funding, and what resources were needed for Bagong Filipinas Studios.
topics.agency_position: PCO said the reduction was principally expected because the FY 2026 budget included funding associated with ASEAN hosting, but acknowledged that additional resources would allow it to perform much better. It sought restoration of items included in its original NEP submission, including funding for digital communications, Bagong Filipinas Studios, and support for attached agencies, and committed to document the cuts and provide justifications.
topics.outcome: The committee did not finally restore or amend the budget during the hearing. The issue was referred for later budget-amendment review, with PCO committed to submit its original request, a list of cuts, and restoration justifications; members expressed support for pursuing additional funding.

positions.position: Questioned why the PCO and attached-agency budget was reduced, why PIA was increased while other offices were cut, and whether continued funding for IBC 13 was appropriate while privatization was pending.

Supported reviewing and restoring the original PCO and attached-agency requests, arguing that increased demand for accurate information, digital services, and anti-disinformation work required additional support.
Supported increasing and restoring PCO funding, saying government communications and state media required resources to compete in the digital information environment and serve the Filipino public.
Indicated that the committee would consider and act on the restoration request at the proper time and would await PCO's supporting submission.

topics.topic: IBC 13 zero budget, privatization, and transitional funding
topics.summary: Representatives Roberto Nazal Jr., Maria Victoria Copilar, Brian Yamsuan, and Antonino Roman III challenged the proposed zero allocation for IBC 13 and questioned the timing and consequences of privatization. The agency said the zero budget was tied to the planned sale, but warned that privatization might not be completed by the end of the year and requested restoration of funding for salaries, station upkeep, programming, and legal obligations. IBC 13 described government-information programming, Congress TV, multiple stations and programs, and employee and arbitration-related needs, including a request cited as 479,000,000 and an arbitration amount generally described as about 50,000,000. Copilar sought a transitional budget, while Secretary Gomez assured the committee that employee welfare would be protected and that Congress TV would move to PTV 4 if needed. DBM said IBC 13's ongoing privatization status explained the zero allocation, but acknowledged that it had not received documentation of the arbitration award. The committee indicated that the matter would be included in a new budget quotation, but the funding amount and final disposition remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why IBC 13 had a zero proposed allocation for FY 2027 despite its continuing operations and government-information programming, and whether transitional funding was needed pending privatization. It also sought clarity on the fate of IBC 13 programs, employees, operating obligations, and the arbitration award.
topics.agency_position: PCO said the zero allocation resulted from IBC 13's inclusion in the planned privatization program, not from a determination that its operations were unnecessary. PCO and IBC 13 asked for restoration or transitional funding because privatization might not be completed by the end of the year, while DBM said the ongoing privatization status explained the zero budget and said it had not received documentation for the arbitration award.
topics.outcome: The committee did not resolve the amount or mechanism for transitional funding. PCO committed to pursuing privatization, protecting employee welfare, and moving Congress TV to PTV 4 if necessary, while the requested restoration and treatment of the arbitration obligation were left for further budget action and documentation.

positions.position: Questioned the reduction and privatization approach and pressed for an explanation of what would happen to IBC 13's responsibilities and mandate.
Strongly urged a transitory IBC 13 budget until privatization was completed and sought protection for Congress TV, IBC programming, and employees.
Opposed the zero allocation, characterized IBC 13 as an effective and fiscally responsible government partner, and argued that it should be supported and fully financed.
Challenged the rationale for defunding IBC 13 and pressed the agency and DBM on continued operations and payment of the arbitration-related legal obligation.
Supported efforts to restore at least some funding for PCO and its attached agencies.

topics.topic: IBC 13 legal obligations, arbitration award, and employee compensation
topics.summary: Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong asked whether IBC 13 had to honor a court or mediation order involving former employees who had been waiting since 1998. An IBC official said the National Mediation Board had ordered payment of 50,000,000 for 26 employees, reduced from more than a 100,000,000, and said it was a legal obligation. Antonino Roman III later questioned IBC 13's defunding and raised 58,000,000, while the agency referred to a 50,000,000 request and DBM cited a separate arbitration award of 15,000,000. DBM said IBC's zero FY 2027 budget resulted from ongoing privatization and that it had received no record or request for the award. Roman pressed whether a budget amendment was required, but DBM said Congress would decide. Secretary Dave asked that IBC 13's funding be restored, and the Chair indicated that a new submission or budget quotation should be made.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the amount and legal status of IBC 13's obligations to former employees, including the arbitration award, and whether FY 2027 funding or a budget amendment was needed. Members also sought to determine why IBC 13 had been given zero funding and how its compensation obligations would be met during the proposed privatization.
topics.agency_position: The agency and DBM said IBC 13's zero FY 2027 allocation resulted from its ongoing privatization, but acknowledged that legal and compensation obligations still had to be settled. Secretary Dave asked the committee to restore or fund IBC 13's proposed amount, while DBM said it had received no record or request for the arbitration award and that any FY 2027 amendment was for Congress to decide.
topics.outcome: The committee did not resolve the conflicting figures of 58,000,000, 50,000,000, and 15,000,000 or determine whether a FY 2027 amendment would be made. The matter was left for a new submission or budget quotation, with the agency seeking restoration or funding.

topics.topic: PTV 4 budget, reach, equipment investment, and operating support
topics.summary: Representative Nazzal asked whether PTV 4's budget, reach, equipment, and staffing were adequate for its state-broadcasting mandate. The PTV 4 general manager said the station had about 136,000,000, also referring to 138,000,000, and requested 1,700,000,000; he said a competitive budget could require roughly five to seven billion. He reported current household reach of about 30%, projected reach of about 42% or more after equipment repairs, and reach above 50% with three additional towers. The general manager also said the current budget could not support a network and that international and regional state broadcasters spent billions in pesos. Members Lemanzeras and Yamsuan supported stronger government-media funding, while the PCO secretary said communications resources were inadequate and committed to pushing the request after a formal submission. The issue was not finally resolved in the hearing and was referred for subsequent committee and BARC discussion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PTV 4's proposed funding, transmission reach, equipment, and staffing were sufficient for it to fulfill its state-broadcasting and developmental-communication mandate. Members also examined the broader adequacy of PCO and government communications funding and whether additional support should be requested.
topics.agency_position: PTV 4 and PCO said the current funding was inadequate for a competitive state broadcaster and insufficient to carry out the government's developmental-communication mandate. PTV 4 requested 1,700,000,000, stating that equipment repairs could increase household reach from around 30% to around 42% or more, while three additional towers could bring reach above 50%.
topics.outcome: The need for additional PTV 4 and broader PCO communications funding received support from the participating members, but no final appropriation was established in the discussion. PTV 4 was to submit a formal request for later consideration by the BARC and the committees.

topics.topic: PIA capital outlay, office rent, and building rehabilitation
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked why PIA's budget had increased, and Secretary Dave M. Gomez said the principal reason was capital outlay for retrofitting its 44-year-old building. Brian Yamsuan then raised PIA's omitted request for 20,000,000 pesos in temporary rent, which Secretary Gomez confirmed was needed while construction proceeded. Members questioned whether retrofitting the deteriorated building was preferable to constructing a new one and requested photographs and videos of its condition. Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong supported maintaining adequate facilities for PCO and its attached agencies. Deputy Speaker Bambi Emano raised the proposed no-cost land donation for a Region 10 PIA office in El Salvador City and sought capital-outlay funding. PIA committed to the infrastructure project if funding was made available, while members committed to work for budget reinstatement or augmentation; no final appropriation was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PIA's budget increased, whether the increase would fund rehabilitation of its 44-year-old building, and why the separate request for temporary office rent was omitted. Members also sought support for capital outlay for PIA and attached-agency facilities, including a proposed Region 10 office in El Salvador City.
topics.agency_position: The PCO said PIA's increased budget was principally for capital outlay to retrofit its severely deteriorated 44-year-old building. Secretary Gomez confirmed that the 20,000,000 rent request had been omitted despite the need for temporary office space during construction, and PIA committed to pursuing the proposed El Salvador City infrastructure project if capital-outlay funding was provided.
topics.outcome: The agency confirmed the need for both PIA building rehabilitation and temporary rent, while members indicated support for restoring the omitted rent appropriation and pursuing capital-outlay funding. PIA's proposed El Salvador City office received an agency commitment contingent on funding, but the transcript does not show a final appropriation, committee ruling, or resolution of the retrofit-versus-new-building question.

topics.topic: PCO digital information services and misinformation response
topics.summary: Secretary Gomez presented a proposed PCO budget of about 2.62 billion, a 6.6% reduction from the 2026 level, while describing expanded digital, media-literacy, and misinformation-response programs. Representative Adiong questioned whether the reduction would impair the PCO's ability to digitalize information services and provide accurate, timely information amid social-media misinformation. Gomez said the PCO could remain effective through organizational agility and streamlined operations, but acknowledged that it could be much better with additional resources. Adiong then asked about the unfunded continuation of Bagong Filipinas Studios, and Gomez identified a request of 128,000,000 for three to five additional studios. Adiong supported the studios as a means of modernizing state media and rebuilding public trust. Representative Yamsuan also supported increased resources and asked the PCO to submit a formal request for committee consideration; the proposed increase therefore remained subject to later action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed reduction in the PCO budget would impair digital information services, media and information literacy, and the government's response to misinformation and disinformation. It also examined whether funding for Bagong Filipinas Studios would continue and whether additional resources were needed.
topics.agency_position: The PCO maintained that it could remain effective despite the reduction by improving organizational agility, streamlining operations, and using available resources more efficiently. Secretary Gomez nevertheless acknowledged that the agency could perform much better with additional resources, and said the 128,000,000 Tier 2 request for additional Bagong Filipinas Studios was not included in the proposed budget.
topics.outcome: The committee received the PCO's explanation that it could continue operating under the reduced budget but would deliver better results with additional resources. The 128,000,000 studios request and broader proposed increases were not resolved during the exchange and were left for formal submission and committee discussion.

topics.topic: PCO communications personnel and vacant critical positions
topics.summary: Secretary Dave M. Gomez reported that PCO proper had 577 available positions but only 469 active personnel, or about 81%, leaving 93 plantilla positions and 15 contractual items unfilled. He also said the proposed personal-services budget covered 185 unfilled positions and 17 non-permanent positions. Representative Nazzal asked why the Director for Communication Service position remained vacant and what prevented other critical positions from being filled. Gomez answered that nominations for some positions were being processed and that others were covered by an optimization plan submitted to the DBM. Nazzal and the PTV 4 general manager also discussed PTV 4’s limited budget, with the manager describing the allocation as 136,000,000 and elsewhere 138,000,000, against a request for 1,700,000,000 and an estimated competitive requirement of five to seven billion. topics.outcome: The vacancy issue was answered procedurally: some appointments were in process, while other positions remained subject to the PCO’s DBM-submitted optimization plan. topics.topic: Government communications ecosystem and developmental communication funding
topics.summary: Brian Yamsuan asked the PTV 4 general manager whether the broadcaster could fulfill its new mandate with its existing funding. The general manager said PTV 4 could probably buy or collaborate on only one show with its budget and could not build a network with about 138 million, while neighboring state broadcasters spent billions in pesos. PCO Secretary Dave Gomez said developmental communication required viewing the communications ecosystem as a whole and corrected the PCO figure to zero point zero three percent, against a government budget of about 7.2 trillion. He also said social-media distribution was cheaper but production was significantly more expensive, and cited 5,000,000,000 in an example involving 10% of potential energy-sector losses. Rep. Brian Yamsuan supported higher PCO funding and the restoration of 1,700,000,000 for PTV and IBC. The matter was left with a request for a formal submission and commitments to pursue the issue in the BARC and committee deliberations.

topics.topic: IBC 13 and attached-agency operating reductions
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned the lower proposed funding for PCO attached agencies and the increase for PIA, while also examining IBC 13's operating needs and planned sale. Secretary Dave M. Gomez attributed the PCO reduction to the one-time higher budget for ASEAN hosting and said PIA's increase would largely fund retrofitting of its 44-year-old building. Gomez asked that at least the agencies' original net plan be restored and said PCO was completing the steps needed to privatize IBC 13. IBC president Jimmy Policarpo cited an arbitration amount of 50,000,000, government-information programming comprising 80% of output, and income of 5,000,000 a month, while saying income covered roughly half of operating needs. Nazal questioned further investment in an entity already slated for sale, and stated that IBC's responsibilities and mandate would transfer to PTV if sold. The issue was left with commitments to advance the privatization process, while budget restoration and the final operating arrangement remained unresolved.

topics.topic: Local Government Support Fund rationale, allocation, and monitoring
topics.summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DILG's authority, monitoring role, transparency, and treatment of unused LGSF balances. DILG said DBM released and validated the assistance while DILG monitored distribution, implementation, and reports, and Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to submit utilization reports covering 2025 and 2026. The agency defended the proposed LGSF of about 58 billion as supplemental funding because the national tax allotment was spread across many provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays. DILG described engineers, project evaluation officers, local monitoring committees, CSO and NGO participation, and the Subay Bayan portal as safeguards. A civil-society-backed line of questioning sought justification after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, evidence against duplication, open-data disclosure, participatory budgeting, and human-rights safeguards. DILG answered these questions in part, but the broader policy and accountability concerns remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why a separate Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) remained necessary after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling increased LGUs' national tax allotment, what programs and fiscal gaps it addressed, and how funds were allocated, validated, implemented, monitored, and disclosed. Members also asked whether DILG or DBM controlled distribution and whether community participation and human-rights safeguards were adequate.
topics.agency_position: DILG maintained that DBM controlled LGSF policy, validation, allocation, and release, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and reported on implementation. It defended LGSF as supplemental funding needed because the national tax allotment was divided among many LGUs and said safeguards included engineers, project monitoring officers, three-tier monitoring, local monitoring committees with CSO participation, reporting portals, and referral of confirmed wrongdoing.
topics.outcome: DILG clarified that DBM controlled LGSF validation, policy, and release, while DILG monitored implementation and relied on COA and other monitoring mechanisms for accountability. The committee received commitments for utilization reports, but questions about the fund's discretionary structure, duplication with national tax allotments, unused prior-year balances, measurable outcomes, and independent safeguards were not fully resolved.

positions.position: Sought clearer accountability for DILG monitoring, investigation of complaints, and referral of wrongdoing involving LGSF assistance.
Raised concerns about the growth and transparency of LGSF, the discretionary role in infrastructure assistance, unused balances from 2016 to 2025, and the need for utilization reports.
Supported stronger DILG ground supervision of LGSF and raised the need for clear implementation timelines and deadlines.

Pressed for a policy justification for retaining LGSF after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, stronger validation and disclosure, meaningful community participation, human-rights safeguards, and evidence supporting SBDP allocations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked DILG to confirm its role in administering and monitoring LGSF financial assistance to LGUs, including assistance for development projects and indigent individuals' education scholarships.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said DILG's sole function was to monitor distribution and present reports. DBM dispersed the money, while COA and DILG monitored its distribution.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked whether DILG had received reports of similar problems in its monitoring of LGSF assistance.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said DILG had seen such reports and was monitoring them, but determining relationships between recipients and disbursement personnel was difficult. DILG remained open to investigating complaints submitted to it.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said confirmed wrongdoing would be referred to the relevant municipality or city authority, or, for more serious cases, to the Ombudsman.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He questioned DILG's role in implementing and monitoring LGSF financial assistance and noted that the proposal had grown from 5,000,000 in the NEP to 37,400,000,000 in the enacted budget process.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked whether DILG had a role in setting the DBM guidelines and distribution levels for financial assistance, including maximum amounts for Ayuda, medical assistance, and infrastructure.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said the guidelines were issued by DBM, not DILG. DILG was strictly a monitoring body and had no policy-making role in the distribution or utilization of the fund.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He cited the DBM guidelines allowing requests to be forwarded to DILG for a recommended amount for each LGU and asked whether this gave DILG discretion.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said DILG had received very few such referrals, which were handled by undersecretaries. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla added that the referrals mostly concerned water systems.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He cited a total 2026 LGSF of 50,000,000,000, more than PHP10 billion in continuing appropriations, for a total of PHP68 billion, and asked DILG to confirm.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla confirmed the figure. The member then stated that PHP57 billion was the 2026 figure and that PHP68 billion had been proposed for the following year.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the utilization rate would be determined at year-end because the program started in 2026. DILG would provide a full report in 2027 after monitoring distribution and use.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He noted that LGUs were required to submit quarterly utilization reports to DBM, DILG, and Congress, and asked for updates covering 2025 and 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla said DILG would submit the requested reports to the committee and undertook to submit them within the day.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: In response to a question on implementation, he stated that implementation was at 100%. He said DILG hired engineers to assess projects, while COA would be needed to determine whether more than 40,000 LGU recipients complied and achieved the required results.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He raised the guideline requiring a Certificate of Reversion for undisbursed balances from completed LGSF financial-assistance projects for fiscal years 2016 to 2025 and asked about unused funds.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla said the 2016 to 2025 period was under Congress's purview rather than DILG's distribution responsibility. He said DILG took full cognizance of the matter only in 2026.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He expressed concern about transparency and the discretionary element of LGSF infrastructure assistance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla said LGU accountability requirements were stringent, including bids and awards committees, post-qualification, post-assessment, and review. He said DILG would file charges if discrepancies were identified.

thread.speaker: Anna York Bondoc
thread.said: She said she supported placing LGSF implementation under stronger DILG ground supervision rather than relying only on DBM monitoring. She also raised the absence of clear LGSF timelines and deadlines as an implementation concern.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: On behalf of civil society organizations, he asked why a separate LGSF was retained after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling expanded the national tax allotment, what fiscal gaps it addressed, and how the government ensured that it supplemented rather than duplicated regular LGU revenues.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said the estimated 2027 national tax allotment was about one point three two to one point four billion trillion pesos, but it was divided among 82 provinces, 149 cities, 1,493 municipalities, and more than 42,000 barangays. The proposed LGSF of 58,000,000,000 was described as additional funding for water and sanitation systems, farm-to-market roads, electrification, health centers, and other basic services.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked DILG to clarify its role in LGSF monitoring, evaluation, implementation, and project validation.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said LGSF was released directly to LGUs, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and checked implementation. DILG had funding to hire engineers and project evaluation officers for deployment to provinces and regions.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked whether DBM handled the validation and vetting of LGU proposals and whether DILG ensured that projects were not duplicates.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said DBM created the portal where LGUs submitted project proposals and handled the validation and vetting. He agreed that DILG did not handle that process and that the question of duplication could be directed to DBM; LGUs identified their own priority projects.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked how local development councils, sanggunians, accredited CSOs, sectoral representatives, and affected communities participated in project identification, procurement, monitoring, and validation, and what outputs and disclosure requirements corresponded to the proposed monitoring allocation.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog described a three-tier monitoring system: local project monitoring committees composed of LGU officials and CSOs, DILG's second-party monitoring, and third-party monitoring involving CSOs and NGOs. He also cited the Subay Bayan portal, where LGUs were required to upload project status updates.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: He said 63,000,000 was allocated for monitoring and evaluation and 560,000,000 was used for salaries of engineers and project evaluation officers hired for field monitoring.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked what performance evidence supported the relative allocations for LGSF and participatory budgeting and how DILG would expand meaningful CSO and community participation throughout the project cycle.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said the Support to Barangay Development Program addressed basic-service gaps in barangays previously influenced by communist armed groups, while participatory-budgeting assistance funded water systems and evacuation centers identified through consultations. He said the latter had a 1,000,000,000 allocation in 2026.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked what safeguards prevented LGSF and SBDP projects from exposing CSOs, human-rights defenders, indigenous peoples, and community leaders to red-tagging, retaliation, or exclusion, and whether complaints and actions would be publicly reported.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog referred the human-rights question to the PNP/related official. The response cited a National Police Commission media-relations manual prohibiting red-tagging and said complaints could be brought to the Commission, which would act on them.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked for the objective criteria, allocations, accomplishment data, audit findings, delays, complaints, outcome evidence, and open-data disclosure supporting the proposed increase in SBDP.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said the apparent SBDP increase was misleading because more barangays would be covered. He said the allocation per barangay actually declined from 10,000,000 to 5,000,000, and referred again to DILG monitoring, its online platform, and CSO and NGO engagement.

topics.topic: Barangay Development Program and SBDP per-barangay allocations
topics.summary: Jose Teves Jr. pressed for a higher SBDP allocation, arguing that 5,000,000 per barangay was insufficient for classrooms, health centers, water, electrification, and other needs. DILG said it had requested 10,000,000 per barangay and would welcome a congressional increase to 7,000,000 or more. Members then sought delivery rates, audits, beneficiary verification, and third-party monitoring, while DILG reported delivery rates ranging from 29% to 100% across the cited years and said 700 monitoring personnel were deployed. Rep. Caroline Agyao obtained clarifications on EL CAC coverage and annual allocations, including 2,500,000 in 2025, 10,000,000 in 2026, and 5,000,000 proposed for 2027. DILG said municipalities implemented the projects, DILG monitored them, and coordination was intended to prevent duplication. A CSO representative questioned the rationale and accountability of the LGSF and SBDP, and DILG described three-tier monitoring, DBM vetting, grassroots consultations, and the SubayBayan portal. The hearing ended with document requests and commitments, while the adequacy of the 2027 allocation and the broader evidence supporting it remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the appropriate per-barangay allocation for the Barangay Development Program/SBDP, the basis for changes in the proposed budget, and whether projects were properly selected, implemented, audited, monitored, and protected against duplication. Members and CSOs also asked what role DILG played in the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), what safeguards existed, and what documents and performance data would be submitted.
topics.agency_position: DILG said the SBDP was a targeted program for barangays previously affected by communist armed groups, with projects selected through grassroots consultations and implemented by municipalities. It maintained that DILG's role was monitoring and evaluation, while DBM administered the LGSF and handled proposal vetting; DILG cited local, second-party, and third-party monitoring, the SubayBayan portal, and additional monitoring personnel as safeguards.
topics.outcome: DILG acknowledged that the 2027 SBDP proposal provided only 5,000,000 per barangay despite DILG's request for 10,000,000, and members' calls for a higher amount were left to Congress. DILG committed to submit accomplishment, coverage, and third-party monitoring documents, but the requested independent outcome, audit, duplication, and open-data evidence was not fully supplied during the exchange.

positions.position: Supported increasing the SBDP allocation from 5,000,000 per barangay, preferably to 7,000,000 or more, because barangays faced substantial classroom, health, water, electrification, and other infrastructure needs.
Sought clarity on EL CAC coverage, the different annual per-barangay allocations, eligible projects, implementing agencies, and safeguards against duplication with DOH and other projects.
Pressed DILG for verified physical and financial accomplishment data, audits, beneficiary verification, and third-party monitoring reports.
Questioned the policy rationale, transparency, performance basis, community participation, safeguards, and independent accountability mechanisms for LGSF and SBDP.
