thread.speaker: DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla referred the legal question to the DILG undersecretary for legal affairs.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary for Legal Affairs
thread.said: The undersecretary answered that DILG had authority to resolve an appeal from an SK chair's dismissal, consistent with section 67(a) of the Local Government Code. The undersecretary also cited section 18 of Republic Act 10742 as recognizing an option to question the dismissal.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary for Legal Affairs
thread.said: In response to Rep. Mano's follow-up, the undersecretary affirmed that DILG could correct the decision on appeal as part of its appellate authority or jurisdiction. The undersecretary added that the propriety of the dismissal was also reviewable under the SK Reform Law of 2015.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bambi Mano
thread.said: Rep. Mano said he would submit his documents to DILG and asked Secretary Remulla to respond before the matter reached plenary.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The minority member asked about capacity building, skills development, awareness, information concerns, and the mandatory training program for SK officials.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official estimated the funding for the next year's mandatory training program at roughly around 70 plus million, while the transcript also recorded the amount as about 72,000,000,000. The official said the NYC was developing modules for Core 1, 2, 3, and 4 and was training trainers from local youth development councils and local youth development offices.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The official said the NYC was part of the National Steering Committee of the SK mandatory continuing training program and was meeting to ensure that the training modules were approved.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The minority member asked about the SK federation's position on postponement of the SK term and the possibility of term extension.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said a quick survey of 120 SK federation presidents nationwide was being conducted, although the NYC had not yet obtained a 100% response. The official said many SK presidents appeared to favor an extension, while some areas without functioning SKs were asking for special elections so that budgets could be executed.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda asked what program the NYC intended to implement after the SK elections, if the elections proceeded.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said continuing training for SK officials would remain available. The NYC was printing SK 101 books and adding SK auditing guidelines because some SK officials had difficulty legally preparing and using their budgets.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The official said the NYC was signing a memorandum of understanding with the Philippine Local Government Accountants Association so accountants could help pre-audit SK plans.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda asked which SK manual was currently being used, including whether it was the SK Reform Bill manual.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said the materials were basic books based on the SK reform framework because not everyone could understand the more complicated SK guide.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: She asked how the three-part training materials, including fiscal management, would be implemented across nearly 2,000 municipal federations.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said the approach was to train local youth development officers and provincial youth development officers, with training ongoing. The official said the NYC had only 10 area offices with two people per office and had requested additional personal-services positions to expand training.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda proposed that SK federation officers or presidents receive training before or during federation elections instead of waiting until afterward, and asked that the training be incorporated with the NYC.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said Republic Act 10742 already required SK chairpersons to undergo one-day orientation before assuming office. DILG would revisit the modules with the Local Government Academy and the National Youth Commission to enhance the one-day orientation.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: Asked about the number of SK federation members suspended or removed, the NYC official said the figure had to be provided later. The official explained that the NYC had no police power and referred complaints to DILG and local governments.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda said every barangay should conduct a KK assembly and every federation should hold at least one meeting each week to discuss programs and plans.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official agreed that planning was central, saying that 50% of the battle was planning.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda asked whether failure to hold meetings for five consecutive months would constitute grounds for removing the federation president from office.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official deferred the removal question to DILG but said the NYC would assist.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said there was a process for removing a Sanggunian Kabataan federation president who failed to comply with the federation's constitution and bylaws.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda urged DILG to reinforce annual reporting and hearing requirements for SK federations and to ensure that SK chairpersons and presidents held monthly meetings, with failure to do so potentially resulting in removal.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said the commission could pass a resolution supporting Jambaranda's manifestation, but emphasized that the NYC could encourage SK officials rather than mandate compliance.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said DILG had already issued several memorandum circulars for guidance and would issue another round in light of Jambaranda's manifestation.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda asked the AILG to provide figures on SK federation members, and the chair directed that the figures be submitted to the committee.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda raised the need to guide out-of-school youth and cited a figure of 10.7 out-of-school youth, although the transcript did not clarify the unit or full description.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said the available out-of-school youth data were flawed because DepEd's information was limited to youth who had applied to DepEd or CHED schools. The official said the actual number could be larger.

thread.speaker: Jambaranda
thread.said: Jambaranda asked that out-of-school youth, including those covered by the senior high school curriculum, be included among the agencies' priorities.

thread.speaker: NYC official
thread.said: The NYC official said the committee could include funding for the NYC policy and research division to undertake the requested work.

topics.topic: Disaster preparedness, LGU capacity, and flood rescue
topics.summary: The chair and members linked disaster resilience and LGU capacity to the DILG budget, citing 50,441 evacuation centers and more than 126,000 deployed uniformed personnel. Teves questioned BFP capital outlay and rescue capacity, while Remulla attributed the earlier reduction to procurement reforms and pointed to planned acquisitions, including 1,500 trucks through a government-to-government transaction. Erice pressed for an integrated Metro Manila flood-control and garbage-management structure, and Remulla said aging drainage systems and fragmented LGU responsibilities required structural reform. Rodriguez sought additional BFP resources from collected fire-code fees, and the chair noted the proposal. York asked about institutional disaster preparation, class-suspension deadlines, and water rescue in flood-prone Pampanga; DILG described operational protocols, Pagasa coordination, monitoring, and continued LGU training. BFP said watercraft and life vests would be distributed geographically and committed to capacity building and future equipment acquisition, while the broader funding and governance issues remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DILG and LGUs were being capacitated for recurring disasters, flooding, and emergency rescue, including the availability and deployment of fire stations, fire trucks, boats, ambulances, personnel, and operating protocols. Members also sought clearer timelines and guidelines for disaster response and class suspensions, and asked whether funding and institutional responsibilities were sufficient.
topics.agency_position: DILG said disaster preparedness depended on coordinated national-agency information, operational protocols, trained LGUs, and monitoring by local officials. It said BFP's response capacity was being improved through procurement reforms, planned government-to-government truck purchases, geographically distributed water-rescue equipment, ambulances, and additional support, but access to trust-fund resources remained dependent on budget action.
topics.outcome: The agency provided its existing disaster-preparedness protocols and described planned improvements in fire-truck procurement, water rescue, ambulances, LGU training, and information sharing. Additional trust-fund support and clearer class-suspension rules were supported or under consideration, but the committee did not finally resolve the funding release, integrated Metro Manila flood governance, or the revised suspension guidelines.

positions.position: Peace, safety, disaster resilience, and capable LGUs warranted sustained and accountable budget support, including resources for fire stations, fire trucks, ambulances, and rescue.
BFP capital outlay and emergency-rescue capacity needed scrutiny, including adequate fire stations, rescue trucks, and personnel.
Metro Manila flooding and garbage required an integrated, regional structure with a clearly accountable agency rather than fragmented LGU systems.
BFP should receive additional resources from collected fire-code fees to address nationwide fire-truck and emergency-response deficiencies.
DILG and LGUs needed stronger institutional disaster preparation, clearer class-suspension timelines, and geographically targeted water-rescue capacity in flood-prone areas.

Continue LGU training, monitoring, and coordination with science agencies and Pagasa for disaster preparedness.
Support capacity building and acquire and geographically place water-rescue equipment for flood-prone localities.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: The chair framed disaster resilience, peace and safety, and LGU capacity to deliver basic services as conditions for economic development, not competing expenses.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the DILG requested budget was 3 and 32,500,000,000, described as 7.1% higher than the FY 2026 General Appropriations Act level.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: The chair cited 50,441 evacuation centers nationwide and more than 126,000 uniformed personnel deployed for disaster response, particularly during the recent habagat.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: Teves cited the BFP budget changes and asked about the department's fire-protection capacity, including new fire stations, rescue trucks, and additional personnel for emergency and rescue response.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: He said the fire item rose from 35,000,000,000 in 2026 to 38,000,000,000 in 2027, while capital outlay fell from 1,400,000,000 to 362,000,000.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: He said natural-disaster capital outlay increased from 2,400,000,000 in 2026 to 6,200,000,000 in 2027.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: Teves referred to 67 new fire stations, eight rescue trucks, and an additional 2,000 PFE personnel.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla explained that the reduction in BFP capital outlay resulted from reconstituting the procurement program after what he described as rampant corruption in prior BFP procurement. He said reforms had been instituted in procurement, recruitment, and deployment and that capital outlay would increase in calendar year 2027.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice asked whether Metro Manila needed one accountable agency and an integrated master plan for flood control, given its population, garbage generation, waterways, and informal-settler issues.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice said Metro Manila had 14,000,000 people and produced 12,000 metric tons of garbage every day.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said some Metro Manila drainage systems were more than 100 years old and still used brick-and-mortar pipes that were too small. He agreed that a proposed Department of Water should address not only water production but also flood mitigation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erice asked whether DILG could use its general-supervision authority to check LGU garbage-collection contracts, arguing that much garbage reached waterways and that the country was approaching a garbage crisis.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla answered that DILG had no supervisory power over LGU contracts and identified COWA as having that authority. He said garbage collection should be treated regionally rather than separately by each LGU and that the Local Government Code needed to be revisited to clarify accountability and oversight.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez cited a budget document with a total amount of 3,430,000,000,427,988,000, in connection with BFP programs and the procurement of fire trucks.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez cited a reported trust-fund balance of 10,536,154,803 pesos and 81 centabos as of 12/31/2025.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez questioned why BFP's request was only 33,000,427,000 pesos despite the reported collections and trust-fund balance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said BFP requested all of the available amount but received only a portion through the DBM budget process.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said BFP asked for everything but DBM allotted it 1,000,000,000 every year.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said a fire truck costing 16,000,000 at comparable quality could cost 10,000,000 under a government-to-government grant.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez moved that the committee consider granting an additional amount to BFP or DILG from collected fire-code fees held in the trust fund, because the request did not cover the country's full fire-truck needs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla thanked the committee and supported assistance from the collected trust-fund fees for BFP requirements.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the proposal was duly noted and expressed support for releasing resources for LGU fire stations, fire trucks, ambulances, and rescue equipment.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said BFP had 5,000 nurses on its payroll but lacked enough ambulances. He said additional funding could allow BFP to acquire class-one ambulances rather than only patient-transfer vehicles for emergencies.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: The chair said BFP personnel numbered 40,000 and that the current pace was 2,000 per year, which would take twenty years; the proposal was 4,000 per year over ten years.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked about repairing fire trucks and providing augmentation or replacement to strengthen fire and emergency-response capability.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said DILG was about to enter a government-to-government transaction with South Korea for the purchase of 1,500 trucks to augment municipal needs. He said broader assistance to municipalities depended on Congress releasing BFP's trust fund.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said the long-term agreement would assure the supply of trucks and that procurement reforms had reduced corruption, allowing BFP to buy more fire trucks.

thread.speaker: Anna York Bondoc
thread.said: York asked how DILG was capacitating itself and LGUs for regular disasters, particularly in flood-prone Pampanga, and what disaster-preparedness measures DILG planned to institutionalize.

thread.speaker: DILG disaster-preparedness official
thread.said: The official said DILG was vice chair for preparedness under the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council and worked with science agencies to provide LGUs timely information on flood-prone and landslide-vulnerable areas. The official said barangays could use the information to prepare constituents in advance.

thread.speaker: DILG disaster-preparedness official
thread.said: The official said DILG had implemented operational protocols since 2016 and 2017 and trained LGUs for typhoons, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, landslides, and El Niño. DILG also maintained contact with Pagasa for updated weather information and monitored LGU preparedness during approaching typhoons.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether DILG could establish a deadline or clearer guidelines for local chief executives declaring class suspensions, noting confusion among parents and businesses.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said an effort was under way to revisit the executive order on class suspensions. The existing policy still left localized suspensions to local chief executives, based on Pagasa forecasts and local conditions.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said the ideal basis for a next-day suspension was the 11PM forecast, so parents and students would not have to go to school before a suspension was declared.

thread.speaker: committee chair
thread.said: York asked how DILG and BFP were training and equipping responders for water rescue, whether specific flooded areas such as Pampanga's 4th District could be identified, and whether boats could be pre-positioned in areas where rescue was needed.

thread.speaker: BFP official
thread.said: The BFP official said BFP played a vital role during flooding and that watercraft, including life vests, were being provided. The official said equipment would be distributed geographically according to the needs of local fire stations.

thread.speaker: BFP official
thread.said: The official undertook to support local disaster-management capacity building, continuing training and acquiring necessary equipment for localities facing hydrometeorological hazards.

topics.topic: Anti-illegal-drug operations and community-based health approach
topics.summary: Rep. Richard Gomez asked the DILG to strengthen anti-drug and peace-and-order support in his district and requested checks on police and CIDG records. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the department was committed and undertook to provide additional police vehicles, ambulances, and two fire trucks, while Gomez expressed full support for the proposed 2027 DILG budget. A PNP representative said anti-illegal-drug operations continued through supply and demand reduction, community engagement, intelligence gathering, and police operations. Minority members questioned barangay drug-watch lists and sought a community-based, health-centered and rehabilitation-oriented approach, but the record did not establish a definitive policy change. NAPOLCOM said it had zero case backlog and committed to submit a 2025–2026 disciplinary-action status report on Tuesday.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the anti-illegal-drug campaign would be sustained and coordinated with peace-and-order programs, including supply and demand reduction. It also questioned the continued use and verification of barangay-level drug-watch lists, rehabilitation-oriented alternatives, safeguards in police operations, and disciplinary action for flawed operations.
topics.agency_position: The PNP said the anti-illegal-drug campaign was continuing through supply and demand reduction, community engagement, intelligence gathering, and police operations. It said target-person lists were based on prior arrests, interviews, and intelligence, while police procedures and body-worn cameras were used to address operational weaknesses; NAPOLCOM said it had no case backlog and agreed to submit the requested disciplinary report.
topics.outcome: The PNP and DILG undertook continued operational and logistical support, including police vehicles, ambulances, and two fire trucks. Questions about barangay drug-watch lists, rehabilitation alternatives, and sanctions were not fully resolved on the record, but NAPOLCOM committed to submit the requested disciplinary report on Tuesday.

positions.position: Supported strengthening the anti-drug campaign and peace-and-order assistance in his district and stated that he fully supported the DILG's proposed 2027 budget.
Supported continuing police and anti-illegal-drug operations and their coordination with peace-and-order programs.
Questioned arbitrary barangay-level drug-watch listings and pressed for a community-based, health-centered and rehabilitation-oriented approach.
Sought confirmation of the barangay drug-watch-list system, verification procedures, and rehabilitation and health-centered alternatives.
Pressed for accountability and a status report on disciplinary action involving police personnel connected with botched operations and enacted arrests.

topics.topic: Seal of Good Local Governance validation and compliance
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice challenged whether the SGLG measured actual governance outcomes or merely documentary compliance. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the DILG had moved to a whole-of-term assessment, reducing the former 10 indicators and as many as 14 categories to resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation; he cited 5,000,000 man hours previously spent annually and an estimated 5,000,000,000 cost for full third-party validation. Erice proposed using an appropriations provision to fund third-party validation, which the secretary welcomed. Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked that electric-bill compliance be added to fiscal-management criteria, and the secretary committed to include it in the next evaluation. In response to Rep. Jambaranda, the secretary committed to an immediate memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and excluding noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG. The request to regulate barangay travel orders was noted but not resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) measured actual improvements in local services and governance, rather than merely documentary compliance. Members also asked whether third-party validation and additional fiscal-management criteria could be incorporated into the SGLG.
topics.agency_position: The DILG said the SGLG had been redesigned as a whole-of-term assessment rather than an annual checklist, with three principal indicators: resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation. The agency supported third-party validation if Congress provided funding and committed to include an electric-bill criterion in the next evaluation and to issue a memorandum circular linking annual development-plan submission to SGLG eligibility.
topics.outcome: The agency answered that the SGLG had been shifted to a whole-of-term, three-area assessment and accepted the possibility of third-party validation if Congress funded it. It also undertook specific follow-up measures on electric-bill compliance and annual development plans, while travel regulation and broader SK concerns remained open.

positions.position: The SGLG should measure actual improvements in local services and governance, including solid waste management, procurement, and contract performance, rather than documentary compliance alone. He supported using appropriations to fund third-party validation.
Fiscal-management evaluation should include whether LGUs comply with electric-cooperative tax exemptions and properly address their electric bills.
The DILG should strengthen guidance for SK and barangay officials, require meaningful local development planning, and regulate or guide barangay officials' travel orders.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He asked whether the SGLG was really a measure of good governance or merely a paper and documentary-compliance exercise, and specifically raised third-party validation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the DILG had changed the SGLG approach for 2024, 2025, and 2026 so that it would be awarded only once every term, rather than assessed annually. The purpose was to evaluate the LGU's whole-of-term performance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the previous annual system required LGUs to commit 5,000,000 man hours each year to reviewing local-government documents. He added that third-party compliance validation was not funded because it could require another 5,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He asked whether actual performance in areas such as solid waste management, bidding, and contracts would be considered, rather than only documentary compliance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla

topics.topic: LGU revenue sharing and local fiscal management
topics.summary: Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked DILG to enforce the local-tax exemption for the 121 electric cooperatives and to include electric-bill compliance in fiscal-management awards. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla assured him of support, and committed to include the criterion in the next evaluation round. Rep. Jambaranda raised SK, barangay development-plan, social-protection, and travel-regulation concerns; the Secretary said DILG could issue a memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and exclude noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG, while taking note of the travel request. Rep. Antonino Roman III asked for the status and timetable of Local Government Code amendments. DILG said consultations were under way, committed to submit available materials by next week, and supported reviewing the LGU share of national tax allocation from 40% to a higher level. The agency also discussed replacing the 25% equal-sharing component with equity sharing, but the allocation changes remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DILG would enforce local-tax exemptions for electric cooperatives, strengthen local planning and fiscal-management requirements, and regulate barangay travel. It also examined the status of proposed Local Government Code amendments, including possible changes to national tax allocation and equalization criteria.
topics.agency_position: DILG and the Secretary committed to support enforcement of electric-cooperative local-tax exemptions and to include electric-bill performance in the next fiscal-management-award evaluation. DILG supported reviewing and potentially increasing LGUs' national tax allocation share, while also considering an equity-based formula that would direct more resources to LGUs with greater geographic, disaster, conflict, or socioeconomic needs.
topics.outcome: The electric-cooperative exemption and fiscal-award issue received affirmative commitments, while the annual development-plan issue also resulted in a proposed immediate memorandum circular. National tax allocation and Local Government Code changes remained under consultation, with DILG committed to provide materials but no final formula or amendment submitted during the hearing.

positions.position: Sought strict LGU enforcement of electric-cooperative local-tax exemptions and inclusion of electric-bill compliance in fiscal-management awards.
Supported stronger SK and barangay guidance, mandatory annual development plans, improved social-protection implementation, and regulation of barangay officials' travel.

Pressed for a timetable on Local Government Code amendments and advocated reviewing the national tax allocation formula and adding equity-related criteria such as income classification and poverty incidence.

topics.topic: Solid-waste management and LGU contract oversight
topics.summary: Jose Teves Jr. asked who was responsible for overseeing LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the Local Government Code assigned waste disposal to municipalities and cities, producing fragmented and potentially inefficient systems, and proposed a regional approach. Rep. Edgar Erice later tied the issue to Metro Manila's 14,000,000 residents and 12,000 metric tons of daily garbage, asking whether DILG could use its general-supervision authority to review LGU contracts. Remulla said DILG had no supervisory power over those contracts and identified COWA as the responsible body as rendered in the transcript. He maintained that the Local Government Code should be revisited because regionalized collection would be more effective than detailed supervision of 40,000 LGUs. The issue remained unresolved, with no specific legal change or oversight mechanism adopted.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which level or agency was responsible for ensuring LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003 and whether DILG could exercise supervisory authority over LGU garbage-collection contracts. Members also examined whether the current LGU-by-LGU system was adequate for the scale of waste and flooding problems, particularly in Metro Manila.
topics.agency_position: DILG said it did not have supervisory power over LGU contracts, identifying COWA as the office with that authority as rendered in the transcript. Secretary Remulla argued that the central problem was the LGU-by-LGU structure required by the Local Government Code and supported revisiting the law to establish a more integrated, regional system with clearer accountability and oversight.
topics.outcome: The agency answered that DILG could not oversee LGU contracts under its current authority and proposed structural and legal reform toward regional garbage management. The committee did not adopt a specific amendment, assign a new oversight agency, or resolve the contract-supervision issue during the hearing.

positions.position: He sought clear oversight of LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations and agreed that the applicable legal framework should be revisited.
He argued that the scale of Metro Manila's waste and flooding problems required an accountable agency with authority to examine LGU garbage contracts and support an integrated metropolitan approach.
He supported regionalizing garbage management and changing the Local Government Code rather than relying on DILG's existing general-supervision authority to conduct detailed contract oversight.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: He asked who was in charge of overseeing LGU implementation of solid-waste management under Republic Act 9003.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the greater defect lay in the Local Government Code, which assigns waste disposal to municipalities and cities. He explained that each municipality develops its own garbage-collection plan, which is not necessarily integrated with other LGUs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said garbage collection is a scaled business and that small municipalities acting independently could face higher and less-efficient costs. He proposed studying whether the Local Government Code could be revised to make garbage management a regional program.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: He agreed that the relevant legal framework should be revisited, referring in the transcript to Republic Act 9003 as a matter for review.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He raised Metro Manila's population and garbage volume in the context of flooding, waterways, and informal settlers. He asked whether there should be one accountable agency and a coordinated metropolitan master plan rather than separate city plans.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He said Metro Manila had 14,000,000 people and produced 12,000 metric tons of garbage every day.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He agreed that a more integrated approach was needed. He linked the waste and flooding problems to aging drainage infrastructure and supported creation of a Department of Water with responsibility not only for water supply but also for mitigating flooding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He returned to garbage collection, saying corruption was a major problem and that only part of the waste was properly handled while the rest entered waterways. He asked whether DILG's general-supervision authority could be used to inspect LGU contracts because the country was approaching a garbage crisis.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He stated that 60% was collected or properly handled and that the rest went to waterways; the transcript does not make the exact referent of the percentage fully clear.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He answered that DILG had no supervisory powers over LGU contracts and said that authority belonged to COWA, as rendered in the transcript. He reiterated that the Local Government Code requires garbage collection to be handled on an LGU basis.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He cited municipalities such as Noveleta in Cavite as examples of LGUs managing their own collection despite limited territory. He said garbage disposal should instead be treated as a regional matter to capture economies of scale.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the Local Government Code needed to be revisited to clarify how garbage should be handled, who was accountable, and who had oversight.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He pointed out that the Constitution gives the President general supervision over local governments and challenged the agency's position that this could not support closer oversight.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He acknowledged the President's general-supervision authority but said that supervising 40,000 local government units at a minute level would not be effective. He maintained that structural reform of garbage collection would be more effective than relying on existing laws, which he described as weak or nearly useless in application.

topics.topic: PNP accountability, body cameras, and public-assembly operations
topics.summary: Jose Teves Jr. raised PNP oversight and anti-hazing accountability, while DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla reported that NAPOCOM had cleared a backlog of about 15,000 cases and had no remaining backlog. Renee Co questioned arrests during mobilizations, police firearms, and the reported more than 700,000 Safer Cities apprehensions. The secretary defended the arrests and initiative but acknowledged that the PNP had only 2,000 body-worn cameras for 320,000 personnel, with another 10 or 20,000 being procured, and said crime reductions ranged from about 30% to 60% depending on the category. The member also challenged the agency’s explanation of school violence and raised arbitrary barangay-level drug-watch listings; officials cited intelligence procedures, supply-and-demand reduction, and operational safeguards. The agency agreed to provide operation reports, incident logs, updated statistics, and a disciplinary report, with the latter committed for submission on Tuesday. The broader questions about firearms, arrests, and enforcement safeguards remained contested.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PNP arrests and public-assembly operations complied with human-rights and public-assembly rules, including restrictions on firearms and requirements for body-worn cameras. Members also sought the factual basis and safeguards for the Safer Cities Initiative, the agency’s approach to school violence and drug-watch listings, and the status of police-accountability cases and reports.
topics.agency_position: The DILG and its police-accountability officials maintained that arrests were based on vandalism or aggression, that firearms were not drawn or used against rally participants, and that the Safer Cities Initiative did not violate constitutional rights. The agency acknowledged obsolete and insufficient body-worn-camera equipment, defended its intelligence and drug-enforcement procedures, reported zero NAPOCOM backlog, and undertook to submit operation, incident, statistical, and disciplinary documents.
topics.outcome: The agency defended its arrest and enforcement practices but acknowledged deficient body-camera coverage and left the legality and proportionality concerns contested. It committed to investigate and submit operational, statistical, and disciplinary records, with the disciplinary report specifically set for Tuesday; the broader accountability questions were not fully resolved during the hearing.

positions.position: Supported stronger PNP supervision, discipline, and accountability, and sought enforcement and resolution of anti-hazing cases.

Questioned the legality and proportionality of mobilization arrests, police firearms, Safer Cities apprehensions, and drug-watch listings. She pressed for functional body cameras, documentary support, safeguards for children and student leaders, and a broader explanation of school violence.
Defended the agency’s operations while acknowledging equipment deficiencies and arguing that the Safer Cities Initiative reduced crime without violating constitutional rights.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: He cited the PNP budget and the amount for supervision, discipline, and accountability, raising the issue of PNP oversight.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He commended NAPOCOM’s performance, saying it had eliminated a backlog of 15,000 cases, including cases dating to 02/2001, and had reached a zero-backlog profile. He said the requested budget and the amount approved by DBM were different and asked that the vice chairman’s budget request be accommodated.

thread.speaker: Jose Teves Jr.
thread.said: He asked for the status of the hazing accident involving the death of a student in Dasmariñas, Cavite.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the hazing case was almost resolved, but the anti-hazing law needed to be strengthened. He said the PNP was vigilant within its own departments but had greater difficulty monitoring school-based and community-based organizations.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He proposed a community-based identification system to identify actors in particular communities and said the case had been solved.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She questioned the PNP’s arrests during a mobilization and asked how the police distinguished people who vandalized property from those who did not.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said the first arrests involved 50 persons allegedly vandalizing a government building with spray-paint cans. He said other participants became aggressive and attacked police, requiring arrests of those who acted aggressively, while maintaining that no human rights were violated.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said that in the “fog of war,” anyone showing aggression toward police or the operation could be considered hostile, but officers were instructed to exercise restraint and avoid seriously injuring anyone.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: Citing BP 880 and its provision on peaceful assembly, she asked why police, particularly civil-disturbance-management ground commanders, carried firearms during mobilizations when the law requires police not to carry firearms in that setting.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said carrying firearms “must have been a mistake” and would be investigated. He maintained that frontline responders did not carry guns, while support groups at the rear could augment the response during a commotion, and said no firearms were drawn or used against rally participants.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She said accounts received by the committee showed police presence within the mobilization area and argued that this created an atmosphere of fear.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said the additional police presence was likely intended to augment frontline police but again maintained that firearms were not drawn or used against participants.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She requested the civil-disturbance-management operation report, ground deployment plan, and official incident logs for the mobilization.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He agreed that the documents should be given to the committee and committed to provide them “by this afternoon.”

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She asked for the operational status of the PNP body-worn-camera system and how many functional cameras were available for public assemblies and police operations in 2025 and 2026, in compliance with Supreme Court AM number 2108.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said the PNP was deficient because its existing body-worn cameras were obsolete. He said a new set of AI-enabled cameras had been ordered in 2026 and was in the procurement and fitting-out process.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She sought confirmation that cameras had been procured for the operations already undertaken.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He clarified that procurement was still in process and that the existing equipment was not up to current industry standards. He said the PNP had only 2,000 units for 320,000 personnel and was ordering another 10 or 20,000 units during the year, with annual augmentation.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He explained that the new system would have a better lens and digital capacity, allowing AI interpretation, whereas the previous cameras had a one-megapixel specification and were obsolete. The new cameras would be AI-enabled and of sufficient quality.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She questioned the Safer Cities Initiative’s reported more than 700,000 apprehensions in Metro Manila and asked how those apprehensions and arrests could be reconciled with the decriminalization of loitering under RA 10158 and with constitutional and statutory rights, particularly those of the urban poor.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said the initiative did not violate constitutional rights. He explained that people drinking in the streets could be warned or arrested and that most people described as loiterers were under the influence of alcohol or other intoxicants; he said few were arrested merely for standing.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She requested updated statistics supporting the reported 700,000 apprehensions.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said the department would provide the statistics later. He asserted that focus crimes in the cities had declined by almost 30%, while rape had declined by 60%, violent crimes by 50%, and physical injuries by 30%, although the exact figures were not available to him at the hearing.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She asked whether body-worn cameras were used as part of the initiative’s implementation and police operations.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said body-worn-camera use was part of standard operating procedures but acknowledged that the PNP remained deficient in cameras and still needed to purchase additional units.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She asked how the department would ensure that police dealing with children at home or in school zones treated them appropriately and did not create a culture of fear, in the context of school shootings and arrests.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said he could not provide the full background of the school shooters in open session and would discuss it in executive session. He maintained that video games played a large part in the shooters’ conduct.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She said school violence resulted from compounded factors, including media, bullying, social conditions, and a broader culture of violence, rather than video games alone. She also raised continuing harassment of student leaders.

thread.speaker: DILG Secretary
thread.said: He said tokhang was no longer state policy and had not been for four years, and that harassment and red-tagging of student leaders were not state policy. He cited an instance in which police took no action when he was heckled by student leaders.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She questioned arbitrary drug-watch-listing reports at the barangay level, including reports from 2021, and asked whether a community-based, health-centered approach would address the drug-watch-list system.

thread.speaker: PNP/PDEA agency official
thread.said: The official said the anti-illegal-drug campaign used supply and demand reduction. Demand reduction included community campaigns, while supply reduction involved police operations based on information and intelligence gathering.

thread.speaker: PNP/PDEA agency official
thread.said: The official said target personalities were identified through prior arrests, interviews, and intelligence gathered over several years, explaining how the agency maintained its lists.

thread.speaker: DILG/PNP agency official
thread.said: The official said the agency followed procedures for verifying individuals and adjudicating cases, and cited Supreme Court rules, intelligence procedures, police-operation controls, and body-worn cameras as safeguards against weaknesses in operations.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She asked about systemic administrative sanctions against police personnel involved in botched operations and alleged or enacted arrests, and sought an update on disciplinary actions.

thread.speaker: NAPOCOM official
thread.said: The official said NAPOCOM had zero backlog and remained active and willing to address such cases.

thread.speaker: Renee Co
thread.said: She requested a disciplinary-action status report for 2025 and 2026, including summaries of dismissals, conviction records, and related outcomes.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair directed the agency to submit the requested report and pressed for a definite deadline.

thread.speaker: NAPOCOM official
thread.said: After initially saying it would be submitted as soon as possible, the official agreed to submit the report on Tuesday.

topics.topic: LGSF and local-project implementation safeguards
topics.summary: Rep. Miro Quimbo raised recurring building-permit delays that had stranded local projects, especially schools and health facilities, and DILG agreed to examine specific cases after receiving data. A member then asked DILG and the PNP to distinguish excavation from quarrying and clarify heavy-equipment impoundment; DILG said local governments generally lacked that authority, while the PNP said it enforced violations in coordination with the DENR and LGUs. A CSO representative questioned the rationale for retaining LGSF despite an estimated national tax allocation of about 1.32 to 1.4 billion trillion pesos, and DILG defended the roughly 58 billion fund as additional support for local basic services. DILG said DBM handled proposal vetting while DILG monitored implementation through technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. Members also sought safeguards against duplicate projects, weak participation, red-tagging, and ineffective implementation, while DILG and NAPOLCOM described existing monitoring and complaint mechanisms. DILG said the proposed SBDP allocation of about 9.74 billion actually reduced the per-barangay amount to 5,000,000 because coverage expanded to 1,904 barangays, leaving several requests for supporting evidence and public accountability information unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DILG would use its supervisory and monitoring powers to address delayed building permits, stranded local projects, and questionable local enforcement actions. It also examined the policy rationale, safeguards, monitoring responsibilities, and proposed funding levels for the Local Government Support Fund and related programs.
topics.agency_position: DILG maintained that compliant building-permit applications should not be delayed and undertook to examine specific cases. It said local governments identified and procured LGSF projects, DBM handled proposal vetting and validation, and DILG monitored implementation through deployed technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. DILG also defended LGSF and SBDP as additional resources for local basic services, while the PNP and NAPOLCOM described enforcement and red-tagging safeguards.
topics.outcome: DILG answered the committee's questions in general terms and undertook to examine the building-permit and local-enforcement cases after receiving supporting details. The LGSF and SBDP safeguards and allocations were explained, but questions about independent validation, public reporting, outcome evidence, and the adequacy of funding remained open.

positions.position: Delayed or overly technical building-permit requirements were stranding locally implemented projects and required DILG intervention and possible administrative action.
Local authorities needed clear guidance on the distinction between excavation and quarrying and on whether they could impound heavy equipment.

The committee needed clearer accountability for LGSF proposal validation, duplicate-project prevention, community participation, monitoring outputs, and the justification for proposed program allocations.
The continued existence and scale of LGSF required policy justification given the increased national tax allotment, along with safeguards against duplication and exclusion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo raised recurring delays in building permits for projects funded under programs in 2025 and 2026, saying additional requirements were sometimes imposed after compliance. He said the delays had stranded projects, particularly schools and health facilities, and asked what recourse was available.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said building-permit requirements were already set and that a permit should be issued when a project proponent faithfully complied with all requirements.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo replied that local officials sometimes applied fine nuances to requirements, such as location plans, in ways that went beyond what was reasonable. He said the matter required DILG attention through its supervisory powers over local governments.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The official undertook to look into the concern raised by Rep. Quimbo.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo said he would provide the available data and asked whether cases involving regular employees who refused building-permit applications could warrant disciplinary or administrative proceedings.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The official asked Rep. Quimbo to provide additional details so DILG could determine the proper course of action.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo said, “I will hold you to that,” referring to the DILG undertaking to examine the matter.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: A member asked DILG and the police to clarify the distinction between excavation and quarrying and whether a task force or provincial government could impound heavy equipment involved in local development activities. The member said a letter on the issue had been received by Secretary Vince Dizon and would also be furnished to the agencies.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member tested the distinction by asking whether canal work, reblocking, and clearing landslides constituted quarrying or excavation.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official classified canal work, reblocking, and landslide clearing generally as excavation, provided the activity was not illegal or prohibited by existing law.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member pressed for a yes-or-no answer on whether local governments were authorized to impound the equipment.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said the authority to impound was not vested in the local government unit.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member described a local situation involving a task force and police action on private land and a fish pond and asked for guidance on what should be done.

thread.speaker: PNP official
thread.said: The PNP official said police must enforce the law when heavy machinery is used in illegal excavation or quarrying activities in violation of special laws, DENR laws, or local ordinances.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether the police acted as deputized enforcers of the DENR.

thread.speaker: PNP official
thread.said: The PNP official agreed, explaining that enforcement was undertaken in coordination with the appropriate agency, including the DENR and the local government.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member was advised to provide an intelligence report or other details so the matter could be investigated. The member said copies would be furnished to DILG and the PNP and asked DILG to examine the issue through its supervisory powers over local governments.

thread.speaker: CSO representative
thread.said: The CSO representative asked why a separate LGSF should be retained when the Mandanas-Garcia ruling had increased the national tax allotment of local governments. The representative also asked what fiscal gaps LGSF addressed and how the government prevented duplication or substitution of regular LGU resources.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said the national tax allotment appeared large but had to be divided among all provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays and was insufficient for LGU priority projects and devolved functions. He said the LGSF provided additional resources for water and sanitation systems, farm-to-market roads, electrification, health centers, and other basic services.

thread.speaker: CSO representative
thread.said: The CSO representative asked what role DILG played in LGSF implementation, particularly whether it vetted and validated project proposals.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said LGSF was released directly to LGUs, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and checked implementation. He said DILG deployed engineers and project evaluation officers to provinces and regions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked whether validation and vetting of proposals were handled by the Department of Budget and Management.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog confirmed that LGUs submitted proposals through a DBM-created portal. Rep. Fuentebella noted that DBM, rather than DILG, handled the vetting and validation relevant to preventing duplicate projects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked what measurable outputs, disclosure requirements, accountability mechanisms, and CSO participation would accompany DILG's monitoring and evaluation allocation for LGSF projects.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog described a three-tier monitoring system: local project monitoring committees composed of LGU officials and CSOs, DILG's second-party monitoring, and third-party monitoring involving CSOs and nongovernmental organizations. He also cited the SubayBayan portal for required project status updates.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked about the relative allocations for LGSF, participatory budgeting, and the Support to Barangay Development Program, and how DILG would expand meaningful community and CSO participation.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said the Support to Barangay Development Program addressed basic-service gaps in barangays previously influenced by communist armed groups and used grassroots consultations to identify projects. He said the participatory budgeting fund supported water systems and evacuation centers in identified municipalities.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked what safeguards and grievance mechanisms protected CSOs, human-rights defenders, Indigenous Peoples, community leaders, and other stakeholders from red-tagging, retaliation, or exclusion in LGSF and SBDP implementation.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog referred the red-tagging question to the National Police Commission.

thread.speaker: National Police Commission official
thread.said: The official said a recently issued media-relations manual prohibited red-tagging and provided for sanctions. The official said the National Police Commission would accept and act on complaints.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked for the evidence supporting the proposed increase in SBDP funding, including beneficiary-selection criteria, allocations, accomplishment rates, audit findings, delays, complaints, outcome evidence, and publication of project-level data.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said the apparent SBDP increase actually reduced the allocation per barangay because more barangays were covered. He said DILG's existing monitoring, evaluation, portal, and CSO/NGO engagement mechanisms were intended to ensure faithful implementation.

topics.topic: NCMF Hajj medical expenses and priority programs
topics.summary: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula raised the adequacy of the NCMF's Hajj operations and medical budget for 2027. The NCMF said its medical allocation was only 600 16,000 pesos, or 95 pesos per projected pilgrim for 6,000 pilgrims, and sought an increase to 6,100,000. The agency also identified three priority programs: Madaris at 87,500,000, the Halal and Muslim community economic empowerment program at the unclear figure "89.04 94,000,000," and Hajj operation modernization at 6,100,000; it stated a total of 24,000,537. A committee member asked for the written request and said the request would be supported and advocated. Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula separately manifested full support for the NCMF budget, but the transcript did not establish final approval of any additional amount.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the NCMF's proposed 2027 budget adequately covered Hajj operations and medical needs for the projected pilgrims. It also asked which NCMF priority programs required additional consideration or funding.
topics.agency_position: The NCMF stated that the proposed medical allocation for Hajj operations was inadequate, providing only 95 pesos per projected pilgrim, and sought an increase. It asked the House to consider its three priority programs—Madaris, the Halal industry and Muslim community economic empowerment program, and Hajj operation modernization—if the full request could not be approved.
topics.outcome: The NCMF's request for additional Hajj medical funding and consideration of its priority programs was supported in principle. The agency was instructed to submit its written request, and a committee member undertook to advocate for it; approval of the requested amounts was not established.

positions.position: Supported increased funding for the NCMF, including its Hajj medical needs and priority programs, and expressed full support for the NCMF's 2027 budget.

topics.topic: Free higher education deficiency payments to SUCs
topics.summary: Members questioned CHED about unpaid free-higher-education deficiencies, SUC budget reductions, and whether continuing and incoming scholarship beneficiaries would be funded. CHED said 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing deficiency, while 667,000,000 remained associated with unpaid 2025 free higher education for 137,000 beneficiaries. The agency attributed future deficiencies partly to SUCs enrolling beyond capacity and to the unrealistic one-is-to-25 faculty-student assumption, and said it was developing a one-is-to-40 formula. Members also highlighted an 11,000,000,000 scholarship funding gap affecting roughly 1,000,000 students and a reported 29,200,000,000 deficit under UACTE alone. The chair required CHED to submit updated enrollment simulations, a prioritized funding request, and aligned beneficiary figures with DSWD before plenary. CHED committed to settle the existing deficiency by the third week of September, but the full 2027 funding requirement remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether free higher education deficiency payments to SUCs had been released, what deficiencies remained for 2025–2027, and whether proposed scholarship and SUC funding would cover continuing and incoming beneficiaries. Members also examined the enrollment-capacity and faculty-ratio assumptions behind the deficiency calculations and requested measures to prevent future shortfalls.
topics.agency_position: CHED said the principal source of free-higher-education deficiencies was the mismatch between SUC enrollment beyond absorptive capacity and the funding assumptions used by DBM, particularly the faculty-student ratio. CHED maintained that 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing deficiency, committed to process remaining requirements by the third week of September, and said it was developing a one-is-to-40 enrollment-capacity formula and coordinating with DBM, PASUC, SUCs, and DSWD.
topics.outcome: CHED stated that 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing SUC deficiency and committed to settle the remaining requirements by the third week of September. However, the broader 2027 scholarship and UACTE deficiencies, including the reported 29,200,000,000 UACTE deficit and possible beneficiary double-counting, remained subject to further CHED-DBM-DSWD review and committee budget action.

positions.position: Supported increased funding for free higher education, faculty, classrooms, and SUC capacity, and later committed to support an increase in CHED's budget.
Opposed SUC and PGH budget reductions and urged restoration of funding, especially for access and inclusive education.

Pressed CHED and the committee to resolve free-higher-education deficiencies, restore SUC funding, and protect student welfare and rights.
Supported increasing TDP funding and using TES or TDP to involve private institutions when SUCs were overcrowded.
Opposed the sharp reduction in tertiary scholarship funding and committed to support efforts to address the 11,000,000,000 gap affecting roughly 1,000,000 students.
Raised constitutional objections to legislative intervention in scholarship implementation and questioned the legal basis and accessibility of program criteria.
Sought to ensure that SUC deficiencies were fully settled, beneficiary figures were not double-counted, and future deficiencies were prevented through better CHED-DBM-SUC coordination.
