topics.topic: Higher-education safety, Safe Spaces compliance and mental health
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno raised reports of restrictions on speech and assembly, red-tagging, online harassment, and potentially harmful active-attack drills, and CHED committed to policy review, student dialogue, and mental-health and campus-safety measures. Minority member Sara Elago focused on Safe Spaces Law enforcement, routine inspection, and CODI functionality. CHED said it was surveying about 2,347 higher-education institutions, including 561 SUCs and campuses, and reported that 66% had functional CODIs for informal anti-sexual-harassment investigations. CHED cited 697,000,000 for scholarship and faculty development and 258,000,000 for monitoring and evaluation, including Safe Spaces monitoring, but promised to submit the precise allocation for Safe Spaces compliance monitoring. Jay Vergara received CHED's account of a student safety portal covering about 5.8 million students and identifying online threats, bullying, violence, and dormitory safety among reported concerns. The agency's commitments were recorded, but the full compliance picture and exact Safe Spaces funding remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED was monitoring and enforcing Safe Spaces compliance and whether its policies and programs adequately protected academic freedom, student dialogue, campus safety, and mental health. Members also asked whether CHED had sufficient monitoring, complaint, and intervention mechanisms for violence, online threats, and psychological risks.
topics.agency_position: CHED said it was actively reviewing higher-education policies, monitoring Safe Spaces compliance through regional offices and institutional programs, and responding to complaints through CODIs and board processes. It also said it was expanding mental-health, campus-safety, anti-terrorism, and student-dialogue initiatives, while acknowledging that compliance data and the exact Safe Spaces monitoring budget still had to be submitted.
topics.outcome: CHED stated that it was undertaking policy review, institutional monitoring, complaint handling, mental-health programming, and campus-safety initiatives. However, the exact Safe Spaces monitoring budget and complete institutional compliance data were not provided during the hearing and were left for submission.

positions.position: CHED should protect academic freedom, freedom of speech and assembly, and students affected by restrictive policies, red-tagging, online harassment, and psychologically harmful violence drills.

CHED should strengthen inspection and enforcement of the Safe Spaces Law, restore funding for Safe Spaces monitoring and related programs, and ensure functional CODIs in both public and private institutions.
CHED should address campus violence and digital or online threats through evidence-based safety policies and adequately funded campus-security measures.
Student-welfare guidelines should protect academic freedom, student organizations, publications, councils, and the exercise of rights within higher-education institutions.

CHED chair Shirley Agrupis added that the concerns would be included in regular consultations and said CHED would work to ensure that students' rights and freedoms inside higher-education institutions were respected.

topics.topic: Private higher-education regulation and tuition-fee sharing
topics.summary: Eli San Fernando questioned CHED's delayed labor-education rules and enforcement of the 70% tuition-fee-sharing requirement in private HEIs. CHED said labor education would be integrated into NSTP and other courses, and it undertook to investigate faculty and staff complaints, coordinate with DOLE, and revise the private-higher-education regulatory manual. Rep. Solomon Chungalao asked about open universities, diploma mills, student complaints, and a campus building; CHED said about 31 of 113 universities were authorized for limited open-university programs, that violations could lead to closure, and that it would receive his documents. Rep. Renee Co raised unresolved free-higher-education deficiencies and student-welfare protections, while CHED acknowledged continuing deficiencies and said it was moving toward a one-to-forty faculty-student ratio and ongoing guideline deployment. Rep. Cheeno Almario cited severe faculty shortages and requested higher TDP funding and possible private-institution partnerships, with the chair taking the budget manifestation into consideration. Rep. Antonio Tinio raised constitutional concerns over legislative intervention in scholarship implementation, and Rep. Jude Acidre urged stronger attention to private HEIs because more than half of college students were enrolled there.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED was enforcing labor-education and tuition-fee-sharing requirements in private higher-education institutions, regulating open universities and diploma mills, and protecting faculty, staff, and student rights. Members also asked how CHED was addressing free-higher-education deficiencies, overcrowding and faculty shortages, the role of private institutions, and regulatory gaps affecting local and private institutions.
topics.agency_position: CHED said it was strengthening regulation of private HEIs, open universities, diploma mills, tuition-fee compliance, and student welfare through guidelines, monitoring, consultations, and coordination with DOLE and DBM. It acknowledged unresolved deficiencies, uneven faculty-student ratios, and the difficulty of monitoring all institutions, while maintaining that violations could result in closure and that private institutions could participate in tuition-subsidy programs.
topics.outcome: CHED undertook to investigate the tuition-fee-sharing complaint, coordinate with DOLE, revise private-HEI regulations, receive documents on complaints, and continue student-welfare consultations. The open-university and enforcement questions received general answers, but the free-higher-education deficiencies, faculty shortages, private-sector partnership model, and constitutional concerns remained subject to further documentation, budget action, or policy work.

positions.position: CHED should directly enforce the 70% tuition-fee-sharing requirement and its memorandum-order obligations toward faculty and staff, rather than simply referring complaints to private-HEI management.
CHED should investigate suspected unauthorized open-university operations, diploma mills, student complaints, and questionable campus practices.
Free-higher-education deficiencies should be resolved, SUC budget cuts restored, and student-welfare guidelines should protect student organizations, publications, councils, and academic freedom.
The TDP budget should be increased, faculty shortages and overcrowding should be addressed, and private institutions should be considered as partners when public institutions lack capacity.

Legislative post-enactment intervention in executive scholarship implementation may be unconstitutional, and access criteria should be open to legal challenge where they are not sufficiently accessible.
CHED should give greater attention to private HEIs because more than half of college students were enrolled in private schools.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked about the delayed implementing rules and regulations for the labor education law, which required issuance within sixty days.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando described the rollout for academic year 2026–2027 as a twelve-hour labor-education component embedded in NSTP or general-education courses, with a plan to expand it into a stand-alone, credit-bearing subject.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said CHED had two implementation tracks with DOLE: curriculum integration and institutional implementation. She said degree programs would integrate the curriculum, including through NSTP.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked about the tuition-fee-increase policy under RA 6728 and the statutory 70% share for educational institutions.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said CHED had developed an equation intended to make the sharing arrangement inclusive and equitable across regions and that CHED had the relevant data.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando pressed CHED on the practical application in private HEIs, asking whether faculty and staff received the 70% share whenever tuition fees increased.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said CHED had met private-HEI heads regarding tuition-fee increases and had asked them to comply with the President's executive order and memorandum order holding increases. She said institutions had to meet criteria before receiving clearance.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked why faculty and staff complaints about the 70% share were being referred back to private-HEI management for appropriate action.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said private HEIs submitted a certification of compliance with Section 5 of RA 6728 as part of the documents required for final tuition-fee clearance. She said she did not know of any faculty complaint and pointed to CHED's strengthened online Itugon system.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando said a teachers' and staff alliance had communicated with CHED and that referral to management was occurring elsewhere in private HEIs. He argued that the matter was also within CHED's mandate under Sections 9.2, 9.3, and 9.4 of Memorandum Order No. 3, series of 2012.

thread.speaker: CHED Director Gorka Banilla
thread.said: Banilla said CHED was already discussing the concern with the teachers' and staff organization and had scheduled a meeting. He said CHED would help coordinate with DOLE because the matter also involved labor jurisdiction.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis thanked San Fernando for raising the memorandum-order provisions and said CHED would look into the matter immediately.

thread.speaker: Eli San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando said he expected CHED to act and would hold the agency accountable.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said CHED had formed technical working groups across SUCs to review its policies, including a comprehensive revision of the manual of regulations for private higher education. She said the final consultation was scheduled for September 17, after which CHED would incorporate private-HEI input and publish the revision.

thread.speaker: Rep. Solomon Chungalao
thread.said: Chungalao asked whether higher education had an open-university concept and whether Philippine universities were authorized to operate one.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said open universities were covered by CHED guidelines and allowed learners to study at a distance through modular curricula. Applications were evaluated partly on internet connectivity and e-learning systems.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said about 31 of 113 universities were accredited or authorized to operate an open-university system, limited to certain degree programs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Solomon Chungalao
thread.said: Chungalao asked whether a university in his area was authorized to operate an open university after reports that students had graduated without physically attending.

thread.speaker: Rep. Solomon Chungalao
thread.said: Chungalao said he wanted to file a complaint because unauthorized distance education could create a diploma mill. He asked what consequences would follow if an investigation confirmed that graduates had not attended physically and whether the board or officials would be liable.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis acknowledged that diploma mills were a real concern and said CHED was strengthening its regulatory function. She said records showed Ifugao had offered an unauthorized open university, but CHED had stopped it after issuing guidelines and was developing a monitoring scheme.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said that when violations were found, CHED ordered institutions to close and had already encountered many such cases.

thread.speaker: Rep. Solomon Chungalao
thread.said: Chungalao raised complaints by students against an executive director, including alleged improper collections and harassment, and asked what action CHED had taken.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis invited Chungalao to bring the complaints to CHED and promised that the agency would attend to them promptly and courageously.

thread.speaker: Rep. Solomon Chungalao
thread.said: Chungalao asked about a campus building allegedly named after a living person and whether the committee could intervene through the budget process.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said CHED would not tolerate the conduct Chungalao was revealing and asked him to visit the office with the supporting documents.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co asked for an update on unresolved free-higher-education deficiencies, including the amount released by DBM, the remaining deficiency, and whether the 2027 budget calculation would minimize the shortfall for SUCs.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The CHED official said the deficiency from 2022 to 2025 had not been solved. The official said CHED and DBM repeatedly validated the figures before finalizing the allotment.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official said the formula for releasing the past four years' free-higher-education deficiency had been covered by a joint CHED-DBM memorandum circular, but a new deficiency was developing for 2025 and 2026. CHED, PASUC, and DBM were agreeing to use a one-to-forty faculty-student ratio instead of one-to-twenty-five, which the official called unrealistic.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co requested documentation on the deficiency calculation and the revised ratio for submission to the committee during the budget season.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co asked about a DBM request that SUCs allocate at least 20% of MOOE and sought CHED's position.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co said budget cuts affecting SUCs should be restored in the budget cycle and reiterated concern over the 20% MOOE issue.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co asked for an update on the student-welfare guidelines for higher-education institutions, including whether the draft had reached implementation and finalization.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official said CMO No. 18, series of 2026, had been issued on 04/06/2026 after consultations and that consultation and deployment were ongoing.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Co
thread.said: Co urged CHED to continue dialogue with student organizations and to ensure that students retained their rights and freedoms, including academic freedom, inside higher-education institutions.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official said CHED had begun consultation with student leaders and would include the concerns raised during regular consultations.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said continuation of the unfunded TDP requirement involved 1,400,000,000 and warned that without continuing funding, the 2026 grant would become a one-time grant.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cheeno Almario
thread.said: Almario asked whether the memorandum circular was intended to safeguard continued enrollment under the General Appropriations Act and prevent the deprivation of 93,000 students.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cheeno Almario
thread.said: Almario proposed that the committee consider increasing the budget allocation for the TDP so learners could continue accessing quality education.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said Almario's manifestation would be taken into consideration.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said SUC faculty-student ratios varied from one-to-twenty-five and one-to-forty to one-to-eighty, one-to-seventy, and one-to-sixty, and said CHED could provide the data.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cheeno Almario
thread.said: Almario cited Davao Oriental State University's 17,000 students, 363 regular faculty, and 260 part-time faculty as an example of overcrowding and faculty shortages that could reduce education quality.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said CHED needed to increase plantilla faculty positions and institutional absorptive capacity through classroom infrastructure. Otherwise, institutions would need stricter admissions policies and enrollment limits consistent with absorptive capacity.

thread.speaker: Rep. Cheeno Almario
thread.said: Almario asked CHED to examine involving private institutions through TES or TDP when public institutions became overcrowded, so students could still receive quality education.

thread.speaker: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis
thread.said: Agrupis said private institutions could be partly subsidized for tuition through the relevant programs and referred to private-school participation guidelines. The response did not fully resolve how partnerships would be expanded to address overcrowding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio questioned whether CHED had authority to accommodate legislative direction concerning a scholarship program and invoked the Supreme Court ruling declaring post-enactment legislative intervention in executive program implementation unconstitutional.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio said the legal basis and eligibility criteria could be challenged by citizens and raised concerns that scholarship access was not sufficiently accessible.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said Tinio's manifestation was noted.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jude Acidre
thread.said: Acidre asked whether local universities and colleges qualified for or were covered by free higher education and whether institutional recognition was required.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The CHED official said there were 170 local universities and colleges, of which 116 had institutional recognition and 54 did not.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jude Acidre
thread.said: Acidre specifically asked whether institutions with institutional recognition were covered by free higher education.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official answered that they were covered, although the response was given with evident concern. The official described compliance with recognition requirements as part of CHED's developmental mandate.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official said local universities and colleges sometimes offered programs beyond their legal mandate, including master's and PhD programs overlapping with recognized SUCs. CHED was developing guidelines and policy reforms to control this proliferation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jude Acidre
thread.said: Acidre noted that more than half of college students were enrolled in private schools and urged CHED to undertake comparable interventions for private institutions.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The CHED official said the agency took the concern seriously.

topics.topic: HEDF portfolio management and travel-tax funding
topics.summary: CHED chairperson Shirley Agropis reported that HEDF had released about 7.8 billion to address free higher-education deficiencies, with Congress adding about 4 billion plus and bringing the cited total to about 12 billion. She also reported remittances of about 12.54 billion and said CHED had submitted about 11.3 billion, while describing the average HEDF release rate as 54%. Nassal asked which government financial institution was the HEDF portfolio manager under Republic Act 7722, and Agropis said the Bureau of the Treasury was involved while CHED had approached Land Bank and other institutions. Nassal challenged that arrangement as a violation of the law and demanded transfer to a qualified government financial institution or an amendatory law. The chair said the issue would be taken up with partner agencies. Brian Yamsoo An later raised the 40% travel-tax collection, and CHED said it did not object provided its HEDF utilization was presented, while warning that it lacked capacity to finance existing programs without another funding source.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) was being managed, whether CHED had appointed the government financial institution required by Section 11 of Republic Act 7722, and how much of requested HEDF funding was actually released. It also asked about the proposed 40% travel-tax collection and whether CHED could finance its existing higher-education programs without that funding window.
topics.agency_position: CHED said it had used and was disbursing HEDF resources for existing higher-education deficiencies and programs, but received only about 54% of its cumulative requests. It did not object to the proposed 40% travel-tax collection, provided HEDF uses were documented, and said another funding source was necessary because CHED lacked the capacity to finance its existing programs.
topics.outcome: CHED's position on the 40% travel-tax collection was recorded as non-objection, subject to showing HEDF utilization and identifying another funding window. The portfolio-manager issue remained contested: CHED identified the Bureau of the Treasury's involvement and discussions with Land Bank, while the member demanded compliance with Section 11 or an amendatory law; the chair referred the matter to CHED and partner agencies.

positions.position: Nassal argued that leaving HEDF under the Bureau of the Treasury instead of appointing a government financial institution as portfolio manager violated Section 11 of Republic Act 7722. He called for immediate transfer to a duly appointed government financial institution or passage of an amendatory law.
An raised the proposed 40% travel-tax collection as a potential source of higher-education funding.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: Agropis said CHED had shared 7,800,000,000 from HEDF savings to cover free higher-education deficiencies from 2022 through 2025. She said Congress later added 4,000,000,000 plus, bringing the total to 12,000,000,000, which CHED was disbursing.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: She said HEDF funding had remained at 799,000,000, although CHED had proposed an amount described as "2 mil billion" for 2027. The wording of the proposed amount was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: Agropis reported that total remittances from 2022 through May 2026 had reached 12,540,000,000, while CHED had submitted a total of 11,300,000,000. She then stated "54,900,000,000," but its meaning was unclear.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: She said CHED had projected HEDF utilization following the release of 7,800,000,000 and had defined program targets for the fund.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: Agropis said CHED and the Department of Tourism had signed a joint administrative circular for tourism-related projects, with 2,000,000,000 allocated to cover an existing project. She said 799,000,000 covered initiatives from prior years.

thread.speaker: Nassal, committee member
thread.said: Nassal cited Section 11 of Republic Act 7722 and asked which reputable government financial institution was presently serving as the HEDF portfolio manager.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: Agropis said CHED had proposed an executive order and that the Bureau of the Treasury was currently involved, but CHED had approached all possible government financial institutions. She identified Land Bank as the first institution approached.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: She said Land Bank had existing scholarship programs and was considering additional scholarship contributions or a funding window, including support for children of farmers, subject to guidelines.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: Agropis referred to an amount of about 6,000,000,000 in discussing the possible funding arrangement, although the specific basis of the amount was not clear from the transcript.

thread.speaker: Nassal, committee member
thread.said: Nassal asked about the proportion of HEDF requests that CHED obtained from the Department of Budget and Management.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: Agropis answered that the average release rate was about 54%, based on CHED's data from 2022 to 2027.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: She said accumulated HEDF requests from 2022 to 2027 totaled about 11,300,000,000, while actual releases were 6,200,000,000, or about 5,400,000,000 and 54% as spoken in the transcript. The relationship between the stated amounts was unclear.

thread.speaker: Shirley Agropis, CHED chairperson
thread.said: When asked about 2027, Agropis again answered that the release rate was about 54%.

thread.speaker: Nassal, committee member
thread.said: Nassal said the situation appeared to violate the law, emphasizing that Republic Act 7722 was not merely a suggestion. He argued that the Bureau of the Treasury should transfer HEDF management to a duly appointed government financial institution or that Congress should pass an amendatory law.

thread.speaker: Nassal, committee member
thread.said: Nassal maintained that if the law needed to be changed, it should be amended, but until then the existing requirement should be followed. He criticized the continued nonuse or lapse of scholarship funds.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair said the matter was well noted by CHED and would also be taken up with the concerned partner agencies.

thread.speaker: Brian Yamsoo An, committee member
thread.said: An raised the issue of the 40% travel-tax collection and sought CHED's position on the matter.

thread.speaker: CHED chairperson
thread.said: The CHED representative said the commission had not objected to the proposal, provided that CHED's HEDF utilization across internationalization, research and development, faculty development, and state universities and colleges was presented.

thread.speaker: CHED chairperson
thread.said: CHED said it did not impose a negative objection to the 40% travel-tax proposal, but stressed that another funding window was needed because CHED did not have the capacity to fund its existing programs.

topics.topic: Scholarship program administration and constitutional authority
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Poe examined CHED's LandBank partnership and sought assurance that the agency could manage a larger scholarship budget. CHED said the system expedited direct distribution, and reported that about 80% of the backlog had been addressed, including 722,000 students with bank accounts. Poe also questioned the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship, for which CHED described eligibility based on grades, household income, first-generation status, priority programs, and regional allocation; the program had 20,000 slots and more than 39,000 applicants, with support figures including 80,000, 90,000, and 45,000 as spoken. Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez then challenged the reduction from roughly 35.5 billion to roughly 17.1 billion, identifying an 11,000,000,000 gap and warning that about 1,000,000 students could be affected. He urged restoration and coordination of barangay scholarship funds with CHED. Rep. Antonio Tinio separately argued that legislative intervention in implementation could violate the PDAF ruling and executive authority, but the chair only noted the manifestation. CHED committed to provide regional distribution data and more accurate figures, leaving the funding and constitutional issues open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether CHED could efficiently administer an expanded scholarship budget, how the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship selected beneficiaries, and why tertiary scholarship funding was being reduced. Members also questioned whether legislative involvement in scholarship implementation raised constitutional concerns under the PDAF ruling.
topics.agency_position: CHED presented the LandBank arrangement as a reform that accelerated scholarship disbursement, reduced school control over funds, and enabled direct student banking. It said the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship used a formula combining grades, household income, first-generation status, and regional graduate counts, while the agency officials did not provide a substantive response to the constitutional objection or the requested explanation of the DBM reductions in the excerpt.
topics.outcome: The committee received CHED's explanation of the LandBank mechanism and scholarship-selection formula, but the proposed tertiary scholarship reduction remained contested. The constitutional objection to legislative intervention was noted without a substantive agency or committee resolution, while CHED undertook to submit supporting distribution and more accurate budget figures.

positions.position: Supported continuing the LandBank scholarship-disbursement reform and sought confidence that CHED could efficiently manage additional funds. He questioned the Barangay Pilipinas program's eligibility rules, distribution formula, and the reduction in CHED's budget.

Supported direct ATM-based scholarship payments and CHED's improved utilization, but opposed the reduction in tertiary scholarship funding and urged restoration or coordination of funds to protect roughly 1,000,000 students. He also questioned the implementation and screening of barangay-level scholarships.
Raised a constitutional objection to legislative intervention in scholarship implementation, citing the PDAF ruling and the executive branch's implementation authority.

Supported the CHED budget and urged increased funding, while expressing support for interventions addressing private higher-education institutions, where more than half of college students were enrolled.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He credited CHED's improvements and its partnership with LandBank, and asked the agency to explain the program to give the committee confidence that additional scholarship funds could be efficiently disbursed.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She said the CHED-LandBank program was intended to expedite scholarship-grant distribution and address delays caused by intervening policies, including problems involving unliquidated downloads. She described a process involving validation by regional and central offices before funds were downloaded, with balances maintained through LandBank.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He said scholarship subsidies should reach students directly through ATMs, rather than being controlled or deducted by schools. He welcomed the reform as providing justice to deserving students.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She reported that about 80% had been distributed, involving more than 700,000 students, and said the agency had a real-time digital system with LandBank. The transcript records a current count as “three thirty seven hundred twenty two thousand seven hundred fifty one students.”

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He clarified that 722,000 students had received bank accounts with zero maintaining balance and said the arrangement improved scholarship efficiency while promoting financial literacy and banking access.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He noted what he understood to be a 150% increase in the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship budget, after correcting an initial reference to 214%, and asked whether that was correct and how many students the program supported.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She said the program was proposed for the top five senior-high-school graduates who enrolled in one of the 10 priority programs identified by EDCOM and were accepted at a top-performing state or private university. The transcript records support of 80,000 for private students, 90,000 for government or state-university tuition, and an allowance of 45,000 per semester academic year.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She said that for 20,000 slots for 2026 graduates, CHED had already received more than 39,000 applicants.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He asked how applicants were selected and how the scholarships were distributed.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She said CHED used a formula based on grades, per-capita income, and whether the student was a first-generation college student. Slots were also distributed proportionately according to the number of senior-high-school graduates in each region.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He asked whether the program was genuinely merit-based and whether economic circumstances gave poorer students an advantage.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She answered that priority was given to households with income from zero to 2,000,000, together with grades. She therefore indicated that the program incorporated both merit and an income-priority criterion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He asked where the scholars were located and whether CHED had regional distribution data.

thread.speaker: CHED chair
thread.said: She said the digital formula made the scholars easier to locate and gave regional examples: Region 1 had 10,000 top-performing graduates and Region 2 had 5,000 under an equity ratio. She undertook to provide the committee a copy of the distribution.

thread.speaker: Rep. Brian Poe
thread.said: He asked which specific budget items had been reduced and whether DBM had made a critical mistake in removing any particular item.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The CHED presentation stated that the prior proposal covered 1,677,000 beneficiaries totaling 35,500,000,000, while the amount being provided was recorded as 17,098,803,000 covering 843 beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He confirmed that the proposed amount had fallen from 35,000,000,000 to 17,000,000,000 and challenged the reduction as a serious problem.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official confirmed the reduction and clarified that the figure covered 843,000 students.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He called the reduction a disaster for free higher education and expressed concern that nearly 1,000,000 students could be affected.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official said free higher education was 667,000,000 for the unpaid and that the displaced figure was 137,000 students.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official gave a combined tertiary education subsidy figure of 29,167,557,000 and said it covered one one million sixty four students.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He asked about the budget difference between 2026 and 2027 and the number of students affected.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official stated that the difference was 11,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He characterized the 11,000,000,000 gap as the amount needed to cover the affected students and linked it to roughly 1,000,000 scholarship beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: CHED official
thread.said: The official listed ongoing and new categories of beneficiaries, including 458,000 incoming tertiary education subsidy beneficiaries, 89,000 4Ps beneficiaries, 100 for continuing PNSL beneficiaries, 397,000 total enrollees, and 150,000 second-year enrollees. The transcript is garbled in parts of this enumeration.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He described the 11,000,000,000 reduction affecting almost 1,000,000 scholarship students as alarming and said he would support efforts to restore funding for deprived and deserving students.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He committed his support, together with the committee leadership and colleagues, to addressing the loss of scholarship funding.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He raised the President's proposed 200,000 per barangay captain for five scholarships of 20,000 and questioned the criteria and implementation. He suggested coordinating the funds with CHED so the agency could screen beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He estimated that the barangay scholarship arrangement could involve about 235,000 new scholars, with 20,000 each, and referred to 15,000 for pre-higher education and 20,000 in another scholarship category. The surrounding transcript is unclear.

thread.speaker: Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez
thread.said: He urged coordination among the Office of the President, CHED, and the committee so implementation would be synchronized.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He praised the CHED chair's data-driven approach and candor, then raised the concern that CHED had no authority to accommodate legislative intervention in program implementation.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair declared a suspension before Rep. Tinio continued his constitutional point.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He cited the Supreme Court ruling declaring the PDAF unconstitutional, including scholarship assistance, and argued that post-enactment intervention by legislators in program implementation was unconstitutional because implementation belonged to the executive.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He said the lack of a legal basis and the scholarship criteria could be challenged by any citizen, and asked the committee to consider the constitutional issue and concerns about access.

thread.speaker: Chair

topics.topic: CHED regional access, monitoring and administrative capacity
topics.summary: CHED Chairperson Shirley Agropis said the commission lacked sufficient personnel, regional-office support, monitoring resources, and digital infrastructure to oversee about 39,000 academic programs across 2,365 higher education institutions. She cited 258,252,500 for monitoring and evaluation, regional-office requirements of 35,600,000 for CAR, 16,640,000 for Caraga, and 12,860,000 for Region 2, as well as an unfunded 331,300,000 ISSP request. Ian Amatong asked for assurances that TES would be released within the semester, requested dormitory design and costing, and sought better access to consultations. CHED said it was targeting full direct delivery by the end of September, agreed to provide the dormitory documents, and accepted a consultation arrangement. Rep. Rommel T. Angara proposed a CHED annex or sub-office in Aurora because travel to Pampanga took about four to six hours; the chair accepted the proposal, committed to interim outreach there, and directed preparation of complete staff work. The issue therefore landed with agency commitments, while the funding and final institutional approval remained open.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish whether CHED had sufficient personnel, regional offices, monitoring resources, digital systems, and consultation capacity to oversee higher education programs nationwide. Members also asked whether CHED could improve access for geographically distant areas, including Aurora, and provide timely assistance and requested documents.
topics.agency_position: CHED said its regional and monitoring capacity was constrained by insufficient personnel, training, IT support, infrastructure, and funding. It maintained that digital systems, stronger monitoring and evaluation, direct payment arrangements, regional outreach, and additional offices or sub-offices were necessary to improve oversight and access.
topics.outcome: The agency's general capacity concerns were presented but the additional regional, monitoring, and digital-system funding remained part of CHED's broader budget request. Specific operational matters produced commitments on TES timeliness, dormitory documents, consultations, and staff work for an Aurora sub-office, but no final appropriation or approval was recorded.

positions.position: He pressed CHED for timely TES releases, requested the dormitory design and costing, and sought a reliable mechanism for consultations with members and districts.
He supported establishing a CHED annex or sub-office in Aurora because of the long travel time to the existing regional office.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARINGS OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (DMW)

topics.topic: OWA's additional 2,000,000,000 request and Emergency Repatriation Fund
topics.summary: Minority member Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether OWA's additional 2,000,000,000 request was the minimum needed for life-and-safety and crisis-response obligations. OWA cited emergency repatriation expenses and geopolitical uncertainty, while Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac expressly endorsed the full request and said utilization alone was not a safe basis for reducing the ERF. Nazal raised the need for contingency planning for nearly 200,000 Filipinos potentially affected by a Taiwan Strait conflict and asked for information on OFWs in China and Hong Kong; DMW said it lacked data on overstayers and secondary employment but had crisis manuals and interagency preparations. DMW reported extensive Action Fund assistance, including 44,445 financial-assistance beneficiaries and 606,921 total assistance and beneficiaries over the longer period reported. Majority member Johanne Monich Bautista supported an additional 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund and restoration of the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000. The chair later sought DBM clarification because the apparent NEP gap depended on how programs and net levels were presented, leaving the final funding decision open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether OWA's requested additional 2,000,000,000 was the irreducible minimum for statutory life-and-safety services, emergency repatriation, and other crisis-response needs. It also examined the adequacy of the Emergency Repatriation Fund (ERF), the basis for its proposed reduction, and whether contingency plans for Taiwan, China, and Hong Kong were costed and funded.
topics.agency_position: DMW and OWA endorsed the full additional 2,000,000,000 request and rejected reliance on historical utilization alone to set a life-and-safety contingency fund. They said at least 1,200,000,000 should be restored for the ERF, while crisis-response planning and additional resources would be coordinated across agencies as conditions developed.
topics.outcome: DMW and OWA secured an express agency-level endorsement of the additional 2,000,000,000 request, while members supported additional Action Fund resources and restoration of the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000. The precise funding level, the costed Taiwan evacuation plan, and the reconciliation of the NEP figures remained subject to further budget clarification and submissions.

positions.position: Supported restoring and increasing DMW and OWA funding, strongly objected to mechanically reducing the ERF based on utilization, and urged preparation for Middle East, Taiwan, China, and Hong Kong contingencies.
Supported an additional 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund and restoration of the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000.
Sought to reconcile the apparent NEP gap by comparing comparable 2026 and 2027 net budget levels before determining how the gap would be bridged.

actions.action: DMW Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac endorsed OWA's full additional 2,000,000,000 request and said DMW would stand by the request.
DMW said it could provide crisis manuals and transport modalities, with precise details potentially disclosed only in confidence for security reasons.
DMW, OWA, DBM, and the Office of the Executive Secretary undertook to submit corresponding budget proposals as a crisis developed.
Johanne Monich Bautista manifested support for an additional 1,000,000,000 for DMW's Action Fund.
Johanne Monich Bautista manifested support for restoring the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000.
The committee chair requested DBM clarification so that 2026 and 2027 net budget levels would be compared on a like-for-like basis.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He referred to OWA Administrator Patricia Yvonne Kaunan's 08/25/2026 letter seeking support for an additional 2,000,000,000. He said the total budget appeared to rise by only 1.48%, while maintenance and other operating expenses, capital outlay, and the ERF were reduced.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked whether OWA's request was already the irreducible minimum for statutory life-and-safety services and implementation-ready requirements, noting that OWA had proposed 12,800,000,000, only 4,300,000,000 was included in the NEP, and the gap was 8,533,000,000.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator gave a garbled response referring to crisis medical repatriation and the US-Iran conflict, stating 900,000,000 and that, at a minimum, 1.2 should be restored. The precise context of the figures was unclear.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the additional 2,000,000,000 request included close to 600,000,000 for emergency repatriation. The request reflected the Middle East crisis and other geopolitical conflicts, not only current utilization.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked how much OWA had spent before and after the crisis.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said that in 2024 and 2025, utilization of the 1,200,000,000 ERF was already at 60%, with the response mentioning a supplemental 700. The wording and the reference to the supplemental amount were partly unclear.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked what the ERF had particularly been spent on before the crisis.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator identified international airfare, hotels or temporary accommodation, medical escorts, medical repatriation, land transportation, domestic flights, accommodation in the Philippines, financial assistance, and medical assistance for repatriated workers.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He followed up on medical repatriation expenses.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator explained that medical repatriation could require a hospital or doctor, medical escort, or nurse, and that these costs were paid from the ERF.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the utilization figures being considered appeared to be based on 2025, but the conflict began on February 28 and remained ongoing. The ERF and Action Fund were described as standby funds for events outside DMW or OWA's control.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac whether DMW fully endorsed the entire 2,000,000,000 request and would defend it through final congressional action.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac answered yes, saying DMW and OWA stood by all their requests and were 'joined at the hip.' He expressly endorsed the request.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He objected to using utilization mechanically to reduce the ERF, saying war, mass displacement, and evacuation could not be predicted. He cited 81.92% utilization of the FY 2026 ERF as of July 31 and an OWA table showing PHP 1,600,000,000 in ERF expenses, including PHP 6 and 63,284,000 for war-related expenses and PHP 967,000,000 for regular repatriation.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked whether the 24% ERF reduction was based wholly or partly on past utilization, and whether DMW agreed that utilization was an unsafe basis for determining a life-and-safety contingency fund.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac said he subscribed to the principle that utilization was a difficult basis because it depended on the geopolitical situation. He said DMW had to keep resources ready for crises that could occur at any time.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac cited a 3,000,000,000 peso supplemental fund as a clear presidential instruction and said DMW's crisis-response level was 3,000,000,000. He said the items needed to reach the 2,000,000,000 DMW request had been justified in the agency's letter.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Responding on the Middle East conflict, Cacdac said that even with a ceasefire, the conflict could reignite at any time. He said the Philippines had to remain prepared to protect and assist Filipino workers in crisis.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: Nazal raised possible Taiwan Strait conflict affecting nearly 200,000 Filipinos and possible immigration enforcement affecting Filipinos in China and Hong Kong. He asked how many Filipinos in those jurisdictions had visa, overstay, or unauthorized secondary-work problems, what minimum ERF and Action Fund support was needed, and whether Taiwan evacuation plans were fully costed and funded.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac said DMW had figures for OFWs in China and Hong Kong but did not have figures identifying overstayers or workers with secondary jobs. He said no unusual distress calls had been received from Hong Kong, while migrant resource centers remained ready to assist.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac again identified the president's 3,000,000,000 support as the benchmark for crisis response. He said DMW could provide crisis manuals and transport modalities, although precise details might not be disclosed publicly for security and confidentiality reasons.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac said Taiwan preparations were an interagency effort, that DMW had been meeting with other agencies under presidential instruction, and that the government was prepared to respond swiftly. He said precise actions could be disclosed in confidence.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac said DMW, OWA, DBM, and the Office of the Executive Secretary stood ready to submit corresponding budget proposals as a crisis developed, with resources depending on the crisis's stages and gravity.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: Nazal urged the committee and the House to support the DMW budget, citing the contribution of overseas workers to GDP.

thread.speaker: Johanne Monich Bautista, majority member
thread.said: Bautista asked DMW to place on record the Action Fund assistance and beneficiaries for 2026, and to provide information on services to Filipino OFWs, including those affected by the Middle East crisis.

thread.speaker: Hans Leo Cacdac, DMW Secretary
thread.said: Cacdac described the Action Fund as providing legal, medical, and financial assistance. He referred to 14,000 OFWs assisted in legal cases and around 5,000 medical cases, then referred the committee to Undersecretary Felicitas Bay for detailed budget data.

thread.speaker: Felicitas Bay, DMW Undersecretary
thread.said: Bay reported Action Fund assistance from January to July 2026: 44,445 OFWs receiving financial assistance, 11.73 for medical assistance, 2,610 for legal assistance, 7,329 for repatriation, and 9,891 for welfare cases. The unit or context for 11.73 was unclear.

thread.speaker: Felicitas Bay, DMW Undersecretary
thread.said: Bay said total Action Fund services and assistance for January to July 2026 covered one hundred and forty five four forty eight beneficiaries, as spoken. She also reported 606,921 total assistance and beneficiaries from July 2023 through July 2026.

thread.speaker: Felicitas Bay, DMW Undersecretary
thread.said: Bay said DMW had 32 legal retainers in various jurisdictions, in addition to in-house counsels at migrant workers' offices.

thread.speaker: DMW agency official
thread.said: The official said DMW had special medical arrangements in Abu Dhabi, Jordan, and Qatar, and a medical retainer in Dubai. The Action Fund covered documented and undocumented OFWs without discrimination.

thread.speaker: Johanne Monich Bautista, majority member
thread.said: Bautista asked about the current Action Fund level and whether the agency could justify an additional 1,000,000,000 based on the rate of emergency response.

thread.speaker: DMW agency official
thread.said: The official said the NEP request was 2,000,000,000, with an additional 1,000,000,000 needed for welfare, financial, medical, repatriation, and legal assistance. The official said this could correspond to the president's additional 3,000,000,000 fund and would cover land-based and seafaring workers.

thread.speaker: Johanne Monich Bautista, majority member
thread.said: Bautista manifested support for DMW's requested increase of 1,000,000,000, saying the Action Fund was continually active and needed additional resources. She then asked OWA to explain an acceptable ERF funding level.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the ERF had served 139,688 OFW clients as of July 31 and was forecast to serve around 240 to 250,000 clients. The administrator thanked the president, Congress, and DBM for an additional 700,000,000 supplemental amount.

thread.speaker: OWA administrator
thread.said: The administrator stated that the ERF should be restored to at least the 1,200,000,000 minimum. The response also referred to an additional 575,000,000 to the 900 plus million level and a figure little below 1,500,000,000, but the precise calculation was unclear.

thread.speaker: Johanne Monich Bautista, majority member
thread.said: Bautista manifested strong support for returning the ERF to at least the minimum 1,200,000,000 level. She then began asking about reintegration-program funding.

thread.speaker: House Appropriations Committee chair
thread.said: After the break, the chair said the apparent gap should first be aligned by comparing 2026 and 2027 net levels and asked DBM to explain how the budget was presented.

thread.speaker: Benjileth Zuniga, DBM director
thread.said: Zuniga said Action Fund, the hospital, migrant workers' offices, and other programs were grouped under one PAP. She stated that the 2026 amount was 4,000,000,000 and the 2027 net level was 4,600,000,000, although the response also contained a contradictory reference to a decrease.

thread.speaker: Benjileth Zuniga, DBM director
thread.said: Zuniga said OWA's ERP under welfare services was 2.3 in 2026 and 3.3 in 2027, again followed by a contradictory reference to a decrease. The figures' units were not stated.

topics.topic: Restoration of 2,000,000,000 in DMW funding
topics.summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez questioned the reduction of DMW's proposed budget and asked for a documented restoration request. Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said DMW was seeking about 2 billion, including about 1 billion for the Action Fund, 60 million for Servicio caravans, 60 million for international labor affairs, 180 million for general administration, and amounts for NMP, the OFW Hospital, migrant protection, and migrant workers' offices. OWWA separately defended an additional 2 billion for MOOE, operations, emergency repatriation, capital outlay, facilities, upskilling, and scholarships. Rodriguez moved to approve both increases, but the chair deferred action because the proceeding was only a budget briefing. Rep. Niko Raul Daza also supported the increases and established that NMP's free maritime training could continue under the proposed budget, while NMP sought 92 million for additional facilities and information systems. The issue therefore remained subject to later committee consideration, with document submissions and facility assessments still expected.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DMW's proposed budget had been reduced, whether DMW and OWWA needed additional funding, and how the requested amounts would be itemized and justified. Members also examined whether the proposed funding would sustain expanded OFW services, including the Action Fund, free maritime training, facilities, and anti-illegal-recruitment programs.
topics.agency_position: DMW said it accepted the NEP as part of the government's fiscal framework but requested a reasonable restoration of 2,000,000,000 to sustain urgent OFW services and programs. OWWA likewise defended an additional 2,000,000,000 for MOOE, operations, emergency repatriation, capital outlay, facilities, upskilling, and scholarships; NMP said its existing personnel and operating budgets could sustain free training but sought 92,000,000 for additional facilities and information systems.
topics.outcome: DMW and OWWA presented and defended separate additional requests of 2,000,000,000 each, and Rep. Rodriguez moved for their approval. The chair did not approve the increases during the briefing, instead deferring the ruling; DMW was asked to submit its itemized request and OWWA committed to present facility assessments.

positions.position: Supported restoring 2,000,000,000 to DMW and providing OWWA an additional 2,000,000,000. He argued that the reductions were excessive and requested itemized submissions to support congressional advocacy.
Supported increased DMW and OWWA funding and specifically supported NMP's request for facilities funding to sustain free maritime training.
Pressed DMW on implementation of the US500 domestic-worker wage, Action Fund disbursement, emergency repatriation, and the need for adequate financial and operational resources.
Supported a 2,000,000,000 restoration for DMW while stating that the agency would cooperate with the NEP and the national government's fiscal framework.
Supported an additional 2,000,000,000 for OWWA to fund operations, repatriation, facilities, global centers, upskilling, and the congressional migrant workers scholarship program.

actions.action: DMW to submit the itemized 2,000,000,000 restoration request to the committee.
OWWA administrator to present the DPWH facility assessments to the committee.
Rep. Rodriguez moved for approval of 2,000,000,000 increases for both DMW and OWWA.
The chair deferred consideration of the motion to the proper time because the hearing was a budget briefing.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac to confirm DMW's proposed 2027 budget and the amount ultimately reflected in the NEP, emphasizing that the agency's budget had been substantially reduced.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He stated that DMW had proposed a total of 24.7992 and that the agency was working within the NEP and the government's limited fiscal space.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He cited the amount given to DMW as 7.26 and described the reduction from the agency's proposal as a major slash, arguing that DMW served overseas workers who were national heroes.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked what DMW was requesting from Congress and whether the document he had received was the agency's consolidated request for additional funding.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He confirmed that DMW had proposed a 24,000,000,000 budget and said it was requesting at least 2,000,000,000 to restore part of the 17,000,000,000 balance. He added that DMW had committed to comply with the NEP while seeking the restoration.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He characterized the request as a reasonable motion for reconsideration and stated that DMW was seeking 2,000,000,000 from its side. He said OWWA was likewise responding with 2,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He pushed back against simply accepting the NEP and requested that DMW itemize the 2,000,000,000 request for inclusion in the official record.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He itemized 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund, increasing it from 2 b to 3 b to match the President's 3,000,000,000 supplemental benchmark.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He requested 60,000,000 for Servicio caravans, citing 25 caravans conducted around the world with 18 other government agencies.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He requested another 60,000,000 for DMW's chairship of the Abu Dhabi Dialogue and promotion of international labor affairs, involving an 18 member state dialogue.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He identified 180,000,000 for general administration and support services, including renovation and reconstruction of portions of the former POEA building and improved facilities for personnel serving OFWs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked whether DMW had considered constructing a new building, potentially through a multiyear arrangement similar to other agencies using GSIS facilities, rather than renovating the old building.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He said the President had allowed DMW to construct its main office on Agham Road and that a DPWH budget of 500,000,000 covered construction.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He referred to another 500,000,000 for a second phase of the planned 10-story building, while explaining that DMW intended to retain the former POEA structure as a regional NCR office.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He listed additional DMW requests of 700,000,000 for the National Maritime Polytechnic, 7,500,000 for the anti-illegal-recruitment campaign, 200,000,000 for the OFW Hospital, and 100,000,000 to establish additional migrant workers' offices.

thread.speaker: Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac
thread.said: He stated that the itemized DMW requests rounded up to 2,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He requested submission of the itemized 2,000,000,000 request, saying the document was not before the committee and would be needed to support a letter to the Speaker and the chair.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: The OWWA administrator presented a separate request for additional 2,000,000,000, beginning with MOOE and personnel-related requirements, vehicles, and services for OFWs and repatriation.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He identified 322,006,000 for MOOE-related requirements and 1,180,000,000 for MOOE operations, including emergency repatriation and OFW-related services.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He identified 575,000,000 for the emergency repatriation fund and discussed OFW lounges and seafarer welfare centers under the Magna Carta for seafarers.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He requested 475,000,000 for the Step Up upskilling program for OFWs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked when committee members could visit OWWA's global centers abroad. The administrator answered, "As soon as possible," and Rodriguez said he would request financing for such visits.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He said DPWH had conducted two assessments of OWWA facilities and that the results would be presented to the committee. The facilities were reportedly only at 10% of the minimum structural-integrity standard for seismic risk.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked whether the facilities request covered construction or renovation, and raised construction of regional offices, particularly in Region 5.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He answered that the request covered renovation, construction of regional offices, an extension of the training center and facilities for Region 2, a seafarer welfare center, and a new office.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He recalled that the congressional migrant workers scholarship program had previously received 150,000,000 from PCSO and 50,000,000 from the CDF, and sought restoration of funding for the program.

thread.speaker: OWWA administrator
thread.said: He summarized the OWWA request as 2,000,000,000: 322,000,000 for MOOE, 1,180,000,000 for MOOE operations, 447,990,000 for capital outlay, and an additional 50,000,000 for the congressional migrant workers scholarship program.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Before moving on the increases, he raised a constituent's case involving nonissuance of residence permits in Saudi Arabia and asked DMW to explain the problem.

thread.speaker: DMW official
thread.said: The official explained that every OFW in Saudi Arabia is required to have a residence permit, but legal problems such as overstaying or perceived violations can affect issuance. DMW addressed these cases through Action Fund legal assistance, retained lawyers, in-house lawyers, and payment of immigration-related penalties where applicable.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He moved for approval of DMW and OWWA increases of 2,000,000,000 each, stating that Congress should support agencies serving overseas workers.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair acknowledged the motion but clarified that the proceeding was only a budget briefing and that the ruling on the proposed increases would be considered at the proper time.

thread.speaker: Rep. Nico Raul Daza
thread.said: He asked whether the National Maritime Polytechnic had begun offering free maritime training courses, noting that NMP was the sole publicly run maritime training center.

thread.speaker: NMP executive director Vic Del Rosario
thread.said: He confirmed that free training began on August 3 under memorandum order 360. NMP had 55 regular training courses, including 23 mandatory STCW courses.

thread.speaker: Rep. Nico Raul Daza
thread.said: He asked how the free courses were funded and whether they were subsidized by the government.

thread.speaker: NMP executive director Vic Del Rosario
thread.said: He answered that NMP was fully subsidized by the national government.

thread.speaker: Rep. Nico Raul Daza
thread.said: He cited a 210,000,000 difference, equivalent to a 52% reduction, between the 2026 GAA and the 2027 NEP and asked whether the free maritime courses were sustainable under the reduced budget.

thread.speaker: NMP executive director Vic Del Rosario
thread.said: He explained that the reduction was primarily in capital outlay because NMP had received 271,000,000 for an infrastructure project that year. He said personnel services and MOOE remained at a level sufficient to continue free training.

thread.speaker: NMP executive director Vic Del Rosario
thread.said: He said NMP expected to train about 28,000 seafarers during the year, including 12,000 Filipino seafarers for free from August to December, and expected to serve about 30,000 Filipino seafarers in 2027, an increase of at least 25%.

thread.speaker: Rep. Nico Raul Daza
thread.said: He asked whether NMP's facilities in Tacloban were sufficient to absorb the expected surge in applications.

thread.speaker: NMP executive director Vic Del Rosario
thread.said: He said DMW had included an additional NMP request of 92,000,000 in its motion for reconsideration. This included 67,000,000 for a proposed 125,000,000 training building, which would provide 15 additional training rooms, and 16,000,000 for the information systems plan.

thread.speaker: Rep. Nico Raul Daza
thread.said: He asked whether the 92,000,000 request was related to NMP's unfunded mandate to establish satellite campuses in Davao and Cavite under a 1978 presidential decree.

thread.speaker: NMP executive director Vic Del Rosario
thread.said: He clarified that the 92,000,000 request was for the additional training building in Tacloban. The proposed Cavite and Davao regional training centers were separate and remained in the feasibility-study and pre-implementation stage, with budgetary requirements potentially proposed for fiscal year 2028.

thread.speaker: Rep. Nico Raul Daza
thread.said: He joined other members in supporting an increased DMW budget and restated that the combined request was 4 b, consisting of 2 b for DMW and 2 b for OWWA, including the Action Fund, Servicio Caravan, international labor affairs, GASS, NMP, migrant protection, OFW Hospital, and migrant workers' offices.

topics.topic: Action Fund disbursement, assistance, and crisis-response funding
topics.summary: Members questioned how the Action Fund had been used for financial, legal, medical, welfare, and repatriation assistance, particularly during the Middle East crisis. DMW reported 80,000 financial-assistance cases, 14,000 legal cases, around 5,000 medical cases, and January-to-July 2026 assistance figures including 44,445 financial beneficiaries, 2,610 legal beneficiaries, 7,329 repatriation beneficiaries, and 9,891 welfare-case beneficiaries. The agency cited general rates of 50,000 for distressed cases, seventy five thousand for medical situations, and one hundred thousand for an OFW, with quick-action assistance ranging from 5,000 to 30,000 and a 30,000 pesos rate for certain trafficking and scam-hub victims. It said the Action Fund covered documented and undocumented OFWs, had no ceiling for certain hospital bills, and could assist in medical disputes and abused dependents. DMW undertook to review and amend the disbursement guidelines, while Johanne Monich Bautista manifested support for an additional 1,000,000,000 for the fund. The funding request and some garbled utilization figures were not finally resolved in the excerpt.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Action Fund was being disbursed, what standards governed legal, medical, financial, and repatriation assistance, and whether its funding was sufficient for ordinary cases and geopolitical crises. Members also asked whether the fund covered medical disputes and abused dependents, and requested utilization and beneficiary records.
topics.agency_position: The DMW said the Action Fund covered legal, medical, financial, welfare, airport, and repatriation assistance for both documented and undocumented OFWs, including abused dependents. It said current resources could cover pending claims and medical-assistance needs, but acknowledged that disbursement rates were under review and requested additional funding for continuing geopolitical and welfare demands.
topics.outcome: The committee received the agency's utilization figures, disbursement rates, coverage assurances, and crisis-response explanation. The agency committed to revise the disbursement guidelines and pursue broader support systems, while the requested additional funding remained a committee-supported request rather than a final appropriation.

positions.position: He supported ensuring that DMW and OWA had enough resources for crisis response and routine OFW protection, while questioning whether the Action Fund and emergency funds were sufficient.
She pressed for timely Action Fund releases, clear disbursement standards, and adequate emergency-repatriation resources during geopolitical crises.
She supported an additional 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund and sought a record of its 2026 assistance and beneficiaries.
He sought safeguards and sufficient assistance for medically repatriated OFWs confronting conflicting medical assessments.
She sought confirmation that abused OFW dependents were covered and supported broader aftercare and mental-health interventions for children left behind.
