topics.topic: Pedestrian, bicycle, sidewalk, and PWD infrastructure
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Co pressed DPWH to prioritize pedestrians and cyclists, separate pedestrian projects from general rehabilitation, and provide wider sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and improved PWD facilities. DPWH cited a pedestrian-walkway expansion cost of about 6 billion, an original EDSA project cost of about 17 billion, EDSA pedestrian widths ranging from a minimum of 2.8 meters to as much as five meters, and a minimum bike-lane width of 1.5 meters. Co also cited a total DPWH budget of roughly 644 billion and a 510 million allocation for PWD, elderly, senior, and gender-responsive facilities, while the secretary said the PWD budget would increase three times from 170 million. Rep. Timothy Titan then asked for stronger anti-overloading enforcement, additional weighing facilities, multiyear bridge funding, and two more pedestrian overpasses along the Maharlika Highway. Secretary Vince Dizon committed to doing his best to enforce anti-overloading rules and suggested multiyear bridge appropriations from 2027 onward, but no definitive action on the overpass request was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's FY2027 program adequately funded pedestrianization, protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and facilities for persons with disabilities, and whether the agency would address unsafe bridges, overloaded trucks, and requested pedestrian overpasses. Members also pressed DPWH on applicable standards, enforcement, and multiyear infrastructure planning.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said pedestrian widths and bike-lane standards were being considered, but pedestrian facilities remained part of broader rehabilitation projects and were constrained by available space. The agency also supported stronger anti-overloading enforcement, indicated that multiyear bridge appropriations could be pursued from 2027 onward, and did not record a clear disposition on the requested pedestrian overpasses.
topics.outcome: DPWH acknowledged the need for pedestrian, bicycle, and PWD facilities and indicated that the PWD allocation would increase, but pedestrian projects were still embedded in broader rehabilitation work. The secretary committed to anti-overloading enforcement and discussed multiyear bridge funding, while the pedestrian-overpass request remained without a recorded agency disposition.

positions.position: Pedestrians, cyclists, PWDs, and commuters should receive priority over a car-centric road approach, with separately identified and adequately funded pedestrianization, protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and accessible facilities.
DPWH should enforce anti-overloading rules more strictly, expand weighing facilities, consider multiyear bridge funding, and construct pedestrian overpasses at identified high-risk locations.
DPWH would seek to enforce anti-overloading regulations and pursue multiyear bridge appropriations, while the transcript does not establish a final position on the requested overpasses.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted, convergence, tourism-road, and special infrastructure projects
topics.summary: Rep. Chel Diokno and another congresswoman pressed DPWH on convergence-program reforms, feasibility-study funding, and responsibility for tourism roads. DPWH said sector departments would identify and prioritize their own projects, while DPWH would participate in joint technical validation and implementation; it also said projects costing 1,000,000,000 and above required a feasibility study. The agency cited 130,000,000 in counterpart funding and 350,000,000 for the Southern Gate to Surigao feasibility study, while Rep. Tan referred to a total DPWH amount of 200 plus billion pesos. Rep. Tan also raised approval documents, foreign-assisted projects, project clustering, and figures that were partly garbled in the transcript. A Pampanga member separately urged progress on the Korea-assisted flood-control project's second part, while DPWH described dredging as a critical and regular maintenance activity. topics.topic: Flood mitigation, drainage, and river-basin master-plan alignment
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented flood mitigation as a 2027 priority and said DPWH would shift toward basin-wide flood management, using major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans. He cited 83.84 billion in locally funded 2027 flood-mitigation projects and described ongoing dredging and desilting needs after more than twelve years without dredging major rivers. Representative Tobit Janko pressed for full publication of projects and allocations by legislative district, while Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula requested complete master-plan data and tables showing whether 2025–2027 projects aligned with those plans. DPWH's flood-mitigation director said the agency was updating plans for all 18 major river basins with catchment areas of 1,400 square kilometer and up, with climate-change updating every three years. Bivensio Dizon undertook to provide the requested alignment information and said a dredging and desilting plan was being prepared. A majority member also identified nationwide lump-sum items of 369,000,000 for dredging and waterway cleaning and 500,000,000 for drainage and flood-mitigation repairs, which DPWH said would be implemented based on need.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's flood-mitigation, drainage, dredging, and desilting projects were guided by current river-basin and local drainage master plans. It also sought the plans' status, the projects aligned with them, and how nationwide flood-mitigation lump-sum items would be allocated.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said flood mitigation should be guided by major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans, with projects coordinated across national, regional, district, and local levels. The department said it was updating plans for all 18 major river basins, incorporating climate-change considerations, and allocating dredging, drainage, and other flood-mitigation works based on need, while relying in some cases on augmentation and savings.
topics.outcome: DPWH answered the committee's questions in principle and undertook to submit master-plan data, project-alignment tables, district-level project information, and a dredging and desilting plan. The record did not show that the requested alignment tables or plan had been submitted during the hearing.

positions.position: Supported full transparency for flood-control and other DPWH projects, including publication by legislative district and line item, and questioned fragmented or unclear project phasing.

Sought complete and current master-plan data and project-by-project alignment tables to determine whether DPWH's proposed budget followed applicable regional, district, national, and river-basin plans.

Questioned how nationwide dredging, waterway-cleaning, drainage-repair, and flood-mitigation lump-sum appropriations would be implemented and expressed support for addressing the country's flooding problem.

Advocated basin-wide, coordinated flood mitigation; updating plans for climate change; completing unfinished projects; and using need-based, transparent implementation rather than disconnected projects.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Bivensio Dizon presented the locally funded flood-mitigation program for 2027 at 83.84 billion, alongside 117,000,000,000 for ongoing foreign-assisted flood-mitigation projects and foreign-assisted projects worth 19,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He said DPWH was reforming its approach by using “flood mitigation” or “flood management” rather than “flood control,” because the latter could suggest that flooding could be completely controlled.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He identified major river-basin master plans and LGU drainage master plans as pillars of the flood-mitigation reforms. He also said the department needed congressional support for project studies, feasibility studies, and master planning.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He said DPWH would focus on closing gaps and completing unfinished flood-mitigation projects nationwide, with savings potentially reprioritized for immediate needs, particularly floodgates.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He said the department's approach would include integrated water-resource management, detention or retarding basins, dams, and coordination with regional development councils, provincial governments, and local governments. He also cited geographic deal-tagging.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He gave examples of the Quezon City drainage master plan and a proposed drainage master plan around G. Araneta, saying coordinated works had reduced flood heights and the speed of flooding in Tatalon.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: For Cebu, he said DPWH was aligning its flood-mitigation master plans with the Metro Cebu integrated flood and drainage system master plan, including consideration of dams and upstream conditions.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He cited the Bicol River Basin, Cagayan Valley, and Central Mindanao River Basin master plans, saying proposed projects should take current master plans into account. He also referred to ongoing foreign-assisted flood-mitigation master plans and related projects.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He returned to flood mitigation and described immediate repair and rehabilitation efforts, including rebuilding the seawall in Albay and other works funded through augmentation and savings.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He said dredging and desilting rivers were critical to flood mitigation and management, but that DPWH had not dredged major rivers for more than twelve years. He said the department had been forced to use augmentation and savings.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He cited the Bicol basin and the GenSan riverbed as examples of areas requiring dredging and desilting after waterways had accumulated silt over many years.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: He said early dredging and desilting efforts had produced success stories and that the department needed to do more to improve river conditions and reduce floodwaters.

thread.speaker: Representative Tobit Janko

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon

thread.speaker: Director Fano Pozas

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon

topics.topic: DPWH FY2027 budget and major program allocations
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented the proposed DPWH FY 2027 budget at 643,950,000,000, roughly about 20% higher than the prior budget. He identified roughly 200 billion for national roads and bridges and roughly about 118 billion for foreign-assisted projects. Flood mitigation figures included eighty three point eighty four billion for locally funded projects, 117 billion for foreign-assisted ongoing projects, and 19 billion for other foreign-assisted projects. The basic infrastructure components included about 105 billion for access roads and bridges, about 41 billion for multipurpose buildings, and smaller allocations for coastal roads and local ports. He also cited allocations for PWD and elderly infrastructure, disaster response, water supply, right-of-way, and general administration. A member requested presentation copies, and Dizon said detailed information would be provided through the committee materials and the National Expenditure Program.
topics.question: What was DPWH's proposed FY 2027 budget, and how was it allocated among national roads and bridges, foreign-assisted projects, flood mitigation, basic infrastructure, and support operations? The committee also sought access to the presentation materials so members could properly examine the proposed allocations.

The agency stated that detailed budget information was available to the committee and would be distributed through the committee staff.

topics.topic: Project rationalization and DPWH absorptive capacity
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon said DPWH had reduced project numbers by eliminating duplicate and overlapping projects, removing projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program, and focusing on larger projects that implementing offices could absorb. He said DPWH had previously reached about 25,000 projects, compared with a typical average of 20,000, and that some offices had carried two to four times their ideal workload. The agency also reported that its 2026 capital outlay involved about 460 billion, with 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded as of 08/23/2026, and targeted 80% awards by the end of September. Representative Mike Tan asked whether DPWH had conservatively estimated implementing-office capacity and requested rough capacity figures. Yusick Ador answered that the ideal was seven projects per PE and requested congressional support for additional engineers. Tan also sought support for ongoing convergence projects, but Dizon deferred the matter to Congress while citing executive policies.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether DPWH had rationalized its project portfolio to match the capacity of its implementing offices and whether the 2027 budget should prioritize projects that could realistically be delivered. It also examined the effect of delayed releases, early procurement, ongoing-project funding, and convergence-program reforms on DPWH’s implementation capacity.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said it was rationalizing projects to eliminate duplication, reduce small-ticket projects, focus on larger priorities, and bring project volume closer to the capacity of district and regional implementing offices. It acknowledged implementation constraints from late release of the 2026 capital outlay, sought additional engineers, committed to help identify priority and unfinished projects, and deferred the treatment and funding of ongoing convergence projects to Congress while complying with executive policies.
topics.outcome: The committee received DPWH’s explanation of project rationalization and the stated implementing-office capacity benchmark, including seven projects per PE and the district-office example. The question of whether ongoing convergence projects would be funded, and the final allocation of projects among implementing offices, was left for congressional consideration and was not resolved in the exchange.

positions.position: Tan pressed DPWH to demonstrate that project volume was conservative relative to implementing-office capacity, asked for criteria and ballpark capacity figures, and advocated consideration and funding of ongoing projects.
Ador stated that the ideal capacity was seven projects per PE and said DPWH needed congressional help to secure additional engineers.
Dizon supported rationalization and prioritization but left further allocation and ongoing-project funding to Congress, subject to executive policies.

actions.action: DPWH said it would implement priority infrastructure programs of other departments through memoranda of agreement and align them with those departments’ priorities.
DPWH said it would provide regional allocation breakdowns and data supporting its needs-based allocation approach.
DPWH committed to help the committee identify priority, unfinished, and flagship projects.
Yusick Ador requested congressional assistance for additional engineers through TBM.
DPWH said it would submit the treatment and funding of ongoing convergence projects to Congress for consideration.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: Bivensio Dizon said budget rationalization and prioritization included rationalizing the convergence and special support program. The purpose was to eliminate duplication and align infrastructure projects with the priorities of other departments.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: He said convergence programs with other departments would be removed from the DPWH program and that priority infrastructure programs of departments such as DTI, DOT, and DOTR would instead be lodged under the appropriate department and implemented through memoranda of agreement.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: He said DPWH typically averaged 20,000 projects, but had reached 25,000 projects in 2024 and 2025.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: He attributed the reduction in the number of projects to eliminating duplicate and overlapping projects and focusing on big-ticket projects rather than small-ticket projects.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: He said the VIP program mandated removal of all projects below 5,000,000 pesos, which also drastically reduced the number of projects.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: Bivensio Dizon said the number of projects had to reflect the capacity of DPWH implementing offices, including district engineers and regional directors. He said each office had a limit on the number of projects it could implement.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: He said some implementing offices were carrying two to four times their ideal number of projects, describing the situation as “triple, quadruple” the ideal in some cases.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: He said the dramatic change in DPWH’s project count resulted from eliminating duplication, focusing on larger projects, and bringing the portfolio closer to implementing-office absorptive capacity.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The presenter said DPWH traditionally began early procurement in October of the preceding year, but the 2026 process was affected by changes in the timing of the budget’s final submission and release.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The presenter said roughly about 460,000,000,000 in projects—essentially the entire 2026 DPWH capital outlay budget—became available only for late release, in late May or early June.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: He said procurement consequently began after the late-May or early-June release and characterized the delayed timing as a factual constraint on DPWH’s implementation schedule, not an excuse.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: He reported a total of 17,764 projects in the 2026 DPWH budget, equivalent to a capital outlay of 460,000,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: As of 08/23/2026, 15,032 projects had been advertised for procurement.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The presenter said the advertised projects represented roughly about 76% or 349,500,000,000 out of the 460,000,000,000 budget. He said 7,467 projects had been awarded, roughly about 32% or 146,100,000,000.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: He said projects continued to be advertised every week and every day as DPWH worked to catch up with the procurement schedule.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The presenter expressed confidence that by the end of September 2026, at least 80% of the projects would have been awarded.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Representative Mike Tan asked whether, in light of the problems DPWH had encountered, it would be safe to assume that the department had been conservative in estimating the capacity of its implementing offices.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: Bivensio Dizon answered, “Definitely,” but pointed to the earlier procurement update and DPWH’s confidence that 80% of the 2026 projects would be awarded by the end of September. He added that the department was moving toward early procurement compared with previous years.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Representative Tan asked for a rough ballpark of the ideal number of projects that could be handled by district, regional, and central implementing offices.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: Bivensio Dizon referred the question to Yusick Ador, identifying him as the most experienced operations official, with the chair’s permission.

thread.speaker: Yusick Ador, DPWH official
thread.said: Ador explained that project capacity depended on the accredited project-engineer classification, with PE three as the relevant capacity level, and stated that the ideal was seven projects per PE. He said this was subject to geographic limits within a province or region.

thread.speaker: Yusick Ador, DPWH official
thread.said: Ador said that if a district office’s limit was 150, the office could implement seven projects multiplied by 150, while noting that project inspectors and resident engineers augmented the workforce.

thread.speaker: Yusick Ador, DPWH official
thread.said: Ador said DPWH was augmenting its technical force with job-order personnel because of limitations in its project staffing. He asked Congress to help DPWH obtain additional engineers through TBM.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Representative Tan explained that he was asking because of implementation concerns and referred to rehabilitation projects for 2026, including the need to bid and implement major rehabilitation work.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Tan referred to a 5,000,000,000 budget for next year’s highway rehabilitation, although the surrounding speech-to-text is incomplete.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DPWH would assist the committee in identifying projects that should be prioritized, particularly unfinished projects and flagship projects.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Tan thanked the officials and continued asking about the assignment of projects between UPMO and regional offices.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Tan asked whether project characteristics, including technically smaller bridge projects, should be considered in determining which implementing office was assigned the work. The transcript identifies a bridge example as less than 20,000,000 and 42 meters, but the surrounding wording is incomplete.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary responded that regional offices were involved and thanked Representative Tan, but the transcript does not provide a detailed explanation of the assignment criteria.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Tan asked whether the rationalization of convergence projects was a determining factor in streamlining the DPWH budget.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: Bivensio Dizon said the reduction was part of DPWH’s rationalization and reform plan, undertaken jointly with DPWH and the other agencies. He cited tourism-road projects and other projects of DOT and DOTR as examples.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: On ongoing projects, the Secretary said DPWH understood that such projects existed and that the department would submit the matter to Congress’s wisdom, subject to DBM and the new executive policies.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Tan asked whether the Secretary would support funding ongoing convergence projects, including projects in tourism areas.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan, committee member
thread.said: Tan urged committee support for funding ongoing projects, consistent with the Secretary’s earlier statement.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon, DPWH Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary reiterated that DPWH would submit the issue to Congress and said the department was constrained by the new policies being implemented by the executive.

topics.topic: District-level project and congressional-allocation transparency
topics.summary: Rep. Tobit Janko raised the need for full, nonselective transparency in DPWH infrastructure allocations and requested publication by region, legislative district, party-list representative, and line item. DPWH said its portal already carried roughly ten years of project records and supporting documents, but acknowledged that its existing summary followed district engineering offices rather than legislative districts. Bivensio Dizon committed to submit and publish the legislative-district NEP and supporting information, initially requested before the end of the meeting and later set by the chair for before 01:00. Rep. Janko also cited a flood-control example involving 900 million, 1 billion, and 100 million to show why phased project amounts should be disclosed. Dizon described multiyear appropriations as the policy direction for ongoing projects and agreed to follow the process for identifying congressional amendments or insertions. The chair clarified that the submission had to cover all legislative districts nationwide, but the transcript did not establish that delivery or publication had already occurred.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's proposed 2027 projects and allocations could be published by region and by legislative district, including party-list districts and project-level amounts. It also examined whether multiyear treatment and disclosure of congressional amendments would improve transparency and manage expectations for phased projects.
topics.agency_position: DPWH stated that its transparency portal already contained project information, including ongoing projects and supporting documents, but acknowledged that its summary was organized by district engineering office rather than legislative district. Bivensio Dizon committed to provide and publish the NEP and supporting information by legislative district and line item, and supported multiyear appropriations as a policy direction for ongoing and phased projects.
topics.outcome: The issue landed with DPWH commitments to submit and publish the NEP and project information by legislative district and line item, and to cover all legislative districts rather than only Rep. Janko's district. The transcript does not confirm that the documents were actually submitted or published during the hearing.

positions.position: Transparency had to be comprehensive rather than selective. He sought publication of DPWH projects and amounts by region, legislative district, and line item; disclosure of congressional insertions or amendments; and clearer identification of phased project funding to manage expectations.
The requested information should be published, and existing DBM, DPWH, House, regional, and district-office portals were cited as sources or possible publication venues.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted projects, delays, and commitment fees
topics.summary: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula asked DPWH for the exact pipeline of foreign-assisted projects and for confirmation of commitment fees paid by taxpayers. Bivensio Dizon reported 50 priority ODA projects, of which seven were completed and 26 were under construction, with the remainder in feasibility study or detailed engineering. A committee member cited about 3,400,000,000 pesos in commitment fees reportedly paid in 2022 and requested data from 2022 to the present on delayed projects, unprogrammed appropriations and lender charges. The committee also asked whether penalties and other fees had resulted from delays. Dizon said most, if not all, of the projects were delayed, agreed that avoidable commitment fees should be avoided, and undertook to submit the requested data and project table. The matter remained pending the agency's submissions.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the exact pipeline of DPWH foreign-assisted or ODA projects, including their completion and implementation status. It also sought data on commitment fees, possible penalties and other charges arising from delays, including the reportedly paid 3,400,000,000 pesos in 2022.
topics.agency_position: DPWH acknowledged that commitment fees were associated with delays and said most, if not all, of the foreign-assisted projects were delayed. Bivensio Dizon agreed that the costs were avoidable and undertook to submit the exact project pipeline and requested information on commitment fees, penalties and related charges.
topics.outcome: The agency provided a top-level ODA pipeline but did not yet provide the exact table or the requested commitment-fee, penalty and delay data. DPWH committed to submit the information through the committee, leaving the financial accountability questions open pending submission.

positions.position: Sought an exact pipeline of foreign-assisted projects and confirmation of taxpayer-funded commitment fees and other delay-related costs.

Pressed DPWH to provide data from 2022 to the present on commitment fees, delayed projects, projects under unprogrammed appropriations, penalties and other lender charges, and said the reported 3,400,000,000 pesos could have funded provincial health infrastructure.

topics.topic: Unfinished, ongoing, and delayed DPWH projects
topics.summary: The DPWH presenter attributed slow 2026 procurement to the late release of roughly 460 billion in capital-outlay projects and reported 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded out of 17,764 projects. DPWH targeted 80% awards by the end of September 2026. Ian Amatong pressed for stronger project-engineer oversight, rapid completion of a hospital, and a policy prioritizing unfinished roads and other ongoing works; Bivensio Dizon agreed but said staffing and DBM rules constrained DPWH. Dizon said the department would seek additional engineer items and a possible exemption for continuing projects, and would provide an update on the Quezon Bridge. Dadah Kiram Ismula requested data on 50 ODA projects, commitment fees, and possible penalties, citing around 3,400,000,000 pesos in fees; DPWH undertook to submit the information. Mike Tan then questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH reiterated the need for additional engineers and agreed to help identify unfinished projects. The issue landed with commitments for follow-up, while key policy and funding questions remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DPWH projects remained unfinished, delayed, or slow to be awarded and whether the department had sufficient implementation and supervisory capacity. Members also asked DPWH to prioritize ongoing works, complete hospitals and other unfinished projects, and account for delay-related commitment fees and other charges.
topics.agency_position: DPWH attributed delays primarily to the late release of roughly 460,000,000,000 in 2026 capital-outlay projects and to limited project-engineer capacity. The department agreed that unfinished and ongoing projects should be prioritized, sought congressional help with DBM for additional engineers and possible exemptions for continuing projects, and undertook to submit project, bridge, ODA, and fee data.
topics.outcome: DPWH acknowledged the delays and capacity constraints and agreed in principle that ongoing and unfinished projects should be prioritized. Several requested datasets and project updates were promised, but the DBM exemption, additional staffing, hospital completion schedule, and broader funding prioritization remained subject to further action.

positions.position: Unfinished hospitals, road links, and other ongoing projects should be completed promptly and prioritized in appropriations rather than repeatedly funded without completion. Project engineers should be physically present and accountable during implementation.

The committee needed a complete accounting of foreign-assisted projects, delays, commitment fees, penalties, and other lender charges because avoidable costs could have supported provincial health infrastructure.
DPWH should assess the absorptive capacity of each implementing office, assign projects according to technical capacity, and prioritize completion of unfinished and ongoing projects.
DPWH should improve preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangay captains before project implementation.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The presenter said roughly 460,000,000,000 of projects, essentially the entire DPWH capital outlay budget for 2026, became available for release only in late May or early June, causing procurement to start late.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: DPWH had 17,764 projects under the 2026 budget, equivalent to a capital outlay of 460,000,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: As of 08/23/2026, 15,032 projects had been advertised for procurement.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The advertised projects represented roughly 76% or 349,500,000,000 out of the 460,000,000,000 budget. A total of 7,467 projects had been awarded, representing roughly 32% or 146,100,000,000.

thread.speaker: DPWH presenter
thread.said: The presenter said DPWH was confident that 80% of the projects would have been awarded by the end of September 2026.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: Amatong asked about institutional reforms and the need for project recipients, regional directors, and district engineers to coordinate with local communities before project implementation and turnover.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon agreed that regional and district offices needed to be on the ground and engage communities, noting that DPWH had 75,000 employees and many regional and district offices.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: Amatong emphasized the role of project engineers and complained that some were not present during structural works, citing a recent project in his district.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon agreed with the observation and said project engineers had limited capacity. He asked Amatong to identify the particular project engineer involved so the department could look into the matter.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said current DPWH rules contemplated one project engineer for a maximum of seven projects, but the actual workload had reached one engineer to 30 projects or sometimes more. He said the ideal ratio was one to seven or one to 10.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said DPWH had requested additional project-engineer items from DBM and would ask the committee's help. He characterized the staffing shortage as a structural problem affecting project monitoring and supervision.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: Amatong raised an unfinished hospital in his district, saying it entailed almost a billion and citing the garbled figure “607,100,000,000,000 million.” He said constituents could not wait four or five years and asked for completion within one year.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon explained that most larger regional hospitals were generally funded through the DOH budget, although some hospital-related works were implemented by DPWH. He said the funding and policy arrangement involved DOH and DBM and was not entirely within DPWH's control.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: Amatong urged that policy should prioritize urgent needs and insisted that hospitals should be finished in one year rather than over the period 2025, 2026, and 2027.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon agreed and said DPWH was willing to seek a DBM exemption for continuing projects, but acknowledged that the matter was then outside DPWH's hands.

thread.speaker: Ian Amatong
thread.said: Amatong argued that projects should not receive repeated approaches over two years and then be left unfinished in the third year. He pressed for a policy of allocating funds to unfinished works, including asphalting and missing road links.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon agreed that unfinished and ongoing projects should be prioritized and said DPWH would strive to do so, including in future-year programming.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said he would obtain and provide Amatong with specific information on the Quezon Bridge.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair suggested that DPWH strengthen preconstruction activities involving local officials and barangay captains to explain project purposes and community impacts before implementation.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said implementing offices considered preconstruction activities critical and that these activities should identify project needs even before budget preparation.

thread.speaker: Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: Ismola asked how many foreign-assisted DPWH projects there were and requested the relevant pipeline and project-status information.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon reported 50 priority ODA projects: seven had been completed, 26 were under ongoing construction, and the remainder were undergoing feasibility study and detailed engineering.

thread.speaker: Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: Ismola asked DPWH to confirm whether Filipino taxpayers paid commitment fees on foreign-assisted projects and whether delays had caused those fees.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The member cited information from DOF that there were around 3,400,000,000 pesos in commitment fees in 2022 and asked DPWH to confirm the amount.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said he would provide the DPWH data and was confident that the commitment fees would reach the billions. He later said most, if not all, of the foreign-assisted projects were delayed.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The member asked whether penalties and other fees, in addition to commitment fees, had been imposed because of project delays, including projects placed under unprogrammed appropriations from 2022 to the present.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said DPWH would provide the requested information. He said ODA project details could be provided within the day, although plotting the projects for a master plan might take longer.

thread.speaker: A minority member
thread.said: The member formally manifested the request for the corresponding data and said the 3,400,000,000 pesos cited by DOF could otherwise have been used for health infrastructure in provincial areas.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon reiterated that DPWH would submit the information and agreed that commitment fees resulting from avoidable delays were a concern.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan
thread.said: Tan asked whether DPWH's implementation problems showed that the department had conservatively low absorptive capacity among its implementing offices.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon agreed that capacity was a problem but maintained that DPWH expected to award 80% of the 2026 projects by the end of September and was working to catch up after the late start.

thread.speaker: Yusick Ador
thread.said: Ador said the ideal workload was seven projects per project engineer. He explained that a district office limit of 150 would correspond to up to seven times one 150, augmented by project inspectors, resident engineers, and job-order personnel.

thread.speaker: Yusick Ador
thread.said: Ador said DPWH was augmenting its technical force with job-order personnel and would appreciate congressional assistance with DBM in securing additional engineers.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan
thread.said: Tan referred to a 5,000,000,000 budget for highway construction for the next year and stressed the importance of finishing unfinished projects rather than focusing only on flagship projects.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said DPWH would assist the committee in identifying and finishing unfinished projects, including projects for 2026 and 2027.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan
thread.said: Tan asked whether technically less complex bridge projects, including a bridge of 42 meters and one costing less than 20,000,000, should be assigned to regional offices rather than specialized implementing offices.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said the issue was tied to DPWH's rationalization plan and coordination with other agencies. He noted that projects involving hospitals and tourism roads could also fall under different agency responsibilities.

thread.speaker: Mike Tan
thread.said: Tan asked whether DPWH would support funding ongoing projects, including projects connected with tourism areas, before expanding to new programs.

thread.speaker: Bivensio Dizon
thread.said: Dizon said DPWH would submit the matter to Congress, but was constrained by new executive policies governing implementation and funding.

topics.topic: Road widening and national road-system priorities
topics.summary: Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan raised the proposed national road system, and Bivensio Dizon said DPWH was rationalizing widening toward the most dilapidated and priority sections. Libanan then pressed for a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, for which Dizon cited allocations of 120,000,000 and later 130,000,000, although the year-by-year breakdown was unclear. Dizon described the bridge as roughly 20 kilometers long, cited economic returns of 33% and 42%, and estimated six years for construction; he also committed to consider tourism in the evaluation. Representative Ian Amatong raised inadequate project-engineer coverage, citing an actual workload of one engineer for 30 projects against an ideal one-to-seven or one-to-10 ratio, and Dizon sought committee help for more DBM items. Amatong also sought faster hospital completion and prioritization of unfinished approach works, while Dizon agreed in principle and said DPWH would pursue a DBM exemption and prioritize ongoing projects. The chair additionally called for stronger preconstruction coordination, and Dizon agreed that such activities were critical.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH was prioritizing road widening within the proposed national road system and whether major inter-island links, particularly the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, were feasible and adequately funded. It also examined whether project oversight, hospital construction, unfinished works, and preconstruction coordination were sufficient to ensure that district infrastructure priorities were delivered.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said road widening should be rationalized and directed to the most dilapidated or otherwise priority sections rather than pursued indiscriminately. It supported a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, sought more project-engineer positions, agreed that unfinished works should be prioritized, and was willing to pursue a DBM exemption for continuing hospital projects, although funding and policy decisions remained partly outside DPWH's control.
topics.outcome: DPWH committed to funding and advancing the Sorsogon–Northern Samar feasibility study, subject to subsequent funding and approval, and agreed to examine tourism considerations. Road-widening priorities were not contested after DPWH's explanation, but the hospital exemption, additional project-engineer items, and Quezon Bridge estimates remained dependent on DBM or later agency follow-up.

positions.position: He pressed for a feasibility study and a clear implementation and funding path for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, and supported advancing the project as a major national and regional link.

He called for stronger project-engineer supervision, rapid completion of the hospital in his district, a policy prioritizing unfinished works and approach roads, and more responsive district-level infrastructure delivery.
He directed attention to tourism in evaluating the bridge and urged DPWH to strengthen preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangay leaders.

topics.topic: Sorsogon–Northern Samar and other major bridge projects
topics.summary: Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan asked DPWH to establish the feasibility of the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, including its economic return, timetable, and financing. Bivensio Dizon said the project was a critical Luzon–Visayas link and cited 120,000,000, later correcting or supplementing the figure with 130,000,000 for the feasibility study. He described the link as roughly 20 kilometers, cited a 42% economic rate of return, identified ADB, Korea, JICA, and AIIB as possible funders, and estimated six years for construction after feasibility and approvals. The Chair required tourism benefits to be considered in the evaluation, and the Secretary agreed. Rep. Ian Amatong and Rep. Mike Tan separately raised concerns about project-engineer workloads, technical assignment, absorptive capacity, and unfinished or ongoing projects; DPWH acknowledged the constraints and sought additional engineer items and continued coordination with Congress and DBM. The bridge feasibility commitment advanced, but financing, final approvals, and implementation remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the feasibility, economic return, financing, timetable, and technical implementation arrangements for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge and other major bridge projects. Members also examined whether DPWH had enough project engineers and absorptive capacity to deliver technically demanding and ongoing bridge works.
topics.agency_position: DPWH supported proceeding with the Sorsogon–Northern Samar feasibility study and considered the bridge a high-value Luzon–Visayas link with strong economic-return potential and possible external financing. The agency acknowledged serious project-engineer capacity constraints, sought additional DBM items, and said it would coordinate with Congress and other agencies on technically complex and ongoing projects.
topics.outcome: The feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge was supported by DPWH, with funding figures stated and possible external financiers identified, but final financing, approvals, and construction remained prospective. The broader issues of engineer capacity, project assignment, and funding for ongoing bridge-related works were acknowledged and referred for further coordination with DBM and Congress.

Wanted tourism benefits included in the bridge's economic evaluation and IRR.
Pressed for stronger project-engineer oversight and faster completion of public-works projects, and supported prioritizing unfinished works.
Questioned whether implementing offices had sufficient absorptive and technical capacity, particularly for technically demanding bridge projects, and advocated support for ongoing projects.

topics.topic: School-building and basic-education facility allocations
topics.summary: A majority member asked DPWH to provide the 2025 and 2026 school-building allocations for Regions 3, 4A, and 5 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund. The member cited 595,000,000 and 261 classrooms for Region 3, 523,000,000 pesos I 48 and 297 classrooms for Region 4A, and 5 hundred seventy eight million and 280 completed classrooms for Region 5, with some accompanying figures unclear. Bivensio Dizon responded that DPWH had a 5,000-classroom catch-up target for 2026 using the 13,000,000,000 Basic Education Fund for 2025. He attributed the 2025 timing problem to an August 2025 DepEd-DPWH agreement and said classroom bidding could begin in October or November, while the 2026 process had started earlier in April and proceeded to procurement in August. He expected construction to start by September and occur in November or December. The transcript did not record a complete regional 2025-2026 breakdown or a formal follow-up submission, so the matter remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the budget intended for school-building construction in Regions 3, 4A, and 5 for 2025 and 2026 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund, which had been assigned to DPWH as implementing agency. It attributed delays in 2025 to the later completion of the DepEd-DPWH memorandum of agreement and said the 2026 process began earlier, with construction expected to begin by September and proceed in November or December.
topics.outcome: DPWH provided a general catch-up target and implementation timetable, but the transcript did not show a complete regional breakdown for both 2025 and 2026 or a formal document submission. The issue therefore remained only partially clarified.

topics.topic: Asset preservation, road rehabilitation, and bridge maintenance
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented road-slip rehabilitation, drainage, safety barriers, aging bridges, flood mitigation, makeshift bridge replacement, and completion of unfinished buildings as asset-preservation priorities. He said many bridges were about 40 to 50 years old and that DPWH had often relied on savings because regular funding was insufficient. Rep. Ian Amatong challenged DPWH on absent project engineers and an unfinished hospital, while Dizon acknowledged workloads that could reach one engineer for 30 projects instead of the ideal one for seven. Dizon agreed that hospitals and other unfinished projects should be prioritized and said DPWH would seek DBM flexibility and additional engineering positions. Rep. Mike Tan then questioned absorptive capacity and project assignments; DPWH cited an expectation to award 80% of 2026 projects by the end of September and an ideal workload of seven projects per engineer. The exchanges ended with commitments to provide information, assist in identifying projects, and submit ongoing-project funding issues to Congress, without a final funding resolution.
topics.question: The committee was examining whether DPWH had sufficient funding, personnel, and implementation capacity to preserve existing roads and bridges, complete unfinished infrastructure, and address hospitals and other ongoing projects. Members also sought to establish whether project-engineer workloads, preconstruction coordination, and budget policies were contributing to delays or quality risks.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said asset preservation, bridge rehabilitation, drainage, flood mitigation, replacement of makeshift bridges, and completion of unfinished buildings required additional and more predictable funding rather than repeated reliance on savings. The agency also maintained that project-engineer shortages and budget-policy constraints limited implementation, and it sought congressional assistance with DBM for additional personnel and possible exemptions for continuing projects.
topics.outcome: The committee received DPWH's explanation of asset-preservation needs and implementation constraints, but no final funding adjustment or policy resolution was made. DPWH undertook to seek DBM assistance, provide project information, and help identify unfinished works.

positions.position: Project engineers needed stronger field oversight, and unfinished hospitals and other infrastructure should be completed quickly and prioritized over starting additional works.

DPWH's absorptive capacity, project assignments, and implementing-office workload needed to be matched more carefully with project volume and technical complexity; ongoing and flagship projects should receive support.
DPWH should strengthen preconstruction coordination with local officials, local governments, and barangay captains before implementation.

thread.said: He identified drainage upgrades, carriageway road safety, and safety barriers as additional asset-preservation needs. He said inadequate drainage along highways contributed to problems that needed to be fixed.

thread.said: Dizon said many bridges across the country were 40 to 50 years old, including critical bridges along the national highway network. He said DPWH lacked enough money to keep responding only after bridges collapsed or required retrofitting.

topics.topic: Project evaluation, geotagging, and right-of-way controls
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's stricter project-evaluation and documentation system. He said projects would require supporting documents, validated on-site geotagged photographs, and certificates covering implementability, right-of-way availability, duplicate-project checks, and specific locations. He also said DPWH would require BP two zero two compliance forms, although the transcript's wording was unclear. Dizon reported that many master plans were about ten or fifteen years old and cited rainfall assumptions associated with 2010, 2013, and 2015. He said DPWH would update outdated plans and seek development-council coordination or certificates of no objection from local government units. The segment ended with the reforms presented as transparency and project-readiness controls, without a recorded committee ruling or unresolved challenge.
topics.question: The committee was seeking to establish how DPWH would evaluate projects before inclusion in the budget, verify project locations and readiness, prevent duplicate funding, and address right-of-way and outdated master-plan risks. The presentation also set out what certifications and supporting documents implementing offices would be required to provide.
topics.agency_position: DPWH stated that it had tightened project evaluation through mandatory technical vetting, supporting documents, geotagged on-site photographs, certificates of implementability, right-of-way certifications, and duplicate-project checks. It also maintained that outdated river-basin, drainage, and related master plans needed updating because climate change and changed rainfall conditions affected infrastructure design.
topics.outcome: The agency presented the reforms and the certifications it said would be required for project inclusion and implementation. No member challenge, separate document request, or committee ruling was recorded in the provided segment.

topics.topic: Road, construction-site, and accessibility compliance
topics.summary: Rep. Percy Sindania questioned DPWH about blacklisted contractors, labor and occupational-safety violations, BP 344 compliance, PWD facilities, and road-crash prevention. Bivensio Dizon estimated that between 10 to 15 contractors or suppliers were blacklisted and committed to submit the complete list, as well as projects awarded to Reddycon in the last three years. Dizon candidly described historical accessibility compliance as poor, but said rehabilitation projects would widen sidewalks and meet accessibility standards, supported by about 100 million previously, 170 million last year, and 500 million this year. He and a DPWH safety official described stricter construction-site enforcement, project-engineer training, and an updated safety handbook. Sindania cited 13,125 road-crash deaths in 2023 and said 94% of commuters were at risk daily, while the agency undertook corrective and reporting measures. The chair was told that PWD structures had a separate funding line item, leaving implementation of the standards as the principal open issue.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH was funding and enforcing standards for road rehabilitation, bridge and construction-site safety, and accessibility under BP 344. topics.agency_position: DPWH acknowledged that past compliance with BP 344 had been poor but said rehabilitation projects were being redesigned to provide sufficiently wide sidewalks and meet accessibility standards. The department said it was separately funding PWD infrastructure, enforcing construction-site safety standards, training project engineers, updating its handbook, and would submit the requested contractor and project lists.
topics.outcome: DPWH acknowledged serious historical accessibility-compliance deficiencies and described ongoing corrective measures, dedicated PWD funding, and tighter road and construction-site safety enforcement. Contractor lists and the updated safety handbook were committed for submission, while the broader questions of actual BP 344 compliance and road-crash reduction remained subject to implementation.

positions.position: He pressed DPWH to strengthen blacklisting for labor and safety violations, comply with BP 344, provide accessible public infrastructure, and address road-crash risks through safer roads and construction practices.

topics.topic: Regional allocation equity and convergence priorities
topics.summary: Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's effort to shift regional allocations toward a more needs-based distribution, reducing Luzon's historical share from about 56% to roughly 52%, while raising the Visayas share to 20% and placing Mindanao at about 28%. He acknowledged that the distribution was not yet fully equitable and invited Congress to consider further reallocations, particularly for high-poverty regions. Dizon also said DPWH had reduced projects from a typical average of about 20,000 and the 2024–2025 level of about 25,000 by removing duplicates, emphasizing larger projects, and eliminating projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program. Representative Mike Tan questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH answered that 80% of the 2026 program was expected to be awarded by the end of September; Yusick Ador gave an ideal capacity of seven projects per project engineer and requested help securing additional engineers. Tan later asked about ongoing convergence projects, including hospital and tourism-road works, and Dizon said their funding would be submitted to Congress subject to executive policies. The issue therefore produced agency commitments and explanations but left final reallocations and ongoing-project funding for congressional action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's regional allocations and convergence projects were distributed according to need and whether implementing offices had sufficient absorptive capacity. It also asked whether ongoing hospital, tourism-road, and related convergence projects would continue to receive funding despite the rationalization of responsibilities.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said it was rationalizing convergence projects to eliminate duplication, assign department-specific priorities to the responsible agencies, and reduce project loads that exceeded implementing-office capacity. It said the 2027 regional distribution was more needs-based but acknowledged that further reallocations might still be warranted, while the continuation of ongoing convergence projects would be submitted to Congress subject to executive policies.
topics.outcome: The committee received DPWH's explanation of the more needs-based regional allocation and its rationale for reducing and transferring convergence projects. The continuation of ongoing convergence projects and any further regional reallocations remained subject to Congress's subsequent judgment.

positions.position: Supported examining DPWH's absorptive capacity, completing unfinished and flagship projects, and continuing funding for ongoing convergence projects serving areas such as tourism destinations.

Supported a more equitable, poverty- and needs-based regional allocation, but said the 2027 distribution was only a start and that Congress could reallocate more. topics.topic: Hospital construction and interagency project coordination
topics.summary: Rep. Ian Amatong raised concerns about absent project engineers, a delayed hospital in his district, and the need to finish unfinished works before starting new projects. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged that engineers were handling workloads as high as one to thirty projects against an ideal one-to-seven ratio and sought additional DBM items. Dizon said hospitals often fell under DOH budgets and that DPWH would seek flexibility for continuing hospital projects, while the chair called for stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangays. Rep. Mike Tan then questioned DPWH's absorptive capacity, and Dizon projected 80% award of the 2026 program by the end of September. DPWH official Yusick Ador reiterated the ideal seven-project workload and requested more engineers. The agency agreed to help identify unfinished projects and said funding for ongoing convergence projects would be submitted to Congress, leaving DBM approvals and several project-specific matters open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate project-engineer and implementing-office capacity to supervise hospital, road, bridge, and other convergence projects. It also examined whether DPWH coordinated sufficiently with local governments and partner agencies before construction, and whether unfinished or ongoing projects should be prioritized and funded.
topics.agency_position: DPWH said project supervision was being strained by workloads far above the ideal one-to-seven engineer-to-project ratio and that additional project-engineer positions were needed from DBM. The department supported coordinating with local governments before construction, prioritizing unfinished and ongoing projects, matching projects to capable implementing offices, and seeking flexibility for continuing hospital and convergence projects, but said DBM and executive policies limited what DPWH could do directly.
topics.outcome: The agency agreed in principle with the members' calls for stronger preconstruction coordination, additional engineering capacity, and prioritization of unfinished and ongoing projects. Specific DBM approvals, additional staffing, the hospital completion timetable, and the status information on the Quezon Bridge remained subject to later action or submission.

positions.position: Hospitals in poverty-stricken districts should be completed quickly, preferably within one year rather than through successive annual funding cycles. topics.topic: Project-engineer oversight and implementation accountability
topics.summary: Ian Amatong raised concerns about project engineers being absent during implementation and asked for stronger transparency, coordination, and accountability before project turnover. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged a structural staffing problem: about 75,000 employees supported a workload that could reach one engineer for thirty projects or more, compared with an ideal ratio of one to seven or one to ten. Amatong also pressed for completion of a hospital in his district within one year rather than four or five years; the transcript gave the hospital amount as "607,100,000,000,000 million," which was unclear. Vince said hospital funding arrangements involved DOH and DBM and offered to seek an exemption for continuing projects, while asking the committee to help persuade DBM. Amatong urged DPWH to prioritize unfinished works and requested exact information on the Quezon Bridge, with Vince undertaking to report back. The chair and secretary also supported stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials, barangay captains, and communities.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH would ensure that project engineers were present and accountable during implementation, and whether the department could improve coordination with local communities before construction. Members also pressed for faster completion and prioritization of unfinished and continuing projects.
topics.agency_position: DPWH acknowledged that project-engineer staffing was inadequate, with actual assignments reaching one engineer for thirty projects or more instead of the ideal one to seven or one to ten. The department supported stronger community and preconstruction coordination, agreed to prioritize unfinished and ongoing projects, and said it would seek DBM assistance or an exemption for continuing projects, but stated that the hospital funding and policy issue was not entirely within DPWH's control.
topics.outcome: DPWH agreed in principle to improve project-engineer oversight, prioritize unfinished and ongoing projects, and strengthen preconstruction coordination. Additional engineer staffing, the hospital's funding and completion schedule, and the requested DBM policy relief remained dependent on DBM or further information, while DPWH undertook to provide an update on the Quezon Bridge.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARINGS OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (DND)

topics.topic: AFP modernization funding, loans, and Horizon Three acquisitions
topics.summary: Secretary Teodoro said AFP modernization required an integrated package of equipment, infrastructure, logistics, secure networks, and support systems. Deputy Majority Leader Panaligan asked for the items charged to the 2026 modernization allocation of about 40 billion and the proposed 2027 allocation of about 50 billion, as well as the appropriate loan-ceiling policy; the Secretary favored retaining a cap controlled by DBM and DOF. The DND confirmed an intent to acquire additional frigates and said multirole fighters remained under consideration, but only as part of a broader force package. Members Poe and Patalbano pressed for a clearer drone-program update, and the DND said drones were funded through modernization but that detailed systems were classified and that control, connectivity, and integration were the immediate priorities. The DND cited about 40 billion for a complete Tagoloan dry dock and said U.S. support for Lumbia was still being scoped. The chair requested a prioritized formal letter identifying omitted capital-outlay and other institutional needs, and the DND committed to submit it within the week.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the AFP modernization program would be financed and implemented, including the items charged to the 2026 and 2027 modernization appropriations, the treatment of unprogrammed appropriations and loans, and the status of Horizon Three acquisitions. Members also asked how modernization funding would support drones, fighters, frigates, infrastructure, EDCA sites, and a proposed naval dry dock.
topics.agency_position: The DND said modernization must be treated as an integrated force package requiring core systems, secure networks, domain awareness, logistics, infrastructure, trained personnel, and sustainment, rather than as isolated platform purchases. It supported retaining a loan cap subject to DBM and DOF control, confirmed that frigate and drone acquisitions were being pursued or studied, but withheld detailed acquisition and agreement information where classified or operationally sensitive.
topics.outcome: The hearing established the DND's broad modernization priorities and elicited commitments for itemized funding and prioritized capital-outlay requests, but the detailed 2026-2027 Horizon Three line items were not supplied on the record. Classified drone systems, modernization agreements, and some exercise-related amounts remained undisclosed, while the loan-ceiling legislation, unprogrammed funding, Lumbia support, and Tagoloan dry dock remained subject to further action or funding.

positions.position: Supported obtaining a detailed accounting of the 2026 and 2027 modernization allocations and pursued legislation to make modernization borrowing more flexible.
Argued that drones and robotic systems should receive serious modernization attention because of their lower relative cost and changing economics of warfare.
Sought accountability for unfinished defense infrastructure and requested reports on modernization agreements and activities.
Supported developing Lumbia, constructing the Tagoloan dry dock, and retaining or expanding the Cagayan de Oro-area military presence as a strategic logistics center.
Supported stronger AFP engineering brigades for disaster mitigation and infrastructure work and pressed for a more developed drone program.
Supported restoring critical DND capital outlays and invited the agency to submit prioritized requests for possible amendment and restoration.
