actions.action: Provide the committee with available updates and copies of drone operational guidelines, subject to withholding details that could compromise sensitive systems.
actions.who: Rep. Vernego and Secretary Gilbert Teodoro

actions.action: Continue developing the framework, backbone, connectivity, and control systems for the AFP drone program.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe said he could not find a Philippine Air Force line item for drone technology or hardware and asked whether there was a specific allocation for procuring drones.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said drones were part of the modernization fund. He said the AFP first needed to integrate the capabilities and establish proper working procedures, noting that it already had UAVs providing ISR services.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the AFP could acquire more drones as it matured, but that the more sensitive issue was what capabilities were placed on them. He said the AFP needed to integrate them fully and acquire them in sustainable quantities.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe cautioned that without the capacity to absorb drones into the AFP and trained personnel to operate them, procurement could produce hardware that was not implementable in the field.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro replied that the principal issue was integration into operations rather than personnel alone. He said each service needed to develop a niche and that connectivity, network capability, and secure near-real-time communications were essential, particularly for ISR.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe said he was looking for a specific drone-technology budget item because the economics of warfare were changing. He asked whether the Navy budget contained a specific drone-procurement item.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the relevant systems were classified and could not be identified because they were highly sensitive, particularly those involving AI. He said the AFP had capabilities but was not at liberty to disclose them.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the DND was in close contact with countries possessing drone expertise, but needed to keep pace with rapid technological change. He said that in one country drones were retooled and reprogrammed at least every three days or they became ineffective.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe said he was not asking the DND to declassify sensitive information, but wanted assurance that drone capabilities were funded, under discussion, and being secured for the future. He asked whether modernization planning accounted for possible restrictions by a neighboring country on critical drone hardware or chip manufacturing.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said allied software-partner countries also needed resilient supply chains for the high technology they used. He said the DND was entering partnerships with them under the applicable SOFAs and was upgrading C4I systems.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe contrasted the cost of larger platforms with drones, saying one F-16 could cost 70,000,000 more or less, equivalent to about 2,000 Shahed-class drones. He argued that the DND needed to prepare for the changing economics of defense.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe said the Secretary's assurances that the modernization program and DND leadership were preparing for drone technology were sufficient for Congress on that point. He then moved to other subjects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Vernego
thread.said: Rep. Vernego asked about arms acquisition beyond small arms, including drones, and whether the DND was pursuing local production.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said drones were part of every country's toolkit and that producing the airframes was relatively easy. He said the important and changing element was the technology placed in them, particularly with the advent of AI.

thread.speaker: Rep. Vernego
thread.said: Rep. Vernego asked whether the AFP had operational guidelines governing military drone use.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the guidelines were still at the evolution stage. He said the AFP was still developing the backbone systems needed to use drones responsibly.

thread.speaker: Rep. Vernego
thread.said: Rep. Vernego flagged the need for written guidelines, saying that responsible use should begin with clear rules.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said there were currently no offensive uses of drones insofar as the DND was concerned and that they were being used for surveillance. He said the DND would conform to guidelines for external-defense uses beyond surveillance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Vernego
thread.said: Rep. Vernego asked the DND to provide the committee with updates and copies of its operational guidelines to help ensure responsible use.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the guidelines could be disclosed insofar as disclosure would not compromise sensitive system details. He indicated that the DND could provide the material while withholding operational granularity that could expose its systems.

thread.speaker: Tony Patalbano
thread.said: Tony Patalbano referred to an earlier discussion on the drone program and asked whether the Chief of Staff was supposed to report its progress. He argued that drone technology was important for a smaller country and requested the program's status.

thread.speaker: Tony Patalbano
thread.said: Tony Patalbano cited Ukraine's conflict with Russia as an example of the significance of drone technology. He said the issue had also been discussed two years ago.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the DND was building the framework and backbone for the drone program and that this was all he could disclose at that point. He said drones were easy to produce, but their payloads, purposes, control systems, and associated capabilities were the difficult elements.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the systems were not autonomous devices and that the DND was developing control systems alongside the required capabilities. He said the AFP already had long-existing capabilities within its engagement framework, but did not provide further details.

topics.topic: Veterans’ pensions, health care, and retirement support
topics.summary: Representative Erline Ayon raised concerns about whether the budget adequately protected veterans’ pensions, benefits, health care, and retirement support, especially for elderly and medically vulnerable veterans. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said pension increases should be decoupled from active-duty salaries and reported a compromise providing 5% increases for three years, or 15% by 2028. He also cited 71,000,000,000 for AFP retirees and JPY 11,000,000,000 for veterans ameliorations in the special-purpose-fund breakdown. The Department described valor clinics, preventive care, mental-health and geriatric programs, and Veterans Memorial Medical Center improvements; it said the center had treated 11,100 inpatients but could accommodate only about nine percent of veterans. Teodoro committed to pursuing a first hospice by the end of the year and assured the committee that the Department would fight for veterans’ benefits. Pension reform, including separate treatment for AFP retirees, was not settled and remained subject to further study.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget adequately protected veterans’ pensions, health care, retirement support, and related welfare programs. It also asked how Congress and the Department of National Defense could ensure that elderly and medically vulnerable veterans would not be left without benefits or care.
topics.agency_position: The Department stated that veterans’ welfare required continued pension support, preventive and specialized health care, socialization, transition assistance, outpatient access through valor clinics, and improved facilities at the Veterans Memorial Medical Center. Secretary Teodoro supported studying pension reform and decoupling veterans’ pensions from active-duty salaries, but opposed treating AFP retirees identically with retirees from other uniformed services and favored preserving retirement security while a sustainable system was developed.
topics.outcome: The Secretary gave assurances on continued advocacy for veterans’ benefits and described ongoing and planned health-care and retirement-support programs, including a hospice targeted for launch by year-end. Pension reform and the legal decoupling of pensions from active-duty salaries remained matters for further study and legislative action.

positions.position: Veterans’ pensions, benefits, health care, and retirement support should receive equal budgetary importance, with concrete safeguards against delayed benefits, insufficient funding, and inadequate care.

Veterans’ pensions should be decoupled from active-duty salaries and AFP retirees should be treated separately in pension reform. The Department should continue defending veterans’ benefits while expanding preventive care, hospice support, clinics, and retirement-wellness programs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said veterans’ welfare was extremely important because retired veterans remained a moral and driving force and could continue contributing technical skills and leadership to the active-duty forces.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He reported that the President had approved the first stage of an annex at the Veterans Memorial Medical Center, intended to house current patients while the more-than-70-year-old Legacy Building was rehabilitated.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said appropriations for valor clinics, or external clinics, had continued so veterans could receive services closer to where they lived. The Department expected three to five clinics to be operating by the end of the year, subject to staffing with competent and security-vetted personnel.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said veterans’ health care was being integrated with active-duty wellness and preventive-health programs. The Department was also developing programs addressing mental wellness, mental health, and geriatric care.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said military retirement could be traumatic because personnel might spend thirty or forty years in a structured environment before suddenly losing that support system. He said the Department was pursuing a more holistic approach to transition and post-retirement wellness, including socialization and mental-health support.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: In the special-purpose-fund breakdown, the presentation listed 71,000,000,000 for AFP retirees and JPY 11,000,000,000 for veterans ameliorations.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the Veterans Memorial Medical Center had treated 11,100 inpatients and that only about nine percent of veterans could currently be accommodated there.

thread.speaker: Representative Erline Ayon
thread.said: Representative Ayon emphasized that veterans, including uniformed personnel and civilian human resources, had devoted many years to national service. She said veterans were concerned about discussions and news regarding their pensions and retirement benefits.

thread.speaker: Representative Erline Ayon
thread.said: She asked whether the Department’s plans and budget priorities gave equal importance to veterans nationwide, particularly elderly veterans facing rising health-care and living expenses. She also asked how lawmakers and the Department could provide concrete programs, adequate benefits, health care, and support for veterans suffering from illness and long-term effects of service-related stress and trauma.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said veterans’ pensions should be decoupled from active-duty salaries so pension adjustments would not automatically require corresponding active-duty pay increases.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said a compromise with veterans had provided for pension-rate increases of 5% for three years, for a total of 15% by 2028.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He explained that, unless pension increases were decoupled by law from active-duty rates, the government would also have to increase active-duty personnel rates.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the Department hoped to launch its first hospice by the end of the year for older veterans who had no home and were being confined in hospitals because no alternative facility was available.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He identified caregiver accreditation and recruitment, as well as construction of the hospice facility, as outstanding implementation issues. He nevertheless said the Department had to begin the program to provide veterans a dignified place to retire.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said socialization was an important part of veterans’ welfare because isolation could cause even younger veterans to withdraw and suffer after leaving their former support systems.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said many veterans’ health problems could be addressed preventively while they were still on active duty. The Department was monitoring diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, heart attacks, and strokes, including strokes affecting personnel at age 35, to anticipate conditions that could later require extensive veterans’ care.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said he was not opposed to pension reform but argued that AFP retirees should not simply be lumped together with retirees from other uniformed services. He said the AFP was a purely sovereign national force and that pension arrangements should reflect the different benefits other agencies and local communities received from targeted services.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He acknowledged that unreformed pensions could eventually consume substantial fiscal space. However, given the AFP’s continuing missions, low troop ceiling, and year-round operational demands, he said active-duty personnel and retirees needed peace of mind while a sustainable pension system was studied.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the old RSPS system had not been sustainable and that any replacement should be foolproof enough to guarantee retirement security and preserve the motivation of active-duty personnel.

thread.speaker: Representative Erline Ayon
thread.said: Representative Ayon asked for assurance that no Filipino veteran who had served honorably would be left behind because of insufficient funds, delayed benefits, or inadequate health care.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro assured the committee that the Department was at the forefront of fighting for veterans’ benefits. He also said he maintained close relationships with veterans’ groups and sought to use retired enlisted personnel, NCOs, and civilian personnel’s expertise after retirement.

thread.speaker: Representative Erline Ayon
thread.said: Representative Ayon thanked the Secretary and indicated that this concluded her intervention.

topics.topic: MUP pension reform and contribution-based financing
topics.summary: Antonio Tinio raised the increase in the MUP pension budget from about 68.6 billion in 2015 to about 154 billion in the proposed 2027 budget and asked about a contribution-based reform. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said the reform required decisions on when it would begin and who would be covered, with the armed forces separated from civilian agencies. He said LGUs might fairly share the pension burden for locally oriented services such as the police, but that the fiscal and actuarial effects needed study. The secretary said the department was open to requiring greater contributions and to proposals easing the national government's burden. He also said a system could be designed to mature gradually before pension drawdown. The issue landed with further study and no definitive contribution or LGU-sharing arrangement.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed MUP pension reform would shift from government-subsidized pensions toward contributions, including when the system would begin and who would be covered. It also asked whether LGUs would share responsibility for the pension burden of civilian uniformed personnel, particularly the police.
topics.agency_position: The DND supported studying a contribution-based MUP pension reform and was open to proposals that would ease the national government's fiscal burden. Secretary Teodoro said the armed forces should be treated separately from civilian agencies, while LGU burden sharing for locally oriented uniformed services should be evaluated through actuarial and fiscal analysis; no definitive plan or contribution level had yet been adopted.
topics.outcome: The department agreed to consider contribution-based reform and possible LGU burden sharing, but left the timing, coverage, contribution level, and allocation of liability for further study. No final reform plan or LGU share was presented.

positions.position: He pressed for clarification of the proposed contribution system, its timing and coverage, the basic contribution required, and whether LGUs should assume part of the pension burden for police and other civilian uniformed personnel.

He favored studying pension reform and possible LGU burden sharing, but said implementation details, fiscal impacts, and actuarial sustainability had to be determined before a final position could be taken.

topics.topic: Disaster-response assets, OCD capacity, and evacuation centers
topics.summary: DND said disaster response required larger airlift platforms, distributed logistics centers, prepositioned supplies, and stronger OCD coordination; it cited about 46 Black Hawk helicopters but said that capacity was insufficient. Representative Poe questioned OCD's 0.96% capital-outlay reduction from a budget of 2,500,000,000, and Secretary Teodoro said the reduction affected capital outlay and that OCD needed relocation from crowded Camp Aguinaldo. Representative Rufus Rodriguez asked for 2027 Ligtas Pinoy sites and selection criteria; the response referred to DNR hazard mapping but did not clearly identify the sites, while the transcript gave inconsistent figures of 60,000,000, 34 centers, and 90,000,000 per center. Members raised delays in rescue and relief processing, the need for Navy dredgers, insufficiently detailed Negros rehabilitation plans, and climate-flooded roads in Central Luzon. Secretary Teodoro committed to national-level coordination, an OCD anticipation deliverable, a revised earthquake-impact study process, and infrastructure referrals, while Representative Salvador cited delivery of 1,200 family packs and supported the FY 2027 DND budget.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DND and OCD had sufficient assets, logistics, evacuation facilities, communications, and coordination systems for disaster response, including prepositioning and response to flooding and a major earthquake. Members also asked how the 2027 evacuation-center program would select sites and whether OCD's reduced capital outlay would impair operations.
topics.agency_position: DND said OCD should concentrate on coordinated awareness, prediction, preemptive response, and logistics rather than directly undertaking rehabilitation or major infrastructure works. The agency identified joint logistics centers, prepositioned supplies and water, improved rescue and airlift capacity, evacuation-site planning, and stronger communications and infrastructure resilience as necessary, while acknowledging that OCD's rehabilitation plans and response procedures still needed improvement.
topics.outcome: The committee received assurances that DND was prioritizing OCD coordination, prepositioned logistics, evacuation planning, and earthquake and flood resilience, but several matters remained dependent on future studies, site identification, interagency action, or additional appropriations. The record included commitments to submit project information, pursue relocation and infrastructure coordination, and elevate national flood and earthquake-resilience measures.

positions.position: Supported attention to OCD and disaster relief capacity and questioned the effect of the capital-outlay reduction.
Sought concrete 2027 Ligtas Pinoy evacuation-center sites and transparent hazard-based selection criteria.
Raised concern that OCD and AFP procedures for rescue and relief requests could produce unacceptable delays.
Supported advance disaster preparation and urged funding or acquisition of Navy dredgers to maintain access to ports and naval facilities.
Pressed for detailed rehabilitation, relocation, and bridge-access measures in flood- and disaster-affected parts of Negros.
Urged national coordination and major, climate-resilient engineering solutions for flooding that had made MacArthur Highway and other connectivity routes inaccessible.
Asked for earthquake preparedness in Bulacan and other flood-prone population centers and supported the FY 2027 DND budget based on AFP humanitarian assistance.

Provide the committee a list of earmarked-revenue projects pledged for payment.
Support or pursue acquisition of Navy dredgers, with one dredger reportedly already in the pipeline.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said DND was increasing its capacity for humanitarian assistance and disaster response. The AFP had about 46 Black Hawk helicopters, but needed larger rotary platforms and palletized aircraft to move heavier loads and supplies.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He said disaster response required reserves and distributed strategic storage points for critical items, supported by infrastructure capable of carrying the weight of the equipment. Modernization therefore included logistics infrastructure and access, not just platforms.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said he had directed OCD to concentrate on disaster response and perfect its coordination function for awareness, prediction, and response before taking on other functions. He asked Congress to allow OCD time to develop those capabilities and said rehabilitation added bureaucracy to the release of funds for infrastructure repairs.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He identified joint logistics centers as OCD's principal need, including prepositioning perishable logistics, medicines, and water with proper inventory management. He said supplies had previously originated mainly from Metro Manila and had to be airlifted or sea-lifted, producing delays when roads or local routes were impassable.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe, member
thread.said: Representative Poe noted that OCD's budget had declined by 0.96% and that 0.96% of 2,500,000,000 was a substantial amount for disaster relief. He asked what the reduction represented.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro answered that the reduction was in capital outlay. He said OCD and the NDCP needed long-term capital outlay to relocate from crowded Camp Aguinaldo; OCD was being directed to look for a site in Bonifacio with unobstructed access for local government executives and civilians.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez, member
thread.said: Representative Rodriguez cited the Ligtas Pinoy requirement for permanent evacuation centers in every city and municipality and asked whether the specific 2027 sites or priority LGUs had already been identified. He also asked what criteria would be used to select them.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez, member
thread.said: He stated that 60,000,000 was proposed for 34 Ligtas Pinoy centers, described in the transcript as two per region at 90,000,000 each. The figures and their relationship are internally inconsistent in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: The response was partly garbled, but referred to identifying areas for evacuees using DNR hazard mapping and considering areas that could support preemptive evacuation. No definitive list of 2027 sites or complete selection criteria was clearly stated.

thread.speaker: Robert Nassau, member
thread.said: Representative Nassau asked whether the AFP's accumulated earmarked revenues were unused because the AFP had not submitted sufficient programs or because DBM had not approved its requests. He later asked for the projects pledged for payment and whether off-budget resources had been considered in preparing the 2027 request.

thread.speaker: Robert Nassau, member
thread.said: He cited 10,285,000,000 in accumulated AFP earmarked revenues from the BCDA share as of 12/31/2025. He also cited 4.02 9,000,000,000 in DND off-budget balances, including 587,000,000 for the Philippine Army, 984,652,000 for the Air Force, and 138,000,000 for the Navy; the first off-budget figure is garbled.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the earmarked BCDA funds already had programs matched to them and that the balances funded existing contracts. He later said the off-budget accounts consisted of ongoing projects, including runway and interagency-transfer works, and that the funds were lodged in the BTR and were not interest earning.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair directed the department to provide the requested information on earmarked-revenue projects pledged for payment.

thread.speaker: Jay Kang Hoon, member
thread.said: Deputy Speaker Kang Hoon asked how OCD processed helicopter rescue missions and delivery of basic food packs, including whether approval was normally required and how long requests took. He described a request that reportedly took almost a week before an airlift was conducted.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said missions depended on available platforms at the GHQ level, weather, and the needs of the affected area. He acknowledged that the process could take several hours to some days and said the experience supported the need for an OCD operations center.

thread.speaker: Anna Bondo, vice chair
thread.said: Vice Chair Bondo commended the AFP's disaster-response work and said it was better to prepare for disasters in advance. She described joint Manila Bay cleanup and dredging work involving the Army, Navy, Coast Guard, DENR, and local government.

thread.speaker: Anna Bondo, vice chair
thread.said: She said more than 1,500 Tupad members participated in the cleanup and reported clearance figures of 9000 in year one, 17000 in year two, and 15000 in year three.

thread.speaker: Anna Bondo, vice chair
thread.said: Vice Chair Bondo urged support for Navy dredgers, arguing that siltation in Manila Bay and naval ports could impair the use of larger modern ships. She said dredgers were a badly needed component of Navy capacity.

thread.speaker: DND agency official
thread.said: The agency official agreed that dredgers were needed for naval bases and ports and said one was already in the pipeline. The official also discussed possible turnover or acquisition arrangements and legal treatment under the tariff and customs code, although parts of the response were garbled.

thread.speaker: Jeffrey Ferrer, member
thread.said: Representative Ferrer asked about ongoing rehabilitation after flooding and Mount Kanlaon activity in Negros, including damage in the fourth and fifth districts. He emphasized the need to restore bridges and access routes serving communities.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the rehabilitation plan lacked sufficient detail, particularly on acquiring land for relocation in unaffected areas. He said OCD Negros would continue coordinating with OCD Central and pressing other agencies, including DBM, for action.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the level of detail raised by Representative Ferrer was what he expected in the rehabilitation plan, but he had not seen it and had returned the plan.

thread.speaker: Anna York Bondoc, vice chair
thread.said: Vice Chair Bondoc warned that MacArthur Highway was inaccessible because of flooding from the Pampanga, Bulacan, and surrounding river systems, threatening trade, national security, and connectivity. She asked whether DND and OCD were addressing the loss of the region's major road routes and could coordinate before disasters occurred.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the problem also affected Tarlac and required a network-wide engineering solution, potentially including major viaduct and elevated-railway works. He stressed that OCD could presently coordinate the response but was not the agency capable of delivering the major infrastructure solution.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He undertook to raise or route the flooding and connectivity problem through the national council as an urgent matter, supporting legislative initiatives and appropriations that might be needed.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said anticipation of disasters was a deliverable that OCD had pending with him. Vice Chair Bondoc said she was willing to work with OCD on pre-disaster coordination.

thread.speaker: Salvador, member
thread.said: Representative Salvador asked DND and OCD to consider the preparedness of Bulacan and other densely populated flood-prone areas for a major earthquake, including the adequacy of AFP and OCD communications, rescue assets, and evacuation logistics when civilian infrastructure failed.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said he had met critical infrastructure and connectivity providers to address resilience and business continuity during an earthquake. He said the Metro Manila earthquake-impact study, dating from about 2003, needed to be revisited and that JICA papers had been approved for Cabinet processing, with DOST designated to shepherd the work.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He said the AFP could operate in an earthquake except where major thoroughfares were blocked, in which case access would depend on aerial capabilities. He distinguished the Manila Trench tsunami risk from the West Valley Fault risks of subsidence, liquefaction, and major damage to connectivity and lives.

thread.speaker: Salvador, member
thread.said: Representative Salvador cited sustained Philippine Air Force humanitarian airlift operations that delivered 1,200 DSWD family packs, ready-to-eat packs, and jerry cans of clean water to isolated barangays in Sarangani. He endorsed prepositioning assets before disasters and expressed strong support for the FY 2027 DND budget.

topics.topic: DND-DPWH military infrastructure and unfinished projects
topics.summary: Representative Sara Hirado questioned Secretary Gilbert Teodoro about the DND-DPWH infrastructure program and projects that remained unfinished or unusable. Teodoro said DND had received 100% of released amounts but that funding was insufficient, citing 27 non-implementable and 51 implementable projects out of 78. Hirado cited an earlier report of 648 completed out of 944 projects and a figure of 15,000,000,000 pesos for uncompleted, idle, and unusable infrastructure, but the discrepancy was not clearly resolved. Teodoro also said reduced capital outlays threatened modernization support and delayed rehabilitation of the 70-year-old DND and Legacy buildings. The chair requested a formal prioritized list of omitted or reduced projects, and Teodoro committed to submit it within the week. The committee indicated that restoration would be considered during the budget amendment process.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status of the DND-DPWH military infrastructure program, particularly projects that remained unfinished or unusable, the accountability measures taken, and the funding needed to complete or rehabilitate them. It also sought to determine whether reduced capital outlays had omitted critical infrastructure support for modernization projects.
topics.agency_position: DND said military modernization could not be sustained without corresponding capital outlays for bases, logistics, maintenance, and other support infrastructure. It said the DND-DPWH project record included 27 non-implementable and 51 implementable projects out of 78, but did not clearly reconcile that figure with the earlier 218-project reference or provide a definitive update on inspections, completion, or possible charges.
topics.outcome: The committee received a partial project-status explanation but the conflicting project counts, completion status, inspection results, and potential filing of charges were not resolved. DND committed to submit a prioritized list of omitted or reduced capital-outlay needs within the week, leaving possible restoration for the budget amendment process.

positions.position: Pressed DND for accountability and a clear status report on unfinished and unusable infrastructure, including the previous commitment to inspect projects and consider charges against responsible parties.
Supported restoring omitted or reduced DND capital outlays and asked DND to submit a prioritized list of critical projects and programs for possible budget amendments.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the President had approved the first stage of constructing an annex at the Veterans Memorial Medical Center so current patients could be moved out while the more than 70-year-old Legacy Building was rehabilitated.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He said modernization required infrastructure to house, support, and maintain new capabilities, but capital outlays had not been financed for several years. The budget was therefore equipment-heavy but not sufficiently support-heavy.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He said the Armed Forces needed logistical bases and strategic reserve points distributed throughout the Philippines, with infrastructure capable of supporting the weight and dimensions of its equipment.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He emphasized that modernization was not merely the acquisition of capabilities but also the provision of adequate infrastructure and access routes that could support the equipment.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He presented a proposed DND budget of 324,632,000,000, with 10% for capital outlay, 55% for personal services, and 35% for maintenance and other operating expenses.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He said the capital-outlay proposal was 239,000,000 and had been specifically matched to modernization items, but the matching had not been made. Without the infrastructure, he said, modernization could not continue and would be a waste of money.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: He said the DND building had required refurbishment because it was molding and contained asbestos, forcing personnel to work off-site in scattered locations. He described it as a legacy building that had to be rehabilitated.

thread.speaker: Sara Hirado, Representative
thread.said: Representative Hirado asked for an update on the implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of the DND-DPWH infrastructure program.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro responded that the Department was developing a new paradigm for constructing main operating bases and major bases to support the infrastructure it needed.

thread.speaker: Sara Hirado, Representative
thread.said: Representative Hirado followed up by asking for an update on projects that were unfinished and unusable as of 2025.

thread.speaker: Gilbert Teodoro, Secretary of National Defense
thread.said: Secretary Teodoro said the DND had received 100% of the amounts released, but the funding was not enough to complete the projects. He reported 27 non-implementable projects and 51 implementable projects, for a total of 78.

topics.topic: Naval bases, dry docks, and strategic military facilities
topics.summary: Members examined AFP modernization allocations, naval frigate plans, base logistics, and the development of Lumbia and Tagoloan facilities. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said the proposed 2027 modernization allocation was tied to fiscal capacity, confirmed an intent to acquire additional frigates, and emphasized that infrastructure was necessary to make advanced equipment useful. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez was told that Lumbia had about 115 million remaining for the current year and a 450 million amount cited for the next year, while no U.S. EDCA counterpart had yet been agreed. DND estimated the proposed complete Tagoloan dry dock at about 40 billion, including equipment, but said titling had to be completed and Sangley was becoming unusable for naval maneuvering. Anna York Bondoc requested Navy dredgers for silted ports, and the secretary agreed that dredging was needed and said one dredger was in the pipeline. Antonio Tinio's security questions about the Sangley-area Chinese-linked company were answered with references to environmental and enforcement actions, but the Navy's need for a dedicated dry dock remained.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DND and the AFP would prioritize modernization, naval-base and dry-dock development, and related logistics facilities within fiscal constraints. Members also asked whether proposed sites were legally, operationally, and securely ready, and what documents or follow-up actions the agency would provide.
topics.agency_position: DND said naval and AFP infrastructure was essential to logistics, readiness, external defense, and disaster response. It supported developing dedicated dry-dock and port capacity, including the proposed Tagoloan facility, but said titling, right-of-way, environmental, and security matters remained prerequisites; it also supported dredging and said a dredger was already in the pipeline.
topics.outcome: The committee received DND's explanations and endorsements for Lumbia, Tagoloan, dredging, and dedicated naval infrastructure, but the Tagoloan project remained dependent on titling and the Lumbia U.S. contribution remained unagreed. Requested modernization and earmarked-fund documents were to be furnished, while the Payao camp and Sangley-area development required further coordination.

positions.position: Pressed for transparency on AFP modernization line items and supported revisiting the statutory modernization-loan ceiling to address fiscal constraints.
Supported Lumbia, the Tagoloan dry dock, and retaining or enlarging the Fourth Infantry Division's Cagayan de Oro-area logistical role as strategic Mindanao facilities.
Supported completing the proposed joint camp in Payao and sought AFP action consistent with the commitments of the other participating agencies.
Supported purchasing Philippine Navy dredgers because siltation affected Manila Bay and naval ports.
Sought assurances that the Sangley-area dry-dock development would protect facility security and would not expose AFP facilities to risks associated with a Chinese-linked company.

thread.speaker: Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: He asked which AFP modernization items would be charged to the PHP 50,000,000,000 proposed for 2027 and the PHP 40,000,000,000 for 2026, noting that repeated Horizon Three reprogramming could affect capability plans.

thread.speaker: Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: He requested copies of the items charged to PHP 40,000,000,000 for 2026 and proposed under PHP 50,000,000,000 for 2027. He also raised his bill concerning the ceiling on modernization loans and asked whether DND preferred retaining, increasing, or removing the ceiling.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the cap should remain because DBM and DOF would set it based on the country's fiscal condition and the type of loan, with DOF ultimately entering into the loan and controlling the government's financial exposure.

thread.speaker: Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: He asked whether the reported proposal to acquire two additional missile frigates, after two previously ordered frigates, could be confirmed, and followed up on sensors and weapon systems for existing frigate classes.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He confirmed that there was an intent to acquire the additional frigates, but said the trigger had not yet been pulled. He said the upgrading and completion of sensors and weapon systems were ongoing.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said multirole fighters, air-defense missiles, and coastal-defense missiles remained under consideration depending on financing, but fighter acquisition required supporting ground control, domain awareness, refueling, and hangar facilities. He said the minimum force package was 40 at any one mission for external defense.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He emphasized that connectivity and infrastructure were necessary to support the weight and operation of the equipment required by the AFP and to address logistics problems.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: Responding to questions about the AFP's accumulated BCDA earmarked revenues, he said programs already existed to match all the earmarked funds and that the balances were tied to existing contracts and pledged payments.

thread.speaker: Appropriations Committee chair
thread.said: The chair agreed to direct the department to provide the requested list of earmarked-revenue projects pledged for payment.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He cited ongoing infrastructure projects, including an Air Force runway and the interagency-transfer refurbishment of Lumbia Air Base, which he said was now a Philippine Air Force base.

thread.speaker: Jay Khonghun
thread.said: He asked for an update and timeline on plans to transfer or expand the naval base referred to in the transcript as Azubik, including the relevant presidential proclamation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the plan was to expand a new shipbuilding area on a net-zero-loss basis and expressed hope that the facility would produce the first Philippine-Korean co-produced logistics supply ship.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked for the DND budget for further development of the Lumbia site for the Fifteenth Strike Wing and asked what the United States would contribute as an EDCA site.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the amount for the current year was 115,000,000 and described it as the remaining amount; he also stated that there was a 450,000,000 budget for the next year, with possible enhancements.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said there was no U.S. counterpart yet. Lumbia development was being hampered by right-of-way and informal-settler issues, and the government was pursuing legal proceedings and relocation to improve base security.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the United States was still scoping possible support, particularly a multipurpose warehouse, while DND was considering air-traffic-control enhancements. No structure had yet been agreed.

thread.speaker: Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked for an update on the proposed naval base at Tagoloan, its location, expected cost, titling status, and construction timetable.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He clarified that the Tagoloan project would be a dockyard in the southern portion of the area identified in the transcript as Phebeetic, pending finalization of titling. A complete dry dock capable of supporting the growing fleet would cost about 40,000,000,000, including equipment.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said the site was strategic because it was relatively free from typhoons and could accommodate large vessels, while Subic could not be used as a dry dock because it remained an operating naval base. He said the government was trying to complete titling because Sangley was shallow, small, and increasingly difficult for naval platforms to maneuver in.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said there was no specific guidance to transfer the Fourth Infantry Division. Instead, the Army was being directed to assess locations for division and brigade headquarters, logistical supply points, motor pools, medical facilities, and connectivity to other strategic bases.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He identified the proposed dockyard, Lumbia as the home of the Fifteenth Strike Wing, and the Northern Mindanao operation center for OCD as areas of prime consideration for Mindanao's defense, maintenance, and disaster-response infrastructure.

thread.speaker: Representative Marlo Bancoro
thread.said: He raised the proposed joint camp in Payao for the Army, PNP, and Coast Guard, noting that the local government would implement it and that an agreement on downloading funds was expected. He asked what remained to be done on the AFP side.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He said AFP units and areas of operation would be guided by logistics requirements and that the service commanders would determine priorities, with attention directed to major logistical bases.

thread.speaker: Anna York Bondoc
thread.said: She linked Manila Bay siltation to naval access and argued that dredgers were essential if the Navy was acquiring and operating larger ships. She urged support for the Philippine Navy's purchase of dredgers.

thread.speaker: Secretary Gilbert Teodoro
thread.said: He agreed that dredgers were needed for naval bases and ports and said one was already in the pipeline. He also discussed possible turnover or allocation of dredgers among the Navy, Coast Guard, and other agencies depending on vessel size and applicable rules.

thread.speaker: Congressman Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked about the industrial-estate area associated with the proposed Sangley dry dock and raised security concerns about a Chinese steel company located there and its possible proximity to a secure AFP facility.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The official identified the company as Sanja Steel and said it was owned by Tony Yang, who was under detention. The official said DND could not allow an attached agency to be used improperly and noted that the company's environmental compliance certificate had been canceled and a cease-and-desist order issued.

thread.speaker: Congressman Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked for the development plan and timeline for the Sangley-area dry dock under the budget proposal.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The official said development and equipment acquisition would proceed as soon as possible, with the dry dock intended to support the Navy. The official described the facility as a separate, sustainable area for servicing Philippine Navy vessels.

thread.speaker: Congressman Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked whether U.S. military personnel would seek access to or use facilities developed in the area, including a possible Navy dry dock.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The official said the area was not environmentally cleared by PNRI and DNR and that the government could not risk allowing people into it. The official ultimately said there was no room for expansion there and that the Navy needed its own dedicated dry dock.

topics.topic: FY 2027 DND budget restorations and institutional amendments
topics.summary: DND presented a proposed budget of about 324.6 billion and identified reduced capital outlay as the principal immediate restoration concern. The agency said the capital-outlay proposal was 239,000,000 and that reductions could delay infrastructure supporting modernization equipment and the restoration of the DND's 70-year-old legacy building. The agency also cited a 50,000,000,000 modernization fund, a 98 or 99% troop-strength fill-up rate, and 10 modernization projects, but no restoration amount was approved. The committee chair asked for a formal and prioritized list of critical programs omitted from the NEP for consideration in the H-GAP. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro committed to submit the list within the week, while the chair committed to have the requests reviewed line by line by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee. Representatives Isidro Ungab and Salvador expressed support for the DND and AFP budgets, with Ungab separately requesting a brief district-related meeting.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which DND and AFP programs or projects had been reduced or omitted from the NEP and should be restored through institutional amendments. It also sought a prioritized, formal list from the agency so the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee could evaluate the requests line by line.
topics.agency_position: DND said the most urgent restoration need was capital outlay, because reductions would leave modernization equipment without the infrastructure needed to house, support, and maintain it. The agency said it would submit a prioritized list of its other institutional amendment needs through the undersecretary and provide a formal letter within the week.
topics.outcome: The committee did not approve specific restoration amounts during the hearing. DND was asked to submit a formal, prioritized list of omitted or reduced programs and institutional amendment requests within the week, after which the subcommittee would conduct line-by-line deliberations.

positions.position: Supported the DND and AFP budgets and requested a brief district-related meeting with DND and AFP officials.
Strongly supported approval of the FY 2027 DND budget, citing the AFP's humanitarian assistance and airlift operations.
Supported restoring critical DND and attached-agency requirements that could be accommodated within available fiscal space and requested a prioritized institutional-amendment list for review.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (COA)

topics.topic: COA FY2027 budget and omitted priority requests
topics.summary: COA presented a FY2027 NEP budget of about 16.46 billion, with no capital outlay, while identifying substantial omitted requests for technology, citizen participatory audit, furniture, vehicles, and pre-audit staffing. Members questioned whether the allocation matched the government’s anti-corruption priority, citing the proposed 107 billion flood-control budget and COA’s reported PHP158 billion in DPWH notices. COA said it had proposed 146 additional pre-audit teams at an estimated 2.5 billion and explained that DBM had excluded several Tier 2 and capital-outlay items. Members also pressed COA on using its existing authority for pre-audit, expanding citizen participatory audit, and supporting a draft bill. Rep. Dumogan moved to seek an augmentation, and the committee requested detailed capital-outlay, omitted-item, and audit-report submissions. The issue landed with possible budget amendments still pending, but with COA commitments to submit the requested documents and add pre-audit personnel funding to its wish list.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish COA’s FY2027 funding level, including which Tier 2, capital outlay, staffing, pre-audit, technology, and citizen-participatory-audit requests were omitted. It also examined whether COA could expand pre-audit and anti-corruption work under its existing authority and what documents COA would submit to support possible budget amendments.
topics.agency_position: COA maintained that its FY2027 NEP allocation excluded important Tier 2 and capital-outlay requests, limiting its ability to expand technology, citizen participatory audit, staffing, and pre-audit capabilities. It supported additional resources and agreed to include pre-audit personnel funding in its wish list, submit detailed capital-outlay information, resubmit audit reports, and provide a position paper supporting the draft bill.
topics.outcome: The committee did not finally resolve COA’s FY2027 augmentation or restore capital outlay during the hearing. It moved toward possible institutional amendments and requested detailed wish-list, capital-outlay, and audit-report submissions; COA committed to provide the materials and include pre-audit personnel funding.

positions.position: Anti-corruption and flood-control oversight should receive stronger COA staffing, technology, special-audit, and capital-outlay support.
COA should use its existing constitutional and statutory authority to conduct pre-audit, and the budget should reflect anti-corruption as a government priority.
COA should prioritize technology and capital outlay, clarify omitted requests, and support the proposed revenue-side draft bill.
COA’s augmentation should include personnel and funding for pre-audit because it was identified as a priority in preventing corruption.
The committee should examine COA’s omitted capital-outlay and other requests through detailed submissions and consider possible institutional budget amendments.

thread.speaker: Nilda Plaras, COA official
thread.said: COA presented a FY2027 National Expenditure Program budget of 16,000,000,000 R16.46 million 527,000, consisting of an agency-specific budget of R14.774 billion and retirement and life insurance premiums of R1.272 billion. Personal services were R14.036 billion and maintenance and other operating expenses were R737.97 million.

thread.speaker: Nilda Plaras, COA official
thread.said: COA said it had no capital outlay in the FY2027 proposal because its capital-outlay request was not considered. It reported a personal-services increase of R179.185 million and a maintenance-and-other-operating-expenses reduction of R254.420 million.

thread.speaker: Gamaliel Cordoba, COA official
thread.said: In response to the member’s concerns about infrastructure and flood-control transactions, COA said its fraud audit office had examined around 50 fraud audits or transactions. COA submitted the relevant matters to the Ombudsman and its auditors served as witnesses.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: A COA official explained that a review of the approved plantilla had identified around 716 positions that had been deducted. COA filed a motion for reconsideration with DBM, which restored 332 positions.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: The official said the remaining balance after restoration was almost 400 positions. COA also reported that auditors were leaving for higher pay, proximity to home, flexible work arrangements, transfers, resignations, and optional retirement at age 60.

thread.speaker: Percival Sindania, member
thread.said: Rep. Sindania cited the 2027 proposed 107,000,000,000 flood-control budget under DPWH and asked about COA’s capacity to audit such projects, including stronger special audit teams and measures against anomalous or fraudulent projects.

thread.speaker: Douglas Malilin, COA official
thread.said: COA identified training in data analytics, stronger technology, and geo-tagging requirements for infrastructure projects as needed improvements. It said budget constraints limited the technology available and that it was coordinating with DPWH on geo-tagging and other requirements.

thread.speaker: Douglas Malilin, COA official
thread.said: On pre-audit, COA said it was looking for a middle ground through continuous audit without treating the process exactly as pre-audit. It also cited upskilling and technology as part of the response.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA said it had proposed 146 additional pre-audit teams composed of audit, technical, and administrative positions. It estimated the cost at more or less 2,500,000,000.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA reported that DPWH notices of suspension were PHP107.771 billion and notices of allowance were PHP51.27 billion, for a combined amount of PHP158 billion issued for DPWH during the year. The official argued that existing COA actions demonstrated the value of additional pre-audit teams.

thread.speaker: Percival Sindania, member
thread.said: Rep. Sindania asked the committee to direct COA to submit a progress report on its efforts concerning license renting and contractor monopolies.

thread.speaker: Gamaliel Cordoba, COA official
thread.said: COA clarified that annual audit reports were transmitted to audited agencies by June 30, after which agencies had 60 days to submit actions taken on audit observations and recommendations. The management responses would be appended before publication, which COA said could be done by October 31.

thread.speaker: Iris Marie Montes, member
thread.said: Rep. Montes said COA already had constitutional and statutory authority to conduct pre-audits and asked why it was not using that authority. She argued that anti-corruption priorities should be reflected in the budget and asked about the budget mechanism involving DBM.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA explained that DBM provided the budget ceiling for maintenance and other operating expenses and capital outlay, while DBM handled the personal-services proposal. COA submitted its Tier 2 requests with justifications, but several items were not included in the National Expenditure Program.

thread.speaker: Gamaliel Cordoba, COA official
thread.said: COA described citizen participatory audit as a program involving NGOs, CSOs, and private citizens who assist in auditing. It said the program remained small and that its expansion depended on the funding available to COA, particularly where manpower was limited.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA compared the FY2026 total allotment of 15,610,000,903 million dollars with the FY2027 amount of 16,046,000,527. It attributed the increase to the fourth tranche of salary standardization and the partial granting of the motion for reconsideration, while noting reductions in MOE and the exclusion of capital outlay.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA said it had prepared a letter requesting reconsideration before the Speaker of the House, subject to the chair’s approval. It identified omitted requests for semi-expendable items, citizen participatory audit MOE, ICT equipment, furniture and fixtures, and motor vehicles.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA listed semi-expendable items at 213,686,000, citizen participatory audit MOE at 40.734 million, ICT equipment at R525.405 million, furniture and fixtures for Building 2 at 1255230000, and motor vehicles for three officials at 5,600,000.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA explained that audit observation memoranda gave agencies an opportunity to explain or correct matters, followed by notices of disallowance or suspension when warranted. Matters indicating possible corruption were endorsed to the Ombudsman, whose preliminary investigation depended on COA’s submissions and prima facie evidence.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA said it agreed with Rep. Roman’s revenue-side proposal and would submit a position paper supporting his draft bill, although the official said the details would first have to be checked.

thread.speaker: Mauricio Domogan, member
thread.said: Rep. Dumogan asked why COA’s augmentation request did not include funding for additional personnel to implement pre-audit, despite COA’s identification of pre-audit as a priority.

thread.speaker: Salvador Pleyto, COA official
thread.said: COA answered that the listed items were those omitted from the NEP despite being proposed by COA. It agreed to add the amount recommended by the chair for pre-audit to its wish list.

thread.speaker: Mauricio Domogan, member
thread.said: Rep. Dumogan moved to ask the House leadership, through the Speaker, to augment COA’s budget for pressing priority needs, particularly the fight against corruption. The transcript records a second.

thread.speaker: Committee on Operations chair
thread.said: The Committee on Operations chair asked why COA’s FY2027 capital outlay was zeroed out and whether DBM had provided an explanation.

thread.speaker: Gamaliel Cordoba, COA official
thread.said: COA answered that DBM had provided no explanation for eliminating the capital-outlay proposal. The chair noted that the proposal included ICT, buildings, and vehicles, including an item for the NIR.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA said its ISSP was a complete five-year roadmap reviewed by DICT and endorsed to DBM. It emphasized digitalization, software subscriptions, and ICT equipment to improve audit quality.

thread.speaker: Committee on Operations chair
thread.said: The chair requested a detailed plan for the ICT capital-outlay request and additional information on building, other-structures, furniture, and fixture proposals.

thread.speaker: Gamaliel Cordoba, COA official
thread.said: COA described the building and infrastructure requests, including modernization of the main-building facade, fire-protection works, renovations, regional offices and training centers, records storage, electrical upgrades, and a powerhouse upgrade. It also identified furniture and fixtures, three vehicles, and ICT equipment and software as capital-outlay components.

thread.speaker: Committee on Operations chair
thread.said: The chair requested a full itemized list of COA’s capital-outlay proposal and a separate wish list of all items omitted from the NEP, so the budget amendments review subcommittee could consider institutional amendments.

thread.speaker: Committee on Operations chair
thread.said: The chair asked COA to provide the wish list within the week because the subcommittee was expected to convene the following week or the week after, before plenary consideration.

thread.speaker: Committee on Operations chair
thread.said: The chair also requested COA audit reports from the previous year, including reports relevant to DPWH, to support the committee’s analysis of agencies’ succeeding-year budget requirements.

thread.speaker: COA official
thread.said: COA committed to resubmit the requested materials and said it would send them again the following morning. The committee accepted the undertaking for use in its budget and DPWH deliberations.

topics.topic: COA capital outlay zeroed out in the FY2027 NEP
topics.summary: COA reported that its FY2027 capital outlay proposal had been excluded from the NEP, leaving the agency with no capital outlay despite requests for ICT, facilities, equipment, vehicles, and related investments. Members argued that the omission was inconsistent with the government's anti-corruption priority and pressed COA on pre-audit capacity, including 146 additional teams and an unclear estimate of around 2,500,000,000. COA explained that DBM set the relevant ceiling, that the omitted items were submitted as Tier Two requests, and that the ISSP had been reviewed by DICT and endorsed to DBM. COA identified a capital outlay request of R656.528 million, including PHP525.405 million for ICT and PHP125.523 million for furniture and fixtures, while other wish-list figures were also cited. Rep. Dumogan moved to seek augmentation, including for pre-audit personnel. The Committee on Operations requested detailed capital outlay and institutional-amendment documents, and COA agreed to submit them, leaving funding itself unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why COA's capital outlay request was omitted from the FY2027 NEP, what investments and capabilities were affected, and whether COA had alternative authority or budget mechanisms to implement pre-audit and other anti-corruption functions. It also sought to determine what additional funding, personnel, and supporting documents should be considered through institutional amendments.
topics.agency_position: COA said its capital outlay proposal was submitted as a Tier Two request but was not included in the FY2027 NEP, and it received no explanation from DBM for the zeroing out. COA maintained that the omitted ICT, facilities, equipment, vehicles, citizen participatory audit, and pre-audit personnel requirements were necessary to improve audit capacity, and agreed to add pre-audit personnel costs to its wish list and submit detailed supporting documents.
topics.outcome: The zeroing out of capital outlay was not explained by DBM and was not resolved during the hearing. COA undertook to submit detailed capital outlay, institutional-amendment, and pre-audit personnel requests for possible committee consideration and augmentation.

positions.position: The absence of capital outlay was inconsistent with the government's stated anti-corruption priority and threatened COA's capacity as a frontline audit institution.
COA already had constitutional and statutory authority to conduct pre-audits, and the authority and anti-corruption priority should be reflected in the budget even without a new bill.
The committee needed to understand the historical budget process and prioritize technology and capital outlay investments that could expand COA's audit capabilities.
Additional funding, including personnel for pre-audit teams, should be included in an augmentation request because pre-audit was a priority for preventing corruption.
The committee should advocate for COA's resources but first needed detailed capital outlay and institutional-amendment information to assess priorities within limited fiscal space.

topics.topic: Funding 146 pre-audit teams with personnel and geotagging
topics.summary: Rep. Percival Sindania and Rep. Mauricio Domogan raised the need for personnel, technology, geotagging, and funding to expand COA's pre-audit capacity. COA said it needed 146 additional pre-audit teams and gave estimates ranging from more or less around 2,500,000,000 to around 2,200,000,000, while citing DPWH notices totaling 158,000,000,000. Rep. Iris Marie Montes pressed COA on its existing constitutional and statutory authority to conduct pre-audit without waiting for legislation, and COA agreed that it could do so but said the bill would strengthen the mandate. Rep. Salvador Pleyto called for continued congressional support for COA's technical manpower and systems. Rep. Mauricio Domogan later noted that COA's listed augmentation did not include pre-audit personnel, after which COA undertook to add the requirement to its wish list and Dumogan moved for budget augmentation. The transcript recorded no final ruling or approved augmentation amount.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA had sufficient personnel, technology, and budget authority to create and operate 146 additional pre-audit teams, including geotagging or geomapping of infrastructure projects. Members also asked whether COA could use its existing authority and budget mechanisms to begin pre-audit and whether additional funding and personnel would be requested.
topics.agency_position: COA said it could conduct pre-audit under its existing constitutional and statutory authority, but it lacked the personnel and resources to implement it at the desired scale. It supported the proposed legislation, estimated the requirement for 146 additional pre-audit teams at around 2,200,000,000, and undertook to resubmit or include the requirement in its budget wish list.
topics.outcome: COA acknowledged that existing authority allowed it to conduct pre-audit but said implementation at scale required additional personnel and funding. It undertook to resubmit and include the pre-audit requirement in its wish list, while Dumogan moved for budget augmentation; no final committee ruling or approved amount was recorded.

positions.position: Supported additional personnel, training, technology, and capital outlay for COA, and questioned whether the budget reflected the government's anti-corruption priority.
Supported mandatory pre-audit coupled with geotagging or geomapping and said he and other members would support budget augmentation for the required personnel.
Argued that COA could already conduct pre-audit under its existing authority and that the authority and anti-corruption priority should be reflected in the budget even without waiting for a bill.
Supported strengthening COA with additional resources, technical manpower, systems, technology, and citizen participation.
Supported augmenting COA's budget, specifically criticizing the omission of additional personnel funding for pre-audit and moving for budget augmentation.

topics.topic: COA staffing losses and restored plantilla positions

COA said about 716 plantilla positions had been deducted from its original plantilla, of which 332 were restored through DBM action, leaving almost 400 positions still unfilled or unrestored; the transcript’s spoken subtraction was unclear. COA attributed auditor attrition to higher pay elsewhere, residence proximity, flexible work arrangements, transfers, resignations, and optional retirement at age 60. The agency said it needed 146 additional pre-audit teams and estimated the requirement at about 2.2 billion, while an earlier estimate was rendered as “2,500,000,000 statistics.” Rep. Mauricio Domogan supported mandatory pre-audit with geotagging and said members would support a budget motion for additional personnel. topics.outcome: The committee received COA’s explanation of the restored and remaining plantilla positions, attrition causes, and the estimated requirement for 146 additional pre-audit teams. COA committed to resubmit its estimate, while member support for funding and legislative action was expressed; final budget action and the requested progress report were not resolved in the excerpt.

De Morgan supported funding 146 additional pre-audit teams and making pre-audit coupled with geotagging or mapping mandatory before payment of government projects. He said members would support a later budget motion for the additional personnel.

topics.topic: DPWH flood-control project audits and notices
topics.summary: Rep. Sindania, Rep. de Morgan, Rep. Renee Co, and the Operations chair pressed COA on DPWH flood-control audits, pre-audit capacity, geotagging, audit notices, and resources. COA reported around 50 fraud-audited transactions or projects and cited DPWH notices of suspension of about 107.8 billion and notices of disallowance or charge of roughly 51.3 billion, with totals also stated as 158 billion. COA said 146 additional pre-audit teams would cost about 2.2 billion to 2.5 billion, while members supported additional resources and pre-audit linked to geotagging. Rep. Co requested a year-specific breakdown of DPWH and flood-control notices, because the issuance year did not necessarily match the year of the underlying transaction. COA undertook to submit flood-control audit materials, a master plan and compliance records, and the requested DPWH reports. The committee also requested detailed capital-outlay and audit-report submissions after noting that COA's capital-outlay proposal had been zeroed out, so the issue remained committed for follow-up rather than finally resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish COA's audit findings and enforcement actions involving DPWH, particularly flood-control projects, and whether COA had the personnel, technology, and capital resources to conduct more effective pre-audits and geotagging. Members also sought specific records on notices of suspension, disallowance, and charge, including figures attributable to flood-control projects.
topics.agency_position: COA said it was already auditing DPWH projects through fraud, compliance, and performance audits, coordinating with DPWH on geotagging, and using available data-analytics tools despite budget and capital-outlay constraints. It maintained that additional pre-audit capacity would require 146 teams and that it would submit more detailed DPWH, flood-control, audit, and capital-outlay records to the committee.
topics.outcome: The committee received COA's broad figures on DPWH notices and its explanation of the need for additional pre-audit teams, but it did not receive a definitive flood-control-specific breakdown. COA undertook to submit the requested flood-control, DPWH audit, CIF, capital-outlay, and institutional-amendment records, leaving the budget augmentation and detailed findings for subsequent committee consideration.

positions.position: Anti-corruption and flood-control oversight should be reflected in COA's resources, including capital outlay, staffing, training, and pre-audit capacity.
Pre-audit coupled with geotagging should be required before payment of government projects, and the budget should support the necessary personnel.
The committee needed year-specific DPWH and flood-control audit notices and records, as well as clearer oversight of confidential and intelligence funds.
COA should receive adequate resources, and the committee needed detailed capital-outlay and audit-report submissions to evaluate possible budget amendments and agency requirements.

topics.topic: Safeguards against manufactured savings and withheld SAROs
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned COA on whether earmarked funds remained traceable after Treasury used cash under the one-fund concept. COA said it monitored the funds, followed the money trail after release, and would flag expenditures outside the authorized purpose; DBM had also committed to place information on its portal. Nazal then raised DPWH projects that had SAROs, bidding, and validation under NDC five ninety five but allegedly lacked SAAs, asking why they were withheld and could later become manufactured savings. COA cited missing supporting documents and prior reversions caused by implementing-office unreadiness, agreed to submit a project list, and undertook to coordinate with DPWH. Nazal warned that withholding Congress-approved projects and augmenting other items with the resulting savings could let the executive rewrite the GAA. In the second round, COA agreed with the concern and promised to confirm reportedly ready projects with the DPWH central office, but no concrete safeguard was finalized.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether COA tracked earmarked funds after Treasury received them and whether cash fungibility could obscure their use. It also sought to determine why DPWH withheld or reverted Congress-approved projects, and what safeguards prevented implementable projects from being converted into manufactured savings and used for augmentation.
topics.agency_position: COA said it tracked earmarked and special funds, followed the money trail after release, and would flag use outside the authorized purpose. On DPWH projects, COA attributed some withheld SAAs to missing supporting documents and cited prior reversions caused by implementing-office unreadiness; it agreed to coordinate with DPWH, submit a project list, and confirm the status of reportedly ready projects.
topics.outcome: COA agreed in principle with the committee's concern and undertook coordination, reporting, and confirmation actions, but the record did not establish a completed safeguard or resolve whether projects had been improperly converted into manufactured savings. The second-round request for a concrete prevention mechanism remained unanswered in the transcript.

positions.position: Cash fungibility should not reduce transparency or accountability. Congress-approved, validated, and implementable projects should not be withheld, reverted, declared savings, or redirected through augmentation in a manner that effectively rewrites the GAA.
