thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Brian Poe asked whether the NBI had funding for attaches or representatives in Philippine embassies abroad, as authorized under RA 10687, section 7(f), with the funding to come from the NBI.

thread.speaker: NBI director
thread.said: The NBI director said placing attaches in selected areas was a future NBI objective because embassies in Europe and the US had helped address transnational crime. He said the plan would require additional agents and that the NBI currently had only about 300 agents in the Philippines.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe said it was alarming that the NBI had no funding for international agents or embassy representatives despite its responsibilities involving POGO, scam networks, cyber fraud, online gambling, Interpol cases, human trafficking, and online sexual exploitation of children. He urged the committee to consider funding for attaches during the budget deliberation.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe asked about legal-aid services for Filipinos without access to counsel, citing about 8,000,000 pesos for the DOJ Action Center or Katarungan Caravan. He asked whether about 15,000 people had been served in 2026 and whether the program was on track to exceed the previous year's 25,000 beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: DOJ official
thread.said: The DOJ official confirmed that the program concerned access to legal services, while identifying the Public Attorney's Office as the primary agency.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe asked whether the DOJ would open more Katarungan regional centers after establishing about nine centers, and whether funding was available for expansion.

thread.speaker: DOJ official
thread.said: The official referred to the DOJ optimization plan and resources for 250 field offices, although the machine-generated response did not clearly state the amount or a definite expansion schedule.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe said that, with only around 8,000,000 pesos, the Katarungan Caravan and DOJ Action Center had served more than 15,000 people and were on track to serve more than 25,000 by year-end. He estimated government spending at about 250 to 300 pesos per person and urged an increase in funding.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe asked PAO whether it could maintain its goal of one attorney per court with its current budget.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The PAO official said some district offices could support one attorney per court but that PAO remained short of personnel because it handled criminal, labor, and preliminary-investigation cases. PAO requested 559 additional items and supported the Katarungang Pambarangay program.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe compared PAO's fiscal year 2026 budget of about 6,600,000,000 with the current net amount of 7,100,000,000 and asked whether the increase of about 400,000,000,000 covered the requested staffing items.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The PAO official said the increase was not for new staffing but for mandatory SSL six increases and deficiencies involving 87 lawyers whose positions had been created previously by DBM.

thread.speaker: Brian Poe
thread.said: Poe clarified that the increase was funding for past creations or deficiencies rather than new positions. The PAO official confirmed that explanation.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The official attributed the increase to the higher salaries of newly hired lawyers, which were at par with new prosecutors, and reported service to 16,000,000 Filipinos in the previous year and about 6,000,000 as of June.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: PAO committed to assign more lawyers to the Katarungan Caravan and grassroots outreach, and said its lawyers were also assisting the DMW and OHA with overseas Filipino workers.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rufus Rodriguez asked the DOJ Secretary about the reduction in OSEC MOOE from 1.9 to 1.6, described as a 203,000,000 decrease, and asked what restoration was needed.

thread.speaker: Eric Bida, DOJ Secretary
thread.said: Secretary Eric Bida requested restoration to the 2026 level so the department would have sufficient resources to fulfill its mandate.

thread.speaker: Eric Bida, DOJ Secretary
thread.said: Bida identified reductions affecting the Office of Cybercrime, NCC, OSI, and IACAT and requested restoration to their 2026 levels. He gave the figure as 45.17 and approximately 30,000,000; the transcript is unclear as to the unit and exact allocation.

thread.speaker: Eric Bida, DOJ Secretary
thread.said: Bida also requested restoration of NBI ICT projects and programs that had been reduced in the proposed budget, citing the NBI's cybercrime and investigative responsibilities.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked whether the NBI budget had fallen from 3,791,000 to 2.9, a reduction of 882000023.2%. The figure and percentage were spoken in a garbled form.

thread.speaker: Ann Matibag, NBI director
thread.said: NBI Director Ann Matibag confirmed the reduction and explained that utilization had been affected by ICT projects requiring alignment and completion. She said the NBI had recognized the issue and was implementing a catch-up plan.

thread.speaker: Ann Matibag, NBI director
thread.said: Matibag said the NBI expected 90% utilization by December, with the remaining 2% for maintenance of ICT installations that had already been obligated.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez proposed restoring 882,000,000 to the NBI budget and asked whether the NBI director was satisfied with that restoration.

thread.speaker: Ann Matibag, NBI director
thread.said: Matibag raised a separate request for higher hazard pay. She said NBI agents were receiving only MXN4000 monthly and requested at least PHP15000 monthly, citing transfers between provinces and 24/7 operations involving OSAEC and cybercrime.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said, "15,000? Approved," expressly characterizing the statement as his own support for the requested hazard-pay level.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The PAO official said PAO needed 559 lawyers and was amenable to receiving half the number. The official also requested 400 staff because no staff positions had been created.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The official estimated that 200 lawyers and 400 staff would cost around 600,000,000, then revised the estimate to around 700,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said the committee would try to provide about 700,000,000 for the requested PAO lawyers and staff.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked why the Bureau of Immigration budget had been reduced by 1,600,000 billion and what priority restoration the BI wanted.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The BI official requested capital outlay for post-construction work on the new BI building and for locally funded IT systems and infrastructure projects for the main building and support offices.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official stated that the total request was billion 227,800 and; the amount is garbled and unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez asked the OSG representative whether additional funding was needed despite an increase in the OSG budget.

thread.speaker: Barrenevil Barabi, OSG official
thread.said: The OSG official said the 248,000,000 increase, bringing the amount to what was transcribed as 2.55, would fund the first installment for a building to be procured through GSIS lease-to-own financing.

thread.speaker: Barrenevil Barabi, OSG official
thread.said: The official cited IISP 123,000,000 for the installment, a total building cost of PHP4.5 billion, and an estimated PHP 800,000,000 to 1,000,000,000 for the OSG main building; the transcript's reference to IISP is unclear.

thread.speaker: Barrenevil Barabi, OSG official
thread.said: Barabi requested 123,000,000 for the OSG computerization and digital-transformation program. Rodriguez said digitalization was very important and supported the request.

thread.speaker: Sarah Elago
thread.said: Sarah Elago asked whether the NBI had a line item for gender-sensitive investigation and interrogation training, particularly for the Division on Violence Against Women and Their Children.

thread.speaker: NBI official
thread.said: The NBI official said the programs were included under the NBI's GAD program, with additional funding through the academy. New academy entrants would receive the training, and agents were also sent to international training programs.

thread.speaker: NBI official
thread.said: The official confirmed that the training applied to all NBI members, particularly agents.

thread.speaker: NBI official
thread.said: In response to Elago's fragmented questions about critical-incident stress debriefing and personnel support, the official cited the human-trafficking division, the Bousi, and the behavioral science unit, with coordination from social workers.

topics.topic: PAO staffing, legal aid, and Katarungan Caravan expansion
topics.summary: Rep. Brian Poe asked whether the DOJ action center and Katarungan Caravan had enough resources to meet demand and expand beyond roughly nine regional centers. DOJ officials confirmed the program's legal-services role and identified PAO as the primary provider, while Poe cited around 8,000,000 pesos in funding, more than 15,000 people served, and a projection of more than 25,000. Poe also asked whether PAO could maintain one attorney per court; PAO answered that some offices could do so but requested 559 additional lawyer items because of its broad caseload. PAO said its budget increase largely covered mandatory increases and past deficiencies, including 87 lawyers, rather than new positions. PAO later estimated that 200 lawyers and 400 staff would cost around 600,000,000 to 700,000,000, and Rodriguez said he would try to secure about 700,000,000. PAO committed to assigning lawyers to the Katarungan Caravan and other outreach, but final funding action was not recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DOJ legal-aid programs, including the Katarungan Caravan and DOJ action center, had sufficient funding to meet demand and expand outreach. It also asked whether PAO could maintain the goal of one attorney per court and what additional personnel and funding were needed.
topics.agency_position: DOJ and PAO officials said legal-aid demand was being addressed through the Katarungan Caravan, DOJ action center, regional centers, field offices, and PAO outreach. PAO said it could staff some courts at one lawyer per court but remained deficient by 559 lawyer items, while the budget increase largely covered mandatory increases and past deficiencies rather than new positions.
topics.outcome: The committee received the agencies' explanations and expressed support for expanding legal aid and PAO staffing. PAO committed to supporting outreach, while the proposed additional personnel funding remained subject to committee action and was not finally approved in the transcript.

positions.position: Supported increasing funding for the Katarungan Caravan, DOJ action center, and PAO so legal aid could reach more poor Filipinos and expand grassroots outreach.
Supported restoring or increasing PAO funding and indicated that he would work to secure about 700,000,000 for a combination of additional lawyers and staff.
Requested 559 additional lawyer items, was amenable to receiving a smaller number of lawyer items, and emphasized the need for staff positions as court branches continued to be created.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez pressed for the cost of providing half the requested lawyers and asked what number of lawyers and staff PAO could accept.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The official's response was garbled, referring to 2,225 new lawyers and a request for 400 staff; the precise intended number of lawyers is unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked for the total cost of the proposed PAO lawyers and staff.

thread.speaker: PAO official
thread.said: The official estimated that 200 lawyers and 400 staff could cost around 600,000,000, then revised the estimate to around 700,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez said 700,000,000 appeared reasonable and said he would try to secure that amount, citing the continuing creation of court branches and the need for prosecutors and PAO lawyers.

topics.topic: Bureau of Immigration modernization, e-gates, and BMIS funding
topics.summary: Rep. Pachernos asked about e-gate operations and modernization procurement, and the Bureau reported 78 e-gates at Terminals 1 and 3 and described Phase one, Phase two, and Phase three funding. Allan Ty then questioned BMIS's purpose, total cost, government share, and relationship to the government-funded e-gates project. The Bureau said the private proponent would shoulder about 10.7 billion for the first five years and described additional twenty-year costs, although the stated government-share figures were unclear. Members identified substantial unobligated allotments, including 4.071 for 2025 and 3,558,000,000 for 2026, which the Bureau attributed to failed bidding, rebidding, and revisions after donated e-gates required changes to the procurement plan. Commissioner Beado and Commissioner Viejo committed to complete procurement and fully obligate the affected funds by November, while some release and disbursement figures were to be verified later. Mr. Erviato clarified that the broader CAES-integrated border-control system was under a PPP arrangement and was distinct from the appropriated e-gates project.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the operational status, procurement progress, costs, funding sources, obligations, and implementation schedule of the Bureau of Immigration's e-gates, modernization, and border-management information system projects. Members also examined why substantial allotments remained unobligated and how the government-funded e-gates project differed from the proposed PPP-based border-control system.
topics.agency_position: The Bureau stated that the government-funded e-gates modernization effort was separate from the larger PPP-based BMIS or enhanced border-control system, although the e-gates would be integrated with the CAES platform. It attributed unobligated allotments and delays to failed bidding, rebidding, and revisions required after donated e-gates created a risk of duplicative procurement, while committing to complete the affected obligations and modernization activities.
topics.outcome: The Bureau attributed the unobligated allotments to failed bidding, rebidding, and procurement revisions and committed to full obligation by November and to completing the modernization program. The committee also established that the government-funded e-gates project was distinct from the proposed PPP-based BMIS or enhanced border-control system, but exact release and disbursement figures remained subject to confirmation.

positions.position: Pressed the Bureau for a concrete status report on e-gate operations, modernization procurement, phase schedules, and service-level arrangements, and commended efforts for the Bureau.
Sought to reconcile the BMIS and e-gates funding figures, identify the government's financial exposure, and explain the large unobligated allotments.

Questioned the classification of BMIS, e-gates, and PPP appropriations under one program and required the Bureau to account for delayed obligations and distinguish the government project from the PPP system.

thread.speaker: Rep. Pachernos
thread.said: Rep. Pachernos asked the Bureau of Immigration for the status of the e-gates and modernization program, including operations at EEA, Clark, MacTan, Cebu, and Davao, procurement for Phases one and two, and service-level agreements with IT providers.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official reported that Terminal 1 had eighteen e-gates, with twelve for arrivals and the remainder for departures, while Terminal 3 had 30 arrival e-gates and 60 departure e-gates, for a total of 78 at Terminals 1 and 3.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said Phase one had been awarded for 2,025,000,000,000, with an intended budget of PHP1.9 billion and PHP400 million. The statement also referred to continuing procurement.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official stated that the Phase II project was worth PHP1.3 billion and that Phase three was 565,000,000. The official committed that the 2025 catch-up plan would be fully obligated by November 2026 and that the Phase II e-gates project worth 1,300,000,000 would be fully obligated by November 2025.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said the Bureau had been conducting weekly meetings, while the projects remained constantly under review.

thread.speaker: Rep. Pachernos
thread.said: Rep. Pachernos made a follow-up inquiry about Phase two, but the exchange was interrupted and the transcript does not capture a complete question.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official reiterated that Phase two would be fully obligated by November 2026.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked Commissioner Beado to explain the border management information system, or BMIS.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: Commissioner Beado described BMIS as a large-scale, technology-, AI-, and biometric-driven border-control system intended to extend Philippine border control beyond the physical border and prevent an unqualified passenger from entering even while still in another country.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked for the total project cost of BMIS and the government's share.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner said the first five years would be shouldered by the private proponent at about 10,700,000,000, while the next twenty years would involve additional capital and maintenance expenses of about US52.5 billion dollars. The stated government-share figure was garbled: the commissioner said it would amount to four passengers, then referred to 4, with 3.80 going to the private proponent and 20¢ to the Philippine government.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the national government had made any allocation for BMIS.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner said the government was adopting a step-ladder approach and that existing government funding was insufficient. The PPP project was intended to cover the resulting border-control shortfalls.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty cited a 2024 allocation of 4 point something billion for BMIS and asked the commissioner to confirm it.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner recalled that the 2024 allocation was 1,900,000,000 for the e-gates project.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty pressed whether government funds had been used for the BMIS project.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner clarified that the government funding was for the e-gates project, not the complete border-control system proposed by the private proponent. The initial funding was around 900,000,000, but the winning bidder's accepted proposal amounted to PHP1.5 billion.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked how much of the 1.5 billion appropriation had been obligated and disbursed.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: Commissioner Beado said he would confirm the figures with a colleague.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner stated that the original allotment was 1,900,000,000 and that 1,500,000,000 had been obligated.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked how much remained unobligated after the DBM release corresponding to 1,900,000,000.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner initially answered that 1,300,000,000 was unobligated, identifying it as Phase two.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty objected that he had asked about Phase one first and directed the commissioner not to move ahead to Phase two.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner clarified that Phase one had been fully obligated.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner said the original amount was R1.9 million, with savings of R400 million, and that R1.5 million had been released.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked how much of the Bureau's 2025 appropriation for the project remained unused.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner identified 1.3 as the 2025 amount and then clarified that it had not yet been obligated because the Phase two terms of reference still had to be transmitted to the Department of Justice for review.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the 2025 allotment had been released through a SARO and then asked for an explanation of the Bureau's 2025 unobligated allotments reported as R4 billion dollars.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner confirmed that the SARO had been released.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty challenged the apparent inconsistency between the earlier 400 figure and the reported R4.071 billion unobligated amount.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner attributed the unobligated amounts to delays in the e-gates phases. Phase one, funded under the fiscal year 2024 GAA in an amount that was unclear in the transcript, went through a failed competitive bidding and rebidding; a donation of e-gates from New NAIA Infrastructure Corporation then required revisions to the technical specifications and deployment plan. The delay in Phase one affected Phase two funded at PHP1.3 billion and Phase three funded at PHP565 million.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The commissioner said the Bureau had completed the required revisions, was expediting procurement, and would award Phase two and the fiscal years 2025 and 2026 projects within the current year.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Beado
thread.said: The Bureau committed to fully implementing the modernization program as scheduled.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked Commissioner Viejo how much had been allocated under the fiscal year 2024 GAA program Enhancement of Border Management Information System.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: After checking the records, Commissioner Viejo stated that the amount was 1,900,000,000, with PHP700,000,000 pertaining to an information, computerization, and technology project.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the amounts were presented under one program, citing his record's 2,600,000,000 figure.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo confirmed that the amounts pertained to one program.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked for the allocation under the same program in the 2025 GAA.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo stated that the 2025 amount was JPY 2,100,000,000, then explained that it included the e-gates Phase two amount of R1.3 billion.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the combined total was 3.8.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo confirmed the total as 3.8 and agreed that it was presented as one program.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked for the 2026 allocation.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo stated that the 2026 allocation was JPY6974542000.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked how much of the 2024 allocation had been obligated and how much had been released.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo said that almost 98% had been obligated in 2024.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo said the Bureau needed to check its records and requested permission to provide the 2024 release figures later.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo stated that the 2026 capital outlay had not been obligated: zero.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the proposed expenditure program confirmed an unobligated allotment of 4.071 for 2025.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo confirmed the 4.071 unobligated allotment and said it pertained to the Enhancement of Border Management Information System program.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether 2026 also had an unobligated allotment of 3,558,000,000.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo confirmed the 3,558,000,000 unobligated appropriation.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked why the allotments for the program remained unobligated.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo attributed the delay to a failure of bidding in the latter part of 2024 and the resulting rebidding process, which took several months.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo committed to fully obligate the amount by November of this year and said the Bureau was holding weekly meetings.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether this program was different from the project discussed earlier.

thread.speaker: Commissioner Viejo
thread.said: Commissioner Viejo said it was different: the e-gates project and an enhanced border-control system were proposed under a public-private partnership arrangement.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked the agency to distinguish the two programs.

thread.speaker: Mr. Erviato
thread.said: Mr. Erviato said the e-gates project would be integrated with the CAES project, which would also connect with Interpol, Advance Passenger Information System, biometrics, digital facial images, reactive screening, and open-source intelligence.

thread.speaker: Allan Ty
thread.said: Allan Ty asked whether the broader system was under the PPP program.

thread.speaker: Mr. Erviato
thread.said: Mr. Erviato confirmed that it was under the PPP program.

topics.topic: CAIS immigration-security PPP, fees, costs, and data control
topics.summary: A minority member and Edgar Erice questioned the status and structure of the proposed CAIS immigration-security PPP, including its proposed fee and reliance on private financing. The agency said the project remained under review, no contract had been signed, and the private proponent proposed capitalization of about 10.7 billion for the first five years, with further upgrades over twenty years. The discussion produced conflicting or unclear figures for total cost and collections, including R10.744 million dollars, R10.7 billion dollars, PHP52.5 billion, about two zero two billion in collections, and a stated 95% private and 5% government sharing arrangement. Erise also challenged foreign access to immigration data, while the agency said sovereign control and data control would remain with the Philippine government. The agency undertook to submit the proposed contract and terms of reference before plenary. Commissioner Viejo separately explained that border-management and e-gates allotments remained unobligated because of failed bidding and rebidding and committed to full obligation by November of this year.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status, structure, cost, funding, fee, and data-governance arrangements of the proposed CAIS immigration-security PPP. Members also sought to determine the relationship between CAIS and existing border-management and e-gates appropriations, and whether the project documents should be provided before plenary consideration.
topics.agency_position: The agency presented CAIS as a necessary integrated aviation and border-security platform that would be privately capitalized and would impose a service fee while remaining subject to government review. It maintained that Philippine government control over immigration functions and data would be retained, that no contract had yet been signed, and that CAIS could be integrated with the e-gates and other border-management systems.
topics.outcome: The CAIS proposal and fee remained under review, with no contract signed. The agency committed to submit documents before plenary, but questions about the fee, project-cost figures, private-government sharing, and data control remained open; related border-management funds were also subject to a later obligation commitment.

positions.position: Questioned the justification for passing modernization costs to travelers through a CAIS fee and pressed for clarification of the fee's status.
Raised concerns about the proposed PPP, the service fee, the large private share of collections, foreign access to immigration data, and the need to review the contract documents before plenary.
Sought to reconcile border-management appropriations, obligations, and unobligated allotments and required clarification of how the e-gates project related to the CAIS PPP.

Defended the border-management and e-gates funding as necessary for operations, attributed unobligated amounts to failed bidding and rebidding, and committed to full obligation by November of this year.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member asked about CAIS and identified a proposed additional "480 pesos fee" for the service.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration commissioner
thread.said: The commissioner confirmed that the proposed CAIS fee was correct.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member asked whether alternative funding sources had been considered and questioned why modernization costs should be passed on to the traveling public under a PPP.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration commissioner
thread.said: The commissioner said no alternative funding source had been discussed because the proposal came from a private proponent. He said the project would provide an integrated border-security platform with biometrics, advanced analytics, and a passenger-information system, and that no national-government program was currently funded at that level.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration commissioner
thread.said: He said the private proponent proposed capitalization of 10,700,000,000 for the next five years, with system upgrades every four years for the next twenty year period, at no cost to the government.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member pressed the commissioner on how the project could be described as having no cost to government while still imposing the fee.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration commissioner
thread.said: The commissioner clarified that the fee was 240 per ticket, or 4.80 for a round-trip ticket. He said the charge was below comparable fees in other countries.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration commissioner
thread.said: He cited passenger charges of about PHP2600 in Australia, PHP2400 in Singapore, about PHP1200 in Japan, about PHP1500 in Hong Kong, and about PHP1800 in Thailand.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member asked whether imposition of the fee would remain.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration commissioner
thread.said: The commissioner said the fee was still under review, no contract had been signed, and the Department of Justice had completed its review while the Department of Finance and other concerned agencies were still reviewing it.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise asked for the status of the CAIS, identified as the Civil Aviation Immigration Security Services project, and requested an explanation of the contract.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said the project was under contract review, with final screening by the Department of Finance, the Office of the Solicitor General, and the PPP Center. The official confirmed that no contract had been signed.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise asked whether the project used a build, train, maintain, and transfer modality.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official confirmed the build, train, maintain, and transfer modality and said the PPP was proposed by Securiport.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official described an integrated aviation and border-security platform using biometrics, advanced analytics, passenger information, facial-image access, risk scoring, biographic comparisons against criminal and sanctions databases, deception-detection analytics, and AI-assisted open-source intelligence.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said the system was intended to help immigration officers combat human trafficking, smuggling of persons, drugs and weapons, terrorism, money laundering, tax evasion, and organized crime.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise asked whether Securiport was foreign or Filipino-owned.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said Security Ports Limited was incorporated in the United States in 2000 and had submitted an unsolicited proposal that went through the PPP Center, DOJ, and the Bureau of Immigration.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise asked whether a foreign company would have access to Philippine immigration data and followed up by asking who would control the servers and whether the company would initially access the data.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said the sovereign function and control would remain with the Philippine government. He said the company would provide tools and train personnel, and stated that, as far as he knew, it would not control the data.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise said he had filed a resolution to investigate the contract and questioned charging a service fee for a function he regarded as a core responsibility of government funded through taxes.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official acknowledged the member's position and said the proposed charge was a security service fee. The remainder of the explanation was garbled in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official reiterated the comparison with other countries, stating that Australia charges about 2,600, Hong Kong 1,800, Japan 1,200, Singapore 2,400, and the Philippines 2.40 pesos.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise stated that the total project cost was R10.744 million dollars.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official described the first five years as R10.7 billion dollars and said the proponent committed to technology, systems, and training upgrades every four years over a twenty year period.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said the initial amount was 10.7 and that an additional PHP52.5 billion was expected over the twenty year period, for a stated total of 62. He said these terms were in the proposed contract and remained under review.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise stated that estimated total collections were about two zero two billion and that the private corporation's share was 192,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official stated that 3.80 goes to the proponent and 0.2 goes to the Philippine government. The transcript then records Erise characterizing this as 95% of collections to the private provider and 5% to government.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice
thread.said: Erise questioned why the government share would fund another project and challenged the characterization of the 5% as something other than profit.

thread.speaker: Bureau of Immigration official
thread.said: The official said the 5% was a sharing arrangement between the private proponent and government, not simply profit, and referred to the Swiss challenge process and notices sent to potential challengers.

thread.speaker: Edgar Erice

topics.topic: Immigration enforcement and border-control staffing
topics.summary: Rep. Percy Sandania asked BI to clarify Agnes Callamard's entry-restriction or blacklist status and raised concerns about restrictions affecting human-rights advocates. Commissioner Oviedo described BI's international and internal blacklist-review processes and said the bureau would review Callamard's status and the applicable guidelines. Edgar Erice raised allegations involving 100,000 fake Filipinos and 200,000 illegal aliens, mostly Chinese, using fraudulent documents, and cited payments of 5,000,010 million pesos; the amount was unclear as spoken. A BI official said the information came from government intelligence sources and undertook to relay the source after the meeting. A DOJ official said Immigration Act amendments were pending and committed to a roadmap and consultation, while Caloy Bolilia pressed BI on alleged multinational groups and border-control funding. BI warned that a decreased border-control budget would substantially affect operations.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the Bureau of Immigration's entry-restriction status for Agnes Callamard and the basis for reported figures on fake Filipinos and illegal aliens. Members also pressed the DOJ and BI on enforcement powers, alleged multinational groups, and whether reduced border-control funding would impair operations.
topics.agency_position: BI said it uses Interpol, fugitive-status information, and its internal blacklist-review process to assess entry restrictions, and it was willing to review Agnes Callamard's status. On immigration enforcement, BI said intelligence could support detention and deportation, while the DOJ said additional Immigration Act powers and a roadmap were needed. BI also stated that a reduced border-control budget would significantly affect operations.
topics.outcome: The Callamard matter was left with BI's undertaking to review her status and applicable guidelines. The alleged fake-Filipino and illegal-alien figures were not independently substantiated during the hearing; the DOJ committed to a roadmap and consultation, while BI warned that reduced border-control funding would impair operations.

positions.position: He opposed using immigration restrictions or blacklist procedures as a political weapon against human-rights defenders and other international advocates, and welcomed a review of the relevant guidelines.

He asserted that large numbers of fake Filipinos and illegal aliens were using fraudulent documents, supported amending the Immigration Act, and emphasized both enforcement and possible government revenue.
He pressed BI to investigate alleged multinational groups and argued that reduced border-control funding would undermine immigration enforcement.

topics.topic: BuCor prison decongestion, NBP closure, and inmate transfers
topics.summary: Rep. Pagenos opened the issue by asking BuCor about regionalization, overcrowding, and the target of closing NBP by 2028. BuCor cited regional-facility and capital-outlay figures, reported additional capacity targets totaling 11,390 PDL, and said an NBP-property initiative could generate 8,000,000,000 over five years. Members later sought confirmation that the 2028 target remained achievable, questioned transfer conditions, and emphasized the Nelson Mandela Rules, especially placement near inmates' homes. Rep. Rennyko specifically cited the reported transfer of 15,730 inmates and asked how transportation, security, infrastructure, medical services, and staffing were funded and provided. BuCor said transfers were made yearly from its MOE budget, costing about 20 to 15 to 20,000 per transfer as spoken, and said NBP congestion had fallen from 300% to almost 200%. BuCor undertook to submit a facility-by-facility transfer list, while the DOJ also undertook to furnish budget-utilization information; conflicting congestion figures and the adequacy of receiving facilities remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether BuCor was on track to decongest and eventually close the New Bilibid Prison by 2028, whether regional prison facilities had sufficient capacity and funding, and how inmate transfers were being conducted. Members also asked about compliance with the Nelson Mandela Rules, the logistical and budgetary requirements of transferring 15,730 inmates, and whether transferred inmates were being placed near their homes where possible.
topics.agency_position: BuCor said it was gradually reducing congestion through yearly transfers, regionalization, and construction or expansion of dormitory and other prison capacity, with 2028 as the target period for decongestion and NBP closure. It said transfers were funded from BuCor's existing MOE budget, NBP congestion had fallen from 300% to almost 200%, and additional capacity for 11,000 plus PDL was expected by 2028.
topics.outcome: BuCor maintained that it was progressing toward the 2028 decongestion and NBP-closure objective, but the hearing did not establish a fully documented transfer schedule, complete receiving-facility capacity assessment, or definitive resolution of the conflicting congestion figures. The requested budget-utilization data and facility-by-facility transfer list remained commitments for subsequent submission.

positions.position: Supported prison decongestion and regionalization but sought clarification of BuCor's overcrowding figures and requested current budget-utilization data.
Sought assurances that BuCor remained on track for the 2028 NBP decongestion target and that inmate transfers were not generating unresolved complaints.
Pressed BuCor to clarify the transfer status of Major General Jovito Palparan and raised continuing concerns about illegal drug activity inside prison facilities.

Supported the NBP closure and decongestion effort but insisted that transfers have adequate logistical, medical, staffing, and infrastructure support and comply with the Nelson Mandela Rules and human-rights safeguards.

topics.topic: BuCor inmate food, facility capacity, and transfer infrastructure
topics.summary: Caloy Bolilia raised an apparent BuCor funding gap involving inmate food requirements and facilities and elicited a reported 204% congestion rate. Rep. Rennyko emphasized the Nelson Mandela Rules, adequate receiving facilities and services, proximity to inmates' homes, due process, and human rights. topics.question: The committee sought to establish the scale of BuCor's inmate food, facility, medical-service, transportation, and security requirements, particularly in light of congestion and the planned closure of New Bilibid Prison. topics.topic: BuCor unaccounted funds and cashless inmate collections
topics.summary: A committee member questioned BuCor about reported trust funds of about 6 to 7 million at the Correctional Institution for Women and asked for an investigation update. BuCor said the investigation had concluded the previous Saturday, that it was awaiting the report, and that unaccounted PERA totaled 6,454,405. The committee also raised collection and cashless-system concerns, and the chair requested the investigation status. Rep. Sarah Elago then asked whether internal auditing could cover cashless transactions in all BuCor prisons and penal farms. BuCor said the audit was already being conducted and committed to do the broader work the following week. It also said its cashless inmate-transaction policy guidelines and procedures were already effective, but the investigation outcome remained pending.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status of the investigation into unaccounted trust funds at the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW), including the amount involved and the responsible office. It also asked whether BuCor could extend internal auditing and harmonize cashless inmate-transaction rules across all prisons and penal farms.
topics.agency_position: BuCor stated that the investigation into the unaccounted PERA had concluded and that it was awaiting the report, with the unaccounted amount identified as 6,454,405. It said cashless-system auditing was already being undertaken, committed to extending the audit to other prisons and penal farms, and said cashless inmate-transaction guidelines and procedures were already effective.
topics.outcome: The investigation remained pending the written report, although BuCor identified the unaccounted PERA as 6,454,405 and committed to provide an update. BuCor also committed to broaden the cashless-system audit, while stating that governing cashless-transaction procedures were already effective.

topics.topic: DOJ vacancies, prosecutorial positions, and NPS staffing
topics.summary: Rep. Pagenos requested comprehensive vacancy data from DOJ, and an agency official reported 7,651 authorized Office of the Secretary positions, with 6,145 filled and 1,506 vacant. DOJ also reported that prosecutorial positions had increased from 2,966 to 3,968, with 103 applicants, and said appointment processing had been reduced to four to five months. Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores questioned why prosecutor positions for newly created courts were triggered only after Supreme Court organization; DOJ acknowledged that this caused delays and said it was pursuing 1,000 additional positions, with a target of about 4,600 positions before June 2028. PAO officials said they needed 559 lawyers, or an alternative package involving 200 lawyers and 400 staff, estimated at around 700,000,000. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez said he would work for the PAO funding, but the record did not show a final appropriation.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the extent of DOJ plantilla and prosecutorial vacancies, how quickly vacant positions were being filled, and whether the National Prosecution Service had enough positions for existing and newly created courts. It also examined whether the Public Attorney’s Office needed additional lawyers and staff to keep pace with court expansion.
topics.agency_position: DOJ officials said the Office of the Secretary had substantial vacancies but that the department was accelerating appointment processing and recruiting for the NPS. They maintained that new prosecutorial positions were triggered only after the Supreme Court organized a court, while acknowledging that court organization and staffing delays were a practical problem. PAO officials said they needed additional lawyers and staff because court expansion was continuing.
topics.outcome: The DOJ agreed to submit comprehensive vacancy data, while the NPS expansion and the timing of prosecutor appointments remained dependent on DBM action and Supreme Court court organization. The committee expressed support for additional PAO staffing, but no final appropriation or staffing authorization was recorded.

positions.position: Supported obtaining a comprehensive vacancy report, including vacancies in DOJ offices and attached agencies and positions open for applications.
Questioned the policy of waiting for Supreme Court organization before requesting prosecutor positions, because newly created courts could remain unorganized and understaffed for years.
Supported additional PAO lawyer and staff positions and undertook to work for funding of around 700,000,000.

topics.topic: DOJ petition-for-review backlog and case-disposition performance
topics.summary: DOJ officials presented high NPS case-disposition and prosecution-success rates, including 395,780 disposed cases out of a 428,779 caseload in 2025 and a 90.84% prosecution success rate. Members then distinguished those field-office indicators from the separate petition-for-review backlog before the Secretary, reported at about 16,000 cases from 2020 to November 11, 2025, plus approximately 10,000 cases filed earlier. Secretary Vida said his office had resolved almost 500, or roughly 2.5% of the 16,000-case group, and had delegated work to eight undersecretaries with a target of 800 cases per month. Members questioned whether the PSR overstated actual conviction performance and requested separate graft, corruption, drug, filing, disposition, and conviction data. Rep. Luizco also sought review and status data for terrorism-related cases under the DOJ's stricter evidentiary standard. The DOJ committed to submit the requested disaggregated data and backlog breakdowns, leaving the underlying backlog unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the size and age of the DOJ's petition-for-review backlog, the rate at which the Office of the Secretary was disposing of those petitions, and whether the DOJ's broader prosecution and conviction indicators accurately reflected case outcomes. Members also asked whether the DOJ's stricter evidentiary standard would improve case quality and requested disaggregated data on prosecution, conviction, dismissal, filing, and terrorism-related cases.
topics.agency_position: The DOJ stated that its NPS performance remained high, but acknowledged that the separate petition-for-review backlog was substantial and was not captured by the field-office disposition indicators. The DOJ said it had delegated new petitions to eight undersecretaries, established a target of 800 monthly dispositions, was reviewing older cases through task forces and publication, and would submit disaggregated backlog, filing, disposition, conviction, and case-type data.
topics.outcome: The DOJ answered that the NPS performance indicators did not include petitions for review pending before the Secretary's office. The petition backlog remained largely unresolved: the DOJ reported about 16,000 cases from 2020 to November 11, 2025, approximately 10,000 older cases, and only around 400 to almost 500 resolved cases; the DOJ committed to submit detailed breakdowns and related prosecution data.

positions.position: The petition-for-review process required scrutiny because of a longstanding backlog and its effect on timely remedies for litigants.

The DOJ's high PSR could obscure lower or category-specific conviction outcomes, particularly in graft, corruption, and drug cases; government agencies needed better coordination and a consolidated conviction database.

The stricter evidentiary standard should be tested against filing, disposition, conviction, and dismissal data, and pending terrorism-related cases should be reviewed for legal and evidentiary deficiencies.
The committee needed a separate performance measure and year-by-year breakdown for petitions for review because the NPS disposition rate did not cover the Secretary's backlog.

topics.topic: DOJ evidentiary threshold and terrorism-financing case review
topics.summary: Rep. Renee Luizco questioned DOJ's 2024 move from a probable-cause threshold to reasonable certainty of conviction and asked whether it had reduced filings or changed conviction rates. DOJ acknowledged fewer filings but characterized them as quality cases, while the Chair cited about 395,000 preliminary investigations and promised disaggregated data. Luizco then raised dismissed terrorism-financing and counterterrorism cases, including cases involving jurisdictional defects, and asked whether older or pending cases would be withdrawn or reviewed. DOJ said older cases would be scrutinized before elevation, while pending cases could not simply be withdrawn and could be challenged through certiorari where appropriate. Luizco requested an update on 106 task-force cases and described coordination questions involving the Anti-Terror Council, military, intelligence community, and Bureau of Immigration. The Chair undertook to submit the requested material, but the disposition of the cited cases and the broader review remained open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how DOJ's 2024 shift from a probable-cause evidentiary threshold to a reasonable-certainty-of-conviction standard affected filing, disposition, and conviction rates. It also sought DOJ's position on reviewing terrorism-financing and counterterrorism cases filed under the former standard, including pending cases and coordination with other agencies.
topics.agency_position: DOJ said the stricter standard resulted in fewer filings but was intended to produce quality cases. It said pre-filing review would test older cases against the department's required quantum, while pending court cases could not automatically be withdrawn; DOJ would consider available legal options, including certiorari, and coordinate with the Anti-Terror Council, military, and intelligence community.
topics.outcome: DOJ answered that older cases would be scrutinized before elevation and that pending cases would be assessed within the limits of ongoing court proceedings, with possible recourse through certiorari. The committee requested case-level and disposition data and additional material on interagency operations; submission of the requested information was committed, while the effect on the cited pending cases remained unresolved.

positions.position: She supported scrutiny of weak, legally defective, or insufficiently supported terrorism-related cases and pressed DOJ to review older and pending cases, provide disposition data, and clarify interagency safeguards.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She requested figures on disposition, conviction, and filing rates and asked whether the data could be submitted to the committee.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair cited 395,000 preliminary investigations and said DOJ would provide disaggregated data showing resolutions for filing and dismissal.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She raised terrorism-financing cases that had been filed in court but were later dismissed, citing People versus Munoz, People versus Aliques, People versus Estolioso, and People versus Lemita. She said the cases involved jurisdictional defects and, in the last case mentioned, a prosecutor's request for additional data and communications.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She asked whether DOJ's evidentiary threshold could prevent cases from being filed, or whether courts would continue dismissing cases after filing.

thread.speaker: Prosecutive Attorney General
thread.said: The Prosecutive Attorney General said prosecutors may be convinced that the evidence meets the beyond-reasonable-doubt standard, while the court may consider factors beyond the prosecution's control. He agreed that cases are sometimes dismissed and emphasized that a prosecutor is only as good as the evidence available.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She asked whether DOJ would dismiss or withdraw cases found by courts to lack sufficient legal basis or to rest on fabricated evidence, particularly cases filed before adoption of the reasonable-certainty-of-conviction standard.

thread.speaker: Prosecutive Attorney General
thread.said: He said cases filed before the new quantum of evidence would be scrutinized before elevation to court. If evidence was insufficient, prosecutors could return the matter for additional evidence, and DOJ would not elevate a case unless it met the department's required quantum.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She asked how DOJ would treat cases already pending in court that did not meet the evidentiary threshold. She referred to previously submitted counterterrorism task-force data and cases dismissed for insufficiency of evidence, saying many involved marginalized sectors and burdensome proceedings.

thread.speaker: Prosecutive Attorney General
thread.said: He said pending cases filed before adoption of the new quantum could not simply be withdrawn, particularly when proceedings were already ongoing. DOJ would consider observations in those cases and could seek certiorari if it believed the court had committed an error or grave abuse.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She requested an update and breakdown of the counterterrorism and terrorism-financing cases filed by the DOJ task force, including whether cases were dismissed or remained under investigation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She also asked whether DOJ was working with other government agencies through a joint task force on terrorism or counterterrorism.

thread.speaker: Prosecutive Attorney General
thread.said: He said DOJ prosecutors coordinated with the Anti-Terror Council, military counterparts, and the intelligence community to help ensure that evidence gathered for case filing was sufficient.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She presented a case study involving a Filipino American whom alleged Bureau of Immigration agents reportedly sought to arrest while wearing anti-terror task-force vests. She asked about the processes, agencies involved, and guidelines governing DOJ task-force or joint-task-force operations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Renee Luizco
thread.said: She requested that the matter be submitted through the committee and said the committee would coordinate on the request.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The Chair responded, "We will submit your honor," indicating that the requested material would be submitted.

topics.topic: Flood-control corruption cases and interagency anti-corruption coordination
topics.summary: Rep. Kjell Jokno raised DOJ's reported flood-control cases and asked whether investigators had coordinated with AMLA, secured bank-secrecy waivers, and independently checked witness accounts. He questioned DOJ's 2025 prosecutorial success rate of 90.8% and sought separate conviction data for graft and corruption cases, contrasting it with a cited 2022 conviction rate of 25%. The DOJ secretary said the data had to be disaggregated and committed to submit it, including clarification on whether drug cases were included. Jokno also warned that witness intimidation or purchase could distort the prosecutorial success rate, and the secretary agreed that DOJ should monitor it. On coordination, DOJ cited its memorandum of agreement with the Ombudsman, with the Ombudsman handling salary grade 27 and above and DOJ handling cases below that level, and described technical work on an anti-corruption code. The secretary agreed that a legal framework and consolidated conviction-tracking effort were needed, but the database issue remained uncompleted.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether DOJ's flood-control investigations were supported by financial-intelligence checks and interagency coordination, rather than relying only on witness accounts. It also asked whether DOJ tracked final convictions separately from its prosecutorial success rate and whether government agencies maintained a consolidated anti-corruption database.
topics.agency_position: DOJ said its available prosecutorial data needed to be disaggregated, particularly to identify graft, corruption, and drug-case results, and committed to submit the requested information. The department agreed that witness intimidation should be monitored and that a government-wide legal framework or consolidated system for tracking convictions was needed, while citing its memorandum of agreement with the Ombudsman and ongoing technical work on an anti-corruption code.
topics.outcome: The secretary agreed with the need for disaggregated conviction data, witness monitoring, and a consolidated framework for tracking corruption convictions. DOJ undertook to submit data and continue internal and interagency work, but no centralized database or final conviction-tracking system was established during the exchange.

positions.position: The member argued that DOJ should verify flood-control witness accounts through AMLA coordination and bank-secrecy waivers, separately track final convictions rather than rely on the broad prosecutorial success rate, monitor witness interference, and develop a consolidated government system for corruption-conviction data.

The secretary agreed that DOJ needed more detailed conviction and case data, should monitor witness interference, and should pursue a legal or institutional framework for monitoring and archiving convictions.

topics.topic: OSG budget, digitalization, and Law of the Sea training
topics.summary: Rep. Cristina Talavera Lopez questioned the OSG's low utilization of the 10,000,000 Law of the Sea allocation, noting that only 422,000, or 5%, had reportedly been obligated. The OSG said the funds were separately managed and committed to second-semester training, workshops, consultations, and activities for around 80 scholars. The official also described a specialized Law of the Sea track and scholarship program for OSG lawyers. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez then asked about the OSG's building and digitalization needs, and the OSG said its 248,000,000 increase would support a new building through GSIS financing and that 123,000,000 was sought for computerization and digital transformation. The OSG placed the whole building cost at PHP4.5 billion and the first-year GSIS installment at PHP 255,000,000, while the committee member expressed support for digitalization and increased OSG operating funds. No final restoration or appropriation decision was recorded.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) would use its appropriations for its aging facilities, digital transformation, and Law of the Sea capacity-building program. Members also asked whether the OSG needed restoration or additional funding in the 2027 proposed budget and how it would ensure that the funds were fully utilized.
topics.agency_position: The OSG said the Law of the Sea allocation was separately managed and would support a series of specialized trainings, workshops, consultations, and scholarships, with major activities scheduled for the second semester. It also said the proposed OSG increase would support a new building through GSIS lease-to-own financing and requested funding for computerization and digital transformation.
topics.outcome: The OSG explained the intended use of the Law of the Sea allocation and identified its building and digitalization requirements. Members expressed support, but the transcript did not record a final committee action restoring or approving the requested OSG amounts.

positions.position: She supported retaining the Law of the Sea allocation for 2027 and sought assurances that the OSG would fully train government lawyers on maritime issues and improve utilization of the funds. She also supported increasing the OSG's maintenance and other operating expenses.
He supported additional OSG funding for the new building and strongly endorsed the OSG's digitalization and computerization request.

topics.topic: LRA special account, lost titles, and Friar Lands reconstitution
topics.summary: Rep. Allan Ty asked the LRA administrator about the proposed special-account allocation of roughly 1.78 billion for 2027 and the destination of the agency's collections. The administrator said the LRA retained 20% while 80% went to the National Treasury, and indicated that about 1.7 billion could potentially support registration of unregistered DENR free patents, subject to DBM approval. The administrator said registries of deeds were repositories of titles and had to conduct annual inventories, but owners generally bore responsibility for judicial reconstitution when records were lost. Administrative reconstitution could be pursued when at least 10% of titles, and not fewer than 500, were lost. On Friar Lands, the LRA said it would explore administrative remedies and the possible use of derivative titles, but the legal basis and procedure remained to be checked. The administrator committed to attend the DENR budget hearing and bring or invite the relevant registries of deeds.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much the LRA would receive through its special account, how those collections could support the registration of DENR-issued free patents, and where responsibility lay for safeguarding and reconstituting lost titles. It also examined whether lost Friar Lands records could be addressed through administrative remedies and derivative-title documentation.
topics.agency_position: The LRA said its special account could potentially fund registration of DENR-issued free patents, subject to DBM approval and the limits of the account. It said owners generally bear responsibility for judicial reconstitution of lost titles, while the LRA can undertake administrative reconstitution when the statutory threshold is met and can otherwise provide documents and explore administrative remedies for Friar Lands cases.
topics.outcome: The committee obtained the LRA's explanation of the special account, the disposition of collections, and the legal framework for lost-title reconstitution. The Friar Lands remedy remained under discussion with the LMB and was carried forward to the DENR budget hearing, with the LRA administrator and relevant registries of deeds expected to participate.

positions.position: He advocated using available LRA special-account resources to address thousands of unregistered free patents and pressed for assistance to owners whose titles were lost in registries of deeds. He also questioned why valid DENR deeds of conveyance and approved subdivision documents should not support Friar Lands derivative titles.
The chair supported continuing the matter through the DENR budget hearing and required the relevant registry of deeds to participate.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked the LRA administrator how much was proposed under the special account in the 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator initially stated that the amount was 1,800,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He clarified whether the amount was 1,780,000,000.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator answered yes.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked for the source of the special account in the General Fund.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator identified it as Fund151, a special account provided by p d fifteen twenty nine, under which the LRA could retain 20% of its collections, subject to DBM approval for releases.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked where the remaining 80% of collections went.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the 80% went directly to the National Treasury, while the LRA retained 20%, subject to DBM approval of releases.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether the 20% amount, described as 1.7, could be used to pay for titling free patents issued by the DENR.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator clarified that 1,700,000,000 represented 15% of the 20% retained amount and said the special account could be used for the purpose because it covered MOOE and capital outlay.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He cited thousands of unclaimed free patents at registries of deeds nationwide and asked whether the LRA could account for them.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator confirmed that LRA visits had found several, if not thousands, of unregistered patents. He said the DENR had previously paid for registration under an agreement, but that funding had later been removed.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: Subject to DBM approval, the LRA could use the special account to register some or all remaining issued patents.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He confirmed that the proposed funding would come from the special account.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator agreed, subject to maximizing utilization of the 20% retained amount.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked about the legal responsibility of registries of deeds and the LRA for the safekeeping and maintenance of certificates of title.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said that under p d fifteen twenty nine, the principal function of registries of deeds was to serve as the main repository of titles and supporting documents.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether registries of deeds were required to inventory titles that had been lost, destroyed, or rendered unusable by deterioration.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said registries of deeds were obliged under p d fifteen twenty nine to conduct an annual inventory, which he understood to include titles lost or damaged in their custody.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked who had legal responsibility for judicial reconstitution when a title was lost.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said that under RA 26 as amended by RA sixty seven thirty two, responsibility rested with the title owner when both the original and registry copy were lost. He added that a Supreme Court decision had removed the registry of deeds' ability to initiate reconstitution cases.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether there was an exception under RA six seven three two.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the LRA could undertake administrative reconstitution if at least 10% of the titles in a registry of deeds had been lost, provided the number was not less than 500 titles.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether registries of deeds had submitted the required inventories of lost titles.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said some registries had complied and that the LRA was closely monitoring the others.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked what the LRA could do for individual owners when the administrative threshold was not met, particularly where the loss occurred in the registry of deeds.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator acknowledged that the burden fell on the registered owner and said the LRA could assist by providing documents needed to file the appropriate reconstitution case in court.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked what would happen to the registration of DENR deeds of conveyance for Friar Lands when the original Friar Lands title had been lost or destroyed.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said original titles were supposedly held by registries of deeds and owners' copies by the LMB, but some registry records and LMB records had been destroyed or damaged. He said the LRA was discussing administrative remedies with the LMB after the moratorium on deeds of conveyance had been lifted.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked what specific administrative remedies the administrator was referring to.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the LRA still had to discuss the remedies with the LMB. A meeting had been postponed because of the weather, but he said they would meet soon and asked for the committee's help in convening the LMB.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He referred to the DENR budget hearing scheduled for Wednesday and asked the administrator to attend in the afternoon.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator committed to attend.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether an approved subdivision plan and technical descriptions could support reconstitution and issuance of derivative titles when the original Friar Lands title had already been subdivided and approved before it was lost.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator referred to RA 26 as amended by RA sixty seven thirty two and said documents, including a subdivision plan, could support reconstitution.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether already-issued derivative titles, together with later DENR deeds of conveyance, could support title issuance for portions of the original Friar Lands.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the LRA would explore using already-issued derivative titles from the original certificate through an administrative remedy.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked under what particular law the proposed remedy would proceed.

thread.speaker: LRA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said the LRA would check, noting that the existing law on reconstitution was RA 26 as amended by RA sixty seven thirty two.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty

topics.topic: Probation and parole staffing, caseloads, and technology
topics.summary: A committee member asked the PPA about its probationer workload, staffing, ideal supervision ratio, and computer systems. The PPA said it processed about 175,000 probationers in 2025, had roughly 875 staff, and was operating at one officer to 400 probationers against an ideal ratio of one to 50. It attributed about 275 vacancies to the promotion of about 300 personnel and reported that 55,000 people had been found unaccounted for or absent from the system. The PPA said its computer system was ISSP-compliant and later identified the 49,000,000 computerization reduction and a training request stated as 8,198,000 and then 8,000,000. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez said the committee would work on restoring those items, but no final restoration was recorded.

topics.topic: DOJ confidential and intelligence funds
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio raised concerns about the increase in DOJ confidential funds, citing 168,000,000 approved in 2024 against reported actual expenses of 271,600,000 and a 2025 allocation of about 1.52 billion. The agency provided partial program breakdowns and said the 2025 funds were fully obligated and liquidated. Tinio questioned cash disbursements, including PHP 1,000,000,000 quarterly and at least PHP 250,000,000, as well as the possibility of a notice of disallowance. He argued that the 2025 DOJ allocation represented almost 15% of the agency budget and called the growth unreasonable. The agency did not clearly answer what activities justified the large amount or what safeguards applied despite procurement exemptions. The chair noted the concern and undertook to discuss it with the committee.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why DOJ confidential-fund appropriations increased sharply, how the funds were obligated, liquidated, and disbursed, and what safeguards applied despite exemptions from ordinary procurement rules. Rep. Antonio Tinio also questioned whether the scale of the funds was reasonable and whether it exposed the agency to notices of disallowance.
topics.agency_position: The agency stated that the 2025 confidential funds were fully obligated and liquidated and provided partial breakdowns for 2025 and 2026. It attributed some budget changes to congressional initiatives, but did not provide a complete, clear answer on the specific activities supporting the large allocations, cash-disbursement safeguards, or protection against disallowance.
topics.outcome: The agency stated that the 2025 funds were fully obligated and liquidated, but key questions about the justification, cash disbursement controls, procurement safeguards, and risk of disallowance were not fully answered. The chair noted the concern for further committee discussion.

positions.position: He opposed the sharp growth and scale of DOJ confidential and intelligence funds, questioned the reported utilization and cash disbursements, and urged stronger procurement safeguards and more rational budgeting.
The chair noted Rep. Tinio's concern and indicated that it would be discussed with the committee.

topics.topic: PCGG recoveries, remittances, and mandate expansion
topics.summary: Rep. Pachernos asked PCGG to compare its budget with its recoveries and remittances and to identify a proposal that would not require additional congressional funding. PCGG said it had recovered about 183 billion in cash and 125 billion in assets over forty years, including PHP8.3 billion in assets during the current administration. It said its historical budget had been below 200 million and that it had remitted 300 million during the current administration, but explained that it now needed a larger budget because it would begin paying rent after previously occupying space provided through an asset sale for PHP 800,000,000. Later, the chair asked about PCGG's institutional needs, and the agency said its civil-forfeiture mandate was limited to a few individuals and should be expanded to all public officials. PCGG cited more than R300 billion recovered through civil forfeiture, while the chair said a bill already existed and committed to coauthor it.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish PCGG's budget in relation to its recoveries and remittances and whether it had a proposal to expand its work without additional congressional funding. It also examined whether PCGG's mandate should be expanded to cover civil-forfeiture cases involving all public officials.
topics.agency_position: PCGG presented its historical recoveries and remittances as evidence that its resources had produced substantial returns, but said it now needed a larger budget because it would have to pay office rent. On mandate expansion, PCGG supported legislation extending civil-forfeiture authority from the currently limited group of individuals to all public officials.
topics.outcome: PCGG's recoveries, remittances, and need for a larger budget were presented but not subjected to a final budget resolution in the quoted exchange. The mandate-expansion issue moved toward legislation, with the chair committing to coauthor the bill.

positions.position: Sought to compare PCGG's budget with its recoveries and remittances and asked whether PCGG could pursue its proposal without additional congressional funding.
Supported pursuing legislation to expand PCGG's mandate and said she would coauthor the bill.
