topics.topic: DOJ-wide budget cuts and prioritized restoration requests
topics.summary: Chair Mika Suansing raised the broad distribution of DOJ budget cuts and asked the department to identify which reductions should be restored first. The DOJ official detailed Bureau of Immigration reductions, including about 673 million in MOE as spoken, multiple ICT and building-related amounts, and a total requirement characterized by the chair as more than 1.1 billion to 1.2 billion. NBI Director Melvin identified hazard pay, operations, vehicles, administrative capability, and cybercrime laboratories and equipment as priorities, citing a proposed increase from 4,000 to 15,000 and a monthly operating figure of 44,000,000,000 whose context was unclear. The chair also catalogued percentage reductions across anti-trafficking, OSIIC, anti-cybercrime, corrections, legal services, and several attached agencies. DOJ officials committed to submit a consolidated, prioritized list within the week and consult the attached agencies. The committee had not approved specific restorations, and the vice chair solicited a motion to terminate the budget briefing.
topics.question: The committee sought to identify which DOJ-wide budget reductions affected priority programs and to obtain a consolidated, agency-ranked list of items for possible restoration. It also asked specific agencies to explain the components of their cuts and their most urgent funding needs.
topics.agency_position: The DOJ and its attached agencies maintained that multiple priority programs and operational requirements had been reduced across the department. DOJ officials agreed to consolidate the requests, consult the attached agencies, and rank the restoration items by priority.
topics.outcome: The DOJ committed to submit a comprehensive prioritized restoration list for consolidation and review by the committee. No final restoration amounts were approved during this exchange; the budget briefing was being brought to termination.

positions.position: The committee should not attempt to restore every reduction because fiscal space was limited; instead, the DOJ should rationalize and prioritize the most essential requests across all attached agencies.
NBI priorities included higher agents' hazard pay, operating funds, administrative-capability improvements, additional vehicles, cybercrime tools, equipment, and regional cybercrime laboratories.
The DOJ would submit a consolidated, agency-by-agency restoration wish list with an order of prioritization.

thread.speaker: NBI Director Melvin
thread.said: Director Melvin said there were six items to address. His first priority was increasing agents' hazard pay from 4,000 to 15,000 to bring it in line with other law-enforcement personnel, citing the difficulty of transfers between provinces.

thread.speaker: NBI Director Melvin
thread.said: He said the NBI was conducting about 200 to two twenty operations per month involving financial scams, cybercrime, and related matters, and needed additional funding for operational expenses.

thread.speaker: NBI Director Melvin
thread.said: Director Melvin said operating expenses averaged a minimum of 100 per operation and referred to 44,000,000,000 a month to continue the NBI's activities; the unit of the figures was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: NBI Director Melvin
thread.said: He also identified administrative-capability improvements, ISO activities, and additional vehicles as priorities, explaining that marked or red-plate vehicles could not be used for undercover operations.

thread.speaker: NBI Director Melvin
thread.said: Director Melvin acknowledged prior-year budget-utilization concerns but said the NBI needed to respond to its congressional mandate, particularly on cybercrime. He said about 80% of crimes were cyber-related and that the NBI wanted regional cybercrime laboratories, tools, and equipment.

thread.speaker: Mika Suansing, committee chair

thread.speaker: Mika Suansing, committee chair

thread.speaker: Mika Suansing, committee chair

topics.topic: PCGG mandate and recovery of hidden wealth, including the PHP70 billion target
topics.summary: A committee member questioned the agency about recovered hidden wealth, remaining assets, and the pending cases. The agency said about 67 cases were pending in the appellate courts and referred to more than PHP70 billion, which the member identified as the target and the agency confirmed. The agency said the PCGG was attached to the Department of Justice and had operated independently without pressure. It also discussed replacing or succeeding the PCGG with a body empowered to pursue unlawfully acquired assets of all public officials under RA thirteen seventy nine. The agency explained the summary judgment process and reported that the government had won an appeal in New York involving enforcement of the Swiss accounts judgment, subject to possible US Supreme Court action. The committee requested a report, which it said it looked forward to receiving.

topics.topic: PCSO FY2027 budget, programs, and charitable mandate
topics.summary: PCSO presented its FY2027 priorities as expanding medical assistance, transport, equipment donations, coastal access, cancer care, digital services, and revenue generation under its charitable mandate. It reported about 8.13 billion in medical assistance from 2024 through the first semester of 2026 and estimated 2027 retail receipts at about 68.55 billion, with 20,150,000,000 identified for the charity fund. Jan Rurik Padiernos asked about the legal and operational feasibility of landing craft vessels and about equitable deployment of ambulances and AI-capable X-rays. General Manager Mel Robles said PCSO would initially procure around 10 vessels for provincial governments, with bidder maintenance and training for three years, and would use need, priority, personnel capacity, and request order in distributing equipment. Members broadly manifested support for the PCSO budget, while Robles indicated that a second round of ambulances and continued outpatient consultation would be pursued. The precise LCV budget allocation and several garbled financial figures remained unspecified.
topics.question: The committee was examining PCSO's proposed FY2027 programs and the resources needed to carry out its charitable mandate, including medical assistance, transport, equipment, remittances, and revenue allocation. Members also sought clarification on the feasibility and intended beneficiaries of landing craft vessels, ambulances, and AI-capable X-ray machines.
topics.agency_position: PCSO maintained that its proposed FY2027 programs were necessary to expand health assistance, medical transport, equipment donations, coastal access, revenue generation, and efficient service delivery under its charitable mandate. It defended the LCV initiative as a medical-mobility program for coastal communities, with an initial procurement of around 10 vessels, provincial-government implementation, and three years of bidder-provided maintenance and training.
topics.outcome: PCSO's programs and charitable mandate were presented without substantive opposition, and members broadly expressed support for the proposed 2027 budget. Questions on LCV procurement, allocation criteria, and expanded ambulance assistance were answered at a general level, with implementation details and the LCV budget allocation not fully specified.

positions.position: Supported PCSO's proposed budget and urged continuation of its assistance programs.
Expressed full support for PCSO's proposed 2027 budget.
Supported the budget and PCSO's medical assistance, outpatient services, ambulances, and other programs, while requesting consideration for additional assistance in her district.
Expressed 100% support for PCSO on behalf of the minority and said he would support it during plenary budget proceedings.
Was grateful for PCSO's support to Rizal province but sought assistance for her district.

thread.speaker: Judge Felix Piraeus, PCSO official
thread.said: He presented PCSO's proposed budget and programs and reaffirmed its mandate under Republic Act No. Eleven sixty nine, as amended, to generate and provide funds for health programs, medical assistance and services, and charitable activities of national character.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: She identified PCSO's 2027 priorities as distributing landing craft vessels to coastal provinces and municipalities, donating medical equipment, participating in a radiation oncology center, developing new games and betting platforms, and digitalizing operations.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: She reported that from 2024 through the first semester of 2026, PCSO provided 8,130,000,000 in medical assistance to 681,099 beneficiaries. The transcript states that 2024 assistance was 240,000,000 for 326,482 beneficiaries and that 2025 assistance increased to an unclear amount despite beneficiaries declining to 236,217.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: She said PCSO had expanded financial assistance to include professional fees for qualified patients, following the expressed desire of House appropriations members.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: Institutional partnership beneficiaries increased from 19 in 2024 to 38 in 2025, while assistance increased from 12,000,000 to 24,600,000; another 19 beneficiaries had been assisted by the first semester of 2026.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: Medical transport vehicle beneficiaries increased from four thirty one in 2024 to ten ninety in 2025, while assistance increased from 913,700,000 to 2,480,000,000. As of 07/31/2026, PCSO had distributed 154 PTVs.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: Medical equipment assistance increased from 20,500,000 in 2024 to 22,000,000 in 2025 and reached 154,580,000 in the first semester of 2026. Outpatient and multispecialty clinic beneficiaries were 7,383 in 2024, 9,416 in 2025, and 8,440 in the first half of 2026.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: Total revenues from major games increased by 4.02 from 62,350,000,000 in 2024 to 64,860,000,000 in 2025. STL increased by 11.99% and the National Instant Sweep Stakes program by 20%; the first-semester 2026 revenue figure was stated only as 'billion' and is unclear.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: Total income increased from 63,420,000,000 in 2024 to 65,870,000,000 in 2025, while operating expenses rose from 51,010,000,000 to 53,860,000,000. Profit after tax declined from PHP11.74 billion to PHP11.52 billion, and financial assistance, subsidies and contributions rose from 7,890,000,000 to 9,540,000,000.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: Net income decreased from 3,840,000,000 in 2024 to 1,980,000,000 in 2025. As of 06/30/2026, PCSO had recorded 31,740,000,000 in total income and PHP 3,350,000,000 in net income.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: For 2023, retail receipts were 61,460,000,000, with 33,220,000,000 allocated to the price fund, 18.11% to the charity fund, and 9,050,000,000 to the operating fund. For 2024, net receipts were PHP 61,300,000,000, with PHP 33,710,000,000 for the price fund, PHP18.39 billion for the charity fund, and PHP9.19 billion for the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: For 2025, the transcript states retail receipts of 4,860,000,000, printing cost of 1.09, and net receipts of 63,770,000,000. Allocations were 35,070,000,000 to the price fund, PHP19.13 billion to the charity fund, and PHP9.57 billion to the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: For 2026, estimated retail receipts were 67,260,000,000 and projected net receipts were stated as NT65.91 billion dollars. The estimated allocations were PHP36.25 billion to the price fund, PHP19.77 billion to the charity fund, and PHP9.89 billion to the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: For 2027, estimated retail receipts were PHP 68,550,000,000. Projected net receipts were stated as TWD67.18 billion, and the allocations were stated as 5% or RMB39.95 billion for the price fund, 30% or 20,150,000,000 for the charity fund, and 15% or 10,080,000,000 for the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: PCSO exceeded its 2025 target of 500 patient transport vehicles by distributing ten ninety PTVs, or 218% of target. For 2026, the target was two fifty eight PTVs, of which 154 had been distributed as of 07/31/2026.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: The 2025 medical assistance target was 3,302,000,000, of which 3,245,000,000 was released to 236,217 patients. For 2026, PCSO allocated 3,650,000,000 and had released 1,640,000,000 to 118,400 patients as of 06/30/2026.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: PCSO reported that portable AI-capable X-ray machines and other medical equipment donated to beneficiary entities amounted to 176,000,000. Charitimba, mobility aids, assistive devices, rescue devices, and evacuation kits distributed under the corporate social responsibility program amounted to 348,600,000.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: PCSO remitted approximately 570,000,000 under the universal health care program for 2025. For 2026, first-quarter remittances were 651,470,000 and second-quarter remittances were 690,670,000; the transcript states a combined amount due and remitted of 3,914,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong, PCSO official
thread.said: She reported that PCSO's total contributions to the National Treasury increased from 14,560,000,000 in 2021 to 21,850,000,000 in 2025. The transcript gives the five-year total and tax amount only as 'billion,' which is unclear, and states dividends of PHP9.93 billion and Universal Healthcare contributions of PHP9.53 billion.

thread.speaker: Attorney Anna Lisa, PCSO official
thread.said: As of 06/30/2026, PCSO had remitted an additional 11,060,000,000, bringing total contributions reflected in the table to 112,350,000,000.

thread.speaker: Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: He questioned the procurement and feasibility of landing craft vessels as a FY2027 strategic thrust, including PCSO's legal mandate, procurement of naval vessels, and the total 2027 budget allocation. The amount sought was not clearly stated in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: He answered that the vessels would operate within municipal islands or coastal areas to provide medical mobility and serve as a 'door to door hospital.' PCSO would begin with around 10 procurements, with provincial governments receiving responsibility for scheduling and maintenance; the winning bidder would maintain each vessel for the first three years and train personnel.

thread.speaker: Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: He asked about equity in the distribution of patient transport vehicles and deployment of AI-capable portable X-rays, citing the reported distribution of sixteen seventy five units, around 730,000,000, and 197,000,000 worth of medical equipment. He asked what criteria PCSO used for geographically isolated, disadvantaged, or urbanized LGUs.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: He said beneficiary LGUs needed personnel who could administer the service and work with the equipment, including radiologist specialization for the X-ray machines. Selection combined priority, demonstrated need, ability to train personnel, and a first-come, first-served order of requests.

thread.speaker: Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: He manifested his full support for PCSO's proposed budget and urged PCSO to continue its programs. He also said the House of Representatives would assist as it could to help more people.

thread.speaker: Representative Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: He congratulated PCSO and expressed full support for its proposed 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: He expressed full support for the budget.

thread.speaker: Representative Christie Gonzales
thread.said: She thanked PCSO for hospitalization and medical assistance, including support when congressional offices had limited guarantee letters, and expressed full support for PCSO's budget request.

thread.speaker: Representative Presley de Jesus
thread.said: As deputy minority leader, he said the minority would support PCSO 100% during plenary budget proceedings and that he would not ask questions in plenary.

thread.speaker: Representative Christie Gonzales
thread.said: She raised the need for additional ambulances for a densely populated city and referred to PCSO's combination of first-come, first-served selection and LGU willingness.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: He said ambulances are emergency vehicles and that one of PCSO's next aspirations was to provide a second round and immediate standby ambulances. He told offices to call PCSO so assistance could be provided.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: He said PCSO had an outpatient clinic and would continue providing free consultation, subject to availability.

thread.speaker: Representative Christie Gonzales
thread.said: She said she would announce the outpatient clinic program through her Facebook program and fully supported all PCSO programs.

thread.speaker: Representative Mia Ynares
thread.said: She thanked PCSO for supporting Rizal province but noted that her district had not received the highlighted assistance apart from charity assistance. She asked PCSO not to forget her district.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: He said Rizal was the first province to achieve 100% distribution of patient transport vehicles or ambulances and indicated that a second round would be pursued.

topics.topic: PhilHealth UHC remittances and 40% net charity fund share
topics.summary: PCSO reported approximately 570 million in UHC remittances for 2025, followed by 651.47 million and 690.67 million for the first and second quarters of 2026. It said the combined amount due and remitted was 3.914 billion pesos and that each period reflected 100% remittance. Rep. Montez asked whether the legally required 40% net charity fund share had been remitted quarterly and on time. A PCSO official answered that remittances were timely and quarterly, with no remembered instances of delay, and said the general manager had personally delivered the latest remittance to the National Treasury. Rep. Montez cited a July 16 turnover of 1.935 billion covering mandatory contributions from the fourth quarter of 2025 through the first and second quarters of 2026. She requested official remittance records so they could be checked against DOF, DBM, and PhilHealth data, and PCSO committed to submit them.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish whether PCSO had remitted the legally required 40% of its net charity fund share for PhilHealth's Universal Health Care program on a quarterly basis. It also sought official PCSO records that could be compared with remittance data from the National Treasury, the Department of Finance, and the DBM.
topics.agency_position: PCSO stated that it had remitted the amounts due under the UHC program in full and on time each quarter, with the amount due matching the amount remitted for each period. It committed to submit official Bureau of the Treasury remittance records covering the 40% net charity fund share for committee verification.
topics.outcome: PCSO asserted that its UHC remittances were complete, quarterly, and timely, but the committee required documentary verification. The issue remained open pending submission of PCSO's official remittance records and comparison with DOF, DBM, and PhilHealth data.

positions.position: She indicated that PCSO appeared to have made its remittances on time, but said she still needed to compare PCSO's records with information from the DBM, DOF, and PhilHealth to determine whether any broader remittance problem existed.

topics.topic: PCSO remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission
topics.summary: Rep. Faustino Michael D. raised the Supreme Court ruling requiring PCSO to remit 30% of charity fund proceeds from six draws per year, including lotto, beginning in 2006. He questioned why PCSO's reported 2025 payment was only 1,500,000 and asked for the exact amount owed, the amount already remitted, and a settlement schedule. A PCSO official discussed the applicable six-digit game mechanics and cited 45,000,000, more or less 73,000,000 for remittances from 2006 to 2025, and other conflicting figures including 122,000,419 and 122,000,000,000. The exchange also referred to a 5% calculation tied to races or draws, without reconciling it with the member's cited 30% obligation. No payment schedule or documentary accounting was committed on the record, leaving the issue unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PCSO had complied with the Supreme Court ruling requiring remittance to the Philippine Sports Commission of 30% of the charity fund proceeds from six draws per year, including lotto, from 2006 onward. It also sought the exact accumulated amount owed, the amount already remitted, and the schedule for settling any balance.
topics.agency_position: PCSO officials stated that remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission were calculated using a percentage tied to the number of races or draws for the six-digit games. They cited remittances of more or less 73,000,000 for 2006 to 2025 and also referred to a total of 122,000,419 and 122,000,000,000, but the figures and their units were inconsistent or unclear in the transcript.
topics.outcome: PCSO provided partial and internally unclear figures on remittances, but did not clearly establish compliance with the cited 30% requirement, the exact accumulated balance, or a schedule for settling any shortfall. The issue remained contested and unresolved.

positions.position: He questioned PCSO's compliance with the Supreme Court ruling, considered the reported 1,500,000 2025 remittance insufficient, and sought an exact accounting of the amount due, the amount remitted, and the settlement schedule.

topics.topic: Landing craft vessels, patient transport, and AI-capable X-rays
topics.summary: Jan Rurik Padiernos asked PCSO about the legal basis and feasibility of procuring landing craft vessels for coastal provinces and municipalities. PCSO general manager Mel Robles said the vessels would support medical mobility, begin with around 10 procurements, be provided to provincial governments, and be maintained by the winning bidder for the first three years, including personnel training. Pajernos also cited 1,675 patient transport vehicles at around 730,000,000 and 197,000,000 in medical equipment, including AI-capable portable X-rays, and asked about equitable deployment. Robles said distribution considered need, priority, personnel and training capacity, and the order of requests, with a first-come, first-served element. Members broadly supported PCSO’s proposed budget and programs. PCSO also indicated that a second round of ambulances and standby support was an aspiration, while Robles said Rizal had already achieved 100% distribution of patient transport vehicles.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish PCSO’s legal mandate and procurement plans for landing craft vessels, including their intended recipients, maintenance, and feasibility. It also sought the proposed allocations and distribution criteria for patient transport vehicles, ambulances, and AI-capable portable X-rays, particularly for geographically isolated or disadvantaged areas and urbanized LGUs.
topics.agency_position: PCSO said the landing craft vessel initiative fell within its medical-mobility and charitable-services mandate, with provincial governments responsible for scheduling and maintenance, subject to Marina licensing. It said patient transport and AI-capable X-ray distribution depended on need and priority, the LGU’s ability to provide and train personnel, and the order of requests, including a first-come, first-served element.
topics.outcome: PCSO answered the questions on intended use, provincial-government responsibility, licensing, contractor maintenance, and distribution criteria. The members expressed broad support, while the timing and scope of the second round of ambulances and the detailed legal and budget basis for the landing craft vessels were not further documented.

thread.said: Jan Rurik Padiernos asked PCSO about the procurement and feasibility of landing craft vessels under the fiscal year 2027 strategy, including whether PCSO had the legal mandate to procure such heavy maritime assets for coastal provinces and municipalities.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Mel Robles said the vessels would operate within municipal islands or the relevant area. He linked the initiative to PCSO’s mandate to provide medical mobility and charity services of national character, with the intention of creating a “door to door hospital” service.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles said LGUs would need to secure licenses from Marina after receiving the vessels. He said PCSO was starting with around 10 procurements and would proceed from there in the next year.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles clarified that the landing craft vessels would be provided to provincial governments, which would schedule and maintain them. The winning bidder would be required to maintain each vessel for the first three years and train the personnel.

thread.speaker: Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: Pajernos asked about equity in the distribution of patient transport vehicles and the deployment of AI-capable portable X-rays. He cited a report that PCSO planned 100% distribution of patient transport vehicles, 1,675 units at around 730,000,000, and 197,000,000 worth of medical equipment, including AI-capable portable X-rays.

thread.speaker: Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: Pajernos asked whether PCSO’s criteria prioritized geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas or urbanized LGUs, and sought the basis for determining the number and order of deployments.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles said PCSO considered whether the LGU had personnel who could provide the services and operate the equipment, including personnel with radiologist specialization. The LGU also had to demonstrate that it could administer the service.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles said allocation was based on a combination of need, priority, the LGU’s ability to train personnel to handle the equipment, and the order of requests. He also described the process as first come, first served.

thread.speaker: Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: Pajernos said he was making a manifestation of full support for PCSO’s proposed budget and hoped PCSO would continue its work for the country. He said the House of Representatives would assist as much as possible to help more people.

thread.speaker: Representative Ramil Hernandez
thread.said: Representative Ramil Hernandez congratulated PCSO for its work and expressed full support for its proposed 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: Representative Christie Gonzales
thread.said: Representative Christie Gonzales thanked PCSO for its financial assistance for hospitalization and MIPS and expressed full support for PCSO’s budget request.

thread.speaker: Representative Presley de Jesus
thread.said: Representative Presley de Jesus expressed support for PCSO and said that, as deputy minority leader, he would not ask questions during plenary budget deliberations and would support PCSO 100 on behalf of the minority.

thread.speaker: Representative Christie Gonzales
thread.said: Gonzales thanked PCSO for its support and referred to the patient transport vehicle distribution as a blend of first come, first served and the willingness and capacity of the LGU. She noted the relevance of the criteria to a densely populated city and its need for ambulances.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles described ambulances as emergency vehicles and said one of PCSO’s next aspirations was to provide a second round and an immediate standby ambulance. He said offices could call PCSO for assistance.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles said PCSO also had an outpatient clinic office available to provide services, including free consultation, subject to availability.

thread.speaker: Representative Mia Ynares
thread.said: Representative Mia Ynares thanked PCSO for supporting Rizal province but said her district had not received the referenced equipment or vehicles, except for charity assistance. She asked PCSO not to forget her district.

thread.speaker: Mel Robles, PCSO general manager
thread.said: Robles said Rizal was the first province to achieve 100% distribution of patient transport vehicles or ambulances, possibly before Ynares took office. He added that she should not worry because a second round would follow.

topics.topic: Ambulance assistance and equitable district medical assistance
topics.summary: PCSO reported that its medical transport vehicle program had grown substantially, including 154 PTVs distributed as of 07/31/2026 and performance of 218% against the 2025 target. Representative Christie Gonzales raised the need for more equitable coverage for densely populated Mandaluyong and additional ambulances. GM Mel Robles said PCSO's next aspiration was a second round of ambulance distribution and offered immediate standby ambulances upon request. Representative Mia Ynares said Rizal province had received strong support but that her district had not received the assistance under discussion. PCSO said Rizal had achieved 100% patient transport vehicle distribution and reiterated the prospect of a second round, but did not give a schedule or specific district allocation.
topics.question: The committee was trying to establish how PCSO distributed patient transport vehicles and whether districts with dense populations or insufficient ambulance coverage could receive additional vehicles. Members also sought clarification on whether PCSO would undertake a second round of ambulance distribution and provide immediate standby assistance.
topics.agency_position: PCSO stated that it had substantially expanded patient transport vehicle distribution and had completed or was pursuing distribution across provinces, cities and municipalities. Its general manager said PCSO aspired to conduct a second round of ambulance distribution and could provide an immediate standby ambulance when an office called.
topics.outcome: PCSO defended its broad PTV distribution and acknowledged requests for denser district coverage and additional ambulances. A second round and standby assistance were indicated, but no timetable, allocation criteria, or specific commitment to Representative Ynares's district was stated.

positions.position: Supported PCSO but sought more equitable ambulance coverage for Mandaluyong, citing its dense population and need for additional ambulances.
Expressed gratitude for PCSO's support to Rizal province but said her district had not received the assistance under discussion and asked not to be forgotten.

topics.topic: PCSO sales, taxes, dividends, and special-law remittances
topics.summary: PCSO presented rising sales and net-receipt estimates, from about 61.46 billion in 2023 to about 68.55 billion in projected 2027 retail receipts. It reported UHC remittances, including about 570 million in 2025 and 651.47 million and 690.67 million in the first two quarters of 2026, and said amounts due and remitted matched. The agency also reported total contributions rising from 14.56 billion in 2021 to 21.85 billion in 2025, with an additional 11.06 billion remitted by June 2026 and a table total of 112.35 billion. Chair Mika Swan Singh questioned why taxes, dividends, and other remittances appeared to decline or remain flat despite rising sales. PCSO's accounting and budget official attributed the pattern to corporate income, final income, and winnings-related taxes, income-based dividends, sales-related UHC and DST computations, and contingent special-law obligations. The chair accepted the explanation, commended PCSO's contributions, and left the matter informational.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PCSO sales and projected revenues were rising while taxes, dividends, and other statutory remittances appeared flat or declining. It also asked whether the decline in remittances under Republic Acts and executive orders reflected specific laws or factors outside PCSO's control.
topics.agency_position: PCSO stated that taxes and dividends were driven principally by corporate income, final income, and winnings-related taxes, while some special-law contributions depended on sales and other contingent factors. It maintained that UHC remittances were fully remitted for the periods reflected and emphasized its significant overall contribution to government revenues and national programs.
topics.outcome: PCSO explained that the differing trajectories reflected the separate statutory and financial bases of taxes, dividends, UHC, and special-law contributions. The chair acknowledged the explanation and commended PCSO; no document request or further undertaking was recorded.

positions.position: Sales and revenues should generally produce a corresponding increase in taxes, dividends, and other government contributions, although she accepted that some remittances were contingent on factors outside PCSO's control.

positions.who: Johann, PCSO accounting and budget department
positions.position: The differing trajectories were explained by the specific bases of each remittance: corporate income and winnings-related taxes, net income for dividends, sales-related computations for UHC and DST, and contingent special-law obligations.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: PCSO reported that total revenues from major games increased by 4.02 from 62,350,000,000 in 2024 to 64,860,000,000 in 2025. The increase was attributed mainly to STL, which grew by 11.99%, and the National Instant Sweep Stakes program, which grew by 20%; the first-semester 2026 revenue figure was stated only as “billion.”

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: For 2023, PCSO reported 61,460,000,000 in retail receipts from Lotto, STL and NISP, with 55% or 33,220,000,000 allocated to the price fund, 30% or 18.11% to the charity fund, and 15% or 9,050,000,000 to the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: For 2024, retail receipts were 62,350,000,000. After deducting 1,060,000,000 in printing costs, net receipts were PHP 61,300,000,000; allocations were 55% or PHP 33,710,000,000 to the price fund, 30% or PHP18.39 billion to the charity fund, and 15% or PHP9.19 billion to the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: For 2025, PCSO reported 4,860,000,000 in retail receipts from Lotto, STL and NISP after deducting 1.09 in printing cost. Net receipts were 63,770,000,000, with 55% or 35,070,000,000 for the price fund, 30% or PHP19.13 billion for the charity fund, and 15% or PHP9.57 billion for the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: For 2026, estimated retail receipts were 67,260,000,000. After deducting the estimated “billion dollars” for printing cost, projected net receipts were NT65.91 billion, with PHP36.25 billion for the price fund, PHP19.77 billion for the charity fund, and PHP9.89 billion for the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: For 2027, estimated retail receipts were PHP 68,550,000,000. After deducting the estimated billion for printing costs, projected net receipts were TWD67.18 billion; the stated allocations were 5% or RMB39.95 billion for the price fund, 30% or 20,150,000,000 for the charity fund, and 15% or 10,080,000,000 for the operating fund.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: PCSO reported that it remitted approximately 570,000,000 under the Universal Health Care program in 2025. For 2026, the first-quarter remittance was 651,470,000 and the second-quarter remittance was 690,670,000.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: PCSO stated that combined 2025 and first-semester 2026 UHC amounts due and remitted totaled 3,914,000,000 pesos. It said the amounts due and remitted were exactly the same for each period, representing 100% remittance of the amounts reflected in the table.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: PCSO presented its contributions to the National Treasury through taxes, dividends, and mandatory contributions for 2021 through the first semester of 2026. The presentation identified taxes as the largest share, followed by dividends of PHP9.93 billion and Universal Healthcare contributions of PHP9.53 billion, although the total five-year figure and tax figure were unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Attorney Lisa Enshong
thread.said: PCSO reported that total contributions increased from 14,560,000,000 in 2021 to 21,850,000,000 in 2025, described as a 50.1 increase.

thread.speaker: Attorney Anna Lisa
thread.said: PCSO stated that it had remitted an additional 11,060,000,000 as of 06/30/2026, bringing the total contributions reflected in the table to 112,350,000,000.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair compared PCSO's sales trajectory with its taxes, dividends, and special-law remittances and asked why the upward trajectory in sales revenues was not matched by the trajectory of government contributions.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair cited sales or net-receipt figures rising from 60,400,000,000 in 2023 to 61.3 in 2024, 63.8 in 2025, 65.9 in 2026, and 67.2 in 2027.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair said total taxes, dividends, and other remittances appeared to be 22,900,000,000 in 2023, 22.26 in 2024, 21.85 in 2025, and 11 in the first half of 2026. She said she assumed the full-year 2026 amount would be 2,021,000,000,000; this figure is unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair asked why sales revenues were consistently increasing from 2023 to 2027 while taxes, dividends, and other remittances were not increasing at the same time.

thread.speaker: Johann, PCSO accounting and budget department
thread.said: Johann explained that taxes were primarily corporate income tax and that net income affected dividends as well. He also cited final income tax and tax on winnings, saying the tax on winnings depended on winnings above 20 or 10020%; the exact threshold was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Johann, PCSO accounting and budget department
thread.said: Johann said other special contributions, including UHC, were affected by sales and that DST was also affected as sales increased. He summarized that taxes and dividends were principally affected by corporate income and final income taxes.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair followed up on the downward trend in the Republic Acts and executive orders column, citing 108, six eighty in 2024, and three forty four in 2025, with the figures and their units unclear. She asked whether particular laws or executive orders caused the erratic trend in support for special laws.

thread.speaker: Johann, PCSO accounting and budget department
thread.said: Johann answered that the Republic Acts and executive orders category depended on sales, including contributions involving the Girl Scouts and Boy Scouts. He also cited the share from dangerous-drugs forfeited prizes; the detailed explanation was partly garbled.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair said the trends were erratic because taxes, dividends, and Republic Acts and executive orders were contingent on factors that were not within PCSO's control, while UHC was a constant earmark under the law. She nevertheless expected contributions generally to rise with sales.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Swan Singh
thread.said: The chair commended PCSO's contributions to the national government and cited roughly 112,000,000,000 pesos from 2021 to 2026 as an important source of funding for government programs and projects.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS - BUDGET BRIEFING/HEARING OF THE FY 2027 PROPOSED BUDGET (OMB)

topics.topic: FY 2027 Ombudsman budget and program allocations
topics.summary: The chair and Christopher Lim presented the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 budget, with the agency citing a recommended level of about 7 billion and allocations for personnel, operations, capital outlay, programs, ICT modernization, facilities, confidential expenses, and proposed marshals. Lim also requested restatement of special provisions on savings, income, retirement benefits, and fiscal autonomy. Iris Marie Montes questioned conviction rates, high-ranking-official cases, political safeguards, digital forensic tools, and regional reach; the agency reported improved conviction rates, said it followed its constitutional mandate without fear or favor, and said digitalization and regional offices were funded or being expanded. The agency could not immediately provide data separating motu proprio investigations or measuring regional-office efficiency and undertook to provide information. Members Rufus Rodriguez, Maisa Sagarbarria, and Girlie Veloso expressed support for the budget, including marshal positions. Committee Chair Micah Swan Singh requested a written and prioritized list of additional funding requests, and Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla committed to submit it and coordinate on the special-provision wording.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 funding requirements, program allocations, and requested special provisions, and whether the proposed resources would improve its anti-corruption, investigative, digital, and regional capabilities. Members also asked what safeguards, performance results, and prioritization would guide any additional funding.
topics.agency_position: The Ombudsman said the FY 2027 recommended budget was necessary to sustain its constitutional anti-corruption, enforcement, public assistance, prevention, digitalization, and regional operations. It requested additional funding, the restatement of FY 2026 special provisions, and support for marshals, facilities, vehicles, positions, and other capability requirements, while committing to use appropriations responsibly.
topics.outcome: The committee expressed broad support for the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 budget and special provisions, but additional requests were not finally resolved during the hearing. The Ombudsman committed to submit a written, prioritized list for subsequent budget-amendment deliberations, while several requested performance data items remained to be provided.

positions.position: Supported scrutiny of the Ombudsman budget and sought evidence on conviction rates, political safeguards, digital-investigation capacity, motu proprio cases, and regional performance.
Supported funding for Ombudsman marshals to protect the office, expedite processes, and enforce final convictions.
Supported the proposed Ombudsman budget as an investment in accountability, institutional integrity, independence, and public trust.
Supported the FY 2027 Ombudsman budget and resources for timely and credible accountability.
Expressed support for the Ombudsman budget and special provisions, while requiring written prioritization of additional funding requests before amendment deliberations.

topics.topic: Additional Ombudsman funding requests and budget amendments
topics.summary: Rep. Toby Tiangco supported the Ombudsman’s budget and urged fiscal-autonomy amendments covering the Ombudsman and other constitutional commissions, saying he had advocated the issue since 2013. Chair Rufus Rodriguez agreed in principle and said the proposed language, including savings, use of income, and retirement benefits, would be recommended to the plenary subject to committee approval. Chairperson Micah Swan Singh then asked the Ombudsman to submit and prioritize in writing its additional funding requests, including confidential funds, marshal positions, motor vehicles, and a new office building. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla committed to comply as soon as possible. The chairperson also said the committee would coordinate on the special-provision wording for the 2027 GAA, building on its inclusion in the 2026 GAA. Final prioritization and appropriations for the additional requests were left for the budget-amendments review process.

topics.topic: Capital outlay for digital forensic tools
topics.summary: Director Christopher Lim reported that the Ombudsman’s FY 2027 budget included total capital outlay of about 157.1 million and an IT modernization requirement described in the transcript as 497,549,000,000, including a capital-outlay component of 250 million. Iris Marie Montes asked whether the capital-outlay increase covered digital forensic tools. An agency official answered that it did, to his understanding, as part of the administration’s digitalization initiative. During a later discussion on fact-finding, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla referred to training and digital-forensics equipment, and Chel Diokno urged that these be included in the budget proposal. The hearing did not establish an itemized amount specifically for digital forensic equipment or a procurement timetable.

topics.outcome: The agency indicated that the capital-outlay request covered digital forensic tools, but the answer was qualified as being based on the official’s understanding. topics.topic: Ombudsman staffing and lawyer recruitment
topics.summary: Christopher Lim presented personnel-services funding of about 3.76 billion and about 1.66 billion for filling positions, while seeking support for additional staffing. Representative Salvador Pleyto questioned whether the unchanged ceiling of 2,439 authorized positions was sufficient, and Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla said it had taken more than ten and a half months to hire 60 lawyers. Chel Diokno then linked staffing and digital-forensics capacity to the Ombudsman's fact-finding workload, citing 2,051 investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases. He requested detailed filing data, including the number of flood-control cases among the 10 filed this year and 12 last year. The Ombudsman identified interagency cooperation, investigator numbers, training, and digital-forensics equipment as needs, but did not provide the requested case breakdown during the hearing. The committee therefore left the data issue for follow-up, while the Ombudsman advocated case-building standards and mandatory continuous trials to reduce delays.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the Ombudsman had sufficient authorized personnel and personnel-services funding to carry out its investigation, prosecution, and public-assistance mandates. Members also asked how recruitment, investigator capacity, digital-forensics capability, and case-processing delays affected the office's workload.
topics.agency_position: The Ombudsman presented personnel-services funding and a substantial allocation for filling positions, while also identifying a need for additional positions, investigators, training, and digital-forensics equipment. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said recruitment was slow—taking more than ten and a half months to hire 60 lawyers—and supported stronger interagency cooperation and faster, continuous trials for corruption cases.
topics.outcome: The hearing established that the Ombudsman had 2,439 authorized positions, unchanged for 2025 through 2027, and that lawyer recruitment was taking more than ten and a half months for 60 hires. The committee's request for detailed case and flood-control data was not answered on the spot and was left for submission or follow-up.

topics.topic: Fact-finding capacity and corruption-case processing delays
topics.summary: Mauricio Domogan questioned the Ombudsman about pending complaints, conflict-of-interest investigations, pre-audit, and processing times. The Ombudsman said fact-finding generally took thirty to sixty days and preliminary investigation another thirty to sixty days, and reported hiring 60 lawyers with 40 more planned. Rep. Chel Diokno raised the absence of a centralized system for tracking final convictions, and the Ombudsman proposed an Ombudsman Marshal office for conviction tracking, process service, and related functions. The Ombudsman also reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks and agreed that a government-wide conviction-rate measure would be useful. Rep. Kjell Jochno cited a report involving 2,051 fact-finding investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases, then requested detailed filing and flood-control data. The hearing ended with commitments on staffing and marshals, but the requested case data and broader solutions to judicial delays remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Ombudsman conducts fact-finding and preliminary investigations, how staffing and resources affect case-processing timelines, and how many corruption cases—particularly flood-control cases—advance to prosecution and conviction. Members also asked how the government tracks final convictions, conducts lifestyle checks, and addresses delays in the justice system.
topics.agency_position: The Ombudsman said fact-finding should take thirty days for non-complex cases and sixty days for complex cases, followed by a preliminary investigation of another thirty to sixty days, and said additional lawyers were being hired to meet those deadlines. It supported centralized conviction tracking, proposed an Ombudsman Marshal office for tracking and process-serving functions, reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks, and favored stronger coordination, digital-forensics capacity, and measures to reduce judicial delay.
topics.outcome: The Ombudsman answered the basic fact-finding timelines and described staffing increases, but several requested datasets—including the annual filing figures and flood-control breakdown—were not clearly provided. The Ombudsman Marshal proposal and additional staffing were commitments, while the constitutional, legislative, and judicial mechanisms for conviction tracking and reducing case delays remained open.

positions.position: Supported the Ombudsman's budget and proposed mandatory pre-audit with geospatial mapping as a tool against ghost projects; he remained concerned about long-pending complaints.
Supported a centralized system for tracking final convictions, a government-wide conviction-rate measure, witness-protection capacity, and revived lifestyle checks.
Supported the Ombudsman Marshal proposal but cautioned that immediate imprisonment after an RTC conviction must be consistent with the constitutional presumption of innocence and the right to appeal.

topics.topic: Flood-control corruption investigations and alleged budget insertions
topics.summary: Representative Antonio Tinio raised allegations involving flood-control corruption, a 2025 budget insertion of 100,000,000,000, an allegedly related 51,000,000,000, and alleged kickbacks totaling 8,000,000,000, including 2,000,000,000 allegedly delivered through armored cars. He asked whether the Ombudsman would investigate the allegations and determine whether appropriations corresponded to projects actually delivered, but the transcript contains no substantive agency answer. Chel Diokno questioned the Ombudsman's fact-finding performance, citing 2,051 investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases, and asked for personnel, digital-forensics, and flood-control case data. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said agency cooperation, personnel, and digital-forensics equipment were needed, but the response on the number of flood-control cases was unclear. Remulla said corruption cases should be filed only after probable cause and a reasonable certainty of conviction had been established, and advocated mandatory continuous trials to avoid extreme delays. The committee's requests for data left the flood-control investigation issue committed for follow-up rather than resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how the Ombudsman was investigating alleged flood-control corruption and budget insertions, including whether complaints had been acted on, how many cases had been filed, and whether its resources and procedures were adequate. Members also asked what institutional or budgetary support would improve fact-finding, digital forensics, case filing, and the eventual prosecution of corruption cases.
topics.agency_position: The Ombudsman said effective fact-finding required cooperation from other agencies, adequate personnel, and digital-forensics equipment. On case delays, Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said the office should file cases only after building probable cause and a reasonable certainty of conviction, while the justice system should adopt mandatory continuous trials for graft cases.
topics.outcome: The hearing did not establish how many flood-control cases the Ombudsman had filed or whether the alleged 2025 budget insertion and kickback allegations had entered a formal investigation. The committee requested case data, while broader support for marshals, personnel, equipment, and faster trials was expressed or discussed.

topics.topic: Conviction rates and tracking of graft cases
topics.summary: Representative Iris Marie Montes asked about the Ombudsman’s conviction rates, comparisons with prior years, high-ranking-official cases, and Moto Propio investigations. The agency reported a Sandigan Bayan conviction rate of sixty five point five two percent, compared with forty two percent previously, and lower-court rates of seventy seven point six percent in 2025 and sixty four point nine one percent as of June 30 of the current year. It could not immediately distinguish Moto Propio cases but committed to provide the data. Representative Chel Diokno raised a decades-old recommendation for a centralized system to track convictions and asked whether the Ombudsman had acted on it. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said the proposed Ombudsman Marshall office, for which funding was requested, would track case and sentence statuses and perform related functions; the chair supported the proposal, although disagreement over imprisonment before final judgment remained. The agency also agreed that a government-wide conviction-rate statistic would be beneficial and reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman’s conviction performance, including comparisons with prior years and between courts, and whether the agency could track cases through final judgment and service of sentence. Members also asked whether the Ombudsman had safeguards against political influence, a centralized conviction-tracking system, a government-wide conviction metric, and active lifestyle-check and marshal programs.
topics.agency_position: The Ombudsman reported improved conviction rates and attributed the gains to procedural changes that accelerated investigations. It supported creating an Ombudsman Marshall office to track convictions and related case statuses, perform process-serving and witness-protection functions, and improve enforcement, and it agreed that a government-wide conviction statistic would be useful.
topics.outcome: The Ombudsman committed to providing missing Moto Propio data and said its budget request included funding for a marshal office that would track convictions and support enforcement-related functions. The need for a government-wide conviction metric was acknowledged, but the centralized system, constitutional issues concerning imprisonment pending appeal, and implementation details remained unresolved.

positions.position: Supported obtaining more detailed Moto Propio investigation data and pressed for measurable safeguards, performance indicators, and accountability in conviction and regional operations.
Supported a centralized system for tracking convictions through appeal and imprisonment, a uniform government-wide conviction-rate gauge, Ombudsman marshals, and renewed lifestyle checks.
Supported Ombudsman marshals but maintained that imprisonment should follow final judgment and emphasized the constitutional presumption of innocence and right to appeal.

Supported immediate implementation of convictions as a policy concern and argued that the presumption of innocence was overturned upon conviction, while also supporting the proposed Ombudsman Marshall office.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Representative Diokno referred to a study from about twenty years earlier involving 110 persons convicted of graft and corruption offenses by final judgment. He said the study recommended a centralized government system to ensure that convicted persons, including those appealing, served their sentences.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Diokno asked Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla for his position on the proposal and what could be done to advance it, noting that it had been pending for more than twenty years.

thread.speaker: Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said the legal system was unclear regarding persons sentenced by the anti-graft or lower courts, particularly because they could usually post bail after conviction. He argued that the system should be reconsidered so convicted persons serve their sentences promptly, while acknowledging that the issue involved the appellate process and should perhaps be raised with the Supreme Court.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Chair Rodriguez cautioned that immediate imprisonment after an RTC conviction could conflict with the constitutional presumption of innocence and the right to appeal, which he said remained until final judgment. He asked Remulla to comment on that concern.

thread.speaker: Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla
thread.said: Remulla agreed that the presumption of innocence was important but maintained that, in his view, it disappeared once a court with jurisdiction convicted and sentenced a person. Rodriguez characterized the exchange as a difference of opinion.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Diokno clarified that his question was not primarily about bail. He asked whether the absence of a centralized system to track cases through lengthy appeals, apprehension, and imprisonment concerned the Ombudsman and whether the office had taken steps to create such a system across the Department of Justice and other agencies.

thread.speaker: Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla
thread.said: Remulla agreed that convictions needed to be tracked and said the Ombudsman’s budget presentation requested funding to create an Ombudsman Marshall office. He said the office would track the status of persons jailed, sentenced to jail, or accused and maintain a complete inventory of persons charged in court.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Diokno said the tracking function was especially important because the Ombudsman was probing about 200 flood control cases, with at least four already in court.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Diokno asked why the Ombudsman’s materials did not contain a proposal for a witness-protection program and sought Remulla’s view.

thread.speaker: Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said the planned Ombudsman Marshall office would also handle witness-protection-related functions, service of subpoenas, and other duties. He said the Ombudsman could delegate these functions to the police but believed its own marshals would be more effective.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Diokno said he wanted to know more about the proposed marshals concept.

thread.speaker: Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla
thread.said: Remulla explained that the Supreme Court had already adopted its own marshals and that the Ombudsman proposal followed that model rather than being an original idea.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno

thread.speaker: An agency official

thread.speaker: Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla
thread.said: Remulla said the Ombudsman was conducting 107 lifestyle checks and was adding more based on information concerning Customs, the LTO, and other income-generating government agencies, including the BII.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Diokno said he was pleased that lifestyle checks were being conducted and remarked that a lifestyle check would have exposed issues concerning the person who had to return R500 million dollars, as spoken in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rodriguez stated that the chair’s representation supported creation of Ombudsman marshals to protect the Ombudsman, expedite processes, and help ensure that persons convicted by final judgment were imprisoned.

topics.topic: Lifestyle checks and investigation safeguards
topics.summary: Representative Iris Marie Montes questioned the Ombudsman about conviction rates, safeguards against political influence, digital investigative tools, moto proprio investigations, and regional reach. The agency reported a Sandigan Bayan conviction rate of about 65.52 percent in 2026, compared with 42 percent previously, and cited lower-court rates of about 77.6 percent in 2025 and 64.91 percent as of June 30. It lacked immediately available data separating moto proprio cases from filed complaints but undertook to provide it, while regional performance indicators were also requested. topics.topic: Pre-audit and geo-mapping support for government projects
topics.summary: Rep. Mauricio Domogan asked whether mandatory pre-audit of government-project payments, combined with geo-mapping, should be pursued to address ghost projects and corruption. He said the pre-audit requirement had been removed in 2011 and that COA supported the proposal with one additional personnel. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla said the measure would be a big help but belonged to COA, which might need more staff. Domogan also asked about investigation timelines; Remulla cited fact-finding periods of about 30 to 60 days and preliminary-investigation periods of about 30 to 60 days. Remulla reported that 60 lawyers had been hired, 40 more were planned, and the total would reach 100 lawyers. The issue ended with member support but without a recorded ruling or final action on the bill.

topics.topic: DOST and attached-agency budget reduction, including 12.5% cut
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio raised the DOST and attached-agency reductions, including the 12.5% cut, and was told that the main reductions were in capital outlay for completed or already funded projects. He also questioned the national AI-compute plan, which DOST described as an in-country, GPU-based capability supported initially by 100,000,000 and targeted for expansion by 26 fold by 2028. The chair then examined the proposed redistribution of about 1.25 billion in grants, while DBM explained that a new policy moved ongoing attached-agency R&D funding into agency-specific budgets. DOST argued that grants were proposal-driven and required flexibility, citing 98% utilization, and the chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards. DOST identified 800,000,000 for the Virology Institute and 309,000,000 for graduate grants, covering 5,000 grantees, and the committee requested supporting tables, project lists, AI documents, and prioritized amendments. The issue remained subject to consultations and subsequent congressional action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why the DOST and attached-agency budgets were reduced, particularly where reductions reflected completed capital-outlay projects, and how DOST's grants should be structured. It also examined the funding needed for national AI-compute infrastructure, the Virology Institute, graduate grants, and priority amendments.
topics.agency_position: DOST said the major agency reductions were primarily capital-outlay reductions caused by projects whose funding or phases had already been completed. It supported retaining flexible, proposal-driven grants under the Office of the Secretary, arguing that agency-specific allocations could not adequately respond to changing R&D, emergency, and disaster-related needs.
topics.outcome: The capital-outlay reductions were explained as reflecting completed projects. The grants issue was not finally resolved in the hearing: DBM deferred to Congress, while the chair proposed possible re-centralization with safeguards and requested further DBM-DOST consultations. DOST was also asked to submit AI, construction, grant, and prioritized amendment information.

positions.position: Pressed DOST and its attached agencies to explain reductions, sought details on national AI-compute and data-sovereignty infrastructure, and requested supporting documents.

Favored preserving DOST's flexibility by potentially re-centralizing the grants in the Office of the Secretary, while allowing safeguards and further DBM-DOST consultation. The chair also supported increasing DOST resources but required prioritization of amendment requests.
Supported DOST flexibility, subject to safeguards against misuse of funds.
Defended the new agency-specific grant allocation as a DBM policy intended to streamline implementation, but deferred the final disposition to Congress.

thread.said: He asked what the proposed high-performance-computing center was, including its scale, power source, hardware, location, and relationship to data centers and data sovereignty.

thread.speaker: the DOST Secretary

thread.said: The ASTI director said the project continued the institute's shared high-performance-computing and storage service for government agencies, R&D institutes, and academe. AI required GPU-based architecture, and DOST was expanding through commercial data-center space while installing its own GPUs to strengthen national AI sovereignty.

thread.speaker: the ASTI director
thread.said: The director said the latest expansion had procured H200 processors. The planned cluster involved five major compute servers, data-storage servers, and network-equipment upgrades, although the exact processor figure was not available.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He requested the national AI strategy and implementation plan.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the major decreases in PAGASA, FNRI, and PNRI reflected completed projects, including a 364,000,000 differential for PAGASA and a 345,000,000 decrease for PNRI.

thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked why grants had been distributed among attached agencies, whether the change was DOST's or DBM's decision, and whether the 1,250,000,000 in grants should instead be re-centralized in the Office of the Secretary.

thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian
thread.said: Director Vivian said DBM had adopted a 2027 policy reallocating ongoing R&D projects of DOST attached agencies from the Office of the Secretary's grants-in-aid to agency-specific budgets. Grants-in-aid would primarily fund projects proposed by external stakeholders, while direct agency funding was intended to speed implementation and streamline transfers.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the new arrangement was a new guideline compared with the 2026 General Appropriations Act and what specifically differed in the 2027 National Expenditure Program.

thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian
thread.said: Director Vivian confirmed that it was a new DBM policy adopted during budget preparation and later said it was covered by an internal memo.

thread.speaker: the DOST Secretary

thread.speaker: the committee chair

thread.speaker: a DOST official
thread.said: The utilization rate was stated as 98%.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair questioned whether fixing an attached agency's grants at a predetermined level, illustrated with 200,000,000, could produce a lower budget utilization rate and reduce flexibility because future grantee needs were dynamic.

thread.speaker: the DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said grants were proposal-driven and could be redirected to experts and institutions responding to emerging needs, such as an oil spill or disaster-risk-reduction work. thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian

thread.speaker: the committee chair

thread.speaker: the committee chair

thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian

thread.speaker: a committee member

thread.speaker: the committee chair

thread.said: The chair questioned whether assigning a fixed grant amount to each attached agency could lower future utilization because grant demand was dynamic and could not be accurately known during budget preparation.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The secretary said grants were proposal-driven and needed to cover emerging needs, including emergency responses such as oil spills requiring university experts. A program for that purpose had been transferred to PAGASA even though PAGASA could not distribute the funds as intended by the OSEC.

thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair pushed back that ongoing projects in the submission might not be the same projects requiring funding in 2027, and said the agency needed flexibility. The chair noted DOST's 98% utilization rate and said the chair sided with DOST on that point.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The secretary explained that centralized, proposal-driven funding allowed DOST to support qualified proposals from different agencies, including disaster-risk-reduction proposals, rather than limiting funds to the agency where the amount had been lodged.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the 1,200,000,000 figure required further assessment and that flexibility was necessary because funds assigned to one agency could not readily be transferred when another agency later had the stronger need.

thread.speaker: Committee chair

thread.speaker: DBM Director Vivian

thread.speaker: DOST official

thread.speaker: Committee chair

topics.topic: National AI infrastructure, high-performance computing, and data sovereignty
topics.summary: Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DOST about the proposed national AI center, the target of increasing high-performance computing capacity by 26 fold by 2028, and whether the expansion was funded in the budget. ASTI said the existing service had evolved from a shared supercomputer into GPU-based infrastructure, with H200 processors, five major compute servers, commercial data-center space, and planned regional expansion. It identified 100,000,000 in initial DOST grant-in-aid seed funding but did not state the total cost of the expansion. The DOST Secretary said DOST would lead research and development infrastructure, talent management, and language models, while DICT would handle connectivity and related private-sector infrastructure. DOST also described a Philippine data-sovereignty platform and a planned government-managed AI hub, while acknowledging insufficient compute power and scale. Tinio supported AI and data sovereignty and requested documents on the National AI Strategy, existing compute capacity, and expansion plans.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish what national high-performance computing and data infrastructure the government was building for artificial intelligence, how large and capable it was, how much expansion would cost, and whether it was reflected in the proposed budget. It also sought to clarify which agency would lead the effort and how the government would protect Philippine data and AI sovereignty.
topics.agency_position: DOST said it should lead research-and-development infrastructure, talent development, and Philippine language-model development, while DICT would lead connectivity and related infrastructure involving the private sector. The agency supported building nationally controlled compute and data capabilities, including regional expansion and a data-sovereignty platform, but acknowledged that compute power and scale remained insufficient.
topics.outcome: DOST explained the institutional division of responsibilities and described existing and planned compute and data-sovereignty initiatives. The committee requested supporting documents and expansion information; the total cost, precise scale, power requirements, and full budget treatment of the 26-fold expansion remained unprovided.

positions.position: Supported data, digital, and AI sovereignty and the development of nationally owned compute and data infrastructure. He opposed excessive reliance on foreign cloud, data, and AI systems and sought a clear expansion plan, cost information, and agency leadership.
Expressed support for the DOST budget and, if possible, an increase in its budget.
Commended the DOST Secretary's position favoring country-specific AI models and data sovereignty.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary described it essentially as a compute center or compute cluster for AI that could be deployed both physically and on the cloud, with the objective of having the capability in-country.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio clarified whether the center would be in the country and whether it would use high-power GPUs and AI processors.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
