thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked how large the cluster would be, where its power would come from, what level of AI infrastructure existed in the Philippines, and whether the plan was reflected in the budget proposal.

thread.speaker: ASTI Director
thread.said: The ASTI Director said the initiative continued a service operated by ASTI for about one decade, originally as a high-performance supercomputer cluster and later as shared computing and storage for government agencies, research institutes, and academia. The AI expansion required GPU-based architecture and was intended to institutionalize and sustain DOST's AI track.

thread.speaker: ASTI Director
thread.said: The Director said the current data center was only a container van behind the office and that DOST was beginning to expand through commercial data centers by leasing space and installing its own GPUs. This was intended to strengthen the country's sovereignty and its ability to deploy AI applications using its own systems.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked about the technological level of the planned infrastructure, including whether it would use current NVIDIA processors such as A100, H100, or Blackwell chips.

thread.speaker: ASTI Director
thread.said: The Director said DOST had procured H200 processors for the latest expansion. He added that the plan included extending compute resources beyond the National Capital Region or Mega Manila to the regions.

thread.speaker: ASTI Director
thread.said: The Director said the H200 cluster had five major compute servers, together with data-storage servers and upgraded network equipment to handle expected data and traffic exchanges. He said he did not have the exact figure for the processors.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether the expansion was included in the current budget and how much the plan to expand computing power by 26 fold by 2028 would cost.

thread.speaker: ASTI Director
thread.said: The Director said the initial seed funding from DOST through grant-in-aid was 100,000,000. He said DOST hoped to increase that support and might also seek assistance from development partners in the future, but he did not provide the total cost of the 26-fold expansion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio said that, whatever terminology was used, the issue was digital or AI infrastructure and data sovereignty. He warned that otherwise the country would remain dependent on cloud, data, and AI services from abroad.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked the chair to require information on the country's existing nationally owned compute capacity, plans to expand it, and plans to extend the resource to the regions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether the Department of Information and Communications Technology was the lead agency for developing indigenous digital or AI infrastructure, or whether another arrangement applied.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said the National AI Strategy had four major components: the AI factory or infrastructure, human resources, policies, and financing. Under the implementation strategy, different government organizations would lead different areas.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DOST would lead infrastructure for research and development, talent management, and language-model development, working with the Department of Trade and Industry, DICT, and industry. DICT would also handle connectivity and infrastructure, primarily in relation to the private sector.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DOST was developing data sovereignty through a geospatial analytics and technology-solutions platform that would transform data using geographic information systems. He said the platform would provide data to fuel AI development and differentiate DOST's role from those of other agencies.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DOST's goal was to develop a government-managed AI hub using Philippine data that could be queried by language models developed in the country. He identified Itano as an existing language model and said Filipino-dataset language models were also being made available through a platform comparable to an app store.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said the principal limitation was a lack of compute power and scale, which constrained the operation of the models.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio requested documents on the National AI Strategy and its implementation plan.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: As a postscript, Tinio said he supported data sovereignty, digital sovereignty, and AI sovereignty under the National AI Strategy. He argued that dependence on foreign systems could leave the Philippines without control over the technology and merely as a paying customer.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio criticized the argument that countries should not reproduce AI capabilities domestically and should instead rely on more advanced foreign systems. He characterized that approach as potentially backward and counterproductive for Philippine sovereignty.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary responded that countries unable to compete with the most advanced systems should develop smaller language models tailored to their specific national or organizational needs. He emphasized that data would be more powerful than AI itself and said DOST's focus was therefore a data-sovereignty platform.

thread.speaker: a committee presiding official
thread.said: The presiding official commended the Secretary for taking that position.

topics.topic: Project SARAI and smart-agriculture climate resilience technologies
topics.summary: Rep. Bella Suansing asked the DOST secretary to explain Project SARAI, its regional coverage, crop recommendations, and links with the Department of Agriculture. DOST said SARAI integrated satellite, GIS, weather, crop, pest, soil, water, nutrient, and mobile-application data, with deployment determined by local commodity needs. The agency said SARAI did not exclude complementary technologies, including seaweed foliar fertilizer that was reported to increase rice production by up to 30%. DOST said it was shifting from pilots toward regional implementation with agriculture agencies, local governments, cooperatives, and farmers, and cited a mobile solar irrigation trailer developed in Region 3. The discussion also covered DOST's customizable disaster platform, its SOS and AI features, and its use of evacuation-site data from the Department of the Interior and Local Government and the Office of Civil Defense. The exchange ended with information provided and a general agency commitment to promote local adoption, without a specific budgetary or documentary action.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how Project SARAI operated, where it was being deployed, and whether its crop, water, and climate-smart technologies were being integrated with the Department of Agriculture, local governments, and disaster-preparedness efforts. It also asked how DOST-developed platforms and technologies could be accelerated in response to El Niño and climate change.
topics.agency_position: DOST stated that Project SARAI and related smart-agriculture technologies were being moved from pilot and use-case applications toward regional implementation with the Department of Agriculture, local governments, cooperatives, and farmer partners. DOST also maintained that its irrigation, information, monitoring, and disaster-response platforms could be customized and adopted locally to address El Niño, climate resilience, and disaster preparedness.
topics.outcome: The committee received an explanation of SARAI's functions, deployment model, interagency links, and related climate and disaster technologies. Wider regional and local adoption was encouraged, but no specific funding, implementation schedule, or additional submission was resolved during the exchange.

positions.position: She supported wider deployment and interagency integration of SARAI and DOST's climate-smart agriculture and disaster-preparedness technologies, particularly in response to El Niño.
The member sought clarification on the source and integration of evacuation-center data in the DOST platform.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She asked the DOST secretary to orient the committee on Project SARAI and its process for applying smarter approaches to Philippine agriculture, including crop nutrient management, agricultural monitoring, and mobile applications.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official said Project SARAI was a DOST R&D program funded by DOST EPIC and previously implemented by UPLB, with operations now at the regional level. It integrated satellite remote sensing, GIS and crop mapping, weather and rainfall data, crop forecasting and modeling, pest and disease monitoring, water and nutrient management, digital mobile applications, and site-specific crop advisories.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She asked in which regions Project SARAI had been rolled out.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official answered that deployment depended on the commodity that local governments and farmers wanted to study. The program could also be used in NCR, including for urban farming.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She asked whether Project SARAI, based on soil sampling, also recommended specific crop varieties.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official said soil health and classification had to be assessed to identify the best possible crop for an area. The official added that SARAI did not restrict the use of other technologies, citing seaweed foliar fertilizer that could increase rice production up to 30%, although it was not part of SARAI.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official said SARAI was supplemented by other smart-agriculture technologies and that DOST was also introducing smart-aquaculture technologies supported and monitored through the Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She asked whether DOST was coordinating with the Department of Agriculture and other national government agencies to promote climate-smart methods across government programs.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official said coordination was occurring through the Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development, whose governing council included the Department of Agriculture. Technologies could be implemented locally through DOST regional and provincial offices and the consortia managed by the council, although utilization would not necessarily be 100%.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She said DOST's technologies should be at the forefront of national attention because DOST co-chaired the Office of Civil Defense under Task Force El Niño. She noted that the presentation had shown completed projects directly addressing climate-smart agriculture, including possible responses to soil acidity caused by climate change.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official said DOST initially promoted agricultural technologies through use cases and pilot projects but concluded that implementation was not accelerating fast enough for the effects of climate change on farmers and fisherfolk. DOST therefore shifted toward regional implementation with the Department of Agriculture, provincial and local governments, cooperatives, and farmer partners.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: For the El Niño task force, the official said DOST had developed a platform to provide information and monitor interventions. DOST had asked that interventions developed by DOST through the council be included, including drip irrigation and furrow irrigation.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official cited a solar irrigation trailer unit developed in Region 3 with Nueva Ecija Science and Technology University. Unlike permanent solarized irrigation systems, the mobile unit could be moved from one farm to another and could draw from surface water or shallow wells.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official said DOST had the relevant technologies and hoped local governments would adopt them to help manage the forthcoming El Niño.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She commended DOST's presentation, including its smart-flood-management approaches, and referred to the establishment of an integrated water-resource and flood-mitigation strategy under 2026.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bella Suansing
thread.said: She asked how the emergency SOS feature of the integrated platform would work and whether it would operate through local government units or the Department of Health central office.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The official described the platform as an integrated system for disaster preparedness and response that combined early-warning systems available to local governments and the public. SOS or incident reporting could be activated by an LGU using the platform, which could be customized for an LGU or the national Office of Civil Defense.

thread.speaker: DOST secretary
thread.said: The platform could use an AI chatbot to identify hazards and plan an evacuation route to the nearest evacuation site. The official said features could be tailored to the needs of each LGU and that the platform had been launched in March of this year.

Using the phone's GPS location, the application could identify the nearest evacuation site and assess the hazard affecting the user.

topics.topic: Fisheries and aquaculture development programs for Bicol and Catanduanes
topics.summary: Rep. Eulogio Rodriguez raised the weak performance of Bicol’s economy and fisheries, citing GDP growth of about 0.5% in 2025, a 2.9% contraction in the agriculture, fisheries and forestry sector, and a 10.7% decline in fishery. He asked where the bottlenecks were and what measurable results DOST, PCAARRD, and partner agencies had achieved in Catanduanes and Bicol. The PCAARRD director said several aquaculture and marine-resources projects were underway, including work involving Catanduanes State University, but identified technology transfer and coordination with local governments and other agencies as challenges. For 2027, the director said PCAARRD would explore expanding the tilapia program and other marine-resource initiatives based on pilot projects elsewhere. PCAARRD committed to reviewing and enhancing its current initiatives, but no quantified outcomes or specific budget figures were provided.

topics.topic: Technology commercialization and sexual-assault-kit procurement
topics.summary: Sarah Elago raised the need to commercialize and scale the DOST-supported sexual-assault-kit technology for use by women-and-children protection units and public hospitals. A DOST official said the agency's role was to support research and development, promote the technology, and maintain dialogue with its UP producer. The official said investors were reluctant to take commercialization risks, so DOST supported production and use cases that could demonstrate the technology to potential adopters such as the DOJ and PNP. The agency also said appropriate agencies needed to procure the kit and expressed hope that the Tatak Pinoy Act would give Filipino-produced, DOST-supported technology preferential treatment. topics.topic: PAGASA and PNRI capital-outlay-related budget decreases
topics.summary: The committee chair asked why PAGASA and PNRI had lower capital-outlay allocations, and the agency-side response attributed the decreases to completed projects, including about 345 million for PNRI. The chair then questioned the transfer of roughly 1.25 billion in DOST grants from the Office of the Secretary to attached agencies. DBM said the distribution reflected a new policy intended to fund ongoing R&D projects directly and streamline implementation, while DOST said the proposal-driven nature of grants required flexibility and that some funds had been transferred to agencies unable to implement the relevant programs. DOST reported 98% utilization under the previous centralized arrangement. The chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards, and DBM deferred to Congress. The chair requested post-hearing DBM-DOST consultations and the drafting of any necessary special provisions.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGASA and PNRI had lower capital-outlay allocations and whether the transfer of DOST grants from the Office of the Secretary to attached agencies should be reversed. It also examined whether the new grant structure would reduce flexibility and utilization, and whether safeguards or special provisions were needed.
topics.agency_position: DBM said the distributed grant structure resulted from a new internal policy intended to place funding for ongoing R&D projects directly with attached agencies, speed implementation, and leave GIA for externally proposed projects. DOST said the transfer had included grants that agencies could not themselves implement and would reduce the flexibility of the proposal-driven system, which had achieved 98% utilization.
topics.outcome: The capital-outlay decreases were explained as resulting from completed projects, including the 345,000,000 PNRI decrease. The grant issue was not finally resolved; DBM deferred to Congress, while the chair sought post-hearing consultations and possible special provisions to preserve flexibility.

positions.position: Supported retaining or restoring flexibility by potentially re-centralizing the grants in the Office of the Secretary, subject to special provisions or safeguards, and favored post-hearing DBM-DOST consultations.

DOST said the reductions were mainly capital-outlay adjustments and described grant-in-aid support for advanced manufacturing, AI, robotics, and other emerging technologies. The AI initiative had initial seed funding of about 100 million, while the agency described a planned 26-fold expansion and regional rollout. The chair asked about 800 million for the Virology Institute and roughly 309 million for master's and PhD grants covering 5,000 recipients, with increases in monthly grant rates. thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Antonio Tinio cited a proposed total budget of 30.8 and 32,100,000,000 for DOST and its attached agencies, and asked about reductions in the Office of the Secretary and attached agencies, including a stated 12.5% reduction.

thread.speaker: DOST agency official
thread.said: The official said the reduction was in capital outlay because projects funded in 2026, including warning systems and an X-band radar in a river basin, were no longer included for the following year. The official clarified that the reduction was in capital outlay, not operations.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked why the Food and Nutrition Research Institute allocation went from 100,000,000.06 to 34,000,000.

thread.speaker: DOST agency official
thread.said: The agency said the change concerned capital outlay and explained that funding had been provided for the Phase 4 building. It stated that the 2027 request for the building was 400,000,000.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio noted a Metals Industry Research and Development Center increase from 360,000,005 and asked about the capital-outlay increase. He then asked what specific grants were covered under the Office of the Secretary grant-in-aid program.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said the grants generally support agencies seeking assistance to develop technologies related to their mandates, particularly Industry 4.0 technologies involving AI, robotics, and automation. The funds may support activities not included in an agency's original program, subject to DBM transferring the amount.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether the Metals Industry Research and Development Center grant specifically concerned robotics and whether it involved mining.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said it was not really about mining but about advanced manufacturing, including metals, robotics, automation, and mechanization.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked about the National AI Center for Research and Innovation, whether it was specifically reflected in the budget, and how the announced goal of increasing high-performance computing capacity by 26 fold would be implemented.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said the AI center was already funded at the grant-in-aid level as a continuing research-and-development program, while the Advanced Science and Technology Institute had proposed increasing compute power. The Secretary confirmed that the capacity was intended for government operations and applications supporting MSMEs and industry.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether the proposed high-performance computing center was physical infrastructure such as data centers, whether it would use high-power GPUs, how large the cluster would be, and whether the expansion was reflected in the budget.

thread.speaker: AST director
thread.said: The AST director described the center as a continuation of ASTI's shared high-performance computing and storage service for government agencies, research institutes, and academia. The AI expansion required GPU-based hardware, and the agency was using commercial data-center space while installing its own GPUs to build national AI capacity.

thread.speaker: AST director
thread.said: The director said the agency had procured H200 processors and planned to expand capacity beyond NCR or Mega Manila to the regions. The director said the H2 cluster had five major compute servers, with data-storage servers and network upgrades, but did not have the exact processor figure.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether the current budget covered the planned 26-fold expansion by 2028 and how much the expansion would cost.

thread.speaker: AST director
thread.said: The AST director said the initial seed funding from DOST through its grant-in-aid program was 100,000,000. The agency hoped to increase this and potentially obtain support from development partners.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio requested information on DOST's existing nationally owned compute capacity, expansion plans, and the planned regional rollout, emphasizing the importance of digital or AI infrastructure and data sovereignty.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio asked whether DICT or DOST was the lead agency for developing indigenous digital or AI infrastructure.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DOST led infrastructure for research and development, talent management, and language-model development, while DICT handled connectivity and infrastructure with emphasis on the private sector. DOST was also developing data sovereignty through geospatial analytics and technology platforms and envisioned a DOST-managed AI hub using Philippine data and models.

thread.speaker: Antonio Tinio
thread.said: Tinio requested the national AI strategy and implementation plan from DOST.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked for an indicative amount needed for the Virology Institute under the Office of the Secretary proposal.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DOST needed 800,000,000 for the following year to complete the Phase 1 and Phase 2 buildings so the institute could operate in New Clark City. The construction was ongoing and lodged under DPWH.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the request for the Virology Institute would come from DOST or DPWH and whether it had been included in DOST's Tier 1 proposal to DBM.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked for an indicative amount for aligning DOST master's and PhD grants with CHED levels and asked how many master's and PhD students were covered.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary stated that the projected amount was 309,000,000 and that 5,000 master's and PhD grant recipients were covered.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said the master's grant would increase from 30 to 38 per month, while the PhD grant would increase from 38 to 50 per month.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair requested a table showing the number of grantees, the amount for each category, and the basis for the 309,000,000 projected 2027 requirement. The Secretary confirmed that the amount was the 2027 projection.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary said DOST had a list of construction projects that had started but were not continued and would submit it.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said fiscal space was limited and that, although members supported increasing DOST's budget, the agency needed to prioritize its requests rather than submit an undifferentiated wish list.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair requested that DOST submit a prioritized list of institutional amendment requests, including partial priorities where appropriate, so the committee could determine how best to assist.

thread.speaker: DOST Secretary
thread.said: The Secretary agreed that DOST would prioritize its requests.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked DOST to submit the institutional amendment requests as soon as possible, preferably within the week, so the budget amendments review subcommittee could deliberate them in time.

thread.speaker: Committee member
thread.said: A committee member expressed support for giving DOST flexibility, subject to safeguards against misuse of funds, citing its performance and reliability in departmental and disaster-related functions.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair commended DOST as a performing agency and said the presentation was overwhelmingly focused on accomplishments. The chair also expressed personal support for DOST's science-high-school, scholarship, grant, and stipend programs.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair recalled that the stipend had once been 500 pesos per month and referenced 2,000 as a minimum at that time, then reiterated that DOST had committee partners who would advocate for its budget.

hearings.title: COMMITTEE ON APPROPRIATIONS (AUGUST 24, 2026)

topics.topic: PAGCOR FY 2026 income decline and FY 2027 revenue outlook
topics.summary: Chair Mika Suansing asked PAGCOR to explain the decline from its 2025 income and to clarify the 2027 outlook. PAGCOR attributed the decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, weaker land-based casino and licensee revenues, and economic conditions affecting its CDE customer market; it projected 2027 total revenues of about 88.33 billion. PAGCOR said first-semester 2026 income was about 43.32 billion, with about 30.16 billion going to nation-building programs, and reported 2026 gaming-operations income of about 80 billion divided roughly equally between land-based and online gaming. Members also questioned the retroactive 37,000,000,000 pesos PSC obligation and online-gaming regulation, including the policing of illegal operators, advertising, influencers, and minors. PAGCOR said it was updating its regulatory framework and disclosed projected 2026 revenues of between 9 and 10 billion for Casino Filipino, about 31.5 billion for licensed casinos, and 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038 for digital e-games. The issue landed with requests for PSC remittance records and detailed revenue data, while stronger online-gaming regulation remained an ongoing commitment rather than a resolved matter.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's 2026 income and net income had declined from the assumptions underlying its approved budget, what the 2027 revenue outlook was, and how the decline would affect government remittances and social-responsibility programs. Members also sought to determine whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory capacity to manage the growth of online gaming and illegal operators.
topics.agency_position: PAGCOR attributed the 2026 income decline mainly to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, weaker land-based casino and licensee revenues, and economic conditions affecting its CDE customer market. It maintained that online gaming remained a significant revenue opportunity but acknowledged regulatory risks and said it was regularly updating its rules and strengthening its structures. PAGCOR also said it was implementing the Supreme Court's retroactive PSC remittance ruling while continuing discussions concerning payment.
topics.outcome: PAGCOR explained the principal causes of the 2026 decline and presented a 2027 revenue projection, but the committee did not resolve the longer-term regulatory and social risks of online gaming. The committee required PAGCOR's PSC remittance records and detailed revenue breakdown for further budget scrutiny.

positions.position: The chair viewed the income decline as requiring clarification but commended PAGCOR for largely maintaining nation-building and social-civic commitments. She said the committee would scrutinize PAGCOR's PSC remittances and the corresponding PSC budget level.
Representative Sanfordado emphasized the social risks of online gaming, the need to control advertising and influencers, and the need for responsible-gaming programs.

Representative Jinger sought a detailed revenue breakdown and suggested considering information dissemination and other public-safety uses alongside or instead of some school-building and calamity-response projects.

Representative Pleyto pressed PAGCOR for concrete measures to reverse declining gross gaming revenue, improve regulation and digital monitoring, address illegal operators, and attract responsible investment, while commending its social-responsibility work.

The minority member regarded the growth of online gaming as a regulatory and social concern, particularly because of its CDE customer base, and urged stronger controls before allowing the sector to expand further.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair said PAGCOR's income and net income for 2026 were projected to be lower than the assumptions underlying its approved corporate operating budget. She said the committee wanted clarification on the downward revisions and a realistic, sustainable 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR assistant vice president Cheryl DeGuilla
thread.said: PAGCOR reported total income of 106,030,000,000 in 2025, total contributions to nation building of around 67,000,000,000, estimated 2026 total revenues of around 7,000,000,000, and projected 2027 total revenues of 88,330,000,000.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR assistant vice president Cheryl DeGuilla
thread.said: For January to June 2026, PAGCOR said operating expenses over total income rose to 26.7%, while net income over total income fell to 3.66%.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR assistant vice president Cheryl DeGuilla
thread.said: PAGCOR said 2025 gaming-operations income was 95,140,000,000, lower by 2,380,000,000, or around 2.5%, than 97,520,000,000 in 2024. It attributed the decline to the closure of Pogo in December 2024, lower revenues from PAGCOR casinos and licensees, and the delinking of e-wallets from online gaming platforms in the third quarter of 2025.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR assistant vice president Cheryl DeGuilla
PAGCOR assistant vice president Cheryl DeGuilla
thread.said: During the first semester of 2026, PAGCOR reported total income of 43,320,000,000, of which 30,160,000,000 went to nation-building programs.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair asked PAGCOR to explain the downturn in total income from 2025 to 2026, citing an 18% decrease from the 2025 actual total income projection of R106 billion to R86.94 PHP 95,000,000,000 in 2026. The wording of the 2026 figure was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco attributed the decline initially to the delinking of payment applications from online-gaming customers in September or the last quarter of 2025. He said gaming activity declined by about 40% after customers had to go through an additional payment process.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the Middle East crisis affected both land-based casinos and online gaming, particularly because the CDE market was PAGCOR's main online-gaming customer base. He reported a gaming-activity increase of about 10% in July and said August remained at the same level, while tourism at integrated resorts had begun to improve.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair noted that estimated total income had decreased by about R20 billion from 2025 to 2026, but contributions to nation building had declined by only point 3% or R5.5 billion. The transcript's currency markings and the complete 2025 contribution figure were unclear.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco explained that PAGCOR was implementing, effective 01/01/2026, the Supreme Court ruling on the Philippine Sports Commission remittance. The ruling required the 5% remittance to be computed on gross income rather than only gaming revenue and was retroactive to 1993.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the retroactive PSC ruling involved 37,000,000,000 pesos. PAGCOR had filed a motion for reconsideration and sought additional time for payment while continuing discussions with PSC.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR's PSC contribution had averaged 190,000,000 pesos a month and that the new interpretation had doubled the impact.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair said the committee would take the additional PSC remittances into account when deliberating the PSC budget. She said the remittance increase was almost double, or more than double, on a monthly basis.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair highlighted that social-civic projects rose from PHP12.4 billion in 2024 to PHP12.8 billion in 2025 and PHP13.99 billion in 2026 despite the income downturn.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco said PAGCOR needed to account for payment of 3,300,000,000 every year for the next ten years in connection with the PSC ruling.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair said the PSC's fiscal year 2027 net level did not yet appear commensurate with the increased remittances from PAGCOR. She undertook to scrutinize the appropriate PSC funding level based on utilization and planned programs and projects.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair requested copies of PAGCOR's remittances to PSC for the whole of 2025 and from the start of 2026 so the committee could consider them in reviewing the PSC budget.

thread.speaker: Minority Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: Representative Sanfordado asked about the reported 30,000,000 registered and 10,000,000 active online-gaming players, noting that many were from the CDE market and appeared to include minimum-wage and low-income earners.

thread.speaker: Minority Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: He asked whether PAGCOR exercised regulatory power over content creators and influencers promoting online gambling, particularly where they had millions of followers.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR official
thread.said: The PAGCOR official said an online-gaming company had been fined 1,000,000 pesos and warned that another violation could lead to suspension and ultimately cancellation of its license.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR official
thread.said: The official stated that 50% of current online-gaming operators were illegal and outside PAGCOR's jurisdiction, while only 8% to 10% were legal at the time the chairman assumed office. The figures were presented in a fragmented response.

thread.speaker: Minority Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: Representative Sanfordado asked about PAGCOR's responsible-gaming projects and measures to address social harm from online gaming.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR official
thread.said: PAGCOR described responsible-gaming efforts involving billboards, a hotline, advice and referrals to rehabilitation centers, and self-exclusion or family-exclusion mechanisms for land-based casinos and online licensees. Some details of the hotline figures were unclear.

thread.speaker: Majority Representative Bong Thebes Jinger
thread.said: Representative Jinger asked for a breakdown of PAGCOR income, including the contributions of online gaming.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR official
thread.said: The PAGCOR official said estimated 2026 gaming-operations income was 80,000,000,000 pesos, divided approximately 50% from land-based casinos and 50% from online gaming, with online gaming at 40,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The minority member asked for projected 2026 income from Casino Filipino operations.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco said Casino Filipino gross gaming revenue was projected at between 9 and 10,000,000,000 only for 2026, down from the comparison raised by the member.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The minority member asked for 2026 revenue from licensed casino operations, excluding Casino Filipino, and requested a list of private casinos and their respective revenues.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco said licensed casinos were expected to generate about 31, 31 and a half billion in 2026, down from the prior comparison of 33.20 24. He agreed to provide a detailed list covering licensed casinos, Casino Filipino, and online gaming.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He projected 2026 digital e-games revenue at 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038. The final figure was spoken unclearly.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco said the shift toward online gaming was both positive and negative: positive because of technological growth and revenue potential, but negative because major licensed casinos were experiencing declining revenue. He cited the Middle East crisis and broader economic conditions as contributing factors.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The minority member questioned the social implications of relying heavily on online gaming, particularly because customers came from the CDE market, while PAGCOR was also spending on social programs.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco identified social-outreach spending of 15 to 18,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The minority member said the concern was not online gaming itself but how minors and other users could be properly policed. He asked what concrete steps PAGCOR had taken to strengthen its regulatory powers and framework.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco said PAGCOR was strengthening its structures and updating online-gaming guidelines, rules, and regulations regularly based on market trends. He acknowledged the difficulty of competing with and policing illegal online operators.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: Mr. Tengco said PAGCOR would need to examine how to strengthen its regulatory structures further.

thread.speaker: Minority member
thread.said: The minority member urged the committee and PAGCOR to develop ways to properly regulate online gaming, especially as technology was evolving rapidly.

topics.topic: Casino Filipino privatization, proceeds, and PAGCOR’s future role
topics.summary: Members asked PAGCOR about the status of privatizing roughly 30 to 40 Casino Filipino properties, its expected proceeds, and the agency's future regulatory role. PAGCOR said the transaction remained pending the GCG recommendation and Office of the President's approval, with estimated proceeds ranging from about 20 billion to 30 billion, and later about 25 billion to 30 billion. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised safeguards for approximately 10,000 employees, while PAGCOR cited retirement and special incentive packages, buyer absorption, and extensive retraining. Rep. Iris Marie Montes and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned how privatization would affect PhilHealth's UHC earmark; PAGCOR said it remitted to the National Treasury, which was responsible for the subsequent 50% UHC remittance. PAGCOR cited about 50 billion pesos remitted in 2025, implying 25 billion for the UHC fund under the statutory formula, and estimated retirement needs of about 28 billion to 30 billion against 12 billion in current retirement funding. PAGCOR agreed to submit remittance and privatization computations within forty eight hours and to study whether any proceeds remaining after retirement costs could support a UHC stabilization fund.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the status, scope, valuation, and proceeds of the proposed Casino Filipino privatization, including PAGCOR's transition from operator-regulator to primarily regulator. Members also asked how privatization would affect employees, PhilHealth's Universal Health Care remittances, PAGCOR's future revenues, and the use of sale proceeds.
topics.agency_position: PAGCOR said the privatization remained subject to the GCG recommendation and approval by the Office of the President. It estimated proceeds in the range of 20,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000, or about 25,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000 under a later estimate, with employee retirement obligations taking priority; it maintained that PAGCOR would continue remitting its share to the National Treasury and that the national government would remain responsible for the 50% UHC remittance.
topics.outcome: The privatization was not yet approved; PAGCOR was still awaiting the GCG recommendation and presidential approval. PAGCOR committed to submit remittance and privatization-related computations within forty eight hours and said a UHC stabilization fund could be studied after employee retirement obligations, but the final proceeds, post-privatization UHC base, and legislative guarantees remained unresolved.

positions.position: She supported clarifying and protecting PhilHealth's UHC income stream and questioned whether privatization proceeds should also benefit PhilHealth.
He emphasized employee protection and questioned whether a 50% to 70% workforce-absorption requirement should take precedence over maximizing sale proceeds.
He sought a quantified before-and-after assessment of UHC funding and advocated consideration of a transitional stabilization fund from privatization proceeds.
He sought the status and expected revenue from Casino Filipino privatization.
He pressed PAGCOR to clarify the post-privatization separation of its operating and regulatory roles.

thread.speaker: Rep. Bong Thebes Jinger
thread.said: He asked for the status of the Casino Filipino privatization initiatives and their expected revenue.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the matter was awaiting a decision or recommendation from the Governance Commission for GOCCs (GCG), which was expected in the last quarter of the year and would then go to the Office of the President.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He reiterated that PAGCOR was waiting for the GCG recommendation to the Office of the President and had been told it would be issued soon. He added that employee retirement and a special incentive package would be needed because the retirement would be involuntary.

thread.speaker: Rep. Iris Marie Montes
thread.said: She asked about the longstanding plan to privatize roughly 40 Casino Filipino branches and noted an expected proceeds range of about thirty to fifty billion. She asked for the exact figures and whether PAGCOR would remain primarily a regulatory body.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR was still awaiting the GCG recommendation and the President's approval. If approved, close to about 30 high-30s Casino Filipino properties would be privatized.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR was looking at anywhere between 20,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000 in proceeds. He cautioned that the current revenue situation could lower the valuation and said PAGCOR could commit only to disposing of the properties at the best possible price.

thread.speaker: Rep. Iris Marie Montes
thread.said: She asked whether PhilHealth would receive a share of the privatization proceeds, expressing concern that privatization could remove an income stream used for PhilHealth.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the proceeds would go to the national government and would first have to cover employee retirement costs, which would run into billions of pesos. The exchange indicated that the regular 50% Universal Health Care share would continue to apply to the relevant income, but the treatment of the sale proceeds was not fully detailed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: He asked about displacement and mass layoffs from privatizing around 40 Casino Filipino properties, potentially affecting approximately 10,000 regular and contractual employees. He asked whether buyers should be required to absorb 50% to 70% of the workforce and whether protecting jobs would reduce bids or proceeds.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said employees would receive the regular retirement package and a special incentive package (SIP). Buyers would be expected to absorb as many employees as they could, with continuity of business and new employment terms considered in determining absorption.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR had begun programs to mitigate employee anxiety and asked PAGCOR's vice president for human resources to describe the measures.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR vice president for human resources Lito Domingo
thread.said: He described management, self-development, personality-development, gaming-related, dealer, slot-machine, and civil-service training. He said 5,000 training initiatives had already been concluded, an initial 80 to 100 people had received civil-service training, and PAGCOR expected to complete about 10,000 training initiatives by year-end.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: In discussing the future market after privatization, he defined an integrated resort as requiring at least 1,000,000,000 US dollars in investment, with lower classifications also subject to minimum investment requirements.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the lowest integrated-resort category required 100,000,000 US dollars. He also referred to the privatization of 30 plus high thirties Casino Filipino branches and to related license fees and investment requirements.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: He asked whether, after Casino Filipino was privatized, PAGCOR would automatically become only the regulator, since it was then both regulator and operator.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He referred to the existing framework and the decoupling of PAGCOR's operating and regulatory roles, but the machine-generated transcript does not capture a complete, definitive answer on the statutory transition.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked how privatizing Casino Filipino and making PAGCOR purely regulatory would affect the Universal Health Care earmark. He specifically asked whether the 50% national-government share would continue to be computed from regulatory fees and license-fee shares from private casinos, e-games, and other licensees, and requested projected PAGCOR contributions for 2026, 2027, 2028, and the first full year after privatization.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the GCG, which includes the Commission Secretary and the Secretary of Finance, with the Secretary of Budget and Management as an ex officio member, was handling the decoupling and privatization-related process. He said operational efficiencies could help offset revenue adjustments in the medium and long term.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He cited 1,500,000,000 pesos a month in salaries, wages, rentals, and other property-related costs and said PAGCOR would continue contributing a minimum of 50% of net profit.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He clarified that PAGCOR remits its share to the national government, while the national government is responsible for remitting 50% of that amount to the Universal Health Care fund. PAGCOR therefore does not control whether the national government makes the subsequent remittance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether PAGCOR had figures for the amount ultimately remitted to PhilHealth. He pressed the distinction between PAGCOR's remittances to the National Treasury and the national government's subsequent remittance to the Universal Health Care fund.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said that in 2025 PAGCOR remitted more or less 50,000,000,000 pesos to the National Treasury, which under the law meant 25,000,000,000 should have been remitted by the national government to the Universal Health Care fund.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether legislation was needed to guarantee the UHC income or share after privatization and requested PAGCOR's internal computations showing the effect of decoupling and privatization.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR would forward its internal computations to the committee, including projections after implementation of the decoupling and privatization.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the priority use of the proceeds was paying employee retirement benefits and the special incentive package. After those obligations were met, using the remaining proceeds for a UHC stabilization fund could be considered.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He estimated that retirement would require about 28,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000 and said PAGCOR was currently close to 12,000,000,000 in available retirement funding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He estimated proceeds at about 25,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000 and repeated that PAGCOR had a current retirement fund of about 12,000,000,000 pesos. He said any resulting extraordinary income would ordinarily be subject to a 50% remittance to the National Treasury.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR would look into prioritizing UHC through the possible use of remaining privatization proceeds and would provide the requested documents within forty eight hours.

topics.topic: Universal Health Care and PhilHealth remittances after privatization
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked whether PAGCOR had complied with the UHC Act and requested a complete remittance history. PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco said PAGCOR had remitted regularly to the National Treasury, while the national government was responsible for transferring 50% to PhilHealth or the UHC Fund; he cited about 50 billion remitted in 2025, implying 25 billion should have gone to the UHC Fund. Montes and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked how privatization of Casino Filipino would affect the PhilHealth earmark and sought projections for 2026, 2027, 2028, and the first full year after privatization. Tengco said privatization proceeds would first cover roughly 28 billion to 30 billion in retirement obligations, against an existing retirement fund of about 12 billion, and that any balance could potentially support a stabilization fund. The requested projections and confirmation of onward remittances were not supplied during the hearing, but PAGCOR committed to provide documents within forty eight hours and to study the stabilization-fund proposal. Rep. Jean Baronda separately sought a contingency plan for UHC and support for hospitals and children with special needs, which PAGCOR said it would consider.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR had complied with the Universal Health Care Act's remittance requirement, how much had been remitted to the National Treasury and ultimately to the Universal Health Care Fund, and how privatizing Casino Filipino would affect the PhilHealth earmark. Members also asked whether a transitional UHC stabilization fund would be needed and whether PAGCOR had a contingency plan to sustain support for Universal Health Care.
topics.agency_position: PAGCOR stated that it had been current and compliant in remitting its required share to the National Treasury, while the national government—not PAGCOR—was responsible for transferring 50% to PhilHealth or the Universal Health Care Fund. PAGCOR said privatization proceeds would first be used for employee retirement and incentive obligations, but any balance could potentially support a transitional UHC stabilization fund; it also agreed to provide records and internal projections.
topics.outcome: PAGCOR's compliance with its own remittance obligation was affirmed, but the committee did not receive during the hearing the requested full remittance history, projected post-privatization UHC contributions, or confirmation of the national government's onward transfers. PAGCOR agreed to submit documents and study a stabilization fund, leaving the fund and the post-privatization revenue treatment unresolved.

positions.position: She sought documentary confirmation of PAGCOR's remittances and pressed for assurance that PhilHealth would retain its 50% earmark after privatization. She also supported reconsidering PAGCOR's infrastructure allocations so other health-related projects could be funded.
He sought before-and-after privatization projections for the UHC contribution and raised the need for a possible transitional health care stabilization fund to protect PhilHealth's subsidy.
She urged PAGCOR to adopt a contingency plan for sustaining Universal Health Care support and to assist hospitals and children with special needs.

He maintained that PAGCOR was compliant with its remittance obligation, prioritized employee retirement liabilities in the use of privatization proceeds, and expressed willingness to study using any remaining funds for UHC stabilization.

topics.topic: PSC retroactive 5% remittance ruling and PAGCOR’s PSC budget
topics.summary: Chair Mika Suansing asked PAGCOR to explain the decline in 2026 income and the effect of the Supreme Court's final PSC remittance ruling. PAGCOR attributed the income decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, and weak casino revenues, while saying gaming activity had begun to recover. PAGCOR said the ruling required 5% of gross income rather than gaming revenue alone, applied retroactively to 1993, and created an obligation of 37,000,000,000 pesos. The agency said its prior average PSC contribution was about 190,000,000 pesos per month and identified a payment of 3,300,000,000 every year for the next ten years. The chair said the PSC's proposed 2027 budget was not yet commensurate with the higher remittances and undertook to scrutinize it. PAGCOR was asked to provide its 2025 and 2026 PSC remittance records, while the payment arrangement remained under discussion.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's 2026 income was projected to decline and how the Supreme Court's final ruling changed PAGCOR's remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). It also sought to determine the ruling's retroactive fiscal impact and whether the PSC's proposed budget adequately reflected the higher remittances.
topics.agency_position: PAGCOR said it was implementing the Supreme Court's final ruling effective 01/01/2026, applying the 5% PSC share to gross income rather than gaming revenue alone. It acknowledged a retroactive obligation of 37,000,000,000 pesos dating to 1993, said discussions on payment were ongoing, and indicated that it was close to an agreement.
topics.outcome: The committee accepted PAGCOR's explanation of the ruling and its effect on remittances but left the adequacy of the PSC budget open for later deliberation. PAGCOR's payment arrangement for the retroactive obligation remained subject to ongoing discussions, and the committee requested remittance records.

positions.position: The chair commended PAGCOR for largely maintaining nation-building contributions despite lower income, but said the committee would scrutinize the PSC budget because the proposed 2027 level did not yet reflect the increased PAGCOR remittances.
Representative De Jesus pressed for clarification of the fiscal effect of the additional PAGCOR remittances on the PSC budget.

thread.said: She identified the PSC, the Renewable Energy Trust Fund, and the Board of Claims as among the entities funded from PAGCOR revenues.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair asked PAGCOR to explain the downturn in total income from 2025 to 2026, noting an 18% decrease from the 2025 actual total income projection of R106 billion to a 2026 figure transcribed as R86.94 PHP 95,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He attributed the decline to the delinking of e-wallets from online gaming, which caused about a 40% decline in gaming activity, the Middle East crisis, and weak land-based casino revenues. He said gaming activity increased about 10% in July and remained at that level in August, while tourist patronage of integrated resorts had begun to improve.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair noted that despite an approximately 20 billion decrease in estimated total income, contributions to nation building declined only about 5.5 billion, and commended PAGCOR for maintaining its commitments.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR was implementing, effective 01/01/2026, the Supreme Court ruling with finality on the PSC remittance formula.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He explained that PAGCOR had previously remitted 5% of gaming revenue under the formula agreed during the administration of then-President Fidel Valdez Ramos. The Supreme Court instead interpreted the 5% PSC share as based on gross income.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the case was filed in 1993, the ruling became final in the last quarter of 2025, and the ruling was retroactive to 1993.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He stated that the retroactive PSC obligation was 37,000,000,000 pesos. He added that PAGCOR had filed a motion for reconsideration and sought additional time for payment while discussions continued.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said the ruling doubled the impact from an average of 190,000,000 pesos a month in PSC contributions.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR had not projected over the years that it would have to make the retroactive payment, but respected the Supreme Court's decision and was implementing it.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair summarized the 37,000,000,000 obligation as spread across ten years, or about 3,700,000,000 per year, with the transcript also recording an unclear reference to more or less 300,000,000 a month.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair said the committee would take the additional PSC remittances into account when it scrutinized the PSC budget and noted that the monthly remittance was almost double or more than double.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He indicated that PAGCOR had clarifications concerning payments to the PSC and referred to the contribution history since 1990, although the remainder of the response was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair directed the PAGCOR official to respond to the query raised by Representative Presley de Jesus.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR official
thread.said: The official said the average PSC contribution had been 180,000,000 to 190,000,000 per month and that, under the Supreme Court ruling, the 5% of revenue had doubled effective January 1. The remainder of the explanation was unclear.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR needed to examine the PSC budget in light of a payment of 3,300,000,000 every year for the next ten years.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair said the PSC's fiscal year 2027 net level was not yet commensurate with the increase in PAGCOR remittances. She said the committee would scrutinize the final PSC level based on utilization, programs, and projects.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR Chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He clarified the 37,000,000,000 retroactive obligation and said PAGCOR was close to reaching an agreement, although the transcript does not specify the terms or timing.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: The chair requested copies of PAGCOR's remittances to the PSC for the whole of 2025 and from the start of 2026, so the committee could consider them during the PSC budget deliberations.

thread.speaker: Representative Presley de Jesus
thread.said: At the close of his questioning, Representative De Jesus reiterated his concern about the budget amount being taken away from PAGCOR in relation to the PSC.

topics.topic: Nation-building contributions and PAGCOR social-responsibility spending
topics.summary: PAGCOR reported that it had contributed about 67 billion to nation building in 2025 and projected about 61 billion in 2026 and 63 billion in 2027, while social-civic projects rose to about 13.99 billion in 2026. It also presented a PHP 7,500,000,000 school-building commitment, PHP 300,000,000 in recent calamity-relief spending, patient transport vehicle donations, and hospital-equipment support. The chair commended PAGCOR for preserving these commitments despite lower income, while the agency explained that the Supreme Court's retroactive PSC ruling created a 37,000,000,000 pesos obligation and could substantially affect its finances. Members pressed for stronger control of illegal online gambling, protection of vulnerable gamblers, and funding for responsible-gaming and mental-health programs; PAGCOR cited KYC requirements, a licensing moratorium, enforcement coordination, and a responsible-gaming partner. Members also sought relief and classroom assistance for General Santos and hospital support for Western Visayas and Pangasinan. The hearing ended with PAGCOR agreeing to provide documents, review requests, and explore equipment assistance, but several allocations and enforcement measures remained for follow-up.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR's nation-building and social-responsibility contributions were being maintained despite lower revenues, including its relief, hospital, school-building, and social-civic programs. Members also examined whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory and responsible-gaming measures to address illegal online gambling and protect vulnerable gamblers.
topics.agency_position: PAGCOR stated that it continued to protect nation-building and social-civic commitments despite lower revenues, including school construction, relief operations, patient transport vehicles, hospital equipment, and universal-health-care support. It said responsible-gaming safeguards, licensing controls, enforcement coordination, and regular rule updates were being used, but acknowledged that illegal operators and rapidly changing technology remained difficult to control.
topics.outcome: The committee received PAGCOR's account of its nation-building and social-responsibility allocations and generally commended its continued spending despite revenue weakness. Several matters remained subject to submissions or follow-up, including PSC remittance records, responsible-gaming data, illegal-site enforcement equipment, classroom requests, and possible hospital-equipment assistance.

positions.position: Commended PAGCOR for keeping nation-building and social-civic contributions broadly intact despite declining income and said the committee would scrutinize PSC funding in light of the Supreme Court ruling.
Supported PAGCOR's disaster-relief and hospital contributions but pressed for stronger revenue recovery, regulation, digital monitoring, and action against illegal operators.
Argued that illegal online gaming could be depriving the government of substantial revenue and sought stronger enforcement technology and funded gambling-addiction services.
Supported PAGCOR's social programs and requested assistance for hospital equipment and children with special needs.

Raised concern that online gaming was becoming the dominant revenue source while vulnerable groups remained exposed, and urged PAGCOR to strengthen its regulatory capacity before expanding online gaming.
Sought stronger safeguards for vulnerable online gamblers and requested relief and classroom assistance for General Santos City.
Questioned whether social-civic spending was appropriately tied to income and pressed for transparency on pending school-building requests and district allocation.
Sought PAGCOR assistance for a Pangasinan hospital project, accepting equipment support as a possible alternative to direct construction funding.
