thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said he particularly liked the proposal concerning special-needs children and that PAGCOR would seriously look into supporting it.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jean Baronda
thread.said: She added that Iloilo City alone had more than 500 children initially diagnosed with special needs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles
thread.said: She asked how PAGCOR operationalized calamity relief, including assistance extended to General Santos City, and whether PAGCOR had committed support for about 1,400 classrooms badly damaged by an earthquake.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said online-gaming safeguards included a stringent know-your-customer process requiring a valid government ID, which was intended to prevent minors and government employees from registering.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR had supported General Santos earthquake victims with financial and relief packages coordinated with the Office of Civil Defense. He added that PAGCOR had sent more than 100,000 relief packs nationwide during the preceding week and a half.

thread.speaker: Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles
thread.said: She renewed her request for help with classroom construction because many classrooms were badly damaged.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR was implementing construction of 125 new school buildings, equivalent to about 200 classrooms. He invited the member to write PAGCOR regarding assistance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles
thread.said: She said her office would send the requested communication to PAGCOR.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Wangkol
thread.said: He asked whether PAGCOR directly funded hospital construction.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR itself did not fund hospital construction; foundations associated with licensees generally funded major hospital projects. He cited a Clark multispecialty hospital funded by the Bloomberry Foundation, with PAGCOR helping purchase equipment.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR had given 100,000,000 pesos during the predecessor's tenure to the Conrado Australia Hospital in Pangasinan and indicated that equipment assistance could also be involved.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Wangkol
thread.said: He said the Pangasinan hospital project was being considered at around the 1,000,000,000 mark and asked whether PAGCOR could help reduce the amount DOH would have to fund.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He explained that assistance had to be liquidated and that an unfinished project could restrict the recipient from receiving further PAGCOR aid. He therefore preferred assistance for a project that could be completed rather than an amount insufficient to finish it.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Wangkol
thread.said: He proposed that PAGCOR fund a portion of the hospital because it would consist of several buildings.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He suggested that hospital equipment would be a more practical form of assistance, particularly equipment that could be used in a completed building.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Wangkol
thread.said: He said Pangasinan's Second District had received the least funding since 2022, by more than 2,500,000,000, and asked PAGCOR to help address the shortfall.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman and CEO Alejandro Tengco
thread.said: He said PAGCOR could possibly work with the district on hospital equipment or other equipment once one of the buildings was nearing completion. He requested a letter so the parties could meet and discuss possible assistance.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Wangkol
thread.said: He undertook to write PAGCOR and pursue the equipment-assistance approach while continuing representations with the government and PAGCOR.

topics.topic: PAGCOR data submissions and supporting budget documentation
topics.summary: Committee members sought documentary support for PAGCOR's remittances, school-building allocations, revenue mix, and the effects of Casino Filipino privatization on UHC funding. PAGCOR said its school-building agreement covered 125 buildings and roughly about 1,500 classrooms at a total cost of about 7.5 billion, with close to about 3.5 billion earmarked for down payments. It maintained that it remitted its shares to the National Treasury, while the National Treasury was responsible for transferring the relevant 50% to PhilHealth or the UHC fund. PAGCOR cited 2025 National Treasury remittances of more or less 50 billion, implying 25 billion for UHC, and estimated privatization proceeds at roughly 25 billion to 30 billion after revisions, with retirement obligations estimated at about 28 billion to 30 billion. Members also requested detailed revenue lists, including projected Casino Filipino revenue of 9 to 10 billion, licensed-casino revenue of about 31.5 billion, and digital e-games revenue stated as 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038. PAGCOR committed to provide the requested records and computations, generally within forty eight hours, but the committee ended the briefing before the submissions could be examined.
topics.question: The committee sought to obtain the records and computations needed to evaluate PAGCOR's proposed budget, including remittances, fund utilization, revenue by source, school-building allocations, and the fiscal effects of privatizing Casino Filipino. It also sought documentation on the Universal Health Care and Philippine Sports Commission remittance bases and on PAGCOR's regulatory and social-civic programs.
topics.agency_position: PAGCOR maintained that it was current and compliant in remitting its statutory shares to the National Treasury and PSC, while the National Treasury was responsible for the downstream PhilHealth or UHC remittance. It said school-building and social-civic programs were being implemented through DepEd and LGU agreements, and it undertook to submit remittance records, revenue lists, fund-utilization information, and privatization-related computations.
topics.outcome: PAGCOR answered portions of the committee's questions but was required to submit substantial remittance, utilization, revenue, and privatization documentation. The briefing was terminated and the documentary issues were left for follow-up rather than resolved during the hearing.

positions.position: The committee should account for PAGCOR's increased PSC remittances when scrutinizing the PSC budget and should obtain PAGCOR's remittance records.
The committee needed a utilization breakdown for the nationwide school-building funds and stronger accountability for foreign illegal operators and problem-gambling support.
The committee needed complete National Treasury remittance records and assurance that privatization or infrastructure realignment would not undermine PhilHealth or other important social projects.
The committee should quantify the UHC effect of privatization and consider a transitional stabilization mechanism to protect PhilHealth funding.
PAGCOR needed to provide revenue-by-source data and strengthen its capacity to police online gaming before the growth of digital gaming created greater regulatory risks.
PAGCOR should explain its social-civic spending methodology and fairly assess pending school-building requests within the nationwide allocation.
A proposed casino in a government facility owned by the city was not ideal.

thread.said: She noted the reported allocation of almost 8,000,000,000 for 125 school buildings and 1,500 classrooms and urged that other important projects also be funded if a budget rebalancing became necessary.

thread.said: He said a rebalancing could be possible, while emphasizing the priority of the 125-school-building program and its 1,500 classrooms.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked whether, after privatization, the Universal Health Care earmark would continue to be computed from PAGCOR's entire gaming-related income, including regulatory fees and license shares, or whether the legal revenue base would become smaller. thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He said operational efficiencies could reduce salaries, wages, rentals, and other costs by 1,500,000,000 pesos a month, while a contribution of at least 50% of net profit could help neutralize longer-term revenue adjustments after privatization.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He reiterated that PAGCOR remitted its share to the National Treasury and that the national government was responsible for remitting 50% of that amount to the Universal Health Care fund.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He pressed whether PAGCOR had figures for the amount actually remitted to PhilHealth.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He said PAGCOR did not control the government's downstream remittance but gave 2025 as an example: PAGCOR remitted more or less 50,000,000,000 pesos to the National Treasury, which would mean 25,000,000,000 should have gone to the Universal Health Care fund.

thread.speaker: PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He said PAGCOR would forward its internal computations to the committee, while making clear that projections after implementation of privatization would remain projections.

thread.speaker: Roberto Nazal Jr., minority member
thread.said: He asked whether the executive would commit, or Congress would need to legislate, a transitional PhilHealth stabilization fund sourced from privatization proceeds to protect the annual UHC subsidy.

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He said the priority use of proceeds was employee retirement and special incentive benefits, but the amount left after those obligations could potentially be considered for a Universal Health Care stabilization fund.

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He estimated retirement needs at about 28,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000, with an existing retirement fund of close to 12,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He estimated privatization proceeds at about 25,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000 and said any extraordinary income would ordinarily result in a 50% remittance to the National Treasury.

thread.speaker: Alejandro H. Tengco, PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He said the requested documentary materials would be delivered within forty eight hours, a commitment repeated by the committee chair.

thread.speaker: A minority member

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman
thread.said: He projected revenue from six licensed casinos, excluding Casino Filipino, at about 31, 31 and a half billion and undertook to provide a detailed revenue list covering licensed casinos, Casino Filipino, and online gaming.

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman

thread.speaker: A minority member

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman

thread.speaker: A minority member

thread.speaker: Alejandro Tengco, PAGCOR chairman

topics.topic: FY2027 budget reductions in health, education, social protection, and agriculture
topics.summary: DBM initially explained that lower social-sector allocations reflected continuing 2026 infrastructure allocations, spillovers, and agency implementation capacity rather than zero funding. Congressman Arnan Panaligan challenged reductions in agriculture, health, social services, and education even as the proposed budget rose from about 6.7 trillions to 7,200,000,000,000. Representative Percival Sindania focused on the health allocation, which fell from approximately PHP 458 billion to PHP 362.7 billion, and was told that the change mainly reflected Facilities Enhancement Program utilization, retained medical assistance, an additional 14,000,000,000 PhilHealth subsidy, and the one-time return of 60,000,000,000 to PhilHealth. Representative Chel Diokno challenged reductions affecting education, SUCs, TESDA, health, PhilHealth, and DSWD, while DBM cited absorptive capacity, implementation status, and one-time expenditures. Jokno also questioned the 3.99% education computation, and DBM said it included national, Bangsamoro, local-government, and SUC-generated funds and undertook to provide a detailed breakdown. The chair directed the requested health reconciliation, while Jokno's call to reprioritize frontline-sector funding remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why proposed FY2027 allocations for health, education, skills development, social protection, and agriculture were lower despite a larger overall budget, and whether the reductions reflected actual service cuts or one-time 2026 expenditures and agency absorptive capacity. Members also questioned the basis for the education-sector computation and requested reconciliations of the affected appropriations.
topics.agency_position: DBM maintained that the apparent reductions in frontline-sector budgets did not generally represent unilateral cuts in services. It attributed them to agency absorptive capacity, implementation status, infrastructure-project timing, one-time 2026 expenditures, the return of the 60,000,000,000 PhilHealth fund balance, and the inclusion of other education-related funding sources in the 3.99% computation.
topics.outcome: DBM provided explanations centered on absorptive capacity, one-time allocations, and funding-accounting differences, but members continued to question whether core frontline services were being underfunded. The committee accepted commitments for a health-sector reconciliation and a detailed education computation; the broader reprioritization issue remained open.

positions.position: He opposed reducing agriculture, health, social services, and education allocations while the overall budget was increasing, arguing that these sectors directly affected poverty reduction and required stronger prioritization.

He questioned whether the roughly PHP 96,000,000,000 health-sector decline represented genuine service reductions or reflected PhilHealth and other one-time 2026 items, and sought detailed reconciliations.

He challenged the reductions in frontline-sector budgets and the use of non-core education-related funds to reach the 3.99% of GDP figure, and urged reprioritization for schools, SUCs, health services, and social protection.
They defended the reductions as the result of absorptive capacity, implementation readiness, and one-time or continuing allocations rather than a single policy to reduce frontline services.

topics.topic: PhilHealth subsidy and universal health-care financing
topics.summary: Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked how much of the proposed budget would expand UHC financing and services and whether PhilHealth would receive funding beyond member contributions and sin-tax shares. DBM cited about 362.73 billion for the health sector, including about 270.98 billion for DOH and about 74.45 billion for PhilHealth, and confirmed that the PhilHealth subsidy came from sin-tax collections. Rep. Percival Sindania later questioned a decline from roughly 458 billion to 362.7 billion in the functional health allocation and asked whether the decrease represented actual service cuts. DBM attributed the change to agency utilization, the Facilities Enhancement Program, medical-assistance treatment, an additional 14,000,000,000 subsidy for expanded zero-balance billing, and the one-time return of 60,000,000,000 to PhilHealth. Chel Diokno also cited substantial reductions in DOH and PhilHealth budgets and urged reprioritization of health services. The chair directed the DBCC to submit a reconciliation of health-related appropriations for 2025 to 2027, leaving the sufficiency of the overall financing unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how much of the proposed 2027 budget would expand universal health-care financing and service capacity, particularly through PhilHealth, and whether reductions in health-sector appropriations reflected real service cuts or one-time adjustments. Members also asked how the proposed allocations would affect out-of-pocket spending and frontline health services.
topics.agency_position: DBM maintained that the apparent decline in health-sector appropriations was driven substantially by changes in utilization, one-time 2026 items, and the 60,000,000,000 return of a PhilHealth fund balance rather than a uniform reduction in services. It also stated that PhilHealth would receive an additional 14,000,000,000 in subsidy to expand zero-balance billing, while medical assistance was retained at the 2026 net level.
topics.outcome: The agency explained the apparent health-sector reduction as largely reflecting one-time and utilization-related factors, while citing an additional 14,000,000,000 PhilHealth subsidy and expanded zero-balance billing. The committee directed the DBCC to submit a detailed 2025–2027 reconciliation, but the broader question of whether health financing was sufficient and whether out-of-pocket costs would rise remained open.

positions.position: She sought assurance that UHC expansion would receive financing beyond existing PhilHealth contributions and sin-tax allocations, and pressed for clarification on whether the PhilHealth subsidy covered the balance-billing expansion.

He questioned whether the roughly PHP96 billion decline in the health-sector allocation represented actual reductions in services and sought a program-by-program reconciliation, including the implications for out-of-pocket health spending.
He questioned the reduction in health and other frontline-sector budgets and urged the committee to review and reprioritize funding for health services.

topics.topic: Unprogrammed appropriations, including 111,984,000,000 in operations
topics.summary: Members questioned the inclusion and scale of unprogrammed appropriations, including the 2027 operations item of about 111.984 billion and the 50 billion AFP modernization item for 2026. DBM said releases depended on triggers such as excess revenue and that foreign-assisted projects were placed in the item because loan agreements and required approvals were not yet certain. Laila Delima challenged the constitutional basis and identified about 57 billion for PDIC restoration, 42.553 billion for foreign-assisted projects, and 3.6 billion for risk management. Alan Teague asked about the 107.23 billion PDIC transfer and was told it had been treated as excess from the unrestricted portion of the Deposit Insurance Fund. DBM reported that proposed 2027 unprogrammed appropriations were 1.56% of the expenditure program and said there was no international maximum benchmark. The executive indicated that PDIC restoration could depend on excess revenue or a Supreme Court order, while DBM committed to provide project-level information before plenary.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and fiscal basis for including unprogrammed appropriations, the projects and triggers covered by them, and whether the proposed amounts—particularly for foreign-assisted projects and PDIC fund restoration—were justified. Members also asked how the proposed level compared with historical levels and any applicable fiscal benchmarks.
topics.agency_position: The executive and DBM maintained that unprogrammed appropriations were justified for limited, necessary uses, particularly foreign-assisted projects awaiting approvals or loan agreements, PPP risk management, and partial PDIC fund-balance restoration. They said releases would depend on statutory or fiscal triggers such as excess revenue, and that the executive would comply with any Supreme Court ruling on constitutionality.
topics.outcome: The committee received the executive's explanation of the limited proposed uses and fiscal triggers but did not resolve the constitutional challenge or establish an agreed maximum benchmark. DBM committed to submit project information, while the full PDIC restoration and the amount released for AFP modernization remained unresolved.

positions.position: Supported AFP and naval modernization as a means of protecting maritime resources and reducing poverty, but sought confirmation of releases from the AFP unprogrammed appropriation.
Pressed DBM for project-level disclosure and monitoring of the 2027 unprogrammed operations item, particularly foreign-assisted projects.
Opposed or seriously questioned the inclusion of unprogrammed appropriations because of pending constitutional challenges and concerns about Congress's power of the purse.
Questioned the legality, fiscal benchmark, and adequacy of the PDIC transfer and proposed restoration, and sought historical comparisons and supporting fiscal data.

topics.topic: PDIC fund-balance transfer and restoration
topics.summary: Leila de Lima raised the constitutional and policy issue of placing PDIC restoration in unprogrammed appropriations. Rep. Alan Teague then asked Secretary Goh about the transfer, which was 107,230,000,000 pesos, its DOF origin, PDIC Board approval, and its effect on depositor protection. Secretary Goh said the amount came from an unrestricted or excess portion of the deposit insurance fund and was more than sufficient for insurance eventualities. DBM reported that FY2027 unprogrammed appropriations were 1.56% of the expenditure program and cited historical percentages from 2022 through 2026. Members questioned why the full transfer was not restored, while the executive said it had proposed 57,000,000,000 because of fiscal-space constraints and could restore the balance in two tranches or later. The Bangko Sentral governor did not finally endorse the amount and said PDIC consultation was required, leaving adequacy of the restoration unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and fiscal rationale for placing PDIC fund restoration in unprogrammed appropriations, whether the 107,230,000,000 transfer had impaired PDIC's ability to protect depositors, and whether the proposed restoration was sufficient. It also examined the scale of FY2027 unprogrammed appropriations and the timetable for restoring the transferred amount.
topics.agency_position: The executive maintained that the transferred 107,230,000,000 was excess from the unrestricted portion of the deposit insurance fund and was considered more than sufficient for depositor-insurance eventualities. It proposed restoring 57,000,000,000 through unprogrammed appropriations, subject to available excess revenue capacity, with possible full restoration in two tranches and further restoration in a later year if needed.
topics.outcome: The hearing established the executive's explanation that the 107,230,000,000 transfer was excess from the unrestricted portion of the deposit insurance fund and that 57,000,000,000 was the fiscal space available for partial restoration. Whether that amount was adequate and acceptable to PDIC remained open, with the Bangko Sentral governor saying consultation with PDIC was still necessary.

positions.position: She questioned the constitutional basis for unprogrammed appropriations and specifically challenged the decision to place PDIC restoration in that category.

He scrutinized the authority and approval of the 107,230,000,000 transfer, whether it came from the deposit insurance fund, its effect on depositor protection, and whether the proposed restoration was adequate.
He stated that the transfer came from an excess or unrestricted portion of the deposit insurance fund and that PDIC had considered it more than sufficient for depositor-insurance needs.

He supported partial restoration of 57,000,000,000 based on available fiscal space and said full restoration could occur in two tranches or in a later year, particularly if ordered by the Supreme Court.
The governor did not take a final position on whether the proposed restoration amount was acceptable and said the matter required consultation with PDIC.

topics.topic: Debt service, deficit targets, revenues, and fiscal consolidation
topics.summary: Members questioned debt ratios, debt service, deficit discipline, revenue forecasts, and the credibility of the 2027 fiscal-consolidation path. Agencies reported a national-government debt-to-GDP ratio of 64.9%, debt service of about 1.1 trillion, and a 2027 deficit of about 3.304 trillion pesos, while explaining that lower growth assumptions reflected external shocks and weaker domestic conditions. DBCC officials said lower GDP assumptions would reduce revenues, and they attributed the 2026 shortfall of about 180 billion mainly to consumption taxes, including about 175 billion in VAT-related effects. The committee also challenged the 2027 revenue projection of about 5.2 trillion and the 101.5 billion privatization assumption, with DOF citing Semirara and CBK proceeds. DBM said contingencies included savings, flexible agency line items, early assistance for El Nino, and reprioritization during execution. The chair directed the DBCC to submit multiple downside scenarios and reconciliations, leaving the issue committed to further documentation rather than fully resolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget's revenue, borrowing, debt-service, deficit, and privatization assumptions were credible and whether fiscal risks had been adequately planned for. Members also asked what spending was being displaced by debt service, how weaker growth would affect revenues and debt, and what contingencies would be available if collections fell short or external shocks occurred.
topics.agency_position: The DBCC and its component agencies said the lower growth, revenue, and deficit assumptions reflected updated macroeconomic conditions rather than a loss of fiscal discipline. They maintained that 2027 revenues could grow in nominal terms because of higher nominal GDP, while privatization proceeds, flexible agency spending, savings, and reprioritization would help manage fiscal and external shocks.
topics.outcome: The agencies answered the principal questions but left several matters dependent on documents, including downside scenarios, forecast reconciliations, health-allocation details, and debt-financing breakdowns. The committee accepted the explanation that nominal growth supported the 2027 revenue increase and that privatization proceeds and budget reprioritization would provide flexibility, but continued to flag the risk of another shortfall.

positions.position: He pressed the executive and fiscal authorities to restore investor and public confidence through action on governance, corruption, budget execution, and infrastructure issues, while questioning spending discipline and project-monitoring capacity.
She questioned whether rising debt service was crowding out programs and sought accountability for commitment fees and the employment effects of the proposed budget.
He questioned the credibility and stability of the fiscal-consolidation path, revenue forecasts, and health-sector allocation, and sought downside scenarios and detailed reconciliations.

She sought a full accounting of debt service, principal amortization, deficit financing, and the use of loan proceeds, while also testing whether allocations and proposed investments were sufficient and properly supported.
The chair stress-tested the 2026 revenue shortfall, the 2027 tax-growth and privatization assumptions, and the availability of contingencies to prevent financing and cash-management problems.

thread.said: DBM said growth targets were reduced because the global economic environment, geopolitical tensions, Middle East conflict, and US tariff changes had changed. It said the lower target was intended to be realistic and support a stronger foundation rather than irresponsibly pursuing unsupported growth.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official said lower GDP assumptions would proportionately reduce tax-revenue assumptions. Revenue projections also used inflation, real GDP growth, borrowing rates, and foreign-exchange rates.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He requested a DBCC downside scenario showing the fiscal consequences of 4% GDP growth, PHP65 to a dollar, higher oil prices, and interest rates 100 basis points above baseline.

thread.speaker: Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: The chair directed the DBCC to submit the requested downside macroeconomic scenario.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He asked why the deficit target had shifted from 4.8% of GDP in 2027 to 5.1%, how often fiscal consolidation could be revised before the original target lost credibility, and what the actual medium-term fiscal anchor was.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official said the DBCC met twice a year and revised assumptions when circumstances changed. Inflation had risen from a projected 3% to 4% to above 6%, while real GDP growth was 2.8% rather than the expected 5% to 6%, requiring new assumptions for the 2027 BASF.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He requested a reconciliation of the 2025, 2026, and 2027 BESF medium-term fiscal programs explaining each major forecast change.

thread.speaker: Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: The chair directed the DBCC to submit the reconciliation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He asked where approximately 161,000,000,000 had been lost from the prior 2027 revenue forecast.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official attributed the reduction to the 2.5-percentage-point drop in GDP growth assumptions and the corresponding slowdown in tax collections.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He asked whether weak collections would hinder proposed tax exemptions and raised lowering VAT or imposing a wealth tax.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official said the administration had submitted the Progress bill, including an increase in the personal-income-tax threshold from 250,000 a year to 350,000 a year and an exemption for micro and small industries from minimum corporate income tax. The bill also contained eight revenue-enhancing measures intended to offset the revenue-eroding provisions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He requested a bridge table reconciling the old and new 2027 revenue forecasts.

thread.speaker: Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: The chair directed the DBCC to submit the bridge table.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He asked DBM to identify program by program the decline in health-sector allocation and distinguish PhilHealth effects, one-time 2026 expenditures, and actual reductions in health services.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: DBM attributed the decline mainly to the Progress Facilities Enhancement Program, the retained level of medical assistance for indigent and financially incapacitated patients, and the one-time return of a fund balance to PhilHealth. It said PhilHealth also received an additional subsidy for expanded zero-balance billing.

thread.speaker: Rep. Percival Sindania
thread.said: He requested a reconciliation of DOH, PhilHealth, health-facilities, medical-assistance, and other health-related appropriations for 2025 through 2027.

thread.speaker: Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: The chair directed the DBCC to submit the health-sector reconciliation.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Sarah
thread.said: She cited debt of 19,100,000,000,000 and a 64.9% ratio, then asked for the domestic and external breakdown of the 2027 fiscal deficit and financing sources.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Sarah
thread.said: She cited a 2027 fiscal deficit of 3,304,000,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: The chair directed the DBCC to submit the requested domestic and external financing breakdown.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Sarah
thread.said: She asked for the amount of principal amortization in addition to the stated debt-interest payment.

thread.speaker: an agency official
thread.said: The official said the principal-amortization figure would need to be computed during the hearing; no final amount was supplied.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official explained that the 19,000,000,000 for DPWH flood control was tied to project loans secured for that purpose and could not be used for another purpose inconsistent with the loan.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked what collections assumption underlay the 2026 budget and how much of the budgeted amount would come from revenues.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official initially cited 4,800,000,000,000 in 2026 emerging revenue, then clarified that the 2026 BSF figure was 4.983.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The revised 2026 collection projection in the 2027 BASF document was 4,807,000,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair identified an approximately 180,000,000,000 shortfall from the 2026 BASF assumption and asked whether tax or nontax revenues were responsible.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official said the shortfall was mainly from tax revenues and was highly correlated with the macroeconomic assumptions.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked which source, including VAT and other consumption taxes, was the largest contributor to the shortfall.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official identified VAT and other consumption taxes as major contributors, with around 175,000,000,000 in shortfall compared with the prior submission.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether projected 2027 revenues were approximately 5.2 trillion and whether that represented 8.3% growth over the revised 2026 target.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official confirmed the 2027 total-revenue projection and the 8.3% growth calculation based on 4.8 trillion.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair challenged the assumption that taxes on domestic goods and services would rise by roughly 180,000,000,000 in 2027 even though that category had driven the 2026 shortfall.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official said the 2027 VAT projection was around 243,000,000,000 lower than the prior BASF 2026 figure, and consumption taxes including sales taxes, VAT, and licenses were about 250,000,000,000 lower.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair compared 1,570,000,000,000 in 2026 taxes on domestic goods and services with 1,750,000,000,000 projected for 2027, a 180,000,000,000 increase.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official said the comparison was year-on-year: the category was projected at 1,574,000,000,000 in 2026 and 1,751,000,000,000 in 2027 because of nominal GDP growth and other macroeconomic assumptions. Compared with the earlier 2026 BASF, however, the amounts were lower.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: The official confirmed that the increase was still expected because nominal GDP was assumed to grow by around 9% in 2027. Another official clarified that revenue growth was measured in nominal terms, while GDP growth assumptions were in real terms.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair questioned the 2027 privatization-revenue assumption because historical collections had been much lower and asked DOF where the assumption came from.

thread.speaker: a DOF official
thread.said: DOF cited several ongoing privatization efforts, including Semirara and CBK. The official said CBK proceeds would include 36 billion received in 2027 from a prior privatization, in addition to other projects.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the 2027 privatization assumption was the highest historically and warned that financing shortfalls could create cash-management problems during implementation.

thread.speaker: a DOF official
thread.said: The official said the pressure from placing 100,000,000,000 in privatization revenues on the budget was shared, stating, "I'm on your side."

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked whether the 2027 budget contained contingencies for another major shock, such as a fuel crisis or El Nino, given the 2026 revenue shortfall.

thread.speaker: a DBM official
thread.said: DBM said contingency resources included lump sums and savings under NBC 602 and 603, with funds being released to the Department of Agriculture to prepare farmers for El Nino. Agencies could also use flexible existing expenditure lines and prioritize vulnerable beneficiaries.

thread.speaker: an executive official
thread.said: The official said budget execution could be reprioritized and some activities deferred if extraordinary circumstances required resources for urgent interventions.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair emphasized the need to balance additional borrowing against deferring expenditures when revenues fell short and said the 2027 assumptions and contingencies should avoid a repeat of the 2026 gap.

topics.topic: Industrialization, manufacturing employment, and quality-job creation
topics.summary: Minority members questioned whether the 2027 budget would create quality jobs, citing a manufacturing-job target of 336 to 396,000 for 2025 alongside declines of about 177,000 in manufacturing employment and 226,000 in industry employment. DBM officials said better-quality jobs were generally wage-and-salaried positions and argued that recovery, infrastructure, energy, connectivity, and business reforms would improve employment. Congressman Arnan Panaligan pressed for a clear industrial policy, while the DBM responded that structural constraints had to be addressed before industry could become competitive. Representative Elijah San Fernando called for greater ambition and raised energy costs, including possible electricity VAT relief; economic officials said relief required replacement revenue. DEPDev also said industrial policy was reflected in the Philippine Development Plan and could work if basic constraints were fixed. The committee did not receive a firm estimate of 2027 industry jobs, and concerns about PACSILICA's strategic, environmental, and social implications remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the 2027 budget and the government's economic program had a credible industrial policy to reverse manufacturing and industry employment declines and create better-paying, higher-quality jobs. Members also asked whether energy costs, infrastructure, coordination, and the PACSILICA initiative would support industrialization.
topics.agency_position: The DBM and economic officials supported industrialization and higher-quality jobs but said the immediate priority was to resolve structural constraints, especially energy costs, infrastructure, connectivity, permitting, and coordination. They said industrial policy could support growth, including through high-value manufacturing and PACSILICA, but the 2027 job numbers had not yet been established.
topics.outcome: The officials defended the budget's recovery and structural-reform strategy but did not provide a quantified 2027 industry-job estimate or a detailed, contested industrialization road map. PACSILICA was described as potentially supportive of industrialization, while Co's questions about its conditions and social and environmental costs remained pending.

positions.position: The member questioned whether the 2027 budget would generate quality jobs rather than mainly low-paying retail and elementary work, citing stagnant wage-and-salaried employment.
Arnan Panaligan argued that premature deindustrialization and import dependence required an aggressive program and road map for industrialization and manufacturing.
Ismula sought a concrete estimate of the number of industry-sector jobs the 2027 NEP would create.

San Fernando advocated a more ambitious industrial policy alongside reforms to reduce energy costs and improve coordination, arguing that the country had deindustrialized and was producing low-paying service jobs.

Co questioned whether PACSILICA would serve Philippine development or strategic interests of competing powers and raised unresolved social, environmental, infrastructure, and Indigenous Peoples' rights concerns.
The secretary maintained that the government had an industrial strategy and national development ambition, but that industrial policy would not succeed without fixing structural constraints.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member asked whether the 2027 NEP would generate more jobs, particularly quality and better jobs.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the employment data came from nationally representative surveys periodically compiled through the Philippine Statistics Authority and covered different types of work and workers.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the budget focused on sectors that could improve job quality, industry competitiveness, and exports, particularly by addressing the country's position relative to neighboring economies.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member cited the government's plan to generate 336 to 396,000 manufacturing jobs in 2025, while manufacturing employment had fallen by 177,000 and industry employment by 226,000; services had increased by 413,000.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member questioned whether the increase in jobs was producing quality employment or mainly low-paying elementary jobs in retail trade.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official distinguished wage and salary workers from informal workers and said wage and salary employment was generally considered better quality because it was more regular and permanent.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the DBM could provide data on the proportion of wage and salaried workers in the total workforce to support the assessment of job quality.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the recent employment and underemployment losses were expected to be recovered if the economy rebounded from the sharp slowdown, describing faster recovery as the thrust of the proposed budget.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member cited the wage-and-salaried worker target of 51.4 to 52.4 for 2025 against an actual figure of 50.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official agreed that the country needed quality and better jobs and said the administration was prioritizing faster execution of programs and projects critical to job creation.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official identified infrastructure, especially energy, as a critical constraint, saying high energy costs would prevent manufacturing from creating sufficiently good employment, particularly for export industries.

thread.speaker: Congressman Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: Arnan Panaligan asked whether the government had a clear program, road map, or industrial policy to reindustrialize and expand manufacturing, citing shipbuilding, steel, pharmaceuticals, and dependence on imports.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said manufacturing had failed to catch up because structural issues had made industry and exports uncompetitive, including poor infrastructure, weak physical and digital connectivity, costly services, and high business costs.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said permitting and other business processes remained slower than in neighboring countries and argued that addressing these structural problems could make local industry more competitive without selecting industrial champions in the manner used by some neighbors.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official emphasized stronger public-private and intergovernmental coordination, saying structural reforms would make investment in factories more profitable and create jobs.

thread.speaker: Congressman Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: Arnan Panaligan agreed that infrastructure, energy costs, and the business environment needed attention but said the country would remain trapped in an import-dependent economy with low-paying jobs without a strong industrial base. He urged a more aggressive industrialization effort.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: Ismula cited projected unemployment of 5.3 to 5.8% in 2026, easing to four to 5% in 2027, and asked how many industry-sector jobs the 2027 NEP would generate.

thread.speaker: economic official
thread.said: The official said the government had assistance and reintegration measures for displaced overseas workers but did not have the details available. On industry jobs, the official said the numbers had not yet been cross-checked and that job gains depended on proper deployment of the budget and economic recovery.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando identified high energy costs as a persistent constraint on quality, better-paying jobs and asked whether value-added tax on electricity could be removed or reduced.

thread.speaker: Secretary of DEPDev
thread.said: The DEPDev secretary said tax changes could be considered in the short or near term but required a replacement for revenues sacrificed and had to be weighed against other development investments.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked whether the Department of Finance opposed any reduction or removal of electricity VAT.

thread.speaker: Secretary Goh
thread.said: Secretary Goh said the Department of Finance was not opposed to removing a tax if a replacement revenue source was identified, but would oppose removing a tax without replacement revenue.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando raised fragmented coordination and implementation as constraints on industry and asked whether the DEPDev secretary agreed.

thread.speaker: Secretary of DEPDev
thread.said: The secretary agreed that coordination problems, including between national and local governments, affected project implementation and efficiency.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando argued that the country needed a more ambitious industrial policy, contrasting its approach with South Korea and Vietnam and calling for meaningful reforms during the remaining two years of the administration.

thread.speaker: Secretary of DEPDev
thread.said: The secretary disagreed that the government lacked ambition, citing the Ambisyon Natin 2040 framework. He said industrial policy could work, but only alongside basic reforms addressing energy, roads, connectivity, and the Internet.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando said the country could pursue industrial policy while addressing structural constraints and objected that manufacturing jobs had declined while services and retail produced low-paying elementary jobs.

thread.speaker: a minority member
thread.said: The member said the economic managers were following the same development model used for 30 years and urged them to take industrial policy more seriously.

thread.speaker: Secretary of DEPDev
thread.said: The secretary referred members to the Philippine Development Plan and its update, saying they clearly contained the country's industrial policy and program. He defended the country's economic progress over the last 15 years and said the priority was to sustain that momentum.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Renee Co
thread.said: Co asked whether the 23-member US-led PACSILICA initiative formed part of the industrial growth strategy and the effort to broaden sources of economic growth.

thread.speaker: DEPDev official
thread.said: The official said PACSILICA could support industrialization if it involved semiconductors, electronics, and high-value manufacturing, but emphasized that the concept was still evolving.

thread.speaker: DEPDev official
thread.said: The official said an industrial hub that created jobs, brought in technology, and added value to local production could diversify growth and support industrialization.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Renee Co
thread.said: Co said PACSILICA was described as part of the Luzon Economic Corridor and an advanced manufacturing and logistics center in the global AI and technology value chain. She questioned whether participation would make the Philippines a pawn in an AI competition between the United States and China.

thread.speaker: DEPDev official
thread.said: The official said the government was pursuing development for the Philippines and would welcome investment from China, the United States, Europe, or the United Kingdom if it served Philippine interests. The initiative was characterized as part of the strategy to industrialize and provide higher-quality jobs.

thread.speaker: Congresswoman Renee Co
thread.said: Co questioned development's beneficiaries and costs, raising land, environmental, electricity, water, and Indigenous Peoples' rights concerns. She said these questions remained pending.

topics.topic: Infrastructure allocation, project selection, and absorptive capacity
topics.summary: Members questioned whether the infrastructure increase was justified by implementation readiness, absorptive capacity, economic multipliers, and regional needs. DBM said the 2027 NEP infrastructure allocation was 4.4% of GDP and that PPP projects could move the ratio closer to the 5% benchmark; it also defended the DPWH increase as funding implementation-ready projects with greater multiplier effects. Members raised traffic losses of about 3.5 billion pesos a day, delayed foreign-assisted projects, right-of-way problems, and LGU permitting and political obstacles. DBM said right-of-way would now precede project approval, agencies were being required to coordinate with LGUs earlier, and DILG intervention could be sought. Rep. Nazal challenged whether SARO releases translated into actual implementation and requested detailed Fisaro project records, while the chair stress-tested the 2027 revenue and privatization assumptions. The hearing produced several commitments for documents and coordination, but did not fully resolve project execution, regional allocation, or financing-risk concerns.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether proposed infrastructure allocations were supported by implementation readiness, absorptive and monitoring capacity, sound project-selection criteria, regional equity, and credible financing assumptions. Members also asked whether delayed releases, local-government obstacles, and weak execution were reducing economic returns and contributing to underspending.
topics.agency_position: DBM maintained that infrastructure allocations and agency-level reductions were guided in part by absorptive capacity, implementation readiness, project evaluation, and expected economic multipliers. It said PPPs could lift infrastructure spending toward the 5% of GDP benchmark, right-of-way requirements had been moved ahead of project approval, and agencies retained primary responsibility for project implementation after allotment release.
topics.outcome: The committee received explanations linking allocations and reductions to absorptive capacity, readiness, multipliers, and implementation status, but several issues remained open. DBM and related agencies undertook to submit project, execution, education-budget, disbursement, and delay-cost information, while LGU obstacles and the soundness of financing assumptions were left for further review.

positions.position: Infrastructure and industrialization should be pursued aggressively, while reductions in agriculture, health, social services, and education required stronger justification and current underspending should not be used to suppress poverty-reducing investments.
Infrastructure spending at 4.4% of GDP was below the 5% to 6% policy target, and allocation criteria should give greater weight to poorer regions, land area, road length, and infrastructure gaps.

Mass-transit and regional-connectivity investment should address traffic losses, unmanaged migration, and the concentration of growth in Metro Manila; delayed foreign-assisted projects required scrutiny of penalties and cost escalation.
The committee should review reductions in frontline-sector budgets and verify the education-sector computation rather than relying on an expanded definition that obscured core education funding.
Release and allotment procedures under NBC 595 required transparency and oversight, particularly where SAROs had been issued but projects remained unawarded, unobligated, or unimplemented.
LGU obstruction and political dynamics could undermine nationally funded projects, and the government needed a concrete remedy to prevent local authority from blocking district infrastructure.
Revenue and privatization assumptions feeding the 2027 BASF required stress-testing because shortfalls could create cash-management problems during budget execution.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official attributed weak industrial competitiveness partly to poor infrastructure quality, connectivity backlogs, and insufficient investment. Physical and digital connectivity remained costly because investment had been inadequate and its quality had often been poor.

thread.speaker: Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: Arnan Panaligan agreed that infrastructure, energy costs, and the cost of doing business had to be addressed, then questioned why sectors directly affecting poverty reduction had been reduced despite the proposed budget rising from 6.7 trillions in 2026 to 7,200,000,000,000 in 2027.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM response indicated that reductions, particularly in infrastructure-related projects, reflected absorptive capacity and implementation considerations, although the response was incomplete and partly garbled.

thread.speaker: Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: Arnan Panaligan pressed whether underspending and failure to obligate and spend current-year allocations had contributed to weaker growth, and urged agencies to accelerate spending in the final two quarters.

thread.speaker: Arnan Panaligan
thread.said: He also asked whether any part of the 50,000,000,000 unprogrammed appropriation for the 2026 AFP modernization program had been released.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM official said release of the unprogrammed appropriation for the revised AFP modernization program depended on a trigger, identified as excess revenue, and therefore could be considered only if that condition was present.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: Rep. Erice questioned whether the government had sufficient absorptive capacity to monitor a large number of local projects and ensure wise use of public resources; the specific figures in his example were garbled.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official referred to implementation through LGUs, standing agreements with the national government, DILG coordination, and regular Commission on Audit functions, but did not provide a quantified monitoring-capacity assessment.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Romeo Momo asked what share of projected 2027 GDP was allocated to infrastructure, citing the medium-term policy of allocating 5% to 6% of GDP.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM said infrastructure projects in the 2027 NEP amounted to 4.4% of GDP.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Romeo Momo calculated the 4.4% allocation as 1,467,000,000,000 and said it was below 1,660,000,000,000, which he associated with 5% of projected GDP.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM explained that public-private partnership projects were expected to raise infrastructure spending as a share of GDP closer to the 5% benchmark.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Romeo Momo cited DPWH's 42.2% share and DOTR's 16.9% share of 2027 infrastructure projects by agency.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: He asked whether absorptive capacity was one of the parameters used in assigning agency infrastructure allocations.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM confirmed that absorptive capacity was among the criteria. On the proposed 36,630,000,000 for DepEd classrooms, it cited ongoing procurement and LGU downloading as an implementation modality.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM acknowledged the status of Farm-to-Market Roads and said the 2026 implementation level was below the amount originally proposed by the agency.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official raised the possibility of DPWH serving as an implementing agency or partner for other infrastructure projects, potentially through a memorandum of agreement.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Romeo Momo questioned the low regionalized allocation share received by CAR and Caraga, arguing that these poorer regions needed greater support and that land area, road length, infrastructure gaps, and the absence of projects should be considered.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM said it would confirm the percentage figures but noted that CAR and Caraga had higher per-capita allocations on average. It thanked Romeo Momo for the suggestion to revisit planning and budgeting criteria.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: In response to a question about high-multiplier projects, the DBM identified infrastructure as the clearest example, estimating a multiplier of probably three to six times the amount spent and emphasizing its lasting benefit.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia cited traffic losses of 3,500,000,000 pesos a day and asked what the economic managers were doing to address congestion, including through mass transit and capital outlays.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM said the overall plan was to improve physical and digital connectivity, connect rapidly urbanizing areas with lagging regions, and develop mass transit and a long-term transport-infrastructure master plan with DOTR and DPWH.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official identified severe underinvestment in mass transit as a root cause of congestion, noting that highways and roads had been prioritized instead. The resulting concentration of growth in Metro Manila had contributed to migration and congestion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia asked about penalties and cost consequences from delays in foreign-assisted projects and suggested demand-driven, shovel-ready projects through bottom-up budgeting.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM said penalty clauses might exist in implementing agencies' contracts, but the more common consequence of delay was cost escalation or a cost overrun; some delayed flagship projects could double in cost.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the ICC had corrected the project-approval sequence by requiring right-of-way acquisition before project approval.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia asked that the committee receive cumulative data on penalties and project costs associated with delays.

thread.speaker: Chel Diokno
thread.said: Rep. Jokno asked why DPWH's budget had increased by 112,000,000,000 despite alleged absorptive-capacity, underutilization, and corruption concerns similar to those cited for frontline departments.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM said DPWH's increase involved a different and largely nonrecurring set of projects that were implementation-ready and expected to have greater multiplier effects under the Build Better More program.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM offered to submit the detailed breakdown supporting its 3.99% education-sector-to-GDP computation, including the items attributed to education.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Rep. Nazal requested a list classifying projects placed under Fisaro and identifying the applicable release conditions.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM undertook to submit the requested list.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM explained that a SARO constituted obligational authority and that an NCA was a separate disbursement authority. An NCA was not principally required for project award and obligation; the requisite authority was the obligational authority.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM said agencies had to submit quarterly financial accountability reports and that actual project implementation remained with the implementing department's technical officials. DBM reviewed aggregate performance but did not make the final per-project implementation determination.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Rep. Nazal asked whether poor execution—where SAROs were released but projects remained unimplemented—could be contributing to weak growth and contracting capital formation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Rep. Nazal said he would submit a formal letter requesting documents and project-status information for fiscal years 2025 and 2026 Fisaro projects, including whether unobligated balances were declared savings and transferred elsewhere.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair said the committee would direct DBM to respond, and the DBM official said it would act upon receiving the details.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: For 2026 through midyear, the official stated that the expenditure program was 3.176 and actual disbursement was about R3.175, leaving about R1 billion short of the program.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: The official said failure to spend appropriated funds limited economic activity and growth and meant other projects had been sidelined while funded projects were prioritized.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Rep. Salamat asked for a remedy when LGUs blocked implementation through permits, location plans, demolition permits, or political decisions, particularly for DPWH projects.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: The DBM said those permits were not required before allotment release and that, for 2027 budget preparation, agencies were being required to coordinate early with localities and secure the necessary manifestations and permits.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: For projects enacted in the GAA, the official identified DILG intervention as an additional recourse because of its supervisory authority over LGUs, while deferring other local-operational remedies to DILG.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: The DBM recognized the problem's implications for succeeding projects and undertook to consult with DILG on possible recourse and actions.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair stress-tested the 2027 BASF assumption of 101,500,000,000 in privatization revenues, noting that historical actuals were only R2 billion in 2025 and R38 billion in 2026.

thread.speaker: DOF official
thread.said: The DOF cited ongoing privatization efforts, including Semirara and the CBK transaction, from which 36 billion was expected next year, along with other projects under review.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: For possible El Nino conditions, DBM said it was preparing early releases for DA from savings under NBC 602 and NBC 603 to assist farmers. It also said agencies could front-load or reprioritize existing expenditure items during execution.

topics.topic: Foreign-assisted projects, delays, and commitment fees
topics.summary: Rep. Edgar Erice requested a breakdown and status report for support to foreign-assisted projects, and DBM committed to submit it before plenary. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula asked about fees and penalties from delayed projects; DOF reported about 3.4 billion in commitment fees since 2022 during the Marcos administration, while clarifying that these were not technically penalties. Rep. Albert Garcia pressed for cumulative data on penalties and delay-related project costs, and DBM said delays more commonly produced cost overruns, with some projects potentially doubling in cost. The agencies identified right-of-way acquisition as a principal cause of delay and said ICC now required it before project approval. Leila de Lima challenged the placement of about 42.553 billion in foreign-assisted-project support in UA, while the executive said the amount covered loan proceeds for projects still awaiting approval or loan signing. The Supreme Court issue and comprehensive penalty and cost data remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how foreign-assisted projects were being programmed, monitored, and delayed; whether delays caused commitment fees, penalties, or cost overruns; and what documentation and corrective measures the executive agencies would provide. It also examined why support for foreign-assisted projects was placed in unprogrammed appropriations and how the executive would respond to constitutional challenges.
topics.agency_position: The agencies said commitment fees were distinct from penalties: DOF had incurred commitment fees when foreign-assisted projects did not proceed, while contractual penalties could apply under implementing agencies' contracts. They said delays were commonly reflected in cost overruns, especially where right-of-way acquisition was incomplete, and that loan-proceeds components of projects still awaiting approval or loan signing were placed in unprogrammed appropriations while government counterpart funding remained programmed.
topics.outcome: The committee received the DOF's figure for commitment fees and the agencies' distinction between commitment fees and contractual penalties, but no total for project-specific penalties or cost overruns was submitted during the hearing. DBM committed to provide the foreign-assisted-project breakdown before plenary, while the constitutional issue involving UA and the status and cost consequences of delayed projects remained open.

positions.position: The committee should receive a detailed breakdown and status report on support to foreign-assisted projects before plenary.
The committee needed to determine the financial burden from delayed foreign-assisted projects, including commitment fees and any penalties.
Long delays, right-of-way problems, penalties, and cost overruns required cumulative reporting and a shift toward demand-driven, shovel-ready projects.
The inclusion of foreign-assisted projects and other items in unprogrammed appropriations raised serious constitutional concerns, including possible undue delegation of Congress's power of the purse.

thread.said: The official said foreign-assisted projects for 2027 required the necessary approvals from the ICC and the ED Council. Ongoing or approved foreign-assisted projects had programmed appropriations, and DBM would submit the breakdown of support to foreign-assisted projects and the projects' review status.

thread.speaker: Rep. Edgar Erice
thread.said: He asked whether the submission could be made one or two weeks before plenary.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official undertook to make the submission before plenary.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked whether programmed appropriations for foreign-assisted projects covered counterpart-funding obligations and whether lenders imposed commitment fees, penalty charges, or nonutilization fees.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked how much in fees and penalties had been incurred from delayed projects transferred to the UA since 2022.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: DBM deferred the question to the Department of Finance.

thread.speaker: DOF official
thread.said: The DOF official reported total commitment fees of 3,400,000,000 pesos during the Marcos administration and confirmed that the period covered 2022 up to the present.

thread.speaker: DOF official
thread.said: The official clarified that the reported amount was not penalties but commitment fees. If a project did not proceed, the commitment fee paid was lost; technically, there was no penalty from the DOF's perspective, although project contracts with agencies such as DOTR or DPWH could contain penalties.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: He asked whether delays in foreign-assisted ODAs caused penalties and whether those penalties were lodged with or paid by implementing agencies such as DOTR and DPWH.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said penalty clauses might appear in the implementing agencies' contracts with service providers or contractors. More commonly, delays increased project costs through cost overruns or additional project costs, and some flagship transportation and DPWH projects had doubled in cost after years of delay.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: He requested information on total penalties or project costs attributable to delays so the committee could study them. He cited right-of-way problems and suggested demand-driven, shovel-ready projects through bottom-up budgeting, noting that some foreign-assisted projects took ten years, fifteen years, or even more.

thread.speaker: DOF official

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: He asked that cumulative delay amounts be provided to the committee for the members' benefit.

thread.speaker: Leila de Lima
thread.said: She asked why the executive continued to include unprogrammed appropriations in the annual NEP despite pending Supreme Court petitions challenging their constitutionality. She also asked whether the DBCC considered unprogrammed appropriations an absolute necessity.

thread.speaker: DBM official

thread.speaker: Leila de Lima
thread.said: She identified the proposed UA items as PHP 57,000,000,000 for restoring PDIC fund balances, R42.553 billion for support to foreign-assisted projects, and R3.6 billion for risk management. She questioned why these items were placed in unprogrammed appropriations and raised concerns about undue delegation of Congress's power of the purse.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline
thread.said: The official explained that the foreign-assisted-projects item covered loan-proceeds components still under ICC or ED Council assessment or awaiting loan-agreement signing. The government counterpart for preliminary and design works remained in the respective agency's programmed budget.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline
thread.said: The official said these projects were placed in UA because loan agreements were not certain when the NEP was prepared; putting them in programmed appropriations could displace ongoing foreign-assisted projects in a zero-sum budget. Once loan agreements were signed, the loan proceeds would become active.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline
thread.said: The official said the executive would stand ready to comply with whatever decision the Supreme Court issued on unprogrammed appropriations.

thread.speaker: DBM official

thread.speaker: Kim Deline

topics.topic: Regional equity and Mindanao's proposed budget share
topics.summary: Rep. Romeo Momo first argued that regional allocation criteria should account for infrastructure deficits, land area, and road length, not only per capita funding. Rep. Jila then questioned the gap between RDC priorities and the central budget process, while DBM and DEPDev officials described ongoing efforts to harmonize planning and budgeting. A DEPDev official said about 30% to 35% of RDC priorities were reflected in the GAA, compared with 50% in the NEP. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez challenged Mindanao's 15.1% share, citing its 22.3% population share, 18% to 19% contribution to gross national product, and seven of the country's 10 poorest provinces. DBM said Mindanao had the highest average increase outside NCR from 2026 to 2027 and that centrally managed funds might not yet be attributed to the region. Rodriguez requested an increase to at least 20%, and DEPDev confirmed receipt of the supporting RDC resolution, but no increase was agreed to.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether Mindanao's 15.1% share of the proposed regional budget was equitable given its population, economic contribution, poverty levels, and development needs. Members also examined whether regional development priorities were being incorporated into the national budget and whether the share could be increased before approval.
topics.agency_position: DBM and DEPDev said they were working to improve regional allocation by prioritizing RDC-endorsed projects, strengthening the planning-and-budgeting linkage, harmonizing calendars and submission systems, and identifying centrally managed funds that could benefit Mindanao. They did not commit to a specific increase to Mindanao's 20% request, but characterized the review as ongoing and confirmed receipt of the Mindanao RDC resolution.
topics.outcome: DBM and DEPDev acknowledged the regional-equity concern, confirmed receipt of the Mindanao RDC resolution, and undertook continuing evaluation and process improvements. The requested increase from 15.1% to at least 20% was not resolved during the hearing.

positions.position: Regional allocations should account not only for per capita funding but also for land area, road length, infrastructure deficits, and the absence of infrastructure, particularly in poorer regions.
The budget process needed to better integrate bottom-up priorities from local and regional development councils with the executive's top-down process.
Mindanao's 15.1% share was inequitable given its 22.3% population share, 18% to 19% economic contribution, and high poverty incidence; he advocated affirmative action and an increase to at least 20%.
The principal problem was the incomplete translation of RDC priorities into the NEP and ultimately the GAA, requiring better prioritization and coordination.
