thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Romeo Momo questioned the regionalized budget, saying CAR and neighboring poorer regions had long received the lowest percentage shares. He asked the agency to reconsider how regional allocations were determined.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM official said the figures cited by Romeo Momo would be confirmed, but emphasized that CAR and Caraga had higher average per capita allocations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Romeo Momo
thread.said: Romeo Momo said per capita allocation was only one criterion and asked that land area, infrastructure deficiencies, road length, and the absence of infrastructure be considered as well.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM official thanked Romeo Momo for the suggestion and said the agency would consider it as it revisited improvements to the planning-and-budgeting linkage.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jila
thread.said: Rep. Jila identified a gap or blind spot between bottom-up priorities developed through local and regional development councils and the top-down budget process. She asked how regional priorities and LGU performance objectives were being incorporated into the executive budget.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair directed the question to the agency official identified as Sec. Kim.

thread.speaker: DBM official Kim De Leon
thread.said: The DBM official said ongoing work with DEPDev sought to improve the linkage between planning and budgeting, harmonize the investment-programming and budget calendars, and establish a harmonized submission portal.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jila
thread.said: Rep. Jila followed up by asking how approved Regional Development Council priorities were reflected in the budget call and how the process determined agency ceilings.

thread.speaker: DBM official Kim De Leon
thread.said: The DBM official said the budget call set ceilings for departments and agencies, after which agency central offices ultimately proposed the projects. Indicative amounts were allocated for regional development councils, and the agency was working to improve coordination between investment programming and budgeting.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jila
thread.said: Rep. Jila requested a second round to continue examining the budget-call process and timelines, but the chair moved the proceedings to the next item.

thread.speaker: DEPDev official
thread.said: The DEPDev official said only about 30% to 35% of priorities identified by regional councils were reflected in the GAA. The official said harmonizing regional investment programming and central budgeting could improve that proportion, with 66% described as a major improvement.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez turned to page 12 of the National Expenditure Program and questioned the proposed budget by region. He said Mindanao received only 15.1%, despite having a 22.3% population share, contributing 18% to 19% of gross national product, and containing seven of the country's 10 poorest provinces.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez said Mindanao required affirmative action and appealed to the National Budget Coordinating Committee to reconsider the 15.1% allocation. He noted that Mindanao's share had been 16% four years earlier and 17% under the prior administration, according to his statement.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair directed Sec. Kim to answer Rep. Rodriguez's question.

thread.speaker: DBM Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: Secretary De Leon said DBM was working with DEPDev to give priority to projects endorsed by Regional Development Councils and improve the planning-and-budgeting linkage. He also said non-regionalized items lodged in central offices or lump-sum funds might be intended for Visayas and Mindanao but could not yet be attributed to a region during NEP preparation.

thread.speaker: DBM Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: Secretary De Leon said Mindanao had the highest average increase outside NCR from 2026 to 2027, and that one region represented by the congressman had increased by 10.6% over its 2026 level.

thread.speaker: DBM Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: Secretary De Leon called the matter a work in progress and said DBM would evaluate how budgets could more accurately identify their intended regional beneficiaries, including centrally managed items distributed during implementation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez pushed back that DBM should be proactive rather than rely only on submissions from RDCs and agencies, including by securing documents because travel to Manila was expensive. He also criticized lump-sum funds as potentially becoming the secretaries' pork barrel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez argued that Mindanao's poverty required an affirmative-action approach and asked whether the share could be increased to 20% before the proposed budget was approved.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez said six Mindanao Regional Development Councils covering Regions 9 to 13 and the Bangsamoro had unanimously passed a resolution requesting that Mindanao receive at least 20%. He asked whether DBM and DEPDev had received the resolution.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez reiterated that the RDC resolution sought 20%, with the transcript also containing an unclear reference to 2025% or one-third. He asked the DEPDev official whether the resolution had been received and urged the agency to fight for Mindanao's allocation.

thread.speaker: DEPDev official
thread.said: The DEPDev official confirmed that the resolution had been received.

thread.speaker: DEPDev official
thread.said: The DEPDev official said the issue returned to prioritization and to translating regional priorities into the GAA. The official noted that 50% of RDC priorities were reflected in the NEP, but only 30% to 35% remained consistent with those priorities in the GAA, and said better executive-legislative coordination was needed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: Rep. Rodriguez requested that the matter continue in the next round, indicating that he considered the response and the proposed Mindanao share unresolved.

topics.topic: Bottom-up budgeting and regional development council priorities
topics.summary: Rep. Jila raised the need for a genuine bottom-up process linking barangay, local, provincial, and regional priorities to agency ceilings and the national budget. DBM and DepDev said they were harmonizing planning and budgeting calendars and portals, but acknowledged that only about 30% to 35% of RDC priorities appeared in the GAA, compared with 50% in the NAP. Rep. Albert Garcia connected weak regional planning and connectivity to traffic losses, migration to Metro Manila, and delayed foreign-assisted projects; DBM answered that mass transit, regional connectivity, and right-of-way reforms were priorities. Rep. Rufus pressed for proactive DBM engagement with RDCs and a 20% Mindanao budget share, while DBM cited a 10.6% increase in one Mindanao region and said the allocation issue remained a work in progress. Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia later questioned bottom-up budgeting, meritocracy, CREATE MORE, and local PPPs; officials described ongoing performance reforms, cited registered investments of about 1.9 trillion, and reported about 50 LGU PPP proposals and three awarded local PPP contracts. The hearing produced commitments on calendar and planning reforms, right-of-way sequencing, and submission of comparative PPP and delay data, but did not resolve the regional allocation gap.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether bottom-up and top-down budgeting processes adequately incorporated priorities identified by local and regional development councils into agency ceilings, the national investment program, and the General Appropriations Act. Members also examined whether regional connectivity, Mindanao's budget share, local government PPPs, and related planning and investment systems were sufficiently decentralized and demand-driven.
topics.agency_position: DBM and DepDev said they were working to strengthen the connection among RDC investment programming, agency budget submissions, national planning, and the GAA, including through harmonized calendars, portals, and a budget code. They acknowledged that regional priorities were not consistently carried through to the GAA, while arguing that centrally managed items and recent increases, particularly in Mindanao, required more accurate attribution and further evaluation.
topics.outcome: The agencies acknowledged that regional priorities were substantially diluted between the NAP and the GAA and committed to improve planning-budgeting integration, local calendars, and project attribution. Mindanao's requested 20% share, cumulative delay data, and pre-PPP Code comparisons remained open for further evaluation or submission.

positions.position: Regional and local priorities should be incorporated through a clear bottom-up process beginning with constituents and development councils, with the gap between RDC priorities and agency ceilings rectified.

Budgeting and investment programming should be more demand-driven and locally identified, while infrastructure planning should improve regional connectivity, manage internal migration, and reduce delays in foreign-assisted projects.
DBM should proactively obtain local and RDC documents, reduce reliance on lump-sum items, and provide Mindanao with affirmative regional support, including consideration of a 20% budget share.
Bottom-up budgeting, meritocracy, and decentralization of economic and PPP authority should be strengthened to make government more responsive, competitive, and capable of regional growth.
DBM recognized weaknesses in the current local-to-national budgeting connection and undertook reforms with DepDev, including integration of local planning and budgeting calendars.
LGU PPP review, negotiation, and approval remained decentralized; the PPP Center's centralized function was limited to completeness and competitive-process checks.

thread.said: The DBM official said DBM and DepDev were improving the linkage between planning and budgeting. The measures included harmonizing the investment-programming and budget calendars and creating a harmonized submission portal.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said these were ongoing measures that DBM hoped to implement in the next budget cycle.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jila
thread.said: Rep. Jila followed up on discussions with regional DepDev officials and regional directors. She asked how approved RDC priorities and the timing of RDC submissions and approvals affected the budget call and the determination of ceilings.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official explained that the budget call for the 2027 budget seeded amounts by department or agency, after which projects were ultimately determined through agency proposals and central offices. Indicative ceilings were allocated to agencies rather than directly fixed by RDC project submissions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jila
thread.said: Rep. Jila requested a second round after the chair ruled that her time had expired.

thread.speaker: DepDev official
thread.said: The official said about 30% to 35% of priorities identified at the various regional levels were reflected in the GAA. The official described this as low and said the target was to improve the proportion, with 66 cited as a major improvement.

thread.speaker: Chair
thread.said: The chair added that a budget code could codify the process and help organize and harmonize the budget calendar.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Albert Garcia cited a JICA study on losses caused by traffic congestion and asked the economic managers what was being done to address the resulting productivity and economic costs.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The DBM official said the National Expenditure Program prioritized investment in more transportation and mass-transit options in urbanizing areas, including the NCR.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia questioned whether continued construction in urban areas could itself create more traffic and asked how congestion could be managed beyond building over, under, or around existing routes.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the overall plan was to improve physical and digital connectivity between highly urbanized and rapidly urbanizing areas and lagging areas. The approach could include mass transit to lower the cost of moving people, goods, and services, supported by a long-term transport-infrastructure master plan being coordinated with the transport and infrastructure agencies.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia suggested considering east-west connectivity, in addition to the traditional north-south alignment, to divert traffic from heavily congested areas, particularly Metro Manila.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official identified underinvestment in connectivity infrastructure, particularly mass transit, as a root cause. The official said reliance on highways and roads contributed to the concentration of growth in NCR, migration to Metro Manila, and weaker development in other regions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia asked whether there was a plan to manage internal migration while regional infrastructure and economic centers were still being developed.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official proposed focusing on areas with strong potential for rapid economic growth, naming Iloilo, Cebu, Bohol, Pangasinan, and Bataan. The official said completed connectivity infrastructure, including the Cavite-Bataan Bridge, could make Bataan an investment magnet, and noted that population growth had declined.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia asked whether foreign-assisted projects incurred penalties or other costs because of long delays and whether the agencies responsible for the projects paid them.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said penalty clauses might be contained in implementing agencies' contracts with service providers or contractors. More commonly, delays increased project costs, sometimes resulting in cost overruns or additional project costs; the official said some flagship transportation and DPWH projects had potentially doubled in cost after years of delay.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia requested information from the DBCC or responsible agencies on cumulative penalties and project costs so the committee could study the causes of delays and reconsider a bottom-up, demand-driven approach based on local, shovel-ready projects.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: The official said the ICC had corrected the project-approval sequence by requiring right-of-way to be secured before project approval, because right-of-way had been a perennial infrastructure-project problem.

thread.speaker: Rep. Albert Garcia
thread.said: Rep. Garcia reiterated that the committee should receive cumulative information on delays and related amounts for the members' benefit.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: DBM said it was working with DepDev to give greater weight to RDC-endorsed projects and improve the planning-budgeting linkage. It also said centrally lodged or lump-sum items could be intended for Visayas and Mindanao but could not be regionally attributed during preparation.

thread.speaker: DBM official
thread.said: DBM said that outside NCR, Mindanao had the highest average increase from 2026 to 2027, citing one region's increase of 10.6%. It acknowledged that the regional allocation issue remained a work in progress because centrally managed items could be distributed only during implementation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus
thread.said: Rep. Rufus pushed DBM to be proactive rather than rely only on submissions from RDCs and agencies, including by seeking documents directly because it was costly for local representatives to travel to Manila. He criticized lump-sum items as potentially becoming the secretaries' pork barrel and argued for affirmative action for Mindanao.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus
thread.said: Rep. Rufus said Mindanao's RDCs had requested that its budget share be increased to 20% before approval of the budget. He said six Mindanao RDCs from Regions 9 to 13 had unanimously adopted a resolution requesting the increase.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus
thread.said: Rep. Rufus asked whether DBM and DepDev had received the Mindanao RDC resolution and pressed them to support the requested increase.

thread.speaker: DepDev official
thread.said: The DepDev official confirmed receipt of the resolution. The official said the issue involved how regional priorities were translated into the GAA and noted that priorities reflected in the national investment program were reduced in the GAA.

thread.speaker: DepDev official
thread.said: The official said 50% of RDC priorities were reflected in the NAP, but only 30 to 35% remained consistent with the original priorities when the GAA was produced. The official said better coordination between the executive and legislative branches was also needed.

thread.speaker: Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia returned to bottom-up budgeting, saying local-level, demand-driven identification was intended to help prevent ghost projects. He asked why projects submitted through local and regional planning instruments had received little consideration in the 2027 budget pipeline.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Secretary Kim said DBM shared the observation. He explained that the existing process generally required submissions through agency central offices and did not yet provide a sufficiently direct connection among local systems, RDC endorsements, and the budget-proposal submission system.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Secretary Kim committed to work with DepDev on improving the linkage among planning, investment programming, and budgeting under the medium-term PFM reform roadmap. He said the effort would include the local budgeting and local planning calendars.

thread.speaker: Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: Senior Vice Chair Garcia asked whether government had an effective meritocracy system for national and local governments and their instrumentalities.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Secretary Kim said DBM monitored performance indicators through the proxy system, midyear and year-end reviews, and other metrics. He said a technical working group under EO 61 was reviewing parameters for assessing agency performance and the performance-based bonus.

thread.speaker: Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: Senior Vice Chair Garcia requested coordination with the EO 61 technical working group because the House was considering a unified and clear meritocracy system for national and local governments.

thread.speaker: Executive official
thread.said: An executive official explained that CREATE had centralized investment-promotion approvals in the Fiscal Incentives Review Board, while CREATE MORE devolved approvals again. The official said CREATE MORE was intended to solve problems created by CREATE.

thread.speaker: Executive official
thread.said: The official said investors could choose between the special corporate income tax and the enhanced deduction regime, and that investments above 50,000,000,000 pesos could receive a customized package. The official cited Samsung's 50,000,000,000 multilayer ceramic capacitor factory in Laguna as an example and said only a small share of applications went to the FIRB.

thread.speaker: Executive official
thread.said: The official said registered investments in all IPAs exceeded PHP 1,900,000,000,000 in both 2024 and 2025, a record level, although the Philippines remained behind its ASEAN neighbors.

thread.speaker: Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: Senior Vice Chair Garcia asked whether the PPP Code had resulted in more local-government PPPs and whether local government economic powers should be further decentralized.

thread.speaker: PPP Center official
thread.said: The PPP Center official said it had received about 50 unsolicited LGU proposals during the first six months of the year. The proposals were at different stages of review and negotiation by the LGUs.

thread.speaker: PPP Center official
thread.said: The official clarified that review, negotiation, and approval authority for LGU PPPs remained decentralized at the LGU level. The PPP Center's centralized role concerned completeness checks and requirements intended to preserve competition and consistency.

thread.speaker: Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia
thread.said: Senior Vice Chair Garcia asked whether any local PPP contracts had actually been consummated.

thread.speaker: PPP Center official
thread.said: The PPP Center official corrected the earlier response and said three local PPP contracts had been awarded in the first quarter of the year. When asked for a pre-PPP Code comparison, the official said the data was not immediately available but committed to submit it.

topics.topic: NTA distribution, LGSF releases, and additional LGU fiscal transfers
topics.summary: Roman Romulo questioned whether the NTA formula gave municipalities an inequitable share compared with cities and whether utilization, poverty, absorptive capacity, and performance should affect distribution. DBM said municipalities generally received less because the Local Government Code formula controlled the allocation, while finance officials said the formula would be studied with the World Bank. Members also questioned additional LGU transfers, including about 58.5 billion in LGSF and other funds, and DBM cited lower-income LGUs, devolved functions, and the Mandanas-Garcia framework as grounds for assistance. Rep. Rami Salamat asked about underspending and LGU obstacles; Secretary Kim reported a midyear 2026 program of 3.176 against actual disbursement of about R3.175, or about R1 billion short, and agreed to submit department-level figures. Rep. Allan Ty examined LGSF releases, including PHP57.872 billion for 2026, almost 54 billion released by July 31, and a little over 7 billion remaining. The hearing also covered savings allocations, including about 6.1 billion identified under the 2026 GAA, although one 2025 savings figure was garbled and required further verification.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish whether the NTA and other LGU transfers were distributed equitably and released under the law, particularly in light of differences between cities and municipalities. Members also examined LGSF availability and releases, savings and unused appropriations, underspending, and obstacles created by LGUs in implementing nationally funded projects.
topics.agency_position: DBM said NTA distribution followed the Local Government Code and that municipalities generally received lower shares because of the statutory formula, although they had greater NTA dependence. It said additional transfers were justified for lower-income LGUs and devolved functions, while LGSF releases reflected programs such as RISE; it also said releases, savings, and implementation problems were governed by statutory rules and would require coordination with DILG and other agencies.
topics.outcome: The existing NTA formula and the legal framework for additional LGU transfers were explained but not changed. DBM committed to provide written underspending data and to coordinate with DILG on remedies for LGU-related implementation obstacles; the savings figures were discussed and partially confirmed, but some figures remained unclear.

positions.position: Roman questioned whether the NTA formula disadvantaged municipalities relative to cities and suggested that population, poverty, absorptive capacity, and performance should be considered in revising the distribution system.
The finance executive agreed that the existing formula raised concerns and supported examining poverty incidence and absorptive capacity, with possible legislative recommendations.
Kawanko questioned the legal and policy basis for additional transfers to LGUs above the NTA, including LGSF and the Growth Equity Fund.
Salamat maintained that underspending and LGU permitting or political obstruction could delay projects and sought a concrete remedy that would protect districts from local political domination.
Ty scrutinized LGSF carryovers, releases, the distinction between unreleased and unobligated amounts, and the legal basis and allocation of declared savings.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman noted that the NTA allocation increased from 2026 to 2027 and asked the Department of Finance to explain its distribution. He cited the Local Government Code formula of 23% for cities, 20% for provinces, 34% for municipalities, and 20% for barangays.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman asked whether 149 cities shared in the 23% city allocation and whether 1,493 municipalities shared in the 34% municipality allocation.

thread.speaker: A finance agency official
thread.said: The official said DBM should reply to Congress, and Roman turned the question over to DBM.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon corrected the municipality figure, stating that there were 1,491 municipalities in 2025.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman asked whether municipalities therefore received less than cities.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon agreed that, considering the allocation percentages and number of LGUs, municipalities tended to receive smaller shares than cities. He added that cities generally had a higher tax base and greater capacity to levy taxes, and that the distribution followed the Local Government Code.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman asked whether municipalities collectively had more people than cities and whether, as a group, they received only 34%.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon said the population comparison was not absolute for every municipality, but confirmed that the allocation was based on the Local Government Code formula.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman asked whether municipal NTA utilization was around 85% to 90% and city utilization around 60%.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon said DBM did not have the actual NTA utilization rates and would need to confirm them. He said the closest available indicator was NTA dependence, which was higher in municipalities than in cities.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman argued that, all other things being equal, greater dependence should justify giving an LGU more resources.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon said that if additional resources could be provided to LGUs needing more assistance, the answer would be yes, while noting that DBM was following the legal allocation formula.

thread.speaker: Roman Romulo
thread.said: Roman confirmed that the NTA was first distributed under the 1991 Local Government Code and then horizontally within each LGU category, with 50% based on population, 25% on land area, and 25% equally distributed.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon confirmed each component of the horizontal distribution formula.

thread.speaker: A finance executive
thread.said: The finance executive said DBM's answer was correct because the agencies were following the law. He said the Department of Finance had discussed with the World Bank whether the formula should be updated, including poverty incidence and absorptive capacity.

thread.speaker: A finance executive
thread.said: The finance executive said the government would work with the World Bank on possible adjustments and could recommend changes for legislative consideration. De Leon added possible merit-based criteria, including outcomes or SGLG, to make MDA distribution more rational.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon asked DBM why LGSF releases appeared higher for cities despite the fund's purpose, and whether unused appropriations averaging about 300,000,000,000 from 2010 to 2022 could have been given to municipalities.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: DBM explained that higher 2026 LGSF releases to cities were primarily due to the President's RISE program, which was population-based. The response said the larger population share of municipalities was given to provinces, with separate allocations directly to cities; other releases were shared between provinces and municipalities based on population.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon clarified that he was referring to unused appropriations and asked whether the question concerned a remaining budget of around 300,000,000,000.

thread.speaker: An agency official
thread.said: The official said unused appropriations could carry over to the next fiscal year if still valid; otherwise, they would eventually revert to the unappropriated surplus of the general fund.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: Kawanko examined transfers to LGUs on top of the NTA. He cited the NTA rising from R1.19 trillion in the 2026 GAA to R1.32 trillion in the 2027 NEP, and identified LGSF, NTF El CAC, Falgo, and the Growth Equity Fund as additional transfers.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: Kawanko asked about transfers above what the Constitution and Local Government Code guaranteed, including the discretionary items that became part of the law when included in the GAA.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim Deline
thread.said: The secretary said higher-income LGUs might have surpluses or excess revenues, making inequality across LGUs important. He cited the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, the Growth Equity Fund mechanism, and devolved functions as reasons for additional assistance, particularly for fourth- and fifth-class municipalities.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim Deline
thread.said: The secretary clarified that the agency was not saying all LGUs required the same assistance. At an aggregate level, lower-income LGUs still required national government support, and the transition under the executive order differed for fourth- and fifth-class LGUs.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat asked for underspending figures for 2025 and, if available, a midyear 2026 comparison.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Secretary Kim said DBM could provide department-level actual disbursements as of the end of 2025 and as of June 30, 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: For midyear 2026, Kim said the expenditure program was 3.176 and actual disbursement was about R3.175, leaving only about R1 billion short of the program.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat clarified whether the figures referred to disbursement or obligations and asked whether the government was practically not underspending.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim clarified that the measure was disbursement. Based on the latest figures as of June, he said the shortfall was only 1,000,000,000 against the program expenditure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat requested the underspending figures by department in writing.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim agreed to provide the figures by department.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim said underspending could limit economic activity and growth and could leave other projects unfunded or delayed while funded projects were prioritized.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat said public works underspending was caused in part by LGU requirements such as building permits, location plans, and demolition permits. He asked what remedy existed when an LGU became an implementation obstacle.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim said permits were not required before allotment release. He emphasized early coordination during planning and said agencies preparing the 2027 budget were required to coordinate with localities and secure necessary permits to avoid similar problems.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat asked what recourse existed when political dynamics within an LGU blocked a project during pre-budgeting.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim referred to the Local Government Code's coordination requirement and said the desired approach was alignment among local, regional, and national development plans.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat pressed for a concrete remedy, saying the problem was not uncommon, particularly in highly urbanized cities, and that mere coordination might not be sufficient.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim said the government should exhaust consultation and coordination remedies and suggested referring specific national projects to the Anti-Red Tape Authority. He later identified intervention by the Department of the Interior and Local Government as another possible recourse.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim asked to defer to DILG on other possible recourse because the matter involved internal local government operations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat said he would seek the chair's intervention on possible budget-language remedies, including treating complete submissions as approved after thirty days. He said his main concern remained pre-budgeting requirements.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: Kim recognized the implications for succeeding projects and said DBM would check and discuss specific recourse or actions with DILG, offering to work with Salamat.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: Salamat accepted the answer for the hearing, while warning that political domination should not come at the expense of a district.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked Secretary Kim De Leon for the total LGSF budget in fiscal years 2025 and 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon stated that total LGSF was PHP57.872 billion for 2026 and PHP58.532 billion for 2027, while clarifying the figures covered the different LGSF uses.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon stated that the 2025 GAA level for LGSF was P22.999 billion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty cited 10,936,000,000 in unreleased 2025 appropriations and asked whether it was carried into 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon confirmed the 10.936 unreleased appropriation figure and agreed that its validity carried it into 2026.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked whether the total available appropriation was around 68,800,000,000.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon confirmed that figure based on the cited page of the NEP.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked how much had actually been released in 2026 out of the available 68,800,000,000.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon reported cumulative 2026 releases of PHP50.9 plus continuing PHP3.7, or almost 54,000,000,000 pesos, as of July 31.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked how much remained available or unreleased from 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon said that, as of July 31, the remaining amount was a little over 7,000,000,000, although releases had also been made during the first two weeks of August.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked De Leon to distinguish unreleased appropriations from unobligated allotments.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon explained that unreleased appropriations were authorized in the GAA but had not been released as obligation authority, while unobligated allotments had already been released but had not yet been obligated by the recipient agency.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked for the legal basis for declaring savings.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon cited the pertinent general provisions and jurisprudence. He said savings could be determined from released allotments when projects or PAPs were abandoned, completed, or discontinued.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked whether savings had been declared in fiscal year 2025.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon initially said there had been no declaration of savings during the 2025 period, subject to checking the timing and figures.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked about National Budget Circular Number six zero three dated 05/04/2026 and whether it allowed agencies to identify savings for fiscal year 2025.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon confirmed that the circular was issued in 2026 but covered available released allotments under the fiscal year 2025 continuing appropriations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty also cited National Budget Circular Number 60T602 dated 04/23/2026 as covering fiscal year 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon confirmed that the circular covered fiscal year 2026 GAA release allotments.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty referred to the January 1 to 07/31/2026 program adjustments and raised a savings figure from the fiscal year 2025 GAA, first stating 3,000,000,000 and 3,240,000,000, then correcting it to around PHP12.287 billion and later around PHP12.87 billion.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: After conferring with Ty, De Leon confirmed the transcript's garbled figure as 1,200,000,000,287,000,000,000 initially declared as savings under the fiscal year 2025 GAA pursuant to National Budget Circular six zero three.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked whether the savings had already been allocated and to which department.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon said 11.287119 went to the Department of Social Welfare and Development and 1,000,000,000 pesos went to DMW OA for measures under the uplift program.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Ty asked about savings under the 2026 GAA.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim De Leon
thread.said: De Leon reported initial 2026 savings of 4.087801, including 3,000,000,000 released to DMWO and 1,087,000,000 to DSWD, plus earmarked amounts of 2,000,000,000 for DA, for about 6,100,000,000 under the 2026 GAA.

topics.topic: Budget execution rules under NBC 595, SAROs, SAAs, and NCAs
topics.summary: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether NBC 595 imposed release conditions beyond the veto message and why specific DPWH projects required SAROs or additional internal allotment documents. DBM said NBC 595 requirements were intended to establish implementation readiness, and that a SARO provided obligational authority while an NCA concerned cash disbursement. DBM deferred questions about withholding SAAs and project-level implementation to the concerned departments, while acknowledging that cash availability should not prevent procurement or obligation. Rep. Rami Salamat raised underspending and LGU permitting or political obstacles; DBM said 2026 midyear disbursement was about 1 billion below program and undertook to provide departmental figures and consult DILG. Rep. Allan Ty then examined LGSF releases, including about 54 billion released as of July 31 and a little over 7 billion remaining, and questioned savings declarations ranging from about 12.87 billion for FY 2025 to about 6.1 billion under the 2026 GAA. The committee obtained commitments for documents and verification, but the precise savings figures and whether delayed obligations became manufactured savings were left open.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish the legal and administrative basis for release conditions under NBC 595, and to clarify the respective functions of SAROs, SAAs, allotment authority, and NCAs. Members also examined whether delayed project awards, LGU permitting obstacles, and declarations of savings contributed to underspending or created manufactured savings.
topics.agency_position: DBM maintained that NBC 595 release requirements were intended to verify implementation readiness for projects not vetted during the NEP or projects with changes, increased allocations, or special-provision requirements. It stated that SAROs provide obligational authority, SAAs concern internal allotment and suballotment, and NCAs concern cash disbursement; project implementation and internal SAA issuance generally remained with the implementing agency. DBM also stated that savings must derive from released allotments and be based on projects or PAPs that were abandoned, completed, or discontinued.
topics.outcome: DBM answered the general distinctions among SAROs, SAAs, allotment authority, and NCAs, but deferred responsibility for internal SAA issuance and project implementation to the concerned departments. The committee required documentary follow-up on SARO projects and underspending, while the precise FY 2025 savings figure and the possibility of manufactured savings remained unresolved.

positions.position: He questioned the legal basis and scope of NBC 595 release conditions, argued that withholding SAAs could delay awards and create manufactured savings, and sought project-level documentation.
He argued that underspending had significant economic and service-delivery effects and pressed DBM to establish a remedy when LGU political or permitting obstacles blocked nationally funded projects.
He sought to reconcile LGSF appropriations, releases, unreleased appropriations, and savings declarations, and questioned the allocation of savings under NBC 603 and NBC 602.

He defended the distinction between allotment and cash authority, deferred agency-specific implementation decisions to the departments, acknowledged the effects of underspending, and agreed to verify or provide supporting figures and coordinate with DILG.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether the President's veto message for the 2025 budget itself contained all additional release conditions imposed by NBC 595 on congressional amendments, requesting a yes-or-no answer.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He answered that the veto message stated that release was subject to the usual DBM rules and regulations. He explained that NBC 595 was issued to implement the veto message.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said the documents listed in NBC 595 were the usual documents proving implementation readiness. The requirements applied because the projects had not been evaluated during budget preparation but were included in the final GAA.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked for the specific legal basis for placing in SAROs projects that were already specific line items in the FY 2026 NEP and retained in the FY 2026 GAA, where there were no congressional amendments, lump-sum items, or attached conditions.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He replied that changes had been introduced to the coordinates of some projects, making renewed vetting necessary before DBM released the allotment orders.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He added that projects with increased allocations could also be subject to SARO, as could items requiring compliance with special provisions identified as SARO items.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He requested from DBM a list specifically classifying the projects covered by the release requirements.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He undertook to submit the requested list.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether the SAROs issued in March 2025 for the questioned DPWH items meant that the NBC 595 requirements, including DPWH certification that projects were shovel-ready or implementation-ready, had been complied with.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said the records showed that release was facilitated upon DPWH's compliance with the requirements, including the necessary approval from the President.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether issuance of a SARO meant that allotment and obligational authority had already been released.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He answered that the SARO was already the obligational authority and that, from DBM's standpoint, the allotment was considered released to the agency.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether an NCA was required before a department could issue an SAA to an implementing office and whether an NCA was required for project award.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He explained that an SAA was an allotment document, while an NCA was a disbursement document, and that the need for an SAA before internal issuance depended on the department's internal guidelines. He said the requisite authority for awarding a project was obligational authority, through an SAA or whichever document was applicable.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He confirmed whether the NCA was principally required for actual cash disbursement or payment.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He agreed that the NCA concerned actual cash disbursement or payment.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He raised DPWH projects that had been bid out but could not be awarded because DPWH central office had not issued the necessary SAA. He asked whether any additional DBM fund-release authority was needed after the SARO before DPWH could proceed with award and obligation.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He responded that the obligational authority had already been given to the agency. He later clarified that DBM was not privy to the specific details of the several projects involved.

thread.speaker: Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: He asked whether there was any valid budgetary or other reason for withholding an SAA after the project had passed the NBC 595 process.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said issuance of an SAA and the manner of suballotting were internal processes within the department, so DBM deferred to the department concerned.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He stated that cash availability was not supposed to hinder procurement or incurrence of obligations because cash was released and programmed based on actual need or infrastructure progress billings.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether a department could withhold an SAA or NCA without reason and thereby prevent award, leaving the corresponding amounts as unobligated allotments.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He again deferred to the agency, explaining that issuance and suballotment were matters peculiar to the implementing department. He said the allotments had already been issued and were reflected in agency reports as available for obligation.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether DBM's responsibility ended once it released authority to obligate funds and whether DBM could compel agencies to proceed with project documentation after NBC 595 compliance.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said agencies were required to submit quarterly financial accountability reports on utilization. He added that actual project implementation rested on the technical expertise and final determination of the respective departments, while DBM would review how agencies obligated and awarded contracts.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said DBM conducted midyear agency performance reviews and received year-end reports, but project-level determinations remained with the agencies because the performance review was aggregate.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether FY 2025 capital-outlay allotments remained valid for release and obligation until 12/31/2026.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He confirmed that, consistent with the GAA, the allotment was valid for obligation until the end of 2026, subject to the agency's determination regarding the projects.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether poor budget execution, where SAROs had been released but projects remained unimplemented, could be contributing to weak economic growth.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member argued that delayed spending meant lost jobs, economic activity, and public services, and raised the possibility of manufactured savings if an unobligated balance caused by withholding an SAA was later declared savings and used for augmentation.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member said he would submit a formal letter to DBM requesting documents and project-status information for FY 2025 and FY 2026 SARO projects, including identified projects, and asked that the letter be included in the committee record.

thread.speaker: the committee chair
thread.said: The chair agreed that the letter would be made part of the committee record and that the committee would direct DBM to respond.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said DBM would act as soon as it received the requested details.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He asked for the 2025 underspending figure and whether it was too premature to provide a 2026 figure based on year-on-year activity.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He said DBM could provide actual disbursement by department as of the end of 2025 and as of June 30, 2026. The transcript's 2025 program, actual-spending, and shortfall figures were garbled and unclear.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: For the 2026 midyear expenditure program, he stated that the program was 3.176 and actual disbursement was about R3.175, with only about R1 billion short of the program.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He asked whether the spending measure referred to obligations or disbursements.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He clarified that the figures referred to disbursement, not obligation.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He said that, based on the latest figures as of June, actual disbursement was only 1,000,000,000 short of programmed expenditure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He requested the figures by department in writing.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He agreed to provide the departmental figures.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He acknowledged that underspending limited economic activity and affected growth, while funded projects displaced other projects that had been placed on the sidelines.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He identified LGU requirements such as building permits, location plans, and demolition permits as obstacles to DPWH implementation and asked what remedy existed when an LGU became the stumbling block.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He said the permits were generally needed after allotment issuance and were not required before release of the allotment. For 2027 budget preparation, DBM was requiring early coordination with localities and confirmation that necessary permits had been addressed.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He pressed for a remedy where political dynamics within an LGU obstructed a project, particularly during pre-budgeting, and said that referral to another authority did not adequately solve the problem.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He said another possible recourse was intervention by the Department of the Interior and Local Government, which exercises supervision over LGUs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He deferred to DILG on other possible recourse because the matter involved internal LGU operations.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim
thread.said: He recognized the implications for succeeding projects in particular localities and undertook to consult with DILG on possible recourse or actions, offering to work with the member.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He said he accepted the answer for the moment because the committee could not allow political domination at the expense of a district.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked for the total Local Government Support Fund budget for FY 2025 and FY 2026.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He stated that the 2026 LGSF was PHP57.872 billion and, although the question concerned 2025 and 2026, he also stated a 2027 figure of PHP58.532 billion.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He later identified the 2025 GAA level for LGSF as P22.999 billion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Referring to Volume III, page 887, he asked whether the unreleased FY 2025 appropriation was 10,936,000,000.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He confirmed the figure as 10.936 in unreleased appropriations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether the unreleased amount had been carried to 2026 and whether total available appropriation was around 68,800,000,000 pesos.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He confirmed both the carryover's validity and the approximately 68,800,000,000 total based on the cited page.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked how much had actually been released in FY 2026 out of the available 68,800,000,000.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He reported cumulative 2026 releases of PHP50.9 plus continuing PHP3.7, or almost 54,000,000,000 pesos as of July 31.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked how much remained available or unreleased from FY 2026.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said the remaining amount as of July 31 was a little over 7,000,000,000, while noting that additional releases had been made during the first two weeks of August.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked the Secretary to distinguish unreleased appropriations from unobligated allotments.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He explained that unreleased appropriations were GAA-authorized appropriations for which no obligation authority had been released, while unobligated allotments were allotments already released to departments or agencies but not yet obligated.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked for the legal basis for declaring savings.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He cited the pertinent general provisions and jurisprudence. He said savings must be determined from released allotments, including whether a project or PAP was abandoned, completed, or discontinued.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether savings had been declared in FY 2025.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He initially said that there had been no declaration of savings during the relevant 2025 period, but stated that he would double-check the timing and figures.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether the Secretary was familiar with National Budget Circular 603 dated 05/04/2026 and whether it allowed agencies to identify savings.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He confirmed that NBC 603 was issued in 2026 but covered available released allotments that could be declared savings under the FY 2025 continuing appropriations.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether NBC 602 dated 04/23/2026 covered FY 2026.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He confirmed that NBC 602 covered FY 2026 GAA released allotments.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: Referring to the January 1–07/31/2026 program-adjustment report, he cited a savings amount that was initially transcribed as 3,000,000,000 3,240,000,000 and then as Ps. 12 point 287 billion from the FY 2025 GAA, asking whether the figure was correct.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said the figure he located appeared to be PHP12.658 billion, while the member stated it was around PHP12.87 billion; the discrepancy was not immediately resolved.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: After conferring with the member, he confirmed the transcript's garbled figure as "1,200,000,000,287,000,000,000" initially declared as savings by agencies from the FY 2025 GAA pursuant to NBC 603.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked whether the savings had already been allocated and to which departments.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He said 11.287119 had been allocated to the Department of Social Welfare and Development and 1,000,000,000 pesos to DMW OA for measures under the uplift program.

thread.speaker: Rep. Allan Ty
thread.said: He asked about savings under the 2026 GAA.

thread.speaker: Kim De Leon, DBM Secretary
thread.said: He stated that offered savings amounted to 4.087801, including 3,000,000,000 released to DMWO and 1,087,000,000 to DSWD, plus 2,000,000,000 earmarked for DA, for about 6,100,000,000 under the 2026 GAA.

topics.topic: DPWH right-of-way, permits, and delayed project implementation
topics.summary: Rep. Mark Kawanko asked whether right-of-way could be funded and acquired before civil works because rising land values and delayed acquisition made projects less implementable. DBM said DPWH's right-of-way budget was a lump sum prioritized by DPWH, supported higher levels in the NEP, and was often reduced before enactment; no specific advance-funding mechanism was settled. DBM also said local autonomy constrained national support for acquiring land for barangay facilities and open spaces. Rep. Rami Salamat linked public-works underspending to LGU requirements such as building, location, and demolition permits and asked for a remedy when LGUs blocked projects. DBM said permits were not required before allotment release, emphasized early coordination for 2027, identified the Anti-Red Tape Authority and DILG as possible avenues, and committed to confer with DILG. The committee requested written department-level disbursement data, including a 2026 midyear shortfall of about 1 billion, while the proposed deemed-approval and other budget remedies remained unresolved.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how right-of-way could be funded and acquired before civil works, whether barangay land and open-space needs could be supported, and how permitting and local-government barriers could be prevented from delaying DPWH projects. Members also sought the executive's remedy when LGUs withheld or delayed required permits and coordination.
topics.agency_position: DBM said DPWH right-of-way funding was proposed as a lump sum and prioritized by DPWH, while DBM supported higher right-of-way levels but said they were often reduced in the enacted GAA. It said early LGU coordination and securing necessary permits during 2027 budget preparation should reduce implementation delays, but acknowledged that further recourse for LGU obstruction required coordination with DILG.
topics.outcome: The committee received DBM's explanation that right-of-way funding was a DPWH-prioritized lump sum and that DBM supported higher allocations, but no decision was made to permit district-specific advance right-of-way items or national acquisition of barangay land. On LGU permitting, DBM undertook to coordinate with DILG and work with the member, while the proposed budget remedy and the broader question of LGU obstruction remained open.

positions.position: Supported increasing and potentially front-loading right-of-way funding before civil works, questioned limits based on project cost, and urged reconsideration of national support for barangay land and open spaces.

Argued that LGU permit and coordination requirements were causing public-works underspending and sought a concrete remedy, potentially through budget language or deemed approval, when LGUs obstructed projects.

Supported higher right-of-way funding and early coordination, but maintained that local autonomy constrained national support for LGU land acquisition and that DILG involvement might be necessary for LGU-related recourse.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She cited foreign-assisted railway projects as an example in which delays in the government counterpart, including right-of-way acquisition, could delay overall implementation.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She said that acquiring the right of way was necessary for implementation and that failure to acquire it would cause further delay to the projects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He asked whether a district representative could concentrate funding on right-of-way acquisition so intended projects would already have their right of way in succeeding years, before real-estate values increased. He also asked whether DOF and DBM would allow funding for barangay open spaces.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She said right-of-way acquisition was precisely intended to prepare projects, but the response was unclear in the transcript.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He said past practice funded civil works before right of way, leaving projects unimplementable. He asked whether a district could buy or fund the right of way ahead of any civil-works appropriation.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She said the issue depended on whether the government was settling or paying for the right of way and on how the government would acquire and evaluate it.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He said DPWH had previously insisted that only a certain percentage of total project cost could be allocated to right of way. He asked whether a representative could request a district budget item for DPWH right-of-way acquisition even when no civil-works component was yet included.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She initially indicated that buying right of way before DPWH implementation could not be done, but the response was interrupted and unclear.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She clarified that DPWH's right-of-way budget was proposed as a lump sum and that prioritization depended on DPWH. She added that right-of-way funding was often reduced between the level proposed in the NEP and the level approved in the GAA.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He asked what was wrong with increasing the right-of-way allocation.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She said DBM fully supported a higher right-of-way allocation and had proposed a higher level every year under the NEP, but said the allocation was reduced during the budget process.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He said they agreed in principle on increasing right-of-way funding, then raised the absence of land for barangay multipurpose buildings, gymnasiums, schoolhouses, and barangay halls.

thread.speaker: Kim Deline, DBM
thread.said: She said the national government could assist LGUs with infrastructure projects but was constrained in supporting land acquisition because of local autonomy. She said national-government acquisition of land for LGU use was therefore constrained.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He said he did not see the rationale for the restriction and suggested that the issue could be discussed further.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: On underspending and project implementation, he said the closest measure was actual disbursement against the program. He said DBM could provide department-level figures for full-year 2025 and midyear 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He said the 2026 midyear expenditure program was 3.176 and actual disbursement was about R3.175, or about R1 billion short.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He asked whether the figures meant the government was practically not underspending, and said this was unexpected.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He replied that, based on the latest figures as of June, actual disbursement was only 1,000,000,000 short of programmed expenditure.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He requested the figures by department in writing.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He agreed to provide the department-level figures.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He said underspending reduced economic activity and growth, and that projects funded for priority implementation displaced other projects that could not be funded.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He said public-works underspending was substantially caused by implementation requirements and LGU support problems, including building permits, location plans, and demolition permits. He asked for a remedy when an LGU itself became the stumbling block.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He said permits were required after allotment release and were not required before the allotment was released. He said DBM was emphasizing early coordination and requiring agencies during 2027 budget preparation to manifest coordination with localities and address necessary permits.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He asked what recourse existed when political dynamics within an LGU obstructed a project during pre-budget coordination or approval.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He referred to the Local Government Code's coordination provisions and said the ideal approach was alignment among local, regional, and national development plans.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He pressed whether coordination was a critical remedy in actual cases, citing his experience that LGU opposition was not uncommon. He asked what concrete remedy existed for a development project in a district.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He said prior consultation and the Local Government Code should be exhausted to implement national priority projects. For a specific project, he said the Anti-Red Tape Authority could be alerted because the projects were national.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He rejected reliance on the Anti-Red Tape Authority as sufficient in highly urbanized cities and argued that it could become local-authority monopoly rather than local autonomy. He said a solution was needed.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He said another possible recourse was intervention by the Department of the Interior and Local Government, which exercised supervision over LGUs.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He said the matter involved internal LGU operations and respectfully deferred to DILG on other possible recourse.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rami Salamat
thread.said: He said he would seek the chair's intervention on a budget remedy, including a provision deeming permits approved if a complete submission remained unacted upon. He clarified that his principal concern was the pre-budget requirement that was obstructing projects.

thread.speaker: Secretary Kim, DBM
thread.said: He acknowledged the implications for succeeding projects in affected localities and committed to check and sit down with DILG on possible recourse or actions. He also said DBM would be willing to work with the member.

topics.topic: Education funding, free higher education, and SUC operations
topics.summary: The DBM presented education and SUC funding separately and reported a release of 10 billion pesos for free higher education arrears. Chel Diokno challenged reductions in frontline-sector budgets and questioned the 3.99% education share, which DBM said included national, Bangsamoro, LGU, and SUC-generated resources; DBM agreed to provide a detailed breakdown. Renee Co questioned the 9.75 billion and 12 billion deficiency releases, additional SUC-reported shortfalls, and the use of enrollment data. DBM said the 2027 formula used actual enrollment and three-year average growth, but it had not yet verified the latest deficiency. DBM also clarified that the MOOE rule applied to 20% of unobligated MOOE, not total MOOE, and agreed to discuss funding for extension campuses. The matter remained dependent on submission of the requested computations and verification of remaining deficiencies.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish how education and free higher education allocations were computed, whether the proposed funding would cover actual SUC needs, and how reductions in frontline-sector budgets were justified. It also examined the treatment of SUC MOOE, extension campuses, and the basis for the 3.99% education-sector share.
topics.agency_position: DBM said the proposed education and SUC allocations were based on actual enrollment, average enrollment growth, agency absorptive capacity, implementation status, and other education-related resources including LGU and SUC-generated funds. It said it was coordinating with CHED, UniFAST, and SUCs on deficiencies and normative financing, and was willing to discuss funding for extension campuses.
topics.outcome: DBM answered the committee's questions on the general computation methodology but did not establish whether all reported SUC free higher education deficiencies had been covered. DBM undertook to submit the education-share and free higher education computation details and to discuss extension-campus funding.

positions.position: He questioned reductions in education and other frontline-sector budgets, challenged the 3.99% education-share computation, and urged the committee to review and reprioritize funding for schools, SUCs, health services, and social protection.
She pressed for adequate funding for free higher education deficiencies, clearer enrollment-based computation, SUC operating needs, and MOOE support for extension campuses.

topics.topic: Confidential and intelligence funds and DBM review authority
topics.summary: Renee Co asked DBM to identify agencies legally authorized to receive confidential and intelligence funds and to explain whether DBM could deny requests based on mandate and physical and financial plans. Secretary Kim said the 2027 proposal retained the same agencies as the 2026 NEP, listed the covered agencies, and said requests were evaluated against the agency's mandate and the governing joint circular. Rep. Ko raised concerns about the Office of the President's confidential-expense increase from 500 million in 2016 to 2.5 billion and sought greater accountability. Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the roughly 10.8 billion total and the Office of the President's roughly 4.56 billion allocation, then pressed whether confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings. DBM answered that eligible expenses could be augmented subject to the general provisions and GAA approvals, but the Chair required a written explanation. DBM also explained that LGU allocations were reviewed for peace-and-order resolutions and other requirements, while actual use was subject to COA post-audit.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish which agencies were legally authorized to receive confidential and intelligence funds, how DBM evaluated requests, and whether confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings. Members also asked how DBM reviewed LGU confidential-fund allocations and whether the Office of the President's confidential-fund level was justified.
topics.agency_position: DBM said it evaluated confidential-fund requests against the requesting agency's legal mandate, applicable joint circulars, physical and financial plans, and GAA requirements. It stated that LGU allocations were reviewed for documentary and statutory compliance, while actual utilization was subject to COA post-audit; it also maintained that eligible confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings subject to required approvals.
topics.outcome: DBM stated that it could review and reject or exclude requests that failed mandate, documentary, or legal requirements, and that eligible confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings subject to GAA requirements and approvals. The classification and augmentation issue remained subject to the written explanation requested by the Chair.

positions.position: DBM should exercise meaningful discretion and accountability in reviewing confidential-fund requests, including requests from national agencies and LGUs, and should require adequate justification and transparency.

The distinction between confidential and intelligence expenses as an object of expenditure and confidential and intelligence funds as a budget concept had implications for whether augmentation from savings was permissible and required written clarification.

topics.topic: Electricity costs, VAT, transmission, and energy-sector regulation
topics.summary: Rep. Sergio Dagooc linked high electricity costs to household burdens, structural market problems, renewable-energy delays, transmission needs, and layered taxes, while agencies cited about 5.3% as the national-average share of household spending devoted to electricity. The agencies supported stronger ERC and PCC coordination and said EPIRA reforms were being pursued sequentially. Rep. Mark Kawanko pressed for advance and higher right-of-way funding and argued that electricity generation had a high multiplier effect, citing Vietnam's 68,000 megawatts against the Philippines' 22,000 megawatts. Rep. Elijah San Fernando asked about reducing VAT on electricity, and DOF said it would be neutral if replacement revenue were identified. Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez separately argued that VAT should not apply to system loss; the BIR said the charge was taxable because it was bundled into distributors' gross sales but reported that the ERC had a draft regulation under preparation. The committee requested the World Bank report and accepted commitments for further data, meetings, and regulatory work.
topics.question: The committee sought to establish why electricity costs were high, how regulation, transmission constraints, taxes, and system loss affected consumers and industry, and what reforms or administrative actions could reduce those costs. It also examined whether right-of-way and electricity-generation investments should receive greater public support and whether VAT on electricity or system loss could be removed.
topics.agency_position: The agencies and economic managers said high electricity costs reflected structural market issues, project and transmission delays, coordination problems, and the tax and subsidy structure. They supported stronger ERC-PCC coordination and higher right-of-way funding, while maintaining that VAT reductions required replacement revenue; the BIR and ERC were nevertheless working administratively to address VAT on system loss.
topics.outcome: The committee received agency explanations and several reform positions, but no final decision was taken on EPIRA amendments, electricity-tax restructuring, government ownership, or higher right-of-way allocations. VAT on system loss was left to an ongoing BIR-ERC regulatory process, while the World Bank report and additional data were to be submitted or discussed further.

positions.position: High electricity costs were driven by structural market weaknesses, delayed renewable-energy implementation, insufficient transmission, and layered taxes and charges. He supported EPIRA and regulatory reforms, a review of multiple taxation, and coordination with the BIR.

Right-of-way funding should be available in advance and at higher levels, and national policy should reconsider restrictions on land acquisition for barangay infrastructure. He argued that electricity generation had a high economic multiplier and that EPIRA had failed, proposing consideration of greater government ownership, including for nuclear generation.

Electricity generation was infrastructure and reducing electricity costs would have significant multiplier effects. Reforms should be informed by evidence on generation costs, project delays, and market-power abuse.

VAT reduction and industrial policy should be pursued alongside structural reforms to lower energy costs and create better-paying jobs. He criticized the government's approach as insufficiently ambitious.
DOF was not categorically opposed to removing VAT from electricity, but required a replacement revenue source.
VAT should not apply to system loss because electricity lost before reaching consumers was not consumed; an administrative exemption might be possible without new legislation.
System loss was currently taxable because it was bundled into distributors' gross sales, but the BIR and ERC were working on a regulatory solution.

thread.said: The official identified studies and proposed strengthening the ERC, improving coordination between the ERC and the Philippine Competition Commission, and giving both agencies stronger mandates to address market abuse and abuse of market power.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sergio Dagooc

thread.said: He asked whether electricity generation was classified as infrastructure and whether generating capacity had a high multiplier effect because electricity enabled economic activity.

thread.speaker: Secretary Arsenio Balisacan

thread.speaker: Secretary Arsenio Balisacan
thread.said: He agreed that generating capacity would have a high multiplier effect if it reduced electricity costs, identifying high electricity costs as one of the most binding constraints to growth and industrialization.

thread.speaker: Rep. Mark Kawanko
thread.said: He said the Philippines had previously been ahead of Vietnam in generating capacity but was now far behind, and argued that EPIRA had failed. He proposed considering 100% government ownership for generating capacity, particularly nuclear generation, and offered to discuss the matter with the executive.

thread.speaker: Secretary Arsenio Balisacan
thread.said: Secretary Balisacan welcomed further discussion and referred to a recent World Bank report identifying the contributions of generation costs, project delays, and possible market-power abuse to high Philippine electricity prices.

thread.said: The Chair asked that a copy of the World Bank report on the Philippine electricity and power market be provided to the committee for further study.
